Proved for the whole class (each of Theorems 1 to 88 was verified independently before insertion; Section 8 dates the
verification, separate-review, analytic-audit and transfer-readback events):
 - beta < 2 is empty (Theorem 1); every profile has beta >= 2.
 - For every beta >= 2, bounded velocity and the critical regime (annular kinetic energy O(R^{4-4/beta})) are
   excluded, so every profile has the natural tail (Theorems 34, 38).
 - Omega <= 0 throughout the open first quadrant Q1 is impossible (Theorem 21), and so is Omega > 0 throughout Q1 at
   beta = 2 (Theorems 12, 21).
 - At beta = 2 every profile has a nonempty open invariant subset of Q1, of infinite area, on which Theta is constant
   and Omega = 0 (Theorem 83); real analyticity of Theta, Omega or U on Q1 is excluded (Theorem 85).

Partial theorems (restricted classes only, not NO): temperature or velocity in L^p for some finite p (so finite kinetic
energy), a single angular mode or finite angular Fourier support of the stream function, and several beta > 2
subclasses defined by zero-set, nondegeneracy and vorticity-sign hypotheses (Theorems 10, 17, 23, 49, 62, 64, 71, 75,
77, 80, 84; list below). Exact exterior solutions with the natural tail exist for beta > 2 and beta = 2 (Theorems 69,
70), and no contradiction among the local and far-field necessary conditions was found (Sections 4, 7).

Best numerical evidence (Section 6): none validated; every examined state is rejected. Representative sampled residuals: the
beta = 3 state N176 (max |R_Omega| = 0.8614, max |R_Theta| = 13.935) and the beta = 2, a0 < 0 state N240 (relative
least-squares misfit 1.096e-3; on 72 points of a circle of radius 0.1 about an interior zero of W, max |R_Omega| =
0.18728, max |R_Theta| = 6.7257, pointwise normalized maxima 0.0145 and 1). These are sampled values far above the
target of about 1e-6, and the joint refits with beta free identify neither a minimizing beta nor a limiting value.

Remaining gap. For beta > 2 the first missing implication is the hypothesis (H1): the only zeros of W = beta X + U in
the closed first quadrant are O and the first positive x-axis zero P. It follows from the far-field vorticity sign
condition of Theorem 81(b) plus nondegeneracy of those zeros (Theorems 84, 86); neither is proved. Under (H1) three
cases stay open (a0 < 0; a0 > 0 with Omega < 0 somewhere in Q1; a0 > 0 with Omega >= 0 on Q1), restricted only by
necessary conditions (Theorems 50, 55, 64, 66, 73, 75, 86, 87, 88). For beta = 2 the open point is the possible flat
endpoints of the stagnation arc through P and their coupling to the equations away from the arc. For every beta >= 2
it is undecided whether an interior solution matches an admissible exterior one (Section 7). Reproduction: Section 9
and the accompanying artifacts.

Overview of results. Neither accepted endpoint has been reached in A2-broad, the smooth full-plane class of Section 2: existence is
unresolved for every beta >= 2 (Section 7). Excluded throughout the class: beta < 2 (Theorem 1); for every beta >= 2,
bounded velocity and the critical regime, in which the annular energy E(R) = int_{R<|X|<2R} |U|^2 dX is O(R^{4-4/beta})
(Theorems 34, 38); vorticity Omega <= 0 throughout the open first quadrant (Theorem 21), and Omega > 0 there at beta = 2
(Theorems 12, 21). Main restricted exclusions: temperature or velocity in L^p(R^2) for some finite p > 0, a stream
function with finite angular Fourier support, and, at beta = 2, real analyticity of W on R^2 or of Theta, Omega, U or W
on the open quadrant (Theorems 17, 23, 49, 85). No numerical state is validated; all examined states are rejected
(Section 6). Among them, the beta = 3 state N176 has sampled maxima |R_Omega| = 0.8614 and |R_Theta| = 13.935, and the
beta = 2 state N240 of the branch a0 < 0 (reported relative least-squares misfit 1.096e-3) has, on 72 points of a circle
of radius 0.1 about a numerically located interior zero of W, maxima |R_Omega| = 0.18728 and |R_Theta| = 6.7257 and
pointwise normalized maxima 0.0145 and 1; these are sampled values, not continuum bounds, and the two sampling sets are
different. Main obstacles (Section 7): at beta = 2, possible flat endpoints of the stagnation arc through P and their
coupling to the equations away from the arc; for beta > 2, the unproved hypothesis (H1) that the zeros of W in the
closed first quadrant are only the origin O and the first positive x-axis zero P, further axis zeros and sign-changing
vorticity configurations, and the global realization of the natural tail; numerically, large transport defects near
stagnation points and in the far field, poor conditioning, and no demonstrated determination of beta (Sections 6, 7). At
beta = 2 every profile has a nonempty open invariant subset of the open quadrant, of infinite area, on which Theta is
constant and Omega = 0 (Theorem 83). For beta > 2, (H1) follows from the far-field sign condition of Theorem 81(b)
together with nondegeneracy of the zeros of W in the closed first quadrant, and under that sign condition nondegeneracy
follows from simple positive zeros of W on the axes and vanishing of Omega on a neighbourhood of each degenerate zero in
the open quadrant (Theorems 84, 86); none of these conditions is proved for any profile. For beta >= 2 and
a0 < 0, the set B of points of the open first quadrant at which Omega > 0, if it has finite area |B|, satisfies
M_B |B|^(1/2) > sqrt(pi) beta L, where M_B = sup_B Omega and P = (L, 0); this is a necessary condition, not an
exclusion (Theorem 87). For beta >= 2, with e = |U|^2/2 + y Theta and the pressure Pi of Theorem 88, the flux of
(e + Pi) U through the quarter circle of radius s, weighted by s^(-n-1) with n = 4 - 2/beta, has an absolutely
convergent integral over 0 < s < infinity; if Theta >= 0 on the open first quadrant, its integral over 0 < s < R is
negative for every R > 0, and so is the integral over all s > 0; this is a necessary condition, not an exclusion
(Theorem 88). Exact solutions on exterior regions with the natural tail exist for beta > 2 and for
beta = 2 (Theorems 69, 70), but whether an interior solution
can be matched to an admissible exterior one remains open; the report derives no contradiction excluding the whole class
A2-broad from its local and exterior analyses (Sections 4, 7). The numerical verification programme is incomplete: among
the missing items are independent fit domains with region-wise evaluation, regional bounds on the inverse error, and
comparisons with controlled objectives and budgets establishing independence from the basis or coordinate map
(Section 6); no tested claim-by-claim reproduction protocol is supplied (Section 9). The accompanying artifacts are
listed in Section 9.

Current status.
 - No A2-broad profile has been constructed, and no theorem here excludes the full class for any fixed beta >= 2;

 - The statements below cite the theorems of Section 3 with their stated hypotheses; Sections 5 and 8 record the

Exclusions in the full class
 - The exponent range beta < 2 is empty (Theorem 1).
 - For every beta >= 2 the critical regime and bounded velocity are excluded (Theorems 34, 38).
 - The vorticity cannot be nonpositive in the open first quadrant (Theorem 21), and it cannot be positive there at
   beta = 2 (Theorems 12, 21).

Restricted exclusions
 - Kinetic energy on the annuli R < |X| < 2R of order o(R^{4-4/beta}) (more precisely O(R^{4-4/beta}) with vanishing
   lower limit) (Theorem 23), which contains vorticity decaying faster than |X|^{-2/beta} (no derivative bounds)
   (Theorems 15, 24), velocity o(|X|^{1-2/beta}) uniformly (for beta > 2 every bounded velocity) (Theorems 19, 23),
   and, at every beta, velocity with a finite integral of |U|^p for some 0 < p < infinity (in particular finite
   kinetic energy) (Theorem 23).
 - Temperature in L^p(R^2) for some finite p > 0 (Theorem 17(b)).
 - Profiles with sgn(a0) d_r(r^{1 + 2/beta} Omega) >= 0 throughout the open quadrant, at every beta >= 2 (Theorem 55);
   this is new only for beta > 2 and a0 > 0, since otherwise it already follows from Theorems 12 and 21.
 - For beta > 2 and a0 < 0, profiles in which {Theta = 0} has no interior point in the open quadrant (in particular
   under (H1)), {Omega > 0} is bounded in the open quadrant, and no ray from the origin carries vorticity of signs
   (-,+,-) at three increasing radii. The last two conditions may be replaced by G <= 0 together with the ray condition

 - For beta > 2 and either sign of a0, with sigma = sgn(a0): profiles in which {Theta = 0} has no interior point in the
   open quadrant (in particular under (H1)), B = {sigma Omega < 0} is bounded and nonempty in the open quadrant, and no

   is nonempty, the ray condition may be imposed only on a dense subset of one open interval of angles meeting the rays

 - For beta > 2 under (H1), with sigma = sgn(a0) and B = {sigma Omega < 0} bounded in the open quadrant, B empty

 - For beta > 2 and either sign of a0, with sigma = sgn(a0): profiles in which the positive zeros of W_1(x, 0) are

Notation in the items below: Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0} is the open first quadrant and Z = {X in R^2 : W(X) = 0}.

Structure theorems (every beta >= 2 unless an item states a range)
 - The first stagnation point P on the positive x-axis has the exactly prescribed eigenvalues beta + 2 and beta - 2,
   so it is a source for beta > 2 (Theorem 2) and lies on a curve of stagnation points for beta = 2 (Theorem 3).
 - No bounded invariant regions (Theorem 4).
 - The origin strain identity holds in the broad class as a centred-disc limit (Theorem 9).
 - With N_L the inward normal derivative at P = (L, 0) of the Green function of the quadrant, the integral of N_L Omega
   over the open quadrant equals beta L, a second explicit weighted integral of Omega vanishes, and the disc limits of
   the integrals of N_L (D Omega + (1 + 2/beta) Omega), D = x d_x + y d_y, vanish; hence sgn(a0) d_r(r^{1 + 2/beta}
   Omega) < 0 on a nonempty open subset of the open quadrant, with no sign assumption (Theorem 55).
 - For beta > 2 the three moments of Omega fixed by Theorems 9 and 55 (against K0 = x y |X|^{-4} and the kernels N_L and
   M_L of Theorem 55) are attained by a positive measure with two atoms in the open quadrant, and every real linear
   combination of the three kernels that is pointwise nonnegative on the open quadrant and not identically zero has a
   positive fixed moment value; so no linear positivity certificate built from these three kernels, with constant
   coefficients, together with Omega >= 0 or Omega > 0 in the open quadrant, can exclude the class (Remark 55.2).
 - Without any sign assumption, Theta_x takes both strict signs on every horizontal half-line in the open quadrant,
   Theta_y on every vertical half-line, and the angular derivative of Theta on every quarter-circle arc (Theorem 57(b)).
   If the vorticity is nonnegative in the open quadrant, then a0 > 0, W_1(x, 0) > 0 for x > x1, W_2(0, y) > beta y,
   Theta_y(x, 0) > 0 and Theta_xx(0, y) > 0 on the positive half-axes (Theorem 57(a)).
 - If a0 < 0, the positive parts of the vorticity moments against the kernels of Theorems 9 and 55 exceed the prescribed
   values, by at least explicit amounts depending on the origin vorticity coefficient b0 (Omega = b0 x y + ...) and on a
   profile-dependent core radius, and Omega_y(x, 0) <= 0 for all x > 0 forces W_1(x, 0) > 0 and Theta_y(x, 0) < 0 for
   x > x1 (Theorem 62(b), (c)).
 - The normal derivative g(x) = Omega_y(x, 0) of the vorticity on the x-axis has an explicit fractional term whose
   coefficient must vanish if the vorticity is C^4 (Theorem 14), and the third y-derivative Theta_yyy(x, 0) of the
   temperature on the x-axis satisfies explicit compatibility conditions at O and at P (Theorem 26).
 - At simple stagnation points on either axis (in a consecutive chain from the origin) the eigenvalues of DW are
   quantized (Theorem 27), and, at the negative-eigenvalue x-axis zeros satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 29
   (Theta_y(x, 0) not identically zero nearby and an integer resonance), smoothness of g imposes an additional Taylor
   condition (Theorem 29).
 - On the y-axis, K(y) = Omega_x(0, y) imposes an additional quantization at the first simple zero of v(y) = W_2(0, y)
   (Theorem 30). Let Y be the largest zero of v on [0, infinity). If E(y) = Theta_xx(0, y)/2 is not identically zero on
   (Y, infinity) (for instance if every positive zero of v is simple), then K/E > 0 there and the transverse outgoing
   derivative of the vorticity is nonzero (Theorem 31(b), (c), (e), with the bounds required in (e) supplied by Theorems
   36 and 42). This condition on E has not been proved for every A2-broad profile (Section 7).
 - For beta > 2, if the temperature is flat at some point, then W has a degenerate zero in the closed first quadrant. If
   every zero of W in the closed first quadrant is nondegenerate, the temperature is flat nowhere, {Theta = 0} has area
   zero, W has finitely many zeros, all hyperbolic sources or saddles, and {Theta = 0} consists of these zeros and
   finitely many orbits, each escaping to infinity or lying on a stable branch of a saddle (Theorem 82). Nondegeneracy
   is not proved for any profile.
 - For beta > 2, nondegeneracy of every zero of W in the closed first quadrant implies that {Theta = 0} has no interior
   point in the open quadrant (Theorem 80(b)), so it may replace that condition in the exclusions of Theorems 62(a) and
   64(b) listed under Restricted exclusions. Set sigma = sgn(a0). Under boundedness of {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0}
   and this nondegeneracy, a failure of (H1) forces a ray in Q1 carrying vorticity of the strict signs (sigma, -sigma,
   sigma) at three increasing radii (Theorem 80(c)). If in addition W has no zero in Q1, the positive zeros of W_2(0, y)
   are even in number; in increasing order the odd-numbered zeros are saddles with d_y W_2(0, y) < 0 and the
   even-numbered zeros are sources with d_y W_2(0, y) = (3 beta + 2)/2. Every orbit in Q1 escapes, and Q1 is the
   disjoint union of the intersections with Q1 of the source basins of P and of the even-numbered sources, and the
   branches in Q1 of the unstable manifolds of those saddles. Theta is nonzero on those source-basin intersections and
   zero on those saddle branches (Theorem 79).
 - For beta > 2, with sigma = sgn(a0) and G as in Theorem 81, assume that sigma G > 0 on (0, pi/2), sigma G'(0) > 0 and
   sigma G'(pi/2) < 0. Then every orbit in the open quadrant on which Omega vanishes identically is bounded, in
   particular every orbit in the open quadrant emerging from a hyperbolic saddle. If moreover every zero of W in the
   closed first quadrant is nondegenerate, then (H1) holds, B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0} is bounded, possibly
   empty, and the conclusions of Theorems 75(a) to (c) apply (Theorem 84). Neither condition is proved for any profile.
 - For beta > 2 under the far-field sign condition of Theorem 81(b) alone: for X in the closed first quadrant outside a
   disc, sigma Omega(X) is at least a positive constant times |X|^(-1/beta) times the angle between X and the nearer
   coordinate axis, so the zeros of Omega in the open quadrant lie in a disc; {Theta = 0} has no interior point in the
   open quadrant; and every ray in the open quadrant on which sigma Omega is somewhere negative carries vorticity of the
   strict signs (sigma, -sigma, sigma) at three increasing radii, the last one arbitrarily large. If moreover every zero
   of W in the closed first quadrant is nondegenerate, then Z = {O, P, -P}, every orbit in the open quadrant comes from
   P and escapes with a limiting polar angle phi_inf in (0, pi/2), and sigma |X|^(1/beta) Omega tends to sigma
   G(phi_inf) > 0 along it (Theorem 86). Neither condition is proved for any profile.
 - If a0 < 0, let B = {X in Q1 : Omega(X) > 0}, with area |B| and M_B = sup_B Omega. Every measurable set E of
   finite area in the open quadrant satisfies int_E N_L <= sqrt(|E|/pi), with a sharp constant; hence, if |B| is
   finite, M_B |B|^(1/2) > sqrt(pi) beta L. For beta > 2 under the far-field sign condition of Theorem 81(b), B is
   bounded, so this bound holds (Theorem 87). It is a necessary condition, not an exclusion.
 - For every beta >= 2, with the pressure Pi of (88.2) normalized by Pi(0) = 0 and e = |U|^2/2 + y Theta,
   div(W e + Pi U) = (4 beta - 2) e. The integral F(R) of e over the quarter disc {X in Q1 : |X| < R} and the flux Q(R)
   of (e + Pi) U through its arc satisfy R^(-n) F(R) = -(1/beta) int_0^R s^(-n-1) Q(s) ds, with n = 4 - 2/beta and
   Q(R) = -pi (2 beta + 2)^2 R^4/8 + O(R^6) as R tends to 0, and R^(-n) F(R) tends to an explicit far-field constant
   C_inf. If Theta >= 0 on Q1, for instance for beta > 2 and a0 > 0 under (H1), then C_inf > 0 and each of these
   weighted flux integrals is negative (Theorem 88). This is a necessary condition, not an exclusion.

Local analysis
 - An exact smooth local family shows that the local identities near the origin and along the axis segment up to P
   cannot by themselves exclude the class (Section 4).
 - Within the separated class Psi = w(x) y every solution with the A2 parities and jet is locally one of two explicit
   families, and none with a0 < 0 has a stagnation point on the positive x-axis (Remark 4.1).

Far field
 - Under a bound |Theta_x| <= C|X|^{-2/beta} the temperature, vorticity and velocity have uniform angular limits at
   the scales r^{1-2/beta}, r^{-1/beta} and r^{1-1/beta}, and either the natural tail (annular energy of exact order
   R^{4-2/beta}) or the critical one occurs (Theorem 32).
 - At beta = 2 this bound holds for every A2-broad profile (Theorem 33), and a sign argument at the origin shows that
   the outgoing amplitude is nonzero (Theorem 34), so every A2-broad profile at beta = 2 has Theta -> H(phi),
   r^{1/2} Omega -> G(phi) uniformly with G not identically zero, max_{|X| = r} |U(X)| of exact order r^{1/2} (no
   lower bound in every direction is asserted) and E(R)/R^3 converging to a positive limit (Theorems 33, 34);
   bounded velocity is impossible at beta = 2 (Theorem 34).
 - Moreover at beta = 2 the angular functions are C^infinity and Theta - H(phi), Omega - r^{-1/2} G(phi) and U minus
   its homogeneous limit are O(r^{-1/2}), O(r^{-1}) and O(1) with all derivatives gaining one power of r^{-1} each
   (Theorem 36).
 - For every beta >= 2 the rescaled vorticity e^T Omega(Phi_T X) converges in distributions to an outgoing
   distribution K, and sgn(a0) K is not nonpositive in any small quarter disc at the origin (Theorem 37).
 - For every beta >= 2 the outgoing distribution is a locally integrable function, the nonescaping set is compact
   and null, and |{|K| > lambda}| = C_K lambda^{-2 beta} exactly, with 0 < C_K < infinity (Theorem 40).
 - For every beta >= 2 the vorticity lies in L^p exactly for p > 2 beta (Theorem 45), the origin strain identities
   hold with absolutely convergent integrals (Theorem 45), and at beta = 2 the first natural correction is explicit
   (Theorem 45).
 - For beta > 2 every A2-broad profile has the natural tail without further hypotheses: the vorticity, the
   temperature gradient and the velocity have angular limits at the scales r^{-1/beta}, r^{-2/beta} and r^{1-1/beta}
   in every finite L^p norm in the angle, the vorticity limit is not identically zero, and E(R)/R^{4-2/beta}
   converges to a positive limit (Theorem 38).
 - Moreover, for beta > 2, |Omega| <= C r^{-1/beta}, |grad Theta| <= C r^{-2/beta} and |DU| <= C r^{-1/beta}
   pointwise, the angular limits are uniform, and the vorticity limit is continuous and has the sign of a0 on an
   interval of angles (Theorem 41).
 - For beta > 2 the angular functions are C^infinity, the remainders of the temperature, vorticity and velocity are
   O_infty(r^{q-h}), O_infty(r^{-2h}) and O_infty(r^{1-2h}) with h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h, where O_infty(r^m) means
   that every derivative of order k is O(r^{m-k}) (a comparison of radial orders, not a relative bound where the
   angular functions vanish), and the first correction of the natural tail is explicit (Theorem 42).
 - If {sgn(a0) Omega < 0} is bounded in the open quadrant (an eventual weak sign of the vorticity), then sgn(a0) G >= 0,
   and the angular stream coefficient satisfies sgn(a0) P > 0 and sgn(a0) P'' < 0 on (0, pi/2), sgn(a0) P'(0) > 0 and
   sgn(a0) P'(pi/2) < 0, at every beta >= 2 (Theorem 64(a)).
 - For beta > 2 the profile equations have a formal natural far-field expansion to every order for every pair (f, G)
   with the parity and axis endpoint conditions of Theorems 41 and 42 and every sequence of harmonic constants
   c_m r^(-2m) sin(2m phi), with coefficients polynomial in log r at the resonances a - delta = -2m; for the explicit
   data f = sgn(a0) sin(phi) cos(phi)^2, G = sgn(a0) sin(2 phi) every truncation has sgn(a0) Theta > 0 and sgn(a0)
   Omega > 0 outside a disc in the open quadrant and satisfies simultaneously the far-field necessary conditions of the
   preceding theorems that apply without additional interior configurations (Theorem 67). This is formal and restricted:
   actual leading pairs are not characterized, global balances are not realized, and it is not shown that far-field
   arguments cannot decide.
 - At beta = 2 the profile equations have a formal natural far-field expansion to every order in powers of r^(-1/2),
   with coefficients polynomial in log r, for every pair (H, G) with the parity and axis endpoint conditions. The only
   freedom is one harmonic constant c_m r^(-2m) sin(2m phi) at each order n = 4m + 3. Nonzero resonant forcing forces a
   logarithm, which Theorems 36 and 45 do not exclude. Nonzero forcing is open dense in the full data space at the first
   resonance and in the full joint space of data and preceding constants at later ones, not relatively within sign or
   plateau subclasses. For either sign sigma there are explicit data with sigma H > 0 on (0, pi/2), H = sigma on
   [pi/6, pi/3], and G = 0 there satisfying the angular necessary conditions and asymptotic axis signs of the
   finite-stagnation-component class; the sigma = +1 data satisfy those of the Omega >= 0 class, and the sigma = -1 data
   those of the a0 < 0 class with bounded {Omega > 0} cap Q1. In all three classes the hypotheses of each cited theorem
   are retained as specified in Theorem 68(d), as hypotheses on the unknown solution, not verified by these data. Every
   truncation solves the equations exactly on the plateau sector (Theorem 68). This is formal: global identities are not
   realized, nothing is shown to converge, and it is not shown that far-field arguments cannot decide.
 - For beta > 2 the natural far field is realized exactly on a distant exterior: for every pair (f, G) with the endpoint
   conditions of Theorems 41 and 42 and every compactly supported odd-odd core vorticity there are exact exterior
   solutions with the canonical whole-plane velocity, the natural tail and the first corrections of Theorem 42, not
   unique without data in the cutoff annulus; for f = sigma sin(phi) cos(phi)^2, G = sigma sin(2phi) they have sigma
   Theta > 0 and sigma Omega > 0 in the distant open quadrant and satisfy the exterior content of the necessary
   conditions proved here, so no condition implied solely by the exterior equations, the canonical inversion and the
   natural tail excludes all of them; the angular implications of Theorems 47(a) and 66(f) fail for some exterior
   solutions, their proofs being interior (Theorem 69). Exterior solutions are not profiles, and neither a global
   profile nor a general limit on methods of proving nonexistence follows.
 - At beta = 2 the natural far field is realized exactly on a distant exterior: for every pair (H, G) with the parity
   and axis endpoint conditions and every compactly supported odd-odd core vorticity there are exact exterior solutions
   with the canonical whole-plane velocity, the natural tail, the first corrections of Theorem 45(f) and the expansion
   of Theorem 68 to every finite order, not unique without data in the cutoff annulus; for the plateau pairs of
   Theorem 68 they have an open forward invariant region of infinite area with Theta = sigma and Omega = 0, so no
   condition implied solely by the exterior equations, the canonical inversion and the natural tail excludes these
   pairs; for H = sin(phi) cos(phi)^2, G = sin(2phi) they have Theta > 0 and Omega > 0 throughout the distant open
   quadrant and G > 0 at a critical point of H, so the angular implication of Theorem 47(a) at beta = 2, and the
   impossibility of a strict vorticity sign throughout the distant open quadrant that follows from it, are not
   consequences of the exterior equations, their proofs being interior (Theorem 70). Exterior solutions are not
   profiles, and neither a global profile nor a general limit on methods of proving nonexistence follows.
 - At beta = 2 every A2-broad profile has the expansion of Theorem 68 to every finite order, with coefficients
   polynomial in log r computed from its leading pair (H, G) and with unique constants c_m determined by the profile;
   the first possible logarithm, (g_7/4) r^(-2) log r sin(2phi) in the stream function, is present exactly when an
   explicit angular coefficient g_7 of the profile is nonzero (Theorem 76). Convergence of the series, further
   restrictions on (H, G) or on the c_m, and an all-order expansion of actual profiles for beta > 2 are not established.
 - For beta >= 2, with sigma = sgn(a0), h = 1/beta, B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0} and r^h Omega(r, .) -> G
   uniformly: if sigma G > 0 on (0, pi/2), sigma G'(0) > 0 and sigma G'(pi/2) < 0, then sigma Omega > 0 on the open
   quadrant outside a disc, so B is bounded (B empty allowed), and this condition may replace boundedness of B in the
   statements that assume it, with the beta range and every other hypothesis retained; at beta = 2 the condition never
   holds, and sigma G < 0 at one interior angle makes B unbounded (Theorem 81). The condition is not proved for any
   profile.
 - Under the critical bound O(R^{4-4/beta}) on the annular energy, Theorem 28 gives a forced homogeneous limit of the
   rescaled far field (the temperature strongly in L^p_loc, the velocity weakly in L^2_loc, the vorticity in
   distributions) and both signs of the vorticity in every large quadrant annulus. This is a conditional consequence,
   not an exclusion; the bound fails for every A2-broad profile at every beta >= 2 (Theorems 34 and 38).

Dynamics of W (every beta >= 2 unless an item states a range)
 - The field (2 beta - 1) W + Omega W^perp - Theta e_2 has a global potential, which gives a strict Lyapunov
   function at beta = 2 (Theorem 44).
 - For beta > 2, the function Ly = Bern + y Theta of Theorem 44 minus the explicit backward-orbit integral Hc of (58.12)
   is a continuous proper function whose derivative along every orbit is (2 beta - 1)|W|^2, for either sign of Theta
   (Theorem 58(e)).
 - Every backward orbit converges to a single zero of W (Theorem 44).
 - Every bounded forward orbit converges to a single zero of W; a nonstationary such orbit also has a backward limit,
   distinct from the forward one, and Ly increases from the backward to the forward limit by (2 beta - 1) times its
   kinetic action; for beta > 2 the temperature vanishes on the whole orbit (Theorem 63(a)).
 - Every finite positive Borel measure with compact support that is invariant under the flow is supported on the
   zero set, and for beta > 2 also on {Theta = 0} (Theorem 44).
 - The backward basin of an open arc of zeros (with grad Theta = 0 on the arc at beta = 2) is an open set of infinite
   area on which Theta is constant and Omega = 0 (Theorem 44).
 - At a hyperbolic saddle of W the temperature gradient and the vorticity vanish, and they vanish on every orbit
   emerging from it (Theorem 46).
 - The temperature gradient is nonzero at the launch point of every outgoing orbit with nonzero vorticity amplitude
   (Theorem 47); consequently the vorticity amplitude vanishes at every double zero of the temperature amplitude
   (beta > 2) and at every critical point of H (beta = 2), H' has a zero in (0, pi/2) (Theorem 47).
 - For beta > 2 the backward limits of these orbits lie in a countable subset of the zero set and both P and -P
   receive an open interval of them (Theorem 47), and at beta = 2 a zero of W whose eigenvalues have positive real
   part has a basin of infinite area with constant temperature and zero vorticity (Theorem 47).

beta = 2
 - The temperature range is carried by the stagnation set (Theorem 5).
 - Every nontrivial component of the stagnation set contains a point Q at which Theta - Theta(Q) and Omega vanish to
   infinite order, so the temperature is not real analytic (Theorem 11).
 - The vorticity vanishes at some stagnation point of the open quadrant where the temperature does not (Theorem 12).
 - Nonnegative vorticity in the open quadrant is not excluded; it gives H'(0) > 0 and H''(pi/2) > 0 (Theorem 57(a)).
 - Under nonnegative vorticity in the open quadrant, Psi > 0 there and W_1(x, 0) < 2x for x > 0; G >= 0 and G is not
   identically zero, the angular stream coefficient is positive and strictly concave, G = 0 and H'' = 0 at every
   interior critical angle of H, G = 0 forces H' >= 0, and G'(pi/2) < 0; the absence of zero components lying wholly in
   the open quadrant is then equivalent to (S), and together with (R) it gives Theta > 0 on the open quadrant and a
   plateau of H strictly inside (0, pi/2); with finitely many components, those lying wholly in the open quadrant have
   total index (1-eps)/2, eps = ind(C). These are necessary conditions (Theorem 59).
 - Under nonnegative vorticity in the open quadrant, along each half-fibre of a regular zero of W in the open quadrant
   the height displacement from the zero satisfies an exact weighted identity, so every escaping branch with L < 0 first
   dips below the height of its zero, with explicit depth bounds in terms of its escape constants and a slope bound;
   under (I) and (R) the exit parameters of the half-fibres near Q+ grow faster than every power of the inverse distance
   to Q+; at a regular zero of W with Omega = 0, DW = diag(4, 0) and D^2 W = 0, and every derivative of Omega of order
   at most 7 vanishes when -8 < Theta_y < 108; an open regular zero arc on which Omega vanishes is vertical, and Omega
   is flat on it except where Theta_y is locally constant with a value 4(k + 1)(4k + 1), k even and k >= 2. These are
   necessary conditions (Theorem 61).
 - The stagnation component through P is an arc with two flat endpoints in the open right half-plane (Theorem 16).
 - An orbit entering an endpoint forces another stagnation point with the same temperature (Theorem 22).
 - Every nontrivial component of the stagnation set is an arc with flat endpoints; a nonstationary orbit in the open
   quadrant with finite limits joins two distinct components, at most one such orbit joins a given pair, and an orbit in
   the open quadrant entering the upper endpoint Q+ of the arc through P comes from a component lying wholly in the open
   quadrant (Theorem 53).
 - A nonstationary orbit anywhere in the plane with finite limits joins two distinct components of the stagnation set at
   equal temperature, at most one such orbit joins a given pair, and the function Ly of Theorem 44 increases along it by
   three times the time integral of |W|^2 (Theorem 56(a)).
 - If no component of the stagnation set lies wholly in the open quadrant, both endpoints of the arc through P are
   outgoing, every nonstationary orbit in the open quadrant escapes, and there is an open connected invariant region of
   infinite area in the open quadrant with Theta = Theta(Q+) and Omega = 0, including when Theta(Q+) = 0 (Theorems 53,
   56(a)).
 - An isolated arc component has index equal to the mean of the signs of its endpoints (+1 outgoing, -1 incoming), an
   isolated arc of constant temperature has two incoming endpoints, and if the stagnation set has finitely many
   components their indices satisfy an explicit balance (Theorem 53).
 - If Q+ is incoming and the orbit through its opposite centre branch meets an open invariant subset of the open
   quadrant on which Theta = Theta(Q+), then the side of a small disc about Q+ opposite to the arc has constant
   temperature and zero vorticity, and the temperature is not constant on any nontrivial terminal subarc ending at Q+
   (Theorem 56(b)).
 - Every isolated stagnation point of index +1 is a hyperbolic source or has spectrum {0, 4} with a drift of odd order
   at least 3 along its centre direction, and in both cases has a full neighbourhood with constant temperature and zero
   vorticity; with finitely many components, an incoming Q+ and k = 0 in (53.9), the components lying wholly in the open
   quadrant have total index 1 (Theorem 56(c)).
 - Every A2-broad profile at beta = 2 has a nonempty open connected invariant set of infinite area in the open quadrant
   on which Theta is constant and Omega = 0, and a nonempty open interval of angles in (0, pi/2) on which H is constant
   and G = 0; the constant is the temperature of a zero of W in the closed first quadrant and is not identified (Theorem
   63(b), (c) when some component of the stagnation set is isolated and has index +1, in particular when there are
   finitely many components; Theorem 83(a) in general).
 - If M = Theta(Q+) > 0 and every zero in the closed first quadrant at temperatures in (0, M) is regular, each level in
   (0, M) is attained at the same number N >= 1 of zeros in the open quadrant and at 2N angles phi in (0, pi/2) of H
   (Theorem 56(d)); if moreover the stagnation set has finitely many components, Q+ is incoming, the closure of
   Theta(Q1) is [0, M] and N = 1, then (R) of Theorem 48 holds, H has a single positive excursion with a plateau of
   positive length at M, and some isolated zero of index +1 at temperature M has a full neighbourhood with constant
   temperature and zero vorticity (Theorem 56(e)).
 - In an accumulating configuration the kinetic actions of the connecting orbits tend to 0 (Theorem 56(f)). If the
   stagnation set has infinitely many components, it contains a point every neighbourhood of which meets infinitely many
   of them; every such point has spectrum {0, 4}, and every neighbourhood of it contains an open set of constant
   temperature and zero vorticity whose backward orbits converge to one zero, a hyperbolic source or a zero with
   spectrum {0, 4} (Theorem 83(b)). These results do not exclude accumulation.
 - For every A2-broad profile at beta = 2 and every lambda > 0 an exact balance weighted by exp(-lambda Ly) holds for
   every C^1 function of the temperature and for the indicator of every temperature level (Theorem 56(g)), and on every
   invariant measurable subset of the open quadrant (Theorem 59(f)); its factor 4 - 3 lambda |W|^2 has no fixed sign.
 - An endpoint with an outgoing centre branch carries an open invariant region of infinite area with constant
   temperature and zero vorticity (Theorem 35).
 - The temperature and the function L = W.grad^perp Theta/|grad Theta|^2 are global coordinates on each component of
   {grad Theta != 0}, in which the flow is linear (Theorem 39).
 - Every regular nonstationary point has a regular stagnation point as backward limit (Theorem 39).
 - Several exact weighted integral balances over the quadrant hold (Theorem 39).
 - Every bounded forward orbit converges to a single zero of W (Theorem 48).
 - No nonstationary orbit has both limits on one arc of zeros (Theorem 48).
 - At every critical point of H in (0, pi/2) where H != 0 the corresponding launch orbit escapes inside
   {grad Theta = 0} (Theorem 48).
 - If the zeros of W in the open quadrant are those of the arc of Theorem 16 (hypothesis (S) of Theorem 48, not proved),
   there is an open connected invariant region of infinite area with Theta = Theta(Q+) and Omega = 0, including when
   Theta(Q+) = 0 (Theorems 35, 48, 53). If moreover grad Theta != 0 on the arc away from its endpoints ((R) of Theorem
   48), then Theta(Q+) != 0 and, after a possible interval next to the x-axis on which H = 0, |H| increases strictly
   from 0 to |Theta(Q+)|, is constant on an interval of positive length and decreases strictly to 0, possibly followed
   by an interval next to the y-axis on which H = 0 (Theorem 48(e)).
 - Under (S) alone, without (R) and for every value of Theta(Q+), near the endpoint the whole side of its strong
   unstable curve that contains the outgoing centre branch has constant temperature and zero vorticity, the complex
   velocity there has no holomorphic continuation across the endpoint, and no real-analytic local invariant curve
   through the endpoint is tangent to the eigenvector for the eigenvalue 4 (Theorems 51, 53).
 - At the end Q of a one-sided arc of zeros at beta = 2 with spectrum {0, 4} and an outgoing zero-free centre branch,
   the temperature and the vorticity are determined on backward invariant neighbourhoods of Q by the velocity and by a
   trace on the arc whose difference from its endpoint value M = Theta(Q) is flat at Q, so the local endpoint
   configuration reduces exactly to one curl equation; in every such configuration the vorticity vanishes on no
   neighbourhood of any point of the strong unstable curve, and under (S), for every value of Theta(Q+), on no
   neighbourhood of any point of the complete orbits through that curve near Q+. A field with div W = 4 and all velocity
   conclusions of Theorem 51 need not extend to a solution (Theorem 72(e)); existence of the endpoint configuration is
   not decided (Theorem 72).
 - In the setting of Theorem 72, an area chart of Theorem 74(a), with det DR = 1 and W(R) = 4t R_t, turns the curl
   equation to which the endpoint configuration (E') reduces into rho - t rho_t = F (74.3), where rho is explicit in the
   chart and F is explicit in the chart and the trace. For a prescribed smooth F this scalar equation has a smooth
   solution exactly when F_t vanishes at t = 0. Thus every (E') configuration satisfies the explicit compatibility
   condition (74.5) in every chart of Theorem 74(a), and its separator Gamma (the strong unstable curve) has zero
   curvature at the endpoint Q. These finite-jet facts do not solve the coupled chart equation. At points with t != 0
   the frozen principal part, for perturbations proportional to exp(lambda s + i eta t), has the rates lambda = i rho
   eta +/- |eta|/|R_t|^2, with growth in both directions. Separately, for the linearization at the exact solution
   W = (0, 4y) with the temperature trace theta unperturbed, the map from the perturbation's data on the fibre {s = 0,
   |t| <= 1} to its second component xi2 at (eL, 0), for fixed L > 0 and e = 1 or e = -1, is not continuous in any C^j
   norm or in the C^infinity topology, among data admitting a smooth linearized solution on a connected rectangle
   meeting t = 0 to that distance. These statements give no nonlinear or general variable-coefficient ill-posedness
   conclusion. For a minus-side field with divergence 4 and curl flat along the dividing curve (in the application, the
   strong unstable curve), smooth matching to a potential side reduces to equality of explicit boundary values ((74.11)
   in a chart); this does not show that the boundary values of any minus-side solution extend holomorphically. No (E')
   configuration has a chart of Theorem 74(a) solving (74.3) on its connected rectangle with affine fibres. Local
   existence of an (E') configuration is equivalent to assertion L of Theorem 74(f), including all its chart, embedding,
   flat temperature trace, holomorphic boundary-extension, zero-set and invariant centre-curve conditions; L remains
   unproved (Theorem 74). If L is false, every A2-broad profile at beta = 2 has a component of {W = 0} wholly in the
   open first quadrant (Remark 74.1).
 - If {sgn(a0) Omega < 0} is bounded in the open quadrant, then at interior angles H'' = 0 wherever H' = 0, sgn(a0)
   H' >= 0 wherever G = 0, and sgn(a0) G > 0 wherever sgn(a0) H' < 0. If it is bounded and nonempty and no ray carries
   vorticity of signs (sigma,-sigma,sigma) at three increasing radii, sigma = sgn(a0), there is an exterior sector with
   Omega = 0 and constant temperature c, on which H = c and G = 0, whose flow saturation is an invariant potential
   region of escaping orbits in the open quadrant; this alternative is not excluded (Theorem 64(g), (h)).
 - At beta = 2 and a0 < 0, if {Omega > 0} cap Q1 is bounded and no ray from the origin into Q1 carries vorticity of
   signs (-,+,-) at three increasing radii, there is a nonempty exterior open sector on which the temperature is
   constant, Omega = 0 and the velocity is harmonic. The same holds if, instead, for a nonempty open interval I of
   angles in (0, pi/2) and some R > 0, the vorticity is positive at some point of a ray from the origin with angle in I,
   is nonpositive at distance at least R from the origin on all these rays, and no ray with angle in I carries these
   signs. This sector is not excluded (Theorem 62(a)).

beta > 2
 - The temperature has no zero in the open quadrant if and only if the stagnation set meets the closed quadrant only
   at O and P (Theorem 13), and then it is determined by the velocity and one scalar (Theorem 8).
 - Every zero of W has real spectrum (Theorem 43).
 - A zero with grad Theta != 0 is a hyperbolic source with eigenvalues kappa and beta + 2 (Theorem 43).
 - The leading temperature jets at sources and saddles are classified (Theorem 43).
 - A source with flat temperature carries an open invariant region of positive lower density with Theta = Omega = 0
   (Theorem 43).
 - The temperature at infinity vanishes at an angle exactly when it vanishes on the corresponding outgoing orbit
   (Theorem 43).
 - The set of points with bounded forward orbit is compact, connected and invariant, contains every zero of W and
   carries Theta = 0 (Theorem 52).
 - (H1) holds exactly when W has no zero on the positive half-axes other than P (Theorem 52).
 - Positive vorticity in the open quadrant forces the stagnation set to be {O, P, -P}; then (H1) holds and Theta > 0
   there (Theorem 21).
 - The same holds when the vorticity is only nonnegative in the open quadrant, and then a0 > 0 and all conclusions of
   Theorem 50 hold (Theorem 57(a)).
 - At the first zero of W after P on the positive x-axis, Theta, grad Theta and Omega vanish and Omega_y(x, 0) has the
   sign of -a0 just before it; hence a further zero of W on the positive x-axis forces both signs of the vorticity in
   the open quadrant (Theorem 54).
 - Below the first positive zero of W_2 on the y-axis, Theta_xx(0, y) and Omega_x(0, y) have the sign of a0, with no
   simplicity assumption; Theta and Omega are flat on the whole set of points whose backward orbit tends to an axis zero
   with zero eigenvalue along the axis (Theorem 54).
 - If the stagnation set in the closed quadrant consists of O, P, one hyperbolic saddle and one hyperbolic source on the
   positive axes, then both lie on the same axis with the saddle first, every point of the open quadrant escapes, and
   the angular limits of the temperature and the vorticity have explicit signs; on the y-axis this configuration is
   impossible when beta is irrational or a reduced ratio of two odd integers (Theorems 30, 54). Neither configuration is
   excluded in general.
 - The dual balance of Theorem 50(d) holds without (H1), also on every invariant measurable subset (Theorem 54).
 - If the positive zeros of W on the x-axis are finitely many and simple, their number is odd, sources and saddles
   alternate, and on each saddle branch entering the open quadrant Theta and Omega vanish to exactly prescribed orders
   with determined signs (Theorem 58(a)). If moreover W has no zero on the positive y-axis and none in the open
   quadrant, the open quadrant is the disjoint union of the intersections with it of the source basins and the saddle
   branches entering it, every point of it escapes, the escape angles of the branches are ordered, the angular limits
   have prescribed orders and signs at these angles, and Theta_x and Theta_y take both signs on every nonempty connected
   component of every horizontal, respectively vertical, slice of the intersection of each source basin with the open
   quadrant (Theorem 58(c), (d)). Each regular source on the positive x-axis has a unit-Jacobian linearization of its
   basin (Theorem 58(b)).
 - If the positive zeros of W_1(x, 0) are finitely many and simple and W_2(0, y) has no positive zero, every bounded
   forward orbit converges to a single zero, and W has a zero in the open quadrant if and only if the upper unstable
   branch of some axis saddle is bounded; if such a branch ends at a hyperbolic zero, the stable-direction exponents i
   and ell of the leading monomials of Theta and Omega there satisfy the integer constraints of Theorem 60(b), and beta
   is rational. Hence for irrational beta and nondegenerate zeros in the open quadrant, W has no zero there and
   Theorem 58(c), (d) apply. With nondegenerate interior zeros the set of bounded forward orbits is a finite tree; in
   the configuration with exactly one interior source and one interior saddle the source has spectrum
   {kappa/p, 2 beta - kappa/p}, p the temperature order of the incoming axis saddle branch, and a signed height moment
   of sign (-1)^k, k = (beta + 1)/a, where -a is the negative eigenvalue of the interior saddle (Theorem 60).
 - If every zero of W is nondegenerate the temperature is flat at no zero (Theorem 52).
 - For beta > 2 and either sign of a0, the corrected Lyapunov function of Theorem 58(e) is smooth on the basin of each
   regular source on the positive x-axis, and its only critical point there is a nondegenerate strict minimum at the
   source, with Hessian (2 beta - 1) diag(beta + 2, beta - 2); no smoothness across basin boundaries is asserted
   (Theorems 62(e), 71(c)).
 - On a connected open set with Omega = 0 and Theta nowhere zero, U is affine and Theta is a power or an exponential of
   an affine function of y; on an unbounded connected open set contained in the open quadrant with Omega = 0 on which
   Theta is not identically zero, U is constant and P and G vanish to infinite order at its limit directions, which lie
   in (0, pi/2) (Theorem 64(d), (e)); no hypothesis on the sign of the vorticity is used here. If {sgn(a0) Omega < 0} is
   bounded in the open quadrant, every unbounded connected open subset of {Omega = 0} in the open quadrant has Theta = 0
   identically, and if moreover {Theta = 0} has no interior point there, the vorticity has the sign of a0 at arbitrarily
   large radii on a dense residual set of angles (Theorem 64(a), (c)).
 - If the vorticity is nonnegative in the open quadrant (so a0 > 0, (H1) and Theta > 0 there, Theorem 57(a)), then
   outside a disc every zero of Omega in the open quadrant has order two or four along its orbit, there are no zero
   orbit segments or flat zeros there, and the vorticity is positive in sectors at both axes; every unbounded sequence
   of zeros in the open quadrant has only interior limit angles, at which G = 0, q cos(phi) f - sin(phi) f' = 0 and the
   angular limit of r^{1/beta} d_x W_2 is nonpositive; every orbit in the open quadrant has positive vorticity at
   arbitrarily large times, and the interior of {Omega = 0} there is bounded. Moreover Theta_y(x, 0) > Theta_y(P) at
   some x beyond P, Omega_y(x, 0) > 0 for all large x, and Omega_y(P) = 0 forces the cubic relation (65.17) at P
   (Theorem 65(b), (c), (e), (f)). If only a0 > 0 and {Omega < 0} is bounded in the open quadrant (Theorem 65(h)), the
   angular inequalities and the radial lower bound persist, and outside a disc: at zeros of Omega with Theta != 0 one
   has grad Omega = 0, Theta_x = 0, W.D^2 Omega W >= 0 and Theta d_x W_2 <= 0, there are no zero orbit segments or flat
   zeros with Theta != 0, every orbit with nonzero temperature has positive vorticity at arbitrarily large times, and
   every interior point of {Omega = 0} has Theta = 0; limit angles of unbounded sequences of zeros with Theta != 0 may
   lie on the axes, and at them G = 0 and q cos(phi) f - sin(phi) f' = 0, while along zeros of fixed temperature sign
   eps the product of eps and the angular limit of r^{1/beta} d_x W_2 is nonpositive. This extension gives neither the
   positive axis sectors nor a global sign of Theta.
 - If, for sigma = sgn(a0), the set B = {sigma Omega < 0} is bounded and nonempty in the open quadrant and {Theta = 0}
   has no interior point there, then on every component D of B, with b = -sigma Omega, the exact balances r int_D
   b^(r-1) sigma Theta_x = (2 beta - r) int_D b^r hold for r >= 1, so Theta_x takes both strict signs in D; if the
   closure of D lies in the open quadrant and grad Omega is nonzero on its boundary, the flux of W through the boundary
   is 2 beta times the area of D, and W crosses the boundary in both directions when sigma Theta > 0 on the closure; a
   dense residual set of the orbits launched from a large circle that meet B has sigma Omega > 0 at arbitrarily large
   later times; interior limit angles of distant vorticity zeros satisfy G = 0, q cos(phi) f - sin(phi) f' = 0 and the
   contact inequalities (66.17). For a0 < 0 under (H1), with w(x) = W_1(x, 0): if w''(L) > 0 a dense residual set of
   these orbits carries vorticity of signs (sigma,-sigma,sigma) at three increasing times, if w''(L) < 0 every orbit in
   the open quadrant meets B, and on every connected component (l, r) of {x > 0 : Omega_y(x, 0) > 0} the trace
   T0 = -Theta_y(x, 0) satisfies T0(r) > T0(l) (Theorem 66). None of these conditions excludes the configuration, and
   the sign of w''(L) is not determined.

beta > 2 under the unproved hypothesis (H1) of Theorem 8
 - The half-plane {x > 0} is the basin of P and is conjugate to the linear flow of DW(P) by a C^1 diffeomorphism
   with unit Jacobian whose second component is Theta/Theta_y(P) (Theorem 50).
 - The escape angle is a strictly decreasing function of the orbit label with an explicit derivative (Theorem 50).
 - With sigma = sgn(a0), the angular limits f of r^{2/beta - 1} Theta and G of r^{1/beta} Omega satisfy sigma f > 0 on
   (0, pi/2), sigma f'(0) > 0, sigma f''(pi/2) > 0 and sigma G'(pi/2) < 0, so sigma G > 0 on an interval of angles next
   to the y-axis (Theorem 50(b), (c)).
 - If moreover, with sigma = sgn(a0), the set B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0} is bounded and nonempty, then the
   common zeros in (0, pi/2) of sigma G and of an explicit angular function K of the leading stream coefficient are
   finitely many and are simple zeros of K; on all but finitely many rays in Q1, sigma Omega >= c r^{-3/beta} beyond a
   radius, and on all but finitely many complete orbits in Q1, sigma Omega >= c |X|^{-3/beta} at all sufficiently late
   points, with c > 0 and the radius or the time threshold depending on the ray or the orbit; if a0 < 0 and w''(L) > 0,
   where w(x) = W_1(x, 0), all but finitely many orbits meeting B carry the vorticity signs (sigma,-sigma,sigma) at
   three increasing times; and, for the orbit through any point of the open quadrant, every maximal time interval
   (connected component of the set of times) on which sigma Omega < 0 along the orbit contains a point with W_2 d_x
   W_2 < 0 (Theorem 73(a)-(d)). These are necessary conditions and do not exclude the configuration; the sign of w''(L)
   is not determined.
 - The finite-exception conclusions and the ray and orbit lower bounds of Theorem 73(a)-(c) hold under (H1) when B is
   only assumed bounded, B empty included. In particular, if Omega >= 0 in the open quadrant (which forces (H1), a0 > 0
   and B empty by Theorem 57(a)), then Omega >= c r^{-3/beta} beyond a radius on all but finitely many rays in Q1, and
   Omega >= c |X|^{-3/beta} at all sufficiently late points of all but finitely many complete orbits in Q1, with c > 0
   and the thresholds depending on the ray or the orbit (Theorem 75). These are necessary conditions and do not exclude
   the class.

Numerical work
 - No tested numerical state has been validated as an exact profile; Section 6 distinguishes diagnostic rejection of
   states from exact exclusions obtained from their stored coefficients, including a certified exclusion of a
   quantitative neighbourhood of one stored state on one disc, also with the exponent free near 2 (Section 6).

Open
 - For every beta >= 2, what remains open is the natural branch (Section 7).

## 1. Problem statement

Physical equations (the sign convention is fixed as stated):
  d_t omega + u.grad omega = d_{z1} theta,  d_t theta + u.grad theta = 0,  u = (-d_{z2} psi, d_{z1} psi),  -Lap_z psi = omega,  z in R^2.
Self-similar ansatz with tau = T - t and unknown beta > 0:
  X = z/tau^beta, omega = tau^{-1} Omega(X), theta = tau^{beta-2} Theta(X), u = tau^{beta-1} U(X), psi = tau^{2beta-1} Psi(X).
Profile equations, with X = (x,y) and W := beta X + U:
  (V) W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x,   (T) W.grad Theta = (beta - 2) Theta,   -Lap Psi = Omega,  U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x).
These four relations together are called (P). Since div U = 0, div W = 2 beta. Note that d_x U_2 - d_y U_1 = Lap Psi = -Omega.

Setting A2 (the only target). Theta(-x,y) = Theta(x,y), Theta(x,-y) = -Theta(x,y); Omega odd in x and odd in y; hence
Psi odd-odd, U_1 odd in x and even in y, U_2 even in x and odd in y, W_2(x,0) = 0, W_1(0,y) = 0 (both axes invariant),
U(0) = 0. Jet: Theta(0,y) = 0 for all y and Theta = x^2 y a(x^2,y^2) near 0 with a(0,0) = a0 != 0 (either sign).

Local identities (verified independently by symbolic computation). With c := Psi_xy(0), the x^2 y coefficient of (T)
gives a0 (3 beta - c) = a0 (beta - 2), so c = 2 beta + 2; then DU(0) = diag(-c, c) and DW(0) = diag(-(beta+2), 3 beta + 2):
the origin is a saddle with stable x-axis and unstable y-axis. If Omega = b0 x y + ..., the x y coefficient of (V) gives
(2 beta + 1) b0 = 2 a0. Symmetry-reduced form: with s = x^2, t = y^2, Theta = y F, Omega = x y G, Psi = x y H,
A = beta - H - 2 t H_t, B = beta + H + 2 s H_s (W_1 = x A, W_2 = y B):
  2 s A F_s + 2 t B F_t + (B - beta + 2) F = 0,  2 s A G_s + 2 t B G_t + (A + B + 1) G = 2 F_s,  4 s H_ss + 6 H_s + 4 t H_tt + 6 H_t = -G.

Spatial scaling. Theta_l = l Theta(X/l), Omega_l = Omega(X/l), U_l = l U(X/l) maps profiles to profiles with
a0 -> a0/l^2 and beta, c unchanged. This dilation is the symmetry used for normalization; no classification of all
symmetries of the class is claimed. Section 2 fixes the velocity gauge, so no strain or harmonic field can be added,
and amplitude scaling is not a symmetry, because W depends on U.

The task description mentions a separate stationary-profile computation for the IPM equation with a C^6 phenomenon. No
exponent, residual figure or regularity threshold from it is used here. The corresponding questions for these Boussinesq
profiles, namely fractional resonances and finite-regularity conditions produced by saddle transport, are treated afresh
in Theorem 14 (an explicit fractional term in Omega_y(x, 0) whose coefficient must vanish if the vorticity is C^4),
Theorem 27 (quantized eigenvalues of DW at simple axis stagnation points) and Theorem 29 (an additional Taylor condition
at integer resonances).

## 2. Admissible class

A2-broad: (beta, Theta, Omega, U) with beta > 0; Theta, Omega in C^infinity(R^2) with the A2 parity and jet;
U in C^infinity with the A2 velocity parities (U_1 odd in x and even in y, U_2 even in x and odd in y), div U = 0,
d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = Omega, U(X) = o(|X|) uniformly as |X| -> infinity; and |Theta| + |Omega| <= C (1 + |X|)^N for some N;
(P) holds. The velocity is canonical: two such fields differ by a divergence-free harmonic field of growth o(|X|),
hence by a constant, which the velocity parities make zero. No strain, harmonic polynomial,
image or uniform flow is added. Finite-regularity variants (C^k) are separate labelled classes.
A2-dec is defined by adding |Omega| <= C (1 + |X|)^{-gamma} for some gamma > 0. Theorem 45(c) proves that A2-dec and
A2-broad have the same solutions: every broad profile with beta >= 2 admits gamma = 1/beta, and both classes are empty
for beta < 2. In A2-dec the velocity is
given by absolutely convergent parity-grouped Green formulas (the ungrouped whole-plane integrals need not converge
absolutely when gamma <= 1; modal form: for Omega = sum_k omega_k(r) sin(2 k phi),
psi_k(r) = (1/(4k)) [r^{-2k} int_0^r rho^{2k+1} omega_k drho + r^{2k} int_r^inf rho^{1-2k} omega_k drho]).

Hypothesis used repeatedly: (G) X.W(X) > 0 for |X| >= R. It follows from U = o(|X|). Under U in C^1 and |U| <= C(1+|X|),
the flow Phi_s of W is global, each Phi_s is a C^1 diffeomorphism of R^2, and det D Phi_s = e^{2 beta s} (Liouville).
(T) is equivalent to Theta(Phi_s X) = e^{(beta-2) s} Theta(X). Z := {W = 0} is compact by (G). kappa := beta - 2.

Physical meaning. For beta > 2 the profile temperature is unbounded on every orbit on which it is nonzero (Theorem 7),
and theta(t,.) is then unbounded; for beta = 2 Theta is bounded (Theorem 5) but does not tend to zero at infinity
(Theorem 6(b), since max Theta > 0). In neither case would an exact profile give blow-up from bounded, spatially
decaying temperature data. No profile has finite kinetic energy, at any beta (Theorem 23); the kinetic energy on
the annuli R < |X| < 2R cannot be O(R^{4-4/beta}) with vanishing lower limit.

Physical reconstruction and conserved quantities (a diagnostic, not an exclusion). Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an
A2-broad profile and define omega, theta, u and psi on R^2 x (-infinity, T) by the ansatz of Section 1. (i) These fields
are smooth, solve the physical equations and have the A2 parities at every time; for each t, u(., t) = o(|z|) uniformly
as |z| -> infinity, so, with its divergence, vorticity and parities, u(., t) is the canonical velocity of omega(., t) in
the sense of Section 2. (ii) Since U is C^1 with |U(X)| <= C (1 + |X|) (Section 2 and Theorem 6), u is C^1 with
|u(z, t)| <= C(t) (1 + |z|), C(t) bounded on compact subintervals of (-infinity, T); hence the particle trajectories
exist throughout (-infinity, T), the trajectory maps between any two such times are area-preserving C^1 diffeomorphisms
of R^2, and theta is constant along trajectories. Therefore sup_z |theta(z, t)| does not depend on t, and neither does
the area of {theta(., t) > lambda} for any real lambda; these quantities may be infinite. The ansatz gives sup_z
|theta(z, t)| = tau^{beta-2} sup |Theta| and |{theta(., t) > lambda}| = tau^{2 beta} |{Theta > lambda tau^{2-beta}}|. If
0 < sup |Theta| < infinity, the first identity and constancy force beta = 2. For beta > 2 every A2-broad profile has sup
|Theta| = infinity (Theorem 7, using a0 != 0), so this diagnostic gives no restriction there, and beta < 2 is excluded
independently (Theorem 1). At beta = 2, Theta is bounded (Theorem 5) and the first identity holds. Under these class
hypotheses, constancy of the distribution function of theta follows from (T), in the form Theta(Phi_s X) = e^{(beta-2)
s} Theta(X), and the Liouville formula det D Phi_s = e^{2 beta s} of Section 2, so it imposes no independent condition
beyond (P). (iii) At every time the integrals of |theta(., t)|^p, 0 < p < infinity, and the kinetic energy are infinite
(Theorems 17(b), 23). Thus finite-integral temperature conservation constraints and a finite global kinetic-energy
balance are unavailable here; local balance laws still hold, and kinetic energy is not generally conserved in
Boussinesq. For the sign convention of Section 1, the conserved total energy is int (|u|^2/2 + z2 theta) dz when both
terms are integrable and the flux at infinity vanishes; those finiteness hypotheses fail here. (iv) The ansatz gives
omega(z, t) = tau^{-1} Omega(z/tau^beta) and grad_z theta(z, t) = tau^{-2} (grad Theta)(z/tau^beta). At beta = 2, Omega
and grad Theta are bounded (Theorem 33(a), together with smoothness on compact sets) and not identically zero (a0 != 0,
and Omega = 0 would give Theta_x = 0 by (V)), so sup_z |omega(z, t)| = tau^{-1} sup |Omega| and sup_z |grad_z
theta(z, t)| = tau^{-2} sup |grad Theta| are finite and positive for t < T and tend to infinity as t -> T. Such a
solution has bounded temperature that does not tend to zero at infinity (Theorem 6(b)) and, at each fixed t, max_{|z|=r}
|u(z, t)| has exact order r^{1/2} as r -> infinity: in polar components, r^{-1/2} (u_r(r, phi, t),
u_phi(r, phi, t)) -> (-P'(phi), (3/2) P(phi)) uniformly in phi as r -> infinity (Theorem 33(d)), with P not identically
zero by Theorem 34(b). No lower bound in every direction is asserted. In particular the kinetic energy is infinite at
every time. It would therefore not be a blow-up from bounded finite-energy data. For beta > 2 the temperature is
unbounded at every time. (v) Four claims are kept separate: an exact global profile in A2-broad for beta >= 2 (neither
constructed nor excluded here); approximate profiles (only rejected numerical trials in Section 6, with no accepted
approximation); nearly self-similar evolution (the dynamic rescaling runs of Section 6 did not converge and establish no
such evolution); and blow-up of a finite-energy solution from bounded smooth data (not established or excluded in
general; by (iv) an exact A2-broad profile alone would not give it).

## 3. Audited theorems and proofs

Each result below was derived or checked independently and then reviewed separately; repairs made during this review
are incorporated.
Standing convention. "A2 profile" means a solution of (P) with the A2 parities; the jet a0 != 0 and the class
conditions of Section 2 are assumed only where stated ("A2-broad profile" includes all of them). Each theorem lists
the hypotheses it uses; a theorem stated for an A2-broad profile with an additional condition uses no bound beyond the
class assumptions unless the condition says so.
Notation. Some symbols are local to the theorem in which they are defined and retain their local
meanings there. In particular, P denotes the first positive x-axis stagnation point (x_1, 0) whenever the point of
Theorem 2 is invoked (for instance in Theorems 2 to 24, 26, 27, 43, 47 and Remark 46.1), and in far-field formulas (for
instance in Theorems 25, 28, 32 to 42 and 45(f)) P(phi) denotes the angular stream-function coefficient; H1 in
Theorem 45(f) is a correction coefficient unrelated to the hypothesis (H1) of Theorem 8; E(y) is an axis trace in
Theorems 27, 30 and 31, E the escaping set and E^c its complement in Theorem 40, E(t) a component of the temperature
gradient along an orbit in Theorems 41 and 42, and E(R) an annular kinetic energy elsewhere; K is a kernel in Theorems 9 and
24, an axis trace in Theorems 30 and 31, and the outgoing distribution in Theorems 37, 38 and 40 (K0 = x y |X|^{-4} in
Theorem 39 is the kernel K of Theorem 9); B is a function in (39.12) and the kernel (z_2, -z_1)/(2 pi |z|^2) in
Theorems 38 and 41 (Lemma 38.2 uses its parity-grouped form), and Bn in Theorems 41 and 42 is a component of the temperature
gradient; (N) is a condition on an axis trace
in Theorem 31 and the natural far-field alternative in Theorems 32 to 37. The coefficient G of the natural tail and
the coefficient B of Theorem 28 have different radial normalizations.

### Theorem 1 (beta < 2 is empty)
Let 0 < beta < 2, U continuous with (G), and Theta in C^1 a solution of (T). Then Theta == 0. For every beta > 0, if
Theta == 0 and Omega in C^1 solves (V), then Omega == 0. No parity, jet or tail assumption is used.
Proof. Fix X0 and R0 = max(R, |X0|). Let Y solve Y' = -W(Y), Y(0) = X0 on a maximal interval [0, S). Where |Y| >= R,
d/ds |Y|^2 = -2 Y.W(Y) < 0. If |Y(s1)| > R0 for some s1, let s0 = sup{s < s1 : |Y(s)| <= R0}; on (s0, s1] we have
|Y| > R0 >= R, so |Y|^2 decreases strictly, contradicting |Y(s0)| = R0 < |Y(s1)|. So |Y| <= R0 and S = infinity. With
X(sig) = Y(-sig), h(sig) = Theta(X(sig)) satisfies h' = (beta - 2) h, so |Theta(X0)| = e^{(2-beta) sig} |h(sig)|
<= M e^{(2-beta) sig} for sig <= 0, M = max_{|X| <= R0} |Theta|; let sig -> -infinity. For Omega with Theta == 0,
k(sig) = Omega(X(sig)) satisfies k' = -k, so |Omega(X0)| <= M' e^{sig} -> 0. QED.

### Theorem 2 (first stagnation point on the positive x-axis)
Assume an A2 profile with beta > 0 and the jet of Section 1 (Theta(0, y) = 0, Theta = a0 x^2 y + O(|X|^5), a0 != 0,
so that c = Psi_xy(0) = 2 beta + 2), Theta in C^2, U in C^1, (G) and U(x,0)/x -> 0 as x -> infinity. Put
w(x) = W_1(x,0), f(x) = Theta_y(x,0), b = beta + 2. Then:
(a) w(x) = -(beta + 2) x + o(x) at 0 and w(x)/x -> beta at infinity, so x1 := inf{x > 0 : w(x) = 0} is in (0, infinity),
    w < 0 on (0, x1), and mu := w'(x1) >= 0.
(b) w f' = (w' - b) f on [0, infinity).
(c) f has the sign of a0 on (0, x1].
(d) mu = beta + 2 exactly, and DW(P) = diag(beta + 2, beta - 2) at P = (x1, 0); for beta > 2, P is a hyperbolic source.
Proof. (a) w = (beta - c) x + o(x) with c = 2 beta + 2. (b) Differentiate (T) in y at y = 0: d_y W_1 = 0 and Theta_x = 0
there (parities), W_2 = 0, and d_y W_2 = 2 beta - w' (div W = 2 beta); so w f' + (2 beta - w') f = (beta - 2) f.
(c) On (0, x1), w != 0 and (b) is a linear first-order ODE with continuous coefficients, so f vanishes nowhere or
everywhere there; f = a0 x^2 + o(x^2) at 0. (d) Let F = sgn(a0) f > 0 on (0, x1). From (b), (w/F)' = (w'F - wF')/F^2 = b/F
on (0, x1). Since w/F < 0, for x0 < x < x1: b int_{x0}^{x} ds/F = w(x)/F(x) - w(x0)/F(x0) <= -w(x0)/F(x0), so
int_{x0}^{x1} ds/F < infinity. If F(x1) = 0 then F(s) <= L (x1 - s) near x1 (F in C^1), and the integral diverges. So
F(x1) > 0, and (b) at x1 gives 0 = (mu - b) f(x1), i.e. mu = b. Off-diagonal entries of DW vanish on the x-axis by
parity and d_y W_2(P) = 2 beta - mu = beta - 2. QED.
Sharpness: with f only continuous the conclusion fails: for t = x1 - x, L = log(1/t), w = -b t (1 + 1/L), f = 1/L solve
(b) with w in C^1, w'(x1) = b, f(x1) = 0.

### Theorem 3 (beta = 2: a curve of stagnation points through P)
Under the hypotheses of Theorem 2 with beta = 2, Theta in C^2 and W in C^1: near P, grad Theta != 0, and W = lam J grad Theta
with J(p,q) = (-q,p) and lam in C^1; Z near P is a C^1 curve Gamma with tangent e_y at P, and Theta restricted to
Gamma has nonzero derivative f(x1) at P. Wherever grad Theta != 0, the Jacobian of (Theta, lam) equals 4 and
W.grad lam = 4 lam.
Proof. grad Theta(P) = (0, f(x1)) != 0. Since W.grad Theta = 0, W is parallel to J grad Theta; lam := W.J grad Theta/
|grad Theta|^2 is C^1 and W = lam J grad Theta, so W = 0 iff lam = 0. At P, lam = 0 and DW(P) = J grad Theta(P) (x) grad lam(P)
with J grad Theta(P) = (-f(x1), 0); comparing with DW(P) = diag(4, 0) gives d_x lam(P) = -4/f(x1) != 0 and d_y lam(P) = 0.
The implicit function theorem gives Gamma. div(lam J grad Theta) = grad lam . J grad Theta = 4 is the Jacobian statement.
QED.

### Theorem 4 (no bounded invariant regions; any beta > 0)
Assume U in C^1, div U = 0 (so div W = 2 beta > 0) and |U| <= C(1 + |X|). If K is compact with Phi_s(K) = K for all s, then R^2 \ K has no bounded
component. No nonempty bounded open set is forward invariant. Hence there are no periodic orbits, no homoclinic loops,
no heteroclinic cycles, and Z contains no Jordan curve. With the A2 reflection symmetry: no connected compact invariant
set C in the closed first quadrant with O not in C meets both open positive half-axes.
Proof. If V is a bounded component of R^2 \ K and X in V, then s -> Phi_s(X) is a path in R^2 \ K, so Phi_s(V) is in V;
applying this to Phi_{-s}, Phi_s(V) = V and |V| = e^{2 beta s}|V| with 0 < |V| < infinity: contradiction. A bounded
open forward invariant set D has e^{2 beta s}|D| = |Phi_s(D)| <= |D|. A periodic orbit, homoclinic loop or heteroclinic
cycle is a compact invariant Jordan curve, whose bounded complementary component is excluded. For the A2 statement,
let K be the union of the four reflections of C (compact, invariant by equivariance W(sigma X) = sigma W(X)). In polar
coordinates C lies in [eps, R] x [0, pi/2] (eps < dist(O, C), R > max |C|) and meets both sides phi = 0 and phi = pi/2;
by the crossing lemma for rectangles, every path in the closed quadrant from {r = eps} to {r = R} meets C. A path in
R^2 from O to infinity folds under (x,y) -> (|x|,|y|) to such a path, and meets K. So the component of O in R^2 \ K is
bounded: contradiction. QED.

### Theorem 5 (beta = 2: the temperature range is carried by the stagnation set)
Assume beta = 2, U in C^1 with div U = 0 and (G), Theta in C^1 solving (T). Then Theta(R^2) = Theta(Z), a compact
interval; Theta is bounded and attains its extrema on Z. Corollary (A2 profile with a0 != 0): Z is uncountable (otherwise Theta(R^2) is a point, Theta == 0 by
oddness in y, contradicting a0 != 0).
Proof. The backward orbit of X0 is bounded (proof of Theorem 1), so A = alpha(X0) is nonempty, compact, connected,
invariant, and Theta = Theta(X0) on A. If A contained no zero of W, by the Poincare-Bendixson theorem it would be a
periodic orbit. This is excluded without the growth hypothesis of Theorem 4: a periodic orbit is a C^1 Jordan curve
to which W is tangent, so the divergence theorem on its interior D gives 0 = int_D div W = 2 beta |D| > 0. So Theta(X0) = Theta(Q) for some Q in Z. Z is compact, so Theta(Z) is compact,
and Theta(R^2) is connected. QED.

### Theorem 6 (stagnation values; level sets)
Part (a) holds for classical solutions of (V) and (T). In (b) and (c) assume U in C^1, div U = 0,
|U(X)| <= C (1 + |X|) and Theta in C^1, and for the attained extrema in (b) also (G); every A2-broad profile satisfies
these hypotheses.
(a) If W(Q) = 0 then Omega(Q) = Theta_x(Q) (any beta), and Theta(Q) = 0 if beta != 2.
(b) beta = 2: every connected component of {Theta > c} and of {Theta < c} is unbounded, for every real c. Hence
    limsup_{|X| -> infinity} Theta = max Theta and liminf_{|X| -> infinity} Theta = min Theta.
(c) beta > 2: the same holds for {Theta > c}, c > 0, and for {Theta < c}, c < 0.
Proof. (a) Phi_s(Q) = Q, so Theta(Q) = e^{kappa s} Theta(Q) for all s; (V) at Q reads Omega(Q) = Theta_x(Q).
(b) Let D be a bounded component of the open set {Theta > c} and X0 in D. Theta o Phi_s = Theta, so Phi_s(D) is a
connected subset of {Theta > c} containing Phi_s(X0); the component containing Phi_s(X0) is locally constant in s,
hence equal to D for all s. Then Phi_s(D) = D and |D| = e^{4 s}|D|: contradiction. For c < max Theta (attained by
Theorem 5) the set {Theta > c} is nonempty with unbounded components. (c) For s >= 0, Phi_s({Theta > c}) =
{Theta > c e^{kappa s}}, contained in {Theta > c} for c > 0; as in (b), Phi_s(D) is in D for s >= 0, and
e^{2 beta s}|D| <= |D|: contradiction. QED.

### Theorem 7 (beta > 2: growth on orbits)
Let beta > 2, U in C^1 with |U| <= C(1 + |X|), Theta in C^1 solving (T). If Theta(X) != 0 then
|Theta(Phi_s X)| = e^{kappa s} |Theta(X)| -> infinity as s -> infinity; hence the forward orbit of X is unbounded and
Theta is unbounded on it. Theta = 0 on Z.
Proof. The flow is global, and Theta(Phi_s X) = e^{kappa s} Theta(X) with kappa > 0. A continuous function is bounded
on compact sets, so the orbit is unbounded. Theta = 0 on Z is Theorem 6(a). QED.

### Theorem 8 (beta > 2: the basin of P and the sign of Theta)
Hypothesis (H1): Z intersected with the closed first quadrant equals {O, P}. Assume an A2 profile with the jet of
Section 1 (a0 != 0), beta > 2, Theta in C^2, U in C^1, (G), U = o(|X|) on the axes, and (H1). Then:
(i) every X in the open quadrant Q1 has alpha-limit set {P};
(ii) Theta has the sign of a0 at every point of Q1;
(iii) on Q1, Theta = f(x1) eta_P, where eta_P is the unique C^2 solution near P of W.grad eta = kappa eta with
     eta(P) = 0, d_y eta(P) = 1, extended by eta(X) = e^{kappa s} eta(Phi_{-s} X). Given W, Theta on Q1 is determined by
     the single number f(x1) = Theta_y(P).
Proof. Under (H1), w < 0 on (0, x1) and w > 0 on (x1, infinity); g(y) := W_2(0,y) has no positive zero and
g'(0) = 3 beta + 2 > 0, so g > 0 on (0, infinity). Hence every point of the positive y-axis has alpha-limit O, the local
unstable manifold of the saddle O is the local y-axis, and W^u(O) is the y-axis.
(i) Q1 is invariant. The backward orbit of X is bounded, so A = alpha(X) is nonempty, compact, connected, invariant and
contained in the closed quadrant. P is a hyperbolic source (eigenvalues beta + 2, beta - 2 > 0), so it attracts all
backward orbits entering a neighbourhood N; if P is in A then A = {P}. Suppose P is not in A, so A intersected with Z
is contained in {O}. A regular point q of A on the positive x-axis has alpha(q) = {P}, contained in A: impossible. A
regular q on the positive y-axis has an unbounded forward orbit (g > 0 without zeros), not contained in the compact
invariant A: impossible. A regular q in A intersected with Q1 has alpha(q) contained in A, with O the only possible
equilibrium; by the Poincare-Bendixson theorem alpha(q) is {O}, a periodic orbit, or a homoclinic loop through O. The
last two are excluded by the divergence theorem as in the proof of Theorem 5 (a homoclinic loop at the hyperbolic
saddle O is a rectifiable, piecewise C^1 Jordan curve, since orbits on the stable and unstable manifolds converge
exponentially to O, and W is tangent to it), so the growth hypothesis of Theorem 4 is not needed; alpha(q) = {O} puts q in W^u(O), the y-axis: impossible.
So A has no regular point, A = {O}, and X is in W^u(O): contradiction with X in Q1. Hence A = {P}.
(ii) Theta(x,y) = y Ft(x,y) with Ft = int_0^1 Theta_y(x, tau y) dtau continuous, Ft(x,0) = f(x). By Theorem 2(c), Ft has
the sign of a0 near P. By (i), Phi_{-s} X -> P inside Q1, so Theta(Phi_{-s} X) has the sign of a0 for large s, and
Theta(X) = e^{kappa s} Theta(Phi_{-s} X).
(iii) Uniqueness: let h1, h2 be C^2 solutions near P with h(P) = 0 and equal d_y h(P). D = h1 - h2 satisfies
DW(P)^T grad D(P) = kappa grad D(P); since DW(P) = diag(kappa + 4, kappa) and d_y D(P) = 0, grad D(P) = 0, so
|D(Y)| <= C|Y - P|^2. In a small backward invariant ball, |Phi_{-s} Y - P| <= e^{-(kappa - eps) s}|Y - P|, and
D(Y) = e^{kappa s} D(Phi_{-s} Y) gives |D(Y)| <= C |Y - P|^2 e^{(-kappa + 2 eps) s} -> 0 for 0 < eps < kappa/2. Existence
and smoothness on Q1 follow from eta_P = Theta/f(x1). Theta(P) = 0 by Theorem 6(a) and d_y Theta(P) = f(x1) != 0. QED.
Remark. (H1) is a hypothesis, not proved. For an existing profile, (iii) and (V) give the necessary reconstruction
identities Theta = f(x1) eta_P[W] and Omega(X) = int_0^inf e^{-s} Theta_x(Phi_{-s} X) ds on Q1 (backward orbits are
bounded). This is not a fixed-point formulation: that would additionally need a function space on which the
temperature reconstruction, the extension across the axes and the canonical inverse are all defined, and none is
constructed here.

### Theorem 9 (origin strain identity in the broad class)
Let Psi be smooth, odd in x and in y, Omega = -Lap Psi, U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x) with U(X) = o(|X|) uniformly. Then
Psi_R(X) := -(1/(2 pi)) int_{|Y|<R} log|X - Y| Omega(Y) dY -> Psi in C^k on compact sets, for every k, and with
K(Y) = Y1 Y2 / |Y|^4,
  c = Psi_xy(0) = (1/pi) lim_{R -> infinity} int_{|Y|<R} K(Y) Omega(Y) dY,
  c - (1/pi) int_{|Y|<R} K Omega dY = (1/pi) oint_{|Y|=R} (K d_r Psi - Psi d_r K) dS.
For an A2 profile with the jet of Section 1 (a0 != 0), c = 2 beta + 2. The integral need not converge absolutely: Psi = chi(r) sin(r) sin(2 phi), with chi a
smooth cutoff (0 for r <= 1, 1 for r >= 2), has bounded velocity and int_{|Y|>2} |K Omega| dY = infinity.
Proof. grad Psi = o(r) and Psi(0) = 0 give Psi = o(r^2) uniformly. Green's identity on the disc gives Psi = Psi_R + B_R
with B_R(X) = oint_{|Y|=R} [Gamma(X,Y) d_r Psi - Psi d_r Gamma(X,Y)] dS, Gamma = -(1/(2 pi)) log|X - Y|. For |X| <= M and
R > 2M, Gamma = -(log R)/(2 pi) + (X.omega)/(2 pi R) + Q with |Q| <= C R^{-2}, |d_r Q| <= C R^{-3} (and the same for X
derivatives). The boundary integrals of Psi and d_r Psi against 1, omega_1, omega_2 vanish by oddness, so constant and
linear terms cancel, and the rest is bounded by C (R^{-2} eps_R R + R^{-3} eps_R R^2) R = O(eps_R), where
eps_R = sup_{|Y| = R} (|Psi|/R^2 + |grad Psi|/R) -> 0. At X = 0, d_x d_y Gamma(0,Y) = K(Y)/pi, locally integrable
against Omega = O(|Y|^2); the boundary term is O(R) o(R) R^{-2} + o(R^2) R^{-3} R = o(1). QED.

### Theorem 10 (restricted: single angular mode)
Let Psi = x y h(x^2 + y^2) with h in C^3 near 0 (h smooth elsewhere is not needed), and suppose (P) holds near the origin
with the A2 parity and jet, beta >= 2. This is impossible. Combined with Theorem 1, no profile of A2-broad has a
stream function of the form x y h(x^2 + y^2).
Proof. Write q = x^2 + y^2 and h = c + d q + e q^2 + o(q^2). Since x y is a harmonic quadratic,
Lap(x y h(q)) = x y (4 q h'' + 12 h'), so Omega = -12 d x y + O(|X|^4). The A2 jet requires Omega = b0 x y + ... with
(2 beta + 1) b0 = 2 a0 != 0 (the x y coefficient of (V)), hence d != 0. Equation (V) gives Theta_x; integrating from
x = 0, where Theta(0, y) = 0 by the A2 jet, determines Theta near 0 up to degree 5 from c, d, e (the o(q^2) part of h
enters Theta only at degree 7). Insert into R_Theta := W.grad Theta - (beta - 2) Theta and take Taylor coefficients.
The x^2 y coefficient is 6 d (2 beta + 1)(c - 2 beta - 2), giving c = 2 beta + 2. With this value the x^4 y and x^2 y^3
coefficients are 6 [3 d^2 - 8 (beta + 2) e] and 2 [(66 beta + 39) d^2 - 16 (3 beta + 2)(8 beta + 5) e]. The
first gives e = 3 d^2/(8 (beta + 2)); the second then reads -6 d^2 (26 beta^2 + 5 beta - 6)/(beta + 2) = 0. The
quadratic 26 beta^2 + 5 beta - 6 has roots (-5 +- sqrt(649))/52, approximately 0.3938 and -0.5861, and is positive
for beta >= 2. So d = 0, a contradiction. QED.
Remark. The computation is local; the growth condition U = o(|X|) is used only through Theorem 1 to remove beta < 2 (at
beta = (-5 + sqrt(649))/52, approximately 0.3938, the fifth-order conditions are compatible, so the local computation
alone does not exclude that value).

### Theorem 11 (beta = 2: flat points on the stagnation set; no analytic temperature)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta = 2. Every connected component C of Z with more than one
point contains a point Q at which Theta - Theta(Q) and Omega vanish to infinite order. The component through P has
more than one point. Corollary: no A2-broad profile with beta = 2 has a real-analytic temperature.
Proof. (i) Regular points. If grad Theta(Q) != 0, then near Q, W = lam J grad Theta with lam smooth (the local calculation in the proof of
Theorem 3, which applies at every regular point), and
div W = grad lam . J grad Theta = 4, so grad lam != 0 and Z = {lam = 0} is locally a smooth arc. Parametrizing it by
gamma' = J grad lam gives d/dt Theta(gamma(t)) = grad Theta . J grad lam = -4: Theta is strictly monotone along the arc.
(ii) Degenerate points. Let Q be in C with grad Theta(Q) = 0. By (V) and Theorem 6(a), Omega(Q) = Theta_x(Q) = 0. A
component with more than one point has no isolated points, so by the inverse function theorem DW(Q) is singular. The
antisymmetric part of DW(Q) is proportional to Omega(Q) = 0, so DW(Q) is symmetric with trace 4 and determinant 0:
eigenvalues 4 and 0. In orthonormal eigencoordinates (u, v) centred at Q (d_u W_u(Q) = 4), the implicit function
theorem gives {W_u = 0} = {u = k(v)} near Q, k smooth, k(0) = k'(0) = 0, and Z is contained in this graph. With
g(v) := W_v(k(v), v), equation (T) on the graph reads g(v) (d_v Theta)(k(v), v) = 0, where d_v is the partial derivative.
Suppose Theta - Theta(Q) is not flat at Q, with first nonzero homogeneous Taylor term P_m (m >= 2). The degree-m part
