of (T) is 4 u d_u P_m = 0, so P_m = C v^m with C != 0, and (d_v Theta)(k(v), v) = m C v^{m-1} + o(|v|^{m-1}) != 0 for
small v != 0. Hence g = 0 near 0 and Z is locally exactly the graph, a smooth arc through Q.
(iii) If no point of C is flat, (i) and (ii) give charts showing that C (closed, hence compact, since Z is compact) is a
compact connected embedded 1-manifold without boundary, i.e. a Jordan curve contained in Z, excluded by Theorem 4.
So some Q in C has Theta - Theta(Q) flat. Then grad Theta(Q) = 0, the eigenvalue argument of (ii) applies, and
Theta_x is flat at Q. If Omega were not flat, its first nonzero homogeneous term R_m would satisfy, by (V),
(4 u d_u + 1) R_m = 0; the multiplier on u^a v^b is 4a + 1 > 0, so R_m = 0: contradiction.
The component through P has more than one point by Theorem 3. If Theta were real analytic, Theta - Theta(Q) would
vanish near Q and hence everywhere, contradicting a0 != 0. QED.
Remark. The local step (ii) is close to a known result on smooth first integrals near curves of equilibria with spectrum
(0, lambda) (X. Zhang, A note on local integrability of differential systems, 2017, Theorem 2).

### Theorem 12 (beta = 2: an interior stagnation point with zero vorticity)
Every A2-broad profile with beta = 2 has a point Q in the open first quadrant with W(Q) = 0, grad Theta(Q) = 0,
Omega(Q) = 0 and Theta(Q) != 0. In particular Omega > 0 on the open first quadrant (or Omega < 0 there) is impossible,
and so is the condition "Omega != 0 wherever Theta != 0". (Omega >= 0 alone is not excluded.)
Proof. Let C be the component of Z through P. By Theorem 3, Theta restricted to C has nonzero derivative at P, so Theta
takes nonzero values on C. C is compact, so |Theta| attains a positive maximum on C at some Q0. Theta = 0 on the x-axis
(oddness in y) and on the y-axis (the class condition Theta(0, y) = 0 for all y; evenness in x alone would not give
this), so Q0 is off the axes. If grad Theta(Q0) != 0, step (i) of the proof of Theorem 11 gives a regular arc of Z through Q0, contained in C,
along which Theta is strictly monotone; since Theta(Q0) != 0, |Theta| is then not maximal at Q0: contradiction. Hence
grad Theta(Q0) = 0 and Omega(Q0) = Theta_x(Q0) = 0. The reflections (x, y) -> (+-x, +-y) preserve Z, the vanishing of
grad Theta and Omega, and the nonvanishing of Theta, so a reflection of Q0 lies in the open first quadrant. QED.

### Theorem 13 (beta > 2: the sign of Theta and the hypothesis (H1))
Let beta > 2 and let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile. Then Theta != 0 everywhere on the open first
quadrant Q1 if and only if (H1) holds. (The direction "(H1) implies Theta has the sign of a0 on Q1" is Theorem 8.)
Proof of the remaining direction. By Theorem 6(a), Theta = 0 on Z, so an interior zero of W in Q1 already contradicts
Theta != 0 on Q1. Suppose W has a zero on the positive x-axis after x1. Since w'(x1) = beta + 2 > 0 and Z is closed,
there is a first such zero R = (L2, 0), with w > 0 on (x1, L2), so mu := w'(L2) <= 0. By parity and div W = 2 beta,
DW(R) = diag(mu, lam) with lam = 2 beta - mu > kappa = beta - 2. In coordinates (xi, eta) = (x - L2, y),
W = (mu xi + F, lam eta + G) with F, G = O(|(xi, eta)|^2) and G = eta g (the x-axis is invariant). Fix a with
max(kappa, lam/2) < a < lam and, for small h > 0, consider on continuous paths with the norm ||Y||_a = sup_{s >= 0} e^{as}|Y(s)|
the map
  xi(s) = int_s^inf e^{mu (t - s)} F(Y(t)) dt,   eta(s) = h e^{-lam s} - int_0^s e^{-lam (s - t)} G(Y(t)) dt.
Since e^{as} int_s^inf e^{mu(t-s)} e^{-2at} dt = e^{-as}/(2a - mu) and e^{as} int_0^s e^{-lam(s-t)} e^{-2at} dt <= 1/(lam - a),
with D = 1/(2a - mu) + 1/(lam - a) the map sends {||Y||_a <= r} into itself and is a contraction there, for r = 2h small
(bounds h + C r^2 D and C r D). Nothing degenerates when mu = 0. The fixed point solves Y' = -W(Y), so X(s) = R + Y(s)
is a backward orbit, with eta(s) = h exp(-lam s - int_0^s g) > 0 and |Y(s)| <= r e^{-as}. Then X(0) = (L2 + xi(0), h)
lies in Q1 for r < L2, and, since Theta(R) = 0 and Theta is C^1,
|Theta(X(0))| = e^{kappa s} |Theta(X(s))| <= C r e^{-(a - kappa) s} -> 0. So Theta(X(0)) = 0 with X(0) in Q1:
contradiction. A first zero (0, L3) on the positive y-axis is treated identically with the roles of the coordinates
exchanged (v(y) := W_2(0, y), v'(0) = 3 beta + 2 > 0, nu = v'(L3) <= 0, transverse eigenvalue 2 beta - nu > kappa).
So Z meets the closed first quadrant only in O and P. QED.

### Theorem 14 (vorticity trace on the x-axis)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile (beta >= 2 by Theorem 1). Put a = beta + 2,
r = (3 beta + 3)/(beta + 2) in [9/4, 3), and g(x) := Omega_y(x, 0). Then g is the unique solution bounded at x1 of
  w g' + (2 beta + 1 - w') g = f'  on (0, x1),
and near 0, g = b0 x + K' x^r + O(x^3), where K' is an explicit finite-part functional of the axis data w on [0, x1]
and the number f(x1). If K' != 0, then g is not C^3 at 0 and Omega is not C^4. K' = 0 occurs for smooth axis data.
Proof. Differentiate (V) in y at y = 0: d_y W_1 = 0 and Omega = 0 on the axis, W_2 = 0, d_y W_2 = 2 beta - w', which
gives the equation. Put s = -w > 0 on (0, x1) and Phi' = 1/s, normalized so that e^Phi ~ x^{1/a} at 0. Then
f = C s e^{a Phi} (Theorem 2), the homogeneous solution is h := s e^{(2 beta + 1) Phi}, and (g/h)' = -I with
I = C (a - w') e^{(1 - beta) Phi}/w^2. At 0, h = a x^r (1 + O(x^2)) and I ~ (2C/a) x^{-r}; at x1, with delta = x1 - x,
h ~ delta^{(1 - beta)/a}, unbounded for beta >= 2, and I = O(delta^{-3/a}) is integrable because a - w' = O(delta). So
the solution bounded at x1 is unique and equals g = h int_x^{x1} I. Writing I = x^{-r} J(x^2) and subtracting the
leading singular part before integrating gives g = G(x) + K' x^r H_0(x^2) with G smooth and odd, H_0 smooth, H_0(0) = 1,
no logarithm (r is not an odd integer), and
  K' = a lim_{eps -> 0} [ int_eps^{x1} I dt - (2C/(a (r - 1))) eps^{1 - r} ].
g is odd in x; if g were C^3 at 0, then g = g'(0) x + O(x^3), forcing K' = 0 since r < 3. Omega in C^4 gives g in C^3.
For w = -(beta + 2) sin x cos x on [0, pi/2] one has f = A sin^2 x and g = A sin(2x)/(2 beta + 1) exactly, so K' = 0. QED.
Remark. This is a compatibility condition on axis data, not an obstruction: the axis data w, f, g are coupled through the
full equations, and the exact local family of Section 4 satisfies all such conditions. Omega in C^3 alone gives only
g in C^2, which the trace does not contradict.

### Theorem 15 (restricted: vorticity decaying faster than |X|^{-2/beta})
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) satisfy the conditions of A2-broad, and suppose
  sup_{|X| >= R} |X|^{2/beta} |Omega(X)| -> 0  as R -> infinity.
Then Theta = Omega = U = 0; in particular there is no A2-broad profile with this decay. No bound on derivatives of
Omega is assumed. This excludes compactly supported vorticity, Schwartz vorticity and |Omega| <= C(1+|X|)^{-gamma} with
gamma > 2/beta. It does not exclude the borderline rate |X|^{-2/beta} or the rate |X|^{-1/beta} of the formal far field
(Section 7).
Proof. (a) Velocity rate. Put eta = min(2/beta, 1), so |Omega| <= C(1 + |X|)^{-eta}. Write U at |X| = r as the parity-
grouped Biot-Savart integral and split the sources into |Y| < r/2, r/2 <= |Y| <= 2r and |Y| > 2r. On centred discs the
mass and first moments of Omega vanish by parity, so in the inner part the kernel may be replaced by its second-order
Taylor remainder, of size C|Y|^2 r^{-3}, giving C r^{-3} int_0^{r/2} rho^3 (1 + rho)^{-eta} d rho = O(r^{1-eta}). In the
middle part the kernel singularity |X - Y|^{-1} is integrable and the source is O(r^{-eta}), giving O(r^{1-eta}). In the
outer part the grouped kernel vanishes at X = 0 and has X-derivative O(|Y|^{-2}), giving C r int_{2r}^infinity
rho^{-1-eta} d rho = O(r^{1-eta}). The integral is a divergence-free field with the required curl and growth o(|X|), so
it equals U by the uniqueness of Section 2. Hence U = O(|X|^{1-eta}).
(b) Angular limit. Suppose Theta is not identically zero. Choose R0 with W_r >= beta r/2 for r >= R0 and with the disc
{|X| < R0} containing a nonempty open set E on which Theta != 0. For alpha in [0, pi/2] the orbit of W from
R0 (cos alpha, sin alpha) meets each circle |X| = r >= R0 once, after time tau(r, alpha), at angle F_r(alpha); since
both axes are invariant and orbits do not cross, F_r is an increasing diffeomorphism of [0, pi/2] fixing 0 and pi/2.
With d := tau - beta^{-1} log(r/R0),
  d_r F_r = U_phi/(r W_r),  d_r d = -U_r/(beta r W_r),
both O(r^{-1-eta}) uniformly by (a), so F_r -> F_inf and d -> d_inf uniformly. Differentiating the crossing point in
alpha and taking the determinant with W (the hitting-time term is parallel to W and drops out, and the flow multiplies
areas by e^{2 beta tau}) gives the exact identity
  F_r'(alpha) = R0 W_r(R0, alpha) e^{2 beta tau(r, alpha)} / ( r W_r(r, F_r(alpha)) ).
Since e^{2 beta tau} = (r/R0)^2 e^{2 beta d} with d bounded, F_r' is bounded above and below uniformly in r, F_inf is
bi-Lipschitz, and the inverse maps converge uniformly. By (T), Theta(r, F_r(alpha)) = (r/R0)^q e^{kappa d(r, alpha)}
theta0(alpha) with q = kappa/beta = 1 - 2/beta and theta0(alpha) = Theta(R0 cos alpha, R0 sin alpha). Hence
r^{-q} Theta(r, phi) -> H(phi) uniformly on [0, pi/2], where H = R0^{-q} (e^{kappa d_inf} theta0) o F_inf^{-1} is
continuous and vanishes at phi = 0 and phi = pi/2 (Theta is odd in y and Theta(0, y) = 0). H is not identically zero:
otherwise theta0 = 0, no forward orbit from E could cross the circle, and Phi_s(E) would stay in the disc while its area
e^{2 beta s}|E| grows without bound.
(c) Weak form of (V). Put Theta_R(Z) = R^{-q} Theta(RZ), Omega_R(Z) = Omega(RZ), W_R(Z) = R^{-1} W(RZ) = beta Z +
R^{-1} U(RZ). By (b) and parity, Theta_R -> T(Z) := |Z|^q H(arg Z) locally uniformly on R^2 \ {0}. Rescaling (V) and
using div W_R = 2 beta,
  d_1 Theta_R = R^{2/beta} [ div(W_R Omega_R) + (1 - 2 beta) Omega_R ].
For a test function phi supported in a compact subset of R^2 \ {0}, |<d_1 Theta_R, phi>| <= C_phi R^{2/beta}
sup_{supp phi} |Omega(R .)| -> 0, the derivatives having been moved onto phi. Hence d_1 T = 0 in distributions away
from 0. T is continuous, so it is constant on every horizontal segment in the open first quadrant, and letting x -> 0+ gives
T(x, y) = T(0, y) = y^q H(pi/2) = 0 there. Thus H = 0: contradiction. So Theta = 0; then Omega = 0 by the second part of
Theorem 1, and U = 0 by uniqueness, contradicting a0 != 0. QED.
Remark. For beta >= 2 Theorem 15 also follows from Theorems 24 and 19 (and is contained in Theorem 23).
Remark. For compactly supported vorticity there is also a direct proof: U = O(|X|^{-3}), Theta_x = 0 outside the
support, the trace C(y) = lim_{x -> infinity} Theta(x, y) solves beta y C' = kappa C and is smooth and odd, so C = 0,
Theta has compact support, and Theorem 17(b) applies.

### Theorem 16 (beta = 2: the stagnation component through P is an arc)
Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile and C the connected component of Z containing P. Then C is a smooth
embedded arc. The reflection R_y(x, y) = (x, -y) reverses C, C meets the x-axis only at P and does not meet the y-axis,
and the endpoints are Q+ in the open first quadrant and Q- = R_y(Q+). At each endpoint Q, grad Theta(Q) = 0, DW(Q) has
eigenvalues 4 and 0, and Theta - Theta(Q) and Omega vanish to infinite order. Omega does not vanish identically, and
Theta is not constant, on any neighbourhood of an endpoint.
Proof. (a) Local structure. Let Q in Z be non-isolated in Z. If grad Theta(Q) != 0, Z is a smooth arc near Q (step
(i) of the proof of Theorem 11). If grad Theta(Q) = 0, DW(Q) has eigenvalues 4 and 0 and Z near Q lies in the smooth
graph {u = k(v)} (step (ii) of the proof of Theorem 11). In both cases there is a closed disc N centred at Q and a smooth arc A, crossing N once with its two ends on dN,
such that Z n N lies in A.
(b) C is an arc. C has more than one point (Theorem 3). For Q in C take N and A as in (a) with C not contained in N.
Every component of the proper closed subset C n N of the continuum C meets the boundary of C n N relative to C, which
is contained in C n dN (the boundary bumping theorem for closed subsets of a continuum). Each component is a closed subinterval of A n N containing one of its two
ends, so there are at most two; if there are two, the one not containing Q has positive distance from Q, and shrinking
N removes it. Hence near Q, C is an interval of A containing Q in its interior or as an end. So C is a compact connected
1-manifold with boundary and with more than one point: an arc or a Jordan curve. A Jordan curve in Z is excluded by
Theorem 4. C is smooth and embedded because it lies locally in smooth arcs.
(c) Endpoints. At an endpoint Q, grad Theta(Q) = 0, otherwise (a) makes Q interior. If Theta - Theta(Q) were not flat at
Q, step (ii) of the proof of Theorem 11 would make Z near Q the whole graph {u = k(v)}, again making Q interior. Flatness of Omega follows as
at the end of step (iii) of the proof of Theorem 11: a first nonzero homogeneous term R_m of Omega would satisfy (4 u d_u + 1) R_m = 0.
(d) Symmetry. W(R_y X) = R_y W(X), so R_y maps Z onto Z; it fixes P, hence maps C onto C. An involutive homeomorphism
of an arc is either the identity or reverses the arc and has exactly one fixed point. The identity would put C in the
x-axis, contradicting the tangent e_y of C at P (Theorem 3). So R_y reverses C, P is its only fixed point on C, so C
meets the x-axis only at P, and R_y exchanges the endpoints. If C met the y-axis at Y, then R_x(Y) = Y, so R_x(C) = C
(R_x(x, y) = (-x, y)) and (-x1, 0) = R_x(P) would be a second point of C on the x-axis. So C lies in {x > 0}, and its
endpoints are Q+ with y > 0 and Q- = R_y(Q+).
(e) Let Q be an endpoint and N a disc centred at Q. If Omega = 0 on N, then W is curl-free with div W = 4 on N, so
W = grad phi with phi - |X|^2 harmonic and phi real analytic. In eigencoordinates (u, v) at Q, phi_uu(Q) = 4, so the
analytic implicit function theorem gives {phi_u = 0} = {u = k(v)} with k analytic, and the analytic function
g(v) = phi_v(k(v), v) vanishes on the interval of v corresponding to C near Q; hence g = 0 near v = 0, the whole graph
lies in Z, hence in C, and Q is interior to C: contradiction. If Theta = M on N, then for X in N and s >= 0, Theta = M
on the open set Phi_{-s}(N) containing Phi_{-s}(X), so Theta_x(Phi_{-s}X) = 0, and (V) gives Omega(Phi_{-s}X) = e^s
Omega(X). The backward orbit is bounded (Theorem 1) and Omega is continuous, so Omega(X) = 0. Thus Omega = 0 on N,
which was just excluded. QED.
Remark. Whether such an endpoint is realized by an A2-broad profile remains open. Near an endpoint Q, a centre manifold
of Q contains Z; on its side opposite to C the centre branch may be outgoing, incoming, or have zeros of W accumulating
at Q. Theorem 35 shows that in the outgoing case Theta = Theta(Q) and Omega = 0 on an open invariant set of infinite
area. (Later results: Theorems 44(b) and 48(a), (b) give single orbit limits and exclude return to the same arc of
zeros; Theorem 53(d) makes Q+ outgoing whenever no component of the zero set of W lies wholly in the open quadrant, in
particular under (S) of Theorem 48, including when Theta(Q+) = 0. No result in this report excludes the incoming or
accumulating configurations for an unrestricted A2-broad profile.)

### Theorem 17 (restricted: analytic velocity at beta = 2; integrable temperature)
(a) There is no A2-broad profile with beta = 2 and W real analytic.
(b) There is no A2-broad profile with Theta in L^p(R^2) for some finite p > 0.
Proof. (a) By Theorem 11 there is a point at which Omega = d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 vanishes to infinite order. Omega is real
analytic, so Omega = 0 on R^2. Then U is divergence-free, curl-free and o(|X|), hence constant, and U = 0 by parity. So
c = Psi_xy(0) = 0, contradicting c = 2 beta + 2 = 6. (b) beta >= 2 by Theorem 1. W has at most linear growth, so its flow
Phi_s is a global diffeomorphism with Jacobian e^{2 beta s}, and Theta o Phi_s = e^{kappa s} Theta. Changing variables,
  e^{(p kappa + 2 beta) s} int |Theta|^p = int |Theta o Phi_s|^p e^{2 beta s} = int |Theta|^p,
and p kappa + 2 beta > 0, so Theta = 0, contradicting a0 != 0. QED.

### Theorem 18 (restricted: finite kinetic energy at beta = 2)
There is no A2-broad profile with beta = 2 and U in L^2(R^2). No decay rate for U and no bound on Omega beyond the
class assumptions is used.
Proof. Choose R0 so large that W_r >= r for r >= R0 and that the disc |X| < R0 contains an open set on which Theta != 0
(if Theta == 0 there is nothing to prove). Let a = pi/2. The orbit of R0(cos alpha, sin alpha), alpha in [0, a], meets
each circle r >= R0 once, at time tau(r, alpha) and angle F_r(alpha); F_r is an increasing diffeomorphism of [0, a]
fixing the endpoints (the axes are invariant). With d = tau - (1/2) log(r/R0) and G_r = F_r^{-1},
  d_r F_r = U_phi/(r W_r),   d_r d = -U_r/(2 r W_r),   J_r := F_r' = R0 W_r(R0, alpha) e^{4 tau}/(r W_r(r, F_r)),
the last identity because det(W, d_alpha X) is multiplied by e^{4 tau} along the flow while the hitting-time
derivative is parallel to W. Since U = o(r) uniformly, J_r + J_r^{-1} <= C_eps r^eps for every eps > 0. Changing
variables phi = F_r(alpha),
  int_0^a (|d_r F_r| + |d_r d|) d alpha <= C r^{-2+eps} int_0^a |U(r, phi)| dphi,
and int_{R0}^inf r^{-2+eps} int_0^a |U| dphi dr <= C ||U||_2 (a int_{R0}^inf r^{-5+2 eps} dr)^{1/2} < infinity for eps < 2.
By Tonelli, F_r(alpha) and d(r, alpha) converge for a.e. alpha, and J_r -> j = (W_r(R0, alpha)/(2 R0)) e^{4 d_inf} > 0
a.e. Fatou's lemma gives lim (F_r(t) - F_r(s)) >= int_s^t j > 0 for s < t in the convergence set, so no interval of
initial angles collapses. From this, the G_r are equicontinuous for large r, and any two subsequential uniform limits
coincide; hence G_r -> G uniformly, G continuous, nondecreasing and onto. Since Theta is invariant at beta = 2,
Theta(r cos phi, r sin phi) = theta_0(G_r(phi)) with theta_0 = Theta on the circle r = R0, so Theta(R Z) -> H(arg Z) with
H = theta_0 o G locally uniformly on R^2 \ {0}; H is continuous, vanishes on both axes, and is not identically zero
(if theta_0 == 0, forward images of an open set E in the disc with Theta != 0 cannot cross the circle, yet have area
e^{4s}|E|). Put V_R(Z) = R^{-1} U(RZ), w_R(Z) = Omega(RZ) = -curl V_R. Then
  d_1 [Theta(R .)] = R [ 2 Z.grad w_R + w_R + V_R.grad w_R ],
and testing against psi in C_c^inf(R^2 \ {0}), using V.grad(-curl V) = -curl div(V (x) V) for div V = 0 and
||V_R||_2 = R^{-2} ||U||_2, gives |<d_1 Theta(R .), psi>| <= C_psi (R^{-1} ||U||_2 + R^{-3} ||U||_2^2) -> 0. So the
continuous limit T(Z) = H(arg Z) satisfies d_1 T = 0, is constant on horizontal segments of the open first quadrant,
and vanishes at their y-axis endpoints: H = 0 on the first quadrant, hence everywhere by parity, a contradiction. QED.

### Theorem 19 (restricted: velocity growth below |X|^{1-2/beta})
Let beta >= 2 and q = 1 - 2/beta. There is no A2-broad profile with sup_{|X| >= R} |U(X)| |X|^{-q} -> 0 as R -> infinity.
For beta = 2 this excludes U -> 0 uniformly at infinity; for beta > 2 it excludes every bounded U.
Proof. With R0, F_r, tau, G_r as in the proof of Theorem 18 and d = tau - beta^{-1} log(r/R0),
  d_r F_r = U_phi/(r W_r),   d_r d = -U_r/(beta r W_r),
and both are O(r^{q-2}) uniformly in alpha, which is integrable since q < 1. So F_r and d converge uniformly, d is
bounded, and J_r = (r/R0) W_r(R0, alpha) e^{2 beta d}/W_r(r, F_r) has uniform positive upper and lower bounds. The limit
F is a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism of [0, pi/2] and G_r -> G = F^{-1} uniformly. Transport gives
Theta(Phi_tau X0) = e^{kappa tau} Theta(X0) and e^{kappa tau} = (r/R0)^q e^{kappa d}, so
  r^{-q} Theta(r cos phi, r sin phi) -> H(phi) := R0^{-q} theta_0(G(phi)) e^{kappa d_inf(G(phi))}
uniformly. H is continuous, vanishes at phi = pi/2 (Theta(0, y) = 0), and is not identically zero (as in Theorem 18).
Hence T_R(Z) := R^{-q} Theta(RZ) -> T(Z) := |Z|^q H(arg Z) locally uniformly on R^2 \ {0}. With V_R(Z) = R^{-1} U(RZ) and
w_R(Z) = Omega(RZ) = -curl V_R,
  d_1 T_R = R^{2/beta} [ (beta Z + V_R).grad w_R + w_R ],
and testing as in Theorem 18 gives |<d_1 T_R, psi>| <= C_psi R^{2/beta} (s_R + s_R^2) with s_R = sup_K |V_R| = o(R^{q-1})
= o(R^{-2/beta}), K the support of psi. So d_1 T = 0. T is continuous, so it is constant on horizontal segments of the
open first quadrant and vanishes at their y-axis endpoints. Hence H = 0, a contradiction. QED.

### Theorem 20 (restricted: integrable velocity at beta = 2)
There is no A2-broad profile with beta = 2 and E_p := int |U|^p dX < infinity for some real p with 0 < p < infinity.
Proof. The proof of Theorem 18 applies with two changes.
(i) Taking eps = 1/2 in J_r^{-1} <= C r^eps gives int_0^a (|d_r F_r| + |d_r d|) d alpha <= C r^{-3/2} int_0^a |U(r, phi)| dphi.
So it suffices that int_{|X| >= R0} |U| |X|^{-5/2} dX < infinity. This holds by Holder for p > 1, since r^{-5p'/2} is
integrable on {r >= R0} when 5p'/2 > 2. It holds directly for p = 1. For p < 1 it follows from |U| <= C r, which gives
|U| r^{-5/2} <= C |U|^p r^{-3/2-p}.
(ii) In the weak form of (V) the linear term is bounded by C_psi R int_K |V_R| and the quadratic term by
C_psi R int_K |V_R|^2. Here int_K |V_R|^p <= R^{-p-2} E_p and s_R = sup_K |V_R| -> 0. The linear term is at most
C R^{-2/p} E_p^{1/p} (p >= 1) or s_R^{1-p} R^{-p-1} E_p (p < 1). The quadratic term is at most C R^{-1-4/p} E_p^{2/p}
(p >= 2) or s_R^{2-p} R^{-p-1} E_p (p < 2). All tend to 0, and the rest of the proof is unchanged. QED.

### Theorem 21 (sign-definite vorticity)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta >= 2 (the proof uses the strain identity of Theorem 9 in
this class). Let w, f, g be the axis traces of Theorems 2 and 14: w = W_1(x, 0), f = Theta_y(x, 0), g = Omega_y(x, 0).
(a) Omega <= 0 on the open first quadrant Q1 is impossible. If a0 < 0, Omega takes both signs in Q1.
(b) If a0 > 0 and g(x) >= 0 for all x > 0, then P is the only zero of W on the positive x-axis.
(c) Omega > 0 on Q1 is impossible for beta = 2. For beta > 2 it implies Z = {O, P, -P}: (H1) holds, and Theta > 0 on Q1.
Proof. (a) By Theorem 9, c = (4/pi) lim_R int_{Q1 cap B_R} Y_1 Y_2 |Y|^{-4} Omega(Y) dY. If Omega <= 0, every truncated
integral is <= 0, while c = 2 beta + 2 > 0. If a0 < 0, then b0 = 2 a0/(2 beta + 1) < 0, so Omega = x y (b0 + O(|X|^2)) is
negative near O in Q1; by the first part it is also positive somewhere in Q1.
(b) Put k = beta + 2 and D = 2 beta + 1. Then w f' = (w' - k) f and w g' + (D - w') g = f'. By Theorem 2, w < 0 on (0, x1),
w'(x1) = k and f > 0 on (0, x1]. Suppose W has a further zero on the axis, and let L2 be the first one after x1. Then
w > 0 on (x1, L2) and w'(L2) <= 0. Also f > 0 on (x1, L2), since the f-equation is regular there. The function h = g/f >= 0
satisfies w h' + (beta - 1) h = (w' - k)/w. Near L2, w' - k <= -k/2, so h' <= -k/(2 w^2). Since w <= C (L2 - x), the
integral of w^{-2} diverges, and h becomes negative before L2, a contradiction. A degenerate zero is included.
(c) At beta = 2 this is Theorem 12. Let beta > 2. Omega > 0 on Q1 gives g >= 0 and b0 > 0, hence a0 > 0. By (b) and
parity, the zeros of W on the x-axis are O and +-P. On the y-axis, W_2(0, y) = beta y + Psi_x(0, y). Differentiating
the disc-truncated potentials of Theorem 9 at (0, y) gives
  Psi_x(0, y) = lim_R int_{Q1 cap B_R} (4 y Y_1 Y_2/pi) Omega(Y) dY / ((Y_1^2 + (y - Y_2)^2)(Y_1^2 + (y + Y_2)^2)) > 0
for y > 0, so the y-axis contains no zero other than O. At a zero Q off the axes, Theta(Q) = 0 (Theorem 7), so
Theta_x(Q) = Omega(Q) != 0. Differentiating (T) gives DW(Q)^T grad Theta(Q) = (beta - 2) grad Theta(Q). Since
tr DW = 2 beta, the eigenvalues of DW(Q) are beta - 2 > 0 and beta + 2, so Q is a source of index +1. Every zero is
therefore isolated, and Z is compact, hence finite. On a large circle X.W > 0, so the index sum is 1. O contributes -1
and +-P (eigenvalues beta + 2, beta - 2) contribute +1 each, so there is no further zero. Theorems 8 and 13 then give
Theta > 0 on Q1. QED.

### Theorem 22 (beta = 2: an orbit entering an endpoint of the arc)
Let beta = 2, let C and Q+ be as in Theorem 16, and put M = Theta(Q+). Suppose a nonstationary orbit gamma in Q1 has
forward limit Q+. Then W has a zero X in the closed first quadrant, not on C, with Theta(X) = M.
Consequently, suppose C is isolated in Z near Q+ and no such X exists. Then the flow on the centre manifold of Q+
points away from Q+ on the side beyond C, and the same holds at Q-. Since O is not on C and Theta(O) = 0, the
statement has content only when M != 0.
Proof. Theta = M on gamma, hence on A = alpha(gamma). A is nonempty, compact, connected, invariant and contained in the
closed quadrant, since backward orbits are bounded. A contains a zero of W, since otherwise it is a periodic orbit
(Poincare-Bendixson), which Theorem 4 excludes.

Suppose no X as in the statement exists. Then A cap Z is contained in the subarc C[P, Q+]. Suppose A contains a
point R of C other than Q+. Then R is interior to C, near R we have Z = C, and DW has eigenvalues 0 and 4 on C. Choose
smooth coordinates (xi, eta) near R in which C = {xi = 0} (a tubular neighbourhood of a slightly extended subarc of C).
Since W vanishes on C, W = xi V with V smooth, so DW = V (x) d xi on C and the xi component of V equals the nonzero
eigenvalue 4 there. In a box |xi|, |eta| <= delta we have 2 <= V_xi <= 6 and |V_eta| <= C_V for a constant C_V > 0. Along a
backward orbit in the box |xi(s)| <= |xi(0)| e^{-2 s} and |eta(s) - eta(0)| <= C_V |xi(0)|/2, so a backward orbit entering
the box at a point with |eta| <= delta/2 and |xi| < min(delta, delta/C_V) stays in it and converges to a point of C. Since R is in A, the backward
orbit of gamma enters such a box around R; hence A = {R}, and gamma together with R, Q+ and the subarc of C from R to Q+
is an invariant Jordan curve. This is excluded by Theorem 4. So A cap Z = {Q+}.

If A = {Q+}, gamma together with Q+ is a homoclinic loop. Otherwise A contains a regular point; let delta be the orbit
through it, which lies in A. Suppose omega(delta) or alpha(delta) contains a regular point p; then p is in A. Let S be a
small transversal through p. Because A is the alpha-limit set of an orbit of a planar flow, S meets A in at most one
point (the lemma in the proof of the Poincare-Bendixson theorem: the successive crossings of gamma with S are monotone
along S, so they accumulate at a single point of S). So S n A = {p}. The orbit delta lies in A and accumulates at p, so
it crosses S near p at arbitrarily large (or arbitrarily negative) times, always at p; hence delta is periodic, which
Theorem 4 excludes. Therefore alpha(delta) and omega(delta), which are nonempty since A is compact, lie in
A cap Z = {Q+}, and delta together with Q+ is a homoclinic loop, which Theorem 4 excludes. No isolation of Q+ is used.

For the consequence: if C is isolated near Q+, the flow on the branch of the centre manifold beyond C has one sign.
If it pointed toward Q+, that branch would be an incoming orbit, contained in Q1 by invariance of the axes. QED.

### Theorem 23 (restricted: annular kinetic energy below the scale R^{4-4/beta})
Let beta >= 2, q = 1 - 2/beta, and E(R) = int_{R < |X| < 2R} |U|^2 dX. There is no A2-broad profile with
  E(R) = O(R^{4-4/beta})  and  liminf_{R -> infinity} E(R) R^{-4+4/beta} = 0;
in particular there is none with E(R) = o(R^{4-4/beta}). Consequences: (a) for every beta > 0 there is no A2-broad
profile with int |U|^p dX < infinity for some real 0 < p < infinity (finite kinetic energy is the case p = 2); (b) every
A2-broad profile with E(R) = O(R^{4-4/beta}) has a strictly positive lower limit of E(R) R^{-4+4/beta}. Theorems 18, 19
and 20 are special cases. No bound on Omega beyond the class assumptions and no bound on derivatives of U is used. The formal far field of Section 7 has
E(R) of order R^{4-2/beta} and is not covered.
Proof. Step 1 (a weighted velocity integral). On a dyadic annulus, Cauchy-Schwarz gives
int_{R<r<2R} |U| r^{-3+eps} dX <= E(R)^{1/2} (C R^{-4+2 eps})^{1/2} <= C R^{q-1+eps}. Hence
I_eps := int_{r >= R0} |U| r^{-3+eps} dX < infinity for 0 < eps < 1 - q = 2/beta.
Step 2 (flow coordinates and travel-time moments). Choose R0 with W_r >= beta r/2 for r >= R0, and let F_r(alpha), tau(r, alpha)
be as in the proof of Theorem 18, d = tau - beta^{-1} log(r/R0), h_r = e^{2 beta d}, A(alpha) = W_r(R0, alpha)/(beta R0),
b_r(alpha) = W_r(r, F_r(alpha))/(beta r). The trajectory and determinant identities are
  d_r d = -U_r/(beta r W_r),   J_r := F_r' = A h_r/b_r.
Uniform sublinearity gives sup_alpha |d| = o(log r) and b_r -> 1 uniformly, so sup_alpha h_r^t <= C_{t,eps} r^eps for every
real t and eps > 0. Since d_r h_r^t = 2 beta t h_r^t d_r d, the change of variables phi = F_r(alpha) gives
  int_0^a |d_r h_r^t| d alpha <= C_{t,eps} r^{-2+eps} int_0^a |U(r, phi)| dphi,   a = pi/2,
whose integral over r >= R0 is at most C I_eps. With h_{R0} = 1 this yields int_0^a sup_{r >= R0} h_r^t d alpha < infinity
for every real t, a.e. limits 0 < h_inf < infinity, and h_r^t -> h_inf^t in L^1(0, a). Hence J_r -> j = A h_inf in L^1,
int_0^a j = a, and F_r -> F, F(alpha) = int_0^alpha j, uniformly. F is an absolutely continuous homeomorphism of [0, a] with
F' > 0 a.e., so F and F^{-1} map null sets to null sets.
Step 3 (weak angular limit of the temperature). Put f_r(phi) = r^{-q} Theta(r cos phi, r sin phi) and
c(alpha) = R0^{-q} Theta(R0 cos alpha, R0 sin alpha). Transport gives Theta(Phi_tau X0) = e^{kappa tau} Theta(X0) and
e^{kappa tau} = (r/R0)^q h_r^{q/2}, so f_r(F_r(alpha)) = c(alpha) h_r(alpha)^{q/2}. Define f a.e. by
f(F(alpha)) = c(alpha) h_inf(alpha)^{q/2}. For continuous zeta,
  int_0^a f_r zeta dphi = int_0^a c A h_r^{1+q/2} zeta(F_r)/b_r d alpha -> int_0^a c A h_inf^{1+q/2} zeta(F) d alpha = int_0^a f zeta dphi,
and sup_r ||f_r||_{L^1(0,a)} < infinity (the same moment bound). Integrating in the radial variable, T_R(Z) := R^{-q} Theta(RZ)
converges in D'(Q1) to T(Z) := |Z|^q f(arg Z). If Theta is not identically zero, choose R0 so large that the disc
|X| < R0 contains an open set E on which Theta != 0. If c were identically zero, Theta would vanish on the whole circle
(parity), the forward images of E (on which Theta stays nonzero) could not cross it, and their area e^{2 beta s}|E|
would be bounded. So c is not identically zero.
Step 4 (weak vorticity equation along low-energy radii). With V_R(Z) = R^{-1} U(RZ) and w_R(Z) = Omega(RZ) = -curl V_R,
  d_1 T_R = R^{2/beta} [ (beta Z + V_R).grad w_R + w_R ].
For psi in C_c^inf supported in Q1 cap {1 < |Z| < 2}, the linear terms are bounded by C_psi int |V_R| after integration
by parts, and the quadratic term, by V.grad(-curl V) = -curl div(V (x) V), by C_psi int |V_R|^2, both over
1 < |Z| < 2. Scaling gives
  |<d_1 T_R, psi>| <= C_psi ( R^{-1-q} E(R)^{1/2} + R^{-3-q} E(R) ).
Along a sequence R_j -> infinity with E(R_j) R_j^{-2-2q} -> 0 both terms tend to 0 (the second is R_j^{q-1} times the
normalized energy), so d_1 T = 0 on Q1 cap {1 < |Z| < 2}, and on Q1 by homogeneity. Hence T = C y^q and
f = C (sin phi)^q a.e.
Step 5 (the y-axis). Pulling back, C (sin F(alpha))^q = c(alpha) h_inf(alpha)^{q/2} for a.e. alpha. If q = 0 this says
c = C a.e., so C = c(a) = 0. If q > 0 and C != 0, then |c(alpha)| <= L (a - alpha) (Theta(0, y) = 0) and sin F(alpha) -> 1 as
alpha -> a give h_inf(alpha) >= c_* (a - alpha)^{-2/q} a.e. near a, which is not integrable since 2/q > 1. So C = 0 and,
since h_inf > 0 a.e., c = 0, a contradiction. Hence Theta = 0, then Omega = 0 (Omega(X) = e^{-s} Omega(Phi_{-s} X) with
bounded backward orbits) and U = 0, contradicting a0 != 0.
Consequence (a). For p >= 2, Holder on the annulus gives E(R) <= C R^{2-4/p} (int |U|^p)^{2/p}. For 0 < p < 2,
E(R) <= (sup_{R<|X|<2R} |U|)^{2-p} int |U|^p = o(R^{2-p}) by uniform sublinearity. Both are o(R^{4-4/beta}). The range
beta < 2 is Theorem 1. QED.

### Theorem 24 (little-o vorticity decay transfers to the velocity)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be A2-broad and 0 < eta <= 1. If sup_{|Y| >= R} |Y|^eta |Omega(Y)| -> 0 as R -> infinity,
then sup_{|X| >= R} |X|^{eta-1} |U(X)| -> 0. Consequently, for beta >= 2, the hypothesis of Theorem 15 implies that of
Theorem 19 (eta = 2/beta), and Theorems 15 and 19 are contained in Theorem 23.
Proof. With K(Z) = (Z_2, -Z_1)/(2 pi |Z|^2), the parity-grouped kernel K(X - Y) - K(X - S_x Y) - K(X - S_y Y) + K(X + Y)
over Y in Q1 (S_x, S_y the reflections in the axes) vanishes at X = 0 and is bounded by C |X| |Y|^{-2} for |Y| > 2|X|,
so the grouped integral converges absolutely; it is divergence-free with curl -Omega, vanishes at 0 and is sublinear by
the estimates below, so it equals U by the uniqueness of Section 2. Fix eps > 0 and R_eps with |Omega(Y)| <= eps |Y|^{-eta}
for |Y| >= R_eps, and let r = |X| > 2 R_eps. Inner region |Y| < r/2: by odd-odd parity the mass and first moments of
Omega vanish on centred discs, so K(X - Y) may be replaced by its Taylor remainder, of size C |Y|^2 r^{-3}; this gives
C_eps r^{-3} + C eps r^{-3} r^{4-eta}. Middle region r/2 <= |Y| <= 2r: int |K(X - Y)| dY <= C r gives C eps r^{1-eta}. Outer
region |Y| > 2r: C eps r int_{2r}^inf rho^{-1-eta} d rho = C eps r^{1-eta}. Hence limsup r^{eta-1} |U| <= C eps. QED.

### Theorem 25 (restricted: bounded velocity at beta = 2 forces a sign-changing far field)
Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile (beta = 2) and suppose U is bounded on R^2. Then:
(i) Theta(r cos phi, r sin phi) -> H(phi) uniformly, where H is C^1, not identically zero, has the parities of Theta and
    H(0) = H(pi/2) = 0;
(ii) with Theta_inf(X) = H(arg X), U(R .) -> U_inf weakly-* in L^inf(R^2), where U_inf is the unique bounded
    divergence-free field with the A2 parities and curl U_inf = d_x Theta_inf; in polar components U_inf = (-P'(phi), P(phi))
    with -(P'' + P) = sin(phi) H'(phi), and U_inf is homogeneous of degree 0;
(iii) R Omega(R .) -> r^{-1} sin(phi) H'(phi) = -d_x Theta_inf in D'(R^2);
(iv) for every sufficiently large R, Omega takes both signs in Q1 cap {R < |X| < 2R};
(v) liminf R^{-2} E(R) >= int_{1 < |X| < 2} |U_inf|^2 > 0.
This does not exclude bounded velocity at beta = 2. It shows that the vorticity of such a profile has a nonzero
distributional scaling limit of degree -1, with an angular factor of both signs. A nonzero homogeneous vorticity term
of degree -1/2 (the natural tail of Section 7) would give unbounded velocity. Theorem 34 shows that bounded velocity
does not occur at beta = 2, so at beta = 2 the theorem is a true implication with a hypothesis that no A2-broad profile
satisfies.
Proof. (i) With the notation of Theorem 18, d_r F_r and d_r d are O(r^{-2}) uniformly, so F_r, d and, by the Jacobian
identity, F_r' converge uniformly, the last to a positive continuous function. So F is a C^1 diffeomorphism of [0, pi/2],
G_r = F_r^{-1} -> G uniformly, and H = theta_0 o G is C^1; H is nonzero as in Theorem 18. Theta is bounded.
(ii), (iii) Put u_R = U(R .) and z_R = R Omega(R .), so z_R = -curl u_R and
  d_x [Theta(R .)] = 2 X.grad z_R + z_R + R^{-1} u_R.grad z_R,
where the last term equals -R^{-1} curl div(u_R (x) u_R) and tends to 0 in D'. A weak-* subsequential limit u of u_R
satisfies (2 X.grad + 1) z = d_x Theta_inf with z = -curl u. Since d_x Theta_inf is homogeneous of degree -1,
D := z + d_x Theta_inf satisfies (2 X.grad + 1) D = 0 and is homogeneous of degree -1/2; but |<D(lambda .), phi>| <= C_phi/lambda
for lambda >= 1 by boundedness of u and Theta_inf, so D = 0 and curl u = d_x Theta_inf. Two bounded divergence-free
solutions with the parities differ by a bounded harmonic field, hence by a constant, hence by 0; so the whole family
converges, and dilation invariance gives homogeneity of degree 0. B(phi) = sin(phi) H'(phi) is odd-odd, so it has only the
modes sin(2n phi), and -(P'' + P) = B is solved by P_{2n} = B_{2n}/(4n^2 - 1). Psi_inf = r P(phi) gives
U_inf = (-P', P) in polar components and -Lap Psi_inf = B/r.
(iv) H is C^1, not identically zero and vanishes at 0 and pi/2, so H', and hence B, takes both signs on open subintervals
of (0, pi/2). Testing (iii) with nonnegative functions supported in 1 < r < 2 and in these angular intervals gives
integrals of R Omega(R .) of both strict signs for all large R.
(v) Weak convergence in L^2(1 < |X| < 2) and lower semicontinuity; U_inf = 0 would give d_x Theta_inf = 0, so H would be
constant on Q1 and hence 0. QED.

### Theorem 26 (temperature traces on the x-axis: necessary compatibility conditions)
Let a smooth profile with the A2 parities solve (P) near the segment [0, L] of the positive x-axis, where L = x1 is the
first positive zero of w(x) = W_1(x, 0). Put k = beta + 2, A = 5 beta + 2, kappa = beta - 2 and
  f(x) = Theta_y(x, 0), g(x) = Omega_y(x, 0), h(x) = Theta_yyy(x, 0), m(x) = d_yy W_1(x, 0).
(a) (without the jet assumption) If c = Psi_xy(0) > beta and f does not vanish identically near 0, then
    c = (2 n beta + 2)/(2 n - 1) for some integer n >= 1, and f = C x^{2n} G(x) near 0 with G smooth, even, G(0) = 1.
    The jet of the class is the case n = 1.
(b) Let beta >= 2 and assume in addition the A2 jet a0 != 0, so that c = 2 beta + 2, w'(0) = -(beta + 2),
    f = a0 x^2 + O(x^4), w'(L) = beta + 2 and f(L) != 0 (the local argument of the proof of Theorem 2(c), (d) at L). (Without the jet the exponents differ: for beta = 2,
    Psi = 3xy - x^3 y + x y^3 and Theta = Omega = 0 give w = -x + x^3, L = 1, and the homogeneous solution x^15 (1 - x^2)^{-3}.)
    Then m = g - w'' and h solves
      w h' + (A - 3 w') h = R,   R := -3 m f' + m' f.
    The homogeneous equation has the positive solution H = s^3 exp(A Phi) on (0, L), s = -w, Phi' = 1/s, with
    H = x^p B(x^2) near 0, p = 8 (beta + 1)/(beta + 2), B smooth, B(0) > 0, and H = (L - x)^{-2 kappa/k} B_L(x) near L,
    B_L smooth and positive.
    (i) beta > 2: h is the unique solution bounded at L, h(L) = R(L)/(2 beta - 4), and near 0, h = h_e + K x^p B(x^2)
        with h_e smooth and even; smoothness of Theta forces K = 0.
    (ii) beta = 2: smoothness at L forces R(L) = 0, equivalently m'(L) = 3 m(L) w''(L)/4. Writing
        w = -4x + w3 x^3 + w5 x^5 + w7 x^7 + O(x^9) and f = a x^2 + O(x^4), smoothness at 0 forces D = 0, where
          D = 3a [-93 a w3^2 - 360 a w5 + 2640 w3^3 + 23760 w3 w5 + 49280 w7]/3520;
        otherwise h contains the term -(D/4) x^6 log x.
These are necessary conditions on axis data, not obstructions. For the traces w = -k sin x cos x, f = a sin^2 x,
g = 2a sin x cos x/(2 beta + 1) on [0, pi/2], which satisfy the lower trace equations exactly,
R(pi/2) = -2a [a - 2k(2 beta + 1)]/(2 beta + 1), and at beta = 2 also D = -2a(a - 40)/5. Both vanish for
a = 2k(2 beta + 1), the member of the exact local family of Section 4 (there m = 0 and h = 0).
Proof. (a) The coefficient of y in (T) gives w f' = (w' - k) f (as in the proof of Theorem 2(b)). Since U_1 = -Psi_y, w(x) = -(c - beta) x a(x^2)
with a smooth, a(0) = 1, so (w' - k)/w = p/x + (smooth odd function) with p = (c + 2)/(c - beta) > 0. Linear uniqueness
makes f nonzero on (0, eps), and integration gives f = C x^p G(x) with G smooth, even and positive. Since f is smooth
and even, p is an even integer 2n, that is c + 2 = 2n (c - beta).
(b) Parity and div W = 2 beta give W_1 = w + (m/2) y^2 + O(y^4), W_2 = (2 beta - w') y - (m'/6) y^3 + O(y^5) and
Theta = f y + (h/6) y^3 + O(y^5); the coefficient of y in Omega = d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 is m + w'', and 6 times the
coefficient of y^3 in W.grad Theta = kappa Theta is the stated equation. H'/H = (3 w' - A)/w, and w = -k x (1 + O(x^2))
near 0, w = k (x - L)(1 + O(x - L)) near L give the two local forms (3 + A/k = p, 3 - A/k = -2 kappa/k).
(i) With a = 2 kappa/k > 0, R/(w H) is (L - x)^{a-1} times a smooth function near L, so
h_* = -H int_x^L R/(w H) is bounded, and the change of variables t = L - (L - x) z shows it is smooth at L; every other
solution differs from h_* by a nonzero multiple of H, which is unbounded at L. At L the equation reads
(A - 3k) h(L) = R(L). At 0, R is even and O(x^2) (m odd, f even, f = O(x^2)); since the operator maps x^{2j} to
k (p - 2j) x^{2j} + O(x^{2j+2}) and 6 < p < 8, an even polynomial h_0 of degree 6 leaves a forcing x^8 Q(x^2), whose
particular solution H int_0^x x^8 Q/(w H) is x^8 times a smooth even function (the integrand is x^{7-p} times a
smooth function, integrable). So h = h_e + K H. The even extension of K |x|^p B(x^2) is not C^7 if p <= 7 and not C^8 if
7 < p < 8, unless K = 0.
(ii) At beta = 2, H is smooth and positive at L, and (h/H)' = R/(w H) = R(L)/(4 H(L) (x - L)) + O(1), so h is bounded at L
only if R(L) = 0. Differentiating w f' = (w' - k) f at L gives k f'(L) = w''(L) f(L), and f(L) != 0 (the local argument of the proof of
Theorem 2(c), (d)), which gives the equivalent form. At 0, p = 6. The coefficients of f and g follow from w f' = (w' - 4) f and the coefficient of y in
(V), w g' + (2 beta + 1 - w') g = f'; then R = R2 x^2 + R4 x^4 + R6 x^6 + O(x^8) and h2 = R2/16, h4 = (R4 + 7 w3 h2)/8. The
operator annihilates the x^6 coefficient of an even polynomial up to the terms -5 w3 h4 - 13 w5 h2 and maps x^6 log x
to -4 x^6 + O(x^8 log x); matching x^6 gives the logarithmic coefficient -D/4 with D = R6 + 5 w3 h4 + 13 w5 h2, which
equals the displayed polynomial (exact symbolic computation, reproduced independently twice). For the trigonometric
traces, w f' = (w' - k) f and w g' + (2 beta + 1 - w') g = f' hold identically, m = (a/(2 beta + 1) - 2k) sin 2x, and
R(pi/2) = m'(pi/2) f(pi/2); D follows from w3 = 8/3, w5 = -8/15, w7 = 16/315. QED.

### Theorem 27 (quantized eigenvalues at simple zeros of W on the axes)
Let a smooth profile with the A2 parities and a0 != 0 solve (P), beta > 0. Put w(x) = W_1(x, 0), f(x) = Theta_y(x, 0),
v(y) = W_2(0, y) and E(y) = (1/2) Theta_xx(0, y). Then
  w f' = (w' - beta - 2) f,   v E' = (2 v' - 3 beta - 2) E.
(x) Let 0 < x_1 < x_2 < ... < x_N be the first N positive zeros of w, all simple (so P = (x_1, 0)). Then w'(x_j) > 0 for
    odd j and
    w'(x_j) < 0 for even j; f does not vanish on (x_j, x_{j+1}) for j < N; w'(x_j) = beta + 2 and f(x_j) != 0 for odd j;
    for even j, w'(x_j) = -(beta + 2)/m_j with m_j a positive integer, and f vanishes at x_j to order exactly m_j + 1.
(y) Let y_1 < ... < y_N be the first N positive zeros of v, all simple. Then v'(y_j) < 0 for odd j and v'(y_j) > 0 for
    even j; E does not vanish on (0, y_1) or on (y_j, y_{j+1}) for j < N; for odd j, v'(y_j) = -(3 beta + 2)/n_j with n_j
    a positive integer, and E vanishes at y_j to order exactly n_j + 2; for even j, v'(y_j) = (3 beta + 2)/2 or
    3 beta + 2, and E vanishes at y_j to order 0 or 1 respectively.
At these zeros DW is diagonal: on the x-axis diag(beta + 2, beta - 2) or diag(-(beta + 2)/m, 2 beta + (beta + 2)/m); on the
y-axis diag(2 beta + (3 beta + 2)/n, -(3 beta + 2)/n), diag((beta - 2)/2, (3 beta + 2)/2) or diag(-(beta + 2), 3 beta + 2).
These are necessary conditions, not obstructions. At a degenerate zero both traces must be flat and may vanish
identically beyond it, so the chain hypothesis is needed. For a profile of finite regularity Theta in C^M the
conclusions at a zero with exponent p (below) are guaranteed if M - 1 > p on the x-axis and M - 2 > p on the y-axis
(equality suffices when p is an integer). The axis condition Theta(0, y) = 0 for all y (Section 1) is assumed in addition to the parities and a0 != 0.
Proof. The first identity follows by differentiating (T) on the x-axis, as in the proof of Theorem 2(b). For the second, Theta(0, y) = 0 and evenness in x give
Theta = x^2 E(y) + O(x^4); W_1 = x A0(y) + O(x^3) with A0 = d_x W_1(0, y) = 2 beta - v' (div W = 2 beta) and
W_2 = v(y) + O(x^2); the coefficient of x^2 in (T) is 2 A0 E + v E' = (beta - 2) E.
Local lemma. Let z be C^2 near s0 with z(s0) = 0, nu = z'(s0) != 0, and let g, not identically zero on (s0 - delta, s0),
solve z g' = (k z' - lam) g there. Then g = C |z|^k exp(-lam int^s dt/z) with C != 0, and since 1/z - 1/(nu (s - s0)) is
bounded, g = |s - s0|^p G(s) with p = k - lam/nu and G(s) -> G0 != 0 as s -> s0-. If g is smooth on a two-sided
neighbourhood of s0, then p is a nonnegative integer: p < 0 contradicts boundedness, and for nonintegral p >= 0 the
Taylor coefficients of order <= floor(p) vanish, so g = O(|s - s0|^{ceil(p)}) = o(|s - s0|^p). Then g^{(p)}(s0) != 0, so g is
not identically zero on (s0, s0 + delta), and by linear uniqueness it has no zero up to the next zero of z.
(x) Here k = 1, lam = beta + 2, p = 1 - (beta + 2)/mu with mu = w'(x_j). Since w'(0) = -(beta + 2) < 0 and x_1 is the first
positive zero, w < 0 on (0, x_1); the zeros are simple and consecutive, so the signs of w' alternate starting with w'(x_1) > 0. For mu > 0, p < 1 forces p = 0, so
mu = beta + 2; for mu < 0, p = 1 + (beta + 2)/|mu| > 1 is an integer m + 1 with m >= 1. f = a0 x^2 + O(x^4) is nonzero
near 0, hence on (0, x_1) by linear uniqueness, and the local lemma with p = 0 gives f(x_1) != 0.
(y) Here k = 2, lam = 3 beta + 2, p = 2 - (3 beta + 2)/nu. E = a0 y + O(y^3) does not vanish on (0, y_1), and v > 0 on
(0, y_1) because v'(0) = 3 beta + 2, so v'(y_1) < 0 and the signs alternate. For nu < 0, p = n + 2 with n >= 1; for nu > 0,
p < 2 forces p = 0 or 1. The off-diagonal entries of DW vanish on the axes by parity and the trace of DW is 2 beta. QED.

### Theorem 28 (restricted: the critical annular energy forces a sign-changing far field)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta >= 2, q = 1 - 2/beta, E(R) = int_{R<|X|<2R} |U|^2 dX, and
assume
  (A) E(R) <= C R^{4-4/beta} = C R^{2+2q} for all large R.
Then:
(i) there is a nonzero angular function f on [0, pi/2], in L^p for every finite p >= 1, extended with the parities of
    Theta, such that T_R(X) := R^{-q} Theta(RX) -> T_inf(X) := |X|^q f(arg X) strongly in L^p_loc(R^2) for every finite p;
(ii) R^{-q} U(R .) -> U_inf weakly in L^2_loc(R^2) (the whole family), where U_inf is the unique divergence-free field
    with the A2 velocity parities, locally in L^2 with energy O(L^{2+2q}) on the disc of radius L, and
    curl U_inf = d_x T_inf. U_inf is homogeneous of degree q; in polar components U_inf = r^q (-P', (q + 1) P) with
    -(P'' + (q + 1)^2 P) = B := sin(phi) f' - q cos(phi) f in distributions;
(iii) R^{1-q} Omega(R .) -> -d_x T_inf = r^{q-1} B(phi) in D'(R^2);
(iv) for every sufficiently large R, Omega takes both signs in Q1 cap {R < |X| < 2R};
(v) liminf E(R) R^{-2-2q} >= int_{1<|X|<2} |U_inf|^2 > 0.
In particular eventually one-signed vorticity in Q1 is incompatible with (A), and so is a vorticity with a nonzero
leading homogeneous term r^{-1/beta} G(phi) (the natural tail of Section 7): R^{1-q} Omega(R .) would then grow like
R^{1/beta}. At beta = 2 a bounded velocity satisfies (A), and (iii) to (v) contain the corresponding parts of Theorem 25.
No pointwise vorticity asymptotics and no strong velocity convergence is asserted under (A) alone. Under (DT),
Theorem 32 gives uniform limits at the natural normalization; in its critical branch it gives only the bounds
Omega = O(r^{-2/beta}), U = O(r^q), and the critical-scale limits are the distributional and weak limits above. (A) does not follow from the class assumptions: the formal natural far field has E(R) of
order R^{4-2/beta}. At beta = 2, (DT) holds for every A2-broad profile (Theorem 33(a)) and (A) holds for none
(Theorem 34). For beta > 2, (A) holds for no A2-broad profile (Theorem 38(e)), and (DT) holds for every one
(Theorem 41).
Proof. Step 1 (moments). As in Steps 1 to 3 of Theorem 23, (A) gives I_eps < infinity, hence for every real t
int_0^a sup_{r >= R0} h_r^t d alpha < infinity, a.e. limits h_inf, the absolutely continuous homeomorphism F with
F' = A h_inf, and f(F(alpha)) = c(alpha) h_inf(alpha)^{q/2}; f is nonzero and in every L^p by the change of variables.
For continuous zeta, int |f_r - zeta|^p dphi = int |c h_r^{q/2} - zeta(F_r)|^p J_r d alpha converges, by dominated
convergence with the moment bounds, to int |f - zeta|^p dphi; density of continuous functions gives f_r -> f in L^p.
Integration in the radial variable gives T_R -> T_inf in L^p on compact subsets of R^2 \ {0}, and the disc |X| < rho
contributes at most C (R^{-2-pq} + rho^{2+pq}) to int |T_R|^p, uniformly in large R.
Step 2 (scaling). With u_R = R^{-q} U(R .) and z_R = R^{1-q} Omega(R .) = -curl u_R,
  d_x T_R = (beta X.grad + 1) z_R + R^{q-1} u_R.grad z_R,   u_R.grad z_R = -curl div(u_R (x) u_R),
and (A) gives int_{|X|<L} |u_R|^2 <= C L^{2+2q} uniformly for R L >= R0. So the quadratic term tends to 0 in D', and
a weak L^2_loc subsequential limit u, with z = -curl u, satisfies (beta X.grad + 1) z = d_x T_inf in D'(R^2).
Step 3 (no residual). z_p := -d_x T_inf is homogeneous of degree q - 1, so (beta X.grad + 1) z_p = -z_p = d_x T_inf.
D := z - z_p satisfies (beta X.grad + 1) D = 0, so <D(lambda .), phi> = lambda^{-1/beta} <D, phi>. On the other hand
z(lambda .) = -lambda^{-1} curl [u(lambda .)] and d_x T_inf(lambda .) = lambda^{q-1} d_x T_inf, and the L^2_loc bound gives
|<D(lambda .), phi>| <= C_phi lambda^{q-1} = C_phi lambda^{-2/beta}. Letting lambda -> infinity gives D = 0, that is
curl u = d_x T_inf.
Step 4 (uniqueness). Two such limits differ by a divergence-free, curl-free field in L^2_loc with energy O(L^{2+2q}) on
discs; it is harmonic, the mean-value property gives gradient O(L^{q-1}) -> 0, and parity makes the constant zero. So
the whole family converges, and dilation invariance of the problem gives homogeneity of degree q. With
Psi_inf = r^{q+1} P(phi), -Lap Psi_inf = -r^{q-1} (P'' + (q + 1)^2 P), and -d_x (r^q f) = r^{q-1} B. B is odd-odd, so only
the modes sin(2n phi) occur and (2n)^2 > (q + 1)^2: there is no resonance.
Step 5 (B changes sign). B = sin^{q+1} (f sin^{-q})'. Suppose B >= 0 in D'(0, pi/2), so g := f sin^{-q} is nondecreasing
(a.e. representative); g is not identically zero. If q = 0, then f(F(alpha)) = c(alpha) is continuous and vanishes at
both ends, so f = 0: contradiction. Let q > 0. If g >= g0 > 0 near a = pi/2, then, since |c(alpha)| <= C (a - alpha)
(Theta(0, y) = 0), h_inf(alpha) >= c' (a - alpha)^{-2/q} near a, which is not integrable since 2/q > 1. Otherwise
g <= -g0 < 0 near 0, so |f(phi)| >= g0 sin^q(phi) there. With |c(alpha)| <= C alpha and Holder with a negative moment,
alpha^{p+1} <= F(alpha)^p int_0^a (A h_inf)^{-p}, so F(alpha) >= c alpha^{1+1/p}, and f(F(alpha)) = c(alpha) h_inf^{q/2} gives
h_inf(alpha) >= c alpha^{-e} near 0 with e = 2/q - 2 - 2/p > 0 for p > q/(1 - q); then int h_inf^n = infinity for n e >= 1,
contradicting the finite moments. B <= 0 is excluded in the same way. So there are nonnegative test functions phi_+,
phi_- on (0, pi/2) with <B, phi_+> > 0 > <B, phi_->.
Step 6. Testing (iii) with chi(r) phi_+-(phi), chi >= 0 supported in 1 < r < 2, gives integrals of R^{1-q} Omega(R .) of
both strict signs for all large R, hence (iv). (v) follows from weak L^2 convergence on 1 < |X| < 2 and lower
semicontinuity; U_inf = 0 would give B = 0, excluded in Step 5. QED.

### Theorem 29 (a vorticity condition at x-axis zeros with negative tangential eigenvalue)
Let a smooth A2 profile solve (P) with beta >= 2; put k = beta + 2, D = 2 beta + 1, w(x) = W_1(x, 0), f(x) = Theta_y(x, 0),
g(x) = Omega_y(x, 0). Let x_* > 0 be a simple zero of w with w'(x_*) = nu = -k/m, m a positive integer, near which f is
not identically zero (as at the even-indexed zeros of Theorem 27(x)). Let rho be the smooth coordinate with
x - x_* = chi(rho), chi(0) = 0, chi'(0) = 1 and w = nu rho chi'(rho), and put b = 1/chi', with Taylor
coefficients b_j = b^{(j)}(0)/j! (all coefficient computations below use finite Taylor expansions with remainder).
If N := 1 + m D/k is an integer, then g is C^N at x_* only if b_{N-m} = 0. This condition does not follow from the
temperature trace: for beta = 2, m = 4 (nu = -1, N = 6) and b = 1 + eps rho^2, the traces w and f satisfy
w f' = (w' - k) f exactly, while every solution of the g equation contains the term -3 C eps rho^6 log|rho|/(1 + eps rho^2).
Proof. With s = x - x_* and w(x_* + s) = nu s a(s), a(0) = 1, rho = s exp(int_0^s [nu/w(x_* + t) - 1/t] dt) is smooth, with
rho'(0) = 1 and w d rho/dx = nu rho; chi is its local inverse. In rho, w d/dx = nu rho d/d rho and w' = nu (1 + rho chi''/chi').
The equation w f' = (w' - k) f gives f = C rho^{m+1} chi'(rho) with C != 0. With g = chi' h, the coefficient of y in (V),
w g' + (D - w') g = f', becomes exactly
  rho h' - N h = (C/nu) [(m + 1) rho^m b - rho^{m+1} b'].
Since 1 < D/k < 2, j := N - m = 1 + m (beta - 1)/(beta + 2) lies in (1, m + 1). The coefficient of rho^N on the right is
(C/nu)(m + 1 - j) b_j = (C/nu)(3m/k) b_j, using 2k - D = 3, and it produces the term (C/nu)(3m/k) b_j rho^N log|rho| in h.
Since chi' is smooth and nonzero, g is C^N only if b_j = 0. In the example the right side is -C (5 rho^4 + 3 eps rho^6),
whose solutions are h = (5C/2) rho^4 - 3 C eps rho^6 log|rho| + K rho^6. QED.
Remark. On the y-axis, K = Omega_x(0, y) solves v K' + (D - v') K = 2E; at the quantized zeros of Theorem 27(y) the
forcing 2E starts strictly above the homogeneous exponent (negative eigenvalue) or the homogeneous exponent is not an
integer (positive eigenvalue), so no logarithm of this kind occurs there.

### Theorem 30 (vorticity quantization at the first simple zero on the y-axis)
Let an A2-broad profile solve (P) with beta >= 2. With v and E as in Theorem 27(y) put K(y) = Omega_x(0, y),
L = 3 beta + 2 and D = 2 beta + 1. Then
  v K' + (D - v') K = 2E,  and where E != 0 the ratio s = K/E solves  v s' + (v' - beta - 1) s = 2.
(a) If the first positive zero y_1 of v is simple, then s > 0 on (0, y_1), and K vanishes at y_1 to order exactly
    ell + 1, where ell = D/|v'(y_1)| is a positive integer. With n = L/|v'(y_1)| (Theorem 27(y)), d := 2n - 3 ell and
    beta d = 2 ell - n are positive integers and v'(y_1) = -1/d. In particular beta is rational.
(b) If also the second positive zero y_2 is simple, then s > 0 on (y_1, y_2) and (beta + 1) d is odd. If
    beta = p/r in lowest terms, this requires p + r odd and d = r m with m odd.
(c) If every positive zero of v is simple, and beta is irrational or beta = p/r in lowest terms with p and r both odd
    (for instance beta = 3), then v has no positive zero.
These are necessary conditions. At beta = 2 they allow d odd, v'(y_1) = -1/d, n = 8d, ell = 5d.
Proof. Smoothness and the parities give Omega = x K(y) + O(x^3) and, as in Theorem 27, Theta = x^2 E + O(x^4),
W_1 = x (2 beta - v') + O(x^3), W_2 = v + O(x^2); the coefficient of x in (V) is (2 beta - v') K + v K' + K = 2E. At O,
v = L y + O(y^3), E = a0 y + O(y^3) and K = b0 y + O(y^3) with D b0 = 2 a0. On an interval where v != 0 let t' = 1/v
(flow time on the axis). Then E = C_E v^2 e^{-L t} (Theorem 27) and the equation for s is equivalent to
  d/dt [s v e^{-(beta + 1) t}] = 2 v e^{-(beta + 1) t}.                                                  (30.1)
(a) On (0, y_1), v > 0 and E != 0, t runs over R, s -> 2/D at 0, and v e^{-(beta + 1) t} -> 0 exponentially as
t -> -infinity because v'(0) = L > beta + 1. So S(t) := s v e^{-(beta + 1) t} = 2 int_{-infinity}^t v e^{-(beta + 1) tau} dtau > 0,
and S has a finite positive limit as t -> infinity (v is bounded on [0, y_1]). With rho = |v'(y_1)| and z = y - y_1,
the local lemma of Theorem 27 gives t = -(1/rho) log|z| + t_* + o(1), hence
  K = E s = C_E v e^{-D t} S(t),  |K| ~ C |z|^{1 + D/rho},  C > 0.
Smoothness of K forces ell = D/rho to be a positive integer. Since 2L - 3D = 1 and 2D - L = beta,
d = 2n - 3 ell = 1/rho and beta d = 2 ell - n.
(b) E is not identically zero on (y_1, y_2) (Theorem 27(y)), v < 0 there, and v'(y_2) = L/2 or L. If v'(y_2) = L/2, then
E(y_2) != 0 and the K equation at y_2 gives s(y_2) = 2/(D - L/2) = 4/beta. If v'(y_2) = L, E has a simple zero, the K
equation at y_2 gives (D - L) K(y_2) = 0 with D - L = -(beta + 1), and first-order coefficients give s -> 2/D. So s > 0
near y_2. If y_* were the largest zero of s in (y_1, y_2), then s'(y_*) = 2/v(y_*) < 0 would make s negative just to
the right of y_*; so s > 0 on (y_1, y_2). The leading Taylor coefficients of E (order n + 2) and K (order ell + 1) at
y_1 are nonzero, so s changes sign across y_1 by the factor (-1)^{n - ell + 1}; hence n - ell + 1 = (beta + 1) d + 1 is
even. If beta = p/r, the integrality of d and p d/r gives d = r m, and (beta + 1) d = (p + r) m.
(c) The zero set of v in (0, infinity) is bounded (v(y)/y -> beta) and consists of isolated points, so it is finite.
Since v > 0 near 0 and for large y, a nonempty set of simple zeros has at least two elements, and (a), (b) apply to
the first two. For irrational beta (a) fails; for p and r odd, (p + r) m is even. QED.

### Theorem 31 (the y-axis beyond its last zero; energy from a nonzero outgoing amplitude)
Let an A2-broad profile solve (P) with beta >= 2; v, E, K, L, D and s as in Theorem 30. Let Y be the largest zero of
v on [0, infinity) (it exists since v(y)/y -> beta), and assume
  (N) E is not identically zero on (Y, infinity).
(N) holds if Y = 0, and by Theorem 27(y) if every positive zero of v is simple. Let t' = 1/v on (Y, infinity). Then:
(a) Y is a simple zero and v'(Y) = L/2 or L.
(b) t -> -infinity at Y and t -> infinity at infinity, and
      S(t) := s v e^{-(beta + 1) t} = 2 int_{-infinity}^t v e^{-(beta + 1) tau} dtau -> I,  0 < I < infinity.
    So s > 0 on (Y, infinity) and s(y) = y^{1/beta + o(1)}. Moreover s(y) ~ C y^{1/beta} for some C > 0 if and only if
    t(y) - beta^{-1} log y converges as y -> infinity.
(c) For y0 > Y let y(t) be the axis orbit with y(0) = y0 and X_1(t) = exp int_0^t (2 beta - v'(y(tau))) dtau (the
    transverse linearization). Writing E = C_E v^2 e^{-L t} with t(y0) = 0,
      J_1(y0) := K(y0) + 2 int_0^infinity e^t E(y(t)) X_1(t) dt = lim_{t -> infinity} e^t K(y(t)) X_1(t) = v(y0) C_E I,
    which is finite, nonzero and of the sign of E on (Y, infinity).
(d) (No derivative bound.) Let J(X) := lim_{t -> infinity} e^t Omega(Phi_t X) where the limit exists. Suppose it exists
    locally uniformly on an open set G0 of points with unbounded forward orbits, and J != 0 at some point of G0 off the
    axes. Then for every eps > 0 there is c_eps > 0 with E(R) >= c_eps R^{4 - 2/beta - eps} for all large R.
(e) Suppose that for some a > 0 and 0 <= sigma < beta a - 1, outside a disc, |Theta_x| <= C r^{-a},
    |grad Theta_x| <= C r^{-a-1}, and the largest eigenvalue of (DU + DU^T)/2 is at most sigma. Then J is C^1 near
    (0, y0), d_x J(0, y0) = J_1(y0) != 0, and the conclusion of (d) holds; in particular (A) of Theorem 28 fails. For
    example DU = o(1), Theta_x = O(r^{q-1}) and grad Theta_x = O(r^{q-2}) suffice (a = 2/beta).
Here E(y) is the axis trace and E(R) the annular energy of Theorem 23. In a smooth forced homogeneous field
Omega_inf = -d_x Theta_inf the ratio Omega_inf,x/Theta_inf,xx on the y-axis equals -1 wherever it is defined, whereas
K/Theta_xx = s/2 > 0 here; this is only a comparison, since the limits of Theorem 28 need not have such traces. The
constant asymptotic in (b) can fail at the level of the trace equations: v = beta y (1 - a'/log y) for large y gives
s ~ C y^{1/beta} (log y)^{a'(beta + 1)/beta}. A degenerate zero can stop (N): the trace equations admit smooth solutions
that are flat at a degenerate zero and vanish beyond it (an example of the axis equations, not of a profile).
Proof. (a) On (Y, infinity), v > 0; t -> -infinity at Y because v(y) <= C (y - Y), and t -> infinity at infinity. By
(N), E = C_E v^2 e^{-L t} with C_E != 0, and d log|E|/dt = 2 v' - L. If v'(Y) < L/2, then 2 v' - L <= -delta < 0 near Y and
|E| -> infinity as t -> -infinity, which is impossible. So v'(Y) >= L/2, Y is simple, and the local lemma of Theorem 27
(exponent p = 2 - L/v'(Y) in [0, 2), an integer) gives v'(Y) = L/2 or L.
(b) s is bounded near Y: if v'(Y) = L/2, E(Y) != 0; if v'(Y) = L, E and K vanish simply at Y as in the proof of
Theorem 30(b); at Y = 0 by the jets. Since v'(Y) - beta - 1 >= L/2 - beta - 1 = beta/2 > 0, v e^{-(beta + 1) t} -> 0
exponentially as t -> -infinity, and (30.1) integrates to the formula for S. For small eps, v <= (beta + eps) y for
large y, so y(t) <= C e^{(beta + eps) t} and v e^{-(beta + 1) t} <= C e^{-(1 - eps) t}: I < infinity. Since v(y)/y -> beta,
t = beta^{-1} log y + o(log y), and s = S e^{(beta + 1) t}/v gives s = y^{1/beta + o(1)}; if t - beta^{-1} log y -> t_inf
then s ~ (I/beta) e^{(beta + 1) t_inf} y^{1/beta}, and conversely, since S -> I and v/y -> beta.
(c) d/dt log X_1 = 2 beta - v' and d/dt log v = v' give X_1 v e^{-2 beta t} = v(y0). Along the orbit,
d/dt [e^t K X_1] = e^t X_1 [K + 2E - (D - v') K + (2 beta - v') K] = 2 e^t E X_1, and
e^t K X_1 = e^t C_E v^2 e^{-L t} s v(y0) e^{2 beta t}/v = C_E v(y0) S(t), because 1 + 2 beta - L = -(beta + 1).
(d) Fix R0 with W_r > 0 outside the disc of radius R0. For alpha in [0, pi/2] let F_r(alpha), tau(r, alpha) be the
hitting angle and time at radius r of the orbit through R0 e(alpha), j_r = d_alpha F_r, and alpha(X) the inverse label.
As in Theorem 18, det D Phi_t = e^{2 beta t} gives j_r = [W_r(R0 e(alpha))/(beta R0)] [beta r/W_r(r, F_r)] e^{2 beta d_r},
d_r = tau - beta^{-1} log(r/R0), and U = o(r) gives d_r = o(log r) uniformly, so C_delta^{-1} r^{-delta} <= j_r <= C_delta r^delta and
e^{-tau} >= c_delta r^{-1/beta - delta}. Differentiating F_r(alpha(r, phi)) = phi gives d_phi alpha = 1/j_r and
d_r alpha = -U_phi/(r W_r j_r), so |grad alpha| = (1 + (U_phi/W_r)^2)^{1/2}/(r j_r) <= C_delta r^{-1+delta}. Transporting a
compact part of G0 on which J has one sign (J(Phi_t X) = e^{-t} J(X)) to the circle gives an interval I in (0, pi/2)
with |J(R0 e(alpha))| >= j0 > 0 of one sign, and the locally uniform limit gives
Omega(r, F_r(alpha)) = e^{-tau} [J(R0 e(alpha)) + o(1)] uniformly on I. So on the tube {alpha(X) in I} Omega has one sign
and |Omega| >= c_delta r^{-1/beta - delta} for large r. Let zeta_R = chi(alpha(X)) psi(|X|/R) with nonnegative chi supported
in I, psi supported in (1, 2), each equal to 1 on a subinterval. Then ||grad zeta_R||_2 <= C_delta R^delta, the set where
zeta_R = 1 has area at least c_delta R^{2 - delta} (dA = r j_r dr d alpha), so |int Omega zeta_R| >= c_delta R^{2 - 1/beta - 2 delta}.
Since curl U = -Omega, int Omega zeta_R = int U.(-d_y zeta_R, d_x zeta_R) <= E(R)^{1/2} ||grad zeta_R||_2, and
E(R) >= c_delta R^{4 - 2/beta - 6 delta}. Take delta = eps/6.
(e) The escaping set is open and invariant (W_r > 0 outside a disc). On a compact neighbourhood V of (0, y0) in it,
c e^{(beta - eps) t} <= |Phi_t X| <= C e^{(beta + eps) t} after a common time, and the symmetric-part bound gives
||D Phi_t(X)|| <= C e^{(beta + sigma) t}. In e^t Omega(Phi_t X) = Omega(X) + int_0^t e^s Theta_x(Phi_s X) ds the integrand
and its X-derivative are bounded on V by C e^{(1 - a(beta - eps)) s} and C e^{(1 - beta a + sigma + (a + 1) eps) s}, both
integrable for small eps. So J is C^1 on V and may be differentiated under the integral. At (0, y0),
D Phi_t (1, 0) = (X_1(t), 0) by parity, Theta_xx(0, y) = 2E and Theta_xy(0, y) = 0, so d_x J(0, y0) = J_1(y0) != 0 by (c).
J is odd in x, hence nonzero at (x, y0) for small x > 0, and (d) applies. QED.

### Theorem 32 (restricted: outgoing-amplitude dichotomy under a temperature-gradient bound)
Let beta >= 2, q = 1 - 2/beta, a = 2 - 1/beta and E(R) = int_{R<|X|<2R} |U|^2 dX. Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be
C^infinity on R^2 and satisfy: Theta is even in x and odd in y, Theta(0, y) = 0 for all y, and Theta is not identically
zero (in particular if a0 != 0); Omega is odd in x and in y; U_1 is odd in x and even in y, U_2 is even in x and odd in
y; div U = 0 and d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = Omega; U(X) = o(|X|) uniformly as |X| -> infinity; (V) and (T) hold. Assume in
addition
  (DT) |Theta_x(X)| <= C |X|^{-2/beta} for |X| >= R_*.
Then:
(a) Omega = O(|X|^{-1/beta}) and U = O(|X|^{1-1/beta}).
(b) For R0 large put X0(alpha) = R0 (cos alpha, sin alpha), and let tau(r, alpha) and F_r(alpha) be the time and the
    angle at which the forward orbit of X0(alpha) meets the circle |X| = r. As r -> infinity,
    tau(r, alpha) - (1/beta) log r converges uniformly to a continuous function of alpha, and F_r converges in C^1 to an
    orientation-preserving C^1 diffeomorphism F of the circle that maps each axis direction to itself; the errors in
    tau - (1/beta) log r, F_r and d_alpha F_r are O(r^{-1/beta}), and F_r^{-1} -> F^{-1} in C^1.
(c) Call X escaping if its forward orbit is unbounded (equivalently |Phi_t X| -> infinity). For every escaping X the
    outgoing amplitude J(X) = int_{-inf}^{inf} e^s Theta_x(Phi_s X) ds converges absolutely, J(Phi_t X) = e^{-t} J(X),
    and e^t Omega(Phi_t X) -> J(X) as t -> infinity.
(d) There are continuous functions f and G on the circle, f with the parities of Theta and G odd in x and in y, such
    that, uniformly in phi and in polar components,
      r^{-q} Theta(r, phi) -> f(phi),   r^{1/beta} Omega(r, phi) -> G(phi),   r^{1/beta-1} U(r, phi) -> (-P', a P)(phi),
    where P is the unique 2 pi-periodic solution of -(P'' + a^2 P) = G; P is odd-odd and C^2. f is not identically zero,
    f and G vanish on both axes, and G == 0 if and only if J = 0 at every escaping point.
(e) Exactly one of the following holds.
    (N) G is not identically zero. Then, as R -> infinity,
        lim E(R) R^{-4+2/beta} = [(2^{4-2/beta} - 1)/(4 - 2/beta)] int_0^{2 pi} (P'^2 + a^2 P^2) dphi > 0.
    (C) G == 0. Then Omega = O(|X|^{-2/beta}), U = O(|X|^{1-2/beta}) and E(R) = O(R^{4-4/beta}); moreover
        liminf E(R) R^{-4+4/beta} > 0 by Theorem 23(b), and the conclusions of Theorem 28 hold.
(f) The following are equivalent: G == 0; J = 0 at every escaping point; Omega = O(|X|^{-2/beta});
    U = O(|X|^{1-2/beta}); E(R) = O(R^{4-4/beta}).
(DT) is stated here as a hypothesis; it holds for every A2-broad profile, by Theorem 33(a) at beta = 2 and by
Theorem 41 for beta > 2. The polynomial bounds of
Section 2 are not assumed (they follow from (a) and (d)), and a0 != 0 enters only through Theta != 0. Neither
alternative is shown to occur, and the theorem neither proves nor excludes the existence of A2-broad profiles. G may
vanish on intervals; P and the angular velocity limit a P vanish on both axes. For beta > 2 no regularity of f or G
beyond continuity is asserted, and no rate is given for r^{1/beta} Omega -> G.
Proof. Step 1 (canonical inverse). Let 0 < eta <= 1, omega continuous and odd in x and in y with
|omega(Y)| <= C (1 + |Y|)^{-eta}, and u continuous and sublinear with the A2 velocity parities, div u = 0 and
d_y u_1 - d_x u_2 = omega in D'(R^2). Then u = O(|X|^{1-eta}); the little-o version is Theorem 24, whose proof uses only
these properties. The grouped kernel of Theorem 24 vanishes at X = 0 and has X-derivative O(|Y|^{-2}) for |Y| > 2|X|, so
it is O(|X| |Y|^{-2}) there; the grouped integral u_K converges absolutely, and centred truncations give div u_K = 0 and
the curl relation. For r = |X| large split at |Y| = r/2 and 2r (ungrouped on the symmetric disc of radius 2r). On
|Y| < r/2 the mass and first moments of omega vanish on centred discs by parity, and the Taylor remainder C |Y|^2 r^{-3}
of K(X - Y) gives C r^{-3} (1 + int_1^{r/2} rho^{3-eta} drho) = O(r^{1-eta}); no logarithm appears, since that needs the
resonance eta = 4 (the stream function of r^{-eta} sin 2phi is r^{2-eta} sin(2 phi)/(eta (4 - eta))). The middle region
gives C r^{-eta} int_{|Z|<3r} |K| = O(r^{1-eta}), the outer one C r int_{2r}^inf rho^{-1-eta} drho = O(r^{1-eta}).
Finally u - u_K is harmonic and o(|X|), hence constant, and zero by parity (Section 2).
Step 2 (orbit integral, first decay). Fix 0 < eps < beta/2 and R0 >= R_* such that
(beta - eps) r <= W_r <= (beta + eps) r for r >= R0 (U = o(r)) and the disc |X| < R0 contains an open set where
Theta != 0. The flow is global and backward orbits stay in the disc of radius max(R0, |X|) (Section 2), so integrating
(V) in the form d/ds [e^s Omega(Phi_s X)] = e^s Theta_x(Phi_s X) gives the absolutely convergent
Omega(X) = int_{-inf}^0 e^s Theta_x(Phi_s X) ds. With X(t, alpha) = Phi_t X0(alpha),
R0 e^{(beta-eps) t} <= |X(t, alpha)| <= R0 e^{(beta+eps) t} for t >= 0; each circle r >= R0 is met once, and each X with
|X| >= R0 lies on exactly one orbit X(., alpha) (its backward orbit meets |X| = R0), so uniformity in alpha is
uniformity on |X| >= R0. By (DT), e^t Theta_x(X(t, alpha)) is dominated, uniformly in alpha, by the integrable function
C e^{-(1 - 2 eps/beta) t}, so J_0(alpha) := Omega(X0(alpha)) + int_0^inf e^s Theta_x(X(s, alpha)) ds is continuous
(a uniform limit). Removing the tail (rho = |X(s, alpha)|, ds = drho/W_r, Theta_x/W_r taken at (rho, F_rho(alpha)))
gives the exit formula
  Omega(r, F_r(alpha)) = e^{-tau(r, alpha)} J_0(alpha) - int_r^inf e^{tau(rho, alpha) - tau(r, alpha)} Theta_x/W_r drho.
Since d_r tau = 1/W_r, the exponent is at most p log(rho/r), p = 1/(beta - eps) < 2/beta, and (DT) bounds the remainder
by C r^{-p} int_r^inf rho^{p-1-2/beta} drho <= C r^{-2/beta}, uniformly in alpha. As e^{-tau} <= (r/R0)^{-eta},
eta := 1/(beta + eps), Omega = O(|X|^{-eta}).
Step 3 (outgoing amplitude, (c)). A forward orbit that meets |X| = R0 escapes; otherwise it stays in the disc. So X is
escaping if and only if Phi_{t0} X = X0(alpha0) for some t0 and alpha0; then J(X) converges absolutely (bounded backward
orbit; Step 2 forward), J(X) = e^{t0} J_0(alpha0), the shift s -> s + t gives J(Phi_t X) = e^{-t} J(X), and
e^t Omega(Phi_t X) = int_{-inf}^t e^s Theta_x(Phi_s X) ds -> J(X). So J = 0 on the escaping set if and only if J_0 == 0.
Step 4 (bootstrap and flow coordinates, (b)). Step 1 with eta = 1/(beta + eps) gives U = O(r^{1-eta}). Lift angles with
F_r(0) = 0 and put, as in Theorem 23, d = tau - beta^{-1} log(r/R0), h_r = e^{2 beta d},
A(alpha) = W_r(R0, alpha)/(beta R0), b_r(alpha) = W_r(r, F_r(alpha))/(beta r). As in Theorems 18, 19 and 23
(det D Phi_t = e^{2 beta t}, and the hitting-time derivative is parallel to W),
  d_r F_r = U_phi/(r W_r),   d_r d = -U_r/(beta r W_r),   j_r := d_alpha F_r = A h_r/b_r
(j_r is J_r of Theorems 18, 19, 23 and 28). The radial derivatives are O(r^{-1-eta}) uniformly, so F_r -> F and
d -> d_inf uniformly with errors O(r^{-eta}); hence b_r -> 1 and j_r -> j := A e^{2 beta d_inf} > 0 uniformly. So
F(alpha) = int_0^alpha j is an orientation-preserving C^1 circle diffeomorphism, F_r -> F in C^1, and F fixes the axis
directions as every F_r does. From F(F_r^{-1}(phi)) - phi = (F - F_r)(F_r^{-1}(phi)) and (F_r^{-1})' = 1/j_r(F_r^{-1}),
F_r^{-1} -> F^{-1} in C^1, and tau - beta^{-1} log r = d - beta^{-1} log R0 converges; no derivative of U is used.
Step 5 (thermal and vorticity limits, (a), (d)). By (T), Theta(Phi_t X) = e^{(beta-2) t} Theta(X), and
e^{(beta-2) tau} = (r/R0)^q h_r^{q/2}, so r^{-q} Theta(r, F_r(alpha)) = R0^{-q} theta_0 h_r^{q/2} with
theta_0(alpha) = Theta(X0(alpha)). Multiplying the exit formula by r^{1/beta}, with
r^{1/beta} e^{-tau} = R0^{1/beta} e^{-d},
  r^{1/beta} Omega(r, F_r(alpha)) = R0^{1/beta} e^{-d(r, alpha)} J_0(alpha) + O(r^{-1/beta})   uniformly in alpha.
The right sides converge uniformly; composing with F_r^{-1} -> F^{-1} gives the limits of Theta and Omega in (d), with
f = R0^{-q} (theta_0 e^{beta q d_inf}) o F^{-1} and G = R0^{1/beta} (e^{-d_inf} J_0) o F^{-1}, which inherit the
parities of Theta and Omega. G vanishes on the axes by parity, f by Theta(x, 0) = 0 and Theta(0, y) = 0
(the only use of the latter). theta_0, hence f, is not identically zero, as in Theorem 18 (forward images of the open
set of Step 2 keep Theta != 0 and have area growing like e^{2 beta t}). As e^{-d_inf} > 0, G == 0 if and only if
J_0 == 0, that is (Step 3) J = 0 on the escaping set. Now Omega = O(r^{-1/beta}); Step 1 with eta = 1/beta gives (a),
and Step 4 with this bound gives the rates O(r^{-1/beta}) in (b).
Step 6 (velocity limit). Since a is in [3/2, 2), P'' + a^2 P = 0 has no nonzero 2 pi-periodic solution, so P is unique
and odd-odd. Odd-odd functions carry only the modes sin(2k phi), k >= 1, and 4k^2 > a^2 (no resonance), so
P_k = G_k/(4k^2 - a^2) is summable, P is continuous and, by the equation, C^2. Let Psi_* = chi r^a P(phi), chi smooth
and radial, 0 near 0 and 1 for r >= 2. Psi_* is C^2 and odd-odd; U_* = (-d_y Psi_*, d_x Psi_*) is C^1, sublinear and
divergence-free with the A2 velocity parities and continuous source Omega_* = -Lap Psi_*; for r >= 2,
Lap(r^a P) = r^{a-2} (P'' + a^2 P) gives Omega_* = r^{-1/beta} G and U_* = r^{1-1/beta} (-P', a P) in polar components.
By (d), Omega - Omega_* = o(r^{-1/beta}) uniformly, so Step 1 (little-o, eta = 1/beta) gives U - U_* = o(r^{1-1/beta}):
the cutoff creates no source at the origin, and no harmonic field is added.
Step 7 (energy, (e), (f)). By (d), |U|^2 = r^{2-2/beta} (P'^2 + a^2 P^2 + o(1)) uniformly, hence the full limit
  E(R) R^{-4+2/beta} -> int_1^2 s^{3-2/beta} ds int_0^{2 pi} (P'^2 + a^2 P^2) dphi
                      = [(2^{4-2/beta} - 1)/(4 - 2/beta)] int_0^{2 pi} (P'^2 + a^2 P^2) dphi.
If G is not identically zero, neither is P, and the constant is positive: (N). If G == 0, then J_0 == 0 and the exit
formula gives Omega = O(r^{-2/beta}); Step 1 with eta = 2/beta <= 1 gives U = O(r^q), so
E(R) = O(R^{2+2q}) = O(R^{4-4/beta}). The bounds of Section 2 hold by (a) and (d), and the proofs of Theorems 23 and 28
use a0 != 0 only through Theta != 0, so Theorem 23(b) and Theorem 28 apply: (C). For (f): the first two conditions are
equivalent by (d); the same arguments give G == 0 => Omega = O(r^{-2/beta}) => U = O(r^q) => E(R) = O(R^{4-4/beta}); and
the last forces G == 0, since otherwise the limit in (N) would be positive while
E(R) R^{-4+2/beta} = O(R^{-2/beta}) -> 0, by the exponent gap (4 - 2/beta) - (4 - 4/beta) = 2/beta > 0. QED.

### Theorem 33 (beta = 2: |grad Theta| <= C/r and the natural/critical alternative)
Let beta = 2, W = 2X + U and E(R) = int_{R<|X|<2R} |U|^2 dX. Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be C^infinity on R^2 and satisfy
the hypotheses of Theorem 32 except (DT): Theta is even in x and odd in y, Theta(0, y) = 0 for all y, and Theta is not
identically zero (in particular if a0 != 0); Omega is odd in x and in y; U_1 is odd in x and even in y, U_2 is even in
x and odd in y; div U = 0 and d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = Omega; U(X) = o(|X|) uniformly as |X| -> infinity; (V) and (T) hold,
that is W.grad Theta = 0 and W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x. Every A2-broad profile with beta = 2 satisfies these
hypotheses. Write X = r e(phi), e(phi) = (cos phi, sin phi), with polar components U_r, U_phi; call X escaping if its
forward orbit is unbounded, and let J be the outgoing amplitude, as in Theorem 32(c). Then:
(a) There are R0 and C with |grad Theta(X)| <= C |X|^{-1}, |Omega(X)| <= C |X|^{-1/2} and |U(X)| <= C |X|^{1/2} for
    |X| >= R0. In particular (DT) holds with beta = 2, and all conclusions of Theorem 32 hold, with q = 0 and a = 3/2.
(b) The escaping set is open, invariant under Phi_t for all real t (both time directions) and under x -> -x and
    y -> -y, contains the exterior of a disc and no zero of W, and has full measure: its complement has Lebesgue
    measure zero (det D Phi_t = e^{4t}).
(c) With Q(a, b) := (b, -a) and lambda := (grad Theta . QW)/|W|^2, for every escaping X (indeed for every X with
    W(X) != 0) and every real t,
      grad Theta(Phi_t X) = lambda(X) e^{-4t} Q W(Phi_t X).                                                  (33.1)
    Hence, on the escaping set,
      J(X) = Omega(X) + int_0^inf e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) dt = Omega(X) + lambda(X) I(X),
      I(X) := int_0^inf e^{-3t} W_2(Phi_t X) dt,
    where the integral I converges absolutely and locally uniformly; I and J are continuous on the escaping set,
    e^t Omega(Phi_t X) -> J(X) locally uniformly, J(Phi_t X) = e^{-t} J(X), and J is odd in x and in y.
(d) There is H in C^1(R/2piZ), not identically zero, with H(-phi) = -H(phi), H(pi - phi) = H(phi) and
    H(0) = H(pi/2) = 0 (H is the function f of Theorem 32(d)), and uniformly in phi and in polar components
      Theta(r, .) -> H in C^1(R/2piZ),   r^{1/2} Omega(r, phi) -> G(phi),   r^{-1/2} U(r, phi) -> (-P', (3/2) P)(phi);
    moreover r d_r Theta(r, phi) = O(r^{-1/2}) uniformly. Here G is continuous, odd in x and in y and zero on both
    axes, and P is the unique 2 pi-periodic solution of -(P'' + (9/4) P) = G; P is odd-odd and C^2.
(e) Exactly one of the following holds.
    (N) G is not identically zero. Then lim_{R -> infinity} E(R)/R^3 = (7/3) int_0^{2 pi} (P'^2 + (9/4) P^2) dphi > 0.
    (C) G == 0. Then U is bounded, Omega = O(|X|^{-1}) and E(R) = O(R^2) (and the remaining conclusions of
        Theorem 32(e)(C) hold).
    The following are equivalent: G == 0; J = 0 at every escaping point; U is bounded; Omega = O(|X|^{-1});
    E(R) = O(R^2); E(R) = o(R^3); liminf_{R -> infinity} E(R)/R^3 = 0.
(DT) is not assumed; it is part of (a). The polynomial bounds of Section 2 are not assumed (they follow from (a) and
(d)), and a0 != 0 enters only through Theta != 0. The proof uses the exact invariance of Theta along orbits (kappa = 0)
and does not extend to beta > 2. Neither alternative is shown to occur here, and the theorem neither proves nor excludes
the existence of A2-broad profiles at beta = 2. G may vanish on intervals; this theorem asserts no regularity of G
beyond continuity and no rate for r^{1/2} Omega -> G. Theorem 36 proves that G is C^infinity and gives a remainder
estimate, and Theorem 76 gives an expansion to every finite order for every A2-broad profile at beta = 2.
Proof. Step 1 (exterior and escaping set; (b)). Fix R0 with |U| <= r/4 for r >= R0 (U = o(r)), so that
  (7/4) r <= W_r <= (9/4) r  and  |W| <= (9/4) r   for r >= R0.                                             (33.2)
The flow Phi_t of W is global and det D Phi_t = e^{4t} (Section 2). Along an orbit dr/dt = W_r, so an orbit that
reaches r >= R0 stays there with r increasing at least like e^{7t/4}: X is escaping if and only if |Phi_t X| >= R0 for
some t >= 0, and otherwise |Phi_t X| < R0 for all t >= 0. In backward time r decreases at rate at least (7/4) r while
r >= R0, so every X with |X| >= R0 meets the circle |X| = R0 exactly once. With X0(alpha) = R0 e(alpha),
X(t, alpha) = Phi_t X0(alpha), and tau(r, alpha), F_r(alpha) the time and angle at which X(., alpha) meets |X| = r,
every point with |X| >= R0 is X(tau(r, alpha), alpha) for exactly one alpha, and by (33.2)
  (4/9) log(r/R0) <= tau(r, alpha) <= (4/7) log(r/R0),   |X(t, alpha)| >= R0 e^{7t/4}   (t >= 0).           (33.3)
The escaping set is open (if |Phi_{t0} X| > R0, the same holds near X), invariant for all real times (Phi_s X has the
same forward tail), invariant under S(x, y) = (-x, y) and S(x, y) = (x, -y) (the parities give W(SX) = S W(X), hence
Phi_t S = S Phi_t), and contains no zero of W. Its complement lies in K0 := {X : |Phi_t X| <= R0 for all t >= 0},
which is closed and satisfies Phi_t(K0) in K0 for t >= 0; so e^{4t} |K0| = |Phi_t(K0)| <= pi R0^2 for all t >= 0, and
|K0| = 0. If K is a compact subset of the escaping set, each point of K has a neighbourhood and a time after which all
orbits from it lie in |X| > R0; a finite subcover gives t_K with |Phi_t X| > R0 for t >= t_K and X in K, and
continuity on [0, t_K] x K with (33.2) gives |W(Phi_t X)| <= C_K e^{9t/4} for t >= 0 and X in K.
Step 2 (cofactor identity). Where W != 0, (T) says that grad Theta is orthogonal to W; QW is orthogonal to W with
|QW| = |W|, so grad Theta = lambda QW with lambda smooth on {W != 0}. Let A = D Phi_t(X). Differentiating
Theta(Phi_t X) = Theta(X) (Section 2, kappa = 0) gives A^T grad Theta(Phi_t X) = grad Theta(X). For every invertible
2 x 2 matrix A, A^{-T} Q = (det A)^{-1} Q A (direct multiplication), and A W(X) = W(Phi_t X) (differentiate
Phi_t(Phi_s X) = Phi_s(Phi_t X) in s at s = 0). With det A = e^{4t},
