grad Theta(Phi_t X) = lambda(X) A^{-T} Q W(X) = lambda(X) e^{-4t} Q A W(X), which is (33.1). No bound on DU or on
D Phi_t is used.
Step 3 (first gradient bound). On |X| = R0, |W| >= W_r >= (7/4) R0, so |lambda| <= C there. (33.1) at X0(alpha) and
t = tau(r, alpha), with (33.2) and (33.3), gives
|grad Theta(r, F_r(alpha))| <= C e^{-4 tau(r, alpha)} r <= C r (r/R0)^{-16/9} <= C r^{-7/9} for r >= R0, uniformly
in alpha, hence on all of |X| >= R0.
Step 4 (vorticity O(r^{-4/9})). By (V), d/dt [e^t Omega(X(t, alpha))] = e^t Theta_x(X(t, alpha)), and by Step 3 and
(33.3) the right side is at most C e^{t (1 - (7/4)(7/9))} = C e^{-13t/36}, uniformly in alpha. So
J_0(alpha) := Omega(X0(alpha)) + int_0^inf e^s Theta_x(X(s, alpha)) ds converges uniformly and is continuous (J_0 of
Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 32, obtained here without (DT)), and the substitution rho = |X(s, alpha)|,
ds = drho/W_r, gives the exit formula
  Omega(r, F_r(alpha)) = e^{-tau(r, alpha)} J_0(alpha)
                         - int_r^inf e^{tau(rho, alpha) - tau(r, alpha)} Theta_x/W_r drho
with Theta_x/W_r taken at (rho, F_rho(alpha)). Since d_r tau = 1/W_r <= 4/(7r), e^{tau(rho) - tau(r)} is at most
(rho/r)^{4/7}, and with Step 3 and W_r >= (7/4) rho the integral is at most
C r^{-4/7} int_r^inf rho^{4/7 - 7/9 - 1} drho = C r^{-7/9}, because 7/9 - 4/7 = 13/63 > 0. The first term is at most
C (r/R0)^{-4/9} by (33.3). So |Omega| <= C r^{-4/9} for r >= R0.
Step 5 (U = O(r^{5/9})). Omega is continuous and odd in x and in y with |Omega(Y)| <= C (1 + |Y|)^{-4/9} on R^2, and U
is continuous and sublinear with the A2 velocity parities, div U = 0 and d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = Omega. The inverse
estimate in Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 32, with eta = 4/9, gives U = O(r^{5/9}).
Step 6 (|grad Theta| <= C/r). Put D(r, alpha) := tau(r, alpha) - (1/2) log(r/R0) (the function d of Theorem 32 at
beta = 2). Then d_r D = 1/W_r - 1/(2r) = -U_r/(2 r W_r) = O(r^{-13/9}) uniformly by Step 5 and (33.2), and D = 0 at
r = R0, so |D| <= C for r >= R0. As e^{-4 tau} = (r/R0)^{-2} e^{-4D}, (33.1) as in Step 3 gives
|grad Theta(r, F_r(alpha))| <= C r^{-2} |W| <= C r^{-1} for r >= R0. This is (DT) of Theorem 32 with beta = 2
(2/beta = 1) and R_* = R0. Steps 1 to 6 use no conclusion of Theorem 32, only Step 1 of its proof, so the argument is
not circular.
Step 7 ((a), (d), (e)). The hypotheses of Theorem 32 now hold with beta = 2, q = 0, a = 3/2, a^2 = 9/4 and
1/beta = 1/2. Theorem 32(a) gives Omega = O(r^{-1/2}) and U = O(r^{1/2}); with Step 6 this is (a). Theorem 32(d) gives
the limits of Omega and U in (d), the stated properties of G and P, and Theta(r, .) -> f uniformly, with f continuous,
not identically zero, with the parities of Theta and zero on both axes. Enlarge R0 so that Theorem 32(b) applies on
|X| = R0. By (T), Theta(r, F_r(alpha)) = theta_0(alpha), where theta_0(alpha) := Theta(X0(alpha)) is smooth, so
Theta(r, .) = theta_0 o F_r^{-1}; as F_r^{-1} -> F^{-1} in C^1 (Theorem 32(b)), Theta(r, .) converges in C^1 to
H := theta_0 o F^{-1}, which is C^1 and equals f. The polar form W_r d_r Theta + (U_phi/r) d_phi Theta = 0 of (T),
with d_phi Theta bounded, U = O(r^{1/2}) and (33.2), gives r d_r Theta = O(r^{-1/2}). This proves (d). At beta = 2 the
exponents of Theorem 32(e), (f) are -4 + 2/beta = -3, 4 - 4/beta = 2, -2/beta = -1 and 1 - 2/beta = 0, and the
constant is (2^3 - 1)/3 = int_1^2 s^2 ds = 7/3; so (N) and (C) are Theorem 32(e), and the first five conditions of
the list in (e) are equivalent by Theorem 32(f) (U = O(1) outside a disc is boundedness of U, by continuity).
E(R) = O(R^2) implies E(R) = o(R^3), which implies liminf E(R)/R^3 = 0; and the last implies G == 0, because under (N)
E(R)/R^3 converges to a positive limit. This proves (e).
Step 8 ((b), (c)). (b) is Step 1, and (33.1) is Step 2. For X escaping, W(X) != 0 and the first component of (33.1)
is Theta_x(Phi_t X) = lambda(X) e^{-4t} W_2(Phi_t X). Integrating
d/dt [e^t Omega(Phi_t X)] = e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) (by (V)) over [0, T] gives
  e^T Omega(Phi_T X) = Omega(X) + int_0^T e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) dt
                     = Omega(X) + lambda(X) int_0^T e^{-3t} W_2(Phi_t X) dt.
On a compact K in the escaping set, W != 0, so lambda is bounded, and |e^{-3t} W_2(Phi_t X)| <= C_K e^{-3t/4} by
Step 1. So the integral converges absolutely and uniformly on K as T -> infinity, I and J are continuous,
e^T Omega(Phi_T X) converges locally uniformly, and by Theorem 32(c) its limit is J(X), which gives both formulas for
J. The relation J(Phi_t X) = e^{-t} J(X) is in Theorem 32(c), and the oddness of J follows from Phi_t S = S Phi_t and
the oddness of Omega in x and in y. QED.
Remark. By (a), Theorem 32 applies in Theorem 35(c) without further hypothesis, and by (c) the limit J of Theorem 31(d)
exists locally uniformly on the whole escaping set. The estimate |grad Theta| <= C r^{-7/9} of Step 3 serves only to start
the argument; the final rate C/r of (a) comes from the bounded correction D of Step 6. The full-measure statement in
(b) is not used in the proofs of (a), (c), (d) and (e).

### Theorem 34 (beta = 2: the outgoing amplitude is nonzero near the origin, so the natural tail is forced)
Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile, and let the escaping set, the amplitude J, the angular functions H, G,
P and the annular energy E(R) be as in Theorem 33. Then:
(a) there is delta > 0 such that sgn(a0) J(x, y) >= (3 |a0|/40) x y at every escaping point with x > 0, y > 0 and
    x^2 + y^2 < delta^2;
(b) alternative (N) of Theorem 33 holds: G is not identically zero, G has the sign of a0 on a nonempty open interval of
    angles in (0, pi/2), and
      lim_{R -> infinity} E(R) R^{-3} = (7/3) int_0^{2 pi} (P'^2 + (9/4) P^2) dphi > 0;
(c) consequently U is unbounded and E(R) is not o(R^3). The hypotheses of Theorems 18, 20 and 25, and of Theorems 19,
    23 and 28 at beta = 2, each imply E(R) = o(R^3) (for Theorem 20 by Holder's inequality on the annuli together with
    |U| <= C |X|^{1/2} from Theorem 33), so at beta = 2 these theorems are contained in (b).
The theorem does not assert that G has one sign in the open quadrant, and it neither constructs nor excludes a profile
in alternative (N).
Proof. Step 1 (jets at the origin). By Section 1 with beta = 2, c = 6, DW(0) = diag(-4, 8) and 5 b0 = 2 a0. Smooth
division, using the parities, gives Theta = x^2 y a, Omega = x y b, W_1 = x A_1, W_2 = y B with a, b, A_1, B smooth
and even in x and in y, a(0) = a0, b(0) = 2 a0/5, A_1(0) = -4, B(0) = 8. As d_x a is odd in x, x d_x a = O(|X|^2),
so Theta_x = x y (2 a + x d_x a) = x y (2 a0 + O(|X|^2)). Fix delta_0 > 0 with B >= 4 on the disc |X| < delta_0;
then W_2 > 0, and so W != 0, at every point of that disc with x, y > 0.
Step 2 (cofactor coefficient). Where W != 0, (T) with kappa = 0 says W . grad Theta = 0, so grad Theta = lambda Q W
with Q(a, b) = (b, -a) and lambda = grad Theta . Q W/|W|^2, and the first component gives Theta_x = lambda W_2. In the
quarter disc of Step 1, lambda = Theta_x/W_2 = x (2 a + x d_x a)/B = x (a0/4 + O(|X|^2)) and
  Omega - lambda y = x y [b - (2 a + x d_x a)/B] = x y (3 a0/20 + O(|X|^2)).
Step 3 (a positive weighted position). Both axes are invariant, so by uniqueness the open first quadrant is invariant
and y(Phi_t X) > 0 for every t when x, y > 0. Fix 0 < eps < 1. Since U = o(|X|), |W(X)| <= (2 + eps)|X| + C_eps, so
|Phi_t X| <= C_X e^{(2 + eps) t} for t >= 0, and
  V(X) := int_0^inf e^{-3t} y(Phi_t X) dt
converges absolutely, with V(X) > 0 for x, y > 0. As d/dt y(Phi_t X) = W_2(Phi_t X), integration by parts on [0, T]
and T -> infinity give int_0^inf e^{-3t} W_2(Phi_t X) dt = -y + 3 V(X), the boundary term e^{-3T} y(Phi_T X) tending
to 0. By Theorem 33(c), J(X) = Omega(X) + lambda(X) int_0^inf e^{-3t} W_2(Phi_t X) dt at escaping X, hence
  J = Omega - lambda y + 3 lambda V   on the escaping set.
Step 4 ((a)). Choose 0 < delta <= delta_0 such that, for x, y > 0 and |X| < delta, sgn(a0) lambda > 0 and
sgn(a0) (Omega - lambda y) >= (3 |a0|/40) x y (Step 2). At escaping points there, 3 lambda V has the sign of a0 or is
0, so sgn(a0) J >= sgn(a0) (Omega - lambda y) >= (3 |a0|/40) x y. No expansion of J itself is used.
Step 5 ((b), (c)). The escaping set is open and of full measure (Theorem 33(b)), so it meets the quarter disc of (a)
in a nonempty open set N, on which J is nonzero with the sign of a0. By Theorem 33(e) G is not identically zero, and
(N) holds. The orbit of a point of N crosses the circle |X| = R0 of Theorem 32 at some angle alpha0 in (0, pi/2), where
J_0(alpha0) = e^{-t0} J(X) has the sign of a0 (J(Phi_t X) = e^{-t} J(X)); J_0 is continuous, so it keeps that sign on
an open interval I containing alpha0, and G = R0^{1/2} (e^{-d_inf} J_0) o F^{-1} (Theorem 32, Step 5) has the sign of
a0 on the open interval F(I), contained in (0, pi/2) since F fixes the axis directions. The limit in (b) is
Theorem 33(e)(N). For (c): a bounded U gives E(R) = O(R^2); the hypotheses of Theorems 18, 19, 23, 25 and 28 at
beta = 2 give E(R) = O(R^2) directly; if int |U|^p < infinity, then on the annulus A_R = {R < |X| < 2R},
int_{A_R} |U|^2 <= (C R^{1/2})^{2-p} int_{A_R} |U|^p for p <= 2 and
int_{A_R} |U|^2 <= (int_{A_R} |U|^p)^{2/p} |A_R|^{1-2/p} for p > 2, and both are o(R^3). Each contradicts (b). QED.
Remark. The argument uses kappa = 0 twice: in grad Theta being parallel to Q W, and in the exact factor e^{-4t} of
Theorem 33(c). Both uses are specific to beta = 2, and no version of the argument is claimed for beta > 2.

### Theorem 35 (beta = 2: an outgoing endpoint carries an invariant region of potential flow)
Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile, and let Q be an endpoint of the arc C of Theorem 16 in the open
first quadrant (so W(Q) = 0 and DW(Q) has eigenvalues 4 and 0). Suppose that a C^2 invariant
centre curve of Q contains no zero of W on its branch opposite to C near Q, and that the flow on that branch points away
from Q. Then:
(a) every neighbourhood of Q contains a nonempty open set D in the open first quadrant which is backward invariant and
    such that every backward orbit from D tends to Q;
(b) S = union_{t >= 0} Phi_t(D) is open, connected, invariant, contained in the open first quadrant and of infinite
    area, and Theta = Theta(Q), Omega = 0 on S; hence U is harmonic, and real analytic, on S;
(c) the angular limits H = f and G of Theorem 32, which apply at beta = 2 by Theorem 33(a), satisfy H = Theta(Q) and
    G = 0 on a nonempty open interval of angles.
Proof. (a) Straighten the centre curve to z = 0 in a C^2 chart (z, s) with Q = (0, 0), C on the side s < 0 and the
outgoing branch s > 0. Invariance of z = 0 and division give
  dz/dt = a(z, s) z,   ds/dt = b(s) + z c(z, s),
with a, c continuous, b of class C^1, a(0, 0) = 4, b(0) = b'(0) = 0 and b(s) > 0 for 0 < s <= delta. Shrink the chart so
that a >= 2, |b'| <= 1/4, |c| <= C0, choose eta > 0 with eta C0 <= 1/2 and let D = {0 < s < delta, |z| < eta b(s)}, an
open set of positive area (b > 0 on (0, delta]). In backward time tau, z' = -a z and s' = -b - z c. In D, |z c| <= b/2,
so -(3/2) b(s) <= s' <= -(1/2) b(s) < 0, and for z != 0, R = |z|/b(s) satisfies
  (log R)' = -a + b'(s)(1 + z c/b(s)) <= -2 + 3/8 < -1.
Hence the boundary parts R = eta and s = delta are entered, z = 0 is invariant, and s stays positive (b(s) <= C s gives
s' >= -(3C/2) s); so D is backward invariant. s decreases to a limit l >= 0, and l > 0 is impossible since s' <= -b/2
is bounded away from 0 near l; |z(tau)| <= |z(0)| e^{-2 tau}. So every backward orbit from D tends to Q. Choosing delta
small puts D in any given neighbourhood of Q, and D lies in the open first quadrant if the neighbourhood does.
(b) The flow is complete since |W| <= C(1 + |X|). For X in D, invariance of Theta (kappa = 0) and continuity give
Theta(X) = lim Theta(Phi_{-tau} X) = Theta(Q). D is open, so Theta_x = 0 on D, and (V) gives
Omega(Phi_{-tau} X) = e^tau Omega(X); the left side stays bounded, so Omega(X) = 0. As D is backward invariant, the sets
Phi_t(D), t >= 0, increase with t; their union S is open and connected, Phi_s(S) = S for all real s, and S lies in the
open first quadrant because the axes are invariant. Theta = Theta(Q) on S by invariance; then Theta_x = 0 on S and
Omega(Phi_t X) = e^{-t} Omega(X) propagates Omega = 0 from D to S. Since det D Phi_t = e^{4t},
|S| >= |Phi_t(D)| = e^{4t} |D| for every t >= 0. On S, div U = 0 and curl U = 0, so the components of U are harmonic.
(c) Take R0 so large that W_r > 0 for |X| >= R0 and D lies in the disc of radius R0. Some orbit from D crosses the circle
|X| = R0, since otherwise Phi_t(D) would stay in the disc, contradicting the area growth. S is open and invariant, so
it contains an open arc I of this circle with closure in the open quadrant, and the orbits from I escape and stay in S.
So Theta(r, F_r(alpha)) = Theta(Q) and Omega(r, F_r(alpha)) = 0 for alpha in I and r >= R0. By Theorem 32(b), F_r -> F
and F_r^{-1} -> F^{-1} uniformly, F a C^1 diffeomorphism; for phi in a compact subinterval of F(I),
F_r^{-1}(phi) lies in I for large r, so Theta(r, phi) = Theta(Q) and Omega(r, phi) = 0 there, and the uniform limits of
Theorem 32(d) (q = 0 at beta = 2) give H = Theta(Q) and G = 0 on F(I). QED.
Remark. With D a small ball, the proof also applies at every stagnation point in the open first quadrant that is a
hyperbolic source. The theorem does not exclude an outgoing endpoint; incoming endpoints and zeros of W accumulating at
Q are not covered.

### Theorem 36 (beta = 2: smooth natural tail with O_infty remainders)
Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 33 (every A2-broad profile with beta = 2 does); no decay,
polynomial or derivative bound is assumed beyond U(X) = o(|X|) uniformly. Let H, G, P be as in Theorem 33(d),
X = r e(phi), e_r = e(phi), e_phi = e(phi + pi/2), and D^k the Cartesian derivatives of order k. For f smooth on
|X| >= R1, f = O_infty(r^m) means: for every integer k >= 0 there is C_k with |D^k f(X)| <= C_k |X|^{m-k} for
|X| >= R1. Put theta_0(X) = H(phi), omega_0(X) = r^{-1/2} G(phi), psi_0(X) = r^{3/2} P(phi) and u_0 = (-d_y psi_0,
d_x psi_0) = r^{1/2} (-P'(phi) e_r + (3/2) P(phi) e_phi). Then -Lap psi_0 = omega_0 for r > 0, and:
(a) H, G and P are C^infinity on R/2piZ; G and P are odd in x and in y, and P is the unique 2 pi-periodic solution of
    -(P'' + (9/4) P) = G.
(b) Theta - theta_0 = O_infty(r^{-1/2}), Omega - omega_0 = O_infty(r^{-1}) and U - u_0 = O_infty(1). In particular,
    for every k >= 0, D^k Theta = O(r^{-k}), D^k Omega = O(r^{-1/2-k}) and D^k U = O(r^{1/2-k}).
(c) For all 0 < a < b and k >= 0 there are C and R2 such that for R >= R2, with C^k norms on {a <= |X| <= b},
      ||Theta(R .) - theta_0|| + ||R^{1/2} Omega(R .) - omega_0|| + ||R^{-1/2} U(R .) - u_0|| <= C R^{-1/2}.    (36.1)
(d) Let R0 >= 1 satisfy (33.2) for r >= R0, let tau(r, alpha) and F_r(alpha) be the time and angle at which the
    forward orbit of R0 e(alpha) meets |X| = r >= R0, and d := tau - (1/2) log(r/R0) (the d of Theorem 32 at beta = 2;
    D in Step 6 of the proof of Theorem 33). Then F_r -> F, F_r^{-1} -> F^{-1} and d(r, .) -> d_inf in every
    C^k(R/2piZ), with errors O(r^{-1/2}) in every C^k; F is a C^infinity orientation-preserving circle diffeomorphism
    fixing each axis direction, and d_inf is C^infinity. The amplitude J(R0 e(.)) of Theorem 33(c) is C^infinity,
    H = Theta(R0 e(.)) o F^{-1} and G = R0^{1/2} (e^{-d_inf} J(R0 e(.))) o F^{-1}.
The constants depend on k and on the annulus.
Proof. Fix 0 < gamma < 1 and R0 as in (d). By Theorem 33(a) and continuity, |Omega| <= C r^{-1/2} and |U| <= C r^{1/2}
for r >= R0. Constants C, C_k do not depend on R, r or the angle.
Step 1 (hitting coordinates). Put X(t, alpha) = Phi_t(R0 e(alpha)); lift angles with F_r(0) = 0. Each X with |X| >= R0
lies on exactly one such orbit (Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 33); the axes are invariant, so F_r fixes the axis
directions and F_r(alpha) - alpha is 2 pi-periodic and bounded. As W is C^infinity and d_t |X| = W_r > 0 for
|X| >= R0, tau, F_r and d are C^infinity on [R0, inf) x R/2piZ (implicit functions). By Step 4 of the proof of
Theorem 32 at beta = 2 (det D Phi_t = e^{4t}; the hitting-time term is parallel to W),
  d_r F_r = U_phi/(r W_r),   d_r d = -U_r/(2 r W_r),   j_r := d_alpha F_r = A e^{4d}/b_r,                       (36.2)
with fields at r e(F_r(alpha)), A(alpha) = W_r(R0 e(alpha))/(2 R0) and b_r = W_r/(2r); no derivative of U enters. By
(33.2), 7/8 <= b_r <= 9/8 and |d_r F_r| + |d_r d| <= C r^{1/2} r^{-2} = C r^{-3/2}; as d(R0, .) = 0, |d| <= C and
C^{-1} <= j_r <= C.
Step 2 (exact transport formulas). Let theta_c, omega_c, lambda_c be the traces of Theta, Omega and lambda
(Theorem 33(c)) on |X| = R0, as functions of alpha; they are C^infinity, as |W| >= (7/4) R0 there. By (T) with
kappa = 0 (Section 2), Theta(r e(F_r(alpha))) = theta_c(alpha). The finite-time formula of Step 8 of the proof of
Theorem 33 at X = R0 e(alpha), T = tau(r, alpha), with e^{-tau} = (R0/r)^{1/2} e^{-d}, rho = |X(t, alpha)|,
dt = drho/W_r, e^{-3t} = (R0/rho)^{3/2} e^{-3d(rho, alpha)} and W_2 = W_r sin phi + U_phi cos phi, gives exactly
  r^{1/2} Omega(r e(F_r(alpha))) = g(r, alpha) := R0^{1/2} e^{-d} [omega_c + lambda_c I_r],
  I_r := R0^{3/2} int_{R0}^r rho^{-3/2} Z(rho, .) drho,   Z := e^{-3d} [sin F_rho + (U_phi/W_r) cos F_rho],     (36.3)
fields at rho e(F_rho(alpha)). As I_r(alpha) = int_0^tau e^{-3t} W_2(X(t, alpha)) dt, I_r -> I(R0 e(.)) =: I_inf, and
J_0 := J(R0 e(.)) = omega_c + lambda_c I_inf by Theorem 33(c).
Step 3 (local div-curl estimate). For 0 < a' < a < b < b', A = {a <= |X| <= b}, A' = {a' <= |X| <= b'} and k >= 0
there is C = C(A, A', k, gamma) such that every C^infinity v near A' with div v = 0, d_y v_1 - d_x v_2 = w obeys
  ||v||_{C^{k+1,gamma}(A)} <= C (sup_{A'} |v| + ||w||_{C^{k,gamma}(A')}),
  ||v||_{C^{0,gamma}(A)} <= C sup_{A'} (|v| + |w|).                                                             (36.4)
This is the interior Schauder estimate for the div-curl system. Take eta in C_c^infinity(int A') with eta = 1 near A,
K(Z) = (Z_2, -Z_1)/(2 pi |Z|^2) and v_N := K * (eta w), the velocity of the Newtonian potential of eta w. D^{k+1} v_N
is a second derivative of the Newtonian potential of D^k(eta w), so Gilbarg-Trudinger, Lemma 4.4 bounds it in
C^{0,gamma} by C ||w||_{C^{k,gamma}(A')}, and |D^j v_N| <= C sup |D^j(eta w)| for j <= k. For sup|w| alone, split
v_N(X1) - v_N(X2) at |X1 - Y| = 2h, h = |X1 - X2|, and use |K(X1 - Y) - K(X2 - Y)| <= C h |X1 - Y|^{-2} on the far
part: the modulus is C sup|w| h (1 + |log h|) <= C sup|w| h^gamma. Near A, v - v_N is div- and curl-free, so harmonic,
and bounded by sup|v| + C sup|w|; interior harmonic estimates bound it in every C^m(A). Scaling: for R >= 8 R0,
u_R(X) := R^{-1/2} U(RX) and w_R(X) := R^{1/2} Omega(RX) satisfy div u_R = 0 and d_y (u_R)_1 - d_x (u_R)_2 =
R^{-1/2} R Omega(RX) = w_R, |u_R| + |w_R| <= C on {1/8 <= |X| <= 8}, and D^j u_R(X) = R^{j-1/2} (D^j U)(RX).
Step 4 (induction on normalized annuli). Let Q = [1/2, 2] x R/2piZ, S = {1/2 <= |X| <= 2}. A function g(r, alpha),
r >= R0, is in N^k if (s, alpha) -> g(Rs, alpha) is bounded in C^{k,gamma}(Q) uniformly in R >= 8 R0 (for circle maps
use F_r(alpha) - alpha). Standard facts: (N1) [1/2, 2] may be replaced by [1/4, 4] (rescalings R/2, 2R; smoothness for
bounded R); (N2) X = s e(phi) identifies C^{k,gamma}(S) with C^{k,gamma}(Q) up to constants, also for polar components
of fields; (N3) C^{k,gamma}(Q) is an algebra stable under exp and 1/g (g >= c > 0), and g(s, phi(s, alpha)) is bounded
in C^{k,gamma}(Q) if g and phi - alpha are and (s, alpha) -> phi is Lipschitz (needed at k = 0); (N4) if
sup_r ||g(r, .)||_{C^{k,gamma}} < infinity and d_s[g(Rs, .)] is bounded in C^{k,gamma}(Q), then g is in N^k: a
derivative of order <= k containing d_s is a derivative of order <= k - 1 of d_s g, hence bounded and Lipschitz, and
d_alpha^k g is C^gamma in alpha and, as d_s d_alpha^k g = d_alpha^k d_s g, Lipschitz in s. Write (u_R)_r, (u_R)_phi
for the polar components of u_R at s e(F_{Rs}(alpha)); so U_r = R^{1/2} (u_R)_r, U_phi = R^{1/2} (u_R)_phi at
Rs e(F_{Rs}(alpha)). Hypothesis H_k: u_R is bounded in C^{k,gamma}(S) uniformly in R >= 8 R0, F_r(alpha) - alpha is in
N^k, and (s, alpha) -> F_{Rs}(alpha) is Lipschitz uniformly in R. H_0 holds by the second bound of (36.4) (a' = 1/4,
a = 1/2, b = 2, b' = 4), j_r <= C and d_s F_{Rs} = R (d_r F_r)(Rs) = O(R^{-1/2}). Assume H_k.
(i) The correction d. With n := W_r/r = 2 + R^{-1/2} s^{-1} (u_R)_r >= 7/4, (36.2) reads
  d_s F_{Rs} = R^{-1/2} s^{-2} (u_R)_phi/n,   d_s d(Rs, alpha) = -R^{-1/2} s^{-2} (u_R)_r/(2n);                 (36.5)
by H_k, (N2) and (N3), R^{1/2} times either is bounded in C^{k,gamma}(Q). At s = 1, ||d_r F_r||_{C^{k,gamma}} +
||d_r d(r, .)||_{C^{k,gamma}} <= C r^{-3/2} (r >= 8 R0); integration from d(R0, .) = 0 (smoothness for r <= 8 R0)
bounds d(r, .) in C^{k,gamma} uniformly, and (N4) puts d in N^k. No angular derivative of order k + 1 is used.
(ii) The hitting map gains one derivative. By (i), H_k and (N3), j = d_alpha F_{Rs} = A e^{4d}/b_{Rs} (b_{Rs} = n/2)
is bounded in C^{k,gamma}(Q), and so is d_s F_{Rs} by (36.5); hence F_r(alpha) - alpha is in N^{k+1}. The gain comes
from det D Phi_t = e^{4t}: j involves u_R only at order k. The inverses B_R(s, .) := F_{Rs}^{-1} satisfy
d_phi B_R = 1/j(s, B_R) and d_s B_R = -(d_s F_{Rs})(s, B_R)/j(s, B_R), with j >= C^{-1}; starting from their Lipschitz
bound, (N3) applied once per order bounds B_R(s, phi) - phi in C^{k+1,gamma}(Q).
(iii) Vorticity, then velocity. Z = e^{-3d} [sin F_{Rs} + R^{-1/2} s^{-1} n^{-1} (u_R)_phi cos F_{Rs}] is in N^k, and
sup_rho ||Z(rho, .)||_{C^{k,gamma}} < infinity. Angular derivatives of order <= k pass under the finite integral in
(36.3), and the gamma-seminorm of an integral is at most the integral of the seminorms, so ||I_r||_{C^{k,gamma}} <=
C R0^{3/2} int_{R0}^inf rho^{-3/2} drho <= C for all r; as d_s I_{Rs} = R0^{3/2} R^{-1/2} s^{-3/2} Z(Rs, .), (N4) puts
I_r, hence g, in N^k. By (ii) and (N3), (Rs)^{1/2} Omega(Rs e(phi)) = g(Rs, B_R(s, phi)) is bounded in C^{k,gamma}(Q);
as w_R(s e(phi)) = s^{-1/2} (Rs)^{1/2} Omega(Rs e(phi)), (N2) and (N1) bound w_R in C^{k,gamma}({1/4 <= |X| <= 4}),
and the first bound of (36.4) bounds u_R in C^{k+1,gamma}(S). This is H_{k+1}. Hence d, F_r(alpha) - alpha, I_r, Z and
g are in every N^k, and B_R(s, phi) - phi is bounded in every C^k(Q).
Step 5 (limits and rates; (d), and (b) for Theta and Omega). By (36.5) at s = 1, d_r I_r = R0^{3/2} r^{-3/2} Z(r, .)
and Step 4, for every k (angular norms, r >= 8 R0)
  ||d_r F_r||_{C^k} + ||d_r d(r, .)||_{C^k} + ||d_r I_r||_{C^k} <= C_k r^{-3/2}.                                (36.6)
So F_r, d(r, .), I_r converge in every C^k(R/2piZ), with errors <= C_k int_r^inf rho^{-3/2} drho = 2 C_k r^{-1/2}, to
C^infinity limits F, d_inf, I_inf; hence J_0 = omega_c + lambda_c I_inf is C^infinity and g(r, .) converges to
g_inf := R0^{1/2} e^{-d_inf} J_0 at the same rate. As |b_r - 1| <= C r^{-1/2}, F' = A e^{4 d_inf} >= C^{-1}, and F
fixes the axis directions as each F_r does: F is an orientation-preserving C^infinity circle diffeomorphism, and
B := F^{-1} is C^infinity. On Q the s-derivatives of F_{Rs}, d(Rs, .) and I_{Rs} are R^{-1/2} times functions bounded
in every C^k ((36.5), (iii)), and the limits do not depend on s; so F_{Rs} - F, d(Rs, .) - d_inf, I_{Rs} - I_inf and
g(Rs, .) - g_inf are O(R^{-1/2}) in every C^k(Q). Next, F(B_R) - F(B) = (F - F_{Rs})(B_R) and F' >= C^{-1} give
|B_R - B| <= C R^{-1/2}. Differentiate the identities of (ii) and B' = 1/F'(B), and split h_1(s, B_R) - h_2(B) =
[h_1(s, B_R) - h_2(B_R)] + [h_2(B_R) - h_2(B)] with h_2 smooth; induction on the order gives ||B_R - B||_{C^k(Q)} <=
C_k R^{-1/2}, which at s = 1 is the rate of F_r^{-1} -> F^{-1}. Now Theta(r e(phi)) = theta_c(F_r^{-1}(phi)) and
r^{1/2} Omega(r e(phi)) = g(r, F_r^{-1}(phi)) converge uniformly to theta_c o F^{-1} and g_inf o F^{-1}, which are H
and G by Theorem 33(d); both are C^infinity, and (d) is proved. The same splitting shows that Theta(Rs e(phi)) -
H(phi) = theta_c(B_R) - theta_c(B) and (Rs)^{1/2} Omega(Rs e(phi)) - G(phi) = g(Rs, B_R) - g_inf(B) are O(R^{-1/2}) in
every C^k(Q). As theta_0(RX) = theta_0(X) and R^{1/2} omega_0(Rs e(phi)) = s^{-1/2} G(phi), (N2) gives
||(Theta - theta_0)(R .)||_{C^k(S)} + R^{1/2} ||(Omega - omega_0)(R .)||_{C^k(S)} <= C_k R^{-1/2}, and
D^j [f(R .)] = R^j (D^j f)(R .) gives Theta - theta_0 = O_infty(r^{-1/2}) and Omega - omega_0 = O_infty(r^{-1}).
Step 6 (velocity; (a), (b) for U, (c)). P is C^2 and unique (Theorem 33(d)); P'' = -G - (9/4) P puts P in C^{m+2} when
P is in C^m, so P is C^infinity, and with Theorem 33(d) and Step 5 this is (a). Lap(r^{3/2} P) = r^{-1/2}
(P'' + (9/4) P) gives -Lap psi_0 = omega_0 for r > 0, and grad psi_0 = r^{1/2} ((3/2) P e_r + P' e_phi) gives the
polar form of u_0. Let chi be smooth and radial, 0 for r <= 1 and 1 for r >= 2, u_* := (-d_y (chi psi_0),
d_x (chi psi_0)) and omega_* := -Lap(chi psi_0). They are C^infinity on R^2; chi psi_0 is odd in x and in y, so u_*
has the A2 velocity parities; u_* is divergence-free and O(|X|^{1/2}), and (u_*, omega_*) = (u_0, omega_0) for r >= 2.
So u := U - u_* is continuous and sublinear with the A2 velocity parities, div u = 0 and d_y u_1 - d_x u_2 = f :=
Omega - omega_*, where f is continuous, odd in x and in y, and |f| <= C (1 + |X|)^{-1} by Step 5. Step 1 of the proof
of Theorem 32 with eta = 1 gives u = O(1), so U - u_0 is bounded on r >= 2. For large R, e_R(X) := (U - u_0)(RX) is
bounded on {1/8 <= |X| <= 8}, div e_R = 0, d_y (e_R)_1 - d_x (e_R)_2 = f_R := R (Omega - omega_0)(R .), and
|D^j f_R(X)| = R^{1+j} |(D^j (Omega - omega_0))(RX)| <= C_j there for every j (Step 5). So f_R is bounded in every
C^{k,gamma}({1/4 <= |X| <= 4}), (36.4) bounds e_R in every C^{k+1,gamma}(S), and D^j e_R = R^j (D^j (U - u_0))(R .)
gives U - u_0 = O_infty(1). The "in particular" bounds follow, as D^j of a smooth function homogeneous of degree m on
R^2 \ {0} is O(r^{m-j}). For (c): f = O_infty(r^m) gives |D^j [f(R .)](X)| <= C_j R^j (R |X|)^{m-j} <= C R^m on
{a <= |X| <= b} for R a >= R1; take m = -1/2, -1, 0 for Theta - theta_0, Omega - omega_0, U - u_0, multiply by 1,
R^{1/2}, R^{-1/2}, and use the homogeneity of theta_0, omega_0, u_0 (degrees 0, -1/2, 1/2). QED.
Remark. This theorem asserts no analyticity, no expansion beyond the first remainder, no sharpness of the exponent -1/2
(the rate produced by the integrable weight r^{-3/2} in (36.6)) and no next-order term; U - u_0 is only shown to be
O_infty(1), not o(1). The next term is identified in Theorem 45(f), where U - u_0 = u_1 + O_infty(r^{-1/2}) with an
order-one term u_1, and Theorem 76 gives an expansion to every finite order for every A2-broad profile; no convergence
of the series is asserted. (a)-(d) do not use G != 0 and hold in both alternatives of Theorem 33(e); for A2-broad
profiles (a0 != 0), G is not identically zero by Theorem 34(b). The argument uses kappa = 0 (Theta is constant on
orbits, and (33.1)); nothing is claimed for beta > 2. The theorem neither constructs nor excludes a profile.

### Theorem 37 (outgoing distribution for beta >= 2; natural tail for beta > 2 under a strain bound)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta >= 2, W = beta X + U, kappa = beta - 2, Q1 the open first
quadrant, Q_rho = {x > 0, y > 0, |X| < rho} and E(R) = int_{R<|X|<2R} |U|^2 dX. Write {f, g} = f_x g_y - f_y g_x; for
smooth f and continuous g, {f, g} := f_x d_y g - f_y d_x g in D'(R^2), that is
  <{f, g}, phi> = -int g {f, phi} dX   for phi in C_c^infinity(R^2).                                          (37.1)
For a distribution L and real s, <L o Phi_s, phi> := e^{-2 beta s} <L, phi o Phi_{-s}>. Put
  V_T(X) = int_0^T e^{-(beta+1) t} y(Phi_t X) dt,   V(X) = int_0^inf e^{-(beta+1) t} y(Phi_t X) dt.           (37.2)
Call X escaping if its forward orbit is unbounded; J(X) := lim_{t -> inf} e^t Omega(Phi_t X) where it exists.
(a) V converges absolutely and locally uniformly, V is continuous, V(0) = 0 and V > 0 on Q1; for T >= 0 and all X,
      e^T Omega(Phi_T X) = Omega(X) + {Theta, V_T}(X).                                                        (37.3)
    As T -> infinity, e^T Omega o Phi_T -> K := Omega + {Theta, V} in D'(R^2); K o Phi_s = e^{-s} K for every real s;
    and (W.grad + 1) K = 0 in D'(R^2), that is <K, W.grad phi + (2 beta - 1) phi> = 0 for all test functions phi.
(b) For every rho > 0 there is phi >= 0 in C_c^infinity(Q_rho) with sgn(a0) <K, phi> > 0: sgn(a0) K is not a
    nonpositive distribution on Q_rho. In particular K is not zero on any Q_rho.
(c) If beta > 2, every X with Theta(X) != 0 is escaping, and Q_rho0 lies in the escaping set for some rho0 > 0.
(d) Let beta > 2, and assume that for constants sigma < 1 and R_*
      (S) the largest eigenvalue of (DU + DU^T)/2 at X is at most sigma for |X| >= R_*.
    Then V is C^1 on the escaping set, e^t Omega(Phi_t X) -> J(X) locally uniformly there, J = Omega + {Theta, V} is
    continuous, J(Phi_s X) = e^{-s} J(X), and J = K in D' of the escaping set. For every rho > 0, sgn(a0) J > 0 on a
    nonempty open subset of Q_rho. Theorem 32(a) to (d) and alternative (N) of Theorem 32(e) hold: G has the sign of
    a0 on a nonempty open interval of angles in (0, pi/2), and, with a = 2 - 1/beta and P as in Theorem 32(d),
      lim_{R -> inf} E(R) R^{-4+2/beta} = [(2^{4-2/beta} - 1)/(4 - 2/beta)] int_0^{2 pi} (P'^2 + a^2 P^2) dphi > 0.
    So E(R) = o(R^{4-2/beta}), the critical regime E(R) = O(R^{4-4/beta}) ((A) of Theorem 28, alternative (C) of
    Theorem 32) and a bounded U are impossible under (S). If DU(X) -> 0 as |X| -> infinity, (S) holds.
Proof. Step 1 (V and (37.3)). U(0) = 0 and |U| <= eps |X| + C_eps for 0 < eps < 1, so the flow is global with det D
Phi_t = e^{2 beta t} and Theta o Phi_t = e^{kappa t} Theta (Section 2), and by Gronwall |Phi_t X| <= (|X| + C_eps)
e^{(beta+eps) t} for t >= 0. On a compact Lambda the integrand of V is O(e^{-(1-eps) t}), so V_T -> V uniformly there,
V is continuous, and V(0) = 0 as O is an equilibrium. The axes are invariant (Section 1), so Q1 is invariant by
uniqueness and V > 0 on Q1. For a diffeomorphism Phi, the chain rule and det(A^T u, A^T v) = det A det(u, v) give
{f o Phi, g o Phi} = (det D Phi) {f, g} o Phi. With Phi = Phi_t, f = Theta, g = y and {Theta, y} = Theta_x,
  {Theta, y o Phi_t} = e^{(2 beta - kappa) t} Theta_x o Phi_t = e^{(beta+2) t} Theta_x o Phi_t.               (37.4)
Differentiating under the integral, {Theta, V_T}(X) = int_0^T e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) dt, and integrating
d/dt [e^t Omega(Phi_t X)] = e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) (by (V)) over [0, T] gives (37.3).
Step 2 (the limit K; (a)). For smooth g, (37.1) is integration by parts, so by (37.3) the functions F_T := e^T Omega o
Phi_T satisfy <F_T, phi> = int (Omega phi - V_T {Theta, phi}) dX -> <K, phi> for every phi in C_c^infinity(R^2). For
functions, L o Phi_s is the composition (put X = Phi_{-s} Y), so F_T o Phi_s = e^{-s} F_{T+s}, and
<F_T o Phi_s, phi> = e^{-2 beta s} <F_T, phi o Phi_{-s}> tends to <K o Phi_s, phi> and to e^{-s} <K, phi>.
Differentiating Phi_T o Phi_s = Phi_s o Phi_T at s = 0 gives D Phi_T W = W o Phi_T, so by the chain rule, (V), (37.4)
  (W.grad + 1) F_T = e^T Theta_x o Phi_T = {Theta, g_T},   g_T := e^{-(beta+1) T} y o Phi_T.                  (37.5)
As |g_T| <= C_Lambda e^{-(1-eps) T} on compact sets Lambda, (37.1) gives {Theta, g_T} -> 0 in D'. As W.grad is
continuous on D' (<W.grad L, phi> = -<L, div(W phi)>, div W = 2 beta), (W.grad + 1) K = 0, the weak form in (a).
Step 3 (jets). By Section 1, c = 2 beta + 2 and (2 beta + 1) b0 = 2 a0. Smooth division (parities, Theta(0, y) = 0)
gives Theta = x^2 y A, Omega = x y B, A and B smooth and even in x and in y, A(0) = a0, B(0) = b0, and Theta_x = x y
(2 A + x d_x A) with x d_x A = O(|X|^2). So B/(2 A + x d_x A) -> b0/(2 a0) = 1/(2 beta + 1) at O. Fix rho0 > 0 with
  A/a0 >= 1/2,   (2 A + x d_x A)/a0 >= 1,   B/(2 A + x d_x A) >= 1/(4 beta + 2)   on |X| < rho0.              (37.6)
Step 4 ((b)). As Q_rho0 is contained in Q_rho for rho >= rho0, let 0 < rho <= rho0 and suppose that
<sgn(a0) K, phi> <= 0 for every phi >= 0 in C_c^infinity(Q_rho). Put h = Theta/a0, psi = (h, y). By (37.6), d_x h =
Theta_x/a0 > 0 on each horizontal slice of Q_rho, an interval, so psi is injective with Jacobian d_x h > 0, a
diffeomorphism onto an open O_rho, and Vt := V o psi^{-1} is continuous. For chi in C_c^infinity(O_rho) and phi = chi
o psi, the chain rule gives {Theta, phi} = a0 h_x (d_y chi) o psi; with dX = dh dy/h_x and (37.1),
  <{Theta, V}, phi> = -a0 int Vt d_y chi dh dy,   int Omega phi dX = a0 int [(Omega/Theta_x) o psi^{-1}] chi dh dy.
As K = Omega + {Theta, V} and Omega/Theta_x = B/(2 A + x d_x A), for chi >= 0 the hypothesis and (37.6) give
  -int Vt d_y chi dh dy = |a0|^{-1} <sgn(a0) K, phi> - int [(Omega/Theta_x) o psi^{-1}] chi dh dy
                        <= -(4 beta + 2)^{-1} int chi dh dy.
So v := Vt + y/(4 beta + 2) has d_y v <= 0 in D'(O_rho), and v is nonincreasing on every vertical segment in O_rho
(mollify with nonnegative kernels of small support and pass to the uniform limit). Fix 0 < delta < rho and a level
0 < h < delta^3 with 2 h^{2/3} < rho^2 - delta^2. For h^{1/3} <= y <= delta, x -> x^2 y A/a0 increases strictly on the
slice, tends to 0 as x -> 0, and is at least h at x = (2h/y)^{1/2} <= 2^{1/2} h^{1/3}, a point of the slice; so a
unique x_h(y) in (0, 2^{1/2} h^{1/3}] has Theta(x_h(y), y) = a0 h, and {h} x [h^{1/3}, delta] lies in O_rho. With
Q_h = (x_h(h^{1/3}), h^{1/3}) and P_h = (x_h(delta), delta), V(P_h) <= V(Q_h) - (delta - h^{1/3})/(4 beta + 2). As
h -> 0, |Q_h| <= 3^{1/2} h^{1/3} gives V(Q_h) -> V(0) = 0, so V(P_h) < 0 for small h, contrary to V > 0 on Q1.
Step 5 ((c)). As |U| <= C (1 + |X|), Theorem 7 shows that X escapes if Theta(X) != 0; Theta != 0 on Q_rho0 by (37.6).
Step 6 ((d): the amplitude). Fix 0 < eps < beta/2 and R0 >= R_* with (beta - eps) r <= W_r <= (beta + eps) r for
r >= R0 (U = o(r)) and such that the disc |X| < R0 contains an open set where Theta != 0. An orbit that meets
|X| >= R0 stays there and escapes, so the escaping set is open and invariant. As tr DU = div U = 0, (DU + DU^T)/2 has
eigenvalues mu, -mu with 0 <= mu <= sigma, so along an orbit in |X| >= R0, z(t) = D Phi_t(X) z0 satisfies
  2 (beta - sigma) |z|^2 <= d|z|^2/dt = 2 z.(beta I + DU) z <= 2 (beta + sigma) |z|^2.                        (37.7)
Each point of a compact subset Lambda of the escaping set has a neighbourhood whose orbits lie in |X| > R0 after a
common time; a finite subcover gives t_1 with |Phi_t X| > R0 for t >= t_1, X in Lambda. Splitting D Phi_t(X) at t_1,
continuity on [0, t_1] x Lambda and (37.7) give ||D Phi_t(X)|| <= C_Lambda e^{(beta+sigma) t} and
||D Phi_t(X)^{-1}|| <= C_Lambda e^{-(beta-sigma) t} for t >= 0. Differentiating Theta o Phi_t = e^{kappa t} Theta,
  grad Theta(Phi_t X) = e^{kappa t} (D Phi_t(X))^{-T} grad Theta(X),                                          (37.8)
so |grad Theta(Phi_t X)| <= C_Lambda e^{-(2-sigma) t} and e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) = O(e^{-(1-sigma) t}) uniformly on
Lambda, and by Step 1 e^T Omega(Phi_T X) converges uniformly on Lambda to a continuous J. The X-gradient
e^{-(beta+1) t} (D Phi_t(X))^T e_2 of the integrand of V is also O(e^{-(1-sigma) t}), so V_T -> V in C^1 on Lambda, V
is C^1 on the escaping set, and (37.3) gives J = Omega + {Theta, V}. Hence J = K in D' of the escaping set, and
J(Phi_s X) = e^{-s} J(X) by definition. For rho <= rho0, Q_rho is in the escaping set by (c); if sgn(a0) J <= 0 on
Q_rho, then <sgn(a0) K, phi> = int sgn(a0) J phi dX <= 0 for every phi >= 0 in C_c^infinity(Q_rho), contrary to (b).
So sgn(a0) J > 0 on an open subset of Q_rho, for rho <= rho0 and hence for all rho > 0.
Step 7 ((d): the far field). In the proof of Theorem 32, (DT) enters only through the domination of e^t Theta_x along
X(t, alpha) = Phi_t X0(alpha), X0(alpha) = R0 (cos alpha, sin alpha), and the remainder of the exit formula
(Steps 2 and 5), and in Step 7 for (C) only; R0 is as in its Step 2, and its other hypotheses hold for A2-broad
profiles. These uses are replaced, since (37.8) gives only the rate e^{-(2-sigma) t} along orbits. The orbits
X(., alpha) stay in |X| >= R0, so (37.8) holds uniformly in alpha with C_Lambda = max_{|X| = R0} |grad Theta|; hence
e^t |Theta_x(X(t, alpha))| <= C e^{-(1-sigma) t}, J_0 of that proof is continuous, and in the exit formula
  Omega(X(tau, alpha)) = e^{-tau} J_0(alpha) - e^{-tau} int_tau^inf e^s Theta_x(X(s, alpha)) ds               (37.9)
the remainder is at most C e^{-(2-sigma) tau} uniformly in alpha. As tau(r, alpha) >= (beta + eps)^{-1} log(r/R0),
Omega = O(|X|^{-eta}) with eta = 1/(beta + eps) < 1/2, the conclusion of Step 2 there. Steps 3 and 4 there give
Theorem 32(c), |d| <= C for d = tau - beta^{-1} log(r/R0), and the convergence assertions of Theorem 32(b) with
preliminary errors O(r^{-eta}). Since r^{1/beta} e^{-tau} = R0^{1/beta} e^{-d} is bounded, (37.9) gives Omega = O(r^{-1/beta});
repeating the inverse estimate and Step 4 with eta = 1/beta then gives U = O(r^{1 - 1/beta}) and the O(r^{-1/beta})
errors of Theorem 32(b). In Step 5 the remainder becomes r^{1/beta} C
e^{-(2-sigma) tau} = C R0^{1/beta} e^{-d} e^{-(1-sigma) tau} = O(r^{-(1-sigma)/beta}), still o(1) uniformly in alpha,
so Steps 5 to 7 give Theorem 32(a), (d) and the energy limit of Theorem 32(e). By Steps 3 and 5 there, G == 0 if and
only if J = 0 at every escaping point, which Step 6 excludes; so (N) holds. Sign of G: for X in Q_rho0 with sgn(a0)
J(X) > 0 (Step 6), the orbit stays in Q1 and meets |X| = R0 at a time t0 and an angle alpha0 in (0, pi/2), and
J_0(alpha0) = e^{-t0} J(X) (Step 3 there). So sgn(a0) J_0 > 0 on an open interval I containing alpha0, and, as in
Step 5 of the proof of Theorem 34, G = R0^{1/beta} (e^{-d_inf} J_0) o F^{-1} has the sign of a0 on F(I), which lies in
(0, pi/2) as F fixes the axis directions. Finally, E(R) = O(R^{4-4/beta}) and bounded U (E(R) = O(R^2)) would give
E(R) = o(R^{4-2/beta}), contrary to the positive limit, and DU -> 0 gives (S) with sigma = 1/2. QED.
Remark (scope). Parts (a) to (c) do not use the polynomial bounds of Section 2, and K is not asserted to be a function
or a measure. For beta > 2 they give no pointwise outgoing amplitude, no angular limit and no bound on the energy: (b)
provides a positive pairing near O, not a pointwise lower bound. At beta = 2 the theorem is weaker than Theorem 34:
J = K on the escaping set, which is open and of full measure (Theorem 33(b), (c)), so (b) follows from Theorem 34(a),
and Theorem 34(b) gives alternative (N) without a strain bound. (S) is stated here as a hypothesis on the far field;
for beta > 2 Theorem 41 derives it for every A2-broad profile. Under (S), (d) uses no bound on Theta or its derivatives
and no hypothesis on the y-axis traces or on simple zeros of W (compare Theorem 31(e)).
Nothing is asserted about the existence of natural-branch profiles: no profile in alternative (N) is constructed or
excluded. Theorem 38 below removes (S) for beta > 2, with the limits of (d) taken in every finite L^p norm in the
angle, and so excludes the critical branch and bounded velocity for every A2-broad profile with beta > 2; Theorem 41
then shows that (S) itself holds, so (d) applies as stated. The natural branch remains open.

### Theorem 38 (beta > 2: every A2-broad profile has the natural tail)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta > 2. Put h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h, a = 2 - h, kappa = beta - 2,
W = beta X + U, A_R = {R < |X| < 2R}, E(R) = int_{A_R} |U|^2 dX, e(phi) = (cos phi, sin phi), and let e_r, e_phi be the
polar frame; angular norms ||.||_p are taken over [0, 2 pi] in dphi or dalpha. Fix R0 >= 1 with |U(X)| <= beta |X|/4
for |X| >= R0, put X0(alpha) = R0 e(alpha), X(s, alpha) = Phi_s X0(alpha) (s real), theta_0 = Theta o X0, and let
tau(r, alpha) and the lifted angle F_r(alpha) (F_{R0}(alpha) = alpha) be the time and angle at which X(., alpha) meets
|X| = r >= R0. Normalize
  d(r, alpha) = tau(r, alpha) - h log(r/R0)
as in Theorem 37 (tau - h log r, used in Theorem 32(b), differs from d by the constant h log R0, which changes no
derivative). Let mu(s, alpha) = X_alpha . W/|W|^2 at X(s, alpha). Neither (DT) nor (S) is assumed. Every assertion that
involves p holds for every p in [1, inf), with constants depending on p; nothing is asserted for p = inf.
(a) (sharp bounds) |U(X)| <= C |X|^{1-h} for |X| >= 1, and for r >= R0, R >= R0,
      ||Omega(r, .)||_p <= C r^{-h},   ||grad Theta(r, .)||_p <= C r^{-2h},
      ||Omega||_{L^p(A_R)} + ||DU||_{L^p(A_R)} <= C R^{2/p - h},   ||grad Theta||_{L^p(A_R)} <= C R^{2/p - 2h};
    in particular int_{A_R} |grad Theta|^2 <= C R^{2-4h} and int_{A_R} Omega^2 <= C R^{2-2h}. There are M >= 1 in every
    L^p(dalpha) and a null set N_* of labels with |mu(s, alpha)| <= M(alpha) and |grad Theta(X(s, alpha))| <=
    M(alpha) e^{-2s} for all s >= 0, alpha not in N_*; mu(s, .) -> mu_inf a.e., and ||mu(s, .) - mu_inf||_p <= C e^{-s}.
(b) (geometry) As r -> inf, d(r, .) -> d_inf, F_r -> F and d_alpha F_r -> F' uniformly, with errors O(r^{-h}), and
    F_r^{-1} -> F^{-1} in C^1. F is an orientation-preserving C^1 diffeomorphism of the circle fixing the four axis
    directions, and F' = j_inf := (W_r(X0)/(beta R0)) e^{2 beta d_inf}. Moreover d_inf is in W^{1,p}, d_inf' = -mu_inf,
    ||d(r, .) - d_inf||_{W^{1,p}} <= C r^{-h}; F' is in W^{1,p}, so F is in W^{2,p} and in C^{1,gamma} for every
    gamma < 1 (no convergence of F_r in W^{2,p} is asserted). r^{-q} Theta(r, .) converges uniformly to
    f := (R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf} theta_0) o F^{-1}; f is in W^{1,p}, has the parities of Theta and is not identically 0.
(c) (outgoing amplitude) B_0(alpha) := |Omega(X0(alpha))| + int_0^inf e^s |Theta_x(X(s, alpha))| ds is finite for alpha
    not in N_* and lies in L^p; J0(alpha) := Omega(X0(alpha)) + int_0^inf e^s Theta_x(X(s, alpha)) ds lies in L^p, is
    not a.e. zero, and
      |e^s Omega(X(s, alpha)) - J0(alpha)| <= M(alpha) e^{-s} (alpha not in N_*),   ||e^s Omega(X(s, .)) - J0||_p <= C e^{-s}.
    The escaping set (Theorem 37) is open and contains Q_rho0 (Theorem 37(c)); (s, alpha) -> X(s, alpha) is a
    diffeomorphism of R x (R/2piZ) onto it, and there the distribution K of Theorem 37(a) is the locally integrable
    function K(X(s, alpha)) = e^{-s} J0(alpha).
(d) (vorticity and velocity) r^h Omega(r, .) -> G := (R0^h e^{-d_inf} J0) o F^{-1} in L^p(dphi); G is odd in x and in y
    and not a.e. zero. Let P be the unique 2 pi-periodic odd-odd solution of -(P'' + a^2 P) = G (a^2 < 4 is not an
    eigenvalue on odd-odd functions); P is in W^{2,p}, hence C^1. Let U_inf = (-d_y Psi_inf, d_x Psi_inf) with
    Psi_inf = r^a P(phi), that is, U_inf has polar components r^{1-h} (-P', a P)(phi), and let Omega_inf = r^{-h} G(phi).
    Then R^{h-1} U(R .) -> U_inf uniformly on compact subsets of R^2 \ {0}, and for 0 < c1 < c2 and
    A(c1, c2) = {c1 <= |X| <= c2}, R^{h-1} U(R .) -> U_inf in W^{1,p}(A(c1, c2)) and R^h Omega(R .) -> Omega_inf in
    L^p(A(c1, c2)).
(e) (energy) lim_{R -> inf} E(R) R^{-(4-2h)} = [(2^{4-2h} - 1)/(4 - 2h)] int_0^{2 pi} (P'^2 + a^2 P^2) dphi > 0. In
    particular U is unbounded, and E(R) is neither O(R^{4-4h}) (the critical regime of Theorems 28 and 32(e)(C)) nor
    o(R^{4-2h}).
(f) (temperature gradient) r^{2h} grad Theta(r, .) -> q f e_r + f' e_phi in L^p(dphi), and for 0 < c1 < c2,
    R^{-q} Theta(R .) -> r^q f(phi) uniformly and in W^{1,p} on A(c1, c2).
(g) (quadratic limits) With C_h = (2^{2-2h} - 1)/(2 - 2h) and Frobenius norms,
      lim R^{-(2-4h)} int_{A_R} |grad Theta|^2 dX = [(2^{2-4h} - 1)/(2 - 4h)] int_0^{2 pi} (q^2 f^2 + f'^2) dphi > 0,
      lim R^{-(2-2h)} int_{A_R} Omega^2 dX = C_h int_0^{2 pi} G^2 dphi > 0,
      lim R^{-(2-2h)} int_{A_R} |DU|^2 dX = C_h int_0^{2 pi} |M_P|^2 dphi > 0,
    where DU_inf = r^{-h} M_P(phi) in the frame (e_r, e_phi), the first column being the derivative along e_r: M_P has
    rows (-(1-h) P', -P'' - a P) and ((1-h) a P, (1-h) P'), and |M_P|^2 = 2 (1-h)^2 P'^2 + (P'' + a P)^2 + (1-h)^2 a^2 P^2.
Scope. The velocity bound of (a), the geometric and temperature limits of (b) and the velocity limit of (d) are uniform.
The vorticity and temperature-gradient bounds and limits are asserted only in every finite L^p (this theorem does not
show that M and B_0 are bounded, and does not assert that they are unbounded); G is only asserted to lie in every
finite L^p, and neither a derivative of G nor a pointwise trace of G on an axis is asserted; no rate is given for the
Eulerian limits of (d), (f). Theorems 41 and 42 strengthen these conclusions.
The theorem neither constructs nor excludes a profile.

Proof. C denotes constants independent of r, R, s, t, k, l, alpha (they may depend on the profile, p and delta);
b := 2 beta/p, and the label circle is S^1 = R/2piZ.
Step 1 (flow coordinates). As |U| <= C(1 + |X|), Phi_s is global (Section 2). For |X| >= R0, W_r := W.X/|X| >=
3 beta |X|/4, so an orbit meeting |X| >= R0 stays there with increasing radius, the backward orbit of X0(alpha) stays in
|X| < R0, and a backward orbit from |X| > R0 reaches |X| = R0. Hence an orbit is escaping iff it meets |X| = R0, at exactly
one time, and (s, alpha) -> X(s, alpha) is a bijection of R x S^1 onto the escaping set, of [0, inf) x S^1 onto
{|X| >= R0}. Both W(X(s, alpha)) and X_alpha solve z' = DW(X) z, so D := det(W, X_alpha) has D' = (tr DW) D = 2 beta D:
  D = D0(alpha) e^{2 beta s},   D0 = det(W(X0), R0 e_phi) = R0 W_r(X0) in [3 beta R0^2/4, 5 beta R0^2/4].          (38.1)
So the map is a local diffeomorphism, the escaping set is open, and dX = D ds dalpha. For 0 < delta <= beta/4 let
R_delta >= R0 with |U| <= delta |X| for |X| >= R_delta; orbits from X0 reach R_delta by a time independent of alpha, so
  C^{-1} e^{(beta-delta)s} <= |X(s, alpha)| <= C e^{(beta+delta)s},  C^{-1} e^{(beta-delta)s} <= |W|, D/|W| <= C e^{(beta+delta)s}
for s >= 0 (38.2). The launch circle is the same for every delta, so all label functions live on one label circle. With
S_k = X([k, k+1) x S^1), D0 bounded above and below, and Holder in s, for 1 <= p < inf,
  int_k^{k+1} ||f(X(s, .))||_p ds <= C e^{-bk} ||f||_{L^p(S_k)},   ||f||^p_{L^p(S_k)} <= C e^{2 beta k} int_k^{k+1} ||f(X(s, .))||^p_p ds.  (38.3)
Let R_i = 2^i R0 (i >= 0) and A_R^* = {R/2 < |X| < 4R}. By (38.2) at most C(1+k) annuli A_{R_i} meet S_k; if A_{R_i} meets
S_k, then A^*_{R_i} meets S_l only for a_delta^{-1} k - m0 <= l <= a_delta k + m0, a_delta = (beta+delta)/(beta-delta),
m0 = m0(delta) (compare the lower radial bound of S_l with 4 R_i <= C e^{(beta+delta)k}, and conversely), hence at most
C(1+k) slabs; the part of A^*_{R_i} in |X| < R0 lies in a fixed compact set.                                     (38.4)
Step 2 (shear and gradient along orbits). Let e_W = W/|W|, n = J e_W with J(v1, v2) = (-v2, v1), mu = X_alpha.W/|W|^2,
nu = D/|W|; then X_alpha = mu W + nu n. With S = Sym(DW) = beta I + Sym(DU), (X_alpha.W)' = 2 X_alpha.S W and
(|W|^2)' = 2 W.S W, so mu' = 2 (X_alpha - mu W).S W/|W|^2 = 2 nu n.S W/|W|^2; as n.W = 0, beta I drops out:
  mu_s = 2 D |W|^{-2} n . Sym(DU) e_W,   |mu(s, alpha)| <= C + C int_0^s e^{2 delta u} |DU(X(u, alpha))| du,       (38.5)
by D/|W|^2 <= C e^{2 delta s} from (38.2). By (T), Theta(X(s, alpha)) = e^{kappa s} theta_0(alpha), so at X(s, alpha)
W.grad Theta = kappa e^{kappa s} theta_0 and X_alpha.grad Theta = e^{kappa s} theta_0'. Solving in the frame (e_W, n),
  grad Theta(X(s, alpha)) = e^{kappa s} [ (kappa theta_0/|W|) e_W + ((theta_0' - kappa mu theta_0)/nu) n ],          (38.6)
so |grad Theta(X(s, alpha))| <= C e^{(-2+delta)s} (1 + |mu(s, alpha)|) by (38.2). By (V), d/ds [e^s Omega(X(s, alpha))] =
e^s Theta_x(X(s, alpha)), so with eta = 1 - 2 delta
  e^s Omega(X(s, alpha)) = Omega(X0(alpha)) + int_0^s e^u Theta_x(X(u, alpha)) du,
  |Omega(X(s, alpha))| <= C e^{-s} [1 + int_0^s e^{-eta u} |mu(u, alpha)| du].                                       (38.7)
Step 3 (Lemma 38.1: local div-curl estimate). Let 1 < p < inf, 0 < c < c' and A' = {c/2 < |X| < 2c'}. There is
C = C(p, c'/c) such that every V in W^{1,p}(A') with div V = 0 and d_y V_1 - d_x V_2 = w in D'(A') satisfies
  ||DV||_{L^p(c < |X| < c')} <= C (||w||_{L^p(A')} + c^{-1} ||V||_{L^p(A')}).                                     (38.8)
Proof. The dilation X -> cX multiplies the three norms by the same power of c, so let c = 1. Take chi in C_c^inf(A'),
chi = 1 on 1 <= |X| <= c', and Z = chi V, a compactly supported W^{1,p} field with div Z = grad chi . V and
curl Z := d_y Z_1 - d_x Z_2 = chi w + (d_y chi) V_1 - (d_x chi) V_2. For Z in C_c^inf, Lap Z_1 = d_x div Z + d_y curl Z
and Lap Z_2 = d_y div Z - d_x curl Z, so each d_j Z_i is a sum of the multipliers xi_j xi_k/|xi|^2 applied to div Z or
curl Z. These are -R_j R_k (R_j the Riesz transforms), bounded on L^p(R^2) for 1 < p < inf (E. M. Stein, Singular
Integrals and Differentiability Properties of Functions, Princeton, 1970, Ch. III; or the Mikhlin multiplier theorem). So
||DZ||_p <= C_p (||div Z||_p + ||curl Z||_p), which extends to compactly supported W^{1,p} fields by mollification, and
(38.8) follows as DZ = DV on 1 < |X| < c'. With c = R, c' = 2R, A' = A_R^* and C does not depend on R.
Step 4 (bootstrap, fixed 1 < p < inf). Let m_p(t) = sup_{0<=s<=t} ||mu(s, .)||_p, H_p(v) = 1 + int_0^v e^{-eta u}
m_p(u) du. By (38.7), Minkowski and (38.3), ||Omega||_{L^p(S_l)} <= C e^{(b-1)l} H_p(l+1) (38.9). By (38.5), Minkowski,
(38.3), the covers (38.4) (each costs (1+k)^{1/p} after summing p-th powers), Lemma 38.1 on A_{R_i}, and |U| <= C|X|
(so R^{-1} ||U||_{L^p(A_R^*)} <= C R^{2/p} with R <= C e^{(beta+delta)k}),
  ||mu(t, .)||_p <= C + C sum_{k<=t} e^{(2 delta - b)k} ||DU||_{L^p(S_k)}
     <= C + C sum_{k<=t} (1+k)^{1/p} e^{(2 + 2/p) delta k} + C sum_{k<=t} (1+k)^{2/p} e^{(2 delta - b)k} max_l e^{(b-1)l} H_p(l+1),
the max over the range in (38.4). H_p increases, so H_p(l+1) <= H_p(a_delta k + m0) (m0 enlarged), while e^{(b-1)l} is
largest at the upper endpoint if b >= 1 and at the lower endpoint if b < 1; so with c_delta = a_delta if b >= 1 and
c_delta = 1/a_delta if b < 1, the max is <= C e^{(b-1) c_delta k} H_p(a_delta k + m0). Absorbing powers of 1+k into
e^{delta k} and setting lambda = (3 + 2/p) delta, gamma_delta = b - 3 delta - (b-1) c_delta (-> 1 as delta -> 0),
  m_p(t) <= C e^{lambda t} + C sum_{k<=t} e^{-gamma_delta k} H_p(a_delta k + m0).
The constant part of H_p gives a bounded sum; for the rest, Tonelli and sum_{k >= (u - m0)/a_delta} e^{-gamma_delta k}
<= C e^{-gamma_delta u/a_delta} give the advanced inequality
  m_p(t) <= C e^{lambda t} + C int_0^{a_delta t + m0} e^{-Q_delta u} m_p(u) du,   Q_delta = eta + gamma_delta/a_delta -> 2. (38.10)
Initialization: |Omega| <= C(1 + |X|)^N (N >= 0) and Lemma 38.1 give ||DU||_{L^p(A_R)} <= C R^{N + 2/p}, and the first
line of the display gives m_p(t) <= C e^{A_0 t} with A_0 = (beta+1)(N+1) for small delta. (The a priori bound is needed:
m(t) = exp(e^t) satisfies (38.10) for a suitable C.) Fix delta so small that gamma_delta > 0, lambda + delta < eta,
Q_delta - lambda > 1 and (a_delta - 1) A_0 - a_delta Q_delta < -1. If m_p <= C e^{At} with A <= A_0, (38.10) gives
m_p <= C e^{A't} with A' = max(lambda, a_delta (A - Q_delta)) <= max(lambda, A - 1) if A > Q_delta, and A' = lambda if
A <= Q_delta (if A = Q_delta the integral is O(1 + t), absorbed by e^{lambda t}). After finitely many steps
  m_p(t) <= C e^{lambda t},   ||Omega(X(s, .))||_p <= C e^{-s},   ||Omega||_{L^p(S_l)} <= C e^{(b-1)l},         (38.11)
the last two by (38.7), (38.9) and lambda < eta. By (38.2), A_R (R >= R0) meets only S_l with (log R)/(beta+delta) - m0
<= l <= (log R)/(beta-delta) + m0, at most C(1 + log R) slabs; taking the worse endpoint and (b-1)/beta = 2/p - h,
  ||Omega||_{L^p(A_R)} <= C R^{2/p - h + C delta}   (R >= R0).                                                      (38.12)
Step 5 (outgoing amplitude). Take p >= 2 in Step 4. By Step 2, (38.11) and Minkowski,
  || int_S^inf e^s |Theta_x(X(s, .))| ds ||_p <= C int_S^inf e^{-(1-delta)s} (1 + e^{lambda s}) ds <= C e^{-(1-delta-lambda)S}.  (38.13)
So B_0 is in L^p for every p >= 2, hence for every p >= 1; N_0 := {B_0 = inf} is null; J0 is defined off N_0 with
|J0| <= B_0; |e^s Omega(X(s, alpha)) - J0(alpha)| <= int_s^inf e^u |Theta_x(X(u, alpha))| du; and e^s Omega(X(s, .)) -> J0
a.e. and in every L^p. A compact subset of the escaping set is X(Lambda) with Lambda compact in R x S^1, so s is bounded
on it. As Phi_T X(s, alpha) = X(T+s, alpha), for T + s >= 0, e^T Omega(Phi_T X(s, alpha)) = e^{-s} e^{T+s} Omega(X(T+s,
alpha)) -> e^{-s} J0(alpha) in L^1(Lambda, ds dalpha) by (38.13), hence in L^1_loc of the escaping set (dX = D0 e^{2 beta
s} ds dalpha). By Theorem 37(a) this limit is K, so K(X(s, alpha)) = e^{-s} J0(alpha) there. Q_rho0 lies in the escaping
set (Theorem 37(c)) and K is not zero on Q_rho0 (Theorem 37(b)), so J0 is not a.e. zero.
Step 6 (Lemma 38.2: grouped inverse). Let B(z) = (z_2, -z_1)/(2 pi |z|^2) = (d_2 Gamma, -d_1 Gamma), Gamma = (2 pi)^{-1}
log |z|, so B * g is divergence-free with d_y(B*g)_1 - d_x(B*g)_2 = g. Let 2 < p < inf, 0 < sigma < 1, and let omega be
odd in x and in y with ||omega||_{L^p(A_rho)} <= L rho^{2/p - sigma} for every rho > 0. Then v(X) := lim_{rho -> inf}
int_{|Y|<rho} B(X - Y) omega(Y) dY exists locally uniformly, v is continuous with the A2 velocity parities, div v = 0 and
d_y v_1 - d_x v_2 = omega in D'(R^2), and |v(X)| <= C(p, sigma) L |X|^{1-sigma}.
Proof. By Holder, int_{A_rho} |omega| <= C L rho^{2-sigma}; summing shells, int_{|Y|<rho} |omega| <= C L rho^{2-sigma}. As
omega(-Y) = omega(Y) and B is odd, B(-Y) omega(Y) has zero integral over every centred annulus, and |B(X-Y) - B(-Y)| <=
C|X| |Y|^{-2} for |Y| > 2|X|. So for 2|X| < rho < rho', int_{rho<|Y|<rho'} B(X-Y) omega = int_{rho<|Y|<rho'} (B(X-Y) -
B(-Y)) omega = O(L |X| rho^{-sigma}): the limit is locally uniform, and continuity, div, curl and parities pass from the
truncations. Each truncation is continuous. Near X0 != 0 split off |Y| < |X0|/2, where the kernel is smooth, and use
omega in L^p and B in L^{p'} on bounded sets for the rest. At 0 the annular hypothesis need not give omega in L^p (if
sigma p >= 2), but int_{|Y|<eps} |B(-Y)| |omega(Y)| dY <= C L sum_{t < eps dyadic} t^{1-sigma} -> 0, and the
three-region estimate below, applied to omega restricted to |Y| < eps (a centred truncation keeps the parity
cancellation), bounds that part of the truncation by C L |X|^{1-sigma} for |X| < eps; so each truncation is continuous
at 0, with value 0 there. For |X| = r split v(X) over |Y| < r/2 (|B(X-Y)| <= 1/(pi r), mass <= C L r^{2-sigma}),
over r/2 <= |Y| <= 2r (Holder, ||B(X - .)||_{L^{p'}(|Y|<=2r)} <= C r^{1-2/p} as p' < 2) and over |Y| > 2r (with B(-Y)
subtracted, at most C L r sum_{t>=2r dyadic} t^{-sigma}); each part is at most C L r^{1-sigma}.
Application. Omega is bounded on |X| <= 2 R0, so ||Omega||_{L^p(A_t)} <= C t^{2/p} for t <= R0; with (38.12) for p = 4
and small delta, Lemma 38.2 applies to Omega with sigma = h - C delta > 0. U - v is divergence-free and curl-free in D',
hence harmonic, and o(|X|), hence constant by the gradient estimate, and U(0) = v(0) = 0 by parity. So U = v (the
canonical velocity of Section 2) and |U(X)| <= C |X|^{1-h+eps} for |X| >= 1, eps = C delta < h.           (38.14)
Step 7 (geometry). Along orbits d|X|/ds = W_r and d(arg X)/ds = U_phi/|X|; as d(R0, .) = 0,
  d_r d = 1/W_r - 1/(beta r) = -U_r/(beta r W_r),   d_r F_r = U_phi/(r W_r).                                         (38.15)
By (38.14) both are O(r^{-1-h+eps}) uniformly, so d -> d_inf and F_r -> F uniformly, |d| <= C, and since |X(s, alpha)| =
R0 e^{beta(s - d)}, C^{-1} e^{beta s} <= |X(s, alpha)| <= C e^{beta s}. Differentiating X(tau(r, alpha), alpha) =
r e(F_r(alpha)) in alpha gives W tau_alpha + X_alpha = r j_r e_phi, j_r = d_alpha F_r. The determinant with W, (38.1),
e^{2 beta tau} = e^{2 beta d} (r/R0)^2, and the scalar product with e_r (n.e_r = -W_phi/|W|) give
  r W_r j_r = D,   j_r = D0 r e^{2 beta d}/(R0^2 W_r),   d_alpha d = tau_alpha = -mu + D W_phi/(|W|^2 W_r).          (38.16)
So j_r -> j_inf = D0 e^{2 beta d_inf}/(beta R0^2) uniformly, and C^{-1} <= j_r, j_inf <= C. Each F_r is a circle
diffeomorphism (each orbit meets |X| = r once, j_r > 0) fixing the axis directions (W_1(0, y) = 0 = W_2(x, 0), W_r > 0).
Hence F is a C^1 diffeomorphism with these properties, |F_r^{-1} - F^{-1}| <= Lip(F^{-1}) ||F_r - F||_inf, and
(F_r^{-1})' = 1/(j_r o F_r^{-1}) -> (F^{-1})' uniformly. By (T) and kappa h = q, r^{-q} Theta(r e(F_r(alpha))) =
R0^{-q} e^{kappa d(r, alpha)} theta_0(alpha) =: theta_r(alpha) -> theta_inf := R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf} theta_0
uniformly, and r^{-q} Theta(r, .) - f = theta_r o F_r^{-1} - theta_inf o F^{-1} -> 0 uniformly. If Theta(X) != 0 then
X escapes (Theorem 37(c)), X = X(s, alpha) and theta_0(alpha) = e^{-kappa s} Theta(X) != 0; so f is not identically 0.
Step 8 (exact powers, shear envelope). Off N_0, |e^s Omega(X(s, alpha))| <= B_0(alpha) for all s >= 0; at s = tau(r,
alpha), e^{-tau} = R0^h r^{-h} e^{-d} <= C r^{-h} gives r^h |Omega(r e(F_r(alpha)))| <= C B_0(alpha). (The bound holds for
all s on each label off N_0, and F_r preserves null sets, so no uncountable union of null sets occurs.) Changing variables
phi = F_r(alpha) (Jacobian j_r <= C) and integrating in r, for all 1 <= p < inf,
  ||Omega(r, .)||_p <= C r^{-h} (r >= R0),   ||Omega||_{L^p(A_R)} <= C R^{2/p - h} (R >= R0).                          (38.17)
With the bounded core, ||Omega||_{L^p(A_t)} <= C t^{2/p-h} for all t > 0, and Lemma 38.2 with sigma = h gives |U| <=
C|X|^{1-h} for |X| >= 1. Then (38.15) is O(r^{-1-h}) and U/r = O(r^{-h}), so the errors of d(r, .), F_r and
d_alpha F_r in (b) are O(r^{-h}) (no rate is asserted for the C^1 convergence of F_r^{-1}, which uses the modulus of
continuity of F'). As |X(s, alpha)| is comparable to e^{beta s}, S_k lies in at most C annuli A_R with R comparable to e^{beta k}; by Lemma
38.1, (38.17) and |U| <= C R^{1-h} on A_R^*, ||DU||_{L^p(A_R)} <= C R^{2/p-h} (1 < p < inf; p = 1 by Holder), so
||DU||_{L^p(S_k)} <= C e^{(b-1)k}, and by (38.3) int_k^{k+1} ||DU(X(s, .))||_p ds <= C e^{-k}          (38.18).
Now D/|W|^2 <= C, so by (38.5), with M(alpha) := C_1 (1 + |mu(0, alpha)| + int_0^inf |DU(X(u, alpha))| du) (C_1 large),
which is in every L^p by Minkowski and (38.18): |mu| <= M, mu(s, alpha) -> mu_inf(alpha) where M < inf, and
  || sup_{s' >= s} |mu(s', .) - mu_inf| ||_p <= C int_s^inf ||DU(X(u, .))||_p du <= C e^{-s}.                         (38.19)
As |W|, nu >= C^{-1} e^{beta s} now, (38.6) gives |grad Theta(X(s, alpha))| <= C e^{(kappa - beta)s} (1 + M) <= M(alpha)
e^{-2s}; so |e^s Omega(X(s, alpha)) - J0(alpha)| <= int_s^inf e^{-u} M du = M(alpha) e^{-s}, and r^{2h} |grad Theta(r e(
F_r(alpha)))| <= C M(alpha), which gives the gradient bounds of (a) as for (38.17). With N_* = N_0 u {M = inf}, (a) and (c)
are proved.
Step 9 (angular vorticity limit). With g := R0^h e^{-d_inf} J0, by Step 8 and e^{-tau} <= C r^{-h},
  g_r(alpha) := r^h Omega(r e(F_r(alpha))) = R0^h e^{-d(r, alpha)} e^{tau} Omega(X(tau, alpha)) = g(alpha) + O(r^{-h}) (|J0| + M)(alpha),
so g_r -> g in L^p(dalpha). As int |psi o F_r^{-1}|^p dphi = int |psi|^p j_r dalpha <= C ||psi||_p^p, for psi continuous
with ||g - psi||_p <= epsilon,
  ||r^h Omega(r, .) - G||_p <= ||(g_r - g) o F_r^{-1}||_p + ||(g - psi) o F_r^{-1}||_p + ||psi o F_r^{-1} - psi o F^{-1}||_p
                               + ||(psi - g) o F^{-1}||_p,
where the first and third terms tend to 0 (the third uniformly) and the others are at most C epsilon. G is odd in x and
in y as each r^h Omega(r, .) is, and not a.e. zero as J0 is not, e^{-d_inf} > 0 and F is a diffeomorphism.
Step 10 (velocity limit and energy). Let omega_R(Y) = R^h Omega(RY), u_R(Y) = R^{h-1} U(RY), z_R = omega_R - Omega_inf.
Since ||Omega||_{L^p(A_t)} <= C t^{2/p-h} for every t > 0 (bounded core and (38.17)), scaling gives ||omega_R||_{L^p(
A_rho)} <= C rho^{2/p-h} for all rho > 0 uniformly in R, and the same holds for Omega_inf; in particular int_{|Y|<rho}
|omega_R| <= C rho^{2-h}. As B(Rz) = R^{-1} B(z) and U = v, u_R is the grouped inverse of omega_R; let U' be that of
Omega_inf (Lemma 38.2, sigma = h), homogeneous of degree 1 - h by the same scaling. For c1 <= |X| <= c2, 0 < rho_1 < c1/2
and rho_2 > 2 c2, u_R(X) - U'(X) is the sum of int_{|Y|<rho_1} B(X-Y) z_R (at most C rho_1^{2-h}/c1), int_{rho_1<|Y|<
rho_2} B(X-Y) z_R (at most ||B||_{L^{p'}(|Y|<2 rho_2)} ||z_R||_{L^p(rho_1<|Y|<rho_2)}, p > 2) and int_{|Y|>rho_2}
(B(X-Y) - B(-Y)) z_R (at most C c2 rho_2^{-h}). Moreover
  ||z_R||^p_{L^p(rho_1 < |Y| < rho_2)} = int_{rho_1}^{rho_2} rho^{1-ph} ||(R rho)^h Omega(R rho, .) - G||_p^p drho -> 0
by dominated convergence: for R rho_1 >= R0 the integrand is at most C rho^{1-ph} by (38.17), and it tends to 0 for each
rho by Step 9. Letting R -> inf, then rho_1 -> 0 and rho_2 -> inf: u_R -> U' uniformly on c1 <= |X| <= c2.
Identification. Odd-odd 2 pi-periodic functions expand in sin(2n phi), n >= 1, and -(P'' + a^2 P) = G means P_n =
G_n/(4n^2 - a^2), 4n^2 - a^2 >= 4 - a^2 > 0; so P exists, is unique and odd-odd, P is in H^2, and P'' = -G - a^2 P is in L^p, so P
is in W^{2,p}. U_inf (polar components r^{a-1}(-P', a P)) is in W^{1,p}_loc(R^2 \ {0}), |U_inf| <= C r^{1-h}, div U_inf =
0 and d_y U_inf,1 - d_x U_inf,2 = -Lap Psi_inf = -r^{a-2} (P'' + a^2 P) = Omega_inf off 0; boundary terms on |X| = eps'
in the weak forms are O(eps'^{2-h}), so these hold in D'(R^2). So U' - U_inf is harmonic and homogeneous of degree
1 - h in (0, 1), hence sublinear, constant and zero: U' = U_inf. By change of variables E(R) R^{-(4-2h)} = int_{A_1}
|u_R|^2 -> int_{A_1} |U_inf|^2 = int_1^2 rho^{3-2h} drho int (P'^2 + a^2 P^2) dphi, which is (e); it is positive, since
otherwise P = 0 and G = 0. Bounded U, E(R) = O(R^{4-4h}) and E(R) = o(R^{4-2h}) each contradict this positive limit.
Step 11 (Sobolev geometry and temperature gradient). In (38.16) the last term is O(r^{-h}) uniformly (D/|W|^2 <= C,
|W_phi| = |U_phi| <= C r^{1-h}, W_r >= beta r/2); as tau(r, alpha) >= h log(r/R0) - C, (38.19) gives
||mu(tau(r, .), .) - mu_inf||_p <= C r^{-h}. So ||d_alpha d(r, .) + mu_inf||_p <= C r^{-h}, and with the uniform
convergence, d_inf is in W^{1,p}, d_inf' = -mu_inf and ||d(r, .) - d_inf||_{W^{1,p}} <= C r^{-h}. As d_inf is bounded
and D0 is smooth and positive, F' = j_inf is in W^{1,p} (one-dimensional chain rule), so F is in W^{2,p}, hence in
C^{1,1-1/p}. Likewise theta_inf = f o F is in W^{1,p} with theta_inf' = R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf} (theta_0' - kappa mu_inf
theta_0), and since F^{-1} is C^1 with derivative bounded above and below, f is in W^{1,p} and f' o F = theta_inf'/j_inf
a.e. In (38.6) at s = tau(r, alpha), times r^{2h}, use e^{kappa tau} = R0^{-q} r^q e^{kappa d}, 2h + q = 1, nu = D/|W|
and (38.16):
  r^{2h} e^{kappa tau}/|W| = R0^{-q} e^{kappa d} r/|W|,      r^{2h} e^{kappa tau}/nu = R0^{-q} e^{kappa d} |W|/(W_r j_r).
As r/|W| = 1/beta + O(r^{-h}), |W|/W_r = 1 + O(r^{-h}), and d, j_r converge with errors O(r^{-h}), the e_W-coefficient
tends uniformly to (kappa/beta) theta_inf = q theta_inf, and by |mu| <= M and the bound on mu(tau(r, .), .) - mu_inf, the
n-coefficient tends in L^p, with error O(r^{-h}), to R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf} (theta_0' - kappa mu_inf theta_0)/j_inf =
f' o F. As |e_W - e_r(F_r)| + |n - e_phi(F_r)| <= C |U|/r <= C r^{-h} and |F_r - F| <= C r^{-h},
  || r^{2h} grad Theta(r e(F_r(.))) - (q f e_r + f' e_phi) o F ||_{L^p(dalpha)} <= C r^{-h},
and the density argument of Step 9, applied componentwise, gives the circle limit in (f) (without rate). As 1 - q = 2h,
d_phi [r^{-q} Theta(r, phi)] = e_phi . r^{2h} grad Theta(r, phi) -> f' in L^p; with (b), r^{-q} Theta(r, .) -> f in W^{1,p}
of the circle. On A(c1, c2), Theta_R := R^{-q} Theta(R .) -> r^q f uniformly; grad Theta_R(Y) = |Y|^{-2h} (R|Y|)^{2h}
grad Theta(RY) and grad(r^q f) = r^{-2h} (q f e_r + f' e_phi), so ||grad Theta_R - grad(r^q f)||^p_{L^p(A(c1, c2))} =
int_{c1}^{c2} rho^{1-2hp} ||(R rho)^{2h} grad Theta(R rho, .) - q f e_r - f' e_phi||_p^p drho -> 0 by dominated
convergence with the circle bound of (a).
Step 12 (velocity in W^{1,p}, quadratic limits). On A' = A(c1/2, 2 c2), v_R := u_R - U_inf is in W^{1,p}, div v_R = 0
and its curl is z_R; Lemma 38.1 gives ||Dv_R||_{L^p(A(c1, c2))} <= C (||z_R||_{L^p(A')} + ||v_R||_{L^p(A')}) -> 0 for
1 < p < inf by Step 10 (applied on A'), and p = 1 follows by Holder. With d_phi e_r = e_phi, d_phi e_phi = -e_r:
d_r U_inf = (1-h) r^{-h} (-P' e_r + a P e_phi) and r^{-1} d_phi U_inf = r^{-h} ((-P'' - a P) e_r + (1-h) P' e_phi), that
is DU_inf = r^{-h} M_P, with tr M_P = 0 and (M_P)_12 - (M_P)_21 = -P'' - a^2 P = G, so |M_P|^2 >= G^2/2. By change of
variables
  R^{-(2-4h)} int_{A_R} |grad Theta|^2 = int_1^2 rho^{1-4h} ||(R rho)^{2h} grad Theta(R rho, .)||_2^2 drho,
  R^{-(2-2h)} int_{A_R} Omega^2 = int_{A_1} omega_R^2,      R^{-(2-2h)} int_{A_R} |DU|^2 = int_{A_1} |D u_R|^2,
which converge, by (f) with dominated convergence, by Step 10 and by W^{1,2} convergence on the closure of A_1, to the
limits in (g) (int_1^2 rho^{1-4h} drho = (2^{2-4h} - 1)/(2 - 4h) with 2 - 4h = 2q > 0, int_1^2 rho^{1-2h} drho = C_h,
|q f e_r + f' e_phi|^2 = q^2 f^2 + f'^2). They are positive because q > 0, f is not 0 and G is not 0. QED.

### Theorem 39 (beta = 2: regular backward sources, global coordinates on the regular set, convergent balances)
Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile, W = 2X + U, and let H, G, P be as in Theorem 36. Write
grad^perp f = (-f_y, f_x), N = {grad Theta != 0} (open), Z_reg = Z cap N, and, on N,
  L := W . grad^perp Theta / |grad Theta|^2                                                                (39.1)
(the function lam of Theorem 3). For X in N \ Z put k0(X) := 1/L(X); this is the number lambda(X) of Theorem 33(c).
(a) For every X in N \ Z the backward orbit converges to a point pi(X) in Z_reg. More precisely, the curve
    z -> Phi_{(log z)/4} X, 0 < z <= 1, extends to a C^infinity curve on [0, 1] with value pi(X) at z = 0, and
      Phi_t X = pi(X) + (L(X)/4) grad^perp Theta(pi(X)) e^{4t} + O(e^{8t})   (t -> -infinity),                (39.2)
    with a nonzero coefficient of e^{4t}. No escape hypothesis and no regular-value hypothesis is used.
(b) On N, W = L grad^perp Theta, {Theta, L} = Theta_x L_y - Theta_y L_x = 4 and W . grad L = 4L. Put pi(q) = q for q in
    Z_reg. Then pi : N -> Z_reg is C^infinity and (pi, L) : N -> Z_reg x R is a diffeomorphism. Each connected
    component of Z_reg is an open arc on which Theta is strictly monotone. On each connected component N' of N,
    (Theta, L) is a diffeomorphism of N' onto I x R for an open interval I, the area element is
    dX = (1/4) dTheta dL, and in these coordinates Phi_t(theta, l) = (theta, e^{4t} l). For theta in I the set
    {Theta = theta} cap N' consists of one point of Z_reg (l = 0) and two orbits (l > 0 and l < 0). If such an orbit
    is not escaping, every accumulation point of its forward half lies in R^2 \ N and has temperature theta.
(c) Omega = -div(L grad Theta) on N; in the coordinates of (b), 4 L Omega_L + Omega = 4 y_L, and with eps = sgn l,
      |l|^{1/4} Omega(theta, l) = int_0^{|l|} s^{-3/4} y_L(theta, eps s) ds.                                  (39.3)
(d) Let X in N \ Z be escaping, q = pi(X), A = lim_{t -> inf} e^{-2t} |Phi_t X| and phi_inf = lim_{t -> inf} of the
    polar angle of Phi_t X (both limits exist, 0 < A < infinity), and J(X) the outgoing amplitude of Theorem 33(c). Then
      I_*(X) := int_{-inf}^{inf} e^{-3t} (y(Phi_t X) - q_y) dt                                                (39.4)
    converges absolutely and
      J(X) = 3 k0(X) I_*(X),   H'(phi_inf) = -2 A^2 k0(X),   G(phi_inf) = A^{1/2} J(X).                       (39.5)
(e) Let F be C^1 on a neighbourhood of Theta(R^2), Q1 the open first quadrant, I0 = (0, pi/2) and K0 = x y |X|^{-4}.
    The following improper integrals over Q1 converge absolutely, and
      int_Q1 F(Theta) Omega^3 Theta_x dX = (1/2) int_I0 F(H) G^4 dphi,                                       (39.6)
      (p - 4) int_Q1 F(Theta) |Omega|^p dX = p int_Q1 F(Theta) |Omega|^{p-2} Omega Theta_x dX   (p > 4),       (39.7)
      int_Q1 F(Theta) grad Theta . (DU grad Theta) dX = -int_I0 F(H) (H')^2 dphi,                            (39.8)
      int_Q1 K0 Omega dX = 3 pi / 2 = int_Q1 K0 Theta_x dX + int_Q1 Omega U . grad K0 dX,                      (39.9)
    and, if F(0) = 0 and b is C^1 on [0, pi/2],
      int_Q1 F(Theta) |X|^{-3} (-2 b U_r + b' U_phi) dX = 2 int_I0 b F(H) dphi.                               (39.10)
    For F = 1 the right sides of (39.6) and (39.8) are > 0 and < 0; for F(s) = s^2, b = 1, (39.10) gives
    int_Q1 Theta^2 U_r |X|^{-3} dX = -int_I0 H^2 dphi < 0.
These are necessary conditions; none of them is contradicted by the other results of this report.

Proof. By Theorem 36(b), with R0 large, |grad Theta| <= C r^{-1}, |Omega| <= C r^{-1/2}, |DU| <= C r^{-1/2} and
|U| <= C r^{1/2} for r >= R0, and W_r >= r there; backward orbits are bounded (proof of Theorem 1) and the flow is
global with det D Phi_t = e^{4t}.
Step 1 (cofactor transport). Theta o Phi_t = Theta gives grad Theta(Phi_t X) = D Phi_t(X)^{-T} grad Theta(X). For an
invertible 2x2 matrix M, M^{-T} R = (det M)^{-1} R M with R(a, b) = (-b, a) (since cof M = R M R^{-1}). On N, W is orthogonal to
grad Theta, so W = L grad^perp Theta = L R grad Theta with L smooth, and grad Theta = -R W / L off Z. With
D Phi_t(X) W(X) = W(Phi_t X):
  grad Theta(Phi_t X) = -(e^{-4t}/L(X)) R W(Phi_t X),   equivalently  L(Phi_t X) = e^{4t} L(X),                (39.11)
which is (33.1). For t <= 0 the backward orbit lies in a compact set on which |grad Theta| <= C_X, so
|W(Phi_t X)| <= |L(X)| C_X e^{4t}; hence Phi_t X converges to some q as t -> -infinity, |Phi_t X - q| <= C e^{4t},
and W(q) = 0.
Step 2 ((a)). Put Y(z) = Phi_{(log z)/4} X. By (39.11), W(Phi_t X) = L(Phi_t X) grad^perp Theta(Phi_t X) =
e^{4t} L(X) grad^perp Theta(Phi_t X), so dY/dz = W(Y)/(4z) = (L(X)/4) grad^perp Theta(Y), a smooth autonomous
equation. Since Y(z) -> q as z -> 0, Y(z) = q + int_0^z (L(X)/4) grad^perp Theta(Y(s)) ds, so Y is C^1 on [0, 1] and,
by induction on the equation, C^infinity. If grad Theta(q) = 0, q is an equilibrium of this equation and uniqueness
gives Y = q, contradicting W(X) != 0. Hence q is in Z_reg, and Taylor expansion at z = 0 gives (39.2).
Step 3 ((b)). div grad^perp Theta = 0, so 4 = div W = grad^perp Theta . grad L = {Theta, L}, and
W . grad L = L grad^perp Theta . grad L = 4L. Thus (Theta, L) is a local chart near every point of N with Jacobian 4,
Z_reg = {L = 0} is a smooth curve along which Theta has nonzero derivative, and in such a chart the flow is
(theta, l) -> (theta, e^{4t} l). A component of Z_reg is a connected 1-manifold; it is not a circle, because a smooth
function on a circle has a critical point, so it is an open arc and Theta is strictly monotone on it. Smoothness of
pi: for X in N \ Z choose T with Phi_{-T} X in a chart box B around pi(X) of the form {|theta - Theta(pi X)| < d,
|l| < d}; in B the backward flow is (theta, e^{-4s} l), so for Y near X, Phi_{-T} Y is in B and pi(Y) is the point of
B with coordinates (Theta(Y), 0); this is smooth in Y, and the same chart shows smoothness on Z_reg. Surjectivity of
(pi, L): given q in Z_reg and l != 0, take the chart point (Theta(q), l0) with 0 < |l0| small and sgn l0 = sgn l, and
flow for the time (1/4) log(l/l0); by (39.11) this point has L = l and source q. Injectivity: points with the same
source q and the same sign of L lie on the same orbit (they enter the chart at q on the same side, where
{theta = Theta(q), l > 0} and {theta = Theta(q), l < 0} are single orbit segments), and on one orbit L(Phi_t X) =
e^{4t} L(X) is strictly monotone. The inverse is the chart inverse composed with a finite-time flow, hence smooth.
Since Theta o pi = Theta and Theta is a diffeomorphism from each arc of Z_reg onto an open interval, (Theta, L) is a
diffeomorphism from N' = (pi, L)^{-1}(arc x R) onto I x R, with area element (1/4) dTheta dL by the Jacobian. If the
forward half of the orbit of (theta, l), l != 0, accumulates at Y in N, then |L(Phi_t X)| = e^{4t} |l| -> infinity along
a sequence converging to Y, contradicting continuity of L at Y; so Y is not in N, and Theta(Y) = theta by continuity.
Step 4 ((c)). The dilation 2X has zero curl, so Omega = d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = -d_y(L Theta_y) - d_x(L Theta_x) =
-div(L grad Theta). Inverting the Jacobian of (Theta, L) gives x_L = -Theta_y/4 and y_L = Theta_x/4, and
W . grad = 4L d_L, so (V) reads 4 L Omega_L + Omega = 4 y_L. With l = eps s this is d/ds[s^{1/4} Omega] =
s^{-3/4} y_L(theta, eps s); since Omega is bounded near the source, s^{1/4} Omega -> 0 as s -> 0, and (39.3) follows.
Step 5 ((d)). For r >= R0, d(log r - 2t)/dt = U_r/r = O(r^{-1/2}) and dphi/dt = U_phi/r = O(r^{-1/2}); since r grows at
least like e^{t} once large, both right sides are integrable in t, so A and phi_inf exist with 0 < A < infinity.
By (39.11), Theta_x(Phi_t X) = k0 e^{-4t} W_2(Phi_t X) = k0 e^{-4t} d/dt y(Phi_t X). The orbit is bounded for t <= 0,
and by (V), Omega(X) = int_{-inf}^0 e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) dt (the term e^t Omega(Phi_t X) tends to 0 as t -> -inf).
With Theorem 33(c), J(X) = int_{-inf}^{inf} e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) dt = k0 int_{-inf}^{inf} e^{-3t} (d/dt)(y - q_y) dt.
The integrand is O(e^{t}) as t -> -inf by (39.2) and O(e^{-t}) as t -> +inf (|W| <= C e^{2t}). Integration by parts,
with boundary terms e^{-3t}(y - q_y) = O(e^{t}) and O(e^{-t}), gives J = 3 k0 I_*, with I_* absolutely convergent.
The polar component of (39.11) is Theta_phi(Phi_t X) = r e_phi . grad Theta = -k0 e^{-4t} r W_r (since
e_phi . R W = e_r . W = W_r); by Theorem 36(b) Theta_phi -> H'(phi) uniformly and W_r/r -> 2, so H'(phi_inf) = -2 A^2 k0. Finally
r^{1/2} Omega -> G uniformly and e^t Omega(Phi_t X) -> J(X), so G(phi_inf) = lim (A e^{2t})^{1/2} e^{-t} J(X) =
A^{1/2} J(X).
Step 6 ((e)). For C^1 functions a (smooth off O), F and B, (T), (V) and div W = 4 give
  div[a F(Theta) B(Omega) W] = F(Theta) { a (4B - Omega B') + a B'(Omega) Theta_x + B W . grad a }.            (39.12)
The axes are invariant, so W is tangent to the straight sides of D_R = Q1 cap {eps < |X| < R} and only the arcs
contribute flux. Near O, Omega, Theta_x = O(r^2), Theta = O(r^3), U = O(r); at infinity Theorem 36(b) gives the decay
rates above, and Theta -> H(phi), r^{1/2} Omega -> G(phi) and Theta_phi -> H'(phi) uniformly, with W_r/r -> 2.
(39.6): a = 1, B = z^4: div[F Omega^4 W] = 4 F Omega^3 Theta_x; the integrand is O(r^{-5/2}); the outer flux
R int_I0 F Omega^4 W_r dphi -> 2 int_I0 F(H) G^4. For F = 1 the right side is positive since G is continuous (Theorem 36)
and not identically zero (Theorem 34(b)). (39.7): B = |z|^p (C^1 for p > 1), a = 1: div[F |Omega|^p W] = F[(4 - p)|Omega|^p +
p |Omega|^{p-2} Omega Theta_x]; for p > 4 both terms are O(r^{-p/2}) and integrable, and the outer flux is
O(R^{2 - p/2}) -> 0. (39.8): g = grad Theta satisfies W . grad g = -(DW)^T g, so div(|g|^2 W) = 4|g|^2 - 2 g . (DW g)
= -2 g . (DU g); multiplying by F(Theta) adds no term since W . grad Theta = 0. The integrand is O(r^{-5/2}). By (T),
r Theta_r = -(U_phi/W_r) Theta_phi = O(r^{-1/2}), so R^2 |g|^2 -> (H')^2 uniformly on |X| = R and the outer flux tends
to 2 int_I0 F(H) (H')^2. For F = 1 the right side is negative because H is not identically zero, H(0) = H(pi/2) = 0, so
H' is not identically zero on I0. (39.9): K0 is homogeneous of degree -2, so 2X . grad K0 = -4 K0 and (39.12) with
a = K0, B(z) = z, F = 1 gives div(K0 Omega W) = K0 Theta_x - K0 Omega + Omega U . grad K0. Near O each term is O(1) and
the inner flux is O(eps^2); at infinity the terms are O(r^{-3}), O(r^{-5/2}), O(r^{-3}) and the outer flux is
O(R^{-1/2}). This gives the second equality. For the first, use the
centered-disc identity of Theorem 9 (K0 is its kernel K): Psi_xy(0) - (1/pi) int_{|Y|<R} K0 Omega dY =
(1/pi) oint_{|Y|=R} (K0 d_r Psi - Psi d_r K0) dS. Since Psi is odd, Psi(0) = 0, and |grad Psi| = |U| <= C r^{1/2} gives
Psi = O(R^{3/2}); with K0 = O(R^{-2}) and d_r K0 = O(R^{-3}) the boundary term is O(R^{-1/2}). As K0 Omega = O(1) near O
and O(r^{-5/2}) at infinity, the integral over R^2 converges absolutely, so Psi_xy(0) = (1/pi) int_{R^2} K0 Omega =
(4/pi) int_Q1 K0 Omega (K0 Omega is even in x and in y), and Psi_xy(0) = 2 beta + 2 = 6 (Theorem 9). (The ungrouped
logarithmic potential is not used: it does not converge absolutely when G is not identically zero.) (39.10): a = |X|^{-2} b(phi), B = 1. Homogeneity gives
4a + 2X . grad a = 0, so div[a F W] = F U . grad a = F |X|^{-3}(-2 b U_r + b' U_phi). Near O, F(Theta) = O(r^3) and the
integrand is O(r); the inner flux is O(eps^3). At infinity the integrand is O(r^{-5/2}) and the outer flux
int_I0 b F(Theta) W_r/R dphi tends to 2 int_I0 b F(H). QED.

Remark 39.1 (formal expansions; verified; see Theorems 68 and 70). At beta = 2 the natural tail admits a formal expansion
Theta ~ sum_j r^{-j/2} H_j, Omega ~ sum_j r^{-(j+1)/2} G_j, Psi ~ sum_j r^{(3-j)/2} P_j whose coefficients satisfy
n H_n = sum_{k+l=n-1} [(l/2) P_k' H_l + ((3-k)/2) P_k H_l'] and
n G_n = sum_{k+l=n-1} [((l+1)/2) P_k' G_l + ((3-k)/2) P_k G_l'] + ((n-1)/2) cos(phi) H_{n-1} + sin(phi) H_{n-1}', with
-(P_j'' + ((3-j)/2)^2 P_j) = G_j. In the odd-odd class (basis sin(2m phi), m >= 1) the elliptic operator has the eigenvalues
4m^2 - (3 - j)^2/4, so it has a kernel exactly when j = 4m + 3 with m >= 1 (j = 7, 11, 15, ...); at
j = 7 a pure-power expansion requires the sin(2 phi) coefficient of G_7 to vanish, and otherwise a term
r^{-2} log r sin(2 phi) enters (-Lap[r^{-2} log r sin 2phi] = 4 r^{-4} sin 2phi). With polynomials in z = log r allowed
as coefficients, every finite order is formally solvable: at order n >= 1 the transport equations have the operator
n - 2 d_z on the unknowns H_n, G_n, invertible on polynomials of degree <= d with inverse (1/n) sum_{k<=d} (2 d_z/n)^k,
and the elliptic equation becomes -(d_phi^2 + ((3 - n)/2 + d_z)^2) P_n = G_n, which on each angular mode is a nonzero
constant plus degree-lowering terms, except on the resonant mode, where it reads -d_z(3 - n + d_z) P_n = G_n with
3 - n != 0 and is solved by one polynomial antiderivative. For the leading data H_0 = sin(phi) cos^2(phi), G_0 = -sin(phi) H_0', the
sin(2 phi) coefficient of G_7 (writing f = sum_m f_m sin(m phi), with H_0 = (sin phi + sin 3phi)/4) was computed in
exact rational arithmetic, in two independent computations, as -248652665830143836372937708761809789 /
5600812026228230278370435051520000000000, which is nonzero, so this leading pair has no
pure-power continuation. Nothing here asserts convergence or realization by a profile.

### Theorem 40 (beta >= 2: the outgoing distribution is a function with an exact weak-L^{2 beta} law)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta >= 2, and let W, Phi_t, V and K be as in Theorem 37. Let
E be the set of escaping points and E^c = R^2 \ E. Since U = o(|X|), fix R0 >= 2 with |U(X)| <= beta |X|/4 for
|X| >= R0/2; then W_r >= c r for |X| >= R0/2 with c = 3 beta/4, and for beta > 2, R0 is admissible in Theorem 38 (at beta = 2 the same exterior construction is used with
Theorem 36). Put e(alpha) = (cos alpha, sin alpha), X(s, alpha) = Phi_s(R0 e(alpha)), D0(alpha) = R0 W_r(R0 e(alpha))
and j(u, alpha) = e^u Omega(X(u, alpha)).
(a) E^c is compact, Phi_t(E^c) = E^c for every real t, and |E^c| = 0. The map (s, alpha) -> X(s, alpha) is a diffeomorphism of
    R x (R/2 pi Z) onto E with dX = D0(alpha) e^{2 beta s} ds dalpha, and s < 0 exactly on E cap B_R0.
(b) For almost every alpha (every alpha if beta = 2) the limit J0(alpha) = lim_{u -> inf} j(u, alpha) exists, J0 is in
