    L^p(dalpha) for every finite p, and K is the locally integrable function
      K(X(s, alpha)) = e^{-s} J0(alpha)   on E                                                           (40.1)
    (no part of K is supported on E^c). For every compact C and 1 <= p < 2 beta, as t -> infinity,
      ||e^t Omega o Phi_t - K||_{L^p(C)} = O(e^{-t}) (p < beta), O((1 + t)^{1/p} e^{-t}) (p = beta),
      O(e^{-(2 beta/p - 1) t}) (beta < p < 2 beta).                                                      (40.2)
(c) C_K := (1/(2 beta)) int_0^{2 pi} D0 |J0|^{2 beta} dalpha satisfies 0 < C_K < infinity, and for every lambda > 0
      |{X in R^2 : |K(X)| > lambda}| = C_K lambda^{-2 beta}.                                               (40.3)
    Hence K is in weak L^{2 beta}(R^2), in L^p_loc for p < 2 beta, in no L^p(R^2) with 1 <= p < infinity, and
    int_{B_{R0/2}} |K|^{2 beta} dX = infinity. The constant C_K does not depend on R0.
(d) V is not in W^{1, 2 beta}_loc(R^2), and {Theta, V} = K - Omega is not in L^{2 beta}_loc(R^2).
(e) If beta = 2, then for every alpha the limits A(alpha) = lim_{u -> inf} e^{-2u} |X(u, alpha)| in (0, inf) and
    phi_inf(alpha) = lim_{u -> inf} arg X(u, alpha) exist (they agree with the quantities of Theorem 39(d) wherever that
    theorem applies), J0 is continuous, J0(alpha) = A(alpha)^{-1/2} G(phi_inf(alpha)), and
    sup_alpha |j(u, alpha) - J0(alpha)| <= C e^{-u} for u >= 0.
Part (d) is a property of the infinite-time integral V, not of the profile fields, which are smooth; it is not a
contradiction.

Proof. Step 0 (exterior input). We use: (AMP) for almost every alpha the limit J0(alpha) exists, J0 is in L^p(dalpha)
for every finite p, and ||j(u, .) - J0||_{L^p(dalpha)} <= C_p e^{-u} for u >= 0. For beta > 2 this is Theorem 38(c), applied with
the same R0 (its X(s, alpha) is the present one). For beta = 2 it follows from
Theorem 36(b) and gives (e): along u -> X(u, alpha), d(log r - 2u)/du = U_r/r = O(r^{-1/2}) and dphi/du = U_phi/r =
O(r^{-1/2}) uniformly in alpha, and r >= R0 e^{cu}; integrating once gives log r = 2u + log A + O(e^{-cu/2}), so
r >= c' e^{2u}, and integrating again gives r = A e^{2u}(1 + O(e^{-u})) and phi = phi_inf + O(e^{-u}), uniformly in alpha,
with A and phi_inf continuous and 0 < A < infinity. Since Omega = r^{-1/2} G(phi) + O(r^{-1}) with G smooth,
j(u, alpha) = A^{-1/2} G(phi_inf) + O(e^{-u}) uniformly. Only (AMP) and Theorem 37(a), (b) are used below.
Step 1 ((a)). Once an orbit reaches |X| >= R0/2 its radius is nondecreasing and grows at least like e^{ct}, so it
escapes and never returns; hence every nonescaping orbit stays in the closed disk B_{R0/2}, and E^c is bounded and
invariant. E is open by continuous dependence, so E^c is compact. Liouville's formula det D Phi_t = e^{2 beta t} and
Phi_t(E^c) = E^c give |E^c| = e^{2 beta t} |E^c| for all t, so |E^c| = 0. An escaping orbit crosses |X| = R0, and does so once
and transversally because W_r > 0 there; so (s, alpha) -> X(s, alpha) is a bijection onto E, with s < 0 exactly on
E cap B_R0. With D = det(X_s, X_alpha) = det(W, X_alpha) and d/ds X_alpha = DW X_alpha, d/ds W(X) = DW W, the identity
det(Ma, b) + det(a, Mb) = (tr M) det(a, b) gives dD/ds = 2 beta D, and D(0, alpha) = det(W, R0 e_phi) = R0 W_r. So
D = D0 e^{2 beta s} > 0 and the map is a diffeomorphism. Check: |E cap B_R0| = (1/(2 beta)) int D0 dalpha =
(1/(2 beta)) int_{|X| = R0} W . n = pi R0^2 by the divergence theorem, consistent with |E^c| = 0.
Step 2 ((b)). Define k by (40.1) on E, with J0 := 0 on the null set of labels where the limit fails (the
cylinder over a null set of labels has zero area by the area formula), and k = 0 on E^c. For p < 2 beta, int_{s < 0} |k|^p dX = (2 beta - p)^{-1}
int D0 |J0|^p dalpha < infinity, and bounded s-intervals give finite integrals, so k is in L^p_loc. Let F_t = e^t
Omega o Phi_t; then F_t(X(s, alpha)) = e^{-s} j(t + s, alpha). Given a compact C, choose R > R0 with C in B_R; points of
E cap B_R have s <= S_R := c^{-1} log(R/R0). Split s < -t and -t <= s <= S_R. For s < -t the point X(t + s, alpha) lies
in B_R0, where |Omega| <= M0, so int_{s < -t} |F_t|^p dX <= M0^p e^{pt} int_{-inf}^{-t} e^{2 beta s} ds int D0 =
O(e^{-(2 beta - p) t}), and the same bound holds for k. On -t <= s <= S_R, by (AMP) and boundedness of D0,
  int |F_t - k|^p dX <= C int_{-t}^{S_R} e^{(2 beta - p) s} ||j(t + s, .) - J0||_p^p ds <= C_p e^{-pt} int_{-t}^{S_R} e^{(2 beta - 2p) s} ds,
which is O(e^{-pt}) for p < beta, O((1 + t) e^{-pt}) for p = beta and O(e^{-(2 beta - p) t}) for beta < p < 2 beta. Taking pth
roots and adding the first part (rate e^{-(2 beta/p - 1) t}, which is at least as fast in each case) gives (40.2) with
k in place of K. So F_t -> k in L^1_loc, hence in D'(R^2); by Theorem 37(a) F_t -> K in D'(R^2), so K = k. In particular
K has no part supported on the null set E^c; strong local convergence, not |Z| = 0 alone, gives this.
Step 3 ((c)). By Tonelli on the cylinder, for lambda > 0,
  |{|K| > lambda}| = int D0(alpha) int_{s < log(|J0(alpha)|/lambda)} e^{2 beta s} ds dalpha = (lambda^{-2 beta}/(2 beta)) int D0 |J0|^{2 beta} dalpha,
finite by (AMP). If C_K = 0 then J0 = 0 a.e. and K = 0, contradicting Theorem 37(b); so C_K > 0. The left side of (40.3)
does not involve R0. By the layer-cake formula int |K|^p = p C_K int_0^inf lambda^{p - 1 - 2 beta} d lambda, which
diverges at 0 for p < 2 beta, at infinity for p > 2 beta and at both ends for p = 2 beta. Backward orbits from the circle
|X| = R0 enter the closed disk B_{R0/2} within the time c^{-1} log 2 and stay there (-W points inward on |X| = R0/2),
so the open disk B_{R0/2} contains the cylinder region s < -c^{-1} log 2, on which int |K|^{2 beta} dX = int D0 |J0|^{2 beta} dalpha
int_{-inf}^{-c^{-1} log 2} ds = infinity (monotone convergence; the angular integral is 2 beta C_K > 0).
Step 4 ((d)). If V were in W^{1, 2 beta}_loc, then {Theta, V} = div(V grad^perp Theta) = grad^perp Theta . grad V, with
grad Theta smooth, would be in L^{2 beta}_loc, and so would K = Omega + {Theta, V}, contradicting (c). QED.

### Theorem 41 (beta > 2: uniform natural bounds; (DT) and (S) hold for every profile)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta > 2, and let h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h, kappa = beta - 2,
W = beta X + U. Then:
(a) There are R1 and C with
      |Omega(X)| <= C |X|^{-h},   |grad Theta(X)| <= C |X|^{-2h},   |DU(X)| <= C |X|^{-h}   (|X| >= R1).        (41.1)
(b) Hypothesis (DT) of Theorem 32 and hypothesis (S) of Theorem 37(d) hold. Hence the conclusions of Theorem 32(a) to
    (d), alternative (N) of Theorem 32(e) and the conclusions of Theorem 37(d) hold. The function f of Theorem 32(d)
    equals the function f of Theorem 38(b), and the continuous function G of Theorem 32(d) is a representative of the
    L^p class G of Theorem 38(d). In particular G is continuous, odd in x and in y, vanishes on both axes, is not
    identically zero, and has the sign of a0 on a nonempty open interval of angles in (0, pi/2); and, uniformly in
    phi, r^{-q} Theta(r, phi) -> f(phi), r^h Omega(r, phi) -> G(phi) and r^{h-1} (U_r, U_phi)(r, phi) ->
    (-P', (2 - h) P)(phi), where P is the unique 2 pi-periodic solution of -(P'' + (2 - h)^2 P) = G.
(c) Let R0 and X(s, alpha) be as in Theorem 38. The integral defining J0 in Theorem 38(c) converges absolutely for every
    alpha and defines a continuous representative of the L^p class J0; this representative satisfies
      sup_alpha |e^s Omega(X(s, alpha)) - J0(alpha)| <= C e^{-s}   (s >= 0).                                      (41.2)
The constants depend on the profile (and in (c) on R0). Scope. The theorem gives no Holder or higher regularity of G,
no rate for the Eulerian angular limits beyond those of Theorem 32(b), and it neither constructs nor excludes a profile.

Proof. Step 1 (Lemma 41.1: a directional inverse estimate). Let 4 < p < infinity, eta = 1 - 2/p,
A = {1 < |x| < 2}, A1 = {1/2 < |x| < 4}, and B(z) = (z_2, -z_1)/(2 pi |z|^2) as in Lemma 38.2. There is C = C(p) such
that, if u, omega, Z are smooth on a neighbourhood of the closure of A1 with div u = 0, d_y u_1 - d_x u_2 = omega, and
  L := sup_{A1} |u| + ||omega||_{L^p(A1)} + ||div(Z omega)||_{L^p(A1)} + sup_{A1} |Z| + [Z]_{eta, A1},
where [Z]_{eta, A1} = sup{|Z(x) - Z(y)| |x - y|^{-eta} : x, y in A1, x != y}, then |Du(x) Z(x)| <= C (L + L^2) for x in A.
Proof. Fix once and for all chi in C_c^infinity(A1) with 0 <= chi <= 1 and chi = 1 on N1 = {3/4 < |x| < 3}, and put
f = chi omega and v = B * f. As f is smooth with compact support, v is smooth, div v = 0 and d_y v_1 - d_x v_2 = f
(Lemma 38.2). Since p > 2, |B(z)| <= C |z|^{-1} is in L^{p'} on bounded sets, so |v| <= C ||f||_p <= C L. On N1, u - v is
divergence-free and curl-free, so its components are harmonic and bounded by C L; interior derivative estimates on
balls of a fixed radius give |D(u - v)| <= C L on A, hence |D(u - v) Z| <= C L^2 there. For the potential part,
d_j v = B * d_j f, and for fixed x in A write
Z(x) . grad f(y) = div(Z f)(y) - f(y) div Z(y) + (Z(x) - Z(y)) . grad f(y). Integrating the last term by parts in y
over A1 minus the disc |y - x| <= eps (f vanishes near the outer boundary; the inner boundary term is O(eps^eta) since
|B| <= C/eps and |Z(x) - Z(y)| <= [Z] eps^eta there) and letting eps -> 0 gives, for x in A,
  Du(x) Z(x) - D(u - v)(x) Z(x) = (B * div(Z f))(x) + int f(y) [(Z(x) - Z(y)) . grad] B(x - y) dy,                (41.3)
where [(Z(x) - Z(y)) . grad] B(x - y) = sum_j (Z_j(x) - Z_j(y)) (d_j B)(x - y). The integration by parts
produces + B * (f div Z) (because div_y (Z(x) - Z(y)) = - div Z(y)), which cancels the term - B * (f div Z) of the expansion.
Here div(Z f) = chi div(Z omega) + (Z . grad chi) omega has L^p norm at most C(L + L^2), so the first term is at most
C(L + L^2). In the second, |Z(x) - Z(y)| |DB(x - y)| <= C [Z] |x - y|^{eta - 2}, and |z|^{eta - 2} is in L^{p'} on
bounded sets because (2 - eta) p' = (p + 2)/(p - 1) < 2, which is equivalent to p > 4; by Holder the second term is at
most C [Z] ||f||_p <= C L^2. This proves the lemma. (No norm of DZ or of div Z enters beyond the given bound on
||div(Z omega)||_p; smoothness of the data is used only to justify the integrations by parts.)
Step 2 (rescaled fields; the derivative of U along W). Fix p in (4, infinity). For R >= 2 put
  u_R(x) = R^{h-1} U(Rx),  omega_R(x) = R^h Omega(Rx),  g_R(x) = R^{2h} grad Theta(Rx),  Z_R(x) = W(Rx)/R = beta x + R^{-h} u_R(x).
Then div u_R = 0 and d_y u_{R,1} - d_x u_{R,2} = omega_R. The region {1/4 < |x| < 8} is covered, up to four circles,
by the five annuli A_c = {c < |x| < 2c}, c = 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 4. By Theorem 38(a), for these c,
||omega_R||_{L^p(A_c)} = R^{h - 2/p} ||Omega||_{L^p(A_{cR})} <= C, ||g_R||_{L^p(A_c)} = R^{2h - 2/p} ||grad Theta||_{L^p(A_{cR})}
<= C, and |u_R(x)| <= C |x|^{1-h}, for R >= R0' := max(2, 4 R0) with R0 as in Theorem 38(a). Hence
sup_{1/4 < |x| < 8} |u_R| + ||omega_R||_{L^p(1/4 < |x| < 8)} + ||g_R||_{L^p(1/4 < |x| < 8)} <= C, with C independent of
R >= R0'. Lemma 38.1 (with c = 1/2, c' = 4) gives ||Du_R||_{L^p(A1)} <= C, and Morrey's inequality on the smooth
bounded domain A1 gives [u_R]_{eta, A1} <= C with eta = 1 - 2/p. So sup_{A1} |Z_R| + [Z_R]_{eta, A1} <= C. Since
grad_x omega_R(x) = R^{h+1} (grad Omega)(Rx), we have R^h W(Rx) . (grad Omega)(Rx) = Z_R(x) . grad omega_R(x); also
div Z_R(x) = (div W)(Rx) = 2 beta. Multiplying (V) at Rx by R^h therefore gives
  Z_R . grad omega_R + omega_R = R^{-h} (g_R)_1,   div(Z_R omega_R) = (2 beta - 1) omega_R + R^{-h} (g_R)_1,         (41.4)
so ||div(Z_R omega_R)||_{L^p(A1)} <= C. Lemma 41.1 gives |Du_R(x) Z_R(x)| <= C for x in A, and |Z_R| >= beta - C
R^{-h} >= beta/2 on A for R large. Since Du_R(x) = R^h DU(Rx) and Z_R/|Z_R| = e(Rx) with e := W/|W|, taking R = 2|X|/3 this is
  |DU(X) e(X)| <= C |X|^{-h}   (|X| >= R2).                                                                      (41.5)
Step 3 (moving frame). By Theorem 38(a), |U| <= C |X|^{1-h} for |X| >= 1, so h |X|^{h-1} |U| <= C3 for |X| >= 1.
Fix R3 >= max(R2, 1) with |U(X)| <= beta |X|/4 for |X| >= R3 and R3^h >= 2 C3. Along an orbit in |X| >= R3 the function
z = |X|^h satisfies z' = h |X|^{h-1} W_r = z + h |X|^{h-1} U_r (as h beta = 1), with |h |X|^{h-1} U_r| <= C3.
Put X(t, alpha) = Phi_t(R3 e(alpha)) (in Steps 3 and 4 only; Step 5 uses the orbits X(s, alpha) of Theorem 38,
launched at radius R0). Then |d/dt (e^{-t} z)| <= C3 e^{-t}, so R3^h - C3 <= e^{-t} z <= R3^h + C3, and
  C^{-1} e^{beta t} <= |X(t, alpha)| <= C e^{beta t},   C^{-1} e^{beta t} <= |W(X(t, alpha))| <= C e^{beta t}   (t >= 0),   (41.6)
uniformly in alpha (|W| lies between (3/4) beta |X| and (5/4) beta |X|). Every X with |X| >= R3 is X(t, alpha) for some
t >= 0 and alpha (Theorem 38, Step 1). Along X(t, alpha) let e = W/|W|, n = J e with J(v1, v2) = (-v2, v1), and write DU
in the positively oriented orthonormal basis (e, n) as [[k1, k2], [k3, -k1]] (k1 = e . DU e, k2 = e . DU n,
k3 = n . DU e; the trace vanishes as div U = 0). The antisymmetric part is invariant under rotations, so
Omega = d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = k2 - k3. By (41.5) and (41.6), |k1| + |k3| <= 2 |DU e| <= C e^{-t}. From d/dt W(X) = DW W
and DW = beta I + DU, e' = (n . DW e) n = k3 n and n' = J e' = -k3 e. Differentiating (T) gives D^2 Theta W = kappa grad Theta - DW^T grad Theta, so g(t) =
grad Theta(X(t, alpha)) satisfies g' = -2 g - DU^T g. Put
  E = e^{2t} g . e,   Bn = e^{2t} g . n,   j = e^t Omega(X(t, alpha)).
By (T), W . g = kappa Theta and Theta(X(t, alpha)) = e^{kappa t} Theta(R3 e(alpha)), so E = kappa Theta(R3 e(alpha))
e^{beta t}/|W| is bounded by (41.6). Differentiating,
  Bn' = 2 Bn + e^{2t} (g' . n + g . n') = e^{2t} (- g . DU n - k3 g . e) = k1 Bn - (k2 + k3) E = k1 Bn - (Omega + 2 k3) E,   (41.7)
using g . DU n = k2 (g . e) - k1 (g . n), and by (V)
  j' = e^t Theta_x(X(t, alpha)) = e^{-t} (E e_1 + Bn n_1),                                                        (41.8)
where e_1, n_1 are the first components of e, n. With Omega = e^{-t} j, (41.7) and (41.8) give
|Bn'| + |j'| <= C e^{-t} (1 + |Bn| + |j|). The initial values are bounded (smooth fields on a circle), so Gronwall
gives |Bn| + |j| <= C for all t >= 0, uniformly in alpha. Hence |Omega(X(t, alpha))| <= C e^{-t},
|g| <= e^{-2t} (|E| + |Bn|) <= C e^{-2t}, |k2| <= |Omega| + |k3| <= C e^{-t} and |DU| <= C e^{-t}. By (41.6) this is
(41.1) with R1 = R3.
Step 4 ((b)). (41.1) gives |Theta_x| <= C |X|^{-2/beta} for |X| >= R1, which is (DT). An A2-broad profile satisfies the
other hypotheses of Theorem 32 (Section 2). By (41.1) the largest eigenvalue of (DU + DU^T)/2 is at most |DU| -> 0, so
(S) holds with sigma = 1/2 and R_* large, and Theorem 37(d) applies, and with it alternative (N). The limit f of
Theorem 32(d) and that of Theorem 38(b) are both the uniform limit of r^{-q} Theta(r, .), so they are equal. The uniform
limit G of Theorem 32(d) is also a limit in L^p(dphi) of r^h Omega(r, .), so it agrees a.e. with the L^p limit of
Theorem 38(d). The remaining properties of G are stated in Theorem 32(d) and Theorem 37(d).
Step 5 ((c)). By Theorem 38(b), d(r, alpha) converges uniformly as r -> infinity, and it is continuous in (r, alpha), so
|d| <= D on r >= R0 for all alpha. At r = |X(s, alpha)| the definition of d gives r = R0 e^{beta (s - d)} >= c0 e^{beta s}
with c0 = R0 e^{-beta D} > 0. Let S = max(0, beta^{-1} log(R1/c0)); then |X(s, alpha)| >= R1 for all s >= S and all alpha,
so by (41.1) e^s |Theta_x(X(s, alpha))| <= C c0^{-2h} e^{-s} for s >= S. On the compact set [0, S] x S^1 the function
e^{2s} |Theta_x(X(s, alpha))| is continuous, hence bounded. So e^s |Theta_x(X(s, alpha))| <= M1 e^{-s} for all s >= 0 and
all alpha, with one constant M1. Hence the integral defining J0 in Theorem 38(c) converges absolutely and uniformly for
every alpha; it agrees with J0 wherever the latter was defined, so it is a representative of the same L^p class.
Integrating (V) along the orbit gives
e^s Omega(X(s, alpha)) - J0(alpha) = - int_s^inf e^u Theta_x(X(u, alpha)) du, so |e^s Omega(X(s, alpha)) - J0(alpha)|
<= M1 e^{-s} for every alpha and s >= 0, which is (41.2). Each j(s, .) = e^s Omega(X(s, .)) is continuous, so J0 is a
uniform limit of continuous functions and is continuous. QED.

Remark 41.2. Part (c) is the beta > 2 analogue of Theorem 40(e). In particular, for beta > 2 the limit
lim_{u -> inf} e^u Omega(Phi_u X) exists for every escaping X (every escaping orbit crosses the launch circle of Theorem
38, and a time shift multiplies the limit by a positive constant), so the limit J0 in Theorem 40(b) exists for every
alpha when beta > 2 as well.

### Theorem 42 (beta > 2: smooth natural tail)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta > 2, and let h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h, kappa = beta - 2,
W = beta X + U, X = r e(phi), e_r = e(phi), e_phi = e(phi + pi/2), D^k the Cartesian derivatives of order k, and
O_infty(r^m) as in Theorem 36. Let f, G and P be as in Theorem 41(b): f is the uniform limit of r^{-q} Theta(r, .)
(Theorems 32(d) and 38(b)), G that of r^h Omega(r, .), and P the unique 2 pi-periodic solution of
-(P'' + (2 - h)^2 P) = G. Let Psi be the stream function with U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x) and Psi(0) = 0 (it is odd in x and in
y, and -Lap Psi = Omega), and put psi_0 = r^{2-h} P(phi) and
u_0 = (-d_y psi_0, d_x psi_0) = r^{1-h} (-P' e_r + (2 - h) P e_phi).
(a) For every k >= 0 there is C_k such that, for |X| >= 1,
      |D^k U| <= C_k r^{1-h-k},  |D^k Omega| <= C_k r^{-h-k},  |D^k grad Theta| <= C_k r^{-2h-k},  |Theta| <= C_0 r^q.
(b) f, G and P are C^infinity on R/2piZ, and
      Theta - r^q f(phi) = O_infty(r^{q-h}),   Omega - r^{-h} G(phi) = O_infty(r^{-2h}),   U - u_0 = O_infty(r^{1-2h}).
(c) (first correction) Put
      f1 = -q P' f + (2 - h) P f',   G1 = h P' G + (2 - h) P G' - q cos(phi) f + sin(phi) f'.
    f1 has the parities of Theta and G1 is odd in x and in y; let P1 be the unique odd-odd solution of
    -(P1'' + (2 - 2h)^2 P1) = G1. The equation is nonresonant: as 1 < 2 - 2h < 2, P1 is also its only 2 pi-periodic
    solution. f1, G1 and P1 are C^infinity. With psi_1 = r^{2-2h} P1(phi) and
    u_1 = (-d_y psi_1, d_x psi_1) = r^{1-2h} (-P1' e_r + (2 - 2h) P1 e_phi),
      Theta = r^q [f + r^{-h} f1] + O_infty(r^{q-2h}),   Omega = r^{-h} [G + r^{-h} G1] + O_infty(r^{-3h}),
      U = u_0 + u_1 + O_infty(r^{1-3h}),   Psi = psi_0 + psi_1 + O_infty(r^{2-3h}).
    Moreover r^{q-h} f1 = u_0 . grad(r^q f) and r^{-2h} G1 = u_0 . grad(r^{-h} G) - d_x(r^q f): the corrections are the
    terms theta1, omega1 of the natural formal regime of Section 7 (there d = h, F = f, B = G).
The constants depend on k and on the profile. Scope. No radial series beyond the first correction, no analyticity, no
sharpness of the remainder exponents and no bound uniform in k is asserted. The remainder powers in (c) are one factor
r^{-h} below the corresponding first-correction powers and two factors r^{-h} below the leading powers; this compares
radial orders and is not a pointwise relative bound where angular coefficients vanish. The remainders need not decay
(q - 2h = 1 - 4/beta >= 0 for beta >= 4). (a) and (b) are the beta > 2 analogue of Theorem 36(a), (b). The theorem
neither constructs nor excludes a profile.

Proof. Fix 0 < sigma < 1. C, C_k do not depend on R, r, t, T, s or the angle; "bounded" means bounded by such a
constant for all sufficiently large R (or T, t); an annulus is a compact set {c <= |x| <= c'}, 0 < c < c'; and
rcurl v := d_y v_1 - d_x v_2. The Holder calculus (products, reciprocals, compositions) is (N3) of Theorem 36, Step 4.
Step 1 (local estimate with divergence). (36.4) holds, with the same proof, for fields v whose divergence need not
vanish, if the norm of div v is added on the right in the same norm as the curl: add K' * (eta div v),
K'(Z) = Z/(2 pi |Z|^2), to v_N (it is curl-free, has divergence eta div v and obeys the bounds of K * (eta w)). Call
this (36.4').
Step 2 (exact identities; derivative gain along W). Let u_R, omega_R, g_R and Z_R = beta x + eps u_R, eps = R^{-h}, be
as in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 41, so div u_R = 0, rcurl u_R = omega_R and (41.4) holds, and put
F_R = Du_R Z_R = (Z_R . grad) u_R. Then, with (Du_R)^2 the matrix square,
  div F_R = eps tr((Du_R)^2),   rcurl F_R = (beta - 1) omega_R + eps (g_R)_1.                                 (42.1)
Indeed div F_R = (d_i Z_{R,j}) (d_j u_{R,i}) + Z_R . grad div u_R = beta div u_R + eps tr((Du_R)^2); and
rcurl((x . grad) u_R) = omega_R + x . grad omega_R, rcurl((u_R . grad) u_R) = u_R . grad omega_R + (div u_R) omega_R, so
rcurl F_R = beta omega_R + Z_R . grad omega_R, and (41.4) gives (42.1). No derivative of omega_R or g_R enters. Hence,
for annuli A inside A': if u_R is bounded in C^{k+1,sigma}(A') and omega_R, g_R in C^{k,sigma}(A') (k >= 0), then
(36.4') bounds F_R in C^{k+1,sigma}(A); if only u_R, Du_R, omega_R, g_R are bounded on A', the second bound of (36.4')
bounds F_R in C^{0,sigma}(A).
Step 3 (orbits and charts). Let R3, X(t, alpha) = Phi_t(R3 e(alpha)), e, n, k1, k2, k3, E, Bn and j be as in Step 3 of
the proof of Theorem 41, and theta_3(alpha) = Theta(R3 e(alpha)). As in (38.1), det(W, X_alpha) = R3 W_r(R3 e(alpha))
e^{2 beta t} at X(t, alpha). Put Y(t, alpha) = e^{-beta t} X(t, alpha); by (41.6) Y stays in a fixed annulus, and
  d_t Y = e^{-t} u_{R(t)}(Y),   R(t) = e^{beta t}.                                                              (42.2)
For T >= L, R = e^{beta T} and (s, alpha) in the strip [-L, L] x S^1 let Y_T(s, alpha) = e^{-beta T} X(T + s, alpha)
= e^{beta s} Y(T + s, alpha). Then d_s Y_T = Z_R(Y_T) and det(d_s Y_T, d_alpha Y_T) = R3 W_r(R3 e(alpha)) e^{2 beta
s} >= c_L > 0. Each X with |X| >= R3 is X(t, alpha) for exactly one (t, alpha) (Theorem 38, Step 1), so by (41.6), for
every annulus A there is L such that for large T, Y_T maps an open part of the strip diffeomorphically onto a
neighbourhood of A; Y_T^{-1} is its inverse on A. With e_R = Z_R/|Z_R| = e(R .) and n_R = J e_R, at t = T + s and
x = Y_T(s, alpha) (so Du_R(x) = R^h DU(Rx), R^{-h} e^t = e^s and e^{beta t}/|W| = e^{beta s}/|Z_R(x)|),
  omega_R(x) = e^{-s} j,   g_R(x) = e^{-2s} [E e_R(x) + Bn n_R(x)],   E = kappa theta_3 e^{beta s}/|Z_R(x)|,
  k1^ := e^t k1 = e^s e_R . F_R(x)/|Z_R(x)|,   k3^ := e^t k3 = e^s n_R . F_R(x)/|Z_R(x)|.                    (42.3)
With Omega = e^{-t} j, (41.7) and (41.8) are the linear system
  d_t Bn = e^{-t} [k1^ Bn - (j + 2 k3^) E],   d_t j = e^{-t} [E e_1 + Bn n_1],                                (42.4)
whose coefficients k1^, k3^, E, e_1, n_1 involve DU only through DU e = R^{-h} F_R/|Z_R|; k2 is eliminated by
Omega = k2 - k3.
Lemma 42.1 (flow charts). If for some m >= 1 u_R is bounded in C^{m,sigma} on every annulus, then Y(t, .) is bounded in
C^{m,sigma}(S^1) for t >= 0, and for every L > 0, Y_T is bounded in C^{m,sigma}([-L, L] x S^1). For every annulus A,
choose a slightly larger annulus A+ and then L = L(A+) so large that, for all large T, the image under Y_T of the
interior of [-L, L] x S^1 contains a neighbourhood of A+; then Y_T^{-1} is bounded in C^{m,sigma}(A). (A strip of
fixed width covers only a bounded region, so the choice of L depends on A.) The constants may depend on A, L, m, sigma
and the profile. If only Du_R is bounded on every annulus, the same holds with C^{0,1} in place of C^{m,sigma}.
Proof. Differentiating (42.2) j times in alpha gives d_t d_alpha^j Y = e^{-t} [Du_R(Y) d_alpha^j Y + Q_j], Q_j a
polynomial in D^i u_R(Y) (2 <= i <= j) and d_alpha^l Y (l < j). Gronwall with the integrable weight e^{-t}, applied
order by order to the values and to the sigma-difference quotients in alpha, bounds Y(t, .) for t >= t_m, and the
smooth flow does so on [0, t_m]; no time derivative of u_R is used. By induction on the order, a derivative of Y_T of
order <= m containing d_s is a derivative of order <= m - 1 of Z_R(Y_T), bounded in C^{0,sigma}, and d_alpha^m Y_T is
C^sigma in alpha and Lipschitz in s (d_s d_alpha^m Y_T = d_alpha^m [Z_R(Y_T)]). By the determinant bound,
D(Y_T^{-1}) = (DY_T)^{-1} o Y_T^{-1} is bounded, so Y_T^{-1} is Lipschitz on A (join two points of A by a path in A+ of
length at most C_A times their distance and lift it; straight chords need not stay in the annulus),
and differentiating Y_T o Y_T^{-1} = id bounds Y_T^{-1} in C^{m,sigma}(A). For C^{0,1} only j = 1 is used.
Step 4 (induction). For k >= -1 let (I_k) be the statement: for large R and T, on every annulus A, omega_R and g_R are
bounded in C^{k,sigma}(A) and u_R in C^{k+1,sigma}(A); on every strip [-L, L] x S^1, Y_T is bounded in C^{k+1,sigma} and
(s, alpha) -> (Bn, j)(T + s, alpha) in C^{k,sigma}; for every annulus A, with the strip chosen for A as in Lemma 42.1,
Y_T^{-1} is bounded in C^{k+1,sigma}(A); and sup_{t >= 0} ||(Bn, j)(t, .)||_{C^{k,sigma}(S^1)} is finite. For k = -1,
C^{-1,sigma} means L^infty and C^{0,sigma} is replaced by C^{0,1} for u_R, Y_T and Y_T^{-1}. Constants and thresholds may
depend on the annulus, the strip and k.
(I_{-1}) holds by (41.1) (|Du_R(x)| = R^h |DU(Rx)|), |U| <= C r^{1-h} (Theorem 38(a)), |Bn| + |j| <= C (Step 3 of the
proof of Theorem 41) and Lemma 42.1. Assume (I_k). The following upgrades, in this order, give (I_{k+1}); each shrinks
the annulus, which costs nothing as (I_k) holds on every annulus.
(i) Coefficients first. Step 2 bounds F_R in C^{k+1,sigma}(A). By (42.3) and the chart bound of (I_k), k1^, k3^, E,
e_1 and n_1 at (T + s, alpha) are bounded in C^{k+1,sigma} of the strip (for k = -1: C^sigma functions composed with
Lipschitz maps); with T = t, s = 0 (and smoothness for bounded t), their C^{k+1,sigma}(S^1) norms at time t are bounded
for all t >= 0. No norm of order k + 1 of Bn, j, omega_R or g_R is used.
(ii) Bn and j by Gronwall. (42.4) is linear with these coefficients and smooth initial data, so
M(t) := ||(Bn, j)(t, .)||_{C^{k+1,sigma}(S^1)} obeys M(t) <= M(0) + C int_0^t e^{-v} (1 + M(v)) dv, and M <= C.
Jointly: a derivative of order <= k + 1 containing d_s is a derivative of order <= k of the right side of (42.4),
bounded in C^{0,sigma} of the strip by (i) and (I_k), and d_alpha^{k+1} (Bn, j) is C^sigma in alpha and Lipschitz in s
((42.4) differentiated k + 1 times in alpha); so (Bn, j)(T + ., .) is bounded in C^{k+1,sigma} of the strip.
(iii) omega_R and g_R via the charts. By (42.3), omega_R(x) = e^{-s} j and g_R(x) = e^{-2s} [E e_R(x) + Bn n_R(x)] at
(s, alpha) = Y_T^{-1}(x); by (ii) and the old chart bound of (I_k), both are bounded in C^{k+1,sigma}(A).
(iv) u_R by (36.4). As div u_R = 0, rcurl u_R = omega_R and |u_R| <= C, the first bound of (36.4) bounds u_R in
C^{k+2,sigma}(A).
(v) The charts last. Lemma 42.1 with m = k + 2 bounds Y_T and Y_T^{-1} in C^{k+2,sigma}. This is (I_{k+1}).
Step 5 ((a)). D^j u_R(x) = R^{h-1+j} (D^j U)(Rx), D^j omega_R(x) = R^{h+j} (D^j Omega)(Rx) and D^j g_R(x) = R^{2h+j}
(D^j grad Theta)(Rx); (I_k) on {1/2 <= |x| <= 2} at x = X/R, R = |X|, gives the first three bounds of (a) for large
|X|, and smoothness gives them for 1 <= |X| <= R1. By (T), Theta(X(t, alpha)) = e^{kappa t} theta_3(alpha), so (41.6)
gives |Theta| <= C e^{kappa t} <= C r^{kappa h} = C r^q. Thus Theta = O_infty(r^q), Omega = O_infty(r^{-h}) and
U = O_infty(r^{1-h}).
Step 6 (radial equations; (b) for Theta and Omega). Put Th(r, phi) = r^{-q} Theta(r e(phi)), Om = r^h Omega and
(v_r, v_phi) = r^{h-1} (U_r, U_phi). Conversion rule: D^k (r^m w) is a combination of r^{m-k} (r d_r)^a d_phi^b w,
a + b <= k, with smooth angular coefficients, and conversely; so r^m w = O_infty(r^{m-l}) if and only if every
(r d_r)^a d_phi^b w is O(r^{-l}) (r >= R1), also for polar components of fields. By Step 5 every (r d_r)^a d_phi^b of
Th, Om, v_r, v_phi is bounded. In polar coordinates W . grad = (beta r + U_r) d_r + (U_phi/r) d_phi and
Theta_x = r^{-2h} [q cos(phi) Th - sin(phi) d_phi Th + cos(phi) r d_r Th]; substituting into (T) and (V) and using
beta q = kappa and beta h = 1 gives exactly
  (beta + r^{-h} v_r) r d_r Th = -r^{-h} [q v_r Th + v_phi d_phi Th],                                         (42.5)
  (beta + r^{-h} v_r) r d_r Om = r^{-h} [h v_r Om - v_phi d_phi Om + q cos(phi) Th - sin(phi) d_phi Th
                                         + cos(phi) r d_r Th].                                                (42.6)
As beta + r^{-h} v_r >= beta/2 for large r and r d_r (r^{-h}) = -h r^{-h}, every (r d_r)^a d_phi^b of r d_r Th and of
r d_r Om is O(r^{-h}). Integrating d_phi^b (r d_r Th) in drho/rho shows that d_phi^b Th(r, .) converges uniformly as
r -> infinity with error O(r^{-h}); for b = 0 the limit is f (Theorem 41(b)), so f is C^infinity and
d_phi^b Th(r, .) -> f^{(b)}. Likewise for Om and G. Hence every (r d_r)^a d_phi^b of Th - f and of Om - G is O(r^{-h})
(for a >= 1 by the bound on r d_r Th, r d_r Om), and the conversion rule gives Theta - r^q f = O_infty(r^{q-h}) and
Omega - r^{-h} G = O_infty(r^{-2h}).
Step 7 (velocity; (b) for P and U). P is C^2 (Theorem 32(d)), and P'' = -G - (2 - h)^2 P puts P in C^{m+2} when it is
in C^m, so P is C^infinity. Lap(r^{2-h} P) = r^{-h} (P'' + (2 - h)^2 P) gives -Lap psi_0 = r^{-h} G for r > 0. Let chi
be smooth and radial, 0 for r <= 1 and 1 for r >= 2, u_* = (-d_y (chi psi_0), d_x (chi psi_0)) and
omega_* = -Lap(chi psi_0).
As chi psi_0 is smooth and odd in x and in y, u_* is smooth, divergence-free and O(r^{1-h}), has the A2 velocity
parities, and (u_*, omega_*) = (u_0, r^{-h} G) for r >= 2. zeta_0 := Omega - omega_* is smooth, odd in x and in y and
O((1 + |X|)^{-2h}) by Step 6, so ||zeta_0||_{L^4(A_rho)} <= C rho^{1/2 - 2h} for all rho > 0, and Lemma 38.2 (p = 4,
sigma = 2h < 1) gives its grouped inverse v_0 with |v_0| <= C |X|^{1-2h}. U - u_* - v_0 is divergence- and curl-free in
D'(R^2) and o(|X|), hence constant, and zero by parity, as in Step 6 of the proof of Theorem 38; so |U - u_0| <=
C r^{1-2h} for r >= 2. For R >= 16, m_R := R^{2h-1} (U - u_0)(R .) is bounded on {1/8 <= |x| <= 8}, div m_R = 0, and
rcurl m_R = R^{2h} (Omega - r^{-h} G)(R .) is bounded there in every C^k by Step 6; the first bound of (36.4) bounds m_R
in every C^{k+1,sigma}({1/2 <= |x| <= 2}), and D^j m_R = R^{2h-1+j} (D^j (U - u_0))(R .) gives
U - u_0 = O_infty(r^{1-2h}).
Step 8 (first correction; (c)). Under phi -> -phi and phi -> pi - phi, f is odd and even and G, P are odd and odd, so
f1 is odd and even and G1 odd and odd. Odd-odd functions expand in sin(2m phi), m >= 1, and 4m^2 - (2 - 2h)^2 >=
4 - (2 - 2h)^2 > 0, so P1 exists, is the only odd-odd solution and is C^infinity (as P in Step 7); as 2 - 2h is not an
integer, P1'' + (2 - 2h)^2 P1 = 0 has no nonzero 2 pi-periodic solution. Let V0 = (-P', (2 - h) P). By Steps 6, 7 and
the conversion rule, every (r d_r)^a d_phi^b of Th - f, Om - G, (v_r, v_phi) - V0 and r d_r Th is O(r^{-h}). Insert
this into (42.5)-(42.6), with 1/(beta + r^{-h} v_r) = h + O(r^{-h}): since h [-q P' f + (2 - h) P f'] = h f1,
h [-h P' G - (2 - h) P G' + q cos(phi) f - sin(phi) f'] = -h G1 and cos(phi) r d_r Th = O(r^{-h}),
  r d_r Th = -h r^{-h} f1 + O(r^{-2h}),   r d_r Om = -h r^{-h} G1 + O(r^{-2h}),                                 (42.7)
with every (r d_r)^a d_phi^b of the remainders also O(r^{-2h}). As r d_r (r^{-h} f1) = -h r^{-h} f1, (42.7) bounds
r d_r (Th - f - r^{-h} f1) and its derivatives by O(r^{-2h}); Th - f - r^{-h} f1 tends to 0 with all angular
derivatives (Step 6), so integration in drho/rho gives Th - f - r^{-h} f1 = O(r^{-2h}) with all derivatives, and the
conversion rule gives the expansion of Theta in (c); that of Omega follows in the same way. Next,
Lap(r^{2-2h} P1) = r^{-2h} (P1'' + (2 - 2h)^2 P1) gives -Lap psi_1 = r^{-2h} G1 for r > 0. With chi as in Step 7,
u_1* = (-d_y (chi psi_1), d_x (chi psi_1)) and omega_1* = -Lap(chi psi_1), zeta_1 := Omega - omega_* - omega_1* is
smooth, odd in x and in y and O((1 + |X|)^{-3h}). The proof of Lemma 38.2 uses sigma < 1 only for continuity at 0,
which is immediate for a source bounded near 0; otherwise it needs only 0 < sigma < 2 (sigma < 2 for the inner mass
sum, sigma > 0 for the outer sum and the limit), so it applies to zeta_1 with p = 4 and sigma = 3h < 3/2. As in Step 7,
U - u_* - u_1* is the grouped inverse of zeta_1, |U - u_0 - u_1| <= C r^{1-3h} for r >= 2, and (36.4) applied to
R^{3h-1} (U - u_0 - u_1)(R .) gives U = u_0 + u_1 + O_infty(r^{1-3h}). Finally grad(Psi - psi_0 - psi_1) is the
velocity remainder rotated by -pi/2, hence O_infty(r^{1-3h}); integrating along rays from r = 2 gives
|Psi - psi_0 - psi_1| <= C + C r^{2-3h} <= C r^{2-3h} (2 - 3h > 1/2), and the derivatives of order >= 1 are those of
the velocity remainder, so Psi = psi_0 + psi_1 + O_infty(r^{2-3h}). The identities for r^{q-h} f1 and r^{-2h} G1
follow from u_0 . grad = r^{-h} (-P' r d_r + (2 - h) P d_phi) and the formula for Theta_x applied to r^q f. QED.

### Theorem 43 (beta > 2: zeros of W, finite-order jets and flat sources)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta > 2, kappa = beta - 2, and let Q be a zero of W, A = DW(Q),
z = X - Q. Write lam1 <= lam2 for the eigenvalues of A when they are real. Let f, G, F, theta_0, J0 and the launch circle
|X| = R0 be as in Theorems 38 and 41.
(a) Theta(Q) = 0, Omega(Q) = Theta_x(Q) and A^T grad Theta(Q) = kappa grad Theta(Q). If grad Theta(Q) != 0, the
    eigenvalues of A are kappa and beta + 2, so Q is a hyperbolic source. If grad Theta(Q) = 0, then Omega(Q) = 0, DU(Q)
    is symmetric and traceless, and the eigenvalues of A are beta - sigma and beta + sigma for some sigma >= 0. In every
    case the eigenvalues are real and A is diagonalizable.
(b) Suppose Theta is not flat at Q (some derivative of Theta at Q is nonzero); let n >= 1 be its order of vanishing and
    H_n the homogeneous Taylor polynomial of degree n of Theta at Q. If lam1 != lam2, let xi_1, xi_2 be linear forms in z
    with A^T grad xi_k = lam_k grad xi_k (so (A z).grad xi_k = lam_k xi_k).
    (b1) If 0 < lam1 <= lam2 (source), then lam1 = kappa/n, lam2 = 2 beta - kappa/n and H_n = c xi_1^n, c != 0.
    (b2) If lam1 < 0 < lam2 (saddle), then H_n = c xi_1^i xi_2^j with c != 0, i > j >= 1, i + j = n (so n >= 3), and
         lam1 = (kappa - 2 beta j)/(i - j).
    (b3) If lam1 = 0 (then lam2 = 2 beta), or if A = beta I, this is impossible: Theta is flat at Q.
    (b4) If Q = (x_Q, 0) with x_Q > 0 is a source, then lam1 = d_y W_2(Q) = kappa/n with n odd and H_n = c y^n; if
         Q = (0, y_Q) with y_Q > 0 is a source, then lam1 = d_x W_1(Q) = kappa/n with n even and H_n = c x^n.
(c) If Q is a source and Theta vanishes at Q to order n (finite), Omega vanishes at Q to order at least n - 1. If Theta is
    flat at Q and Q is a source or lam1 = 0, Omega is flat at Q.
(d) Suppose Q is a hyperbolic source at which Theta is flat, and let B = {X : Phi_{-t} X -> Q as t -> infinity}. Then B
    is open, connected and invariant, Theta = Omega = 0 on B, and there is c_B > 0 with |B cap {|X| < rho}| >= c_B rho^2
    for all large rho. The intersection of B with the launch circle contains an open arc {R0 e(alpha) : alpha in I_0},
    and f = G = 0 on the open interval F(I_0) of angles (with the continuous representative of G of Theorem 41(b)).
(e) In general, for alpha in the circle, f(F(alpha)) = 0 if and only if Theta(R0 e(alpha)) = 0. In particular, under the
    hypotheses of Theorem 8, f has the strict sign of a0 at every angle in (0, pi/2).
Scope. (b) lists necessary conditions on the leading jet; nothing is said about their realizability. (d) does not by
itself exclude a flat source: it shows only that one forces an open invariant set of positive lower density on which
Theta and Omega vanish (a dead zone). If every zero of W is nondegenerate, Theorem 52(c) excludes flat zeros and Theorem
80(b) excludes every open subset of Q1 on which Theta vanishes. No statement here alone proves or disproves (H1).

Proof. (a) Theta(Q) = 0 and Omega(Q) = Theta_x(Q) are Theorem 6(a). Differentiating (T) gives
DW^T grad Theta + D^2 Theta W = kappa grad Theta, and W(Q) = 0. If grad Theta(Q) != 0 it is an eigenvector of A^T with
eigenvalue kappa; tr A = div W = 2 beta, so the other eigenvalue is beta + 2, and the two are distinct and positive. If
grad Theta(Q) = 0 then Omega(Q) = 0. DU(Q) is traceless, and its antisymmetric part is (Omega(Q)/2) times a fixed
rotation generator, so DU(Q) is symmetric with eigenvalues -sigma, sigma, and A = beta I + DU(Q) is symmetric. In both
cases A is diagonalizable over the reals.
(b) Insert the Taylor expansion of W at Q (W = A z + O(|z|^2)) and of Theta (Theta = H_n + O(|z|^{n+1})) into (T); the
part of degree n is (A z).grad H_n = kappa H_n. If A = beta I this reads n beta H_n = kappa H_n, impossible as
0 < kappa < beta. Otherwise lam1 < lam2 and xi_1, xi_2 are coordinates; on the monomial xi_1^i xi_2^j the operator
(A z).grad acts as multiplication by i lam1 + j lam2, so H_n = sum c_ij xi_1^i xi_2^j with c_ij = 0 unless
i lam1 + j lam2 = kappa, i + j = n. For fixed n this linear equation in i has at most one solution because
lam1 != lam2, so H_n is a single monomial. (b1) lam2 >= beta > kappa forces j = 0 and n lam1 = kappa. (b2)
lam2 = 2 beta - lam1 > 2 beta > kappa and lam1 < 0 exclude j = 0 and i = 0; then kappa = 2 beta j + (i - j) lam1 with
kappa < 2 beta <= 2 beta j forces (i - j) lam1 < 0, i > j. (b3) If lam1 = 0, i lam1 + j lam2 = 2 beta j = kappa has no
integer solution since 0 < kappa < 2 beta; so no H_n exists, Theta is flat. (b4) On the positive x-axis A is diagonal
by parity, the eigen-coordinates are x - x_Q and y, and every Taylor monomial of Theta has odd degree in y (Theta is odd
in y). If xi_1 were x - x_Q, H_n = c (x - x_Q)^n would be even in y. So xi_1 = y, lam1 = d_y W_2(Q), n is odd. On the
positive y-axis, Theta is even in x and Theta(0, y) = 0, so every monomial has even positive degree in x; xi_1 = y - y_Q
is impossible, so xi_1 = x and n is even.
(c) Let W_d, theta_m, omega_m denote the homogeneous parts of degree d, m of the Taylor series of W, Theta, Omega at Q
(W_1 = A z); the identities below are identities between Taylor jets, not between convergent series. The degree-m
part of the Taylor series of (V) is
  ((A z).grad + 1) omega_m = d_x theta_{m+1} - sum_{d=2}^{m+1} W_d . grad omega_{m-d+1}.                         (43.1)
In the eigen-coordinates, (A z).grad + 1 acts on degree-m monomials by 1 + i lam1 + j lam2 with i + j = m. At a source
these numbers are positive, and if lam1 = 0 they are 1 + 2 beta j > 0; so the operator is invertible on every degree.
If theta_k = 0 for k <= n - 1, induction on m in (43.1) gives omega_m = 0 for m <= n - 2. If Theta is flat, the same
induction gives omega_m = 0 for all m.
(d) Let lam1 > 0 be the smaller eigenvalue and fix c0 in (0, lam1). Since A is diagonalizable with positive
eigenvalues, there is an inner product with <A z, z> >= ((lam1 + c0)/2) |z|^2; for a small ball V around Q in its norm,
d/dt |Phi_{-t} X - Q|^2 = -2 <W(Phi_{-t} X), Phi_{-t} X - Q> <= -2 c0 |Phi_{-t} X - Q|^2 for Phi_{-t} X in V. So V is
backward invariant and |Phi_{-t} X - Q| <= e^{-c0 t} |X - Q| for X in V, t >= 0. Hence B = union_{t >= 0} Phi_t(V):
it is open (each Phi_t is a diffeomorphism), connected (each Phi_t(V) is connected and contains Q) and invariant. For
X in B choose T with Phi_{-T} X in V; for t >= T, flatness gives |Theta(Phi_{-t} X)| <= C_N e^{-N c0 (t - T)} for
every N, so Theta(X) = e^{kappa t} Theta(Phi_{-t} X) -> 0 (take N c0 > kappa): Theta = 0 on B. As B is open,
Theta_x = 0 on B, and (V) along orbits in B gives Omega(X) = e^{-t} Omega(Phi_{-t} X) -> 0 (Omega is bounded near Q):
Omega = 0 on B.
Density. By Theorem 38(a) and smoothness, |U(X)| <= C1 (1 + |X|^2)^{(1-h)/2} on R^2, h = 1/beta. For
rho(t) = (1 + |Phi_t X|^2)^{1/2}, d rho/dt = Phi_t X . W/rho <= beta rho + C1 rho^{1-h}, so
d(rho^h)/dt <= rho^h + h C1 (beta h = 1) and rho(t)^h <= e^t (rho(0)^h + h C1). Hence Phi_t(V) lies in
{|X| < C_V e^{beta t}} with C_V = (sup_V rho^h + h C1)^beta. Phi_t(V) is contained in B and has area e^{2 beta t}|V|
(det D Phi_t = e^{2 beta t}). Taking e^{beta t} = rho/C_V gives |B cap {|X| < rho}| >= |V| C_V^{-2} rho^2 for
rho >= C_V. In particular B is unbounded. Since |U| <= beta|X|/4 on |X| >= R0, W has no zero there, so Q lies inside
the launch circle; B is connected, contains Q and points outside the circle, hence meets the circle, in a relatively open
set, which contains an open arc {R0 e(alpha) : alpha in I_0}. For alpha in I_0, theta_0(alpha) = 0, and J0(alpha) =
Omega(X0(alpha)) + int_0^inf e^s Theta_x(X(s, alpha)) ds = 0 since the orbit X(., alpha) lies in B (J0 is the
continuous representative of Theorem 41(c)). By Theorem 38(b), (d), f = (R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf} theta_0) o F^{-1} and
G = (R0^h e^{-d_inf} J0) o F^{-1} a.e., where F is a C^1 diffeomorphism of the circle and d_inf is continuous (a uniform
limit of the continuous functions d(r, .)). With the continuous J0 of Theorem 41(c), the right side of the formula for G
is continuous, and so is the representative of G in Theorem 41(b); two continuous functions equal a.e. are equal, so
the formula for G holds at every angle, and f = G = 0 on the open interval F(I_0).
(e) The first statement is the formula for f in Theorem 38(b): R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf} > 0. Under the hypotheses of
Theorem 8, theta_0 has the sign of a0 on (0, pi/2) (Theorem 8(ii)), and F maps (0, pi/2) onto itself (it is an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism fixing the four axis directions). QED.

Remark 43.1 (what a failure of (H1) requires, beta > 2). By Theorem 13, a failure of (H1) means a zero of W in Q1 or a
further zero on a positive half-axis. By Theorem 43 every such zero has real spectrum and is of one of the following
kinds: a hyperbolic source with Theta of finite order n and lam1 = kappa/n (for n = 1, eigenvalues kappa, beta + 2, grad
Theta != 0, and {Theta = 0} is a smooth curve through it); a hyperbolic source with Theta flat, which forces a dead zone
as in (d); a saddle with a resonant temperature jet as in (b2) or with Theta flat (at a saddle a flat Theta does not
force Omega to be flat: for an integer m >= 1 the local fields W = (-x/m, (2 beta + 1/m) y + x^{m+1}), Theta = 0,
Omega = -(m + 1) x^m, Psi = (beta + 1/m) x y + x^{m+2}/(m + 2) solve (P) near Q = 0, which is a saddle; they are a local
example, not an A2-broad profile); or a degenerate zero (eigenvalues 0 and 2 beta) at which Theta and Omega are flat. If
all zeros are isolated, they are finitely many (Z is compact) and the index sum over them is 1 (X.W > 0 on a large
circle); O and +-P contribute -1 + 1 + 1, so the further zeros have total index 0, and if they are nondegenerate the
fourfold symmetry gives 4 (s_1 - d_1) + 2 (s_2 - d_2) = 0, where s_1, d_1 count sources and saddles in Q1 and s_2, d_2
those on the two positive half-axes other than P. If all further zeros lie off the axes, the smallest nonempty balance
is one source and one saddle in Q1 with their reflections (eight zeros); one source and one saddle on the positive
half-axes with their reflections (four zeros) also balance. These are index possibilities, not existence assertions.
Theorem 52(b) excludes every configuration in which all further zeros lie off the axes, in particular the first of these
balances; the second is not excluded. If every zero of W in the closed first quadrant is nondegenerate, the flat
alternatives are excluded by Theorem 52(c); if in addition {X in Q1 : sgn(a0) Omega(X) < 0} is bounded, Theorem 77
excludes further x-axis zeros and permits a positive y-axis zero only for beta = N/M in lowest terms with N even and M
odd.

### Theorem 44 (beta >= 2: a global potential, single backward limits and arc basins; a Lyapunov function at beta = 2)
Let beta >= 2, kappa = beta - 2, and let Theta, Omega, U be C^infinity on R^2 with div U = 0, d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = Omega,
U(X) = o(|X|) uniformly as |X| -> infinity, satisfying (V) and (T) with W = beta X + U. Parts (a)-(e) use no parity or
jet assumption and no growth or tail assumption beyond these. Write W^perp = (-W_2, W_1), e_2 = (0, 1), Z = {W = 0},
Crit = {grad Theta = 0}.
(a) The field Xi := (2 beta - 1) W + Omega W^perp - Theta e_2 is curl-free, Bern(X) := int_0^1 Xi(tX).X dt is the unique
    C^infinity function with grad Bern = Xi and Bern(0) = 0, and Ly := Bern + y Theta satisfies
      W.grad Ly = (2 beta - 1) |W|^2 + kappa y Theta.                                                        (44.1)
    At beta = 2, Ly is strictly increasing along every nonstationary orbit.
(b) For every X the backward orbit Phi_{-s} X (s >= 0) lies in a compact disc, int_0^infinity |W(Phi_{-s} X)|^2 ds is
    finite, and Phi_{-s} X converges as s -> infinity to a single point pi(X) of Z. The map pi : R^2 -> Z is Borel,
    pi(Phi_t X) = pi(X) for all real t, pi(Q) = Q for Q in Z, and Theta(pi(X)) = 0 if beta > 2. For an A2-broad profile
    at beta = 2, pi agrees on {grad Theta != 0} \ Z with the map pi of Theorem 39(a).
(c) Every finite positive Borel measure with compact support that is invariant under the flow is supported in Z, and in
    Z cap {Theta = 0} if beta > 2.
(d) Crit is invariant, Omega = 0 on Crit, Crit is contained in {Theta = 0} if beta > 2, and grad Ly = (2 beta - 1) W on
    Crit. At every Q in Z cap Crit, DW(Q) is symmetric with trace 2 beta.
(e) Let I be a connected one-dimensional C^infinity embedded submanifold of R^2 without boundary contained in Z (an open
    arc of zeros; Z contains no closed embedded curve, since it would bound a domain D with 2 beta |D| = int_D div W =
    int_{dD} W.n = 0), and B_I = {X : pi(X) in I}. Then B_I is open, connected, invariant, contains I and has infinite
    area, and:
    (e1) if beta > 2, Theta = Omega = 0 on B_I;
    (e2) if beta = 2 and grad Theta = 0 on I, then Theta is a constant M on I, and Theta = M, Omega = 0 on B_I.
    In both cases U is harmonic on B_I.
(f) Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be A2-broad and I as in (e), with grad Theta = 0 on I if beta = 2. Then there is a
    nonempty open interval of angles on which f = G = 0 (beta > 2; f, G of Theorem 38, G the continuous representative
    of Theorem 41(b)), respectively H = M and G = 0 (beta = 2; H, G of Theorems 32 and 36).
Proof. By Section 2 the flow is global and (G) holds; as in the proof of Theorem 1 the backward orbit of X0 stays in K =
{|X| <= max(R, |X0|)}, on which all fields and their derivatives are bounded.
(a) For a planar field V put rc V = d_y V_1 - d_x V_2, so V is curl-free iff rc V = 0, and rc W = Omega (rc X = 0). Then
rc(Omega W^perp) = d_y(-Omega W_2) - d_x(Omega W_1) = -div(Omega W) = -W.grad Omega - 2 beta Omega and rc(-Theta e_2) =
Theta_x, so rc Xi = (2 beta - 1) Omega - W.grad Omega - 2 beta Omega + Theta_x = 0 by (V). With d_j Xi_i = d_i Xi_j, d_j
Bern(X) = int_0^1 [Xi_j(tX) + t X_i d_i Xi_j(tX)] dt = int_0^1 d_t[t Xi_j(tX)] dt = Xi_j(X) (summation over i); a second
such function differs by a constant, which is zero. Since W.W^perp = 0, W.Xi = (2 beta - 1)|W|^2 - Theta W_2, and
W.grad(y Theta) = W_2 Theta + kappa y Theta by (T); adding gives (44.1). At beta = 2, d_t Ly(Phi_t X) = 3 |W(Phi_t
X)|^2, positive off Z.
(b) Fix X0 and put Y(s) = Phi_{-s} X0. By (T), Theta(Y(s)) = e^{-kappa s} Theta(X0), so by (44.1)
  d_s Ly(Y(s)) = -(2 beta - 1)|W(Y(s))|^2 - kappa e^{-kappa s} Theta(X0) y(Y(s)),
and integration over [0, T], with kappa int_0^T e^{-kappa s} ds <= 1, gives (2 beta - 1) int_0^T |W(Y)|^2 ds <= 2 max_K
|Ly| + |Theta(X0)| max_K |y| for every T. The function g(s) = |W(Y(s))|^2 is integrable on [0, infinity) and |g'| =
2|W.DW W| is bounded on K, so g -> 0. The alpha-limit set A = cap_{T >= 0} closure{Y(s) : s >= T} is a nested
intersection of nonempty compact connected sets, hence nonempty, compact and connected, and W = 0 on A. If beta > 2,
Theta = 0 on A since Theta(Y(s)) -> 0.
A is a single point. Suppose Q != P both lie in A. Since tr DW(Q) = 2 beta != 0, grad W_i(Q) != 0 for some i, and by the
implicit function theorem there are an open neighbourhood U_Q of Q with P not in U_Q and a C^infinity diffeomorphism chi
of U_Q onto (-2, 2)^2 with chi(Q) = 0 and chi({W_i = 0} cap U_Q) = (-2, 2) x {0}; hence chi(Z cap U_Q) lies in (-2, 2) x
{0}. If there were a in (-1, 0) and b in (0, 1) with chi^{-1}(a, 0) and chi^{-1}(b, 0) not in A, then R = chi^{-1}([a,
b] x [-1, 1]) would be compact with boundary disjoint from A (its boundary meets chi^{-1}((-2, 2) x {0}) only in these
two points), so A cap R = A cap int R would be a relatively open and closed subset of A, nonempty (it contains Q) and
proper (P is not in U_Q), contradicting connectedness. So chi^{-1}((-1, 0) x {0}) or chi^{-1}((0, 1) x {0}) lies in A,
hence in Z; fix Q* = chi^{-1}(u*, 0) in it and d > 0 with |u - u*| <= 2d, v = 0 inside this segment.
Trapping. In the coordinates (u, v) = chi the field -W becomes a C^infinity field (f1, g1) vanishing for v = 0, |u - u*|
< 2d, so f1 = v A1, g1 = v B1 with A1, B1 C^infinity (Hadamard). At (u, 0) the derivative of (f1, g1) is [[0, A1], [0,
B1]], conjugate to -DW, so B1(u, 0) = -tr DW = -2 beta. Shrink d and choose eta > 0 so that on the closed rectangle |u -
u*| <= d, |v| <= eta (inside the chart) B1 <= -beta and |A1| <= M1. Let 0 < eta0 <= eta with M1 eta0/beta < d/4. For a
backward orbit with |u(0) - u*| < d/2 and |v(0)| < eta0, as long as it stays in the rectangle, |v(s)| <= |v(0)| e^{-beta
s} and |u(s) - u(0)| <= M1 |v(0)|/beta < d/4; so it never reaches the boundary of the rectangle, these bounds hold for
all s >= 0, u(s) converges to some u_inf with |u_inf - u*| < 3d/4 and |u(s) - u_inf| <= M1 |v(0)| e^{-beta s}/beta. So
every backward orbit that enters V* = chi^{-1}({|u - u*| < d/2, |v| < eta0}) converges to a point of the segment, at the
rate C e^{-beta s}. Since Q* is in A, Y(s_n) is in V* for some s_n, so Y converges and A is a single point, a
contradiction.
Hence A = {pi(X0)}, and as Y stays in the compact set K, Y(s) -> pi(X0). pi = lim_n Phi_{-n} is a pointwise limit of
continuous maps, hence Borel; pi(Phi_t X) = pi(X) because the two backward orbits differ by a time shift; pi(Q) = Q on
Z; Theta(pi(X)) = 0 for beta > 2 was shown above. For an A2-broad profile at beta = 2 and X in {grad Theta != 0} \ Z,
Theorem 39(a) gives the limit of the same orbit.
(c) Let nu be such a measure with support S and f in C^infinity(R^2). For 0 < |t| <= 1 and X in S, |f(Phi_t X) -
f(X)|/|t| <= sup{|W.grad f(Y)| : Y in Phi_{[-1, 1]}(S)}, so by invariance and dominated convergence int W.grad f dnu =
lim_{t -> 0} t^{-1} int (f o Phi_t - f) dnu = 0. If beta > 2, f = Theta^2 gives 2 kappa int Theta^2 dnu = 0, so nu is
carried by the closed set {Theta = 0}. Then f = Ly gives (2 beta - 1) int |W|^2 dnu = -kappa int y Theta dnu = 0 (kappa
= 0, or Theta = 0 nu-a.e.), so nu is carried by Z.
(d) Differentiating (T), d_t grad Theta(Phi_t X) = (kappa I - DW(Phi_t X)^T) grad Theta(Phi_t X), a linear equation, so
grad Theta(Phi_t X) vanishes for one t iff for all t: Crit is invariant. For X in Crit, Theta_x = 0 along the orbit and
(V) gives Omega(Phi_{-s} X) = e^s Omega(X); the left side is bounded on K, so Omega(X) = 0. If beta > 2, (T) gives kappa
Theta = W.grad Theta = 0 on Crit. grad Ly = Xi + Theta e_2 + y grad Theta = (2 beta - 1) W + Omega W^perp + y grad
Theta, which is (2 beta - 1) W on Crit. At Q in Z cap Crit, d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = Omega(Q) = 0, so DW(Q) is symmetric, and
tr DW = div W = 2 beta.
(e) For Q in I choose a C^infinity chart chi straightening I near Q, with a segment |u - u_Q| <= 2d, v = 0 contained in
I, and apply the trapping step of (b) with Q* = Q: there is an open connected neighbourhood V_Q of Q such that for X in
V_Q the backward orbit converges to a point pi(X) of I with |Phi_{-s} X - pi(X)| <= C_Q e^{-beta s} (the chart has
bounded derivatives on the compact rectangle). If pi(X) = Q' in I, then Phi_{-t} X lies in V_{Q'} for some t >= 0;
conversely pi is invariant. Hence B_I = union_{Q in I, t >= 0} Phi_t(V_Q): B_I is open, invariant, and contains I (pi =
identity on Z); it is connected, since I is connected and each connected set Phi_t(V_Q) contains Q (W(Q) = 0). B_I is
nonempty and open, and Phi_t(B_I) = B_I with |Phi_t(B_I)| = e^{2 beta t} |B_I|, so |B_I| = infinity.
(e1) For X in V_Q, Theta(pi(X)) = 0 by (T) and Theta is Lipschitz on K, so |Theta(Phi_{-s} X)| <= C e^{-beta s}, and
Theta(X) = e^{kappa s} Theta(Phi_{-s} X) -> 0 since kappa - beta = -2. So Theta = 0 on each V_Q, and on B_I by
Theta(Phi_t X) = e^{kappa t} Theta(X).
(e2) The derivative of Theta along the connected curve I vanishes, so Theta = M on I; by (T) with kappa = 0, Theta(X) =
Theta(Phi_{-s} X) -> Theta(pi(X)) = M for X in B_I.
In both cases Theta is constant on the open invariant set B_I, so Theta_x = 0 along every orbit in B_I and (V) gives
Omega(X) = e^{-s} Omega(Phi_{-s} X) -> 0 (bounded backward orbits). With div U = 0 and curl U = 0, U is harmonic on B_I.
(f) Fix the launch radius R0 of Theorem 38 (beta > 2), respectively of Theorem 36, with (33.2) (beta = 2); in both cases
Z lies in {|X| < R0}. B_I is connected, contains I and has infinite area, so it is unbounded and meets the circle |X| =
R0 in a nonempty relatively open set, which contains an open arc of labels I_0 (no reflection is used: a reflection R of
the A2 group maps B_I onto B_{R I}, but changes the constant M to -M when it reverses y). For alpha in I_0 the whole
orbit of X0(alpha) lies in B_I.
beta > 2: theta_0(alpha) = 0 and J0(alpha) = Omega(X0(alpha)) + int_0^infinity e^s Theta_x(X(s, alpha)) ds = 0 for alpha
in I_0, with the continuous representative J0 of Theorem 41(c). By Theorem 38(b), (d), f o F = R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf}
theta_0 and G o F = R0^h e^{-d_inf} J0, the second a.e.; both sides are continuous (d_inf is a uniform limit of
continuous functions, G is the continuous representative of Theorem 41(b)), so it holds everywhere, and f = G = 0 on
F(I_0). This is the final step of the proof of Theorem 43(d), which uses only that the orbits from I_0 lie in an
invariant set where Theta = Omega = 0.
beta = 2: Theta(r, F_r(alpha)) = M and Omega(r, F_r(alpha)) = 0 for alpha in I_0 and r >= R0. For a compact interval J
in F(I_0), F_r^{-1} -> F^{-1} uniformly (Theorem 32(b)) gives F_r^{-1}(J) in I_0 for large r, so Theta(r, phi) = M and
Omega(r, phi) = 0 for phi in J and large r, and the uniform angular limits (Theorem 32(d); Theorem 32 applies at beta =
2 by Theorem 33(a)) give H = M and G = 0 on J, hence on F(I_0). This is the argument of Theorem 35(c). QED.

Remark 44.1. (i) In the proof of Theorem 22, (b) replaces the appeal to Poincare-Bendixson: the alpha-limit set of gamma
is the single zero pi(gamma), and Theta(pi(gamma)) = M. (ii) For beta > 2, at a zero Q of W differentiating (T) gives
DW(Q)^T grad Theta(Q) = kappa grad Theta(Q); if grad Theta(Q) != 0 the eigenvalues of DW(Q) are kappa > 0 and 2 beta -
kappa = beta + 2, so DW(Q) is invertible and Q is isolated (as in Theorem 43(a)). A non-isolated zero Q therefore lies
in Crit, DW(Q) is symmetric with trace 2 beta by (d), and it is singular (otherwise Q is isolated by the inverse
function theorem), so its characteristic polynomial is lam (lam - 2 beta): the eigenvalues are 0 and 2 beta. This does
not show that Q is interior to an arc of zeros. (iii) At beta = 2 the whole arc C of Theorem 16 is not an admissible I in (e),
because C has endpoints. Its interior is eligible for the open-basin conclusion of (e). A subarc containing P does not
satisfy the additional hypothesis grad Theta = 0 required in (e2) and (f), since grad Theta(P) != 0 by Theorem 3. Its
regular part is described by Theorem 39. (iv) Theorem 44
does not exclude isolated degenerate zeros, endpoints of arcs of zeros, or non-isolated zeros that are not interior to
an arc of zeros, and it is not a nonexistence statement.

### Theorem 45 (beta >= 2: vorticity integrability, the decay class, absolute strain identities, axis growth, and the first correction at beta = 2)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta >= 2, h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h, kappa = beta - 2,
W = beta X + U, Psi the stream function with U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x) and Psi(0) = 0 (odd in x and in y, -Lap Psi = Omega),
Q1 the open first quadrant and K0 = x y |X|^{-4}. Let G be the angular vorticity function (Theorems 33 and 36 at
beta = 2, Theorems 41 and 42 for beta > 2). Then:
(a) There are R1 and C such that for |X| >= R1
      |Omega| <= C r^{-h},  |U| <= C r^{1-h},  |grad Theta| <= C r^{-2h},  |Theta| <= C r^q,  |Psi| <= C r^{2-h},
    and there are delta > 0, R2 >= R1 and a closed interval I of positive length in (0, pi/2) such that
      sgn(a0) Omega(r e(phi)) >= delta r^{-h}   for phi in I and r >= R2.
    In particular, for every R there is X in Q1 with |X| > R and sgn(a0) Omega(X) > 0.
(b) For 0 < p < infinity, Omega is in L^p(R^2) if and only if p > 2 beta. There are C, c > 0 and lambda0 > 0 with
      |{|Omega| > lambda}| <= C lambda^{-2 beta}  (lambda > 0),    |{|Omega| > lambda}| >= c lambda^{-2 beta}  (0 < lambda <= lambda0),
    so Omega lies in weak L^{2 beta} and not in L^{2 beta}.
(c) Omega satisfies the bound defining A2-dec with gamma = h, and no bound |Omega| <= C (1 + |X|)^{-gamma} with
    gamma > h holds. Hence A2-dec and A2-broad have the same solutions (for beta < 2 both are empty by Theorem 1). The
    hypothesis of Theorem 15, which is that of Theorem 24 with eta = 2h, fails for every A2-broad profile; the
    hypothesis of Theorem 24 holds for 0 < eta < h and fails for h <= eta <= 1.
(d) The functions K0 Omega, K0 Theta_x, Omega U . grad K0 and Theta y (3 x^2 - y^2) |X|^{-6} are bounded on Q1 near O and
    O(r^{-2-h}) as r -> infinity, hence absolutely integrable on Q1, and
      int_Q1 K0 Omega dX = (pi/4)(2 beta + 2) = int_Q1 K0 Theta_x dX + int_Q1 Omega U . grad K0 dX
                         = int_Q1 Theta y (3 x^2 - y^2) |X|^{-6} dX + int_Q1 Omega U . grad K0 dX.            (45.1)
    At beta = 2 the first line is (39.9).
(e) Let v, Y, t and s be as in Theorem 31 (v(y) = W_2(0, y)). Then |v(y) - beta y| <= C y^{1-h} for y >= R1, so
    t(y) - beta^{-1} log y converges as y -> infinity. Hence, if (N) of Theorem 31 holds, s(y) ~ C y^{1/beta} for some
    C > 0.
(f) (beta = 2, first correction.) Let H, G, P, theta_0, omega_0, psi_0, u_0 be as in Theorem 36 and put
      H1 = (3/2) P H',   G1 = (1/2) P' G + (3/2) P G' + sin(phi) H'.
    H1 has the parities of Theta and G1 is odd in x and in y. Let P1 be the unique solution of -(P1'' + P1) = G1 that is
    odd in x and in y (the equation also has the 2 pi-periodic solutions P1 + a cos(phi) + b sin(phi), which are not
    odd-odd unless a = b = 0). H1, G1 and P1 are C^infinity. With psi_1 = r P1(phi) and
    u_1 = (-d_y psi_1, d_x psi_1) = -P1' e_r + P1 e_phi,
      Theta = H + r^{-1/2} H1 + O_infty(r^{-1}),    Omega = r^{-1/2} G + r^{-1} G1 + O_infty(r^{-3/2}),
      U = u_0 + u_1 + O_infty(r^{-1/2}),            Psi = psi_0 + psi_1 + O_infty(r^{1/2}).
    Moreover r^{-1/2} H1 = u_0 . grad H(phi) and r^{-1} G1 = u_0 . grad(r^{-1/2} G) - d_x H(phi). These are the formulas of
    Theorem 42(c) at h = 1/2, q = 0 (f = H).
The constants depend on the profile (and in (f) on k). Scope. The theorem is a list of necessary conditions; it neither
constructs nor excludes a profile. (b) is a bound on the distribution function of the smooth function Omega and is
different from the exact level-set law of Theorem 40, which concerns the outgoing distribution. This theorem asserts no
asymptotic series beyond the first correction at beta = 2; Theorem 76 gives an expansion to every finite order for every
A2-broad profile at beta = 2, with no convergence assertion. Applicability of an external nonexistence theorem to the
integrability in (b) requires checking its complete hypotheses; this is not done here.

Proof. (a) At beta = 2, Theorem 36(b) gives Theta - H = O_infty(r^{-1/2}), Omega - r^{-1/2} G = O_infty(r^{-1}) and
U - u_0 = O_infty(1) with H, G, P smooth; so |Theta| <= C, |grad Theta| <= C r^{-1}, |U| <= C r^{1/2} and
|r^{1/2} Omega(r e(phi)) - G(phi)| <= C r^{-1/2}. For beta > 2, Theorem 38(a) gives |U| <= C r^{1-h}, Theorem 41(a)
gives the bounds on Omega and grad Theta, Theorem 42(a) gives |Theta| <= C r^q, and Theorem 42(b) gives
|r^h Omega(r e(phi)) - G(phi)| <= C r^{-h}. Since Psi(0) = 0 and |grad Psi| = |U|, integration along the segment from 0
to X gives |Psi(X)| <= C + C |X|^{2-h} <= C' |X|^{2-h} for |X| >= R1. G is continuous (Theorem 36(a) at beta = 2, Theorem 41(b)
for beta > 2), and sgn(a0) G > 0 on a nonempty open interval of angles in (0, pi/2) (Theorem 34(b) at beta = 2,
Theorem 41(b) for beta > 2); choose a closed
interval I of positive length inside it and delta > 0 with sgn(a0) G >= 2 delta on I. With the uniform bound
|r^h Omega - G| <= C r^{-h}, sgn(a0) r^h Omega >= delta on I for r >= R2 := max(R1, (C/delta)^beta).
(b) Let M = max_{|X| <= R1} |Omega|. If p > 2 beta, then hp > 2 and
int |Omega|^p <= pi R1^2 M^p + 2 pi C^p int_{R1}^infinity r^{1 - hp} dr < infinity. If 0 < p <= 2 beta, then
1 - hp >= -1 and, by (a), int |Omega|^p >= |I| delta^p int_{R2}^infinity r^{1 - hp} dr = infinity. For the upper level
bound, {|Omega| > lambda} is contained in {|X| <= R1} union {r < (C/lambda)^beta}, and is contained in the second set
alone if lambda >= M; so |{|Omega| > lambda}| <= pi (C/lambda)^{2 beta} for lambda >= M and
<= pi R1^2 + pi (C/lambda)^{2 beta} <= (pi R1^2 M^{2 beta} + pi C^{2 beta}) lambda^{-2 beta} for lambda < M. For the
lower bound, {|Omega| > lambda} contains {r e(phi) : phi in I, R2 <= r < (delta/lambda)^beta}, of area
(|I|/2)((delta/lambda)^{2 beta} - R2^2) >= (|I|/4)(delta/lambda)^{2 beta} when (delta/lambda)^{2 beta} >= 2 R2^2.
(c) By (a) and boundedness of Omega on compact sets, |Omega| <= C (1 + |X|)^{-h}. If |Omega| <= C (1 + |X|)^{-gamma}
with gamma > h, then r^h Omega -> 0, contradicting the lower bound of (a). The same lower bound contradicts
Omega = o(|X|^{-2h}), since r^{2h} |Omega| >= delta r^h on the sector, and for h <= eta <= 1 it gives
r^eta |Omega| >= delta there. For 0 < eta < h, sup_{|Y| >= R} |Y|^eta |Omega(Y)| <= C R^{eta - h} -> 0.
(d) Near O: Omega and Theta_x are odd in x and in y and smooth, so they are O(r^2); Theta is even in x, odd in y and
vanishes on the y-axis, so by the parities and Theta(0, y) = 0 its Taylor polynomial of degree 2 vanishes and
Theta = O(r^3); |U| <= C r since
U(0) = 0. With |K0| <= r^{-2}, |grad K0| <= C r^{-3} and |y (3x^2 - y^2)| |X|^{-6} <= 3 r^{-3}, all four functions are
bounded for r <= 1. At infinity, by (a): |K0 Omega| <= C r^{-2-h}, |K0 Theta_x| <= C r^{-2-2h},
|Omega U . grad K0| <= C r^{-h} r^{1-h} r^{-3} = C r^{-2-2h} and |Theta y (3x^2 - y^2) |X|^{-6}| <= C r^{q-3} =
C r^{-2-2h}; as int^infinity r^{-2-h} r dr < infinity, all four are absolutely integrable on Q1.
First equality. By Theorem 9, 2 beta + 2 = Psi_xy(0) = (1/pi) lim_{R -> infinity} int_{|Y|<R} K0 Omega dY. K0 Omega is
even in x and in y, so int_{|Y|<R} K0 Omega = 4 int_{Q1 cap {|Y|<R}} K0 Omega, and by absolute integrability the limit
is 4 int_Q1 K0 Omega. Hence int_Q1 K0 Omega = (pi/4)(2 beta + 2).
Second equality. K0 is homogeneous of degree -2, so X . grad K0 = -2 K0 and W . grad K0 = -2 beta K0 + U . grad K0. With
div W = 2 beta and (V),
  div(K0 Omega W) = K0 W . grad Omega + Omega W . grad K0 + 2 beta K0 Omega = K0 Theta_x - K0 Omega + Omega U . grad K0.
Integrate over A(eps, R) = Q1 cap {eps < |X| < R}. K0 vanishes on both axes, so the flat sides contribute nothing. On
|X| = R the flux is at most (pi/2) R sup |K0 Omega W| <= C R R^{-2} R^{-h} R = C R^{-h}; on |X| = eps it is at most
C eps eps^{-2} eps^2 eps = C eps^2. Letting eps -> 0 and R -> infinity, with the absolute integrability above, gives
int_Q1 K0 Omega = int_Q1 K0 Theta_x + int_Q1 Omega U . grad K0.
Third equality. d_x K0 = y |X|^{-4} - 4 x^2 y |X|^{-6} = -y (3 x^2 - y^2) |X|^{-6}, and
div(K0 Theta e_1) = K0 Theta_x + Theta d_x K0. On A(eps, R) the flat sides contribute nothing (K0 = 0 there), the outer
arc at most C R R^{-2} R^q = C R^{-2h} and the inner arc at most C eps eps^{-2} eps^3 = C eps^2; so
int_Q1 K0 Theta_x = int_Q1 Theta y (3 x^2 - y^2) |X|^{-6}.
(e) v(y) = beta y + U_2(0, y), so |v(y) - beta y| <= |U(0, y)| <= C y^{1-h} for y >= R1 by (a). Enlarging R1 so that
C y^{-h} <= beta/2, v(y) >= beta y/2 there and |1/v(y) - 1/(beta y)| = |beta y - v(y)|/(beta y v(y)) <= (2C/beta^2)
y^{-1-h}. Since t' = 1/v, t(y) - beta^{-1} log y = t(y1) - beta^{-1} log y1 + int_{y1}^y (1/v - 1/(beta eta)) d eta
(y1 >= max(R1, Y + 1)), and the integrand is absolutely integrable on [y1, infinity). So the limit exists, and
Theorem 31(b) gives s(y) ~ C y^{1/beta} under (N).
(f) Parities. Under phi -> -phi (y -> -y) and phi -> pi - phi (x -> -x), G and P are odd and odd (Theorem 36(a)) and H
is odd under phi -> -phi and even under phi -> pi - phi (Theta is odd in y and even in x). So P' and G' are even under
both maps, H' is even under phi -> -phi and odd under phi -> pi - phi, and sin(phi) is odd under phi -> -phi and even
under phi -> pi - phi. Hence each of P' G, P G', sin(phi) H' is odd under both maps, so
G1 is odd-odd, and P H' is odd under phi -> -phi and even under phi -> pi - phi, so H1 has the parities of Theta.
Odd-odd 2 pi-periodic functions expand in sin(2 m phi), m >= 1, on which -(d^2 + 1) acts by 4 m^2 - 1 >= 3 > 0; so there
is exactly one odd-odd P1, and P1 is C^infinity since G1 is (P1'' = -G1 - P1 and bootstrap). The kernel of d^2 + 1 on
2 pi-periodic functions is spanned by cos(phi) (even in y) and sin(phi) (even in x), neither odd-odd.
Expansions. Put Th = Theta, Om = r^{1/2} Omega, (v_r, v_phi) = r^{-1/2} (U_r, U_phi) and V0 = (-P', (3/2) P). By
Theorem 36(b) and the conversion rule of Step 6 of the proof of Theorem 42 (which does not use beta > 2), every
(r d_r)^a d_phi^b of Th - H, Om - G, (v_r, v_phi) - V0 and r d_r Th is O(r^{-1/2}) for r >= R1. The equations (42.5) and
(42.6) were derived from (T), (V) using only beta q = kappa and beta h = 1, which hold at beta = 2 (q = kappa = 0); at
beta = 2 they read
  (2 + r^{-1/2} v_r) r d_r Th = -r^{-1/2} v_phi d_phi Th,
  (2 + r^{-1/2} v_r) r d_r Om = r^{-1/2} [(1/2) v_r Om - v_phi d_phi Om - sin(phi) d_phi Th + cos(phi) r d_r Th].
With 1/(2 + r^{-1/2} v_r) = 1/2 + O(r^{-1/2}) (with all derivatives) and cos(phi) r d_r Th = O(r^{-1/2}),
  r d_r Th = -(1/2) r^{-1/2} H1 + O(r^{-1}),   r d_r Om = -(1/2) r^{-1/2} G1 + O(r^{-1}),
with every (r d_r)^a d_phi^b of the remainders O(r^{-1}). This is (42.7) at h = 1/2, and the remainder of Step 8 of the
proof of Theorem 42 applies without change: integration in d rho/rho gives the expansions of Theta and Omega
(Th - H - r^{-1/2} H1 and Om - G - r^{-1/2} G1 tend to 0 with all angular derivatives by Theorem 36(b)); Lap(r P1) =
r^{-1} (P1'' + P1) gives -Lap psi_1 = r^{-1} G1 for r > 0; zeta_1 := Omega - omega_* - omega_1* (cutoffs as in Steps 7
and 8 there) is smooth, odd in x and in y and |zeta_1(Y)| <= C (1 + |Y|)^{-3/2}. With B(Z) = (Z_2, -Z_1)/(2 pi |Z|^2)
put v_1(X) = int B(X - Y) zeta_1(Y) dY; the integral converges absolutely (|B(Z)| <= |Z|^{-1}/(2 pi) and
int^infinity rho^{-3/2} d rho < infinity), so it equals the grouped inverse, v_1 is continuous, div v_1 = 0 and
d_y v_1,1 - d_x v_1,2 = zeta_1 in D'(R^2), and v_1 has the velocity parities. For r = |X| >= 2, splitting into
|Y| < r/2, r/2 <= |Y| <= 2r and |Y| > 2r gives the bounds C r^{-1} int_0^{r/2} rho (1 + rho)^{-3/2} d rho,
C r^{-3/2} int_{|Z| <= 3r} |Z|^{-1} dZ and C int_{2r}^infinity rho^{-3/2} d rho, each at most C r^{-1/2}; so
|v_1(X)| <= C |X|^{-1/2}. U - u_* - u_1* - v_1 is divergence- and curl-free in D'(R^2), hence smooth and harmonic, and
o(|X|), hence constant (interior gradient estimate), and zero by the velocity parities (chi (psi_0 + psi_1) is odd in
x and in y); so |U - u_0 - u_1| <= C r^{-1/2} for r >= 2, and (36.4) applied to R^{1/2} (U - u_0 - u_1)(R .), whose
curl R^{3/2} (Omega - r^{-1/2} G - r^{-1} G1)(R .) is bounded in every C^k on fixed annuli uniformly in R, gives
U = u_0 + u_1 + O_infty(r^{-1/2}). Integrating grad(Psi - psi_0 - psi_1) = O_infty(r^{-1/2}) along rays from r = 2
gives |Psi - psi_0 - psi_1| <= C + C r^{1/2} <= C' r^{1/2} for r >= 2, so Psi = psi_0 + psi_1 + O_infty(r^{1/2}).
Finally u_0 . grad = r^{-1/2} (-P' r d_r + (3/2) P d_phi), so u_0 . grad H(phi) = r^{-1/2} (3/2) P H' = r^{-1/2} H1 and
u_0 . grad (r^{-1/2} G) = r^{-1} ((1/2) P' G + (3/2) P G'), while d_x H(phi) = -r^{-1} sin(phi) H'; this gives the
last identities. QED.

Remark 45.1. (b) and (c) determine, for A2-broad, which finite positive powers of Omega are integrable (Omega is also
bounded). They do not by themselves exclude a profile: the sector lower bound of (a) is incompatible with the faster
decay assumed in Theorem 15, Theorem 17(b) excludes finite integrals of |Theta|^p and Theorem 23(a) finite integrals of
|U|^p; none of these concerns finite integrals of |Omega|^p. In (e) the logarithmic counterexample at
the end of Theorem 31 is incompatible with A2-broad: it has beta y - v of order y / log y, not O(y^{1-h}).

### Theorem 46 (beta >= 2: orbits emerging from saddles, and the backward limits of labels with nonzero amplitude)
Let beta >= 2, kappa = beta - 2, and let Theta, Omega, U be as in Theorem 44 (C^infinity on R^2, div U = 0,
d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = Omega, U(X) = o(|X|) uniformly, (V) and (T) with W = beta X + U). Let pi be the backward-limit map
of Theorem 44(b). A zero Q of W is a hyperbolic saddle if DW(Q) has real eigenvalues -a < 0 < c (then c = 2 beta + a)
and a hyperbolic source if both eigenvalues of DW(Q) have positive real part.
(a) At a hyperbolic saddle Q, grad Theta(Q) = 0, Omega(Q) = 0 and DW(Q) is symmetric.
(b) Let Q be a hyperbolic saddle and X a point with Phi_{-s} X -> Q as s -> infinity. Then grad Theta = 0 and
    Omega = 0 at every point of the orbit of X, and Theta = 0 (beta > 2), respectively Theta = Theta(Q) (beta = 2), on it.
(c) Let the profile be A2-broad, let R0, X0(alpha), X(s, alpha), F_r and F be as in Theorem 32(b), which applies by
    Theorem 41(b) (beta > 2) and Theorem 33(a) (beta = 2), with R0 also admissible in Theorem 38 if beta > 2, and let
    f and G be the continuous functions of Theorem 32(d) (f = H at beta = 2; for beta > 2, f and G are those of
    Theorems 38(b) and 41(b)). Suppose that Omega(X(s, alpha)) = 0 for all s >= 0. Then G(F(alpha)) = 0, and if
    beta > 2 the integral defining J0(alpha) in Theorem 38(c) vanishes. Independently of this hypothesis,
    f(F(alpha)) = Theta(X0(alpha)) if beta = 2, and f(F(alpha)) = 0 if beta > 2 and Theta(X0(alpha)) = 0. By (b), all of
    this applies when pi(X0(alpha)) is a hyperbolic saddle Q; then G(F(alpha)) = 0, and f(F(alpha)) = 0 (beta > 2),
    respectively f(F(alpha)) = Theta(Q) (beta = 2).
(d) (beta > 2) Let the profile be A2-broad. If G(F(alpha)) != 0, then Q = pi(X0(alpha)) is either a hyperbolic source
    at which Theta vanishes to a finite order n >= 1, with eigenvalues kappa/n and 2 beta - kappa/n, or a zero of W at
    which DW(Q) has eigenvalues 0 and 2 beta and Theta and Omega are flat.
(e) (beta = 2) Let the profile be A2-broad. If G(F(alpha)) != 0, then DW(pi(X0(alpha))) has eigenvalues 0 and 4.
Scope. Parts (a) and (b) use no A2 parity, prescribed jet, or decay estimate for Theta or Omega. They are stated
under the smoothness and sublinearity hypotheses above; the saddle arguments require no additional assumption at
infinity. Part (b) asserts vanishing only on the set of points tending backward to Q, and asserts no vanishing on a
neighbourhood of Q. The local fields of Remark 43.1 have Omega != 0 when x != 0 and have x = 0 as their set of points
tending backward to the saddle; they illustrate this local distinction, but do not satisfy the global sublinearity
hypothesis. (d) and (e) are necessary conditions; they do not
exclude degenerate zeros, and by Theorems 34(b) and 41(b) the set of labels with G(F(alpha)) != 0 is a nonempty open
set. The theorem is not a nonexistence statement.

Proof. (a) Put A = DW(Q). Differentiating (T) and using W(Q) = 0 gives A^T grad Theta(Q) = kappa grad Theta(Q). The
eigenvalues of A^T are -a < 0 and c > 2 beta > kappa >= 0, so kappa is not one of them and grad Theta(Q) = 0. Then (V)
at Q gives Omega(Q) = Theta_x(Q) = 0, so d_y W_1(Q) = d_x W_2(Q) and A is symmetric.
(b) Choose orthonormal coordinates z = (xi, eta) centred at Q in which A = diag(-a, c). The reversed field -W reads
  -W(Q + z) = (a xi, -c eta) + N(z),   N(0) = 0,   DN(0) = 0,
and |z|_m := max(|xi|, |eta|). Fix gamma with kappa + a < gamma < c (possible since c - kappa - a = beta + 2 > 0) and
delta > 0 with delta < gamma - kappa - a and delta/a, delta/c, delta/(a + gamma), delta/(c - gamma) all < 1/2. Since
sup_{|z| <= 2 rho} |DN| = o(1) and sup_{|z| <= 2 rho} |N| = o(rho) as rho -> 0, for a smooth cutoff chi equal to 1 on
|z| <= 1 and 0 on |z| >= 2 the field N~ = chi(z/rho) N is, for small rho, C^infinity on R^2 with N~(0) = 0 and
|N~_i(z) - N~_i(z')| <= delta |z - z'|_m (i = 1, 2), and equals N on |z| <= rho. Shrink rho so that also the symmetric
part of DW(Q + z) is >= -(a + delta) I for |z| <= rho.
Let Y(s) = Phi_{-s} X - Q = (xi(s), eta(s)). After a time shift, |Y(s)| <= rho for all s >= 0, Y(s) -> 0, and
xi' = a xi + N~_1(Y), eta' = -c eta + N~_2(Y). Integrating xi' between s and T, multiplying by e^{-aT} and letting
T -> infinity (xi is bounded and a > 0) gives
  xi(s) = -int_s^infinity e^{a(s - t)} N~_1(Y(t)) dt,   eta(s) = e^{-cs} eta(0) + int_0^s e^{-c(s - t)} N~_2(Y(t)) dt.  (46.1)
Let T be the map that sends a continuous z : [0, infinity) -> R^2 to the right sides of (46.1) with Y replaced by z. On
bounded continuous functions with the norm sup_s |z(s)|_m, T is a contraction with constant max(delta/a, delta/c) < 1,
so Y is its unique bounded fixed point. On the space with norm ||z||_gamma = sup_s e^{gamma s} |z(s)|_m, using
|N~_i(z)| <= delta |z|_m,
  |(Tz)_1(s)| <= delta ||z||_gamma int_s^infinity e^{a(s - t) - gamma t} dt = delta ||z||_gamma e^{-gamma s}/(a + gamma),
  |(Tz)_2(s)| <= e^{-cs} |eta(0)| + delta ||z||_gamma int_0^s e^{-c(s - t) - gamma t} dt
             <= e^{-gamma s} (|eta(0)| + delta ||z||_gamma/(c - gamma)),
and the same estimates for differences show that T is a contraction there with constant
max(delta/(a + gamma), delta/(c - gamma)) < 1. Its fixed point in this space is bounded, hence equals Y, and so
|Y(s)| <= C e^{-gamma s} for s >= 0.
Let g(s) = grad Theta(Phi_{-s} X). Since grad Theta(Q) = 0 and grad Theta is Lipschitz near Q, |g(s)| <= C e^{-gamma s}.
Differentiating (T) along the flow gives d_t grad Theta(Phi_t X) = (kappa I - DW(Phi_t X)^T) grad Theta(Phi_t X), so
g' = (DW^T - kappa I) g and d_s |g|^2 = 2 g . (Sym DW) g - 2 kappa |g|^2 >= -2 (kappa + a + delta) |g|^2. Hence
|g(0)| <= e^{(kappa + a + delta) s} |g(s)| <= C e^{(kappa + a + delta - gamma) s} -> 0, so g(0) = 0. The set
{grad Theta = 0} is invariant (Theorem 44(d)), so grad Theta = 0 on the whole orbit. Then Theta_x = 0 on the orbit, and
(V) gives Omega(Phi_{-s} Y0) = e^s Omega(Y0) for every orbit point Y0; the left side is bounded since the backward orbit
converges, so Omega(Y0) = 0. Theta is constant on the orbit (W . grad Theta = 0 there); if beta > 2, (T) gives
kappa Theta = 0, and if beta = 2 the constant is lim Theta(Phi_{-s} X) = Theta(Q).
(c) Along the orbit, (V) reads d_s Omega(X(s, alpha)) + Omega(X(s, alpha)) = Theta_x(X(s, alpha)), so Omega = 0 for
s >= 0 gives Theta_x(X(s, alpha)) = 0 for s >= 0, and the integral Omega(X0(alpha)) + int_0^infinity e^s
Theta_x(X(s, alpha)) ds defining J0(alpha) is 0. For r >= R0 the orbit meets |X| = r at r e(F_r(alpha)), where Omega = 0.
With the uniform limit r^h Omega(r, .) -> G of Theorem 32(d) (h = 1/beta), the uniform convergence F_r -> F of
Theorem 32(b) and the continuity of G,
  |G(F(alpha))| <= |G(F(alpha)) - G(F_r(alpha))| + |G(F_r(alpha)) - r^h Omega(r, F_r(alpha))| -> 0   (r -> infinity).
In the same way, r^{-q} Theta(r, F_r(alpha)) = r^{-q} e^{kappa tau(r, alpha)} Theta(X0(alpha)) by (T) (q = 1 - 2h,
tau(r, alpha) the time at which the orbit meets |X| = r), which is Theta(X0(alpha)) if beta = 2 and 0 if
Theta(X0(alpha)) = 0; the uniform limit r^{-q} Theta(r, .) -> f of Theorem 32(d) and the continuity of f give
f(F(alpha)) = Theta(X0(alpha)), respectively f(F(alpha)) = 0. If pi(X0(alpha)) = Q is a hyperbolic saddle, (b) gives
Omega = 0 on the orbit, Theta(X0(alpha)) = 0 if beta > 2 and Theta(X0(alpha)) = Theta(Q) if beta = 2.
(d) Let Q = pi(X0(alpha)), a zero of W (Theorem 44(b)), and A = DW(Q). By Theorem 43(a) there are two cases.
If grad Theta(Q) != 0, the eigenvalues are kappa and beta + 2, Q is a hyperbolic source, and Theta(Q) = 0 with
grad Theta(Q) != 0, so n = 1 and the eigenvalues are kappa/n and 2 beta - kappa/n.
If grad Theta(Q) = 0, the eigenvalues are beta - sigma and beta + sigma with sigma >= 0. If sigma > beta, Q is a
hyperbolic saddle and (c) gives G(F(alpha)) = 0, which is excluded. If sigma = beta, the eigenvalues are 0 and 2 beta,
Theta is flat at Q by Theorem 43(b3), and Omega is flat at Q by Theorem 43(c). If sigma < beta, Q is a hyperbolic
source. If Theta vanishes at Q to a finite order n, Theorem 43(b1) gives the eigenvalues kappa/n and 2 beta - kappa/n.
If Theta is flat at Q, X0(alpha) lies in the set B of Theorem 43(d), which is invariant and on which Omega = 0; so
Omega = 0 on the orbit of X0(alpha) and (c) gives G(F(alpha)) = 0, which is excluded.
(e) Let Q = pi(X0(alpha)) and A = DW(Q); here kappa = 0 and tr A = 4. If grad Theta(Q) != 0, A^T grad Theta(Q) = 0, so
the eigenvalues are 0 and 4. If grad Theta(Q) = 0, then Omega(Q) = Theta_x(Q) = 0 by (V), so A is symmetric with
eigenvalues 2 - sigma and 2 + sigma, sigma >= 0. If sigma > 2, Q is a hyperbolic saddle and (c) gives G(F(alpha)) = 0,
which is excluded. If sigma < 2, A is positive definite; fix 0 < c0 < 2 - sigma and eps > 0 with
W(Q + z) . z >= c0 |z|^2 for |z| <= eps (W(Q + z) = A z + O(|z|^2)). For |Y0 - Q| < eps,
d_s |Phi_{-s} Y0 - Q|^2 = -2 W . (Phi_{-s} Y0 - Q) <= -2 c0 |Phi_{-s} Y0 - Q|^2 while the orbit is in the ball, so it
stays in the open ball V of radius eps and tends to Q. Hence B = {X : Phi_{-s} X -> Q} = union_{t >= 0} Phi_t(V) (a
backward orbit tending to Q enters V) is open and invariant. For X in B, Theta(X) = Theta(Phi_{-s} X) -> Theta(Q), so
Theta = Theta(Q) on B, Theta_x = 0 on the open set B, and (V) gives Omega(X) = e^{-s} Omega(Phi_{-s} X) -> 0. So
Omega = 0 on the orbit of X0(alpha), which lies in B, and (c) gives G(F(alpha)) = 0, which is excluded. The remaining
case sigma = 2 gives the eigenvalues 0 and 4. QED.

Remark 46.1. (i) By Theorems 34(b) and 41(b), G is continuous and not identically zero, and F is a homeomorphism of
the circle, so the labels alpha with G(F(alpha)) != 0 form a nonempty open set; (d) and (e) restrict their backward
limits. Let P = (x1, 0) be the point of Theorem 2. A2 parity gives Theta(P) = 0, and Theorem 2(c) gives
Theta_y(P) != 0, so Theta has vanishing order n = 1 at P. Theorem 2(d) gives DW(P) = diag(beta + 2, kappa); for
beta > 2, P is therefore a hyperbolic source, and A2 reflection in x gives the same conclusions at -P. At beta = 2,
DW(P) = diag(4, 0), as in (e). Theorem 47 sharpens (d) and (e). Whether every such
backward limit is +-P (beta > 2), respectively lies on the arc of Theorem 16 or its reflections (beta = 2), is not
decided here. (ii) At beta = 2 the proof of (e) shows that every hyperbolic source Q
has an open invariant basin on which Theta = Theta(Q) and Omega = 0 (compare the remark after Theorem 35). (iii) A
degenerate zero with eigenvalues 0 and 2 beta is not excluded by Theorems 43, 44 or 46.

### Theorem 47 (labels with nonzero outgoing amplitude: launch gradient and backward limits)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta >= 2, kappa = beta - 2, q = 1 - 2/beta, and let R0,
X0(alpha), X(s, alpha), F, f and G be as in Theorem 46(c) (f = H if beta = 2). Put theta_0 = Theta o X0, let pi be the
