backward-limit map of Theorem 44(b), Z = {W = 0}, Crit = {grad Theta = 0}, N = R^2 \ Crit, Z_reg = Z cap N,
P = (x1, 0) as in Theorem 2 (labels alpha and angles phi are taken modulo 2 pi), and
  O = {alpha : G(F(alpha)) != 0},
a nonempty open set of labels (Remark 46.1(i)).
(a) grad Theta(X0(alpha)) != 0 for every alpha in O. Consequently, if beta > 2, then G(phi) = 0 at every angle phi
    with f(phi) = f'(phi) = 0; if beta = 2, then G(phi) = 0 at every angle phi with H'(phi) = 0, and H' has a zero in
    (0, pi/2).
(b) (beta > 2) There is a countable set C contained in Z such that pi(X0(alpha)) lies in C for every alpha in O. Every
    point pi(X0(alpha)) with alpha in O is of one of the two types of Theorem 46(d). The set {alpha in O : pi(X0(alpha)) = P} contains a
    nonempty open interval, and so does {alpha in O : pi(X0(alpha)) = -P}.
(c) (beta = 2) For alpha in O, X0(alpha) lies in N and Q = pi(X0(alpha)) lies in Z_reg, so grad Theta(Q) != 0 and
    DW(Q) has eigenvalues 0 and 4. Every zero Q of W equals pi(X0(alpha)) for at most two labels alpha with X0(alpha)
    in N, hence for at most two alpha in O; in particular pi(X0(O)) is an uncountable subset of Z_reg.
(d) (beta = 2) Let Q be a zero of W at which both eigenvalues of DW(Q) have positive real part, and
    B_Q = {X : pi(X) = Q}. Then grad Theta(Q) = 0, DW(Q) is symmetric positive definite, B_Q is open, connected,
    invariant, contains Q and has infinite area, Theta = Theta(Q) and Omega = 0 on B_Q, and there is a nonempty open
    interval of angles on which H = Theta(Q) and G = 0.
Scope. These are necessary conditions on a hypothetical profile. On the axes the conditions in (a) hold automatically
(f and H vanish at 0 and pi/2 and are even about pi/2, and G vanishes on both axes), so (a) has content only in the
open quadrants. (b) does not decide which points of C other than P and -P are backward limits of labels in O; the
argument does not show that C is finite or that its closure is countable. (d) does not assert that such a zero exists. Nothing here contradicts
the other results of this report, and the theorem is not a nonexistence statement.

Proof. On the launch circle W_r > 0 (|U| <= beta |X|/4 there), so no zero of W lies on it, and with
theta_0'(alpha) = R0 e_phi . grad Theta(X0(alpha)) equation (T) at X0(alpha) reads
  W_r d_r Theta + (W_phi / R0) theta_0'(alpha) = kappa theta_0(alpha).                                     (47.1)
Hence grad Theta(X0(alpha)) = 0 if and only if theta_0'(alpha) = 0 and kappa theta_0(alpha) = 0.
(a) If grad Theta(X0(alpha)) = 0, then X0(alpha) lies in Crit, which is invariant with Omega = 0 on it
(Theorem 44(d)); so Omega = 0 on the whole orbit of X0(alpha), and Theorem 46(c) gives G(F(alpha)) = 0.
beta > 2. By Theorem 38(b), f o F = R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf} theta_0 at every label (f is defined by this formula), d_inf
is continuous and F is a C^1 diffeomorphism of the circle; f is C^infinity by Theorem 42(b) (and is the f of
Theorem 32(d) by Theorem 41(b)). Let f(phi) = f'(phi) = 0 and alpha = F^{-1}(phi). Then theta_0(alpha) = 0, and since
theta_0 is C^1 and vanishes at alpha while e^{kappa d_inf} is continuous,
  R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf(alpha)} theta_0'(alpha) = lim_{t -> 0} t^{-1} [f(F(alpha + t)) - f(F(alpha))]
                                              = f'(phi) F'(alpha) = 0.
So theta_0'(alpha) = 0, grad Theta(X0(alpha)) = 0 by (47.1), alpha is not in O, and G(phi) = 0.
beta = 2. By Theorem 46(c), H(F(alpha)) = theta_0(alpha) for every alpha; F is a C^1 diffeomorphism (Theorem 32(b),
which applies by Theorem 33(a); F is C^infinity by Theorem 36(d)) and H is C^infinity (Theorem 36(a)). If H'(phi) = 0
and alpha = F^{-1}(phi), then theta_0'(alpha) = H'(phi) F'(alpha) = 0, so grad Theta(X0(alpha)) = 0 by (47.1) with
kappa = 0, and G(phi) = 0. By Theorem 33(d), H is not identically zero, H(0) = H(pi/2) = 0, H(-phi) = -H(phi) and
H(pi - phi) = H(phi); so H is not identically zero on [0, pi/2], and |H| attains a positive maximum on [0, pi/2] at an interior point,
which is a critical point of H in (0, pi/2) with H != 0 there.
(b) Step 1 (nonisolated zeros). Z is compact (it lies inside the launch circle), and so is the set Z' of its
accumulation points. By Remark 44.1(ii), at every Q in Z', grad Theta(Q) = 0, Omega(Q) = 0, and DW(Q) is symmetric
with eigenvalues 0 and b := 2 beta. The isolated points of Z are countable (assign to each a disc with rational centre
and radius containing it and no other point of Z).
Step 2 (rapid graphs). Fix Q_* in Z' and orthonormal coordinates zeta = (zeta_1, zeta_2) centred at Q_* in which
DW(Q_*) = diag(0, b); write |zeta|_m = max(|zeta_1|, |zeta_2|). Then -W(Q_* + zeta) = (0, -b zeta_2) + R_rem(zeta) with
R_rem(0) = 0, D R_rem(0) = 0. Fix delta with 0 < delta < 1/8. As in the proof of Theorem 46(b), there are rho > 0 and a
C^infinity field R_cut on R^2 with compact support, equal to R_rem on |zeta| <= rho, with
|R_cut_i(zeta) - R_cut_i(zeta')| <= delta |zeta - zeta'|_m (i = 1, 2) for all zeta, zeta'; shrink rho so that also
Sym DW(Q_* + zeta) >= -delta I for |zeta| <= rho (possible as Sym DW(Q_*) >= 0). Put V(zeta) = (0, -b zeta_2) + R_cut(zeta),
so that V = -W on |zeta| <= rho.
Zero set. Fix r with 0 < 4r < rho. Since |d_2 R_cut_2| <= delta and |R_cut_2(zeta)| <= delta |zeta|_m (R_cut(0) = 0),
d_2 V_2 <= -b + delta < 0 everywhere and, for |zeta_1| < 2r, V_2(zeta_1, r) <= -b r + 2 delta r < 0 < V_2(zeta_1, -r).
So for each zeta_1 in (-2r, 2r), V_2(zeta_1, .) has exactly one zero k(zeta_1), which lies in (-r, r); k is
C^infinity, k(0) = 0 and |k'| = |d_1 V_2 / d_2 V_2| <= m := delta/(b - delta) < 1/15. Every zero of W in
(-2r, 2r) x (-r, r) has the form (x, k(x)) with x in E := {x in (-2r, 2r) : V_1(x, k(x)) = 0}, a relatively closed
subset of (-2r, 2r).
Graphs. For a zero Q = (q1, q2) of W in (-2r, 2r) x (-r, r) and a real number a, let T_{Q,a} act on continuous
z : [0, infinity) -> R^2 with ||z|| := sup_{s >= 0} e^{beta s} |z(s)|_m < infinity by
  (T_{Q,a} z)_1(s) = -int_s^infinity [R_cut_1(Q + z(t)) - R_cut_1(Q)] dt,
  (T_{Q,a} z)_2(s) = e^{-b s} a + int_0^s e^{-b (s - t)} [R_cut_2(Q + z(t)) - R_cut_2(Q)] dt.
Since |R_cut(Q + z) - R_cut(Q)|_m <= delta |z|_m, int_s^infinity e^{-beta t} dt = e^{-beta s}/beta and
int_0^s e^{-b(s - t)} e^{-beta t} dt <= e^{-beta s}/(b - beta) = e^{-beta s}/beta, T_{Q,a} maps this complete space into
itself and is a contraction with constant delta/beta < 1/8. Its fixed point z_{Q,a} satisfies ||z_{Q,a}|| <= 8|a|/7 and
||z_{Q,a} - z_{Q,a'}|| <= 8|a - a'|/7, and solves z' = V(Q + z) - V(Q) = V(Q + z) (V(Q) = -W(Q) = 0). Fix a_* with
0 < a_* <= r and 4r + 4a_* < rho. For |a| <= a_*, |Q + z_{Q,a}(s)| <= sqrt(2) (2r + 8 a_*/7) < rho, so Q + z_{Q,a}(s) is the
backward orbit Phi_{-s}(Q + z_{Q,a}(0)) of W, and |Phi_{-s}(Q + z_{Q,a}(0)) - Q| <= 2 a_* e^{-beta s}. Put
h_Q(a) = (z_{Q,a}(0))_1; then h_Q(0) = 0 (z = 0 is the fixed point for a = 0) and
|h_Q(a) - h_Q(a')| <= (delta/beta) ||z_{Q,a} - z_{Q,a'}|| <= L_lip |a - a'| with L_lip := 1/7. For a zero Q with |q2| <= a_*/2
let G_Q(y) := q1 + h_Q(y - q2) for |y| <= a_*/2 and Gamma_Q = {(G_Q(y), y) : |y| <= a_*/2}; since (z_{Q,a}(0))_2 = a,
Gamma_Q = {Q + z_{Q,a}(0) : |a + q2| <= a_*/2}, and every point of Gamma_Q has backward limit Q, at the rate e^{-beta s}.
(i) Continuity in Q. Let omega be a modulus of continuity of the entries of D R_cut. For zeros Q, Q' as above,
[R_cut(Q + z) - R_cut(Q)] - [R_cut(Q' + z) - R_cut(Q')] = int_0^1 [D R_cut(Q + tz) - D R_cut(Q' + tz)] z dt has max norm at most
2 omega(|Q - Q'|) |z|_m, so ||z_{Q,a} - z_{Q',a}|| <= (2 omega(|Q - Q'|)/beta) ||z_{Q',a}|| / (1 - delta/beta)
<= 3 omega(|Q - Q'|) a_* and |G_Q(y) - G_{Q'}(y)| <= |q1 - q1'| + L_lip |q2 - q2'| + 3 omega(|Q - Q'|) a_*.
(ii) Disjointness. If Q != Q', Gamma_Q and Gamma_{Q'} are disjoint: a common point would have two backward limits.
Fix r' in (0, r] with |k| < a_*/4 on (-r', r') and put R_* = (-r', r') x (-a_*/4, a_*/4), an open rectangle containing
Q_* and contained in |zeta| <= rho; every zero of W in R_* is (x, k(x)) with x in E cap (-r', r'), and has |q2| < a_*/4.
(iii) Order. Let Q = (q1, k(q1)), Q' = (q1', k(q1')) be zeros in R_* with q1 < q1'. For x between q1 and q1',
|k(x) - q2| < a_*/2, and g(x) = x - q1 - h_Q(k(x) - q2) satisfies g(x'') - g(x') >= (1 - L_lip m)(x'' - x') > 0 for
x' < x'', and g(q1) = 0; so g(q1') > 0, that is, G_Q(q2') < q1' = G_{Q'}(q2'). The continuous function G_{Q'} - G_Q on
[-a_*/2, a_*/2] has no zero by (ii), so G_Q < G_{Q'} there; in particular G_{Q'}(q2) > G_Q(q2) = q1.
Step 3 (barrier). Let Q = (q1, k(q1)) be a zero in R_* such that q1 is an accumulation point of E both from the left
and from the right, and let Y(s) = Phi_{-s} X -> Q. Choose s1 with Y(s) in R_* for s >= s1. Suppose
Y_1(s0) > G_Q(Y_2(s0)) for some s0 >= s1. Take x_n in E cap (q1, r') with x_n -> q1 and Q_n = (x_n, k(x_n)), zeros in
R_* with Q_n -> Q; by (i), G_{Q_n}(Y_2(s0)) < Y_1(s0) for some fixed n. The function
sigma(s) = Y_1(s) - G_{Q_n}(Y_2(s)), s >= s0, is continuous, positive at s0, and never zero (a zero would put Y(s) on
Gamma_{Q_n}, so Y would tend to Q_n != Q); so sigma > 0. But sigma(s) -> q1 - G_{Q_n}(q2) < 0 by (iii), a
contradiction. If Y_1(s0) < G_Q(Y_2(s0)), zeros Q_n with first coordinate in E cap (-r', q1) give the symmetric
contradiction. Hence Y(s) lies on Gamma_Q for s >= s1, and |Y(s) - Q| <= 2 a_* e^{-beta (s - s1)}.
Since Q is in Z', grad Theta(Q) = 0, so g(s) = grad Theta(Y(s)) satisfies |g(s)| <= C e^{-beta s}. As in the proof of
Theorem 46(b), g' = (DW^T - kappa I) g and d_s |g|^2 = 2 g . (Sym DW) g - 2 kappa |g|^2 >= -2 (kappa + delta) |g|^2 for
s >= s1, so |g(s1)| <= e^{(kappa + delta)(s - s1)} |g(s)| <= C' e^{(kappa + delta - beta) s} -> 0
(beta - kappa = 2 > delta): g(s1) = 0. By Theorem 44(d), grad Theta = 0 and Omega = 0 on the whole orbit of X, so if
X = X0(alpha), Theorem 46(c) gives G(F(alpha)) = 0.
Step 4 (countability). In each chart the points of E cap (-r', r') that are not accumulation points of E from both
sides are countable: such a point is an endpoint of a component of the open set (-2r, 2r) \ E, and these components are
disjoint open intervals, each containing a rational number. Cover the compact set Z' by finitely many rectangles R_*
of Step 3 and let C consist of the isolated points of Z and, for each of these finitely many charts, of the zeros
(x, k(x)) with x such an exceptional point; C is countable. If Q is in Z \ C, then Q is in Z', it lies in one of the
rectangles, and its coordinate is an accumulation point of E from both sides; by Step 3 no alpha with
pi(X0(alpha)) = Q lies in O. Each point pi(X0(alpha)), alpha in O, is of one of the types of Theorem 46(d).
Step 5 (P and -P). DW(P) = diag(beta + 2, kappa) (Theorem 2(d)) is symmetric positive definite, so there is eps > 0
with W(P + z) . z >= (kappa/2)|z|^2 for |z| <= eps; for |Y0 - P| < eps, d_s |Phi_{-s} Y0 - P|^2 =
-2 W . (Phi_{-s} Y0 - P) <= -kappa |Phi_{-s} Y0 - P|^2, so the backward orbit stays in the ball V = {|X - P| < eps} and
tends to P. Hence B_P := {X : pi(X) = P} = union_{t >= 0} Phi_t(V) is open and invariant. Near the origin,
W_1 = x (-(beta + 2) + O(|X|^2)) and W_2 = y (3 beta + 2 + O(|X|^2)) (parities and DW(0) = diag(beta - c, beta + c),
c = 2 beta + 2). By Theorem 2(a), w = W_1(., 0) < 0 on (0, x1), and W_2 = 0 on the x-axis; so the backward orbit of
(x, 0), 0 < x < x1, stays on the axis, increases, and converges to a zero of w in (x, x1], which is x1: (0, x1) x {0}
is contained in B_P. Fix d1 in (0, x1) with -W_1 >= (beta + 2) x/2 and -W_2 <= 0 on [0, d1]^2, and, as B_P is open
and contains (d1, 0), e1 in (0, d1) with {d1} x [0, e1) contained in B_P. For 0 < x < d1, 0 < y < e1 the backward orbit
of (x, y) keeps 0 < y(s) <= y (the x-axis is invariant) and has x(s) >= x e^{(beta + 2) s/2} while it stays in
(0, d1] x (0, e1), so it reaches {d1} x (0, e1), and (x, y) is in B_P. Thus (0, d1) x (0, e1) is contained in B_P.
By Theorem 41(b) the conclusions of Theorem 37(d) hold: with rho0 as in Theorem 37(c) and rho = min(e1, rho0),
sgn(a0) J > 0 at some X* in Q_rho, which lies in (0, d1) x (0, e1), hence in B_P. X* is escaping (Theorem 37(c)), so
X* = X(s*, alpha*) for some (s*, alpha*) (Theorem 38(c)), and by (41.2), with J0 the continuous representative of
Theorem 41(c), J(X*) = lim_t e^t Omega(X(t + s*, alpha*)) = e^{-s*} J0(alpha*); so J0(alpha*) != 0. By the proof of
Theorem 43(d), or by the proof of Theorem 44(f), G(F(alpha)) = R0^{1/beta} e^{-d_inf(alpha)} J0(alpha) for every alpha, so
G(F(alpha*)) != 0. X0(alpha*) = Phi_{-s*} X* lies in the open invariant set B_P, and X0 and G o F are continuous, so
there is an open interval I* containing alpha* with X0(I*) contained in B_P and I* contained in O. The reflection
R(x, y) = (-x, y) maps the profile to itself (W(RX) = R W(X), Omega(RX) = -Omega(X)), so Phi_t o R = R o Phi_t,
pi o R = R o pi, X0(pi - alpha) = R X0(alpha), F(pi - alpha) = pi - F(alpha) and G(pi - phi) = -G(phi); hence the
interval pi - I* is contained in {alpha in O : pi(X0(alpha)) = -P}.
(c) By (a), X0(alpha) lies in N for alpha in O, and it is not a zero of W; Theorem 39(a) gives pi(X0(alpha)) in Z_reg
(the maps pi of Theorems 39(a) and 44(b) agree there, Theorem 44(b)). At Q in Z_reg, differentiating (T) with
kappa = 0 gives DW(Q)^T grad Theta(Q) = 0 with grad Theta(Q) != 0, so 0 is an eigenvalue of DW(Q), and tr DW(Q) = 4.
With N the regular set defined above and L the function (39.1), Theorem 39(b) gives a diffeomorphism
(pi, L) : N -> Z_reg x R, under which Phi_t acts by l -> e^{4t} l; so
{X in N : pi(X) = Q} is empty if Q is not in Z_reg, and otherwise it consists of Q and two orbits (l > 0 and l < 0).
An orbit meets the launch circle at most once: d|Phi_t X|/dt = W_r > 0 wherever |Phi_t X| >= R0, so after a crossing
the orbit stays outside the circle and before it inside. Hence at most two labels alpha with X0(alpha) in N have
pi(X0(alpha)) = Q. As O is a nonempty open set, it is uncountable, and so is pi(X0(O)).
(d) DW(Q)^T grad Theta(Q) = 0 (differentiate (T) at Q, kappa = 0), and 0 is not an eigenvalue, so grad Theta(Q) = 0;
then Omega(Q) = Theta_x(Q) = 0 by (V), DW(Q) is symmetric (Theorem 44(d)) with eigenvalues of positive real part, hence
positive definite. By the proof of Theorem 46(e) there is an open ball V centred at Q such that every backward orbit
starting in V stays in V and tends to Q, B_Q = union_{t >= 0} Phi_t(V) is open and invariant, and Theta = Theta(Q),
Omega = 0 on B_Q. Each Phi_t(V) is connected and contains Q, so B_Q is connected; it is nonempty, open and invariant,
and |Phi_t(B_Q)| = e^{4t} |B_Q|, so |B_Q| = infinity. B_Q is therefore unbounded; being connected, it meets the launch
circle (Q lies inside it), and B_Q cap {|X| = R0} is relatively open, so it contains X0(I_0) for an open interval I_0.
For alpha in I_0 the orbit of X0(alpha) lies in B_Q, so Omega = 0 on it and Theta(X0(alpha)) = Theta(Q); Theorem 46(c)
gives G = 0 and H = Theta(Q) on the open interval F(I_0). QED.

Remark 47.1. (i) Part (a) is a necessary condition on the angular limits of an A2-broad profile that can be tested at
infinity: at beta = 2, G must vanish at every critical point of H in (0, pi/2), and there is at least one; at beta > 2,
G must vanish at every phi in (0, pi/2) with f(phi) = f'(phi) = 0 (no such interior point is asserted to exist). Its
proof follows complete backward orbits (Theorem 44(d)), and it is not a consequence of the exterior equations alone:
Theorem 69 gives exact exterior solutions for beta > 2 with f = 0 and G != 0, and Theorem 70(e) gives exact exterior
solutions at beta = 2 with G > 0 at a critical point of H. (ii) At beta = 2, (c) sharpens Theorem 46(e): the backward
limit of a label in O has grad Theta != 0, and is neither a hyperbolic source nor a saddle. (iii) For beta > 2 the
points of C reached from O include P and -P, and by Theorem 54(c) no axis zero whose eigenvalue tangent to the axis is
zero is reached from O; whether there are other points, for instance degenerate zeros with eigenvalues 0 and 2 beta in
the open quadrant or on an axis with zero transverse eigenvalue, is not decided.

### Theorem 48 (beta = 2: forward limits, no return to an arc of zeros, and the angular profile under (S) and (R))
Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile, W = 2X + U, Z = {W = 0}, Crit = {grad Theta = 0}, N = R^2 \ Crit,
Z_reg = Z cap N, Q1 the open first quadrant, sigma = sgn(a0), and let C, Q+, Q- be as in Theorem 16 and M = Theta(Q+).
Let H, G be as in Theorem 36, L as in (39.1), and R0, X0(alpha) = R0 (cos alpha, sin alpha) and F as in Theorem 46(c)
(labels alpha and angles phi modulo 2 pi; R0 >= 1 is so large that (33.2) holds for r >= R0, possible by Theorem
33(a), so that R0 is admissible in Theorems 36(d) and 46(c) and W_r >= |X| on |X| >= R0). Put w(x) = W_1(x, 0),
f(x) = Theta_y(x, 0), v(y) = W_2(0, y), E(y) = Theta_xx(0, y)/2, and consider the hypotheses
  (S) Z cap Q1 = C cap Q1;   (R) C \ {Q+, Q-} is contained in N;   (X) w > 0 on (x1, infinity);   (Y) v > 0 on (0, infinity).
(a) (Forward limits.) If X is not escaping, its forward orbit stays in {|X| < R0} and converges to a single point S of
    Z, and Theta(S) = Theta(X). If moreover X is in N \ Z, then S is in Crit and Omega(S) = 0.
(b) (No return.) No nonstationary orbit has its backward limit and its forward limit on one embedded arc contained in
    Z. In particular no nonstationary orbit has both limits on C.
(c) (A critical outgoing orbit.) H has a critical point in (0, pi/2) at which H != 0. For every phi_c in (0, pi/2) with
    H'(phi_c) = 0 and H(phi_c) != 0, the orbit of X0(F^{-1}(phi_c)) lies in Crit and escapes, Theta = H(phi_c) and
    Omega = 0 on it, and its backward limit is a point of Z cap Crit cap Q1 with temperature H(phi_c). (This
    proves the existence conclusion of Theorem 12 with the additional property that the zero is the backward limit
    of a critical escaping orbit whose temperature is a nonzero critical value of H.)
(d) Assume (S). Every nonstationary orbit with backward limit on C and nonzero temperature escapes. If M != 0, there is
    an open, connected, invariant set of infinite area contained in Q1 on which Theta = M and Omega = 0, and a nonempty
    open interval of angles on which H = M and G = 0.
(e) Assume (S) and (R). Then M = sigma m with m > 0, and there are angles 0 <= phi_1 < phi_2 < phi_3 < phi_4 <= pi/2
    such that: H = 0 on [0, phi_1] and on [phi_4, pi/2]; sigma H increases strictly from 0 to m on [phi_1, phi_2], with
    H' != 0 on (phi_1, phi_2); H = M on [phi_2, phi_3]; sigma H decreases strictly from m to 0 on [phi_3, phi_4], with
    H' != 0 on (phi_3, phi_4); G = 0 on [0, phi_1], [phi_2, phi_3] and [phi_4, pi/2]. Each value sigma u, 0 < u < m, is
    taken by H at exactly two angles in (0, pi/2). If moreover (X) holds, then phi_1 = 0 and H'(0) = R0 f(R0)/F'(0)
    with sigma f(R0) > 0. If (Y) holds, then phi_4 = pi/2 and H''(pi/2) = 2 R0^2 E(R0)/F'(pi/2)^2 with sigma E(R0) > 0.
(f) (Isothermal balances.) Let b be C^1 on [0, pi/2] and K_b = |X|^{-3} (-2 b(phi) U_r + b'(phi) U_phi). For every
    c != 0, K_b is absolutely integrable on {Theta = c} cap Q1 and, with dX planar Lebesgue measure and dphi linear
    Lebesgue measure,
      int_{{Theta = c} cap Q1} K_b dX = 2 int_{{phi in (0, pi/2) : H(phi) = c}} b(phi) dphi;                  (48.1)
    in particular int_{{Theta = c} cap Q1} |X|^{-3} U_r dX = -|{phi in (0, pi/2) : H(phi) = c}|. Under (S) and
    M != 0, the set {Theta = M} cap Q1 has infinite area and int_{{Theta = M} cap Q1} |X|^{-3} U_r dX =
    -|{phi in (0, pi/2) : H(phi) = M}| < 0; under (S) and (R) this angular level set is [phi_2, phi_3], so the integral
    equals -(phi_3 - phi_2).
Scope. These are necessary conditions on a hypothetical profile. (S), (R), (X) and (Y) are hypotheses, not proved.
(a), (b), (c) and (48.1) use none of them; (d) uses (S); the last sentence of (f) uses (S) (and (R) for its final
identification); (e) uses (S) and (R), and the
refinements at phi = 0 and phi = pi/2 in (e) use in addition (X), respectively (Y). (d), (e) and the last sentence of
(f) describe what a profile satisfying the corresponding hypotheses must look like, and are neither a
construction nor a contradiction: smooth angular functions with the shape of (e), the A2 parities, and G = 0 wherever
H' = 0 exist, and whether a profile realizes such a configuration is open. The set in (d) need not contain a
neighbourhood of Q+, so (d) does not contradict Theorem 16. The theorem is not a nonexistence statement.

Proof. Throughout, Theta is constant on orbits, div W = 4, backward limits pi(X) exist and lie in Z (Theorem 44(b)), Crit
is closed and invariant with Omega = 0 on it (Theorem 44(d)), and Ly of Theorem 44(a) satisfies W.grad Ly = 3|W|^2.
For |X| >= R0, d|Phi_t X|/dt = W_r >= |Phi_t X|; hence an orbit that reaches {|X| >= R0} stays there with radius
growing at least like e^t, so it escapes, and it meets the circle {|X| = R0} at most once.
(a) Suppose X is not escaping, i.e. its forward orbit is bounded (Theorem 32(c)). By the preceding remark, Phi_t X
stays in the disc K = {|X| < R0} for t >= 0. If X is in Z, S = X. Let X not be in Z.
Ly is bounded on K and t -> Ly(Phi_t X) is nondecreasing, so int_0^infinity 3 |W(Phi_t X)|^2 dt is finite. Since
d/dt |W(Phi_t X)|^2 = 2 W . (DW W) is bounded on K, |W(Phi_t X)| -> 0 (otherwise there are disjoint time intervals of a
fixed length on which |W|^2 exceeds a fixed positive number). Hence the omega-limit set A is a nonempty, compact,
connected subset of Z.
Fact 1. Let I be an embedded open arc contained in Z, R a point of I, and X a point not in Z. Then R is not in the
omega-limit set of X. Indeed, since tr DW(R) = 4, some component W_i has nonzero gradient at R, so near R the set Z
lies in the smooth curve {W_i = 0}, and I fills a neighbourhood of R in that curve. Take C^infinity coordinates (u, v)
near R in which I = {v = 0} near R and R = (0, 0). The field
vanishes on {v = 0}, so in these coordinates W = v (a(u, v), b(u, v)) with a, b smooth, and the derivative of W at
(u, 0) has eigenvalues 0 and b(u, 0); its trace is that of DW, namely 4, so b(u, 0) = 4. Choose eps > 0 with b >= 2 and
|a| <= M0, M0 >= 1, on the closed rectangle B = [-eps, eps]^2 (in (u, v)), with X not in B. In backward time
du/ds = -v a, dv/ds = -v b, so while a backward orbit stays in B, |v(s)| <= |v(0)| e^{-2s} and
|u(s) - u(0)| <= M0 |v(0)|/2. Hence every backward orbit starting in B' = {|u| < eps/2, |v| < min(eps, eps/(2 M0))}
stays in B for all s >= 0 (a first exit would contradict these bounds). If R were in the omega-limit set of X, then
Phi_T X would lie in B' for some T > 0, and X = Phi_{-T}(Phi_T X) would lie in B: a contradiction.
Fact 2. A compact connected subset A of Z with more than one point contains an embedded open arc. Indeed, let Q be in
A and Q' != Q in A. Since tr DW(Q) = 4, some component W_i has grad W_i(Q) != 0, so in suitable C^infinity coordinates
(u, v) on a closed box B around Q, not containing Q', {W_i = 0} cap B = {v = 0} cap B, and Z cap B is contained in
{v = 0}. Suppose that on each side of Q there are points of {v = 0} cap B not in A arbitrarily close to Q; choose such
p1 = (u1, 0), p2 = (u2, 0) with u1 < 0 < u2 and a small eta > 0 so that B'' = [u1, u2] x [-eta, eta] lies in B. Then the
boundary of B'' meets Z only in {p1, p2}, which lie outside A, so A cap B'' = A cap int B'' is open and closed in A,
contains Q and misses Q': this contradicts connectedness. Hence on one side of Q an interval {(u, 0) : 0 < u < u3} (or
its mirror) lies in A, and this is an embedded open arc contained in Z.
If A had more than one point, Fact 2 would give an embedded open arc in Z contained in A, and Fact 1 would exclude its
points from A. So A = {S}, and Phi_t X -> S. Theta(S) =
Theta(X) by continuity. If X is in N \ Z, Theorem 39(b) (last sentence) gives S in R^2 \ N = Crit, and Omega(S) = 0.
(b) Let gamma be a nonstationary orbit with backward limit S1 and forward limit S2 on an embedded arc I contained in Z.
If S1 = S2, then Ly(S2) - Ly(S1) = lim (Ly(Phi_t X) - Ly(Phi_{-t} X)) = int_{-infinity}^{infinity} 3 |W(Phi_t X)|^2 dt > 0,
a contradiction. If S1 != S2, map [-1, 1] to R^2 by tau -> Phi_{tan(pi tau/2)} X for |tau| < 1, -1 -> S1, 1 -> S2. This
map is continuous and injective (gamma is not periodic, since Ly strictly increases on it, and contains no zero), so
its image gamma' is a compact embedded arc meeting Z only at S1, S2. With the compact subarc I' of I from S1 to S2,
J = gamma' cup I' is a Jordan curve. Each Phi_t maps J onto itself (it preserves gamma and fixes Z pointwise), so it maps
the bounded component D of R^2 \ J onto a bounded component of R^2 \ J, that is, onto D. Then |D| = |Phi_t D| =
e^{4t} |D| with 0 < |D| < infinity: a contradiction. C is an embedded arc contained in Z (Theorem 16).
(c) H is not identically zero on [0, pi/2], H(0) = H(pi/2) = 0 (Theorem 33(d)), so |H| attains a positive maximum on
[0, pi/2] at an interior point, where H' = 0 and H != 0. Let phi_c be as stated and alpha_c = F^{-1}(phi_c). By
Theorem 46(c), H o F = theta_0 := Theta o X0, and F is a C^1 diffeomorphism, so theta_0'(alpha_c) = H'(phi_c) F'(alpha_c)
= 0; (47.1) with kappa = 0 and W_r > 0 then gives grad Theta(X0(alpha_c)) = 0 (as in the proof of Theorem 47(a)). So the
orbit lies in Crit, Omega = 0 on it, and Theta = theta_0(alpha_c) = H(phi_c) on it. It starts on the launch circle,
so it escapes. Its backward limit S lies in the closure of the orbit, hence in Crit, has Theta(S) = H(phi_c) != 0,
and lies in the closed quadrant (Q1 is invariant and X0(alpha_c) is in Q1); since Theta = 0 on both axes, S is in Q1.
(d) Let gamma have backward limit on C and temperature theta != 0. C lies in {x > 0} (it is connected, contains P and
misses the y-axis), the axes are invariant and carry Theta = 0, so gamma lies in Q1 or in Q4 = {x > 0, y < 0}. The
reflection (x, y) -> (x, -y) maps orbits to orbits, preserves Z and C, and changes the sign of Theta; it maps (S) to
Z cap Q4 = C cap Q4. So we may assume that gamma lies in Q1. If gamma does not escape, (a) gives a forward limit S in
Z cap closure(Q1) with Theta(S) = theta != 0, so S is off the axes and in Z cap Q1 = C cap Q1 by (S); this contradicts
(b). Now let
M != 0. By (S), Q+ (which lies in Q1) has a neighbourhood in which Z coincides with C, and every zero of W in the closed
quadrant that is not on C lies on an axis, where Theta = 0 != M. The second statement of Theorem 22 therefore applies: the
flow on the centre manifold of Q+ points away from Q+ on the side beyond C, where by isolation there is no zero of W
near Q+. We verify the hypotheses of Theorem 35 at Q = Q+. DW(Q+) has eigenvalues 4 and 0 (Theorem 16), so Q+ has a
local C^2 invariant centre curve tangent to ker DW(Q+) (the centre-manifold fact used after Theorem 16 and in Theorem
22). In C^2 coordinates (s, z) straightening it to {z = 0}, the normal equation is z' = a(s, z) z with a continuous and
a(0, 0) = 4; shrinking, a > 0, so every zero of W near Q+ has z = 0 and lies on the centre curve. In particular the
part of C near Q+ lies on it (C is tangent to ker DW(Q+) at Q+), and we orient s so that C is {s <= 0} near Q+. By the
local isolation given by (S), the branch 0 < s < delta carries no zero of W, so the flow on it has one sign, and by the
second statement of Theorem 22 it points away from Q+. Theorem 35 then gives the open, connected, invariant set of
infinite area in Q1 with Theta = M, Omega = 0 (35(b)) and the interval of angles with H = M, G = 0 (35(c)).
(e) Assume (S) and (R). Let D+ = C cap Q1 \ {Q+}; by (R) it lies in Z_reg, and since C is an arc that meets the x-axis
only at P and is reversed by (x, y) -> (x, -y) (Theorem 16), D+ is the open subarc of C from P to Q+. By Theorem 3,
Theta restricted to C has derivative f(x1) at P in the direction e_y, with sgn f(x1) = sigma (Theorem 2(c)); by
Theorem 39(b), Theta is strictly monotone on the component of Z_reg containing D+. Hence M = sigma m with m > 0, and for
0 < u < m there is exactly one q(u) in D+ with Theta(q(u)) = sigma u. By Theorem 39(b), the nonstationary orbits in N
with backward limit q(u) are exactly two, gamma_+(u) (sgn L = -sigma) and gamma_-(u) (sgn L = sigma), and both lie in
Q1 (near q(u) and invariant axes). Both escape by (d); each meets the launch circle exactly once, and we write
phi_+(u), phi_-(u) for the angles F(alpha) of their labels.
Exit angles. For an escaping X in N \ Z with exit angle phi_inf, (39.5) gives H'(phi_inf) = -2 A^2 / L(X) != 0. Let
X_+(u) be the point of gamma_+(u) with L = -sigma; in the coordinates (Theta, L) of Theorem 39(b) on the component of
N containing D+, X_+(u) has coordinates (sigma u, -sigma), so u -> X_+(u) is C^infinity; the (possibly negative)
time at which its orbit meets the launch circle is unique and is C^infinity in u by the implicit function theorem
(W_r > 0 on the circle), so phi_+ is C^infinity on (0, m) (F is C^infinity, Theorem 36(d)), and H(phi_+(u)) = sigma u
(Theorem 46(c)). Differentiating, phi_+'(u) = sigma/H'(phi_+(u)) > 0, since H' has sign sigma at phi_+(u). So phi_+ is
strictly increasing; likewise phi_-'(u) = sigma/H'(phi_-(u)) < 0 and phi_- is strictly decreasing. So phi_+((0, m)) = (phi_1, phi_2) and phi_-((0, m)) = (phi_3, phi_4) are open intervals, with
H(phi) -> 0 at phi_1 and phi_4 and H(phi) -> M at phi_2 and phi_3; they are disjoint, since an angle determines its
label and the orbit through it.
Values. Every point of the closed quadrant has its backward limit in Z cap closure(Q1), which by (S) is contained in
C cap closure(Q1) union the axes; on the axes Theta = 0 and on C cap closure(Q1) Theta takes values between 0 and M.
So H takes values in the closed interval between 0 and M. Let phi in (0, pi/2) with H(phi) = sigma u, 0 < u < m, and
X = X0(F^{-1}(phi)). Its backward limit has temperature sigma u, so it is q(u), which lies in N; since Crit is closed
and invariant, X is in N, and by Theorem 39(b) its orbit is gamma_+(u) or gamma_-(u), so phi is phi_+(u) or phi_-(u).
Hence each such value is taken at exactly two angles, and outside (phi_1, phi_2) cup (phi_3, phi_4), H takes only the
values 0 and M.
Order. Suppose phi_4 <= phi_1. Then H(phi_3) = M and H(0) = 0, so H takes every value sigma u, 0 < u < m, on
(0, phi_3), which is disjoint from both intervals: a contradiction. So phi_1 < phi_2 <= phi_3 < phi_4. On each of the
connected sets [0, phi_1], [phi_2, phi_3], [phi_4, pi/2], H is continuous with values in {0, M}, hence constant, equal
to H(0) = 0, M, H(pi/2) = 0 respectively. So {phi in [0, pi/2] : H(phi) = M} = [phi_2, phi_3]. By (d) there is an
open interval of angles with H = M; it lies in [phi_2, phi_3], so phi_2 < phi_3. On every one of the three sets that
is a nondegenerate interval, H' = 0 on its interior and, by continuity of H', at its endpoints, so G = 0 there by
Theorem 47(a). If [0, phi_1] = {0} or [phi_4, pi/2] = {pi/2}, then G = 0 at that axis angle by Theorem 33(d) (G
vanishes on both axes). (No claim H'(0) = 0 is made; under (X), H'(0) != 0 below.)
(X). By Theorem 2(b), w f' = (w' - 4) f, which is a regular homogeneous linear equation on (x1, infinity) under (X);
f(x1) has sign sigma (Theorem 2(c)), so sigma f > 0 at some x* > x1 near x1, and uniqueness for the regular equation
gives sigma f > 0 on [x1, infinity). Hence the segment [x1, infinity) x {0} lies in N and in the component of N
containing D+, and at Y0 = (R0, 0), Theta = 0 and L(Y0) = -w(R0)/f(R0) has sign -sigma. In the coordinates (Theta, L)
of Theorem 39(b) the points with coordinates (sigma u, L(Y0)) lie on gamma_+(u) and tend to Y0 as u -> 0, so their
hitting times of the launch circle tend to 0 and phi_+(u) -> F(0) = 0. So phi_1 = 0. Differentiating
H(F(alpha)) = Theta(R0 cos alpha, R0 sin alpha) at alpha = 0 gives H'(0) F'(0) = R0 f(R0), and F'(0) > 0.
(Y). Near O, W_1 = x(-4 + O(|X|^2)), W_2 = y(8 + O(|X|^2)) and Theta_x = 2 a0 x y (1 + O(|X|^2)) (parities and the jet).
Choose delta, e > 0 such that on (0, delta) x (0, e), W_2 > 0 and sigma Theta_x > 0. This rectangle lies in N, and so
does (0, delta) x {0} (f has sign sigma on (0, x1]); so it lies in the component of N containing D+, and
L = W_2/Theta_x has sign sigma there (W = L grad^perp Theta). Under (Y), the backward orbit of (0, R0) runs down the
y-axis to O, so Phi_{-T}(0, R0) = (0, y*) with 0 < y* < e for some T; by continuity there is eps > 0 such that
Phi_{-T} X0(alpha) lies in (0, delta) x (0, e) for pi/2 - eps < alpha < pi/2. For these alpha, X0(alpha) is in N with
sgn L = sigma (L(Phi_t X) = e^{4t} L(X)) and with temperature sigma u(alpha), where 0 < u(alpha) < m: its backward
limit is in Z_reg cap closure(Q1) (Theorem 39(a)), hence by (S) in D+ or on an axis; zeros on the y-axis are in Crit;
and a regular zero (x', 0) on the x-axis has w'(x') = 4 (DW is diagonal on the x-axis by parity, with entries w' and
4 - w', and DW^T grad Theta = 0 with grad Theta = (0, f(x')) != 0), so w has the sign of x - x' near x', and the two
x-axis half-segments adjacent to (x', 0) are local pieces of two distinct complete orbits in N with backward limit
(x', 0); by Theorem 39(b) these two complete orbits, which stay on the invariant x-axis, exhaust the nonstationary part
of its fibre in N. The orbit of X0(alpha) lies in Q1, so its backward limit is in D+. So F(alpha) = phi_-(u(alpha)), and
H(F(alpha)) -> 0 as alpha -> pi/2 gives phi_4 = pi/2. By the linear equation v E' + (8 - 2 v') E = 0 (the x^2
coefficient of W.grad Theta = 0, using Theta = x^2 E(y) + O(x^4), W_1 = x(4 - v'(y)) + O(x^3), W_2 = v(y) + O(x^2)),
which is regular on (0, infinity) under (Y), and E(y) = a0 y + O(y^3), E has sign sigma on (0, infinity). At
alpha = pi/2 the first and second derivatives of Theta vanish except Theta_xx (the y-axis lies in Crit and Theta = 0
on it), so theta_0''(pi/2) = R0^2 Theta_xx(0, R0) = 2 R0^2 E(R0); with H'(pi/2) = 0 (H(pi - phi) = H(phi)) and
theta_0 = H o F (F is C^infinity, Theorem 36(d)), H''(pi/2) F'(pi/2)^2 = 2 R0^2 E(R0).
(f) Let c != 0 and choose a C^1 function rho on R with 0 <= rho <= 1, rho(0) = 1 and support in [-1, 1], and put
F_n(s) = rho(n (s - c)). For n > 2/|c|, F_n(0) = 0, so (39.10) applies to F_n. The set V = {X in Q1 : |Theta(X) - c|
<= |c|/2} has positive distance from O (Theta(O) = 0), and |K_b| <= C |X|^{-3} |U| <= C' |X|^{-5/2} for large |X|
(Theorem 33(a)), while K_b is bounded on V cap {|X| <= R} for each R; since int_{Q1 cap {r >= R}} r^{-5/2} dX < infinity,
K_b is absolutely integrable on V, hence on {Theta = c} cap Q1, which is contained in V. On V, |F_n(Theta) K_b| <= |K_b| and F_n(Theta) -> 1 on
{Theta = c}, -> 0 elsewhere; on (0, pi/2), |F_n(H) b| <= |b| and F_n(H) -> 1_{H = c}. Dominated convergence in both
sides of (39.10) gives (48.1); b = 1 gives the second formula. Under (S) and M != 0, (d) gives an open set of infinite area in
{Theta = M} cap Q1 and a nonempty open interval in {H = M} cap (0, pi/2), so the right side with c = M is negative;
under (S) and (R), {H = M} cap (0, pi/2) = [phi_2, phi_3] by (e), so it is -(phi_3 - phi_2). QED.

### Theorem 49 (restricted: finite angular support)
Let beta > 0 and let Psi, Theta be smooth real functions on R^2 satisfying (V) and (T), with Omega = -Lap Psi, U =
(-Psi_y, Psi_x), W = beta X + U, and U(X) = o(|X|) uniformly as |X| -> infinity. In polar coordinates (r, phi) suppose
that
  Psi = sum_{n even, 2 <= n <= N} h_n(r) sin(n phi),   Theta = sum_{l odd, 1 <= l <= L} theta_l(r) sin(l phi),
with N >= 2 even, L >= 1 odd, and h_N, theta_L not identically zero on (0, infinity).
(a) This is impossible.
(b) The same holds if the assumption on Theta is replaced by: Theta is not identically zero, even in x and odd in y
    (with Psi as above). Precisely, Theta then has only odd sine frequencies at most 3N - 1 on every circle, so (a)
    applies.
Consequently no A2-broad profile has a stream function with finite angular Fourier support, whatever the angular
support of its temperature.
Scope. Part (a) uses smoothness, the two equations, the parities encoded in the two sine series and U = o(|X|), the last
only through h_N = o(r^2); part (b) uses U = o(|X|) uniformly for every angular coefficient of U_2. Neither part uses
the jet, the axis condition, the canonical inverse or the growth bounds of Section 2. Some growth condition is needed:
Psi = -2 x y, Theta = y (so Omega = 0, U = (2x, -2y)) satisfy (V) and (T) for every beta, with N = 2 and L = 1. The
theorem concerns exact finite support with one fixed bandwidth N; it gives no lower bound for residuals of finite
approximations and says nothing about limits of such approximations as N, L -> infinity.
Proof. The coefficients h_n, theta_l are smooth on (0, infinity). Write h = h_N, theta = theta_L, and g = -h'' - h'/r +
N^2 h/r^2, so that Omega = sum_{n <= N} g_n(r) sin(n phi) with g_N = g. In polar form U_r = -Psi_phi/r and U_phi =
Psi_r. For a stream mode h_n sin(n phi) and a scalar mode a_m sin(m phi),
  U.grad(a_m sin(m phi)) = [(m h_n' a_m - n h_n a_m') sin((n+m) phi) + (m h_n' a_m + n h_n a_m') sin((n-m) phi)]/(2r),
  d_x(a_m sin(m phi)) = [(a_m' - m a_m/r) sin((m+1) phi) + (a_m' + m a_m/r) sin((m-1) phi)]/2,
while r d_r and multiplication by a constant preserve frequencies. Write [F]_k for the coefficient of sin(k phi). Only
the pair (n, m) = (N, L) reaches frequency N + L in U.grad Theta, only (N, N) reaches 2N in U.grad Omega, and only
theta_L reaches L + 1 in Theta_x, so
  [U.grad Theta]_{N+L} = (L h' theta - N h theta')/(2r),  [U.grad Omega]_{2N} = N (h' g - h g')/(2r),
  [Theta_x]_{L+1} = (theta' - L theta/r)/2.
All other terms of (T) have frequencies at most L < N + L, so (T) at frequency N + L gives
  L h' theta - N h theta' = 0 on (0, infinity).                                                        (49.1)
The cosine coefficient of U_r at frequency N is -N h/r, and Fourier coefficients are bounded by the angular supremum, so
h = o(r^2).
Case L + 1 > 2N. The terms of (V) other than Theta_x have frequencies at most 2N < L + 1, so theta' = L theta/r and
theta = C r^L with C != 0. Then (49.1) gives h' = N h/r, so h = D r^N with D != 0, contradicting h = o(r^2) (N >= 2).
Case L + 1 < 2N. Theta_x and the linear terms of (V) have frequencies at most max(L + 1, N) < 2N, so (V) at frequency 2N
gives h' g - h g' = 0. On a component of {h != 0} this says g = lambda h with a constant lambda, so h'' + h'/r +
(lambda - N^2/r^2) h = 0 there. Let Y be the solution of this linear equation on (0, infinity) that agrees with h on
that component, and let r0 > 0 be a finite endpoint of a maximal interval on which h = Y. If Y(r0) != 0, then h != 0
near r0; on the part of that neighbourhood where h = Y, g = lambda h, so the constant ratio g/h on the component of {h
!= 0} containing r0 is lambda, and uniqueness gives h = Y on that component, contrary to maximality. If Y(r0) = 0, then
Y'(r0) != 0 (Y is a nontrivial solution of a regular linear equation), so h has a simple zero at r0 and is nonzero on
both sides; since g(r0) = 0 and g is C^1, the constant ratio g/h on each side equals g'(r0)/h'(r0), so the constants
agree and linear uniqueness gives h = Y beyond r0, again contrary to maximality. Hence g = lambda h on (0, infinity)
with one lambda, and every positive zero of h is simple. Put p = L/N, which is positive and not an integer (L is odd, N
is even). On each component I of {h != 0}, (49.1) gives theta = C_I |h|^p. Since theta is not identically zero and the
zeros of h are isolated, C_I != 0 for some I. If I had a finite positive endpoint r0, then near r0 on that side theta =
C_I |v|^p |r - r0|^p with v smooth and v(r0) != 0, whose derivative of order floor(p) + 1 is unbounded, contrary to
smoothness. So I = (0, infinity) and h has no positive zero. Taylor expansion of Psi at the origin to degree N + 1 (a
homogeneous polynomial of degree j has frequencies j, j - 2, ..., so degrees below N and degree N + 1 contribute nothing
at frequency N) gives h = gamma r^N + O(r^{N+2}) and h' = N gamma r^{N-1} + O(r^{N+1}). Put f = h/r^N, so f(0) = gamma,
f' = O(r) and (r^{2N+1} f')' = -lambda r^{2N+1} f. If lambda = -a <= 0, then f'(r) = a r^{-2N-1} int_0^r s^{2N+1} f(s)
ds. If gamma = 0, then M_R = max_{[0,R]} |f| satisfies M_R <= a R^2 M_R/(4N + 4), so f = 0 near 0 and h = 0 by linear
uniqueness, a contradiction; replacing f by -f (the equation for f is linear) we may take gamma > 0, and then the
formula excludes a first zero of f and gives f >= gamma, i.e. h >= gamma r^N, contradicting h = o(r^2). If lambda > 0,
replace h by -h if necessary (the equation is linear) so that h > 0, and put v = r^{1/2} h, so v'' + [lambda - (N^2 -
1/4)/r^2] v = 0. On a tail where the bracket is at least a1 = lambda/2, w = v'/v satisfies w' <= -a1 - w^2, hence
(arctan(w/sqrt(a1)))' <= -sqrt(a1), which is impossible on an interval longer than pi/sqrt(a1).
Case L = 2N - 1. Then (V) at frequency 2N = L + 1 and (49.1) give
  L h' theta - N h theta' = 0,   N (h' g - h g')/r = theta' - L theta/r.                                (49.2)
Let I0 be a component of {theta != 0}. The first equation is linear and homogeneous in h on I0, so h is either nowhere
zero or identically zero on I0. In the second case the second equation gives theta = C r^L on I0, which does not vanish
at a finite positive endpoint, so I0 = (0, infinity) and h = 0, a contradiction. So there is a component I of {h != 0}
on which theta = C |h|^p with C != 0 and p = 2 - 1/N. Write h = e k and g = e j with e = +-1 and k = |h|. The second
equation of (49.2) becomes (j/k)' = p C [k^{-1/N} - (r/N) k^{-1-1/N} k'] = p C (r k^{-1/N})', so j/k = lambda + p C r
k^{-1/N} on I, and f = k/r^N satisfies on I
  f'' + (2N + 1) f'/r + lambda f + mu f^nu = 0,   f > 0,   nu = 1 - 1/N,   mu = p C != 0.             (49.3)
Tail. No positive solution of (49.3) on an interval (R1, infinity) tends to 0. Put J = r^{2N+1} f'. If mu > 0, then for
small f, lambda f + mu f^nu >= c f^nu with c > 0, so J' <= -c r^{2N+1} f^nu < 0; J cannot stay nonnegative (f would not
decrease to 0), so after some R2 >= R1, J < 0 and f decreases, and J(r) <= -(c/(2N + 2)) (r^{2N+2} - R2^{2N+2}) f(r)^nu
gives f' <= -c1 r f^nu for r >= 2 R2, so (f^{1-nu})' <= -(1 - nu) c1 r, contradicting f > 0. If mu < 0, then for small
f, J' >= c r^{2N+1} f^nu > 0, so J < 0 throughout (otherwise f eventually increases), f' < 0, and f'' >= c f^nu > 0; the
increasing negative f' tends to 0 (a negative limit would make f negative), and integrating f' f'' <= c f^nu f' to
infinity gives f'^2 >= (2c/(nu + 1)) f^{nu+1}, so f' <= -c2 f^{(nu+1)/2} with (nu + 1)/2 < 1, which forces f to vanish
in finite distance. Since h = o(r^2) gives f -> 0, I is bounded.
Endpoints. At a finite positive endpoint R of I, h(R) = 0, and h'(R) = 0, since otherwise theta = C |h|^p with 1 < p < 2
would not be C^2 at R; so f, f' -> 0 at R. The energy E = f'^2/2 + V(f), V(f) = lambda f^2/2 + mu f^{nu+1}/(nu + 1),
satisfies E' = -(2N + 1) f'^2/r. If I had two finite positive endpoints, E would tend to 0 at both, so E would be
constant and f' = 0 on I, a contradiction. So I = (0, R). Near R, J' = -r^{2N+1} (lambda f + mu f^nu) has the sign of
-mu and J(R) = 0. If mu > 0, then J > 0 to the left of R, so f increases to 0, which is impossible. So mu < 0, f' < 0
near R, V(f) <= -c3 f^{nu+1}, and E(r) >= E(R) = 0 gives -f' >= c4 f^{(nu+1)/2}; with b = (1 - nu)/2 = 1/(2N), (f^b)' <=
-b c4, so f(r) >= c5 (R - r)^{2N} for r < R near R. Hence h is not flat at R, and being smooth it is nonzero on (R, R +
delta) for some delta > 0. Let I2 be the component of {h != 0} with left endpoint R. By the first equation of (49.2),
theta is either nowhere zero or identically zero on I2. In the second case the second equation gives g = lambda2 h on
I2, and the linear equation with h(R) = h'(R) = 0 forces h = 0 on I2, a contradiction. So theta is nowhere zero on I2,
and the analysis of I applies to I2: its right endpoint is neither infinite (tail) nor finite (energy, since R > 0).
This contradiction proves (a).
Proof of (b). Let F = W.grad Omega + Omega. By the frequency rules above (beta r d_r preserves frequencies, and the
products of modes of frequencies n and k have frequencies n + k and |n - k|), F has only even sine frequencies at most
2N. For even m, sin(m phi) = cos(phi) p_{m-1}(sin phi) with p_{m-1} an odd polynomial of degree at most m - 1 (expand
Im (cos phi + i sin phi)^m and replace cos^2 by 1 - sin^2). Hence, with s = x^2 + y^2, there are smooth functions b_j on
(0, infinity) such that F = x sum_{j=0}^{N-1} b_j(s) y^{2j+1}. Put Q(s, y) = (1/2) sum_{j=0}^{N-1} y^{2j+1}
int_1^s b_j(t) dt. Then d_x [Q(x^2 + y^2, y)] = F = Theta_x by (V), and on each circle Q(r^2, y) has only odd sine
frequencies at most 2N - 1. So Theta - Q(x^2 + y^2, y) is independent of x on each horizontal half-line in {x > 0}, and
with the smooth odd function A(y) = Theta(1, y) - Q(1 + y^2, y),
  Theta(x, y) = Q(x^2 + y^2, y) + A(y)
for x > 0, for x < 0 by evenness and for x = 0, y != 0 by continuity. Substituting into (T),
  (beta y + U_2) A'(y) - (beta - 2) A(y) = (beta - 2) Q - W.grad Q =: B.                                   (49.4)
The term beta X.grad Q preserves frequencies, and U.grad Q = (Psi_r Q_phi - Psi_phi Q_r)/r has frequencies at most
N + 2N - 1, so on each circle |X| = r, B is an odd sine polynomial of frequency at most D = 3N - 1. Since sin(k phi) is
a polynomial of degree k in sin phi for odd k, B(sqrt(r^2 - y^2), y) = B_r(y) for |y| < r, with B_r a polynomial of
degree at most D. Next, U_2 = Psi_x has only odd sine frequencies at most N + 1, its coefficients are bounded by twice
sup_{|X| = r} |U| = o(r), and |sin(k phi)| <= k |y|/r; so U_2(sqrt(r^2 - y^2), y) -> 0 as r -> infinity, uniformly for
y in compact sets. Evaluating (49.4) at (sqrt(r^2 - y^2), y), the polynomials B_r converge pointwise to
P(y) = beta y A'(y) - (beta - 2) A(y). Evaluation at D + 1 fixed distinct points (an invertible Vandermonde system)
shows that the coefficients of B_r converge, so P is a polynomial of degree at most D, odd since A is odd. With
P = sum_{m odd} p_m y^m, the odd polynomial A0 = sum p_m y^m/(beta (m - 1) + 2) (every denominator is positive)
satisfies beta y A0' - (beta - 2) A0 = P, so a = A - A0 is smooth, odd and solves beta y a' = (beta - 2) a. On y > 0
this gives a = c y^{1 - 2/beta}, and a(y) = O(y) at 0 forces c = 0 because 1 - 2/beta < 1; by oddness a = 0. Thus A is
a polynomial of degree at most D, and Theta = Q + A has only odd sine frequencies at most 3N - 1 on every circle, with
coefficients smooth on (0, infinity). Since Theta is not identically zero, it has a largest frequency L with theta_L not
identically zero, and (a) applies. This proves (b).
Consequence. For an A2-broad profile the parities make the angular series of Psi and Theta sine series in the even,
respectively odd, frequencies, and U = o(|X|) uniformly (Section 2). Theta is not identically zero (a0 != 0). If Psi
were identically zero, then Omega = 0, (V) gives Theta_x = 0, and Theta(0, y) = 0 forces Theta = 0. So if the series of Psi were finite, h_N would be nonzero for its largest frequency N, which (b)
excludes; in particular the two series are not both finite. QED.

### Theorem 50 (beta > 2 under (H1): a unit-Jacobian linearization of the basin of P, the escape law of the orbit label, axis signs, a dual balance and sign changes of grad Theta)
Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta > 2 satisfying (H1) of Theorem 8. Put kappa = beta - 2,
lambda = beta + 2, h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h, p = lambda/kappa, d = 2 beta - 1, sigma = sgn(a0), A = Theta_y(P) (so
sgn A = sigma, Theorem 2(c)), eta = Theta/A, L_t = diag(e^{lambda t}, e^{kappa t}), and let w, T(x) = Theta_y(x, 0) (the
function f of Theorem 2),
v(y) = W_2(0, y) and E(y) = Theta_xx(0, y)/2 be the axis traces (Theorems 2, 27, 30). Let f, G be as in Theorem 41(b) and
R0, X0(alpha), F, d_inf as in Theorem 38. Q1 is the open first quadrant.
(a) (Linearization.) Every X with x > 0 has backward limit P, and no other point does. There is a C^1
    diffeomorphism Hc = (xi, eta) of {x > 0} onto R^2 with second component eta = Theta/A, Hc(P) = 0, DHc(P) = I,
    det DHc = 1 and Hc o Phi_t = L_t o Hc for all t. Hc is C^infinity off the x-axis, and on all of {x > 0} if p is
    not an even integer; xi is even in y, Hc maps Q1 onto {eta > 0}, and on the axis
      xi(x, 0) = A w(x) / (lambda T(x))   (x > 0),                                                         (50.1)
    which vanishes only at x1. Any C^1 map with these properties and the same second component coincides with Hc on
    Q1 up to xi -> xi + B eta^p (B a constant). (Conversely, xi + B |eta|^p gives such a C^1 map for every B; if p is
    not an even integer, it is smooth across the x-axis only for B = 0.)
(b) (Orbit label and escape law.) c = xi/eta^p is a C^infinity first integral on Q1; Z(c, s) := Hc^{-1}(c s^p, s)
    (c real, s > 0) is a C^infinity diffeomorphism of R x (0, infinity) onto Q1 with Phi_t Z(c, s) = Z(c, e^{kappa t} s)
    and dX = s^p dc ds. Every orbit in Q1 escapes; its escape angle phi(c) is a strictly decreasing C^infinity
    diffeomorphism of R onto (0, pi/2), and
      phi'(c) = -q (f(phi(c))/A)^{2/q}.                                                                      (50.2)
    In particular sigma f > 0 on (0, pi/2).
(c) (Axis signs.) sigma f'(0) > 0, sigma f''(pi/2) > 0 and sigma G'(pi/2) < 0. In particular sigma G > 0 on an interval
    (pi/2 - eps, pi/2). For an A2-broad profile with beta > 2, the conclusion sigma f'(0) > 0 requires, instead of
    (H1), only w != 0 on (x1, infinity); the conclusions sigma f''(pi/2) > 0 and sigma G'(pi/2) < 0, and the resulting
    interval sign of G, require only v > 0 on (0, infinity).
(d) (Dual balance.) With K0(X) = x y |X|^{-4}, the function phi_K(X) = int_0^infinity e^{d t} K0(Phi_t X) dt is finite,
    positive and continuous on Q1, satisfies (1 - 2 beta) phi_K - W.grad phi_K = K0 along orbits, phi_K Theta_x is
    absolutely integrable on Q1, and
      int_{Q1} phi_K Theta_x dX = int_{Q1} K0 Omega dX = (pi/2)(beta + 1).                                     (50.3)
(e) (Sign changes.) For every y > 0, x -> Theta_x(x, y) takes both signs on (0, infinity); for every x > 0,
    y -> Theta_y(x, y) takes both signs on (0, infinity).
(f) (Lyapunov function, a0 > 0.) If a0 > 0, the function Ly of Theorem 44(a) is proper (this holds for every A2-broad
    profile with beta > 2, without (H1) and for either sign of a0), strictly increasing along every
    nonstationary orbit, and its critical points are exactly O (a nondegenerate saddle, D^2 Ly(O) =
    d diag(-lambda, 3 beta + 2)) and +-P (nondegenerate minima, D^2 Ly(P) = diag(d lambda, d kappa + A)); Ly(O) = 0 and
    Ly(P) = d int_0^{x1} w(x) dx < 0.
Scope. These are necessary conditions on a hypothetical profile satisfying (H1). (H1) is a hypothesis, not proved
(Theorem 21(c) shows that Omega > 0 on Q1 implies it). The linearization changes coordinates for a given W; it does not
solve the coupled system. No contradiction between these necessary conditions is established here. Their angular sign
and parity requirements are consistent (for example f = sigma sin(phi) cos^2(phi) and G = sigma sin(2 phi) have the
parities and the signs of (b) and (c)); their simultaneous realization by an A2-broad profile satisfying the coupled
equations is not proved. Part (e) rules out a globally fixed sign of Theta_x or Theta_y on Q1, and neither the
representation Omega(X) = int_0^infinity e^{-s} Theta_x(Phi_{-s} X) ds of the Remark following Theorem 8 nor (50.3), by
itself, establishes Omega >= 0 throughout Q1. The positive balance (50.3) does imply Omega > 0 somewhere in Q1; for
a0 < 0 the origin jet and this balance force both signs, as in Theorem 21(a). The theorem is not a nonexistence
statement.
Remark 50.1. The basin statement on Q1 and the sign of Theta are Theorem 8(i),(ii), and Theorem 8(iii) already fixes
the second component eta; escape of every orbit in Q1 is Theorem 7 with W_r > 0 outside a disc; the second equality in
(50.3) is Theorem 9 with the decay of Theorem 41(a); an interval of angles with sigma G > 0 is in Theorem 41(b), and
(c) locates one adjacent to the y-axis (compare Theorem 31(b),(c)). New here are the global unit-Jacobian conjugacy,
the escape law (50.2), the three endpoint inequalities of (c), the dual weight phi_K with the first equality in (50.3),
the sign changes (e), and the classification in (f).

Proof. Throughout, backward orbits are bounded (proof of Theorem 1), W_r > 0 outside the disc of radius R0, and Q1, the
axes and the half-planes {x > 0}, {x < 0} are invariant.
(a) Under (H1), Theorem 8(i) gives backward limit P on Q1, and by reflection (x, y) -> (x, -y) on Q4. On the positive
x-axis w < 0 on (0, x1) (Theorem 2(a)) and w > 0 on (x1, infinity) (opening paragraph of the proof of Theorem 8), so
axis points tend backward to P. The y-axis and {x < 0} are invariant, so no other point tends to P. T has the sign
sigma on (0, x1] (Theorem 2(c)); on (x1, infinity), where w != 0, Theorem 2(b) is a regular homogeneous linear
equation, and its solution, which has the sign sigma just to the right of x1 by continuity, keeps that sign. So T has
the sign sigma on (0, infinity); this uses only w != 0 on (x1, infinity).
Local chart. Near P put u = x - x1 and s = eta(x, y); since eta_x(P) = 0 (Theta_x = 0 on the x-axis) and eta_y(P) = 1,
(u, s) are C^infinity coordinates on a neighbourhood V0 of P. Write the inverse as y = Y(u, s), shrink V0 so that
Y_s > 0, and put z(u, s) = int_0^u Y_s(t, s) dt. Then z_u = Y_s = 1/eta_y, so the Jacobian of (z, s) with respect to (x, y)
is z_u eta_y = 1, and D(z, s)(P) = I (z(0, s) = 0). In (z, s) the field has s-component kappa s (W.grad eta = kappa eta),
and, the change of variables having unit Jacobian, divergence 2 beta; hence its z-component Z1 satisfies d_z Z1 = lambda,
so Z1 = lambda z + b(s) with b C^infinity, b(0) = 0 (P is a zero) and b'(0) = 0 (DW(P) = diag(lambda, kappa), Theorem
2(d)). eta is odd in y, so Y is odd in s, z is even in s, and since the field is equivariant under y -> -y, b is even.
Shear. xi = z + g(s) gives W.grad xi = lambda xi if and only if kappa s g' - lambda g = -b. Take N > p, write
b = sum_{2 <= j <= N} b_j s^j + r_N with r_N = O(s^{N+1}) together with its derivatives in the usual Taylor sense, and
put g = sum_{j != p} b_j s^j/(lambda - j kappa) + g_p + g_R, where g_p = 0 unless p = j is an integer, in which case
g_p = -(b_p/kappa) s^p log|s|, and g_R(s) = -(1/kappa) int_0^1 t^{-p-1} r_N(t s) dt. Since d/dt [t^{-p} r_N(t s)] =
t^{-p-1} [t s r_N'(t s) - p r_N(t s)] and t^{-p} r_N(t s) -> 0 as t -> 0, g_R solves the equation with right side -r_N;
differentiation under the integral sign is valid at every order (the k-th s-derivative of r_N(t s) is
t^k r_N^{(k)}(t s), which on a compact s-interval is at most C t^{k + max(N + 1 - k, 0)} <= C t^{N + 1}, so the
differentiated integrand is O(t^{N - p}) with N - p > 0), so g_R is C^infinity. The monomial terms solve their equations directly (for g_p, kappa s g_p' - lambda g_p = -b_p s^p). So g is
even, g(0) = g'(0) = 0, g is C^infinity for s != 0, C^infinity at 0 unless p is an integer with b_p != 0, and C^1 in all
cases (p > 1, so s^p log|s| is C^1). If p is an odd integer, b_p = 0 since b is even. Hence Hloc = (z + g(s), s) is a
C^1 local diffeomorphism with determinant 1, DHloc(P) = I, conjugating the field to (lambda xi, kappa eta).
Globalization. W(P + Z') . Z' >= (kappa/2) |Z'|^2 for small Z' (DW(P) symmetric positive definite), so there is a ball V
around P contained in V0 with Phi_{-s}(V) contained in V for s >= 0. For x > 0, choose s >= 0 with Phi_{-s} X in V and put
Hc(X) = L_s Hloc(Phi_{-s} X); this is independent of s by the local conjugacy, satisfies Hc o Phi_t = L_t o Hc, and is C^1
with det DHc = e^{(lambda + kappa) s} e^{-2 beta s} = 1 (det D Phi_{-s} = e^{-2 beta s}); its second component is
e^{kappa s} eta(Phi_{-s} X) = eta(X). Hc is injective (move two points with equal image backward into V and use
injectivity of Hloc), its image is open, invariant under L_t for all t and contains a neighbourhood of 0, hence is R^2
(L_{-t} contracts every point into that neighbourhood). The inverse function theorem gives a C^1 inverse; regularity off
the axis, evenness of xi and Hc(Q1) = {eta > 0} (sigma Theta > 0 on Q1, Theorem 8(ii)) follow. On the axis, eta_x = 0
and eta_y = T/A, so det DHc = 1 gives xi_x = A/T, and W.grad xi = lambda xi gives w xi_x = lambda xi, that is (50.1).
Uniqueness. If (xi~, eta) is another such map, then on Q1 xi~ = xi + g~(eta) (unit Jacobian, same second component, so
d xi~/d xi = 1 in the coordinates (xi, eta)), and the conjugacy gives kappa eta g~' = lambda g~, so g~ = B eta^p on
{eta > 0}.
(b) In the coordinates (xi, eta) the flow is L_t, so c = xi/eta^p is invariant (lambda = p kappa), and
(c, s) -> (c s^p, s) is a C^infinity diffeomorphism of R x (0, infinity) onto {eta > 0} with Jacobian s^p; composing with
Hc^{-1} (unit Jacobian, C^infinity on Q1) gives the statements on Z. Every X in Q1 has Theta(X) != 0 (Theorem 8(ii)), so
its forward orbit is unbounded (Theorem 7), leaves the disc of radius R0 and escapes. Each orbit in Q1 meets the arc
{X0(alpha) : 0 < alpha < pi/2} exactly once (W_r > 0 on and outside the circle), so alpha -> c(X0(alpha)) is a bijection
of (0, pi/2) onto R. The tangent R0 e_phi of the arc and W at X0(alpha) have determinant det(W, R0 e_phi) = R0 W_r > 0;
in the coordinates (xi, eta), where W = (lambda xi, kappa eta) and xi = c eta^p, this determinant equals
lambda xi eta_alpha - kappa eta xi_alpha = -kappa eta^{p+1} c_alpha (using kappa p = lambda). Hence c_alpha < 0. By
Theorem 38(b), F' = (W_r(X0)/(beta R0)) e^{2 beta d_inf} and f(F(alpha)) = R0^{-q} e^{kappa d_inf} theta_0(alpha), with
theta_0 = A eta(X0). So, at c = c(X0(alpha)) and phi = F(alpha),
  phi'(c) = F'(alpha)/c_alpha = -(kappa/(beta R0^2)) eta^{p+1} e^{2 beta d_inf} = -q (f(phi)/A)^{2/q},
since (p + 1) = 2/q and (2/q) kappa = 2 beta. This is a C^1 bijection with negative derivative, and it is C^infinity because
the right side of (50.2) is a C^infinity function of phi (f is C^infinity, Theorem 42(b), and f/A > 0 on (0, pi/2) by
the displayed formula for f o F) and phi solves this autonomous equation.
(c) If w != 0 on (x1, infinity), T has sign sigma on (x1, infinity), by the argument in (a). Theorem 2(b) gives
T'/T = (w' - lambda)/w there, and by Theorem 42(a), w = beta x + O(x^{1-h}) and w' = beta + O(x^{-h}), so T'/T = -2h/x + O(x^{-1-h}), and
x^{2h} T(x) tends to a nonzero limit of sign sigma. By Theorem 42(b) (derivative of Theta - r^q f on the axis),
T(x) = x^{q-1} f'(0) + O(x^{q-1-h}) with q - 1 = -2h; so sigma f'(0) > 0. On the y-axis, by Theorem 27,
v E' = (2 v' - 3 beta - 2) E (the x^2 coefficient of equation (T)), and E = a0 y + O(y^3) at 0; if v > 0 on (0, infinity) (which
holds under (H1) by the opening paragraph of the proof of Theorem 8), E has sign sigma on
(0, infinity). With v = beta y + O(y^{1-h}) and v' = beta + O(y^{-h}) (Theorem 42(a)), E'/E = -(1 + 2h)/y + O(y^{-1-h}),
so y^{1+2h} E(y) tends to a nonzero limit C_y of sign sigma. Theorem 42(b) gives Theta_xx(0, y) = y^{q-2} (f''(pi/2) +
q f(pi/2)) + O(y^{q-2-h}), and f(pi/2) = 0, q - 2 = -1 - 2h, so f''(pi/2) = 2 C_y. For K(y) = Omega_x(0, y),
Theorem 30 gives v K' + (D - v') K = 2E with D = 2 beta + 1, and K = b0 y + O(y^3) with D b0 = 2 a0. Let
H0(y) = v(y) exp(-D int_1^y dt/v(t)) > 0, a solution of the homogeneous equation; since v = (3 beta + 2) y + O(y^3) at 0,
H0(y) ~ C0 y^{(beta + 1)/(3 beta + 2)} at 0, and since D/beta = 2 + h, H0(y) ~ C_inf y^{-1-h} at infinity (C0, C_inf > 0).
As K/H0 -> 0 at 0, variation of constants gives K(y) = H0(y) int_0^y 2E/(v H0) dt; the integrand has sign sigma, is
O(t^{-(beta + 1)/(3 beta + 2)}) at 0 and O(t^{-1-h}) at infinity, so y^{1+h} K(y) tends to a nonzero limit of sign sigma.
Theorem 42(b) gives K(y) = -y^{-1-h} G'(pi/2) + O(y^{-1-2h}) (d_x (r^{-h} G(phi)) = -y^{-1-h} G'(pi/2) on the positive
y-axis), so sigma G'(pi/2) < 0, and since G(pi/2) = 0, sigma G > 0 just below pi/2.
(d) For X in Q1 and t large, outside the disc of radius R0, d log|Phi_t X|/dt = W_r/r = beta + O(r^{-h}) and r grows at
least exponentially, so |Phi_t X| >= c_X e^{beta t}, locally uniformly in X (for a compact set of Q1 there is a
common time after which all its forward images lie outside the circle: by continuous dependence each point has a
neighbourhood that is outside at one finite time, a finite subcover gives a common time, and the exterior of the
circle is forward invariant). As 0 < K0 <= |X|^{-2}, the integrand is at most C e^{-t}: phi_K is finite, positive and
continuous, and phi_K(Phi_s X) = e^{-d s} (phi_K(X) - int_0^s e^{d t} K0(Phi_t X) dt) gives the equation along orbits.
Put B(Y) = int_0^infinity e^{-t} |Theta_x(Phi_{-t} Y)| dt. For |Y| <= 1 the backward orbit stays in the disc of radius
R0 (W_r > 0 outside), where |DW| <= M0 (M0 > 1) and |Theta_x| <= C; Theta_x(0) = 0 and |Phi_{-t} Y| <= e^{M0 t} |Y| give
|Theta_x(Phi_{-t} Y)| <= C min(e^{M0 t} |Y|, 1), and splitting at t = M0^{-1} log(1/|Y|) gives B(Y) <= C |Y|^{1/M0}. For
|Y| = r large, fix R* so large that W_r >= beta r/2, |U| <= C r^{1-h} and the bounds of Theorem 41(a) hold for
r >= R*, and let S be the backward time at which rho(t) = |Phi_{-t} Y| reaches R*. For 0 <= t <= S,
d log rho/dt = -beta + O(rho^{-h}) and int_0^S rho^{-h} dt <= (2/beta) int_{R*}^r u^{-h-1} du <= (2/(beta h)) R*^{-h}, so
C^{-1} r e^{-beta t} <= rho(t) <= C r e^{-beta t} and |S - h log(r/R*)| <= C, uniformly in Y; in particular
e^S <= C r^h and e^{-S} <= C r^{-h}. By Theorem 41(a), the part of B before S is at most
C r^{-2h} int_0^S e^{(2 beta h - 1) t} dt <= C r^{-2h} e^S <= C' r^{-h}, and the part after S is at most C e^{-S} <= C r^{-h}
(the backward orbit then stays in a fixed disc). B is bounded on compact sets. Hence K0 B is integrable on Q1.
By Tonelli and the change of variables Y = Phi_t X (Jacobian e^{2 beta t}, Phi_t(Q1) = Q1),
  int_{Q1} phi_K |Theta_x| dX = int_0^infinity e^{d t} e^{-2 beta t} int_{Q1} K0(Y) |Theta_x(Phi_{-t} Y)| dY dt
                             = int_{Q1} K0 B dY < infinity,
and the same computation with the signed integrand (Fubini) and Omega(Y) = int_0^infinity e^{-t} Theta_x(Phi_{-t} Y) dt
(Remark after Theorem 8; backward orbits are bounded) gives int_{Q1} phi_K Theta_x = int_{Q1} K0 Omega. K0 Omega is
absolutely integrable on R^2 (Omega = O(|xy|) at 0 since Omega is odd in x and in y, |Omega| <= C r^{-h} at infinity by
Theorem 41(a)), so the limit in Theorem 9 is the integral, int_{R^2} K0 Omega = pi (2 beta + 2), and K0 Omega is even in
x and in y, which gives (50.3).
(e) Fix y > 0. sigma Theta(x, y) > 0 for x > 0 (Theorem 8(ii)), Theta(0, y) = 0, and for x large, Theta(x, y) =
int_0^y Theta_y(x, t) dt is at most C y x^{-2h} in absolute value (Theorem 41(a)), so it tends to 0 as x -> infinity.
Choosing x' > 0 and then x'' > x' with sigma Theta(x'', y) < sigma Theta(x', y), the mean value theorem on [0, x'] and
[x', x''] gives points where sigma Theta_x > 0 and < 0. Fix x > 0. Theta(x, 0) = 0, and since Theta(0, t) = Theta_x(0, t) = 0,
|Theta(x, t)| = |int_0^x (x - s) Theta_xx(s, t) ds| <= C x^2 t^{-1-2h} for t large (Theorem 42(a) with k = 1); the same
argument gives both signs of Theta_y(x, .).
(f) For a0 > 0, y Theta >= 0 everywhere (Theta > 0 on Q1 by Theorem 8(ii), hence for y > 0, x != 0 by evenness in x;
Theta = 0 on the y-axis; Theta is odd in y). Theorem 44(a) gives W.grad Ly = d |W|^2 + kappa y Theta > 0 where W != 0, so Ly strictly increases on
nonstationary orbits. By (H1) and reflection, Z = {O, P, -P}. By the identity grad Ly = d W + Omega W^perp + y grad Theta
(proof of Theorem 44(d)), the critical points of Ly are zeros of W (where W != 0, W.grad Ly > 0), and each zero of W is
critical. Differentiating the identity, with (a (x) b)_ij = a_i b_j and J v = v^perp,
D^2 Ly = d DW + W^perp (x) grad Omega + Omega J DW + grad Theta (x) e_2 + y D^2 Theta. At O, W = Omega = grad Theta = 0 and
y = 0, so D^2 Ly(O) = d DW(0) = d diag(-lambda, 3 beta + 2). At P, W = Omega = 0, y = 0 and grad Theta = (0, A), so
D^2 Ly(P) = d DW(P) + A e_2 (x) e_2 = diag(d lambda, d kappa + A), positive definite (the second derivatives of Theta
are multiplied by y = 0); -P by reflection. On the x-axis, d_x Ly = d w (W^perp has no x-component
there and y = 0), and Ly(O) = 0 by the normalization of Theorem 44(a), so Ly(P) = d int_0^{x1} w < 0. By Theorems 41(a)
and 42(a), grad Ly = d beta X + O(r^{1-h}), so Ly = (d beta/2) |X|^2 + O(r^{2-h}) and Ly is proper; this growth
estimate uses neither (H1) nor the sign of a0. QED.

### Theorem 51 (beta = 2 under (S): a potential side of the strong unstable curve at the end of the arc, and no holomorphic continuation across the endpoint)
Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile, W = 2X + U, Z = {W = 0}, Q1 the open first quadrant, C, Q+, Q- as in
Theorem 16 and M = Theta(Q+). Assume (S) of Theorem 48 (Z cap Q1 = C cap Q1) and M != 0. By Theorem 16, DW(Q+) is
symmetric with eigenvalues 4 and 0; let e4 be a unit eigenvector for the eigenvalue 4. A local invariant curve through
Q+ is a regular embedded curve containing Q+ as an interior point to which W is tangent. A local C^infinity invariant
curve through Q+ tangent to e4 exists (the strong unstable curve, Step 1); fix any such curve Gamma. Identify X = (x, y)
with x + i y and put f = U_1 - i U_2.
(a) (A potential side.) Fix any local C^2 invariant centre curve K through Q+. There is an open disc B centred at Q+,
    contained in Q1, such that B \ Gamma has exactly two components B+ and B-, C cap B is contained in B- u {Q+}, and
    the branch of K opposite to C lies in B+ near Q+. Every point of B+ has backward limit Q+; Theta = M and Omega = 0
    on B+, and f is holomorphic on B+; every derivative of Theta - M and of Omega vanishes at every point of
    Gamma cap B.
(b) (No holomorphic continuation.) There is no holomorphic function g on a disc B' centred at Q+ with g = f on
    B+ cap B'.
(c) (No analytic strong unstable curve.) There is no local real-analytic invariant curve through Q+ tangent to e4.
The corresponding statements hold at Q- by the reflection R_y, with temperature -M.
Scope. These are necessary conditions on a hypothetical profile; neither (S) nor the existence of a profile satisfying
(S) is proved. Part (c) excludes an additional analyticity property of the transverse invariant curve; it does not
exclude a smooth profile satisfying (S) and M != 0. The hypotheses (S) and M != 0 may be replaced by
  (51.H1) Z = C in a neighbourhood of Q+, and
  (51.H2) no point of Z in the closed first quadrant outside C has temperature M;
only (51.H1) is local, and (51.H2) implies M != 0 because O lies in Z \ C with Theta(O) = 0. In a purely local
formulation the argument needs only the two equations near Q+, the spectrum of DW(Q+), the one-sided smooth zero arc C
ending at Q+, and a C^2 centre curve whose branch opposite to C is zero-free and outgoing; M may then be any real
number. Part (a) strengthens the local basin of Theorem 35(a) from a cuspidal region to a full side of a smooth
transverse invariant curve, with flatness along that curve beyond the endpoint flatness of Theorems 11 and 16. The
global invariant region and the angular plateau under (S) and M != 0 are already given by Theorem 48(d); no hypothesis
(R) is used here. Step 4 adapts the analytic continuation argument of step (e) of the proof of Theorem 16 to a field
defined on one side; that step needs neither (S) nor M != 0, and Theorem 17(a) excludes a globally real-analytic
velocity without these hypotheses. A one-sided neighbourhood does not contain a full disc about Q+, so (a) does not
contradict Theorem 16.

Proof. Step 0 (the outgoing branch). Theorem 16 gives Q+ in Q1 and the smooth arc C ending at Q+, with Theta - M and
Omega flat at Q+; so Omega(Q+) = 0, DW(Q+) is symmetric, and its eigenvalues are 4 and 0. Since Q+ is in the open set
Q1, (S) gives Z = C on a disc about Q+, which is (51.H1). Every zero of W in the closed first quadrant outside C lies on
an axis, where Theta = 0 (Theta is odd in y and Theta(0, y) = 0), so none has temperature M != 0, which is (51.H2).
Local C^2 centre curves of Q+ exist (centre manifold theorem, as in Theorems 22 and 35). Such a curve contains every
nearby zero of W: in a C^2 chart straightening it to {z = 0}, the normal component of W is z a(s, z) with a continuous
and a(0, 0) = 4, so a != 0 near Q+ and zeros have z = 0. In particular it contains the terminal part of C. By (51.H1)
its branch opposite to C contains no zero near Q+, so the flow on it has one direction. If that direction were towards
Q+, a nonstationary orbit in Q1 would have forward limit Q+, and Theorem 22 would give a zero outside C in the closed
first quadrant with temperature M, contrary to (51.H2). So every such branch is outgoing.

Step 1 (a smooth strong unstable curve). Translate Q+ to 0 and use orthonormal coordinates (u, v) along (e4, e0), where
e0 is a unit eigenvector for the eigenvalue 0. Then
  du/dt = 4u + P(u, v),   dv/dt = R(u, v),
with P, R and their first derivatives zero at 0. Multiplying by a smooth cutoff supported in a small ball, extend P and
R to C^infinity functions on R^2 with all derivatives bounded and with Lipschitz constant L < 1 in the maximum norm (P,
R = O(|(u, v)|^2) and DP, DR = O(|(u, v)|), so the cutoff contributes O(r) to the first derivatives when its support has
radius r). Let E be the Banach space of continuous paths X(t) = (u(t), v(t)), t <= 0, with
  ||X||_E = sup_{t <= 0} e^{-2t} max(|u(t)|, |v(t)|) < infinity,
and for real a consider the map T_a on E,
  (T_a X)_u(t) = e^{4t} a - int_t^0 e^{4(t - r)} P(X(r)) dr,   (T_a X)_v(t) = int_{-infinity}^t R(X(r)) dr.
Since int_t^0 e^{4(t - r)} e^{2r} dr <= e^{2t}/2 and int_{-infinity}^t e^{2r} dr = e^{2t}/2, T_a maps E to E and is a
contraction with constant at most L/2; its fixed point X_a satisfies ||X_a||_E <= |a|/(1 - L/2). The map (a, X) -> T_a X
is C^infinity on R x E: its j-th derivative in X applies the same integral operators to bounded derivatives of P or R
times j increments, each bounded by its norm times e^{2r}, and e^{2jr} <= e^{2r} for r <= 0. Since its derivative in X
has norm at most L/2 < 1, the implicit function theorem in Banach spaces gives that a -> X_a is C^infinity. The fixed
path solves the differential equations, has u_a(0) = a and tends to 0 as t -> -infinity; for small a it stays in the
ball where the extended field equals W. Hence a -> (a, v_a(0)) is a C^infinity embedded curve through 0, tangent to e4
(the derivative at a = 0 is the path (e^{4t}, 0)). For t0 < 0 the shifted path X_a(. + t0) is the fixed point of T_{a'}
with a' = u_a(t0), so X_a(t0) lies on the curve: the curve is backward invariant; W is tangent to it, and uniqueness for
the differential equation gives local forward invariance. Uniqueness of this curve is not used below; the argument
applies to any Gamma as in the statement.

Step 2 (coordinates). Orient e0 so that C leaves Q+ in the direction -e0 (C is tangent to the kernel of DW(Q+):
differentiate W = 0 along C). Choose C^infinity coordinates (s, v) centred at Q+ with Gamma = {s = 0} and with e0 mapped
to a positive multiple of d/ds. The C^2 curve K is a graph v = h(s) with h(0) = h'(0) = 0; put z = v - h(s). In the C^2
chart (s, z), Gamma = {s = 0}, K = {z = 0}, C = {z = 0, s <= 0} near Q+, and the outgoing branch is {z = 0, s > 0}. In
the chart (s, v), invariance of Gamma and Hadamard's lemma give ds/dt = s Bt(s, v) with Bt of class C^infinity. Hence
  ds/dt = s B(s, z),   dz/dt = z A(s, z),                                                                   (51.1)
with B(s, z) = Bt(s, z + h(s)); the z-component of the field is C^1 and vanishes on K, so A is continuous, and A(0, 0) =
4 because the z-direction at Q+ is the direction of Gamma. On a closed box {|s| <= delta, |z| <= eps0}, A >= 2 and |B(s,
z) - B(s, 0)| <= K0 |z| for a constant K0 >= 0 (Bt is Lipschitz in its second variable). By Step 0, B(s, 0) > 0 for 0 <
s <= delta.

Step 3 (part (a)). Choose 0 < eps < eps0 with exp(K0 eps/2) < 2 and put D = {0 < s < delta/2, |z| < eps}. For a backward
orbit from (s0, z0) in D, with tau = -t and while the orbit is in the box, |z(tau)| <= |z0| e^{-2 tau} and
  d log s/d tau = -B(s, z) <= -B(s, 0) + K0 |z| <= K0 |z0| e^{-2 tau},
so 0 < s(tau) <= s0 exp(K0 |z0|/2) < delta (s cannot reach 0, since {s = 0} is invariant). These strict bounds exclude
an exit from the box, so the orbit stays in it for all tau >= 0. Put I(tau) = K0 int_0^tau |z| and q = s e^{-I}; then
dq/d tau <= -q B(s, 0) <= 0 and I has a finite limit, so s has a limit l >= 0. If l > 0, then B(s, 0) >= c > 0 for large
tau, and since z -> 0, d log s/d tau <= -c/2 eventually, a contradiction. So every point of D has backward limit Q+. The
backward saturation E0 = union_{tau >= 0} Phi_{-tau}(D) is open and all its points have backward limit Q+; Theta is
constant on orbits and continuous, so Theta = M on E0 and Theta_x = 0 there. By (V), Omega(Phi_{-tau} X) = e^tau
Omega(X) for X in D; the left side is bounded, so Omega = 0 on D. Choose an open disc B centred at Q+, contained in Q1
and in the chart, so small that Gamma cap B is a single arc crossing B and B cap {s > 0} is contained in D. Then B \
Gamma has the components B+ = B cap {s > 0} and B- = B cap {s < 0}, and the positions of C and K follow from Step 2. On
B+, Theta = M and Omega = 0; every derivative of these smooth functions vanishes on B+, hence by continuity on Gamma cap
B. Finally div U = 0 and Omega = d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = 0 give d_x U_1 = -d_y U_2 and d_y U_1 = d_x U_2, the Cauchy-Riemann
equations for f = U_1 - i U_2. (B+ need not be backward invariant; its backward orbits are controlled in the larger
box.)

Step 4 (part (b)). Suppose g is holomorphic on a disc B' centred at Q+, B' contained in B, with g = f on B+ cap B'. Put
Wa = 2X + (Re g, -Im g), a real-analytic field on B'. Then Wa = W on B+ cap B', so every derivative of W - Wa vanishes
at Q+ and |W - Wa|(X) <= C_n |X - Q+|^n for every n near Q+; in particular DWa(Q+) = DW(Q+). In the coordinates (u, v)
of Step 1, d_u Wa_u(0) = 4, and the analytic implicit function theorem gives {Wa_u = 0} = {u = k(v)} near 0 and Wa_u(u,
v) = a(u, v)(u - k(v)), with k and a real analytic, k(0) = k'(0) = 0 and a(0, 0) = 4. By the smooth implicit function
theorem for W_u and the endpoint structure of C (step (ii) of the proof of Theorem 11, and Theorem 16), C is near Q+ the
set {(c(v), v) : v <= 0} with c smooth, c(0) = c'(0) = 0. On C, W = 0 and |(c(v), v)| <= C |v|, so for every n and v <=
0 near 0, |Wa(c(v), v)| <= C_n |v|^n, and |c(v) - k(v)| = |Wa_u(c(v), v)|/|a(c(v), v)| <= C_n' |v|^n. The real-analytic
function g0(v) = Wa_v(k(v), v) satisfies |g0(v)| <= |Wa_v(c(v), v)| + L0 |c(v) - k(v)| <= C_n'' |v|^n for v <= 0, with
L0 a bound for d_u Wa_v; a first nonzero Taylor coefficient of g0 of order m is impossible (take n = m + 1 and v -> 0-),
so g0 = 0 on (-v0, v0) and Wa = 0 on {(k(v), v) : |v| < v0}. Near Q+, Gamma is a graph v = gam(u) with gam(u) = O(u^2),
and k(v) = O(v^2), so v - gam(k(v)) = v + O(v^4) > 0 for small v > 0; the side {v > gam(u)} is B+, since it contains the
outgoing branch of K, which leaves Q+ in the direction e0. So for small v > 0 the point Y_v = (k(v), v) is in B+ cap B',
hence in Q1 and not on C, and W(Y_v) = Wa(Y_v) = 0. This contradicts (51.H1).

Step 5 (part (c)). Suppose Gamma' is a local real-analytic invariant curve through Q+ tangent to e4. It is C^infinity,
so Steps 2 to 4 apply to Gamma' and give a disc B, the side B+ and part (b) for Gamma'. Let gamma be a regular
real-analytic parametrization of Gamma' with gamma(0) = Q+. It extends holomorphically to a disc Delta = {|zeta| < rho}
with gamma' != 0, and is a biholomorphism of Delta onto a neighbourhood N of Q+ contained in B, mapping (-rho, rho) onto
Gamma' cap N. The images of the two half-discs are connected, disjoint from Gamma' and lie on different sides of it;
replacing gamma(zeta) by gamma(-zeta) if necessary, the upper half-disc Delta+ is mapped onto N cap B+. Put gamma*(zeta)
= conj(gamma(conj zeta)), holomorphic on Delta, and on Delta+
  Hf(zeta) = gamma'(zeta) f(gamma(zeta)) + 2 gamma'(zeta) gamma*(zeta),                                    (51.2)
which is holomorphic on Delta+ and continuous up to (-rho, rho). With w = W_1 + i W_2 = 2X + conj(f) (X = x + i y), for
real t one has Hf(t) = gamma'(t) conj(w(gamma(t))); tangency of W to Gamma' means w(gamma(t)) = alpha(t) gamma'(t) with
alpha(t) real, so Hf(t) = alpha(t) |gamma'(t)|^2 is real. By the Schwarz reflection principle (with continuous real
boundary values; Morera's theorem), Hf extends holomorphically to Delta. Then g = (Hf o gamma^{-1})/(gamma' o
gamma^{-1}) - 2 gamma* o gamma^{-1} is holomorphic on N and equals f on gamma(Delta+) = N cap B+. For a disc B' centred
at Q+ and contained in N, B+ cap B' = gamma(Delta+) cap B', so g on B' contradicts (b) for Gamma'. The statements at Q-
follow by applying R_y. QED.

Remark 51.1 (independently checked). Taylor identities at the endpoint do not decide the configuration. The following
local example realizes a one-sided zero arc, either orientation of the centre branch and a potential cone, and satisfies
every Taylor identity of the two equations at the endpoint; it does not satisfy (V) on any neighbourhood of the
endpoint, has no potential side as in part (a), and is not an A2-broad profile. At the origin, let chi be an even smooth
function with chi = 1 on [-1/4, 1/4] and chi = 0 outside (-1/2, 1/2), let e = 1 or e = -1, let M be real, F(y) =
-exp(-1/y^2) for y < 0 and F(y) = 0 for y >= 0, and q(x, y) = -e chi(x/y) Im exp(-1/(y - i x)^2) for y > 0, q = 0 for y
<= 0. Put Psi = -2xy + q, U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x), W = 2X + U = (4x - q_y, q_x), Omega = -Lap q and Theta = M + F(y). On the
support of q, |x| <= y/2 and Re (y - i x)^{-2} = (y^2 - x^2)/(y^2 + x^2)^2 >= 12/(25 y^2), so every derivative of q is
O(y^{-N} exp(-12/(25 y^2))); hence all fields are smooth near 0, DW(0) = diag(4, 0), and Theta - M and Omega are flat
at 0. Exactly, div W = 4 and W.grad Theta = 0 (W_2 = 0 for y < 0, F' = 0 for y >= 0), and Theta_x = 0. As q is odd in x and
3 <= d_x W_1 <= 5 on a small disc, the zero set of W there is {x = 0, y <= 0}, with W_2(0, y) = 2 e y^{-3} exp(-1/y^2)
for y > 0: the branch {x = 0, y > 0} is outgoing for e = 1 and incoming for e = -1. On the zero arc, F'(y) = -2 y^{-3}
exp(-1/y^2) > 0, so the temperature is regular and strictly monotone there. On the cone {y > 0, |x| < y/4}, W =
grad(2x^2 + e Re exp(1/z^2)) with z = x + i y, so Theta = M, Omega = 0 and both equations hold there, as they do for y <
0 and outside the support of chi(x/y). The residual Rv = W.grad Omega + Omega - Theta_x of (V) is flat at 0 but does not
vanish on any neighbourhood of 0: Omega is supported in {y > 0, 1/4 <= |x|/y <= 1/2}; on a small disc, W_1/x >= 3, |W_2|
<= y and |W| <= 6|X|, so along an orbit in this region d log(|x|/y)/dt >= 2, and an orbit starting there within radius r
e^{-6} reaches |x|/y = 1/2, where Omega = 0, in time at most (log 2)/2 inside radius r. If Rv = 0 on the disc of radius
r, then dOmega/dt = -Omega along orbits, so Omega = 0 on the disc of radius r e^{-6}; then q is harmonic there and
vanishes for y < 0, so q = 0, contradicting q_x(0, y) != 0 for y > 0. For the same reason (q is not harmonic on any disc
about 0) Omega is nonzero at points arbitrarily close to 0 in {y > 0, 1/4 <= |x|/y <= 1/2}, which near 0 lies on the
side containing the centre branch of every curve through 0 tangent to the x-axis.

### Theorem 52 (beta > 2: axis characterization of (H1) and nonflatness when all zeros are nondegenerate)
