Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta > 2, kappa = beta - 2, W = beta X + U, and Phi_t the flow
of W. Let P = (x1, 0) be the first positive zero of W on the x-axis (Theorem 2), put Z = {W = 0}, and let K be the set
of points whose forward orbits are bounded.

(a) K is nonempty, compact, connected and invariant under Phi_t for every real t. Moreover, Z is contained in K and
    Theta = 0 on K.

(b) Hypothesis (H1) of Theorem 8 holds if and only if W has no zero on {(x, 0) : x > x1} and no zero on {(0, y) : y >
    0}. In this case, K = [-x1, x1] x {0} and Z = {O, P, -P}.

(c) If DW(Q) is invertible at every Q in Z, then Theta is not flat at any point of Z. Consequently, if Theta is flat at
    some zero, then Z contains a zero Q' with det DW(Q') = 0. If the flat zero is hyperbolic, Q' is a different zero.

Scope. Part (b) reduces (H1), which concerns the closed first quadrant, to two axis conditions; it does not prove those
conditions. Under boundedness of {X in Q1 : sgn(a0) Omega(X) < 0} and nondegeneracy of every zero of W in the closed
first quadrant, Theorem 77 proves the first condition, and the second when beta is irrational or has odd reduced
numerator. Theorems 27 and 30 impose further restrictions under their stated simplicity and consecutiveness hypotheses.
No general exclusion or realization of further axis zeros for the coupled profile equations is asserted here. Part (a),
apart from Theta = 0 on K, uses only smoothness, beta > 0, U = o(|X|) uniformly and W(O) = 0. Part (c) does not exclude
flat hyperbolic zeros when a degenerate zero is present. No strain hypothesis or numerical input is used.

Proof. (a) Choose R0 > 0 so that

  X.W(X) >= (beta/2)|X|^2  for |X| >= R0.

Sublinear growth of U also gives |W(X)| <= C(1 + |X|), so the smooth flow is defined for all real times and each Phi_t
is a diffeomorphism. Let D = {|X| <= R0}. Strict outward pointing on its boundary prevents a forward orbit in {|X| >=
R0} from entering {|X| < R0}. Consequently, if |Phi_t0 X| >= R0, then

  |Phi_t X|^2 >= |Phi_t0 X|^2 exp(beta(t - t0))  for t >= t0.

Such a forward orbit is unbounded. Therefore

  K = {X : Phi_t X in D for every t >= 0}
    = intersection_{t >= 0} Phi_{-t}(D).

The outward boundary condition makes D invariant under the backward flow. For s,t >= 0,

  Phi_{-s}(D) is contained in D,
  Phi_{-(t+s)}(D) is contained in Phi_{-t}(D).

Each Phi_{-t}(D) is compact and connected and contains O. Their intersection is nonempty, compact and connected. For
completeness, monotonicity allows the intersection to be taken over integer times. If it had two disjoint nonempty
compact pieces, choose disjoint open neighbourhoods of those pieces. Compactness and nesting would force some
Phi_{-n}(D) to lie in their union while meeting both, contradicting its connectedness.

A finite time shift preserves boundedness of a forward orbit: for a negative shift only a compact finite orbit segment
is added. Thus Phi_s(K) = K for every real s. Every zero has a constant orbit, so Z is contained in K. Finally, (T)
gives

  Theta(Phi_t X) = exp(kappa t) Theta(X).

For X in K the left side is bounded for t >= 0. Since kappa > 0, Theta(X) = 0.

(b) Hypothesis (H1) immediately implies the two axis conditions.
For the converse, assume those conditions and write

  w(x) = W_1(x, 0),  v(y) = W_2(0, y),  T(x) = Theta_y(x, 0).

The axes are invariant. Theorem 2 gives w < 0 on (0, x1), w'(x1) = beta + 2 > 0, and T(x) of the strict sign of a0 on
(0, x1], including at x1. The absence of further positive x-axis zeros then gives w > 0 on (x1, infinity). The origin
strain identity gives v'(0) = 3 beta + 2 > 0, and the absence of positive y-axis zeros gives v > 0 on (0, infinity).

Put S = [-x1, x1] x {0}. The scalar flow x' = w(x) leaves [0, x1] invariant, and reflection gives S contained in K. An
orbit starting at (x, 0) with x > x1 is increasing on that axis. If bounded, its coordinate would converge to a zero of
w greater than x1, which is impossible. The same argument applies on the positive y-axis, and reflection handles the
negative axes. Thus

  K intersect ({x = 0} union {y = 0}) = S.

Near O, smoothness, evenness in x, oddness in y and Theta(0, y) = 0 give, by repeated division by the vanishing
coordinates,

  Theta(x, y) = x^2 y k(x, y),  k(0, 0) = a0 != 0.

After shrinking this neighbourhood, k has no zero there, so the only temperature zeros there lie on the axes. At every
(x, 0) in S other than O,

  Theta(x, y) = y H(x, y),
  H(x, y) = integral_0^1 Theta_y(x, tau y) dtau,
  H(x, 0) = T(|x|) != 0.

Continuity makes H nonzero in a neighbourhood of each such point, including P and -P. Hence there is an open set V
containing S such that {Theta = 0} intersect V is contained in the axes.

Since S is compact, choose a bounded open neighbourhood N of S with closure(N) contained in V. Part (a) and the axis
calculation give

  K intersect closure(N) = S.

In particular S is both open and closed relative to K. Equivalently, K is the union of the disjoint closed sets S and K
\ N. Connectedness and S != empty imply K = S. By the first-zero property of P and reflection, the only zeros of W on S
are O, P and -P. Since Z is contained in K, this proves (H1) and the asserted identities.

(c) The set Z is closed and contained in compact K. Invertibility of
DW at each zero makes every zero isolated, so Z is finite. By Theorem 43(a), DW has real eigenvalues at every zero, with
sum 2 beta > 0. They are nonzero under the present hypothesis, so every zero is a hyperbolic source or a hyperbolic
saddle.

Fix X in K \ Z and write X(t) = Phi_t X. By (a) its entire orbit lies in K and Theta(X(t)) = 0. Theorem 44(a) gives

  d/dt Ly(X(t)) = (2 beta - 1)|W(X(t))|^2.

Boundedness of Ly on K implies that |W(X(t))|^2 is integrable over [0, infinity). Its derivative is

  d/dt |W(X(t))|^2 = 2 W(X(t)).DW(X(t)) W(X(t)),

which is bounded on K. A nonnegative integrable function with bounded derivative tends to zero: otherwise uniform
continuity supplies disjoint intervals of uniformly positive length on which it is bounded below by a fixed positive
number. Thus W(X(t)) -> 0.

The omega-limit set is a nonempty connected compact subset of the finite set Z, so it is a single zero Q_+. Compactness
then gives X(t) -> Q_+. The stable manifold of a hyperbolic source is just the source, so Q_+ is a saddle. Every such
orbit is one of the two nonstationary branches of the stable manifold of its forward saddle. Each branch is one complete
orbit: on a local one-dimensional stable branch the vector field has no zero, and all its points are related by finite
flow times. Consequently K \ Z consists of finitely many complete orbits, at most two for each saddle.

Theorem 44(b) gives a backward limit Q_- in Z for each of these orbits. The stable and unstable manifold theorem gives
exponential convergence to Q_+ in forward time and to Q_- in backward time, with possibly different positive rates. The
closure of each orbit is exactly that orbit together with its two endpoints, and is compact. The endpoints are distinct
because Ly increases strictly along a nonstationary orbit.

Fix one such orbit. For m >= 0 let J_m be the vector of all partial derivatives of Theta of order at most m. For a
multi-index alpha, differentiating (T) gives

  W.grad(partial^alpha Theta)
    = kappa partial^alpha Theta
      - sum_{0 < nu <= alpha} binom(alpha, nu)
          (partial^nu W).grad(partial^(alpha-nu) Theta).

Every derivative of Theta in the sum has order at most |alpha|. Thus, along the orbit,

  d/dt J_m(X(t)) = B_m(X(t)) J_m(X(t)).

The coefficients involve derivatives of W of order at most m and are bounded on the compact orbit closure. In a fixed
induced operator norm, put C_m = sup_t ||B_m(X(t))||. The evolution operator E_m(s,t), mapping data at time t to time s,
satisfies

  ||E_m(s,t)|| <= exp(C_m |s-t|)

for both time directions, by Gronwall's inequality.

Suppose Theta is flat at either endpoint E. Exponential convergence in the corresponding time direction gives

  |X(t) - E| <= A exp(-c |t|)

for all sufficiently large |t| in that direction, with c > 0. For fixed m and every integer n >= 1, Taylor's theorem and
flatness give

  |J_m(Y)| <= C_{m,n} |Y - E|^n

near E. Therefore, after absorbing A^n into the constant,

  |J_m(X(t))| <= C'_{m,n} exp(-n c |t|),
  |J_m(X)| <= C'_{m,n} exp((C_m - n c)|t|).

Choose n with n c > C_m and let t tend to the chosen endpoint. Then J_m(X) = 0. Uniqueness for the linear system makes
J_m vanish at every finite point of the orbit. Since m is arbitrary, Theta is flat along the orbit and, by continuity of
each derivative, at its other endpoint.

Let F be the subset of Z at which Theta is flat. Each of the finitely many nonstationary orbits has both endpoints in F
or both in Z \ F. Let K_F be F together with the closures of the orbits whose endpoints lie in F, and let K_N be Z \ F
together with the closures of the remaining orbits. These are finite unions of compact sets. They are disjoint and cover
K. The prescribed origin jet gives

  partial_x^2 partial_y Theta(O) = 2 a0 != 0,

so O belongs to K_N. Connectedness of K forces K_F to be empty. Hence F is empty. QED.

Remark 52.1 (consequences, independently checked). By part (b) and Theorem 13, the following are equivalent for beta >
2: (H1); Theta has the strict sign of a0 throughout the open first quadrant; W has no zero on {(x, 0) : x > x1} and none
on {(0, y) : y > 0}. Consequently a nonempty additional zero set cannot lie entirely off the axes. In particular, a
configuration consisting only of one additional source and one additional saddle in the open first quadrant and their
reflections is excluded.

The associated axis segments can be specified without any nondegeneracy assumption on the additional zeros. If w has a
zero after x1, let

  x2 = min{x > x1 : w(x) = 0}.

This minimum exists because w'(x1) > 0 leaves a zero-free interval immediately after x1 and the zero set is compact. On
(x1, x2) one has w > 0. Every point there moves monotonically to x2 in forward time: uniqueness prevents crossing x2,
and any smaller limiting coordinate would be another zero. Thus [x1, x2] x {0} is contained in K. If v has a positive
zero, define

  y1 = min{y > 0 : v(y) = 0}.

The same argument, using v'(0) > 0, gives {0} x [0, y1] contained in K. If (H1) fails, at least one of these two cases
occurs; if both axis conditions fail, both segments occur. Their temperatures vanish by (a), also directly by the A2
axis conditions.

Assume every positive zero of v is simple. If beta is irrational or beta = p/r in lowest terms with p and r both odd,
Theorem 30(c) excludes positive zeros of v. Under these hypotheses, (H1) holds if and only if w has no zero on (x1,
infinity).

Finally, a dead zone arising from a flat hyperbolic source as in Theorem 43(d) requires a distinct degenerate zero
somewhere in Z. No location for that degenerate zero, and no converse existence statement, is asserted.

### Theorem 53 (beta = 2: zero components, connections and endpoint direction)

Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile. Put W = 2X + U, Z = {W = 0}, Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, and Crit = {grad
Theta = 0}. Let P = (x1,0) be the first positive zero of W_1(x,0), let C be its component in Z, let Q+ and Q- be the
endpoints of C, and put M = Theta(Q+). Write R_x(x,y) = (-x,y), R_y(x,y) = (x,-y), and Phi_t for the flow of W. Let H, G
and the exit-angle maps be as in Theorem 36. In particular,

  div W = 4,    d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = Omega,
  W.grad Theta = 0,    W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x.       (53.1)

At an endpoint of a zero arc, call the opposite branch of a local invariant centre curve outgoing or incoming according
as its forward flow points away from or towards the endpoint. These terms require that branch to be zero-free
sufficiently near the endpoint. Otherwise the endpoint is accumulating. A component is isolated if some neighbourhood
meets Z in precisely that component.

(a) Every nontrivial component of Z is a compact smooth embedded arc. Its tangent is ker DW, and the eigenvalues of DW
on it are 0 and 4. Every regular zero, meaning a zero outside Crit, is interior to its component. Theta is strictly
monotone on each connected regular subarc.

At every endpoint Q, Theta-Theta(Q) and Omega vanish to infinite order. Theta is not constant, and Omega does not vanish
identically, on any full neighbourhood of Q.

Every singleton component is critical. If its point has spectrum {0,4}, Theta-Theta(Q) and Omega are flat there. A
singleton component need not be isolated; if it is not isolated, its spectrum is {0,4}.

An arc meeting an axis is either contained in that axis or crosses it exactly once, transversely, at an interior point.
In the crossing case reflection interchanges its endpoints. No arc meets both axes.

(b) Let gamma be a nonstationary orbit in Q1 with backward limit A and finite forward limit B. Then

  Theta(A) = Theta(B),

  Ly(B)-Ly(A)
    = 3 int_{-infinity}^{infinity} |W(Phi_t X)|^2 dt > 0,
    X in gamma.                                             (53.2)

Here Ly is the function of Theorem 44, and the integral is finite. The limits belong to distinct components of Z. At
most one connecting orbit joins any fixed unordered pair of distinct components.

If one limit belongs to C, the component containing the other limit is wholly contained in Q1. Consequently, an incoming
Q+ requires a component D wholly contained in Q1 and a point A in D satisfying

  Theta(A) = M,    Ly(A) < Ly(Q+).                            (53.3)

The point A is the actual backward limit of the incoming orbit. If A is regular, M is an interior temperature value on D
and on Q1. If A is critical, the entire connecting orbit lies in Crit and Omega vanishes on it. No assumption M != 0 is
used.

(c) Suppose zeros outside C accumulate at Q+. There are pairwise distinct components D_n^-, D_n^+ wholly contained in
Q1, points A_n in D_n^- and B_n in D_n^+, and zero-free intervals of one local invariant centre curve which, oriented by
the flow, are complete orbits from A_n to B_n. They satisfy

  max_{X in D_n^- union D_n^+} |X-Q+| -> 0,

  Theta(A_n) = Theta(B_n) = m_n -> M,

  Ly(A_n) < Ly(B_n),
  Ly(A_n), Ly(B_n) -> Ly(Q+).                                (53.4)

Both limits and every point of each connecting orbit are critical, and Omega vanishes on each orbit. For every integer
k >= 1, there is C_k such that, for sufficiently large n,

  |m_n-M| <= C_k max(|A_n-Q+|, |B_n-Q+|)^k.                   (53.5)

No equality m_n = M or ordering of either Ly endpoint value relative to Ly(Q+) is asserted.

(d) If no component of Z is wholly contained in Q1, Q+ is outgoing. In particular, assume

  (S) Z cap Q1 = C cap Q1.                                  (53.6)

Then Q+ and Q- are outgoing for every real M, and every nonstationary orbit in Q1 escapes to infinity in forward time.

All conclusions of Theorem 35 at Q+ hold. Arbitrarily small neighbourhoods contain an open backward invariant set whose
backward orbits tend to Q+. Its forward saturation is open, connected, invariant, contained in Q1, and of infinite area,
with Theta = M and Omega = 0. On this saturation U is harmonic and real analytic. There is a nonempty open interval of
angles on which H = M and G = 0.

All conclusions of Theorem 51 at Q+ also hold. A smooth local strong unstable curve Gamma exists. For any such curve and
any local C^2 invariant centre curve, a sufficiently small disc B in Q1 has two sides B+ and B- separated by Gamma. The
terminal zero arc lies in B- union {Q+}, and the opposite centre branch lies in B+. Every point of B+ has backward limit
Q+; Theta = M and Omega = 0 there. All derivatives of Theta-M and Omega vanish on Gamma cap B.

The function f = U_1-i U_2 is holomorphic on B+, has no holomorphic extension to a disc about Q+ agreeing with it on
that side, and no real-analytic local invariant curve through Q+ is tangent to the eigenvector for 4. The reflected
conclusions hold at Q- with temperature -M.

(e) A terminal zero subarc on which Theta is constant cannot have an outgoing endpoint. Hence an isolated
constant-temperature arc component has two incoming endpoints.

(f) Let D be an isolated arc component. Give each endpoint the sign eps_i = +1 for outgoing and eps_i = -1 for incoming.
Then

  ind(D) = (eps_1+eps_2)/2.                                  (53.7)

The same formula applies at an isolated zero with spectrum {0,4}, using its two centre half-branches. Hyperbolic sources
have index +1 and hyperbolic saddles have index -1. In particular, the isolated constant-temperature arcs in (e) have
index -1.

A component accumulated by other components has no individual index defined by a zero-free boundary isolating that
component alone.

Suppose Z has finitely many components. Put eps = ind(C). Let I_Q be the sum of the indices of components wholly in Q1.
Let I_A be the sum over one representative of every other axis reflection pair, chosen to meet a positive half-axis;
exclude O, C and R_x C. Then eps is +1 or -1, and

  -1 + 2 eps + 4 I_Q + 2 I_A = 1,

  eps + 2 I_Q + I_A = 1.                                    (53.8)

More precisely, for an integer k >= 0,

  I_A = -2k,    I_Q = k + (1-eps)/2.                         (53.9)

These are finite sums. No componentwise infinite index sum is asserted.

(g) Let Q be a hyperbolic saddle, and suppose Theta-Theta(Q) is flat at Q. Both complete stable separatrices and both
complete unstable separatrices lie in Crit, have temperature Theta(Q), and have Omega = 0. This assertion does not
establish flatness of Omega at Q.

(h) The temperature ranges satisfy

  H([0,pi/2]) = closure(Theta(Q1))
             = Theta(Z cap closure(Q1)).                   (53.10)

This is a compact interval. If c != 0 and every zero in the closed quadrant with temperature c is regular, there are
finitely many such zeros, every nonstationary orbit in Q1 with temperature c escapes, and

  #{phi in (0,pi/2): H(phi)=c}
    = 2 #{Q in Z cap Q1: Theta(Q)=c}.                        (53.11)

At every angle counted on the left, H' != 0.

(i) The isothermal identity of Theorem 48 also holds at c = 0. For every real c and b in C^1([0,pi/2]), put K_b =
|X|^{-3}(-2b U_r+b' U_phi). Then K_b is absolutely integrable on {Theta=c} cap Q1, and

  int_{{Theta=c} cap Q1} K_b dX
    = 2 int_{{phi in (0,pi/2): H(phi)=c}} b(phi) dphi.        (53.12)

The measures are planar and angular Lebesgue measure, respectively. Under (S), {Theta=M} cap Q1, with M = Theta(Q+),
has infinite area, including when M = 0, and

  int_{{Theta=M} cap Q1} |X|^{-3} U_r dX
    = -|{phi in (0,pi/2): H(phi)=M}| < 0.                   (53.13)

Scope. These are necessary conditions on a hypothetical A2-broad profile. Neither existence, (S), finiteness of the
number of zero components, nor outgoing direction without the component exclusion in (d) is proved. No assumption that
all arc interiors are regular is made.

The first assertion of Theorem 22 already has no M != 0 hypothesis. Part (b) strengthens it by locating the actual
backward limit on an entire component inside Q1. The actual-backward-limit conclusion outside C already
follows from Theorems 44 and 48. The original consequence of Theorem 22 excludes every same-temperature zero outside C
in the closed quadrant. Its premise remains impossible when M = 0 because of O; part (d) uses a different exclusion.

Theorem 35 already allows M = 0. The new result supplies its outgoing hypothesis under (S).

Theorem 48(a)-(c) and its no-return statement are unchanged. In particular, the nonzero critical value in (c), used to
exclude axis backward limits, is not removed here. Under (S), escape holds for all nonstationary orbits in Q1. One
cannot simply delete "nonzero temperature" from the unrestricted backward-limit-on-C statement: the x-axis orbit from P
to O is bounded.

The potential-region conclusion of Theorem 48(d), the infinite-area and negative-integral conclusions of Theorem 48(f),
and all conclusions of Theorem 51 hold without M != 0. The integral conclusion uses the separate zero-level proof below.
Theorem 51 is applied through its local outgoing formulation; its alternative exclusion of all other closed-quadrant
zeros of temperature M remains impossible at M = 0.

Theorem 48(e) retains (R), meaning that C minus its endpoints is contained in {grad Theta != 0}. Its axis refinements
retain (X), W_1(x,0)>0 for x>x1, and (Y), W_2(0,y)>0 for y>0. Under (R), M != 0 is already a consequence. The
identification in Theorem 48(f) of the angular level set as one interval retains (R).

Proof. The flow is complete, Z is compact, and every backward orbit is bounded. Theorems 44 and 48 give a single
backward zero for every orbit and a single forward zero for every bounded forward orbit. By Theorem 44,

  grad Ly = 3W + Omega W^perp + y grad Theta,
  W.grad Ly = 3|W|^2,
  d Ly = y d Theta on a zero arc.                           (53.14)

The last identity supplies no ordering between different components.

1. Components and reflection.

Since tr DW = 4, at every zero some component of W has nonzero gradient. The implicit function theorem puts Z locally
inside one smooth curve.

Let D be a nontrivial component. Choose a closed curve chart about Q in D, small enough not to contain D, with the
containing curve meeting the chart boundary at exactly two points. The boundary-bumping argument of Theorem 16 applies
to D: every component of its intersection with the chart meets the boundary. These components are closed intervals in
the containing curve, so there are at most two. Shrinking about Q removes the interval not containing Q, if present.
Thus D is locally an interval or a half-interval. It is a compact connected smooth one-dimensional manifold with
boundary. The circle alternative is excluded by Theorem 4. Hence D is an arc.

At a regular zero, Theorem 39 gives coordinates (Theta,L) with Z = {L=0} and nonzero coordinate Jacobian. Thus the zero
is interior to its arc, and Theta is strictly monotone on every connected regular subarc. Differentiating W = 0 along an
arc gives a zero eigenvalue, so the spectrum is {0,4}. At a critical zero, Theorem 44 gives Omega = 0 and symmetry of
DW.

An endpoint cannot be regular. In orthonormal eigencoordinates (u,v) at an endpoint Q, DW(Q) = diag(4,0), and {W_u=0} is
a graph u=h(v), with h(0)=h'(0)=0. If Theta-Theta(Q) has a first nonzero homogeneous term P_m, the lowest-degree
transport equation gives 4u partial_u P_m=0. Hence P_m=c v^m with c != 0. On the graph,

partial_v Theta(h(v),v)=mc v^{m-1}+o(|v|^{m-1}),

which is nonzero for small v != 0. The transport equation restricted to W_u=0 forces W_v=0 there. Thus the entire graph
consists of zeros, contradicting the endpoint property.

The same argument excludes a nonflat temperature jet at a singleton with spectrum {0,4}. A first nonzero vorticity term
would then solve (4u partial_u+1)omega_m=0. Its multipliers on u^i v^j are 4i+1, all positive, so Omega is flat. A
singleton cannot be regular because regular zeros belong to full zero arcs. At a non-isolated zero DW is singular by the
inverse function theorem; its trace then gives spectrum {0,4}.

If an arc meets an axis, reflection fixes an intersection point and preserves the component. Its restriction to the arc
is an involution of an interval. An increasing involution is the identity, putting the whole arc on the axis. Otherwise
it reverses the interval, has exactly one fixed point, and interchanges the endpoints. Its derivative at the fixed point
in a smooth parameter is -1, so the tangent is perpendicular to the axis.

No arc contains O, which is an isolated hyperbolic saddle. If an arc met both axes, neither reflection could restrict to
the identity. Both would reverse the interval. Their commuting product would be an increasing involution and hence the
identity, whereas R_x R_y fixes only O. This is impossible.

2. Connections.

Temperature invariance and integration of (53.14) between times -T and T give (53.2) as T tends to infinity. Continuity
at the two limits gives finiteness; nonstationarity gives strict positivity. Equal limits are impossible. Two different
limits on one arc are excluded by Theorem 48. Part (a) therefore excludes both limits on any one component.

The closure of an orbit with distinct finite limits is an embedded closed arc: compactify its time parameter and use
uniqueness and absence of periodic orbits for injectivity. Distinct connecting orbits have disjoint interiors. If two
join the same components, join their endpoints by the corresponding zero subarcs, omitting a subarc when its endpoints
coincide. The result is an invariant Jordan curve, forbidden by Theorem 4.

Suppose one limit lies on C. It cannot be P. An interior point of a zero arc cannot be a nonstationary forward limit, by
Theorem 48. The two nonstationary orbits with backward limit P are its two x-axis orbits, by Theorem 39. Neither is
gamma. Thus the limit on C lies in Q1.

Neither limit can be O, whose stable and unstable manifolds lie on the axes. Suppose the other component meets an axis.
If its limit lies in Q1, part (a) gives a zero subarc from that limit to the unique axis intersection R, otherwise
inside Q1. If the limit itself is on an axis, take R to be that limit. Adjoin the closed orbit and the subarc of C
leading to P. They form a compact invariant embedded arc from P to R, otherwise inside Q1 and avoiding O.

If R is on the positive x-axis, append the axis interval from R to P. This interval is invariant because its endpoints
are zeros, including when it contains other zeros. The resulting invariant Jordan curve contradicts Theorem 4.

If R is on the positive y-axis, the constructed compact connected invariant set avoids O and meets both open positive
half-axes. This is exactly the configuration excluded by the A2 assertion of Theorem 4.

Thus the other component misses both axes. Since it meets Q1, connectedness puts it wholly in Q1.

Apply this to an incoming centre orbit at Q+ to obtain (53.3). At a regular backward limit, Theta is a local coordinate
on the zero arc and takes values on both sides of M. At a critical backward limit, a regular orbit point would
contradict Theorem 39. Thus the orbit is critical, and Theorem 44 gives Omega = 0.

3. Accumulation.

Fix an arbitrarily small closed curve chart about Q+, contained in Q1, with the containing curve meeting its boundary
twice. The terminal part of C occupies one boundary point. Choose zeros outside C tending to Q+ on pairwise distinct
components; every fixed other component is compact and has positive distance from Q+.

Any such component leaving the chart must contain a boundary point of the containing curve. It cannot contain the
boundary point on C. At most one component can contain the other boundary point, and that fixed component stays a
positive distance from Q+. Consequently all sufficiently late components lie wholly inside the chart. Applying this to
arbitrarily small charts proves that the full components shrink to Q+.

Choose a local C^2 invariant centre curve. In coordinates straightening it to n=0, the transverse equation is
n'=a(s,n)n, with a(0,0)=4 and a>0 near Q+. Thus the curve contains every nearby zero. Parametrize it so Q+ has parameter
0 and C occupies s<=0.

The closed zero-parameter set has positive points arbitrarily close to 0, but contains no interval (0,epsilon), since
that would extend C. Its complement therefore has bounded intervals (a_n,b_n), with 0<a_n<b_n->0 and zero endpoints. On
each interval the scalar velocity has a fixed nonzero sign. Smooth uniqueness prevents reaching either endpoint
equilibrium in finite time, so it is a complete connecting orbit.

A gap endpoint cannot be regular, since a regular zero fills a neighbourhood in the centre curve with zeros. Both
endpoints are critical. Theorem 39 makes the whole connecting orbit critical, and Theorem 44 gives Omega=0. Part (b)
puts the endpoints on distinct components. Those components shrink to Q+ by the chart argument. Taking successively
smaller gaps avoids any finite list of earlier components, so all components can be chosen pairwise distinct.

Equation (53.2) gives the strict Ly ordering. Continuity gives (53.4), and flatness at Q+ gives (53.5).

4. Outgoing direction and escape.

The opposite centre branch is either zero-free with one fixed direction near Q+, or has zeros accumulating there. Part
(b) excludes incoming direction when no component is wholly in Q1; part (c) excludes accumulation. Hence Q+ is outgoing.
Hypothesis (S) implies the required component exclusion.

Under (S), a bounded nonstationary orbit in Q1 would have two zero limits on C or on the axes. Two on C contradict
Theorem 48. One on C and one on an axis contradict part (b). A limit O is impossible by its axis stable and unstable
manifolds. Equal limits contradict (53.2).

Two distinct limits on one positive half-axis, together with the interval between them, give an invariant Jordan curve.
Two limits on different positive half-axes give a compact connected invariant orbit closure avoiding O and meeting both
open positive half-axes. The respective assertions of Theorem 4 exclude both possibilities. Thus every such orbit
escapes.

Theorem 35 requires the zero-free outgoing branch and no restriction on M. The local formulation of Theorem 51 requires
the smooth equations, spectrum {0,4}, the one-sided zero arc, and the zero-free outgoing centre branch. These hypotheses
now hold. Reflection gives the conclusions at Q-.

The analytic continuation argument in Theorem 51 does not assume analyticity of W on both sides. A hypothetical
holomorphic extension of U_1-i U_2 gives an analytic field W_a agreeing with W on the potential side. Hence W_a-W is
flat at Q+. The analytic graph {W_{a,u}=0}, written u=k(v), is flatly close for v<=0 to the actual terminal zero arc
u=c(v). Therefore W_{a,v}(k(v),v) is an analytic function flat as v tends to 0 from below, so it vanishes identically.

For v>0 this graph enters the potential side: k(v)=O(v^2), while the strong unstable curve has the form
v=gamma(u)=O(u^2). It supplies zeros on the side whose points have backward limit Q+, a contradiction. The Schwarz
reflection argument excluding an analytic transverse invariant curve uses its real tangency boundary values and is
likewise independent of M.

5. Constant terminal arcs.

Let Q have a terminal zero subarc of constant temperature m. Use the simultaneous centre and strong unstable coordinates
of Theorem 51, with Q=(0,0), the zero arc at z=0, s<=0, and the strong unstable curve at s=0. In a small box,

  s'=s B(s,z),    z'=z A(s,z),    A>=2,

  |B(s,z)-B(s,0)| <= K|z|,
  B(s,0)=0 for s<=0.                                        (53.15)

The last equality is used only on the specified terminal subarc. Choose the negative extent of the box within it.

For backward time tau and initial data s_0<0, while the orbit stays in the box,

  |z(tau)| <= |z_0| exp(-2tau),

  |log(-s(tau))-log(-s_0)| <= K|z_0|/2.                     (53.16)

Start with |s_0| less than half the s-width and |z_0| small enough that exp(K|z_0|/2)<2. These bounds prevent exit. They
keep s negative and bounded away from 0 for each fixed initial point, and the logarithmic derivative is absolutely
integrable. Hence s tends to s_infinity<0 on the chosen terminal subarc. Temperature invariance gives Theta=m on a full
smaller negative side.

This negative side is not the backward basin of Q.

Suppose the opposite branch is outgoing. Then B(s,0)>0 for s>0. Step 3 of Theorem 51 applies on that side. Explicitly,
put I(tau)=K int_0^tau |z(r)| dr and q=s exp(-I). The backward equation gives q'<=-q B(s,0)<=0. The same trapping
estimate prevents exit; I has a finite limit, so s has a limit. A positive limit would make d log s/dtau eventually
bounded above by a negative constant. Thus s tends to 0. These points, and the points on s=0, have backward limit Q and
temperature m.

Consequently Theta=m on a full neighbourhood of Q. Theorem 44 gives Omega=0 there. Since W has zero curl and constant
divergence, its components are harmonic and real analytic.

In eigencoordinates (u,v), the analytic implicit function theorem gives {W_u=0} as u=h(v), since partial_u W_u(Q)=4. The
analytic function W_v(h(v),v) vanishes on the interval corresponding to the terminal arc. The one-variable identity
theorem makes it vanish on both sides of 0. This extends the same zero component through Q, contradicting its endpoint
property.

The same analytic argument excludes Omega=0 on any full neighbourhood of any arc endpoint. Local constancy of Theta
would imply that vanishing by Theorem 44. This completes (a).

At an isolated arc endpoint accumulation is impossible. Excluding outgoing direction therefore leaves incoming
direction, proving (e).

6. Indices.

Extend an isolated arc a short distance beyond each endpoint along invariant centre curves. These agree with the arc on
their overlaps and give an embedded invariant C^2 curve. Construct a C^2 tubular chart using a smooth transverse vector
field. The transformed field has the form

  s'=b(s)+n c(s,n),    n'=n a(s,n),    a>0.                  (53.17)

On the zero arc a(s,0)=4. Positivity persists on sufficiently short extensions and in a sufficiently thin tube.
Isolation makes b nonzero on the end extensions.

Choose a rectangle [l,r] x [-eta,eta] enclosing the arc and no other zero. For 0<=t<=1 use

  V_t(s,n) =
    (b(s)+(1-t)n c(s,n), n((1-t)a(s,n)+t)).                  (53.18)

The second coefficient stays positive. On the horizontal faces the second component is nonzero. On either end face, a
possible zero must have n=0, where the first component is b(l) or b(r), both nonzero. Thus the entire boundary stays
zero-free throughout the homotopy.

Coordinate invariance of the vector-field index and the degree of the product field (b(s),n) give

  ind(D) = (sgn b(r)-sgn b(l))/2.                            (53.19)

Left outgoing means b(l)<0; right outgoing means b(r)>0. This proves (53.7). The same calculation applies at a single
isolated degenerate zero. At a hyperbolic zero the index is sgn det DW. A singleton is critical, so DW is symmetric with
trace 4; a hyperbolic zero is therefore a source or a saddle. Part (e) gives index -1 for an isolated
constant-temperature arc.

A component accumulated by other components has no neighbourhood isolating it alone, so this construction assigns it no
individual index.

If Z has finitely many components, all are isolated. On a sufficiently large circle X.W>0, so the total degree is 1. The
origin has index -1. Reflection acts on both the domain and vector values and preserves index. Part (a) gives the pair
C,R_x C, quartets of components off the axes, and pairs for all other axis components. Reflection R_y exchanges the ends
of C and preserves their types, so eps=+1 or -1. Index additivity gives (53.8).

For the refinement, let j(D) be the scalar index of the intersection of an axis representative D with its positive
half-axis. That intersection is one point or one interval. We claim

  ind(D)-j(D) is either 0 or -2.                             (53.20)

For an axis-contained arc, the transverse eigenvalue is 4 and the product argument gives ind(D)=j(D). For a crossing
arc, its tangent is perpendicular to the axis, so the axis eigenvalue is 4 and j(D)=1. Reflection gives equal endpoint
types, hence ind(D)=+1 or -1.

For an isolated axis point, DW is diagonal in axis and transverse directions; write its eigenvalues d and 4-d. If d<0
both indices are -1. If 0<d<4 both are +1. If d>4 the planar index is -1 and the scalar index is +1. If d=0, the
invariant axis is a centre curve with positive transverse coefficient, and the product argument gives equality.

If d=4, use coordinates (u,v) along and perpendicular to the axis. The equation W_u=0 has a graph u=h(v). Reflection
makes h even and g(v)=W_v(h(v),v) odd. Isolation makes g nonzero for small v!=0. Eliminating the positive u-direction
gives the scalar degree of g, hence planar index +1 or -1, while j(D)=+1. This proves (53.20).

On the positive x-axis the scalar field is negative near O and positive at infinity. Its total scalar index away from O
is 1, already contributed by P, whose derivative is 4. The additional x-axis scalar indices sum to 0. On the positive
y-axis the field is positive near O and at infinity, so the scalar indices also sum to 0.

Therefore I_A is the sum of terms in (53.20), hence a nonpositive even integer. Substitution in (53.8) proves (53.9).

7. Flat saddle temperatures.

At a saddle Q, differentiating transport gives DW(Q)^T grad Theta(Q)=0. Invertibility gives criticality; Theorem 44
gives symmetry and zero vorticity. Theorem 39 excludes regular points on an orbit with backward limit Q, so the unstable
separatrices are critical and have zero vorticity. This conclusion is already contained in Theorem 46.

For X on a stable separatrix, hyperbolicity gives |Phi_t X-Q|<=C exp(-lambda t) for large t and some lambda>0. On its
compact forward orbit DW is bounded, so ||D Phi_t(X)||<=C exp(Kt). Differentiating Theta o Phi_t=Theta and using
flatness gives, for every N,

  |grad Theta(X)|
    = |D Phi_t(X)^T grad Theta(Phi_t X)|
    <= C_N exp((K-N lambda)t).                              (53.21)

Choose N lambda>K and let t tend to infinity. Thus grad Theta(X)=0. Invariance of Crit and Theorem 44 extend criticality
and Omega=0 along the complete separatrix. Temperature invariance and continuity give Theta=Theta(Q) on all four
separatrices.

8. Ranges and regular labels.

Backward limits and temperature invariance put Theta(Q1) inside the compact set Theta(Z cap closure(Q1)). Conversely,
interior zeros contribute values of Theta(Q1), while axis zeros contribute only 0, which belongs to its closure. This
proves equality of the last two sets in (53.10).

Escaping points are dense by Theorem 33. Their temperatures equal H at their exit angles by Theorem 36. Approximation by
escaping points puts closure(Theta(Q1)) inside H([0,pi/2]). The reverse inclusion follows from the angular limit,
including the axis value 0. Connectedness of Q1 gives the interval assertion.

For the specified c, the zero set at temperature c is compact and locally discrete, since Theta is a coordinate along Z
at each such zero. It is finite and lies in Q1 because c!=0.

Each such regular zero has exactly two outgoing orbits by Theorem 39. Every nonstationary orbit of temperature c has one
of these regular backward limits. It is regular near that limit, hence everywhere by invariance of Crit and its
complement. If it were bounded forward, Theorem 48 would give a critical forward zero of temperature c, contrary to the
hypothesis. Thus every such orbit escapes.

Every launch label with temperature c has one of these backward limits. Distinct escaping orbits have distinct exit
labels, proving (53.11). The formula for H' in Theorem 39 gives its nonvanishing.

9. The zero isotherm.

Only c=0 in (53.12) needs an additional argument. The exact A2 factorization is Theta=x^2 y a(x^2,y^2) near O, with
a(0,0)!=0. Choose rho>0 so small that Theta has no zero in Q1 cap {|X|<=rho}. Thus E={Theta=0} cap Q1 stays away from O.
By Theorem 36, K_b=O(r^{-5/2}) at infinity, so K_b is absolutely integrable on E.

For r>0 put a_b(X)=r^{-2}b(phi). Direct differentiation gives

  div(a_b W) = K_b,

  div(F(Theta) a_b W) = F(Theta) K_b                         (53.22)

for every C^1 function F.

Use these identities on a fixed annular quadrant. Choose smooth eta with 0<=eta<=1, eta(0)=1 and support in [-1,1], and
put F_n(s)=eta(ns). Integrate (53.22) over Q1 cap {rho<r<R}. The axis fluxes vanish because W is tangent to the axes.

At fixed rho and R, dominated convergence as n tends to infinity selects the exact zero level. The inner-circle
contribution vanishes because Theta(rho,phi)!=0 for 0<phi<pi/2. Consequently,

  int_{E cap {r<R}} K_b dX
    = int_{{phi in (0,pi/2): Theta(R,phi)=0}}
                           b(phi) W_r(R,phi)/R dphi.         (53.23)

For R at least the launch radius, let E_0 be the launch labels with temperature 0. Exact transport identifies the
angular integration set with F_R(E_0). Changing variables makes the right side the integral over E_0 of

b(F_R(alpha)) [W_r(R,F_R(alpha))/R] F_R'(alpha).

Theorem 36 gives F_R->F in C^1 and W_r/R->2 uniformly. Dominated convergence therefore gives 2 int_{E_0}
b(F(alpha))F'(alpha) d alpha, equal to 2 int_{H=0} b(phi) dphi. Absolute integrability gives convergence on the left.

This proves (53.12) at zero without using the condition F_n(0)=0 required by the existing proof of Theorem 48. Under
(S), part (d) gives infinite area and a positive-length angular interval at temperature M. Taking b=1 proves (53.13).
QED.

### Theorem 54 (beta > 2: further axis zeros, minimal axis configurations and a dual balance)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2. Put W = beta X + U, kappa = beta - 2, b
= beta + 2, L = 3 beta + 2, D = 2 beta + 1, d = 2 beta - 1, h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h and sigma = sgn(a0). In particular
the fields are smooth, U is uniformly sublinear, and

  W.grad Theta = kappa Theta,   W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x,
  div W = 2 beta,   d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = Omega.                    (54.1)

The A2 hypotheses include Theta even in x and odd in y, Theta(0,y) = 0, the nonzero jet Theta = a0 x^2 y + O(|X|^5), and
Omega odd in each coordinate. The component U_1 is odd in x and even in y, while U_2 is even in x and odd in y, so both
axes are invariant. The fields Theta and Omega have polynomial growth, and U is the canonical velocity. Let Phi_t be the
flow, Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, O = (0,0), and P = (x1,0) the first positive x-axis zero of W. Define

  B_Q = {X : Phi_(-t) X -> Q as t -> infinity},
  w(x) = W_1(x,0),   T(x) = Theta_y(x,0),   g(x) = Omega_y(x,0),
  v(y) = W_2(0,y),   E(y) = Theta_xx(0,y)/2,
  K_y(y) = Omega_x(0,y),
  r^(-q) Theta(r,phi) -> f(phi),   r^h Omega(r,phi) -> G(phi).     (54.2)

The last limits, with every angular derivative, are those of Theorem 42. An orbit escapes if its radius tends to
infinity in forward time. Hypothesis (H1) means that the zero set of W in the closed first quadrant is exactly {O,P}.
Flatness means vanishing of all Cartesian derivatives, including the value. Exact transverse order j along a regular
curve means a local factorization u^j H, where u defines the curve, du != 0, and H is nonzero at the point in question.
Total order means the degree of the first nonzero Taylor polynomial.

(a) Suppose w has a zero after x1. Its first such zero x2 exists. With Q_x = (x2,0) and a = -w'(x2), one has a >= 0 and

  DW(Q_x) = diag(-a, 2 beta + a),
  Theta(Q_x) = grad Theta(Q_x) = Omega(Q_x) = 0.                  (54.3)

On (x1,x2), T has sign sigma. Immediately to the left of x2,

  sgn T' = sgn g = -sigma,
  g(x)/T'(x) -> 1/(beta - 1 + a)  as x increases to x2.           (54.4)

These conclusions include a = 0. Consequently, any further positive x-axis zero forces Omega to take both signs in Q1.

If a > 0, there is a positive integer m such that

  a = b/m,
  ord_(Q_x) Theta = m + 2,   ord_(Q_x) Omega = m + 1.             (54.5)

The unstable branch gamma_x in Q1 has exact transverse orders m + 1 for Theta and m for Omega at every nonstationary
point. On this branch Theta = grad Theta = Omega = 0. If the branch escapes, its limiting angle phi_* lies in (0,pi/2),
and

  ord_(phi_*) f = m + 1,   ord_(phi_*) G = m,
  f^(m+1)(phi_*) G^(m)(phi_*) < 0.                               (54.6)

(b) Suppose v has a positive zero. Its first such zero y1 exists. With Q_y = (0,y1) and a = -v'(y1), one has a >= 0 and

  DW(Q_y) = diag(2 beta + a, -a),
  Theta(Q_y) = grad Theta(Q_y) = Omega(Q_y) = 0.                  (54.7)

Without a simplicity assumption,

  sgn E = sgn K_y = sigma  on (0,y1),
  K_y(y)/E(y) -> +infinity  as y increases to y1.                 (54.8)

If a > 0, then

  n = L/a,   ell = D/a,   d0 = 1/a
  are positive integers, and beta d0 is a positive integer.     (54.9)

The exact total orders of Theta and Omega at Q_y are n + 4 and ell + 2. On the unstable branch gamma_y in Q1 their exact
transverse orders are, respectively,

  p = n + 2,   k = ell + 1 < p - 1.                            (54.10)

On this branch Theta = grad Theta = Omega = 0. If it escapes at phi_* in (0,pi/2), then f and G have exact orders p and
k there. In particular, an irrational beta excludes a hyperbolic first positive y-axis zero, without any assumption on
subsequent zeros.

(c) Let Q be any axis zero whose eigenvalue tangent to that axis is zero. Its transverse eigenvalue is 2 beta. Then

  D^j Theta(X) = D^j Omega(X) = 0
  for every X in B_Q and every integer j >= 0.                  (54.11)

This includes backward approaches with no prescribed rate. If an orbit in B_Q escapes, f and G are flat at its limiting
angle. Thus such a Q cannot be the backward limit of an outgoing label with nonzero G.

(d) Suppose the zero set in the closed first quadrant is exactly {O,P,Q,S}, where Q is a hyperbolic saddle, S is a
hyperbolic source, and Q,S lie on the positive axes. Then Q and S lie on the same axis, with Q preceding S. The unstable
branch gamma of Q in Q1 escapes at an angle phi_* in (0,pi/2), every point of Q1 escapes, and

  Q1 = (B_P intersect Q1) disjoint-union gamma
       disjoint-union (B_S intersect Q1).                      (54.12)

Both source basins in this decomposition are nonempty.

In the x-axis case, write Q = (x2,0), S = (x3,0), with x1 < x2 < x3, and use m from (a). Put tau = (-1)^(m+1) sigma. The
angular interval below phi_* belongs to B_S and the interval above it belongs to B_P, and

  sgn f(phi) = tau    for 0 < phi < phi_*,
  sgn f(phi) = sigma  for phi_* < phi < pi/2.                    (54.13)

The orders and derivative inequality in (54.6) hold. For some eps > 0,

  sgn G(phi) = tau     for phi_* - eps < phi < phi_*,
  sgn G(phi) = -sigma  for phi_* < phi < phi_* + eps.            (54.14)

Also sigma G'(pi/2) < 0, so G has sign sigma immediately below pi/2. Hence G takes both signs in the angular interval
belonging to B_P and has a further zero strictly between phi_* and pi/2.

In the y-axis case, write Q = (0,y1), S = (0,y2), with y1 < y2, and use n, ell, d0, p, k from (b). Necessarily

  d0 and beta d0 are positive integers,
  (beta + 1)d0 is odd.                                         (54.15)

Put tau = (-1)^n sigma. The interval below phi_* belongs to B_P and the interval above it belongs to B_S. For some eps >
0,

  sgn f(phi) = sigma  for 0 < phi < phi_*,
  sgn f(phi) = tau    for phi_* < phi < pi/2,
  sgn G(phi) = sigma  for phi_* - eps < phi < phi_*,
  sgn G(phi) = tau    for phi_* < phi < phi_* + eps.             (54.16)

Moreover,

  ord_(phi_*) f = p,   ord_(phi_*) G = k,
  p - k = (beta + 1)d0 + 1 is a positive even integer,
  f^(p)(phi_*) G^(k)(phi_*) > 0.                                (54.17)

This minimal y-axis configuration is excluded when beta is irrational, or when beta is a reduced ratio of two odd
positive integers.

(e) No assumption (H1) is needed for the following balance. Let K be the full-plane set of points with bounded forward
orbit, and let E_esc = Q1 \ K. The set K is compact, invariant and of area zero. On E_esc define

  K0(X) = xy |X|^(-4),
  phi_K(X) = int_0^infinity e^(dt) K0(Phi_t X) dt.               (54.18)

This function is finite, positive and continuous on E_esc. Along every orbit there it satisfies

  -d phi_K - W.grad phi_K = K0.                                 (54.19)

Extend phi_K by zero on K intersect Q1. Then phi_K Theta_x is absolutely integrable. For every measurable A contained in
Q1 with Phi_t(A) = A for all real t,

  int_A phi_K Theta_x dX = int_A K0 Omega dX.                    (54.20)

In particular,

  int_Q1 phi_K Theta_x dX = int_Q1 K0 Omega dX
                         = (pi/2)(beta + 1).                   (54.21)

In either configuration of (d), this gives

  I_P + I_S = (pi/2)(beta + 1),
  I_R = int_(B_R intersect Q1) phi_K Theta_x dX
      = int_(B_R intersect Q1) K0 Omega dX,   R = P,S.           (54.22)

There is no additional separatrix term.

Scope. The quantization a = b/m and the trace orders used in (a) are from Theorem 27. The simple first y-axis
quantization in (54.9), including rationality of beta, is already Theorem 30(a); its positive limiting homogeneous
coefficient follows from the origin jet and the first-zero condition. No extra nonvanishing hypothesis is needed at that
first zero. At an arbitrary later simple zero, such a coefficient must be proved nonzero before its exponent can be
quantized. The arithmetic restriction (54.15) is already Theorem 30(b).

The additional conclusions concern the degenerate first-zero trace limits, the exact total and transverse orders, their
outgoing coefficients, flatness on the entire unstable set in (c), and the basin and angular sign conclusions in (d).
The y-axis endpoint sign used in (d) is already the version of Theorem 50(c) assuming only v > 0 on the positive
half-axis. Part (e) extends Theorem 50(d) by removing (H1) and allowing restriction to invariant measurable sets; the
strain constant itself is already Theorem 45(d). No continuity across K or distributional equation for the zero
extension of phi_K is asserted.

The complete parameter exclusions here are the exclusion of a hyperbolic first positive y-axis zero for irrational beta,
and the exclusion of the minimal y-axis configuration for irrational beta or a reduced ratio of two odd integers. Part
(c) excludes the indicated degenerate axis zeros as origins of nonzero outgoing amplitude. Part (a) also excludes a
fixed vorticity sign on Q1 whenever a further positive x-axis zero exists. These do not exclude all A2-broad profiles at
any beta > 2. In particular, the odd-over-odd restriction does not exclude the first positive y-axis zero alone without
the subsequent simplicity hypothesis.

No existence or complete exclusion of the minimal x-axis configuration, or of an arithmetically permitted minimal y-axis
configuration, is proved. If {X in Q1 : sgn(a0) Omega(X) < 0} is bounded, the minimal x-axis configuration is excluded
by Theorem 71, and also by Theorem 77 since all its zeros are nondegenerate. For the minimal y-axis configuration,
boundedness of {X in Q1 : sgn(a0) Omega(X) < 0} forces the arithmetic condition of Theorem 77(b) and a ray of the kind
described in Theorem 80(c); these conditions do not exclude that configuration. For general zero sets, the outgoing
conclusions about a specified saddle branch remain conditional on its escape. Part (c) does not assert that B_Q is open,
does not cover an axis zero with tangential eigenvalue 2 beta and transverse eigenvalue zero, and does not remove the
remaining interior degenerate possibility in Theorem 46(d). No sign or separately prescribed value for I_P or I_S
follows from (54.22).

Proof. Step 1 (axis equations and first zeros). Theorem 2 gives w'(0) = -b, w'(x1) = b, T(x1) != 0, and sign sigma for T
on (0,x1]. The origin jet also gives v'(0) = L. Sublinearity gives w(x)/x -> beta and v(y)/y -> beta. The zero set is
compact, and the positive derivative at x1 leaves a zero-free interval after x1. Thus x2 exists whenever there is a
further zero. The argument for y1 uses v'(0) > 0. One has w > 0 on (x1,x2) and v > 0 on (0,y1); hence the derivatives at
the respective right endpoints are nonpositive.

Parity makes DW diagonal on either axis, and its trace is 2 beta. At either first zero its eigenvalues are -a and 2
beta + a. At any zero, (54.1) and its first derivative give Theta = 0, Omega = Theta_x and DW^T grad Theta = kappa grad
Theta, as in Theorem 43(a). Neither eigenvalue here equals kappa, proving (54.3) and (54.7).

Differentiation on the x-axis, and extraction of the x^2 and x coefficients on the y-axis, give

  w T' = (w' - b)T,       w g' + (D - w')g = T',
  v E' = (2v' - L)E,      v K_y' + (D - v')K_y = 2E.            (54.23)

For the second x-axis identity, W_(2y) = 2 beta - w', while W_(1y), Omega_x and W_2 vanish on that axis. On the y-axis,
Theta = x^2 E(y) + O(x^4), Omega = x K_y(y) + O(x^3), W_1 = x(2 beta - v') + O(x^3) and W_2 = v + O(x^2). These
expansions prove both y-axis equations, including their factors 2. They are the identities of Theorems 27 and 30.

On (x1,x2), use flow time x' = w(x). Then t -> infinity as x increases to x2: smoothness gives w(x) <= C(x2-x) near that
endpoint. The first equation in (54.23) gives

  T = C w e^(-bt),   sgn C = sigma,
  T' = C e^(-bt)(w' - b).                                      (54.24)

The sign of C follows from T(x1) != 0 and uniqueness of the homogeneous trace equation away from zeros of w. Since w' ->
-a, the last factor tends to -a-b < 0. This establishes the asserted sign of T', including a = 0.

Put A0 = beta - 1 and H(t) = e^(A0 t)/w(x(t)). The second equation in (54.23) implies

  d/dt (e^(Dt) g/w) = -C H' - 3C H,
  g/(C e^(-bt)) = -1 + C1/H
                 - 3 (int_(t0)^t H(s) ds)/H(t).                (54.25)

Here H'/H = A0 - w' -> A0 + a > 0, so H -> infinity and the ratio of its integral to H tends to 1/(A0+a). Consequently
g/(C e^(-bt)) tends to -(b+a)/(A0+a), while T'/(C e^(-bt)) tends to -(b+a). This proves (54.4). The expansion Omega(x,y)
= yg(x) + O(y^3) gives sign -sigma at some points of Q1 near this interval. The origin expansion Omega = (2a0/D)xy +
O(|X|^4) gives sign sigma at other points.

Step 2 (y-axis positivity and simple trace orders). On (0,y1), let y' = v(y). Its flow time ranges over the whole real
line. The origin expansions are E = a0 y + O(y^3), K_y = (2a0/D)y + O(y^3) and v = Ly + O(y^3). Solving (54.23) gives

  E = C_E v^2 e^(-Lt),   sgn C_E = sigma,
  K_y = C_E v e^(-Dt) S(t),
  S(t) = 2 int_(-infinity)^t v(y(s)) e^(-(beta+1)s) ds.          (54.26)

Indeed, for s_y = K_y/E one has

d/dt(s_y v e^(-(beta+1)t)) = 2v e^(-(beta+1)t).

Its boundary value at negative infinity is zero because s_y -> 2/D and v grows there like e^(Lt), with L > beta+1. The
integrand is positive. It is integrable at negative infinity by this exponent inequality, and at positive infinity
because v is bounded and beta+1 > 0. Thus

  0 < S(t) -> S_infinity < infinity,
  K_y/E = S(t)e^((beta+1)t)/v(y(t)) -> +infinity.                (54.27)

This proves (54.8), also for a degenerate first zero.

If a > 0 and z = y-y1, smoothness of v gives t = -(1/a)log|z| + t_* + o(1). Formula (54.26), with S_infinity > 0, gives
nonzero leading powers E of order 2+L/a and K_y of order 1+D/a. A smooth function asymptotic to a nonzero constant times
|z|^r must have nonnegative integral r: for nonintegral r, Taylor's theorem would give O(|z|^(ceil(r))), contradicting
that asymptotic. Hence n = L/a and ell = D/a are positive integers. Moreover,

  2n - 3ell = 1/a = d0,
  2ell - n = beta/a = beta d0.                                 (54.28)

Both are positive integers. This reproduces Theorem 30(a), with no hypothesis on later zeros.

For the x-axis, Theorem 27 applies to the consecutive simple zeros x1,x2 and gives a = b/m and exact order m+1 of T. For
the y-axis it gives exact order n+2 of E. The finite nonzero leading derivatives also continue the traces nontrivially
through these zeros. This is the precise consecutiveness and simplicity needed from Theorem 27.

Step 3 (orders near the unstable curve). Fix either simple saddle and put c = 2 beta + a. Its local stable manifold is
its axis. Its smooth unstable curve is transverse to that axis and invariant under reflection in it. Thus it is an even
graph chi, with chi(0) = chi'(0) = 0. Use coordinates

  (u,eta) = (x-x2-chi(y),y)       in the x-axis case,
  (u,eta) = (y-y1-chi(x),x)       in the y-axis case.
  W_u = u A(u,eta),   W_eta = eta C(u,eta),
  A(0,0) = -a,   C(0,0) = c.                                   (54.29)

The invariant axes u = 0 and eta = 0 justify the smooth factors. The smooth stable and unstable manifold construction
applies because the eigenvalues are strictly negative and strictly positive. Theorem 46 gives Theta = grad Theta = Omega
= 0 on the whole unstable branch.

Let H_j(eta) = partial_u^j Theta(0,eta)/j!. If the lower H_i vanish, differentiating the temperature equation gives

  eta C(0,eta) H_j' = (kappa-jA(0,eta))H_j,
  rho_j = (kappa+ja)/c.                                        (54.30)

A nonzero solution on eta > 0 equals a nonzero constant times eta^(rho_j) times a smooth positive factor. This follows
by subtracting rho_j/eta from the logarithmic derivative; the remainder is smooth at zero.

In the x-axis case each H_j is odd in eta. With p = m+1, one has 0 < rho_j < 1 for j < p and rho_p = 1. Smoothness
therefore forces H_j = 0 for j < p, while H_p'(0) = T^(p)(x2)/p! != 0.

In the y-axis case each H_j is even in eta and vanishes at eta = 0. With p = n+2, one has 0 < rho_j < 2 for j < p and
rho_p = 2. Hence H_j = 0 for j < p, while H_p''(0)/2 = E^(p)(y1)/p! != 0. In both cases the first nonzero coefficient
stays nonzero on the local branch.

Let R_j(eta) = partial_u^j Omega(0,eta)/j!. When lower coefficients and the corresponding forcing vanish,

  eta C(0,eta) R_j' + (1+jA(0,eta))R_j = 0,
  the nonzero solution exponent is (ja-1)/c.                   (54.31)

All R_j are odd in eta. In the x-axis case partial_x = partial_u, so the forcing starts at order m = p-1. For j < m the
exponent in (54.31) is less than 1. A negative exponent contradicts boundedness, exponent zero contradicts oddness, and
an exponent between zero and one contradicts smoothness. Thus R_j = 0 for j < m. At j = m the forcing is p H_p, so
comparison of the coefficients of eta gives

  R_m'(0) = p H_p'(0)/(c+1-ma)
          = p H_p'(0)/(beta-1+a) != 0.                          (54.32)

In the y-axis case partial_x = partial_eta - chi'(eta)partial_u, so the forcing has transverse order at least p-1. With
k = ell+1, one has k < p-1. The exponent in (54.31) is less than 1 for j < k and equals 1 at j = k. Hence R_j = 0 for j
< k, and R_k'(0) = K_y^(k)(y1)/k! != 0.

The leading Taylor polynomials in these coordinates are therefore

  x-axis: Theta_lead = C_x u^(m+1) eta,
          Omega_lead = ((m+1)C_x/(beta-1+a))u^m eta;
  y-axis: Theta_lead = C_y u^(n+2) eta^2,
          Omega_lead = B_y u^(ell+1) eta,
  C_x != 0,   C_y B_y != 0.                                    (54.33)

Parity supplies the displayed eta factors for all remaining coefficients. Since chi(eta) = O(eta^2), returning to the
original coordinates does not change these first homogeneous polynomials. This proves all total orders.

Every finite flow map preserves the exact transverse temperature order, and Theta_x has order at least p-1 along the
branch. The vorticity equation preserves all lower vanishing coefficients. In the y-axis case its order-k coefficient
has no forcing and cannot vanish under finite propagation. The corresponding x-axis assertion requires the following
signed integral.

Step 4 (the forced x-axis coefficient). Parametrize gamma_x by gamma(t) = (x(t),y(t)), with gamma(t) -> Q_x as t ->
-infinity. Choose a transverse section S(z) through gamma(0), oriented so that J_* = det(W(gamma(0)),S'(0)) > 0. Put
X(t,z) = Phi_t S(z). At z = 0,

  det(X_t,X_z) = e^(2 beta t) J_*,
  z_x = -y'(t)/(e^(2 beta t)J_*).                               (54.34)

Write Theta(S(z)) = theta_p z^p + O(z^(p+1)), with p = m+1 and theta_p != 0, and Omega(X(t,z)) = omega_m(t)z^m +
O(z^(m+1)). Since Theta(X(t,z)) = e^(kappa t)Theta(S(z)), the leading order-m coefficient of Theta_x is p e^(kappa
t)theta_p z_x. The term involving the derivative of t has order p and does not enter. Hence

  d/dt(e^t omega_m(t))
    = -(p theta_p/J_*)e^(-(beta+1)t)y'(t).                      (54.35)

The boundary value of e^t omega_m at negative infinity is zero. To verify it, fix eps > 0 sufficiently small. On the
local graph, y' = y C(0,y), so |gamma(t)-Q_x| <= C e^((c-eps)t) for t negative. The variational equation and Sym DW >=
-(a+eps)I give |X_z(t,0)| <= C e^(-(a+eps)t). All derivatives of Omega below order m vanish on the branch, and D^m
Omega(Q_x) = 0 by (54.33); hence |D^m Omega(gamma(t))| <= C|gamma(t)-Q_x|. The chain rule gives

  |e^t omega_m(t)|
    <= C e^([1+c-ma-(m+1)eps]t) -> 0,
  1+c-ma = beta-1+a > 0.                                       (54.36)

Integrating (54.35) yields

  e^t omega_m(t) = -(p theta_p/J_*) I(t),
  I(t) = int_(-infinity)^t e^(-(beta+1)s)y'(s) ds
       = e^(-(beta+1)t)y(t)
         +(beta+1)int_(-infinity)^t
                     e^(-(beta+1)s)y(s) ds > 0.                (54.37)

The integration by parts is justified at negative infinity by c > beta+1 and the preceding exponential estimate, with
eps < c-beta-1. The branch remains in Q1, so y(s) > 0. No sign for y'(s) is required. Thus omega_m never vanishes,
proving the asserted finite transverse order along all of gamma_x.

If the branch escapes, Theorems 41 and 42 imply |gamma(t)| is comparable to e^(beta t) for large positive t and
|W(gamma(t))| <= C e^(beta t). Both weighted integrals in (54.37) converge absolutely at positive infinity, and the
boundary term there is O(e^(-t)). Therefore

  I_infinity
    = int_(-infinity)^infinity e^(-(beta+1)s)y'(s) ds
    = (beta+1)int_(-infinity)^infinity e^(-(beta+1)s)y(s) ds
    is finite and strictly positive.                          (54.38)

Step 5 (passing the coefficients to infinity). Choose a sufficiently large circle S(alpha) = R(cos alpha,sin alpha), put
X(t,alpha) = Phi_t S(alpha), and Y(t,alpha) = e^(-beta t)X(t,alpha). The natural velocity bound gives |X(t,alpha)|
comparable to e^(beta t), uniformly for t >= 0, so Y stays in a fixed annulus. With U_t(Z) = e^(-(beta-1)t)U(e^(beta
t)Z),

  partial_t Y = e^(-t) U_t(Y).                                 (54.39)

Theorem 42(a) bounds every spatial derivative of U_t on that annulus. Differentiation in alpha and induction, using
Gronwall with the integrable coefficient e^(-t), bound every alpha derivative of Y. Equation (54.39) then bounds every
alpha derivative of partial_t Y by C_j e^(-t). Thus Y converges in every C^j to Y_infinity = rho_infinity e(F), with
rho_infinity > 0 smooth.

Liouville's formula, divided by e^(2 beta t) and passed to the limit, gives

  beta rho_infinity(alpha)^2 F'(alpha)
    = R W_r(S(alpha)) > 0.                                     (54.40)

Axis invariance fixes F(0) = 0 and F(pi/2) = pi/2, so interior launch labels have interior limiting angles. Theorem
42(b), composed with these uniformly smooth rescaled trajectories, and exact temperature transport give

  e^t Omega(X(t,alpha)) -> J(alpha)
     = rho_infinity(alpha)^(-h) G(F(alpha))  in every C^j,
  Theta(S(alpha))
     = rho_infinity(alpha)^q f(F(alpha)).                      (54.41)

The convergence of the first line and all its derivatives has error O(e^(-t)): the spatial remainder in Theorem 42(b),
after this rescaling, has that bound on the fixed annulus, and Y-Y_infinity has that bound in every C^j.

Positive smooth factors and composition with F, whose derivative is positive, preserve orders and the signs of leading
coefficients. For an escaping x-axis branch choose its launch section to be this circle, with z = alpha-alpha_*.
Equations (54.37)-(54.38) show that the leading coefficients of Theta on the section and J have opposite signs. This
proves (54.6). For a y-axis branch, the order-k coefficient of e^t Omega(X(t,alpha)) is a nonzero constant in t because
k < p-1. This proves its asserted outgoing orders.

Step 6 (degenerate axis zeros). At the Q of (c), Theorem 43(a),(b3),(c) gives a symmetric DW(Q) with eigenvalues 0,2
beta and flatness of both fields at Q. Propagation to all of B_Q uses an additional argument.

Smooth division gives

  x-axis: Theta = y H,   W_2 = y C,
          W.grad H = lambda H,
          lambda = kappa-C,   lambda(Q) = -b;
  y-axis: Theta = x^2 H,   W_1 = x C,
          W.grad H = lambda H,
          lambda = kappa-2C,   lambda(Q) = -L.                  (54.42)

These are smooth equations also on the axis. The x^2 factor uses both Theta(0,y) = 0 and evenness in x.

Fix X in B_Q and Y(s) = Phi_(-s) X. The scalar equation is d_s H(Y(s)) = -lambda(Y(s))H(Y(s)). For large s its
coefficient is bounded below by a positive number, while H(Y(s)) remains bounded. Therefore H vanishes on this orbit.

Suppose inductively that all derivatives of H below order j vanish along it. Differentiate (54.42). Terms involving a
derivative of W of order at least two or a positive-order derivative of lambda multiply lower derivatives of H and
vanish. For the Euclidean symmetric covariant tensor T_j = D^j H(Y(s)), the remaining equation is

  T_j' = [sum_(nu=1)^j DW(Y(s))^T_nu
          - lambda(Y(s))I]T_j.                                 (54.43)

The subscript denotes action on one tensor slot. At Q the symmetric part of this operator has all eigenvalues at least
-lambda(Q) > 0, because DW(Q) is positive semidefinite. For each fixed j it follows by continuity that d_s |T_j|^2 >=
2delta_j |T_j|^2 eventually, for some delta_j > 0. A bounded solution must be zero. Induction proves flatness of H and
therefore of Theta at every point of the orbit.

All derivatives of Theta_x now vanish along the orbit. In backward time the vorticity equation is Omega' = Omega, so
boundedness forces Omega = 0. Induction for its derivatives gives (54.43) with -lambda I replaced by +I. Its limiting
symmetric part is bounded below by I, and the same argument proves flatness of Omega. The constant orbit is included. No
convergence rate for Y(s) has been used.

For an escaping orbit, let phi_r be its angle on the circle of radius r, with phi_r -> phi_*. All angular derivatives of
the fields vanish at phi_r. Uniform convergence of every angular derivative in Theorem 42(b), followed by continuity at
phi_*, proves flatness of f,G there.

Step 7 (minimal configurations and signs). Under (d), all positive axis zeros are simple. The signs of w near zero and
infinity are negative and positive; those of v are positive and positive. Thus the number of additional positive x-axis
zeros is even, and the number of positive y-axis zeros is even. The two additional zeros must lie on the same axis, with
the first having negative tangential derivative. Theorem 27 gives

  x-axis: DW(Q) = diag(-b/m, 2 beta+b/m),
          DW(S) = diag(b,kappa);
  y-axis: DW(Q) = diag(2 beta+L/n,-L/n),
          DW(S) = diag(kappa/2,L/2).                            (54.44)

The other positive-derivative possibility v'(y2) = L in Theorem 27 would make S a saddle, contrary to the hypothesis.
Smooth continuation through the finite trace zero therefore gives sign (-1)^(m+1)sigma for T(x3), and sign (-1)^n sigma
for E(y2).

The branch gamma cannot have bounded forward orbit. On it Theta = 0 by Theorem 46. If it were bounded, Theorem 44(a)
would give

  d_t Ly(gamma(t)) = d |W(gamma(t))|^2,
  d = 2 beta-1 > 0.                                            (54.45)

Boundedness of Ly and boundedness of the derivative of |W|^2 on the compact orbit closure imply W(gamma(t)) -> 0. Its
omega-limit set is nonempty, compact and connected; since the zero set is finite it is one zero. A source cannot receive
a nonconstant forward orbit. The stable manifolds of the only saddles O and Q lie on their respective invariant axes, so
neither can receive an orbit from Q1. This is a contradiction. Outward radial motion outside a sufficiently large circle
now gives escape; (54.40) gives its interior angle.

By Theorem 44(b), every point of Q1 has a single backward zero. The unstable manifold of O lies on the y-axis, and the
part of the unstable manifold of Q in Q1 is exactly gamma. The remaining backward limits are P and S. This proves
(54.12).

Near P the factor Theta/y has sign sigma. Near an x-axis S, Theta/y has sign (-1)^(m+1)sigma; near a y-axis S, Theta/x^2
has sign (-1)^n sigma. The respective coefficients at the sources are nonzero by Theorems 2 and 27. Source basins are
open and contain nearby points of Q1, and transport preserves these strict signs throughout each basin. Every such point
escapes because its temperature grows like e^(kappa t). Together with escape of gamma this proves escape of all Q1.

The launch arc meets gamma once. Its two remaining connected intervals lie in the open source basins. In the x-axis case
the outward x-axis orbit has backward limit S, so the interval next to angle zero belongs to S. The basin of P has a
nonempty launch set because it contains escaping points of Q1; hence the other interval belongs to P. In the y-axis case
the outward x-axis and y-axis orbits have backward limits P and S, respectively. Openness assigns the intervals
accordingly. Formula (54.41) proves the temperature sign tables.

In the x-axis case the leading coefficient of f at phi_* has sign sigma, because f has this sign for phi > phi_*.
Formula (54.6) makes the leading coefficient of G have sign -sigma. Its order m yields (54.14).

There are no positive y-axis zeros in this case, so v > 0 for y > 0. Here is the required argument from Theorem 50(c)
without (H1). Equation (54.23) keeps E of sign sigma everywhere on that half-axis. Theorem 42(a) gives v = beta y +
O(y^(1-h)) and v' = beta + O(y^(-h)), hence

  E'/E = -(1+2h)/y + O(y^(-1-h)),
  y^(1+2h)E(y) -> C_y != 0,   sgn C_y = sigma.                  (54.46)

Let H0(y) = v(y) exp(-D int_1^y dz/v(z)), which is positive and solves the homogeneous K_y equation. At zero H0(y) is
asymptotic to a positive constant times y^((beta+1)/L); at infinity it is asymptotic to a positive constant times
y^(-1-h). Since K_y/H0 -> 0 at zero, variation of constants gives

  K_y(y) = H0(y) int_0^y 2E(z)/(v(z)H0(z)) dz.                  (54.47)

The integrand has sign sigma. It is O(z^(-(beta+1)/L)) near zero, with (beta+1)/L < 1, and O(z^(-1-h)) at infinity. Its
full integral is finite and nonzero, of sign sigma. Thus y^(1+h)K_y(y) has a nonzero limit of sign sigma. Theorem 42(b)
gives

  K_y(y) = -y^(-1-h)G'(pi/2) + O(y^(-1-2h)),                   (54.48)

proving sigma G'(pi/2) < 0. Since G(pi/2) = 0, G has sign sigma just below pi/2, and the further zero asserted after
(54.14) follows by continuity. Only v > 0, the origin jet, the trace equations and Theorem 42 were used.

For the y-axis case, Theorem 30(b) applies to the first two positive simple zeros. Its parity condition can be seen
directly. On (y1,y2), E != 0, v < 0, and s_y = K_y/E solves

  v s_y' + (v'-beta-1)s_y = 2.                                 (54.49)

At S, E(y2) != 0 and (54.23) gives s_y(y2) = 4/beta > 0. At every zero of s_y in (y1,y2), (54.49) gives s_y' = 2/v < 0.
Such a zero can cross only from positive to negative, so positivity near y2 implies positivity throughout the interval.
The nonzero leading orders p and k at y1 then force p-k even. By (54.28), p-k = (beta+1)d0+1, which proves (54.15).

The coefficient B_y in (54.33) has sign (-1)^k sigma, because K_y has sign sigma below y1. This is also the sign of the
leading angular coefficient of G. To check orientation, in the local coordinates x = eta, y = y1+u+chi(eta), a
positively oriented flow section has

  det(W,X_z) = eta C(0,eta) u_z > 0
  on u = 0, eta > 0.                                          (54.50)

Thus u_z > 0. The order-k coefficient propagates homogeneously and nonvanishingly, and (54.41) preserves its sign. Since
p-k is even and p = n+2, one has (-1)^k = (-1)^n. These signs give (54.16) and the positive derivative product in
(54.17).

If beta = p0/r0 in lowest terms, integrality of d0 and beta d0 gives d0 = r0 M with M a positive integer. Oddness of
(beta+1)d0 means (p0+r0)M is odd. Therefore p0+r0 and M must both be odd. This excludes odd p0,r0; irrational beta was
already excluded in Step 2.

Step 8 (the balance without (H1)). By Theorem 52(a), K is compact and invariant. Liouville's formula gives |K| = |Phi_t
K| = e^(2 beta t)|K|; finiteness of |K| implies |K| = 0. Its complement in Q1 is precisely the open escape set, since a
forward orbit reaching a sufficiently large radius remains outside and grows exponentially.

On a compact subset of E_esc, continuous dependence and a finite covering give a common time after which every orbit
lies outside a fixed large circle. The natural velocity bound then gives |Phi_t X| >= c e^(beta t), uniformly on that
subset for large t. Since K0 <= |X|^(-2) and d-2 beta = -1, the integrand in (54.18) is bounded by C e^(-t). This proves
finiteness, positivity and continuity. Shifting the time variable in (54.18) proves (54.19) as a derivative along the
orbit.

All backward orbits are bounded by Theorem 44(b). Integrating the vorticity equation backward therefore gives

  Omega(Y) = int_0^infinity e^(-t)Theta_x(Phi_(-t)Y) dt.
  B(Y) = int_0^infinity e^(-t)|Theta_x(Phi_(-t)Y)| dt.            (54.51)

The discarded initial term tends to zero because Omega is bounded along each backward orbit.

We verify K0 B is integrable. For |Y| small, all backward orbits stay in one fixed disc. Choose M > 1 bounding |DW|
there. Since W(O) = 0 and Theta_x(O) = 0, the Lipschitz estimate gives |Theta_x(Phi_(-t)Y)| <= C min(e^(Mt)|Y|,1).
Splitting at t = (1/M)log(1/|Y|) yields B(Y) <= C|Y|^(1/M), so K0 B is integrable near O.

For r = |Y| large, let S be the backward time to a fixed sufficiently large radius R_*. With rho(t) = |Phi_(-t)Y|, the
natural velocity bound and outward radial motion give

  d_t log rho = -beta + O(rho^(-h)),
  int_0^S rho(t)^(-h) dt <= C,
  rho(t) comparable to r e^(-beta t),
  S = h log r + O(1),   e^(-S) comparable to r^(-h).             (54.52)

The integral bound follows from |rho'| >= beta rho/2 and integration of rho^(-1-h) between R_* and r. All constants are
independent of the initial angle. By Theorem 41(a), the part of B before time S is at most C r^(-2h)int_0^S e^t dt <= C
r^(-h). The remaining part is at most C e^(-S) <= C r^(-h), because the subsequent backward orbit stays in a fixed disc.
On compact sets away from O, B is bounded. These estimates prove K0 B in L^1(Q1).

Tonelli and Y = Phi_t X now give

  int_Q1 phi_K |Theta_x| dX
    = int_Q1 K0(Y) int_0^infinity
                  e^(-t)|Theta_x(Phi_(-t)Y)| dt dY
    = int_Q1 K0 B dY < infinity.                               (54.53)

Initially perform the change of variables on E_esc; its invariant null complement does not affect the integrals. The
exponent is e^(dt)e^(-2 beta t) = e^(-t). Fubini and (54.51) give the signed equality. The same calculation restricted
to any invariant measurable A proves (54.20). The value in (54.21) is Theorem 45(d), whose A2-broad hypotheses hold
without (H1).

In (d), the two basins are invariant and the intervening smooth curve has area zero. Applying (54.20) to each basin and
adding proves (54.22). This derivation uses area integrals and creates no interface term. QED.

### Theorem 55 (an axis identity and a necessary radial sign change)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta >= 2. Use -Lap Psi = Omega, U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x), W = beta
X + U and D = x partial_x + y partial_y. Let Q1 = {(x,y): x > 0, y > 0}, B_R = {Y: |Y| < R}, P = (L,0) be the first
positive x-axis zero of W, and sigma = sgn(a0). Put h = 1/beta, gamma = 1 + 2h and S = D Omega + gamma Omega.

For ell > 0 and Y = (a,b) in Q1 define

  (55.1) Q_ell(Y) = [(ell-a)^2+b^2][(ell+a)^2+b^2],
         N_ell(Y) = 4 ell a b / (pi Q_ell(Y)).

The kernel N_ell is strictly positive on Q1. Define also

  (55.2) M_L = L partial_ell N_ell|_{ell=L} + 2h N_L
              = N_L [1+2h - 4L^2(L^2-a^2+b^2)/Q_L]

              = 4Lab/(pi Q_L^2) [
                  (1+2h)(a^2+b^2)^2
                  + 2(1-2h)L^2(a^2-b^2) + (2h-3)L^4 ].

Then

  (55.3) integral_Q1 N_L Omega dY = beta L,
         integral_Q1 M_L Omega dY = 0,
         lim_{R -> infinity} integral_{Q1 cap B_R} N_L S dY = 0.

The first two integrals are absolutely convergent. The last limit follows using only smoothness, the A2 parities, the
axis data of Theorem 2, the Green representation of Theorem 9 and Omega = O(r^(-h)). For actual A2-broad profiles, the
last integrand is also absolutely integrable: Theorem 36(b) supplies derivative decay at beta = 2, and Theorem 42(a)
supplies it at beta > 2.

There is a nonempty open subset of Q1 on which

  (55.4) sigma [D Omega + (1+2/beta) Omega] < 0.

At X = r(cos(theta),sin(theta)) in Q1, this inequality is equivalent to either of

  (55.5) sigma partial_r [
             r^(1+2/beta) Omega(r cos(theta),r sin(theta))
         ] < 0,

         sigma [Theta_x - U.grad Omega + (beta+1) Omega] < 0.

Consequently no such profile satisfies sigma partial_r(r^(1+2/beta) Omega) >= 0 throughout Q1. No sign assumption on
Omega is imposed.

Scope. Theorem 2 gives the first axis zero and its slope for every A2-broad profile. Theorem 9 applies to its smooth
odd-odd stream function and uniformly sublinear velocity. The scalar decay used here is Theorem 33(a) at beta = 2 and
Theorem 41(a) at beta > 2; neither requires a sign condition. Theorem 36 is not needed for the disc-limit proof.

The displayed radial balance is a further consequence of these results and is not stated in Theorems 9, 14, 21, 25, 28
or 50(d). There is, however, overlap in the sign conclusion. At beta = 2, and when a0 < 0 at any beta >= 2, the
monotonicity exclusion already follows from Theorem 21: monotonicity and the origin jet would force sigma Omega > 0
throughout Q1. The necessary radial sign change then also follows by the mean value theorem along a ray. The additional
restricted exclusion concerns the positive class at beta > 2.

Theorem 14 concerns axis-trace compatibility. Theorems 25 and 28 require, respectively, bounded velocity at beta = 2 and
the critical annular-energy bound. Those additional hypotheses are absent here. Theorem 50(d) uses a different weight
and is stated for beta > 2 under (H1); Theorem 54(e) removes (H1), with that weight defined on the escape set and
extended by zero. No claim of priority beyond the report, or of unrestricted nonexistence, is made.

Proof. Set p(ell) = Psi_y(ell,0) and w(x) = W_1(x,0). By Theorem 2,

  (55.6) p(x) = beta x - w(x),
         p(L) = beta L,       p'(L) = -2.

Differentiate the disc-truncated potentials of Theorem 9 in the inward normal direction at (ell,0), grouping the four
reflected sources. Their kernel is

  (55.7) N_ell(a,b)
           = b/pi [1/((ell-a)^2+b^2) - 1/((ell+a)^2+b^2)],

         p(ell) = integral_Q1 N_ell Omega dY,
         p'(ell) = integral_Q1 (partial_ell N_ell) Omega dY.

We justify the infinite integrals and the derivative. For ell in a compact subinterval of (0,infinity), N_ell and
partial_ell N_ell are O(r^(-2)) at infinity, uniformly in ell. Their products with Omega are O(r^(-2-h)), hence
integrable.

Near P_ell = (ell,0), smooth oddness in b gives Omega = O(b) and D Omega = O(b). With delta = |Y-P_ell|, the singular
terms satisfy

  (55.8) N_ell = O(b/delta^2),
         |(partial_ell N_ell) Omega| <= C/delta,
         |N_ell Omega|
           + |N_ell(D Omega + alpha Omega)| <= C

for each fixed real alpha. These bounds are locally integrable. There is no singularity at O.

To justify differentiation despite the moving singularity, choose a smooth cutoff chi, even in b, supported near P and
equal to one on a smaller neighbourhood. Its support is separated from a = 0. Write Omega = g + (1-chi)Omega, where g =
chi Omega. For ell close to L, the second summand stays away from the singularity. Dominated differentiation applies to
it, including at infinity.

For the singular term involving g, extend g by zero in a outside its support and set z = a-ell. Its integral becomes

  integral_{b>0} integral_R
      b g(ell+z,b)/(pi(z^2+b^2)) dz db.

Differentiate g rather than the kernel. Since g_a = O(b) and the translated supports lie in a fixed compact rectangle,
