the derivative integrand is bounded there by C b^2/(z^2+b^2). Dominated convergence applies. For each b > 0, integration
by parts in a transfers the derivative back to the kernel; (55.8) justifies integration of this equality over b. The
reflected term in (55.7) is smooth. This proves the derivative formula near L; the same argument centred at P_ell works
for every ell > 0. The formula for p follows from the C^1 convergence in Theorem 9 and the absolute bounds above.

Equations (55.6) and (55.7) give the first two identities in (55.3). For the last one, homogeneity gives

  (55.9) N_{t ell}(tY) = t^(-1) N_ell(Y),
         D_Y N_ell = -N_ell - ell partial_ell N_ell,
         div_Y(Y N_ell) = N_ell - ell partial_ell N_ell.

Apply the divergence theorem on Q1 cap B_R with the half-disc |Y-P_ell| <= epsilon removed, where R > 2ell. Letting
epsilon decrease to zero gives

  (55.10) integral_{Q1 cap B_R}
              N_ell(D Omega + alpha Omega) dY
            = integral_{Q1 cap B_R}
                [ell partial_ell N_ell + (alpha-1)N_ell] Omega dY
              + integral_{Q1 cap partial B_R}
                  (Y.n) N_ell Omega dS.

Here n is the outward unit normal. The straight axis pieces have Y.n = 0. On the small half-circle about P_ell, |Y.n| <=
ell+epsilon, N_ell Omega is bounded, and the length is pi epsilon. Its boundary contribution is O(epsilon). On the outer
arc, Y.n = R, N_ell = O(R^(-2)), Omega = O(R^(-h)), and the length is O(R). Its contribution is O(R^(-h)). Both boundary
terms therefore vanish in their respective limits, without decay assumptions on grad Omega.

Take ell = L and alpha = gamma in (55.10). Absolute convergence of M_L Omega proves the last identity in (55.3).

Smooth division by xy near O, using the origin jet, gives

  (55.11) Omega = xy [b0 + O(r^2)],       b0 = 2a0/(2beta+1),
          S = xy [(3+2h)b0 + O(r^2)].

The remainder may be differentiated here because the quotient is smooth and even in both variables. Thus sigma S > 0 in
a sufficiently small open quarter-disc.

Suppose sigma S >= 0 throughout Q1. The nonnegative functions 1_{B_R} N_L sigma S increase to N_L sigma S. Monotone
convergence and (55.3) would give integral_Q1 N_L sigma S = 0, although its integral over a fixed small interior ball is
positive. Equivalently, every sufficiently large disc integral would be bounded below by that fixed positive number.
This argument is valid when only disc-limit convergence has been established. Hence sigma S is negative somewhere, and
continuity gives an open set.

Finally, partial_r(r^gamma Omega) = r^(gamma-1) S, while (V) gives Theta_x - U.grad Omega + (beta+1)Omega = beta S. This
proves (55.4) and (55.5).

For actual A2-broad profiles, Theorems 36(b) and 42(a) give D Omega = O(r^(-h)). Together with (55.8) and N_L =
O(r^(-2)) at infinity, this proves absolute convergence of the radial integral. This strengthening is separate from the
derivative-free argument.

The exponent and other axis zeros. The same calculation proves, for every ell > 0 and every real alpha,

  (55.12) lim_{R -> infinity}
            integral_{Q1 cap B_R}
                N_ell(D Omega + alpha Omega) dY
              = ell p'(ell) + (alpha-1)p(ell).

These integrals are absolutely convergent for A2-broad profiles. At any positive x-axis zero P_ell, put mu = w'(ell).
Then p(ell) = beta ell and p'(ell) = beta-mu, so

  (55.13) integral_Q1 N_ell(D Omega + alpha Omega) dY
              = ell(alpha beta-mu).

No simplicity or nonzero-temperature-trace hypothesis is needed for this formula. Its right-hand side vanishes precisely
at alpha = mu/beta. At the first zero this is gamma, uniquely within this family of balances. The same gamma works at
another x-axis zero precisely when its slope is beta+2.

For example, Theorem 27 gives that slope at odd-indexed zeros when the first N positive zeros are all simple. At an
even-indexed zero in that chain, it gives mu = -(beta+2)/m for a positive integer m. The chain hypothesis cannot be
omitted. No uniqueness assertion among different kernels, or analogous assertion at an arbitrary interior point, follows
from this calculation. QED.

Remark 55.1 (checked obstructions to positive-weight arguments).

Assume beta > 2 and Omega > 0 on Q1. Theorem 21(c) gives a0 > 0, Theta > 0 on Q1 and (H1), so Theorem 50 applies. Let
Phi_t be the flow of W, and write Jac for the derivative matrix of a map. Put

  (55.14) kappa = beta-2,   lambda = beta+2,   d = 2beta-1,
          h = 1/beta,     q = 1-2h,
          K0(X) = xy/|X|^4,
          phi(X) = integral_0^infinity e^(dt) K0(Phi_t X) dt.

Then phi > 0, phi is C^1 on Q1, and phi_x takes both signs on every horizontal line y > 0. The ordered identity is

  (55.15) -integral_0^infinity [
              integral_0^infinity Theta(x,y) phi_x(x,y) dx
            ] dy = (pi/2)(beta+1).

Every inner integral is absolutely convergent, and its signed value is absolutely integrable in y. Nevertheless, with
z_+ = max(z,0) and z_- = max(-z,0),

  (55.16) integral_Q1 (Theta phi_x)_+ dX = infinity,
          integral_Q1 (Theta phi_x)_- dX = infinity.

Thus Theta phi_x has no two-dimensional Lebesgue integral.

Proof of regularity and (55.15). Theorems 41 and 42 give U = O(r^(1-h)) and Jac U = O(r^(-h)). For sufficiently large
initial radius r, the radial and variational equations give, uniformly for t >= 0,

  (55.17) Phi_t X = e^(beta t)[X + O(r^(1-h))],
          Jac Phi_t(X) = e^(beta t)[I + O(r^(-h))],
          phi = K0 + O(r^(-2-h)),
          phi_x = y(y^2-3x^2)/r^6 + O(r^(-3-h)).

Indeed, r(t) first grows at least exponentially. Integrating d log r(t)/dt = beta + O(r(t)^(-h)) then makes r(t)
comparable to r e^(beta t). Variation of constants gives the velocity correction, and the normalized variational
equation has coefficient Jac U(Phi_t X) with time integral O(r^(-h)). Homogeneity of K0 and its gradient makes the
integrands for phi and grad phi equal to e^(-t) times their respective leading terms and errors in (55.17). These
estimates justify differentiation under the integral.

Every orbit in Q1 escapes by Theorem 50(b). Compact neighbourhoods have a common finite escape time, so splitting the
defining integral at that time extends C^1 regularity to all of Q1. Under (H1), positive y-axis orbits and x-axis orbits
with x > L also escape. The same argument gives a C^1 extension across those axis segments, where phi = 0.

Positivity of K0 along Q1 orbits gives phi > 0. For fixed y > 0, phi tends to zero both as x decreases to zero and as x
tends to infinity. The mean value theorem gives both signs of phi_x on that line.

On a fixed horizontal line, near x = 0,

  phi = O(x),  phi_x = O(1),
  Theta = O(x^2),  Theta_x = O(x).

At infinity,

  phi = O(x^(-2)),  phi_x = O(x^(-3)),
  Theta = O(x^q),  Theta_x = O(x^(-2h)).

Thus both row integrands are absolutely integrable and the boundary product Theta phi vanishes. Horizontal integration
by parts gives integral Theta phi_x dx = -integral phi Theta_x dx. Theorem 50(d) gives integral_Q1 phi |Theta_x| <
infinity and integral_Q1 phi Theta_x = (pi/2)(beta+1), proving (55.15).

Proof of (55.16). Use the C^1 conjugacy H = (xi,eta) of Theorem 50(a), with A = Theta_y(P) > 0, eta = Theta/A, H(P) = 0,
Jac H(P) = I and det Jac H = 1. It is smooth inside Q1. Set

  (55.18) m = lambda/kappa > 1,
          rho = d/kappa = 2+3/kappa > 2,
          c = xi/eta^m,
          Z(c,s) = H^(-1)(c s^m,s).

Theorem 50(b) gives Phi_t Z(c,s) = Z(c,e^(kappa t)s) and dX = s^m dc ds. Consequently,

  (55.19) M(c) = (1/kappa) integral_0^infinity
                       v^(rho-1) K0(Z(c,v)) dv,

          Rem(c,s) = s^(-rho)/kappa integral_0^s
                       v^(rho-1) K0(Z(c,v)) dv,

          phi(Z(c,s)) = s^(-rho) M(c) - Rem(c,s).

The factor s^(-rho) is part of Rem.

Uniformly for c in a compact interval, the inverse chart gives K0(Z(c,v)) = O(v) and partial_c[K0(Z(c,v))] = O(v^m) near
v = 0. At infinity, a common escape time and (55.17) give |Z(c,v)| comparable to v^(beta/kappa) and |partial_c Z(c,v)| =
O(v^(beta/kappa)). The integrand defining M and its c derivative are therefore O(v^(-1-1/kappa)) there. These integrable
bounds prove M > 0 and M in C^1.

Fix a sufficiently small xi0 > 0 and set s_c = (xi0/c)^(1/m) for large positive c. The point H^(-1)(xi0,0) is on the
escaping x-axis segment x > L. The C^1 extension gives phi(H^(-1)(xi0,s_c)) = O(s_c). For 0 < v < s_c, the chart points
have 0 <= c v^m <= xi0 and remain in a fixed small rectangle near P, where K0(Z(c,v)) = O(v) uniformly. Equation (55.19)
gives

  (55.20) M(c) = O(s_c^(rho+1)) -> 0 as c -> +infinity.

A positive C^1 function tending to zero at positive infinity has negative derivative somewhere. Continuity gives a
compact interval I of positive length and m0 > 0 with M' <= -m0 on I.

Uniformly on I, differentiation gives

  (55.21) Rem = O(s),       Rem_c = O(s^m),       Rem_s = O(1),
          eta_x = O(s),    xi_x = 1+o(1),
          c_x = s^(-m)xi_x - m c s^(-1)eta_x,

          phi_x(Z(c,s))
              = s^(-rho-m)[M'(c)+o(1)] + O(s^(-rho)).

The first line follows from the small-v estimates; explicitly, Rem_s = -rho Rem/s + K0(Z(c,s))/(kappa s). Also Theta_x =
O(y) near P by oddness in y, and eta is comparable to y, giving eta_x = O(s). The C^1 normalization gives xi_x -> 1
uniformly. On differentiating the last equation of (55.19), the terms containing eta_x are O(s^(-rho)), while Rem_c
c_x + Rem_s eta_x is O(1). This proves the stated remainder and requires only C^1 regularity at the axis, including resonant
values of m.

Hence phi_x <= -C s^(-rho-m) on I for small s. Since Theta(Z(c,s)) = A s and dX = s^m dc ds,

  (55.22) integral_{Z(I x (0,epsilon))} (Theta phi_x)_- dX
              >= C integral_0^epsilon s^(1-rho) ds = infinity.

Let B(y) and N(y) be the x integrals of (Theta phi_x)_+ and (Theta phi_x)_-. Both are finite for every y > 0 by the row
estimates, and B-N is absolutely integrable in y by (55.15). If integral B were finite, N <= B+|B-N| would contradict
(55.22). This proves both assertions in (55.16).

Temperature-only weights. Every continuous F:(0,infinity) -> [0,infinity) that is not identically zero satisfies

  (55.23) integral_Q1 F(Theta) Omega dX = infinity.

Write v(y) = W_2(0,y), E(y) = Theta_xx(0,y)/2 and K(y) = Omega_x(0,y). Under (H1), v > 0 on the positive y-axis. The
trace calculation in Theorem 50(c) gives

  E(y) ~ e0 y^(-1-2h),    K(y) ~ k0 y^(-1-h),

with e0,k0 > 0. To check strict positivity of the constants, its temperature equation gives E'/E = -(1+2h)/y +
O(y^(-1-h)), with E positive. For the vorticity equation, the positive homogeneous solution

  H0(y) = v(y) exp(-(2beta+1) integral_1^y dt/v(t))

is asymptotic to positive multiples of y^((beta+1)/(3beta+2)) at zero and y^(-1-h) at infinity. Variation of constants
gives

  K(y) = H0(y) integral_0^y 2E(t)/(v(t)H0(t)) dt.

The integrand is positive, O(t^(-(beta+1)/(3beta+2))) at zero, and O(t^(-1-h)) at infinity. Its total integral is finite
and strictly positive, proving k0 > 0.

For z in a compact subinterval of (0,infinity), set x = z y^(1/2+h). Since h < 1/2, x/y tends to zero. Parity and
Theorem 42(a), using fourth derivatives of Theta and third derivatives of Omega, give uniformly in z

  (55.24) Theta(x,y)
              = E(y)x^2 + O(x^4 y^(-3-2h))
              = e0 z^2 + o(1),

          Omega(x,y)
              = K(y)x + O(x^3 y^(-3-h))
              = y^(-1/2)[k0 z+o(1)].

The temperature Taylor error is O(y^(-1+2h)); the vorticity Taylor error has the same relative order. Both vanish.
Choose a z interval on which F(e0 z^2) has a strictly positive lower bound. Uniform convergence preserves a positive
lower bound for F(Theta). Since dx = y^(1/2+h) dz, this interval contributes at least C y^h to the x integral for all
sufficiently large y. Nonnegativity and Tonelli prove (55.23).

Exact local compatibility. For every beta > 0, with lambda = beta+2, the fields

  (55.25) Psi = [beta x + (lambda/2)sin(2x)]y,
          Omega = 2lambda sin(2x)y,
          Theta = 2lambda(2beta+1)sin^2(x)y

solve the profile equations on the whole plane and have the A2 parities and origin jet. Direct differentiation gives

  W_1 = -(lambda/2)sin(2x),
  W_2 = [2beta+lambda cos(2x)]y,
  -Lap Psi = Omega,
  W.grad Omega = 2beta Omega,
  Theta_x = (2beta+1)Omega,
  W.grad Theta = (beta-2)Theta.

Thus both transport equations hold. Theta and Omega are positive on 0 < x < pi/2, y > 0. For beta >= 2, the smooth
vorticity trace 2lambda sin(2x) realizes the zero fractional coefficient in the axis calculation of Theorem 14; that
calculation uses only the axis equations and boundedness at the first zero. The first positive axis zero is pi/2 and has
slope beta+2.

However, U_1(x,0)/x tends to -beta, so these fields fail A2-broad. This family is already present in the report. It
proves local compatibility and does not construct an admissible profile.

Weak sign. Every assertion of this remark, including (55.23), remains true when Omega > 0 on Q1 is weakened to
Omega >= 0 on Q1. Under the weak sign, Theorem 57(a), whose proof does not use this remark, gives a0 > 0, Theta > 0 on
Q1 and (H1), so Theorem 50 applies, and (57.3) gives v > 0 and E > 0 on the positive y-axis. The arguments above use the
sign of Omega only through these facts and through the nonnegativity of the integrand in (55.23).

All assertions of this remark are proved under their stated hypotheses. Positivity of phi and the balance before
horizontal integration by parts are already in Theorem 50(d). The ordered identity, both infinite parts in (55.16), and
the divergence in (55.23) follow from the checks above. None supplies an exclusion of the positive A2-broad class. QED.

Remark 55.2 (the fixed moments of Theorems 9 and 55 admit a positive measure).

Fix beta > 2 and L > 0, let h = 1/beta, and use N_L and M_L of (55.1), (55.2) and K0(Y) = ab/|Y|^4 for Y = (a,b) in Q1.
For an A2-broad profile whose first positive x-axis zero of W is (L,0), (55.3) fixes the N_L and M_L moments of Omega,
and Theorem 9 with c = 2 beta + 2, together with the parities, gives

  (55.26) lim_{R -> infinity} integral_{Q1 cap B_R} K0 Omega dY = (pi/2)(beta+1).

As a linear moment, the third identity in (55.3) adds nothing to the second: its proof, (55.10) with ell = L and
alpha = gamma, converts it into the M_L moment.

For t > 0 put Y_t = (L t^(1/4)/sqrt(2))(1,1), and let

  eta = 2(beta+3)/(beta(3beta+5)),   t_* = 1/(beta+2),
  (55.27) mu = beta L [ (1-eta) delta(Y_3)/N_L(Y_3) + eta delta(Y_{t_*})/N_L(Y_{t_*}) ],

where delta(Y) is the unit point mass at Y. Then mu is a positive measure on Q1 with two atoms, and

  (55.28) integral N_L dmu = beta L,   integral M_L dmu = 0,   integral K0 dmu = (pi/2)(beta+1).

Moreover, if u, v, w are real and H = u K0 + v N_L + w M_L is nonnegative on Q1 and not identically zero, then

  (55.29) u (pi/2)(beta+1) + v beta L > 0.

Consequently no linear positivity certificate built from these three fixed kernels (with coefficients constant on Q1), together with Omega >= 0 on Q1, or
Omega > 0 on Q1, can exclude the class. Such an argument needs a nonnegative H, not identically zero, whose moment value
u(pi/2)(beta+1) + v beta L is negative, or is zero when Omega > 0 on Q1 is assumed; (55.29) rules out both. The measure
mu is not a profile and is not claimed to satisfy either transport equation. The remark does not concern arguments that
use the transport equations, flow-dependent weights such as phi_K in (50.3) or phi in (55.14), the origin jet beyond
these moments, or the source basin of the first positive x-axis zero (L, 0) of W.

Proof. Here 1 - eta = 3(beta-1)(beta+2)/(beta(3beta+5)) > 0 and eta > 0, and N_L > 0 on Q1, so mu is positive. At Y_t,
a = b and a^2 + b^2 = L^2 t^(1/2), so Q_L(Y_t) = (L^2 + a^2 + b^2)^2 - 4L^2 a^2 = L^4(1+t), and (55.1) and the second
form of (55.2) give

  K0/N_L = pi(1+t)/(4Lt),   M_L/N_L = 1 + 2h - 4/(1+t)   at Y_t.

At t = 3 these are pi/(3L) and 2h. At t = t_*, where 1/t_* = beta+2 and 1 + t_* = (beta+3)/(beta+2), they are
pi(beta+3)/(4L) and -3(beta+2)(beta-1)/(beta(beta+3)). The N_L moment of mu is beta L(1 - eta + eta) = beta L. The M_L
moment is L[2(1-eta) - 3 eta (beta+2)(beta-1)/(beta+3)] = 0, because both terms equal 6(beta-1)(beta+2)/(beta(3beta+5)).
The K0 moment is

  pi beta [(1-eta)/3 + eta(beta+3)/4] = pi[2(beta-1)(beta+2) + (beta+3)^2]/(2(3beta+5))
                                      = pi(3beta+5)(beta+1)/(2(3beta+5)) = (pi/2)(beta+1).

This proves (55.28). For (55.29), the left side equals integral H dmu >= 0. Suppose it is zero. Since both atoms have
positive mass, H(Y_3) = 0, so H/N_L has an interior minimum 0 at Y_3 and its gradient vanishes there. The map
(a,b) -> (t,d) = (|Y|^4/L^4, (a^2-b^2)/L^2) has Jacobian determinant -16ab(a^2+b^2)/L^6 != 0 on Q1, and since
Q_L = L^4(1 + t - 2d),

  K0/N_L = pi(t + 1 - 2d)/(4Lt),   M_L/N_L = 1 + 2h - 4(1-d)/(t + 1 - 2d).

At (t,d) = (3,0) the t and d derivatives of H/N_L are -pi u/(36L) + w/4 and -pi u/(6L) + w/2. Their vanishing gives
u = w = 0, the determinant being pi/(36L) != 0. Then H(Y_3) = v N_L(Y_3) = 0 gives v = 0, contradicting that H is not
identically zero. QED.

Scope. This rules out one strategy, a linear positivity certificate built from the three fixed kernels, in the stated
restricted sense. It is not a statement about profiles. The coupled transport identities, including (50.3) and (55.15),
are not fixed kernels acting on an arbitrary measure and are not covered.

### Theorem 56 (beta = 2: connections, incoming endpoints and conditional sources)

Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2. In particular, the fields are smooth on R^2, Theta and
Omega have at most polynomial growth, U(X) = o(|X|) uniformly, and U has zero divergence. The temperature is even in x
and odd in y, Omega is odd in both variables, U_1 is odd in x and even in y, and U_2 is even in x and odd in y. The A2
jet is Theta(0,y) = 0 and Theta = x^2 y a(x^2,y^2) near O = (0,0), where a is smooth and a(0,0) != 0.

Write X = (x,y), W = 2X + U, Z = {W = 0}, Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, and Crit = {grad Theta = 0}. The equations are

  div W = 4,    d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = Omega,
  W.grad Theta = 0,    W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x.       (56.1)

Let Phi_t be the complete flow of W and pi(X) its backward limit, whose existence for every X is supplied by 44(b). Let
P = (x1,0) be the first positive x-axis zero, C its zero component, Q+ the endpoint of C in Q1, Q- its reflection across
the x-axis, and M = Theta(Q+). Write r = |X| and phi for the polar angle, and U_r and U_phi for the radial and angular
components of U. Write H and G for the smooth angular limits Theta(r,phi) and r^(1/2) Omega(r,phi) from 36. Let Ly be
the function of 44, normalized by Ly(O) = 0. With W^perp = (-W_2,W_1),

  grad Ly = 3W + Omega W^perp + y grad Theta,
  W.grad Ly = 3|W|^2,    d Ly = y d Theta on Z.              (56.2)

The last equality means equality after restriction to a smooth zero arc. An endpoint is incoming or outgoing only when
the opposite branch of a local invariant centre curve is zero-free sufficiently near it; the terms refer to forward flow
towards or away from that endpoint. Otherwise it is accumulating. A zero is regular if grad Theta != 0. An isolated zero
has a neighbourhood containing no other zero.

(a) Let gamma be a nonstationary orbit anywhere in R^2, with backward limit A and finite forward limit B. The limits lie
in distinct components of Z. At most one orbit joins a fixed unordered pair of distinct zero components. Moreover,

  Theta(A) = Theta(B),
  Ly(B) - Ly(A) = 3 int_{-infinity}^{infinity}
                         |W(Phi_t X)|^2 dt > 0,  X in gamma. (56.3)

If gamma lies in Q1, at least one of its endpoint components lies wholly in Q1. Consequently, if no component of Z lies
wholly in Q1, both Q+ and Q- are outgoing and every nonstationary orbit in Q1 escapes to infinity in forward time. This
assertion requires neither isolation nor finiteness of the zero components.

Under this component exclusion, all the potential-region and local-side conclusions of 35 and 51 hold at Q+, for the
actual value M = Theta(Q+), including M = 0. Specifically, arbitrarily small neighbourhoods of Q+ contain a connected
open backward invariant set tending
backwards to Q+. Its forward saturation is an open connected invariant subset of Q1 of infinite area, with Theta = M and
Omega = 0; U is harmonic and real analytic on this region. There is a smooth local strong unstable curve Gamma through
Q+. For any such curve and any local C^2 invariant centre curve, a sufficiently small disc B about Q+ in Q1 has a side
B+ opposite to the terminal zero arc, every point of which has backward limit Q+. On B+, Theta = M and Omega = 0; all
derivatives of Theta-M and Omega vanish on Gamma cap B. The function U_1-i U_2 is holomorphic on B+, has no holomorphic
continuation agreeing with it to a disc about Q+, and no real-analytic local invariant curve through Q+ is tangent to
the eigenvector for 4. The reflected statements hold at Q- with temperature -M.

There is a nonempty open angular interval on which H = M and G = 0. In particular,

  |{Theta = M} cap Q1| = infinity,
  int_{{Theta=M} cap Q1} r^(-3) U_r dX
    = -|{phi in (0,pi/2): H(phi)=M}| < 0.                  (56.4)

Here and below the two measures in this formula are planar and angular Lebesgue measure. Identifying the angular level
set with one interval still requires additional hypotheses, as in 48(e).

(b) Suppose Q+ is incoming. Let gamma be the complete orbit containing its opposite centre branch, and suppose gamma
meets an open set V contained in Q1 such that Phi_t(V) = V for all real t and Theta = M on V. For a smooth local strong
unstable curve Gamma, the side B+ of a sufficiently small disc B opposite to C satisfies

  B+ subset V,    Theta = M and Omega = 0 on B+.            (56.5)

Every derivative of Theta-M and Omega vanishes on Gamma cap B. The full flow saturation of B+ is open, connected,
invariant, of infinite area, and has Theta = M and Omega = 0. It supplies an open angular interval with H = M and G = 0,
and (56.4) holds.

If V is the open backward basin {X in Q1: pi(X)=S} of a zero S, every point of B+ has backward limit S. This does not
include Gamma, whose sufficiently small points have backward limit Q+.

Under these hypotheses Theta cannot be constant on any nontrivial terminal subarc of C ending at Q+. No sign restriction
on M and no finiteness hypothesis are needed in this part.

(c) Suppose Z has finitely many components, Q+ is incoming, and k = 0 in (53.9). With eps = ind(C), I_Q the sum of the
indices of components wholly in Q1, and n_+ and n_- their respective numbers of components of index +1 and -1,

  eps = -1,    I_Q = 1,    n_+ = n_- + 1.                 (56.6)

Components of index zero do not enter this equality. Here k is the integer defined by I_A = -2k in (53.9). The sum I_A
takes one component from each other axis reflection pair, chosen to meet a positive half-axis, and excludes O, C and the
reflection of C across the y-axis. The integer k is not the number of all such pairs.

Independently of finiteness or the direction of Q+, every isolated zero S of index +1 is either a hyperbolic source with
two positive real eigenvalues summing to 4, or has spectrum {0,4} and two outgoing centre half-branches. In both cases a
full neighbourhood of S has backward limit S and satisfies Theta = Theta(S), Omega = 0.

In the second case W is real analytic near S. In orthonormal coordinates (u,v) centred at S with DW(S) = diag(4,0),
solve W_u = 0 as u = h(v) and put g(v) = W_v(h(v),v). There exist an integer j >= 1 and a constant a > 0 such that

  g(v) = a v^(2j+1) + O(v^(2j+2)).                         (56.7)

The scalar velocity on a C^2 invariant centre graph u = kappa(v), with the same v-coordinate, has the same leading term.
No analyticity of that invariant graph is asserted.

The remaining positive-index component type is an isolated arc with two outgoing endpoints. Its classification and the
impossibility of a constant terminal temperature at either endpoint are already given by 53(e)-(f). Such an arc need not
be a source with a single-point backward basin.

(d) Assume M > 0 and every zero in the closed first quadrant with temperature in (0,M) is regular. There is one integer
N >= 1, independent of c in (0,M), such that

  #{Q in Z cap Q1: Theta(Q)=c} = N,
  #{phi in (0,pi/2): H(phi)=c} = 2N.                       (56.8)

Every angle counted here has H' != 0. The number of these zeros on the half-arc C[P,Q+] is odd. The set {phi in
(0,pi/2): H(phi)>0} has exactly N components. Each has a strictly increasing passage through (0,M), a nonempty connected
central set where H >= M, and a strictly decreasing passage through (0,M). On the two passages H' is nonzero.

If, in addition,

  closure(Theta(Q1)) = [0,M],                              (56.9)

each central set is a closed interval on which H = M, possibly a single point. Every nonconstant zero arc wholly in Q1
has temperature range [0,M], hence contributes at least one zero at each intermediate level. If its endpoint
temperatures agree, it contributes at least two. Part (d) does not require finiteness of all zero components.

(e) Assume Z has finitely many components, Q+ is incoming, M > 0, (56.9) holds, all zeros in the closed first quadrant
at temperatures in (0,M) are regular, and N = 1 in (56.8). Let q(c) be the unique zero of temperature c in Q1 and put
L_C = Ly(Q+). The temperature along C[P,Q+], oriented from P to Q+, is nondecreasing, and

  q(c) in C[P,Q+],    Ly(q(c)) -> L_C as c increases to M.  (56.10)

Every zero in the set

  S_M = {S in Z cap Q1: Theta(S)=M, Ly(S)<L_C}              (56.11)

is isolated and has a full neighbourhood on which Theta = M and Omega = 0. The set S_M is nonempty and finite. Every
minimizer of Ly on S_M is an isolated index +1 source of one of the two types in (c).

The actual backward limit of the orbit entering Q+ belongs to S_M, but need not be this minimizer. Part (b) applies to
that orbit without requiring its backward limit to have an open individual basin. The arc C satisfies

  (R) C minus {Q+,Q-} is contained in {grad Theta != 0}.     (56.12)

There is one positive angular excursion, with a strictly increasing part, a plateau of positive length at M, and a
strictly decreasing part. Zero intervals next to either axis are still allowed. These conclusions use no assumption
k = 0.

(f) In the accumulating configuration of 53(c), let gamma_n be its connecting orbit from A_n to B_n, and choose X_n in
gamma_n. Then

  0 < int_{-infinity}^{infinity} |W(Phi_t X_n)|^2 dt
      = (Ly(B_n)-Ly(A_n))/3 -> 0.                          (56.13)

The necessity of infinitely many distinct components is already part of 53(c). Formula (56.13) is its energy corollary,
not an exclusion of accumulation.

(g) For every lambda > 0 and every real C^1 function F on a neighbourhood of Theta(R^2),

  int_Q1 F(Theta) exp(-lambda Ly)
                  (4 - 3 lambda |W|^2) dX = 0.             (56.14)

The integral is absolutely convergent. The same statement holds with F(Theta) replaced by 1_{Theta=c}, for any fixed
real c.

Scope. All parts are necessary conditions on a hypothetical profile. They establish neither existence nor nonexistence
in A2-broad at beta = 2. M > 0 and (56.9) are additional hypotheses in the parts that use them; they are not a sign
normalization or consequences of an incoming endpoint. The range and fixed-level counting identities, the finite index
balance, and the accumulating-component assertion are those of 53. The hyperbolic source conclusion is already in 47(d).
The outgoing potential-region and analytic conclusions are applications of 35 and the local formulation of 51. No new
isothermal identity is asserted beyond 53(i). Here (S) means Z cap Q1 = C cap Q1, (R) is (56.12), (X) means W_1(x,0) > 0
for x > x1, and (Y) means W_2(0,y) > 0 for y > 0. None is automatic; the axis refinements in 48(e) retain (X) and (Y).
The weighted identity (56.14) supplies no nonexistence conclusion.

Proof.

Theorems 44(b) and 48(a) give single backward limits for every orbit and single forward zero limits for bounded forward
orbits. Uniform sublinearity gives a radius R0 with W_r >= r for r >= R0. An orbit reaching this region escapes, so a
nonescaping forward orbit is bounded. Theorem 53(a) gives the structure of every zero component: a singleton or a
compact smooth embedded arc. A component meeting an axis is contained in it or crosses it transversely exactly once; no
arc meets both axes. We use these facts without any assumption that all components are isolated.

(a) Integration of (56.2) along an orbit, followed by passage to its two finite limits, proves (56.3). Its integrand is
positive somewhere and nonnegative everywhere. In particular A != B.

The closure of gamma is an embedded closed arc with endpoints A and B. Indeed, compactify the time parameter to a closed
interval. The resulting map is continuous and injective: an interior repetition would make the orbit periodic, contrary
to strict increase of Ly, and an interior orbit point cannot be a zero. A continuous injection of a compact interval
into the plane is an embedding.

If A and B belonged to one zero component, that component would be an arc, and its subarc between A and B would close
gamma to a Jordan curve. This curve is invariant under every Phi_t, since the orbit is preserved and its zero subarc is
fixed pointwise. Its bounded complementary domain is therefore invariant. Its area would equal exp(4t) times itself,
which is impossible for a nonempty bounded open domain. This is the argument of 48(b), and it applies in the whole
plane.

If two distinct orbits joined the same two distinct components, their interiors would be disjoint by uniqueness. Join
their endpoints within each zero component by its unique zero subarc, allowing a subarc to collapse to a point when the
endpoints coincide. These two zero subarcs and the two orbit closures form a Jordan curve: their only intersections are
the prescribed endpoints. It is invariant and gives the same area contradiction. The orientations of the two connections
are irrelevant.

Now let gamma lie in Q1, and suppose neither endpoint component lies wholly there. Neither limit can be O. At O, DW(O) =
diag(-4,8); its local stable and unstable curves are respectively the invariant x- and y-axes. A nonstationary orbit
with forward or backward limit O must therefore lie on an axis, contrary to gamma subset Q1.

For an endpoint already on an axis, choose that endpoint as R_A or R_B. For an endpoint in Q1, its component meets an
axis: otherwise connectedness and avoidance of both axes put the whole component in Q1. Such a component is a crossing
arc. Join the endpoint to its unique axis intersection by the zero subarc, whose remaining points lie in Q1. These
constructions produce an embedded compact invariant arc J from R_A to R_B, with its interior in Q1. The two endpoints
are different because their zero components are different. Both lie on positive half-axes and neither is O.

If R_A and R_B lie on the same positive half-axis, close J by the axis interval between them. If they lie on different
positive half-axes, close J by the two axis intervals from them to O. Every added interval is invariant: its endpoints
are equilibria and the axis flow cannot cross them. These intervals meet J only at its endpoints, so in each case the
union is an invariant Jordan curve. The same area contradiction excludes both cases. This includes connections with an
endpoint on C, since C meets the positive x-axis at P.

Under the component exclusion in (a), a nonstationary orbit in Q1 cannot have a bounded forward orbit, by the preceding
argument and the two limit theorems. Thus it escapes. An incoming Q+ would itself give a nonstationary orbit in Q1 with
finite forward limit. Accumulation at Q+ would give components wholly in Q1 by 53(c). Both alternatives are excluded, so
Q+ is outgoing; reflection gives the same at Q-.

The hypotheses of 35 and of the local outgoing formulation of 51 are now satisfied: the endpoint is in Q1, has spectrum
{0,4}, terminates a smooth zero arc, and its opposite centre branch is zero-free and outgoing. Those proofs do not
require M != 0. In the continuation argument of 51, the purported analytic extension produces zeros on B+; these are
impossible because every point of B+ has backward limit Q+. Thus the argument uses no further zero exclusion. The
angular interval follows from 35, and (56.4) follows by taking b = 1 in (53.12), including when M = 0. Only the escape
assertion here enlarges the escape hypothesis in 53(d); its outgoing conclusion was already stated under the present
component exclusion.

(b) The coordinate construction in 51 first straightens the smooth strong unstable curve to s = 0 and then a C^2
invariant centre curve to z = 0. This construction uses their transversality and invariance, not the direction of the
centre flow. It gives a box about Q+ = (0,0) with

  s' = s B(s,z),    z' = z A(s,z),    A >= 2,
  |B(s,z)-B(s,0)| <= K |z|,
  B(s,0) < 0 for s > 0,    B(s,0) = 0 for s <= 0.         (56.15)

The terminal zero arc is z = 0, s <= 0. The last equality holds because W vanishes there, regardless of its temperature.
The estimate for B follows by dividing the smooth s-component by s before making the C^2 centre change; division of an
arbitrary C^1 transformed field is not being used to assert this Lipschitz estimate.

The terminal incoming orbit lies in z = 0. Otherwise its nonzero |z| would grow at least exponentially while its forward
orbit remains in the box, preventing convergence to Q+. Choose a small d > 0 on this orbit. Invariance of V puts (d,0)
in V, and openness gives a strip {s=d, |z|<eta} contained in V.

In backward time tau, until a trajectory starting with 0 < s0 < d and |z0| < eta leaves that strip-shaped box, (56.15)
gives

  |z(tau)| <= |z0| exp(-2tau),
  s(tau) >= s0 exp(-K |z0|/2) > 0.                        (56.16)

For the second inequality, integrate d_tau log s = -B(s,z) >= -K|z|. Thus exit cannot occur through s = 0 or |z| = eta.
If the trajectory never reaches s = d, its s-coordinate remains in a compact subinterval of (0,d]. On that interval
B(s,0) is bounded above by a negative constant. Since z tends to zero, d_tau log s is eventually bounded below by a
positive constant. This contradicts s <= d. Every such point therefore reaches the chosen strip in finite backward time.
Choosing B small enough puts its entire positive side in this box, proving B+ subset V.

Theta = M on the open set B+, hence B+ lies in Crit. By 44(d), Omega = 0 there. All derivatives of both smooth functions
Theta-M and Omega vanish on B+ and therefore on its boundary portion Gamma cap B. Flow invariance of Theta and Crit
propagates these properties to the full saturation E = union_{t in R} Phi_t(B+). This is open and connected, the latter
because it is the continuous image of R times B+. It is invariant and has positive area. If its area were finite, |E| =
exp(4t)|E| would be impossible. Thus its area is infinite.

Choose a launch radius beyond R0 and larger than |X| for every X in B+. The connected unbounded set E meets this circle,
and its openness gives a nonempty open arc on it. The corresponding orbits escape and remain in E. The exit-angle
diffeomorphism of 36 gives an open angular interval with H = M and G = 0. Formula (56.4) follows from 53(i). In the
basin case, B+ subset V also proves the asserted backward limit S.

Suppose now that the terminal zero arc has temperature M. For negative s, (56.15) and backward decay of z give

  |log(-s(tau)) - log(-s0)| <= K |z0|/2.                   (56.17)

Start in a smaller negative half-box, with |s0| less than half the available width and exp(K|z0|/2) < 2. The bounds
prevent exit, keep s away from zero for each fixed starting point, and make d_tau log(-s) absolutely integrable. Thus s
converges to a negative value on the chosen terminal zero arc and z tends to zero. Temperature invariance gives Theta =
M on a full smaller negative side. Together with (56.5) and continuity on Gamma, this makes Theta constant on a full
neighbourhood of Q+, contrary to 16. This proves the terminal-subarc exclusion.

(c) Under finiteness, every component is isolated: each compact component has positive distance from the finite union of
the others. Reflection across the x-axis interchanges the endpoints of C and preserves the vector field and its forward
direction. Thus both endpoints are incoming. Formula (53.7), not k = 0, gives eps = (-1-1)/2 = -1. Formula (53.9) then
gives I_Q = 1. Every component index is -1, 0 or +1 by 53(f) and the classification below, so (56.6) follows.

For precision about k, let j(D) be the scalar index of the intersection of an additional axis representative D with its
positive half-axis, as in the proof of 53(f). That proof gives ind(D)-j(D) in {0,-2} and sum_D j(D) = 0. Thus k counts
the representatives with deficit ind(D)-j(D) = -2. Representatives with zero deficit may still be present when k = 0.

An isolated singleton is critical by 53(a). By 44(d), its derivative is symmetric with trace 4, so its eigenvalues are
real. If neither is zero, its index is the sign of their product. Index +1 forces both positive; 47(d) supplies the
stated basin and potential neighbourhood. If an eigenvalue is zero, the spectrum is {0,4}. Formula (53.7) for its two
centre half-branches shows that index +1 means both are outgoing.

To check the basin assertion in this degenerate case, use the simultaneous coordinates of (56.15), now with B(s,0) > 0
for both signs of s != 0. On either side put r_s = |s|. In backward time,

  |z(tau)| <= |z0| exp(-2tau),
  d_tau log r_s <= -B(s,0) + K |z|,
  r_s(tau) <= |s0| exp(K |z0|/2).                          (56.18)

Starting in a smaller box prevents exit. Put I(tau) = K int_0^tau |z(v)| dv. The quantity r_s exp(-I) is nonincreasing
and I has a finite limit, so r_s has a limit. A positive limit would make B(s,0) uniformly positive eventually,
contradicting convergence of r_s and (56.18). Hence s and z tend to zero. Points on the strong unstable curve do so as
well. A full neighbourhood therefore has backward limit S. Temperature invariance and 44(d) give Theta = Theta(S), Omega
= 0 there.

Zero curl and constant divergence make both components of W harmonic in this neighbourhood, hence real analytic. The
analytic implicit function theorem gives h in (56.7). Isolation implies that the analytic germ g is not identically
zero. Also g(0) = g'(0) = 0. Eliminating the positive u-direction preserves local degree; equivalently, in coordinates
u-h(v), the first component is a positive factor times u-h(v), and the remaining component can be homotoped to g(v)
without introducing boundary zeros. Its scalar degree is therefore +1. The first nonzero Taylor term of g consequently
has positive coefficient and odd order at least three, proving (56.7).

This nullcline is not assumed invariant. To compare it with a C^2 invariant centre graph u = kappa(v), factor W_u(u,v) =
a_1(u,v)(u-h(v)), where a_1(0,0) = 4. Write q(v) = W_v(kappa(v),v). Invariance and the mean value formula give

  kappa-h = kappa' q/a_1,
  q = g + b_1(kappa-h),
  q (1 - b_1 kappa'/a_1) = g.                             (56.19)

Here a_1 is evaluated on the centre graph and b_1 is the average of partial_u W_v between the two graphs. Both graphs
are O(v^2), kappa' = O(v), and partial_u W_v(0,0) = 0, so b_1 = O(v). The parenthesis is 1 + O(v^2). This proves that q
has the same leading term as g. It does not imply that the centre graph is analytic.

(d) Fix c0 in (0,M). Formula (53.11) and its hypotheses give finitely many regular zeros of temperature c0, all in Q1.
Near each, 39(b) makes Theta a coordinate on its zero arc. Choose disjoint such neighbourhoods. The remainder of Z in
the closed quadrant is compact after removing these open neighbourhoods and contains no zero of temperature c0. Its
temperature stays a positive distance from c0. Shrinking a temperature interval about c0 therefore gives exactly one
zero in each of the chosen neighbourhoods and no others. The number of zeros is locally constant, hence constant on
(0,M). It is positive because Theta on C[P,Q+] joins 0 to M. Formula (53.11) now gives (56.8) and the nonvanishing
angular derivatives.

At a specified regular level c, the crossings along C[P,Q+] are transverse. Its endpoint values are below and above c,
so the number of upward crossings minus downward crossings is one. The total number is odd.

Each positive component of H has value zero at both ends, including an axis endpoint if present. Its positive maximum
cannot belong to (0,M), since H' does not vanish at such a value. Thus the component reaches M. If two points of its set
{H >= M} had an intervening point with H < M, the minimum between them would be a positive critical value below M,
impossible. This central set is therefore connected. Before it H increases strictly through (0,M), and after it H
decreases strictly through (0,M); any derivative zero there is excluded by (56.8). Each positive component supplies
exactly two roots of every intermediate level. There are exactly N such components.

Under (56.9), 53(h) gives 0 <= H <= M, so every central set is a closed M-level interval. For a nonconstant compact zero
arc wholly in Q1, both its extrema are critical zero values. An endpoint is critical by 53(a); at an interior extremum,
regularity would contradict the local coordinate property of Theta on Z. The extrema therefore cannot lie in (0,M). They
must be 0 and M. Endpoints themselves have temperatures in {0,M}; if equal, any intermediate level is crossed at least
twice. This proves the remaining assertions.

(e) Since C[P,Q+] joins temperatures 0 and M, the unique zero q(c) lies on this half-arc. If the temperature decreased
between two ordered points of the half-arc, an intermediate value between their temperatures would also be crossed
before the first and after the second, using the endpoint values 0 and M. This would give at least three distinct zeros
at that intermediate level. Thus the temperature is nondecreasing.

Its M-level set is a terminal closed subarc, possibly just Q+. On this subarc d Theta = 0, so (56.2) makes Ly constant,
with value L_C. Every subsequential limit of q(c) as c increases to M lies in that subarc. Compactness and continuity
prove (56.10).

For every X in Q1 with Theta(X) = c in (0,M), 44(b) gives a backward limit in Z cap closure(Q1). Its temperature is c.
It cannot lie on an axis, where Theta = 0, so it equals q(c). Monotonicity of Ly yields

  Ly(X) >= Ly(q(c)).                                       (56.20)

Fix S in S_M and choose ell with Ly(S) < ell < L_C. By (56.10), Ly(q(c)) > ell for c < M sufficiently close to M. Choose
a ball about S inside Q1 on which Ly < ell and Theta is this close to M. By (56.9), Theta <= M throughout the ball. Any
smaller value would contradict (56.20). Hence Theta = M on the ball, and 44(d) gives Omega = 0.

It remains to prove that the component of S is a singleton. It is not C, since the M-level portion of C in Q1 has Ly =
L_C. If its component were an arc meeting an axis, the zero subarc from that axis, of temperature 0, to S would provide
an additional zero at each intermediate level, contrary to N = 1. If it were a nonconstant arc wholly in Q1, part (d)
gives the same contradiction. The only remaining arc possibility is a constant-temperature arc at M wholly in Q1. Ly is
constant on it by (56.2), with value below L_C. The preceding neighbourhood argument would then apply at either
endpoint, making Theta = M and Omega = 0 on a full neighbourhood of that endpoint, contrary to 53(a). Thus the component
is a singleton; finiteness of the components makes it an isolated zero.

The incoming orbit at Q+ has an actual backward limit A in a component wholly in Q1, with Theta(A) = M and Ly(A) < L_C,
by 53(b). Thus S_M is nonempty. Its points belong to distinct singleton components, so it is finite. The potential
neighbourhood just proved for A meets the incoming orbit at sufficiently negative time. Its full saturation is an open
invariant constant-temperature set in Q1. Part (b) applies and excludes a nontrivial terminal M-subarc of C.

The initial zero-temperature subarc of C[P,Q+] is also trivial. Otherwise Theta would have zero derivative along C at P,
contrary to its regularity from 2 and the regular zero coordinate in 39(b). Monotonicity now puts every other interior
point of C[P,Q+] at a temperature in (0,M), so it is regular by hypothesis. Reflection and regularity at P give (56.12).
Part (d) gives one positive angular excursion; part (b) makes its central M-level interval have positive length.

Choose any minimizer S of Ly on the finite nonempty set S_M. It has no nonstationary incoming orbit. Indeed, such an
orbit lies in Q1 because it is eventually near S and the axes are invariant. Its backward limit T exists by 44(b);
temperature invariance and M > 0 put T in Q1. Formula (56.3) gives Ly(T) < Ly(S) < L_C and Theta(T) = M. Thus T belongs
to S_M, contradicting minimality.

By 44(d), DW(S) is symmetric with trace 4. A hyperbolic saddle would have incoming stable separatrices. In the
degenerate case {0,4}, isolation makes both centre half-branches zero-free near S. If one is incoming, its scalar flow
is monotone towards S and converges to S in forward time. It cannot reach S in finite time by uniqueness for a C^1
vector field. The complete global flow extends it backwards, and 44(b) supplies its backward zero limit. It is therefore
an incoming orbit in exactly the sense just excluded; local attraction alone is not being substituted for a complete
connection. The only remaining types are a hyperbolic source or a degenerate zero with both centre half-branches
outgoing. They have index +1 and the properties proved in (c).

(f) Theorem 53(c) gives pairwise distinct shrinking endpoint components and Ly(A_n), Ly(B_n) both tending to Ly(Q+).
Apply (56.3) to their connecting orbits. Positivity and convergence of the difference prove (56.13). No positive lower
bound for these energies follows, and no ordering of either endpoint value relative to Ly(Q+) is asserted.

(g) The bounds in 36(b), respectively with zero, zero and one Cartesian derivatives, give U = O(r^(1/2)), Omega =
O(r^(-1/2)) and grad Theta = O(r^(-1)), uniformly in angle. Hence W = 2X + O(r^(1/2)). Substitution into (56.2) shows
that Omega W^perp = O(r^(1/2)) and y grad Theta = O(1). Integrating the resulting gradient estimate along rays from a
fixed circle gives

  grad Ly = 6X + O(r^(1/2)),
  Ly = 3r^2 + O(r^(3/2))                                  (56.21)

uniformly in angle. The bounded values of Ly on that fixed circle make the integration constant uniform. In particular
Ly >= 2r^2 for all sufficiently large r, and |W| <= C(1+r).

The temperature range is compact, by 53(h) and reflection, so F is bounded on it. Formula (56.21) proves absolute
convergence in (56.14). Direct differentiation gives

  div(F(Theta) exp(-lambda Ly) W)
    = F(Theta) exp(-lambda Ly)(4-3 lambda |W|^2).            (56.22)

Integrate over a quarter-disc of radius R. The axes give zero flux since W is tangent there. The outer flux is bounded
in absolute value by

  C R^2 exp(-3 lambda R^2 + C lambda R^(3/2)) -> 0.         (56.23)

There is no singularity at O; alternatively an inner quarter-circle of radius epsilon has flux O(epsilon^2). The
divergence theorem and absolute convergence give (56.14).

For a fixed c choose a smooth compactly supported eta with 0 <= eta <= 1, eta(0) = 1, and put F_n(s) = eta(n(s-c)). Then
F_n(Theta) tends pointwise to 1_{Theta=c}. The integrable bound exp(-lambda Ly)(4+3 lambda |W|^2) permits dominated
convergence and proves the level version.

The nonescaping set in Q1 is invariant and contained in the disc of radius R0. Its finite area must equal exp(4t) times
itself, so it has area zero. Every escaping orbit crosses the launch circle exactly once: a backward orbit starting
outside that circle reaches it in finite time, since W_r >= r outside. Thus the escaping set has global coordinates
X(t,alpha) = Phi_t(R0 e(alpha)), where e(alpha) = (cos alpha,sin alpha) and 0 < alpha < pi/2. The area Jacobian is
D0(alpha) exp(4t), where D0(alpha) = R0 W_r(R0 e(alpha)) > 0. Along each orbit,

  d_t exp(4t-lambda Ly(X(t,alpha)))
    = exp(4t-lambda Ly(X(t,alpha)))
                       (4-3 lambda |W(X(t,alpha))|^2).     (56.24)

As t tends to minus infinity the orbit has a finite zero limit, so the exponential tends to zero. As t tends to
infinity, r grows at least exponentially and (56.21) again makes it tend to zero. Thus its integral in t is zero for
each label. F(Theta) is constant along that orbit, so multiplication by it preserves this cancellation. Absolute
convergence permits integration over labels. The weighted identities are not algebraic consequences of the single scalar
equality with F = 1, but all follow from this same orbitwise cancellation. Formula (56.14) supplies no independent
nonexistence obstruction arising from temperature weights.

For the exact comparison W = 2X and Ly = 3r^2, take F = 1. The two terms in the quadrant integral are

  4 int_Q1 exp(-3 lambda r^2) dX = pi/(3 lambda),
  12 lambda int_Q1 r^2 exp(-3 lambda r^2) dX
                                      = pi/(3 lambda).    (56.25)

Their difference is zero. This comparison is a check of the balance; U = 0 does not have the required nonzero A2 jet.

Remark 56.1 (isothermal marginals, a signed density and remaining cases).

For c in R define, for almost every phi in (0,pi/2),

  A_c(phi) = int_0^infinity 1_{Theta(r,phi)=c}
                                      U_r(r,phi)/r^2 dr,
  B_c(phi) = int_0^infinity 1_{Theta(r,phi)=c}
                                      U_phi(r,phi)/r^2 dr. (56.26)

Both functions are in L^1. The second has an absolutely continuous representative on [0,pi/2], and

  B_c' = -2(A_c + 1_{H=c}) almost everywhere,
  B_c(0) = B_c(pi/2) = 0.                                 (56.27)

These statements are an equivalent angular formulation of (53.12), not an additional isothermal identity. To verify the
integrability, use the absolute convergence in 53(i) first with b = 1, which controls r^(-3) U_r on the level, and then
with b(phi) = phi. Subtracting the already controlled radial term controls r^(-3) U_phi. Fubini now gives (56.26) and

  int_0^(pi/2) (-2 b A_c + b' B_c) dphi
                 = 2 int_0^(pi/2) b 1_{H=c} dphi.          (56.28)

Compactly supported tests give the derivative in (56.27) distributionally. Its right side is L^1, so B_c has the
asserted representative. Integration by parts in (56.28), allowing independent endpoint values of b, gives both zero
traces. Conversely (56.27) gives (56.28) for every C^1 weight b.

For a plateau I = [phi_2,phi_3] with {H=M} = I, the formal marginal data A_M = -1_I and B_M = 0 satisfy every angularly
weighted isothermal identity and give int A_M = -|I|. More generally, for every c the assignments A_c = -1_{H=c}, B_c =
0 satisfy (56.27) simultaneously. For the single positive excursion, intermediate levels have angular measure zero, the
M-level gives the plateau, and the zero level can include the intervals next to the axes. These are compatible marginal
data only. No common velocity or temperature field realizing them, and no satisfaction of the other profile equations,
is asserted.

There is also a direct obstruction to a fixed-sign use of the weight b = H' in the F(s) = s^2 instance of (39.10).
Assume (S) and (R) of 48 and M > 0. Use the angles from 48(e), so H rises on (phi_1,phi_2), is M on [phi_2,phi_3], and
falls on (phi_3,phi_4). Then

  int_Q1 Theta^2 r^(-3)
                    (-2 H' U_r + H'' U_phi) dX = 0.        (56.29)

Indeed, its angular side is 2 int H' H^2 dphi = 0 because H vanishes on both axes. This is exactly (39.10), whose
absolute convergence applies.

The full spatial density in (56.29) takes both signs arbitrarily near O within each of the rising and falling angular
intervals. The A2 strain and parities give

  U_r = -6r cos(2phi) + O(r^3),
  U_phi = 6r sin(2phi) + O(r^3),
  r^(-3)(-2H' U_r + H'' U_phi)
     = 6r^(-2) d_phi(H' sin(2phi)) + O(1).                (56.30)

On the rising interval H' sin(2phi) is positive and vanishes at both ends. At an axis end the sine factor vanishes; at a
plateau end H' vanishes. Its derivative therefore takes a positive and a negative value in the interval, by the mean
value theorem. On the falling interval the same function is negative with zero endpoint values, so its derivative again
takes both signs. Fix angles giving these signs. At each such angle the A2 jet makes Theta^2 strictly positive for all
sufficiently small r, and (56.30) fixes the sign of the remaining factor. This proves the density claim. It excludes
this particular fixed-sign argument, not all angular weights.

The following configurations remain unexcluded by these results.

1. Under (S) and (R), with M > 0, both endpoints are outgoing and H has the rising, positive-length plateau, falling
shape of 48(e). The version with M < 0 is expressed using sigma H, where sigma = sgn(a(0,0)). The shape requires (R);
(S) alone does not prove it. Possible zero intervals adjacent to the axes remain unless the corresponding extra axis
hypotheses are imposed. The potential side and failure of analytic continuation do not contradict smoothness.

2. With finitely many components, an incoming endpoint and the range, regular-level and N = 1 hypotheses of 56(e), an
isolated index +1 source at temperature M and Ly below Ly(Q+) is required. Either source type in 56(c) remains possible
under the proved conditions. At the level of the index, range and counting data, one such interior source is compatible
with eps = -1, k = 0 and I_Q = 1; its temperature M does not add a zero at an intermediate level. This is not a
construction. More general incoming configurations are not classified by 56(e), and the Ly-minimal source there is not
identified with the actual backward limit of the orbit entering Q+.

3. Accumulation at Q+ with infinitely many components remains unexcluded. The critical connections, shrinking
components, endpoint Ly limits and flat temperature estimates are those of 53(c); their positive energies tend to zero
as in (56.13). Neither a positive energy gap nor an infinite componentwise index sum is available.

These are remaining possibilities under the stated hypotheses, not an assertion that any of them is realized by an
A2-broad profile.

### Theorem 57 (weak vorticity sign and signs of temperature derivatives)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta >= 2. Thus the fields are smooth on R^2, U(X)
= o(|X|) uniformly, Theta and Omega have at most polynomial growth, and the velocity is canonical. The temperature is
even in x and odd in y, Omega is odd in each coordinate, and U_1 is odd in x and even in y while U_2 is even in x and
odd in y. Write

  W = beta X + U,    div W = 2 beta,
  W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x,
  W.grad Theta = (beta - 2) Theta,
  -Lap Psi = Omega,    U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x).                  (57.1)

The axis condition and jets are

  Theta(0,y) = 0,    Theta = a0 x^2 y + O(|X|^5),
  Omega = b0 x y + O(|X|^4),
  a0 != 0,    b0 = 2 a0/(2 beta + 1).                      (57.2)

Let O = (0,0), Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, Z = {W = 0}, and P = (x1,0) be the first positive x-axis zero from Theorem 2. Put
sigma = sgn(a0), h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2/beta, w(x) = W_1(x,0), v(y) = W_2(0,y), T(x) = Theta_y(x,0), and E(y) =
Theta_xx(0,y)/2. Hypothesis (H1) means Z cap closure(Q1) = {O,P}. Let H be the angular temperature limit at beta = 2
from Theorem 33(d), and f the limit of r^(-q) Theta at beta > 2 from Theorem 41(b).

(a) Suppose Omega >= 0 on Q1. Then a0 > 0 and

  w(x) > 0  for x > x1,    v(y) > beta y  for y > 0,
  T(x) > 0  for x > 0,    E(y) > 0  for y > 0.             (57.3)

If beta > 2, then

  Z = {O,P,-P},    (H1) holds,    Theta > 0 on Q1,          (57.4)

and all conclusions of Theorem 50(a)-(f) hold, including its Lyapunov conclusion for a0 > 0.

If beta = 2, the axis conclusions (57.3) still hold. The component of Z through P has the off-axis endpoints of Theorem
16, so (H1) fails. Moreover,

  H'(0) > 0,    H''(pi/2) > 0.                             (57.5)

For every beta >= 2, without a vorticity sign assumption, a further positive x-axis zero of W forces Omega to take both
strict signs in Q1.

(b) For every y > 0 and every x > 0, respectively,

  Theta_x(.,y) takes both strict signs on (0,infinity),
  Theta_y(x,.) takes both strict signs on (0,infinity).    (57.6)

Each of these horizontal and vertical half-lines contains a point where sigma Theta > 0. For every r > 0 the open
quadrant arc also contains such a point, and

  phi -> Theta_phi(r,phi) takes both strict signs
  on (0,pi/2).                                           (57.7)

No sign assumption on Omega or Theta, and no hypothesis (H1), is used in (b).

(c) Fix phi in (0,pi/2). If Theta(r,phi) -> 0 as r -> infinity, then Theta_r(.,phi) takes both strict signs. In
particular this holds at beta = 2 whenever H(phi) = 0. At beta > 2,

  Theta_r(r,phi)
    = q r^(q-1) f(phi) + O(r^(q-h-1)).                    (57.8)

Consequently, if a0 f(phi) < 0, Theta_r(.,phi) takes both strict signs. If f(phi) != 0, its sign for all sufficiently
large r is the sign of f(phi). If 2 < beta < 3 and f(phi) = 0, Theta(r,phi) -> 0 and the first assertion of (c) applies.

Scope. Part (a) replaces strict positivity by nonnegativity in the beta > 2 implication of Theorem 21(c). Its axis
argument uses Theorems 2, 9 and 21(b); Theorem 52(b) then supplies (H1), Theorem 8 supplies the temperature sign, and
Theorem 50 supplies its conclusions. No index count or assumption that off-axis zeros are nondegenerate is needed. The
statement about a further x-axis zero is already a consequence of Theorem 21(a),(b) for every beta >= 2; Theorem 54(a)
gives stronger information near the first further zero when beta > 2. At beta = 2, nonnegativity of Omega gives (57.3)
and (57.5), but neither an exclusion nor existence, nor strict positivity of Theta on Q1, is established here. It does
not supply the additional zero-component or regularity hypotheses in Theorems 48 and 53. Part (b) removes (H1) from
Theorem 50(e) and includes beta = 2. Its additional inputs are the unbounded superlevel components of Theorem 6 and the
gradient bounds of Theorems 33(a) and 41(a). The angular and radial assertions concern coordinate circles and rays, not
trajectories of W. Part (c) makes no assertion of two radial derivative signs on every ray with f(phi) != 0.

Proof.

(a) Oddness of Omega in both variables and smoothness give Omega = x y B(x,y) near O, with B smooth and B(O) = b0.
Nonnegativity along x = y > 0 gives b0 >= 0. Since a0 != 0, b0 != 0, so b0 > 0 and a0 > 0. Shrinking the neighbourhood
makes B positive; hence Omega > 0 on a small open quarter disc.

For every fixed x > 0, oddness in y and smoothness give

  g(x) := Omega_y(x,0)
        = lim_(t -> 0+) Omega(x,t)/t >= 0.                 (57.9)

Theorem 21(b) applies for every beta >= 2. It excludes all further positive x-axis zeros, including degenerate ones.
Since w'(x1) = beta + 2 by Theorem 2, w > 0 on (x1,infinity).

We justify the y-axis kernel with the prescribed velocity gauge. For the centred-disc potentials of Theorem 9,
differentiation and grouping the four reflected source points give, with Y = (s,t) in Q1 and y > 0,

  Psi_x(0,y) = lim_(R -> infinity)
                int_(Q1 cap B_R) K_y(s,t) Omega(s,t) ds dt,

  K_y(s,t) = 4 y s t /
       (pi (s^2 + (y-t)^2) (s^2 + (y+t)^2)).              (57.10)

Indeed, the derivative of -log|X-Y|/(2 pi) at X = (0,y) is s/(2 pi (s^2+(y-t)^2)). Reflection in x doubles this
contribution, and reflection in y gives the difference of the denominators with y-t and y+t. This is exactly K_y.
Theorem 9 gives convergence of the differentiated potentials to Psi_x locally uniformly, since Psi is smooth and odd-odd
and grad Psi = o(|X|). Thus the limit in (57.10) is finite.

The only possible finite singularity of the grouped integrand is at (s,t) = (0,y). There the second denominator is
bounded below by a positive constant depending on y, and

  K_y(s,t) <= C_y s/(s^2+(t-y)^2),
  |Omega(s,t)| <= C_y s.                                 (57.11)

The latter bound follows from Omega(0,t) = 0 and smoothness. Their product is bounded by C_y s^2/(s^2+(t-y)^2), so it is
locally integrable. There is no singularity at O for fixed y > 0.

For completeness, the class also gives absolute convergence at infinity without the sign assumption. Theorems 33(a) and
41(a), in their respective parameter ranges, give |Omega(Y)| <= C |Y|^(-h) outside a disc. If |Y| > 2y, each
squared-distance denominator in (57.10) is at least |Y|^2/4 and st <= |Y|^2/2. Therefore, for R sufficiently large,

  int_(Q1 cap {|Y|>R}) |K_y Omega| dY
       <= C_y int_R^infinity rho^(-1-h) drho
       <= C_y R^(-h).                                   (57.12)

This decay is a proved consequence of A2-broad, not an added assumption. Under Omega >= 0, absolute convergence also
follows directly from the finite limit in (57.10) and monotone convergence.

Choose a closed disc D of positive radius contained in the small quarter disc where Omega > 0. For fixed y > 0 the
kernel is positive and continuous on D, so

  int_D K_y Omega dY > 0.                                (57.13)

Every sufficiently large truncation in (57.10) is at least this fixed positive number. The limit is therefore strictly
positive. Hence v(y) = beta y + Psi_x(0,y) > beta y for all y > 0.

The two trace equations are those of Theorems 2 and 27:

  w T' = (w' - beta - 2) T,
  v E' = (2v' - 3 beta - 2) E.                           (57.14)

Theorem 2 gives T > 0 on (0,x1], including at P. The first equation is regular on (x1,infinity), so linear uniqueness
and continuity at x1 give T > 0 there. The second equation is regular on (0,infinity), since v > 0. Its initial sign is
fixed by E(y) = a0 y + O(y^3) near zero. Linear uniqueness gives E > 0 on the whole positive half-axis. This proves
(57.3).

Suppose beta > 2. The axis conditions just proved are exactly the right-hand side of the equivalence in Theorem 52(b).
That theorem assumes A2-broad and beta > 2, with no additional nondegeneracy or sign hypothesis. It gives (H1) and Z =
{O,P,-P}. Theorem 8(ii) gives Theta > 0 on Q1. Every hypothesis of Theorem 50 is now satisfied, and its additional
assumption in part (f) holds because a0 > 0. This proves (57.4) and the asserted applications.

Suppose beta = 2. Theorem 16 supplies the arc through P and its endpoints in the open quadrants, so (H1) is false. To
prove (57.5), choose a launch radius R0 as in Theorem 36(d). Write

  theta_0(alpha) = Theta(R0 cos alpha, R0 sin alpha),
  H = theta_0 o F^(-1),    F(0) = 0,    F(pi/2) = pi/2,
  F' > 0.                                                (57.15)

At alpha = 0, theta_0'(0) = R0 T(R0). At alpha = pi/2, both first Cartesian derivatives of Theta vanish: Theta_x
vanishes by evenness in x, and Theta_y vanishes because Theta(0,y) = 0. Thus theta_0'(pi/2) = 0 and theta_0''(pi/2) = 2
R0^2 E(R0). The chain rule gives

  H'(0) = R0 T(R0)/F'(0) > 0,
  H''(pi/2) = 2 R0^2 E(R0)/F'(pi/2)^2 > 0.              (57.16)

These computations do not use the hypotheses (S) or (R) of Theorem 48.

Finally suppose a further positive x-axis zero exists, with arbitrary beta >= 2. If a0 < 0, Theorem 21(a) already gives
both signs of Omega. If a0 > 0, the contrapositive of Theorem 21(b) gives x_* > 0 with g(x_*) < 0. Smoothness and
Omega(x_*,0) = 0 imply Omega(x_*,y) < 0 for all sufficiently small y > 0. Theorem 21(a) excludes Omega <= 0 on Q1, so
Omega is positive somewhere as well. This proves the companion assertion.

(b) Theorems 33(a) and 41(a) give constants C,R with

  |grad Theta(X)| <= C |X|^(-2h)  for |X| >= R.            (57.17)

Both axis values of Theta are zero. If x >= R, the entire segment {(x,t): 0 <= t <= y} lies outside the disc of radius
R. If y >= R, the entire segment {(s,y): 0 <= s <= x} does so. Integration along these segments gives

  |Theta(x,y)| <= C y x^(-2h)  for x >= R, y >= 0,
  |Theta(x,y)| <= C x y^(-2h)  for y >= R, x >= 0.         (57.18)

In particular each horizontal or vertical restriction tends to zero at its infinite end. The estimates are uniform on
every strip of bounded height or bounded width, respectively.

We show that none of these restrictions is identically zero. For c > 0 let D be a nonempty connected component of {sigma
Theta > c} which meets Q1. Since Theta vanishes on the axes, D is contained in Q1. By Theorem 6(b),(c), D is unbounded.
The reason applies to either value of sigma: Theta(Phi_t X) = exp((beta-2)t) Theta(X) keeps the component forward
invariant, and a nonempty bounded component would have positive finite area whereas its forward images have area exp(2
beta t) times that area.

Each coordinate projection of D is unbounded above. If y <= L throughout D for some finite L, the first estimate in
(57.18) bounds x throughout D: for sufficiently large x it gives |Theta| < c. This would bound D, a contradiction. If x
<= L throughout D, the second estimate bounds y and gives the same contradiction.

Fix y0 > 0. The smooth factorization Theta = x^2 y a(x^2,y^2), with sigma a positive near O, gives a point X_* in Q1
with y_* < y0 and sigma Theta(X_*) > 0. Choose 0 < c < sigma Theta(X_*) and take its component D. The y-coordinate takes
a value below y0 on D and is unbounded above. Its image is an interval, because D is connected. Hence D meets y = y0, at
a point where sigma Theta > c. Starting instead with x_* < x0 and using the x-projection proves the corresponding
assertion for every vertical line x = x0 > 0.

Here is the elementary derivative argument. Let u be C^1 on [0,infinity), with u(0) = 0, u(s) -> 0 as s -> infinity, and
u(s0) != 0 for some s0 > 0. Choose s1 > s0 with |u(s1)| < |u(s0)|/2. The mean value theorem on [0,s0] gives a derivative
of the sign of u(s0); on [s0,s1] it gives a derivative of the opposite sign. Apply this to u(s) = Theta(s,y0) and u(s) =
Theta(x0,s), using (57.18) and the points just constructed. This proves (57.6).

For a fixed radius r > 0, choose X_* near O with |X_*| < r and sigma Theta(X_*) > c > 0. Its component D is connected
and unbounded in Q1. The continuous radius function therefore takes the value r on D. Thus the quadrant arc contains a
point where sigma Theta > 0. The function u(phi) = Theta(r cos phi,r sin phi) vanishes at phi = 0 and phi = pi/2.
Applying the mean value theorem between these endpoints and the nonzero interior point gives both strict signs of u' =
Theta_phi. This proves (57.7).

(c) On every fixed interior ray the smooth jet gives

  Theta(r,phi) = a0 cos(phi)^2 sin(phi) r^3 + O(r^5),
  Theta_r(r,phi) = 3 a0 cos(phi)^2 sin(phi) r^2 + O(r^4).
                                                               (57.19)

The restriction is nonzero near r = 0 and its radial derivative initially has sign a0. If its limit at infinity is zero,
the same one-dimensional argument used in (b) gives both derivative signs. At beta = 2, Theorem 33(d) identifies this
limit with H(phi). For beta > 2, differentiation of the O_infty remainder in Theorem 42(b) gives (57.8). If f(phi) != 0,
the remainder is smaller than its leading term by a factor O(r^(-h)), proving the eventual sign and the conclusion when
a0 f(phi) < 0. Finally, if f(phi) = 0, Theorem 42(b) gives Theta(r,phi) = O(r^(q-h)); for 2 < beta < 3, q-h =
1-3/beta < 0. QED.

### Theorem 58 (beta > 2: finite x-axis chains, source basins and a corrected Lyapunov function)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2, with beta > 2. Thus the fields are smooth on R^2, U is
the canonical velocity and is uniformly sublinear, Theta and Omega have polynomial growth, and

  W = beta X + U,                 div W = 2 beta,
  W.grad Theta = kappa Theta,     W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x,
  U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x),             -Lap Psi = Omega.

Here Theta is even in x and odd in y, Omega is odd in each coordinate, U_1 is odd in x and even in y, and U_2 is even in
x and odd in y. Moreover,

  Theta(0,y) = 0,    Theta = a0 x^2 y + O(|X|^5),    a0 != 0.

Put kappa = beta-2, b = beta+2, d = 2 beta-1, h = 1/beta, q = kappa/beta, nu = b/kappa and sigma = sgn(a0). Write O =
(0,0), Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, Phi_t for the complete flow of W, and

  w(x) = W_1(x,0), T(x) = Theta_y(x,0), g(x) = Omega_y(x,0),
  v(y) = W_2(0,y),
  B_R = {X : Phi_(-t)X -> R as t -> infinity}.

Total order is the degree of the first nonzero Taylor polynomial. Exact transverse order k along a regular curve means a
local factorization u^k A, where u defines the curve, du!=0 and A!=0 at the point under consideration.

Let f,G be the smooth angular limits of Theorem 42, normalized by r^(-q)Theta(r,phi) -> f(phi) and r^h Omega(r,phi) ->
G(phi). Set W^perp = (-W_2,W_1) and e_2 = (0,1). Use the normalization of Theorem 44:

  Xi = d W + Omega W^perp - Theta e_2,
  Bern(X) = integral_0^1 Xi(tX).X dt,    Ly = Bern + y Theta.

(a) Suppose all positive zeros of w form a finite sequence of simple zeros. Their number is 2n+1 for some integer
n >= 0. Write

  0 < x_1 < ... < x_(2n+1),
  R_j = (x_(2j+1),0), 0 <= j <= n,    R_0 = P,
  Q_j = (x_(2j),0),   1 <= j <= n.

There are positive integers m_j such that, with a_j = b/m_j, c_j = 2 beta+a_j and p_j = m_j+1,

  DW(R_j) = diag(b,kappa),   DW(Q_j) = diag(-a_j,c_j).

Define sigma_0 = sigma and sigma_j = sigma (-1)^(p_1+...+p_j). With x_0 = 0 and x_(2n+2) = infinity, T has sign sigma_j
on (x_(2j),x_(2j+2)). Its only positive zeros are x_(2j), of exact orders p_j. At Q_j the total orders of Theta and
Omega are m_j+2 and m_j+1. On the unstable branch gamma_j entering Q1, Theta = grad Theta = Omega = 0; at every
nonstationary point their exact transverse orders are p_j for Theta and m_j for Omega. Immediately to the left of
x_(2j), T' and g have sign -sigma_(j-1); immediately to the right both have sign sigma_j, and

  g(x)/T'(x) -> 1/(beta-1+a_j) on either side.             (58.1)

(b) Let R=(r,0), r>0, be any zero with A=T(r)!=0 and DW(R)=diag(b,kappa). This part does not require (a). There is a C^1
diffeomorphism H_R=(xi_R,eta_R): B_R -> R^2 such that

  eta_R = Theta/A, H_R(R) = 0, DH_R(R) = I, det DH_R = 1,
  H_R(Phi_t X) = (e^(bt)xi_R(X),e^(kappa t)eta_R(X)).      (58.2)

It is smooth off the x-axis and can be chosen smooth everywhere if nu is not an even integer. It is equivariant under y
reflection: xi_R is even and eta_R is odd. It maps B_R cap Q1 onto {eta > 0}. On the x-axis part of B_R,

  xi_R(x,0) = A w(x)/(b T(x)),    xi_R(r,0) = 0.           (58.3)

Every upper-basin orbit escapes. Its label and coordinates are

  c = xi_R/eta_R^nu,
  Z_R(c,s) = H_R^(-1)(c s^nu,s),    c in R, s>0,
  dX = s^nu dc ds.

Its escape angles form an open interval J_R in (0,pi/2). The escape map phi_R: R -> J_R is a decreasing smooth
diffeomorphism, with

  phi_R'(c) = -q (f(phi_R(c))/A)^(2/q),    f/A > 0 on J_R. (58.4)

At the source,

  T'(r) = A w''(r)/b,
  g(r) = A w''(r)/[b(beta-1)].                            (58.5)

If w''(r)!=0, Omega has sign sgn(A w''(r)) in a sufficiently small upper neighbourhood of R.

(c) In addition to (a), suppose v has no positive zero and W has no zero in Q1. Every gamma_j escapes, every point of Q1
escapes, and

  Q1 = disjoint-union_(j=0)^n (B_(R_j) cap Q1)
       disjoint-union_(j=1)^n gamma_j.                    (58.6)

There are ordered angles

  0 = phi_(n+1) < phi_n < ... < phi_1 < phi_0 = pi/2

such that gamma_j escapes at phi_j and J_(R_j) = (phi_(j+1),phi_j). On this interval sgn f = sigma_j. At every internal
angle phi_j,

  ord f = p_j,    ord G = m_j,
  f^(p_j)(phi_j) G^(m_j)(phi_j) < 0,
  sgn G = -sigma_(j-1) immediately above phi_j,
  sgn G = sigma_j immediately below phi_j.                (58.7)

The endpoints satisfy

  sigma_n f'(0) > 0,    sigma f''(pi/2) > 0,
  sigma G'(pi/2) < 0.                                    (58.8)

For 0 <= j < n, G takes both signs in J_(R_j), and has an additional zero there. No sign of G'(0) is asserted.

(d) Under the hypotheses of (c), Theta_x takes both signs on every nonempty connected component of every horizontal
slice of each B_(R_j) cap Q1. Theta_y takes both signs on every nonempty connected component of every vertical slice of
that basin. Put

  K0(X) = xy |X|^(-4),
  phi_K(X) = integral_0^infinity e^(dt) K0(Phi_t X) dt
  for X in Q1.

This weight is finite, positive and continuous. The following integrals are absolutely convergent:

  I_j = integral_(B_(R_j) cap Q1) phi_K Theta_x dX
      = integral_(B_(R_j) cap Q1) K0 Omega dX,
  sum_(j=0)^n I_j = (pi/2)(beta+1).                        (58.9)

The integrand phi_K Theta_x takes both signs in each basin. The full-plane zero set has 2(n+1) sources and 2n+1 saddles,
including O, and its index sum is 1.

If all sigma_j=+1, equivalently sigma=+1 and every m_j is odd, Ly is a proper smooth strict Lyapunov function whose
critical points are exactly the zeros of W. The sources are nondegenerate minima and the other zeros are nondegenerate
saddles. For an x-axis zero R, with A=T(R),

  D^2 Ly(R) = d DW(R) + A e_2 (x) e_2.                    (58.10)

Here (u (x) v)_ij = u_i v_j. For every sign pattern, the axis connections satisfy

  Ly(Q_j) > Ly(R_(j-1)),    Ly(Q_j) > Ly(R_j),
  Ly(O) > Ly(P).                                         (58.11)

(e) For every A2-broad profile with beta>2, without any of the additional zero-set hypotheses in (a)-(d), define

  Hc(X) = kappa Theta(X) integral_0^infinity
                         e^(-kappa s) [Phi_(-s)X]_2 ds,
  L_tilde(X) = Ly(X)-Hc(X).                                (58.12)

The integral converges locally uniformly, Hc and L_tilde are continuous, and

  |Hc(X)| <= C(1+|X|)^(1+q),
  Ly(X) = (d beta/2)|X|^2 + O(|X|^(2-h)),
  L_tilde(X) -> +infinity as |X| -> infinity.              (58.13)

The function L_tilde is proper and differentiable along every orbit, with

  d_t L_tilde(Phi_t X) = d |W(Phi_t X)|^2.                (58.14)

It therefore strictly increases along every nonstationary orbit, for either sign of Theta. On {Theta=0}, L_tilde=Ly. A
nonconstant connection from a zero Z_1 to a zero Z_2 satisfies L_tilde(Z_2)>L_tilde(Z_1). This recovers the absence of
periodic orbits, homoclinic loops and cycles of connections (Theorem 4). No transverse differentiability or Morse
classification of L_tilde is asserted.

Scope. These are necessary conditions on a hypothetical A2-broad profile; no existence or exclusion of that class is
proved. Finiteness and simplicity of all positive x-axis zeros are extra hypotheses in (a). Absence of positive y-axis
zeros and of interior zeros are extra hypotheses in (c),(d). Theorem 52(b) supplies absence of interior zeros from the
two axis conditions only when n=0, and does not supply it for a longer chain. Part (b) concerns each specified regular
source and does not require exhaustion by its basin. Part (e) is unconditional within the stated A2-broad class. The
consistency statements in Remark 58.1 concern charts, local germs and angular data, not a coupled global realization.

Proof.

First record the exterior flow facts used below. Theorem 42(a) gives U=O(r^(1-h)) with every derivative gaining a power
of r^(-1). Uniform sublinearity gives a radius R_* outside which X.W(X)>0, with X.W(X)>=(beta/2)|X|^2, and also
|W(X)|<=C(1+|X|). Thus the flow is complete, each backward orbit stays in {|X|<=max(R_*,|X_0|)}, and any unbounded
forward orbit escapes. These facts are also in Theorems 44(b) and 52(a).

On a sufficiently large launch circle S(alpha)=R_* e(alpha), every escaping orbit has exactly one intersection, allowing
either sign of the crossing time. As in the proof of Theorem 54, Step 5, put Y(t,alpha)=e^(-beta t)Phi_t S(alpha).
Integrating d_t log|Phi_t S|=beta+O(|Phi_t S|^(-h)) first gives |Phi_t S| comparable to e^(beta t), uniformly for t>=0.
Then

  partial_t Y = e^(-t) U_t(Y),
  U_t(Z) = e^(-(beta-1)t)U(e^(beta t)Z).

Every derivative of U_t is bounded on the fixed annulus containing Y. The variational equation and induction give
uniform bounds on all alpha derivatives of Y; their time derivatives are O(e^(-t)). Consequently Y converges smoothly to
rho(alpha)e(F(alpha)), where rho>0. Liouville's formula and Theorem 42(b) give exactly (54.40)-(54.41):

  beta rho^2 F' = R_* W_r(S) > 0,
  Theta(S(alpha)) = rho(alpha)^q f(F(alpha)),
  e^t Omega(Phi_t S(alpha))
       -> rho(alpha)^(-h)G(F(alpha)) in every C^j.          (58.15)

The last error is O(e^(-t)) in each C^j. Axis invariance gives F(0)=0 and F(pi/2)=pi/2. These exterior identities use no
finite chain or exhaustion hypothesis. Positive factors and the increasing diffeomorphism F preserve exact orders and
leading signs.

(a) Theorem 2 gives w'(0)=-b, w<0 near zero and w(x)/x->beta. Every simple zero reverses the sign of w, so its finite
number is odd. Theorem 27(x) applies to the first N consecutive simple zeros for every N, not only to x_1,x_2. Its local
trace lemma continues nonvanishing through each zero of finite integral order. Starting with T=a0 x^2+O(x^4), it gives
the stated spectra, nonzero source traces and saddle trace orders. Between zeros of w the equation

  w T' = (w'-b)T                                          (58.16)

preserves nonvanishing. This also applies on the final unbounded interval. Smooth continuation across order p_j changes
the sign by (-1)^p_j. This proves every trace sign in (a).

We give the local and propagated order argument for an arbitrary Q_j, so that no first-saddle hypothesis is implicit.
Suppress j and put a=b/m, c=2 beta+a and p=m+1. The smooth unstable manifold, invariant under y reflection, is locally
x=x_(2j)+chi(y), where chi is even and chi=O(y^2). In the smooth coordinates u=x-x_(2j)-chi(y), eta=y, invariance of
this graph and of the axis gives

  W_u = u A(u,eta), W_eta = eta C(u,eta),
  A(0,0)=-a, C(0,0)=c.

Theorem 46(b) gives Theta=grad Theta=Omega=0 on the branch. Let H_k(eta)=partial_u^k Theta(0,eta)/k!. If all lower
coefficients vanish, differentiating the temperature equation gives

  eta C(0,eta) H_k' = (kappa-k A(0,eta))H_k.                (58.17)

The logarithmic derivative minus (kappa+ka)/(c eta) is smooth at zero. Hence a nonzero solution on eta>0 is a nonzero
constant times eta^((kappa+ka)/c) times a smooth positive factor. For k<p the exponent is strictly between zero and one.
Smoothness forces H_k=0, inductively. At k=p it is exactly one, since kappa+pa=2 beta+a=c. Further,

  H_p'(0)=T^(p)(x_(2j))/p! != 0.

Thus H_p is nonzero for positive eta sufficiently small.

Let R_k(eta)=partial_u^k Omega(0,eta)/k!. The lower unforced equations have nonzero-solution exponent (ka-1)/c. For k<m
it is less than one: a negative exponent contradicts boundedness, zero contradicts oddness in eta, and an exponent in
(0,1) contradicts smoothness. Thus R_k=0 for k<m. At k=m the forcing is p H_p because partial_x=partial_u. Comparing
coefficients of eta gives

  R_m'(0)=p H_p'(0)/(c+1-ma)
         =p H_p'(0)/(beta-1+a) != 0.                      (58.18)

The leading polynomials are therefore

  Theta_lead = C_* u^p eta,
  Omega_lead = [p C_*/(beta-1+a)]u^m eta,    C_* != 0.

All other coefficients are odd in eta, so there are no terms of smaller total degree. Replacing u by x-x_(2j)-chi(y)
leaves these first homogeneous polynomials unchanged. On eta=0 the resulting trace expansions prove (58.1). The
right-hand sign of T is sigma_j; differentiating its leading power gives the two claimed signs of T' and g.
