It remains to prove that the forced vorticity coefficient cannot vanish later on the branch. Parametrize
gamma(t)=(x(t),y(t)), with gamma(t)->Q_j as t->-infinity. Choose a transverse section S(z) through gamma(0), oriented so
J=det(W(gamma(0)),S'(0))>0, and put X(t,z)=Phi_t S(z). Write

  Theta(S(z)) = theta_p z^p + O(z^(p+1)),
  Omega(X(t,z)) = omega_m(t) z^m + O(z^(m+1)).

Temperature transport preserves its exact order under finite flow, and the vorticity equation preserves all lower
vanishing coefficients. At z=0, Liouville's formula gives

  det(X_t,X_z)=e^(2 beta t)J,
  z_x=-y'(t)/(e^(2 beta t)J).

Differentiating Theta(X(t,z))=e^(kappa t)Theta(S(z)) in physical x, the term containing t_x has order p and does not
enter order m=p-1. The vorticity equation therefore gives

  d_t(e^t omega_m(t))
    =-(p theta_p/J)e^(-(beta+1)t)y'(t).                    (58.19)

We check its negative-time boundary condition. For sufficiently small eps>0 and all sufficiently negative t,
|gamma(t)-Q_j|<=C e^((c-eps)t). Continuity of the symmetric part of DW near its diagonal value gives Sym DW>=-(a+eps)I
there. Applied backward to the variational equation, this yields |X_z(t,0)|<=C e^(-(a+eps)t). All Cartesian derivatives
of Omega of order below m vanish on the regular branch: this follows from its transverse divisibility. Also D^m
Omega(Q_j)=0 by the total order just proved. The chain rule consequently gives

  |e^t omega_m(t)|
    <= C e^([1+c-ma-(m+1)eps]t) -> 0,                    (58.20)

because 1+c-ma=beta-1+a>0. Higher derivatives of X do not enter this estimate, since their coefficients contain lower
derivatives of Omega.

Integrating (58.19) and integrating once by parts gives

  e^t omega_m(t)=-(p theta_p/J) I(t),
  I(t)=e^(-(beta+1)t)y(t)
       +(beta+1) integral_(-infinity)^t
                       e^(-(beta+1)s)y(s) ds > 0.         (58.21)

The boundary term at negative infinity vanishes because c>beta+1 and eps can be chosen smaller than c-beta-1. Every
regular point of the branch has y>0. Thus I(t)>0 without requiring y'(t)>0. This proves exact transverse order m for
Omega everywhere on gamma_j, and completes (a).

(b) We spell out the extension of Theorem 50(a) to an individual source. Near R put u=x-r and s=Theta/A. Since s_y(R)=1
and s_x(R)=0, (u,s) are smooth coordinates. Write y=Y(u,s); Y_s>0 after restriction to a smaller neighbourhood. Set

  z(u,s)=integral_0^u Y_s(v,s) dv.

The coordinate change to (z,s) has determinant one and derivative I at R. Its vector field has s component kappa s.
Preservation of divergence under this coordinate change implies that its z component is b z+B(s). Reflection gives B
even, and the source linearization gives B(0)=B'(0)=0.

The shear xi=z+k(s) gives the required linear field if

  kappa s k'(s)-b k(s)=-B(s).                              (58.22)

Choose an integer N>nu and subtract the Taylor polynomial of B through degree N, leaving r_N(s)=O(s^(N+1)). For its term
B_l s^l, use k_l=B_l s^l/(b-l kappa) when l!=nu. If nu is integral, the resonant term is -(B_nu/kappa)s^nu log|s|; it is
absent when nu is odd by evenness of B. For the remainder use

  k_rem(s)=-(1/kappa) integral_0^1 t^(-nu-1)r_N(ts) dt.

Differentiating t^(-nu)r_N(ts) verifies (58.22). The kth s derivative of r_N(ts) is O(t^(N+1)) for k<=N+1 on compact s
sets, and O(t^k) for k>N+1, so all these integrals converge. The remainder is smooth. The possible logarithm is C^1
because nu>1, even when present, and all terms have k(0)=k'(0)=0. This gives the local chart with the stated parity and
regularity.

For a sufficiently small ball V about R, W(R+z).z >= (kappa/2)|z|^2. Thus V is backward invariant, every point of V
tends backward to R, and B_R=union_(t>=0)Phi_t(V). Define

  H_R(X)=diag(e^(bt),e^(kappa t))H_loc(Phi_(-t)X)

whenever Phi_(-t)X lies in V. Backward invariance and the local conjugacy make the definition independent of t. Its
determinant is e^((b+kappa)t)e^(-2 beta t)=1. Moving two points into V proves injectivity. Its image is open, contains a
neighbourhood of zero and is invariant under the linear flow for all times; linear contraction shows that the image is
all R^2. The inverse function theorem gives a global C^1 inverse.

Axes are invariant. No point with x<=0 can tend backward to R, and near R the sign of s is the sign of y. Transport
preserves that sign and nonvanishing throughout the basin. This proves the upper-half-plane image. On its axis segment
s_x=0 and the determinant condition gives xi_x=A/T. In particular T is nonzero there. Conjugacy gives w xi_x=b xi,
proving (58.3).

The map (c,s)->(c s^nu,s) has determinant s^nu. It gives the coordinates in (b) and identifies time translation with
s->e^(kappa t)s. Temperature is nonzero on each upper orbit, so it cannot remain bounded forward by Theorem 7. It
escapes by the exterior radial inequality.

Represent each orbit by Z_R(c,1). Its unique launch-circle intersection depends smoothly on c, since W_r>0 there.
Conversely each basin point on that circle has a unique label c. This launch set is open and connected, hence an
interval. Let c(alpha) be its label and eta=Theta(S(alpha))/A. The determinant computed in the area-preserving source
coordinates is

  det(W,S')=-kappa eta^(nu+1)c'(alpha)
           =R_* W_r(S)>0.

Divide this identity by the first identity in (58.15) and use eta=rho^q f(F(alpha))/A and nu+1=2/q. It follows that

  dc/dphi=-(1/q)(f(phi)/A)^(-2/q).

This is nonzero and gives (58.4), smoothness of its inverse and the asserted angular interval. Smoothness here is away
from the axis, where the source chart is smooth.

Finally differentiating (58.16) at a source, with w'=b, gives b T'(r)=w''(r)A. The second trace equation (54.23),

  w g'+(2 beta+1-w')g=T',

gives (beta-1)g(r)=T'(r). This proves (58.5). The smooth quotient Omega/y has value g(r) at R and has its sign in a
sufficiently small neighbourhood when this value is nonzero.

(c) There are exactly the listed zeros and O in the closed quadrant. Since v'(0)=3 beta+2 and v has no positive zero,
v>0 on that half-axis. The origin is the saddle DW(O)=diag(-b,3 beta+2).

Suppose gamma_j were bounded forward. Theorem 46(b) gives Theta=0 on it, so (44.1) yields d_t Ly=d|W|^2 there. On its
compact orbit closure Ly and d_t|W|^2 are bounded. Therefore |W|^2 is integrable in forward time and uniformly
continuous, and tends to zero. Its omega-limit set is nonempty, compact, connected and contained in the finite zero set,
so consists of one zero. A source has no nonconstant orbit tending to it in forward time. At each Q_j and at O the local
stable manifold is on the x-axis. Indeed the invariant axis has the stable eigenvector and supplies the local stable
manifold; uniqueness of that manifold identifies it. Any orbit converging to this zero eventually lies in that local
stable manifold. Its earlier points are its inverse-flow images, still on the x-axis. Thus the entire stable set, not
merely the local stable manifold, lies on the x-axis. No orbit in Q1 can have such a forward limit. This contradiction
proves escape of gamma_j.

Every point has a single backward limit by Theorem 44(b). The unstable set of O is on the y-axis, by the same
local-manifold and invariance argument. The unstable set of Q_j in Q1 is exactly gamma_j. All other points of Q1
therefore belong to one of the source basins. These sets are disjoint, proving (58.6). Near each source Theta/y has sign
sigma_j; transport preserves this sign on the upper basin. Its orbits escape by (b). This proves escape of all Q1.

Choose the launch quarter-circle larger than all the zeros. The portion of gamma_j between Q_j and that circle,
including its endpoints, is a simple compact arc with interior in the quarter-disc. It is an embedded crosscut: the
local unstable graph supplies continuity and injectivity at its initial endpoint, and flow uniqueness supplies them
elsewhere. Different such arcs do not intersect, since their backward limits differ. A crosscut separates the boundary
arc containing larger x coordinates from the one containing O and the y-axis. If k>j, the endpoint Q_k is on the first
side. Its crosscut must end at a smaller launch angle than that of Q_j; otherwise it must cross gamma_j by Jordan
separation. Applying the increasing map F gives the strict ordering of the phi_j.

The sectors between consecutive crosscuts contain near the x-axis the corresponding sources R_j. Their launch intervals
are connected and partitioned, by (58.6), into relatively open source-basin sets. Such a partition of an interval has
one nonempty member. Upper points sufficiently near R_j cannot cross the bounding branches, and escape, so that member
is B_(R_j). This also treats the outer sectors, with the invariant axes as their other boundaries. The second identity
in (58.15) transfers the strict basin signs to f.

For an escaping gamma_j, the exterior estimate gives y(t),|y'(t)|=O(e^(beta t)). Consequently the two weighted integrals
in (58.21) converge at positive infinity and

  I(t) -> (beta+1) integral_(-infinity)^infinity
                       e^(-(beta+1)s)y(s) ds
       = I_infinity in (0,infinity).                     (58.23)

The boundary term at positive infinity is O(e^(-t)). Take S to be the launch circle and z=alpha-alpha_j, so J>0.
Equations (58.19)-(58.23) show that the first nonzero coefficient of the outgoing vorticity amplitude has sign opposite
to theta_p. Smooth convergence in (58.15) preserves this nonzero coefficient and all lower zero coefficients. Hence the
angular orders are p_j,m_j and their leading coefficients have opposite signs. Since f has sign sigma_(j-1) above phi_j,
these coefficients have signs sigma_(j-1),-sigma_(j-1). Crossing the zero of order m_j gives sign sigma_j below it. This
proves (58.7).

On the final x-axis interval, Theorem 42 and (58.16) give

  T'/T=-2h/x+O(x^(-1-h)).

The error is integrable. Thus x^(2h)T tends to a nonzero constant of sign sigma_n. Differentiated angular asymptotics
identify this constant as f'(0). For the y-axis inequalities, the version of Theorem 50(c) assuming only v>0 applies. To
make the nonvanishing input explicit, put E=Theta_xx(0,y)/2 and K_y=Omega_x(0,y). The trace equations (54.23) give E of
sign sigma on y>0 and

  E'/E=-(1+2h)/y+O(y^(-1-h)),
  y^(1+2h)E -> C_y != 0,    sgn C_y=sigma.

With D=2 beta+1, let H0(y)=v(y)exp(-D integral_1^y dz/v(z)), which is positive. It is asymptotic to positive multiples
of y^((beta+1)/(3 beta+2)) at zero and y^(-1-h) at infinity. Smoothness at O fixes the homogeneous constant, giving

  K_y(y)=H0(y) integral_0^y 2E(z)/(v(z)H0(z)) dz.

The integrand has sign sigma, is integrable at zero because (beta+1)/(3 beta+2)<1, and is O(z^(-1-h)) at infinity. Its
full integral is nonzero of sign sigma. Thus y^(1+h)K_y has that sign in its nonzero limit. Theorem 42 identifies the
two limits as f''(pi/2)/2 and -G'(pi/2). This proves (58.8).

On J_(R_0), G has signs -sigma near its lower endpoint and sigma near pi/2. For 1<=j<n it has signs -sigma_j near its
lower endpoint and sigma_j near its upper endpoint. Continuity proves each asserted additional zero and both signs.

(d) The basin is open and Theta has one strict sign there. By (58.6), every boundary point inside Q1 is on a gamma_j,
where Theta=0. A connected horizontal slice component is an open interval. Its finite endpoints have zero temperature,
also when an endpoint lies on the y-axis. At an infinite endpoint, Theorem 41 gives, for fixed y>0 and large x,

  |Theta(x,y)|
    =|integral_0^y Theta_y(x,t) dt| <= C_y x^(-2h) -> 0.

For a vertical slice, finite endpoints again have zero temperature, including the x-axis. Evenness in x and Theta(0,y)=0
give Theta_x(0,y)=0. Theorem 42(a) gives

  |Theta(x,y)|
    =|integral_0^x (x-s)Theta_xx(s,y) ds|
    <= C_x y^(-1-2h) -> 0

for fixed x and large y. A differentiable function of one strict sign on an interval, tending to zero at both endpoints,
has derivatives of both signs: choose an interior nonzero value and smaller absolute values on both sides, and apply the
mean value theorem on the two subintervals. This proves the two slice assertions. Positivity of phi_K preserves the two
signs of Theta_x.

Theorem 54(e) applies without (H1). Here the entire quadrant escapes by (c), so its weight is finite, positive and
continuous there. Each basin is invariant and measurable. Restrict (54.20) to each basin and sum. The finitely many
smooth separatrices have area zero, so (54.21) gives (58.9), with absolute convergence and no interface term. Both signs
of the integrand prevent a pointwise sign argument for I_j; no prescribed individual value or arbitrary realizability is
claimed.

Reflection gives two copies of every positive x-axis source and saddle, together with O. The sum of their nondegenerate
indices is 2(n+1)-(2n+1)=1, agreeing with the degree of the outward field on a large circle.

If all sigma_j=+1, the basin signs, branch zeros and parities give y Theta>=0 on the full plane. Equation (44.1) gives
W.grad Ly=d|W|^2+kappa y Theta>0 off the zero set. The identity from Theorem 44,

  grad Ly=d W+Omega W^perp+y grad Theta,                    (58.24)

shows that every axis zero is critical. The strict derivative excludes any other critical point. At an x-axis zero
W=Omega=0 and y=0, while grad Theta=A e_2. Differentiating (58.24) proves (58.10). At R_j the Hessian is diag(db,d
kappa+T(R_j)), positive definite. At Q_j it is diag(-d a_j,d c_j); at O it is d diag(-b,3 beta+2). Reflection gives the
corresponding matrices at negative zeros. The properness of Ly is proved just below without sign assumptions. Finally
Ly_x=d w on the entire x-axis. Integrating the strict alternating signs of w proves (58.11) for every sign pattern.

(e) The backward radial bound at the beginning of the proof gives

  |[Phi_(-s)X]_2| <= max(R_*,|X|) for every s>=0.

Since kappa>0, the integral in (58.12) converges uniformly on compact sets of initial points. Finite-time continuous
dependence, followed by this uniform tail estimate, proves its continuity. Theorem 42(a) gives |Theta(X)|<=C(1+|X|)^q;
therefore

  |Hc(X)| <= |Theta(X)|max(R_*,|X|)
           <= C(1+|X|)^(1+q).                              (58.25)

For a fixed complete orbit, temperature transport gives

  Hc(Phi_t X)=kappa integral_(-infinity)^t
                  [Phi_u X]_2 Theta(Phi_u X) du.           (58.26)

The integral converges at negative infinity, since the orbit is bounded there and Theta(Phi_u X)=e^(kappa u)Theta(X).
The fundamental theorem of calculus gives d_t Hc(Phi_t X)=kappa [Phi_t X]_2 Theta(Phi_t X). Subtracting this from (44.1)
proves (58.14). This argument does not differentiate an infinite-time integral transversely.

By Theorems 41-42, (58.24) gives grad Ly=d beta X+O(r^(1-h)): the term Omega W^perp has this order, and y grad
Theta=O(r^(1-2h)) is smaller. Integration along rays, with a bounded contribution from a fixed disc, proves the stated
expansion of Ly. Since 1+q=2-2h<2 and 2-h<2, (58.25) gives properness of L_tilde.

At every zero Theta=0, so L_tilde=Ly there. A nonconstant connection has positive integral of d|W|^2 on any nontrivial
finite segment. Integrate (58.14) and use continuity at its two limits to obtain L_tilde(Z_2)>L_tilde(Z_1). The same
identity excludes a periodic orbit or a cycle, including a homoclinic loop. QED.

Remark 58.1 (consistency statements, not exclusions).

The following chart, local and angular observations do not construct an A2-broad profile and do not exclude one.

(i) The charts cannot be continued with finite first component through a separating saddle branch. Under (c), fix
gamma_j, put C_j=f^(p_j)(phi_j)/p_j! and E_j=2p_j/q-1. For the inverse escape labels on its two sides, (58.4) and (58.7)
give

  c_(R_(j-1))(phi)
    ~ (|T(R_(j-1))|/|C_j|)^(2/q)/(q E_j)
                          (phi-phi_j)^(-E_j)
       as phi decreases to phi_j,
  c_(R_j)(phi)
    ~ -( |T(R_j)|/|C_j|)^(2/q)/(q E_j)
                          (phi_j-phi)^(-E_j)
       as phi increases to phi_j,
  E_j = nu c_j/a_j.                                      (58.27)

Indeed dc/dphi=-(1/q)|A/f|^(2/q), and integration of |phi-phi_j|^(-2p_j/q) gives these constants; E_j>0. The exponent
identity follows by substituting a_j=b/m_j. It agrees with the linear saddle passage exponent and is not a nonlinear
gluing assertion.

On a smooth transverse section through a regular point of gamma_j, take z=0 on the branch and z>0 on the R_(j-1) side.
The local flow to the launch circle is a smooth transverse diffeomorphism, and (58.15) gives a nonzero derivative of the
escape angle. The temperature has exact transverse order p_j by (a), with eta_R positive on its own side. Thus eta_R is
asymptotic to a positive constant times |z|^p_j. Multiplying the inverse-label asymptotics by eta_R^nu gives

  xi_(R_(j-1)) ~ C_+ z^(-m_j) as z decreases to zero,
  xi_(R_j) ~ -C_- |z|^(-m_j) as z increases to zero,
  C_+,C_->0,

since p_j nu-E_j=1-p_j=-m_j. Neither first component has a finite continuous extension. Independently, grad Theta=0 on
the branch, so any C^1 extension retaining eta_R=Theta/T(R) has a zero second derivative row and cannot retain
determinant one. This obstruction concerns these prescribed coordinates; it is not an obstruction to smoothness of the
original fields.

(ii) The source spectrum and A alone do not determine the sign of the upper vorticity at the level of exact local
solutions. For r>0, k!=0, u=x-r, define on a neighbourhood of (r,0)

  w=(b/k)(exp(k u)-1),
  Psi=(beta x-w)y,
  Theta=b(beta-1)exp(k u)y,
  Omega=b k exp(k u)y.                                    (58.28)

Direct differentiation gives

  U=(w-beta x,(beta-w')y),
  W=(w,(2 beta-w')y),    div W=2 beta,
  -Lap Psi=w''y=Omega.

With T=b(beta-1)exp(k u), g=b k exp(k u), one has T'=kT, g'=kg and w'-b=kw. It follows exactly that

  W.grad Theta=[kw+2 beta-w']Theta=kappa Theta,
  W.grad Omega+Omega=[kw+2 beta+1-w']Omega
                    =(beta-1)Omega=Theta_x.

Thus both transport equations, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), and -Lap Psi=Omega hold, not merely their leading jets. At the source
DW=diag(b,kappa), T(r)=b(beta-1)>0 and g(r)=bk, allowing either sign. Reflection supplies disjoint germs at the negative
source with the A2 x parities. This does not supply the origin jet, canonical global inverse or uniform sublinearity.

For comparison, the all-ell kernel identities are already (55.7),(55.12),(55.13). With

  N_ell(u,v)=4 ell u v /
      (pi [((ell-u)^2+v^2)((ell+u)^2+v^2)]),
  F_axis(ell)=integral_Q1 N_ell Omega,

they give

  F_axis=beta ell-w(ell), F_axis'=beta-w'(ell),
  integral_Q1 N_ell(D Omega+alpha Omega)
    =ell(beta-w'(ell))+(alpha-1)(beta ell-w(ell)),           (58.29)

where D=X.grad. These integrals and the first differentiated kernel integral are absolutely convergent by Theorems 42
and 55. At a zero of slope mu the last value is ell(alpha beta-mu). In the three-zero case, F_axis(x_i)=beta x_i,
F_axis'(x_1)=F_axis'(x_3)=-2 and F_axis'(x_2)=beta+a. The signs of F_axis-beta ell on the four intervals are +,-,+,-.
For alpha=b/beta the last integral is zero at the sources and x_2(b+a)>0 at the saddle. No new kernel identity is
asserted.

(iii) Here are angular functions satisfying the scalar angular conditions in (c) for every beta>2 and every list
m_1,...,m_n. Choose

  1=t_0>t_1>...>t_n>t_(n+1)=0,
  t_(j+1)<z_j<t_j,    0<=j<n,

and define on the whole angle circle

  f(phi)=sigma sin(phi) cos(phi)^2
             product_(j=1)^n (sin(phi)^2-t_j)^(m_j+1),
  G(phi)=sigma sin(2phi)
             product_(j=1)^n (sin(phi)^2-t_j)^m_j
             product_(j=0)^(n-1) (sin(phi)^2-z_j).          (58.30)

Empty products are one. Put phi_j=arcsin(sqrt(t_j)). These are smooth nonzero trigonometric polynomials, with the
temperature and vorticity parities. In particular f(0)=f(pi/2)=f'(pi/2)=G(0)=G(pi/2)=0.

To check the signs, put t=sin^2(phi), increasing on the open quadrant. On (t_(j+1),t_j) exactly the temperature factors
indexed 1,...,j are negative, so sgn f=sigma_j. At t_j, the leading coefficient of f has sign sigma_(j-1). Just above
t_j, exactly the first j-1 saddle factors and exactly j of the z factors are negative in G. Its sign is

  sigma (-1)^(m_1+...+m_(j-1)+j)=-sigma_(j-1).

Crossing order m_j gives sign sigma_j below. Since t'(phi_j)>0, the angular orders are exactly p_j,m_j and the leading
derivative product is negative. There is precisely one additional simple zero t=z_j in each J_(R_j), 0<=j<n. The
endpoint derivatives are nonzero with the signs in (58.8), by direct differentiation of the sine and cosine factors.

For n=1, writing t_*=t_1, z=z_0 and tau=(-1)^(m+1)sigma, the exact endpoint values are

  f'(0)=tau t_*^(m+1),
  f''(pi/2)=2 sigma(1-t_*)^(m+1),
  G'(pi/2)=-2 sigma(1-t_*)^m(1-z),
  G'(0)=2 tau t_*^m z.                                    (58.31)

The last sign is a choice of the example, not a necessary condition. The simultaneous zeros of f,f' in the quadrant are
the internal phi_j and pi/2; G vanishes at all of them. The reflected statement verifies Theorem 47(a) on the whole
circle. Also sigma G>0 next to pi/2, as required by Theorems 41 and 50(c).

For each J_(R_j) and any nonzero amplitude A of sign sigma_j, choose phi_c in that interval and set

  c(phi)=-(1/q) integral_(phi_c)^phi
                          (A/f(theta))^(2/q) dtheta.      (58.32)

The ratio is positive. The map is smooth and decreasing. The zero orders of f at its endpoints are one at zero, two at
pi/2 and p_j>=2 internally. Each exponent 2k/q is greater than one, so the integral diverges at both endpoints: c tends
to +infinity at the lower endpoint and -infinity at the upper. Its inverse is a smooth bijection R->J_(R_j) satisfying
(58.4). This verifies the scalar escape laws only.

The other purely angular checks are as follows. The inverse -(partial_phi^2+(2-h)^2)P=G in Theorems 38,41,42 is
nonresonant, since 3/2<2-h<2. It gives a smooth nonzero odd-odd P. Thus the angular energy integral
integral(P'^2+(2-h)^2 P^2) is positive, and all angular norms appearing in Theorem 38 are finite. Its three
quadratic-limit integrals are also strictly positive: q>0 and f!=0 give integral(q^2 f^2+f'^2)>0; G!=0 gives integral
G^2>0; and the term (1-h)^2(2-h)^2 P^2 in |M_P|^2 gives integral |M_P|^2>0. Theorem 42(c) defines smooth coefficients

  f1=-q P' f+(2-h)P f',
  G1=h P' G+(2-h)P G'-q cos(phi)f+sin(phi)f'.

They have the required parities, and f1(0)=f1(pi/2)= f1'(pi/2)=0. The P1 inverse is also nonresonant, since 1<2-2h<2.
The angular expression for the constant in Theorem 40(c) is

  C_K=(1/2) integral_0^(2 pi) |G(phi)|^(2 beta) dphi,

which is finite and positive. Indeed inserting (58.15) and J0=rho^(-h)G(F) into (40.3) cancels the factors rho^2 and
changes variables by F. This checks that constant, not the existence of K or its transport law.

Theorems 36,39 and 48 concern beta=2 and impose no conditions here. Theorem 49 excludes an entire stream function with
one fixed finite angular bandwidth. It does not exclude a leading angular coefficient P with finite Fourier support. The
source assignment of nonzero-G labels in Theorems 46(d) and 47(b) is compatible at the level of labels: the assigned
sources have nonzero temperature gradient, and R_0 and its reflection each receive an open nonzero-G interval. It is not
a construction of the backward-limit map.

No fields or radial remainders are defined by (58.30). Consequently the history identities of Theorems 37-40, the
canonical velocity, the separatrix coefficient magnitude in (58.19)-(58.23), the finite-radius moments of Theorem 55,
and the invariant-set balances of Theorem 54(e) have not been realized. For n>=1 the interval with sigma G<0 next to
phi_1 would already give the negative radial-sign set of Theorem 55 far out, because D
Omega+(1+2h)Omega=(1+h)r^(-h)G+O(r^(-2h)). For n=0 the example has sigma G>0 throughout the open quadrant, so the sign
reversal required by Theorem 55 would have to occur at finite radius; the example makes no assertion about that.
Remark 55.1, including its weak-sign paragraph, applies under beta > 2 and Omega >= 0 on Q1; it concerns full spatial
fields and weights, not an additional condition on leading angular functions alone.

The distinction from earlier results is precise. The trace quantization and its continuation are Theorem 27; the exact
orders and outgoing calculation extend Theorem 54(a) to every saddle of a finite chain, and (58.6)-(58.8) extend Theorem
54(d). Part (b) extends the construction of Theorem 50 from its single exhaustive basin to each regular x-axis source
basin. Equation (58.9) is already covered by Theorem 54(e). The slice localization in (d) is finer than a sign change
somewhere on a half-line. Theorem 57(b) proves that latter conclusion for every beta>=2 without the chain hypotheses,
but does not localize it to each basin slice component; it is not used as a premise here.

Finally Theorem 44(a),(b) contains the potential and the backward integrability needed for (58.12), but states no
continuous proper correction with (58.14) for beta>2. The properness of Ly itself is already in Theorem 50(f). Theorem 4
already excludes periodic orbits, homoclinic loops and cycles. A bounded connection has Theta=0 by temperature
transport, so its strict ordering by Ly is already a consequence of (44.1). The new assertion in (e) is one explicit
continuous proper function, with the exact positive orbit derivative, on the full plane for either temperature sign. It
does not provide a new exclusion.

### Theorem 59 (beta = 2: nonnegative vorticity, angular restrictions and the remaining alternatives)

Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2. Thus the fields are smooth on R^2, the velocity is
canonical and uniformly o(|X|), the temperature and vorticity have at most polynomial growth, and

  W = 2X + U,    div W = 4,
  W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x,    W.grad Theta = 0,
  -Lap Psi = Omega,    U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x).                 (59.1)

The stream function is normalized by Psi(O) = 0. The temperature is even in x and odd in y, Omega and Psi are odd in
both coordinates, and

  Theta(0,y) = 0,    Theta = a0 x^2 y + O(|X|^5),
  Omega = (2a0/5)xy + O(|X|^4),    a0 != 0.               (59.2)

Put Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, O = (0,0), Z = {W = 0}, Crit = {grad Theta = 0}, and N = R^2 \ Crit. Let Phi_t be the flow and
pi(X) its backward limit from Theorem 44(b). Let P = (x1,0), C, Q+ and Q- be the point, zero component and endpoints of
Theorems 2 and 16, and put M = Theta(Q+). Write A = pi/2 for the quadrant angle; pi(X) always denotes the backward-limit
map when it has an argument.

Use p for the angular stream-function coefficient denoted P in Theorems 33, 36 and 45. Their smooth angular functions
satisfy

  Theta(r,phi) -> H(phi),    r^(1/2) Omega(r,phi) -> G(phi),
  r^(-1/2)(U_r,U_phi) -> (-p',(3/2)p),
  -(p'' + (9/4)p) = G,    p(0) = p(A) = 0.               (59.3)

Here H(0) = H(A) = 0, H is odd about 0 and even about A, and G and p are odd about both axes. Define

  (V+) Omega >= 0 on Q1;
  (T+) a0 > 0 and Theta >= 0 on Q1;
  (S)  Z cap Q1 = C cap Q1;
  (R)  C \ {Q+,Q-} is contained in N.

Set w(x) = W_1(x,0), v(y) = W_2(0,y), T(x) = Theta_y(x,0), and E(y) = Theta_xx(0,y)/2.

(a) Under (V+), Psi > 0 on Q1 and w(x) < 2x for every x > 0. The only components of Z meeting the boundary of the closed
first quadrant are {O} and C. Every other component meeting that closed quadrant lies wholly in Q1. Consequently the
following alternatives are exhaustive and disjoint:

  (I)  no component of Z lies wholly in Q1, equivalently (S);
  (II) some component of Z lies wholly in Q1.             (59.4)

(b) Under (V+),

  G >= 0,    G not identically zero,
  p > 0 and p'' < 0 on (0,A),
  p'(0) > 0,    p'(A) < 0.                               (59.5)

There is a unique phi_* in (0,A) with p'(phi_*) = 0. At interior angles,

  H' = 0 implies G = 0 and H'' = 0,
  G = 0 implies H' >= 0,
  H' < 0 implies G > 0.                                  (59.6)

At the axes,

  G'(0) >= 0,    G'(A) < 0.                              (59.7)

On every compact angular subinterval of (0,A), U_phi > 0 for all sufficiently large radii. On such subintervals to the
left of phi_*, U_r < 0 eventually; to its right, U_r > 0 eventually. The function U.grad Theta takes both strict signs
arbitrarily far out in Q1.

(c) Assume (V+) and (I). The conclusions of Theorem 53(d) apply at Q+, for its actual temperature M, including M = 0.
Define

  D = Q1 cap int_{R^2}{Theta = M}.                        (59.8)

This invariant open set contains the potential region of that theorem. In addition, U_r < 0 on D in a sufficiently small
neighbourhood of Q+, and D meets every sufficiently small neighbourhood of Q+.

If (R) also holds, then Theta > 0 throughout Q1. In the notation of Theorem 48(e), phi_1 = 0 and phi_4 = A, so its
plateau has endpoints

  0 < phi_2 < phi_3 < A.                                 (59.9)

On that plateau G = 0; on (phi_3,A), G > 0. On (0,phi_2) the asserted vorticity condition is only G >= 0.

(d) Under (V+), at every zero Q in the closed first quadrant,

  Theta_x(Q) = Omega(Q) >= 0.                            (59.10)

At every X in Q1 where Omega(X) = 0,

  grad Omega(X) = 0,    Theta_x(X) = 0.                   (59.11)

If also W(X) = 0, then

  Theta_xx(X) = Theta_xy(X) = 0.                          (59.12)

A regular such zero has a nonzero vertical temperature gradient, and its horizontal direction is the eigenspace of DW
for eigenvalue 4.

If Z has finitely many components, let eps = ind(C), and let n_+ and n_- count the components wholly in Q1 with indices
+1 and -1. Then

  eps is +1 or -1,    I_Q = (1-eps)/2,
  n_+ - n_- = (1-eps)/2,                                 (59.13)

where I_Q is their total index. Components of index zero are allowed.

Suppose, in addition, Z has finitely many components, Q+ is incoming, M > 0, closure(Theta(Q1)) = [0,M], every zero in
the closed quadrant with temperature in (0,M) is regular, and each such temperature is attained at exactly one zero in
Q1. Then the one positive angular excursion of Theorem 56(e) reaches both axes: its increasing passage starts at 0, its
decreasing passage ends at A, and G is strictly positive on the decreasing passage.

(e) Under (T+), an interior zero of Theta belongs to Crit and has Omega = 0. Moreover,

  T(x) >= 0 and E(y) >= 0 for x,y > 0,
  H'(0) >= 0,    H''(A) >= 0.                            (59.14)

(f) Let Ly be the function of Theorem 44, normalized by Ly(O) = 0. For every Lebesgue measurable set B contained in Q1
with Phi_t(B) = B for all real t, and every lambda > 0,

  int_B exp(-lambda Ly)(4 - 3lambda |W|^2) dX = 0.         (59.15)

The integral is absolutely convergent. If B has positive area, the mean of |W|^2 for the weight exp(-lambda Ly) on B is
4/(3lambda).

For a regular escaping point X in Q1, write q = pi(X), L(X) = W.grad^perp Theta/|grad Theta|^2, and let J(X), a(X) and
phi_inf be its outgoing amplitude, positive radial amplitude and exit angle as in Theorem 39(d). Define

  I_*(X) = int_{-infinity}^{infinity}
              e^(-3t)(y(Phi_t X)-q_y) dt.

Under (V+), J(X) >= 0. If J(X) > 0, the sign of I_*(X) is opposite to the sign of H'(phi_inf). If J(X) = 0, then I_*(X)
= 0 and H'(phi_inf) > 0.

(g) The angular conditions in (59.3), (59.5)-(59.7), the strict endpoint conditions H'(0) > 0 and H''(A) > 0, and the
shape in Theorem 48(e) with phi_1 = 0 and phi_4 = A are mutually consistent. Explicit smooth data are given below with
H > 0 on (0,A), G > 0 on both open passages, and

  {phi in [0,A]: G(phi) = 0} = {0,A} union [phi_2,phi_3].

Their p solves p'' + (9/4)p = 0 on the plateau. This is a consistency statement for the listed angular conditions.

Scope. These are necessary conditions on a hypothetical A2-broad profile at beta = 2. Neither existence nor nonexistence
is asserted. The sign conditions, (I), (R), finiteness, and the further incoming-endpoint hypotheses in (d) are
additional wherever used. Under (V+), (I) is equivalent to (S); that equivalence is not asserted under (T+) alone.
Theorem 53 supplies the general component classification and range identity, Theorem 48 supplies the conditional angular
shape, and Theorem 56 supplies the connection, source and incoming-endpoint results cited here. They are not new
assertions of this theorem. Part (f) extends Theorem 56(g) from the whole quadrant and temperature levels to arbitrary
invariant measurable subsets. Part (g) does not realize its data by a stream function and flow satisfying (59.1). All
proof inputs are earlier theorems or arguments proved below. The axis facts shared with Theorem 57(a) are reproved
below; that theorem is not used as an input.

Proof.

1. Axis facts used in the proof.

Smooth oddness in both variables gives Omega = xy B near O with B smooth and B(O) = 2a0/5. Under (V+), evaluation on x =
y > 0 gives B(O) >= 0. Since a0 != 0, B(O) > 0, so a0 > 0 and Omega > 0 on a sufficiently small open quarter disc. At
each x > 0,

  Omega_y(x,0) = lim_{t -> 0+} Omega(x,t)/t >= 0.

Theorem 21(b), whose hypotheses are now satisfied, excludes every positive x-axis zero after P. Theorem 2 gives w'(x1) =
4 and hence w > 0 on (x1,infinity).

For X = (x,y) and Y = (s,t) in Q1, group the four reflections in the centred-disc formula of Theorem 9. The resulting
kernel is

  K_D(X,Y) = (1/(2pi)) log(
      |X-(-s,t)| |X-(s,-t)| / (|X-Y| |X+Y|)).

Let d = |X|^2 + |Y|^2, u = 2xs > 0 and z = 2yt > 0. The square of the ratio in this logarithm is

  [d^2-(u-z)^2]/[d^2-(u+z)^2] > 1

away from X = Y. At X = Y the kernel has a positive logarithmic singularity. It is locally integrable, and for fixed X
it is O_X(|Y|^(-2)) at infinity: the numerator minus denominator is 4uz = O_X(|Y|^2), whereas the denominator is of
order |Y|^4.

Theorem 33(a) gives Omega = O(|Y|^(-1/2)). Thus K_D Omega is absolutely integrable at infinity, with a radial majorant
proportional to rho^(-3/2). Theorem 9 identifies its integral with the canonical Psi. In particular no harmonic term at
infinity is being discarded. More explicitly, U = o(r) and Psi(O) = 0 give Psi = o(r^2); Theorem 9 proves that the
parity-cancelled boundary term tends to zero under precisely these bounds. Consequently

  Psi(X) = int_Q1 K_D(X,Y) Omega(Y) dY > 0.

Strictness follows by integrating over a small disc where Omega > 0. Also -Lap Psi >= 0 and Psi vanishes on the axes.

Differentiating the same canonical formula on the positive axes gives

  Psi_y(x,0) = int_Q1
    4xst Omega(s,t) /
    (pi [(x-s)^2+t^2][(x+s)^2+t^2]) ds dt,

  Psi_x(0,y) = int_Q1
    4yst Omega(s,t) /
    (pi [s^2+(y-t)^2][s^2+(y+t)^2]) ds dt.

The first is also the normal kernel in Theorem 55. Both kernels are positive in Q1. At their possible boundary
singularities, oddness gives respectively Omega = O(t) and Omega = O(s). The products are bounded by a constant times
t^2/((s-x)^2+t^2), respectively s^2/(s^2+(t-y)^2), and hence are locally integrable. At infinity each kernel is
O(r^(-2)), so the preceding decay gives absolute convergence. Theorem 9 justifies the differentiated limit on compact
sets. The same positive disc gives strict positivity of both integrals. Therefore w(x) = 2x-Psi_y(x,0) < 2x for all x >
0, and v(y) = 2y+Psi_x(0,y) > 2y for all y > 0.

Differentiating temperature transport on the axes gives

  w T' = (w'-4)T,    v E' = (2v'-8)E.

For the second equation, differentiate twice in x at x = 0, use Theta = Theta_x = Theta_y = 0 there and W_1,x = 4-v'.
Theorem 2 gives T > 0 on (0,x1], including T(x1) > 0. Continuity first gives positivity just after x1, and uniqueness
for the regular linear ODE on (x1,infinity) propagates it. Since v > 0, its ODE is regular on (0,infinity), and E(y) =
a0 y + O(y^3) near zero gives E > 0 everywhere on that half-axis.

Choose the launch radius R0 of Theorem 36(d), and put theta_0(alpha) = Theta(R0 cos alpha,R0 sin alpha). That theorem
gives theta_0 = H o F, where F is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism fixing the axes. Direct differentiation gives
theta_0'(0) = R0 T(R0). At A both Cartesian derivatives of Theta vanish, by evenness in x and Theta(0,y) = 0, so
theta_0'(A) = 0 and theta_0''(A) = 2R0^2 E(R0). Hence

  0 < w(x) < 2x for x > x1,    v(y) > 2y for y > 0,
  T(x) > 0,    E(y) > 0,
  H'(0) = R0 T(R0)/F'(0) > 0,
  H''(A) = 2R0^2 E(R0)/F'(A)^2 > 0.                     (59.16)

The x-axis zeros in the closed quadrant are now O and P, and the y-axis has only O. The origin is isolated since DW(O) =
diag(-4,8). By Theorem 16, C crosses the positive x-axis only at P and avoids the y-axis. A connected zero component
meeting Q1 but avoiding both axes lies entirely in Q1, since the four open quadrants are the connected components of the
complement of the axes. This proves (a), including both directions of (59.4). It also proves (X) and (Y) of Theorem 48.

2. Angular restrictions.

The uniform limit in Theorem 36 gives G >= 0. Its nonvanishing follows from Theorem 34, which applies to every A2-broad
profile at beta = 2. For k = 3/2, the Dirichlet kernel for -(d_phi^2+k^2) on (0,A) is

  K_k(phi,s) =
    sin(k min(phi,s)) sin(k(A-max(phi,s))) /
    (k sin(kA)).

It vanishes at the boundary, solves the homogeneous equation away from phi = s, and its first derivative in phi has jump
-1 there. It is strictly positive in the open square because kA = 3pi/4 < pi. The homogeneous Dirichlet problem has only
the zero solution since sin(kA) != 0. Thus

  p(phi) = int_0^A K_k(phi,s) G(s) ds > 0.

The equation gives p'' = -(9/4)p-G < 0. Differentiation at the endpoints gives

  p'(0) = int_0^A sin(k(A-s)) G(s)/sin(kA) ds > 0,
  p'(A) = -int_0^A sin(ks) G(s)/sin(kA) ds < 0.

The derivative p' is strictly decreasing and has opposite endpoint signs, proving the uniqueness of phi_*.

Theorem 45(f) supplies, with remainders differentiable to every order at the stated radial scales,

  H1 = (3/2)p H',
  G1 = (1/2)p'G + (3/2)pG' + sin(phi)H',
  Theta = H + r^(-1/2)H1 + O_infty(r^(-1)),
  Omega = r^(-1/2)G + r^(-1)G1 + O_infty(r^(-3/2)).
                                                               (59.17)

If G vanishes at an interior angle, nonnegativity makes G' vanish there. On that fixed ray, multiplication of the
vorticity expansion by r gives G1 >= 0. Hence sin(phi)H' >= 0, which proves G = 0 implies H' >= 0, and its
contrapositive.

We give the critical-angle argument, including the additional second-derivative conclusion. Let H'(phi_c) = 0, alpha_c =
F^(-1)(phi_c), and X(t,alpha) = Phi_t(R0 e(alpha)). On the launch circle W_r > 0. Therefore theta_0'(alpha_c) = 0 and
W.grad Theta = 0 imply grad Theta(X(0,alpha_c)) = 0. By Theorem 44(d), its entire orbit is critical and has Omega = 0,
so its outgoing amplitude and G(phi_c) vanish. This reproves the implication of Theorem 47(a) being used.

Put lambda(alpha) = (grad Theta . (W_2,-W_1))/|W|^2 at the launch point. Theorem 33(c) gives

  Theta_x(X(t,alpha)) = lambda(alpha)e^(-4t)W_2(X(t,alpha)),
  theta_0'(alpha) = -R0 W_r(X(0,alpha)) lambda(alpha).

For every fixed t, the smooth function alpha -> Omega(X(t,alpha)) is nonnegative near alpha_c and vanishes at alpha_c.
Its alpha derivative is zero there for every t. Differentiating its transport equation in alpha consequently gives
partial_alpha Theta_x(X(t,alpha_c)) = 0. Since lambda(alpha_c) = 0, the preceding cofactor formula now gives

  lambda'(alpha_c) W_2(X(t,alpha_c)) = 0.

The orbit escapes with interior angle phi_c. Thus W_2/|X| tends to 2sin(phi_c) > 0, and lambda'(alpha_c) = 0.
Differentiating the launch identity and theta_0 = H o F gives

  0 = theta_0''(alpha_c) = H''(phi_c) F'(alpha_c)^2.

This proves the first implication in (59.6). It does not assert that every critical point is flat to all orders.

Nonnegativity and the zero axis values give G'(0) >= 0 and G'(A) <= 0. If G'(A) = 0, differentiate (59.17) at A. Since
p(A) = G(A) = H'(A) = 0,

  G1'(A) = 2p'(A)G'(A) + H''(A) = H''(A) > 0.

The differentiated remainder then gives Omega_phi(r,A) = r^(-1)H''(A) + O(r^(-3/2)) > 0 for large r. This contradicts
the nonpositive left derivative at A of the nonnegative function Omega(r,.) vanishing at A. Hence G'(A) < 0.

The velocity conclusions follow uniformly on the stated compact intervals from (59.3). Temperature transport and (59.17)
give

  U.grad Theta = -2r Theta_r
              = r^(-1/2)(3/2)pH' + O(r^(-1)).

There are interior angles with H' > 0 near 0, by (59.16), and angles with H' < 0 near A, by H'(A) = 0 and H''(A) > 0.
Positivity of p proves the two asserted signs arbitrarily far out.

3. The component alternatives.

Under (V+) and (I), part (a) supplies (S), so Theorem 53(d) gives outgoing Q+, escape of every nonstationary orbit in
Q1, and all its stated applications of Theorems 35 and 51. In particular the local outgoing formulation of Theorem 51
applies even at M = 0; its alternative exclusion of other zeros with temperature M is not being used.

The connected open invariant saturation in Theorem 35 is contained in D, and meets every small neighbourhood of Q+.
Since every flow map preserves both Theta and Q1, it preserves D. On D the temperature gradient vanishes. Bounded
backward orbits and vorticity transport give Omega(X) = e^(-s)Omega(Phi_{-s}X) -> 0 as s -> infinity. Thus Omega = 0 on
D, and U is harmonic and real analytic there. The contained saturation has infinite area. This proves these properties
of D without asserting that D is connected or that its complement in the full temperature level is null.

At any zero Q in Q1,

  U_r(Q) = -2|Q| < 0,    U_phi(Q) = 0.                  (59.18)

Continuity gives U_r < 0 near Q+, and the preceding saturation ensures nonempty open intersections with D arbitrarily
close to Q+.

Suppose also (R). By (59.16), a0 > 0, (X) and (Y) hold. Theorem 48(e) therefore gives M > 0, phi_1 = 0, phi_4 = A, its
two strict passages, and the nonempty plateau between phi_2 and phi_3. It also gives exactly two angular preimages of
each value in (0,M). The strict inequality for G on the decreasing passage follows from (59.6). This argument
establishes no strict positivity for G on the increasing passage.

To prove the additional spatial positivity, orient C[P,Q+] from P upwards. By (R), Theorem 39(b) makes Theta strictly
monotone on this regular half-arc; its initial derivative is positive since T(x1) > 0. Hence its only zero-temperature
point is P. By (a) and (S), the only zero-temperature zeros of W in the closed quadrant are O and P.

If X in Q1 had Theta(X) = 0, temperature invariance and Theorem 44(b) would give Theta(pi(X)) = 0. An interior orbit
cannot have backward limit O, whose unstable manifold is the invariant y-axis. If its backward limit were P, it would
enter N near P and then remain in N by gradient transport. By Theorem 39(b), the only two nonstationary orbits with
backward limit P are its two regular fibres. They are the x-axis orbits on (0,x1) and (x1,infinity), so neither contains
X. The stationary case is already excluded by the zero set just described. Finally every interior backward limit has
nonnegative temperature. Therefore Theta > 0 on Q1, proving (c).

For (d), equation (59.1) at a zero of W gives Theta_x = Omega. Its sign in (59.10) uses membership in the closed first
quadrant. At an interior zero of the nonnegative smooth function Omega, grad Omega = 0. Substitution in vorticity
transport gives Theta_x = 0, proving (59.11). Differentiating the same equation gives

  grad Theta_x = (DW)^T grad Omega + (D^2 Omega)W + grad Omega.

At a zero of W satisfying (59.11) every term on the right vanishes, proving (59.12). If the point is regular, its
remaining temperature derivative Theta_y is nonzero. The matrix DW is symmetric because Omega = 0 there. Differentiated
temperature transport gives (DW)^T grad Theta = 0; trace DW = 4 then makes the vertical direction its kernel and the
horizontal direction its eigenspace for 4.

The classifications needed for the remaining alternatives are exactly Theorem 53(a): components wholly in Q1 are compact
smooth arcs or critical singletons; arc spectra are {0,4}, endpoints are critical with flat Theta-Theta(Q) and Omega,
and regular subarcs have strictly monotone temperature. Flatness does not make either field locally constant at an
endpoint. Theorem 56(c) supplies the isolated index +1 singleton source alternatives, including the analytic odd-order
centre drift in the degenerate case. Theorem 53(e)-(f) gives index -1 for an isolated constant-temperature arc. None of
these classifications excludes case (II).

Under finiteness, part (a) removes every additional axis component in Theorem 53(f), so I_A = 0 and its integer k = 0.
Formula (53.8) and the identity displayed before it read

  eps + 2I_Q = 1,    -1 + 2eps + 4I_Q = 1.

The same theorem gives eps in {+1,-1}. Its component index formula and the source/saddle cases show that the interior
indices belong to {-1,0,+1}. Thus I_Q = n_+-n_-, proving (59.13). No infinite componentwise index sum is used.

For clarity, an incoming Q+ still requires an actual backward zero B on a component wholly in Q1 with

  Theta(B) = M,    Ly(B) < Ly(Q+),                        (59.19)

by Theorem 53(b). The connection and accumulation assertions are those of Theorems 53(b)-(c) and 56(a),(f); they
introduce no positive lower bound for connecting actions. Under all the further hypotheses of Theorem 56(e), that
theorem gives (R), its potential side and its single positive excursion. A nontrivial zero interval next to 0 would
contradict H'(0) > 0; one next to A would contradict H''(A) > 0. The derivatives on the two passages are nonzero by
Theorem 56(d), so (59.6) gives G > 0 on the decreasing passage. This proves the last assertion of (d) without applying
Theorem 48(e), whose hypothesis (S) is absent in this incoming case.

4. The temperature sign.

Theorem 53(h) states the range equality

  H([0,A]) = closure(Theta(Q1))
           = Theta(Z cap closure(Q1)).

Consequently, for every profile in the theorem,

  Theta >= 0 on Q1
    iff Theta >= 0 on Z cap closure(Q1)
    iff H >= 0 on [0,A].                                 (59.20)

This equivalence is an application of that theorem, not an additional result. Under (T+) the common range is [0,m] for
some m > 0, since the local jet is positive in Q1. At an interior zero of Theta the minimum condition gives grad Theta =
0, and Theorem 44(d) gives Omega = 0.

One-sided differentiation at the x-axis gives T >= 0. At the y-axis, Theta = Theta_x = 0 and nonnegativity give
Theta_xx >= 0, so E >= 0. The same arguments for H give H'(0) >= 0 and, using H'(A) = 0, H''(A) >= 0. They give no strict trace
inequality. This proves (e).

For this subclass, G has a positive open interval by Theorem 34 and vanishes at critical angles of H by Theorem 47(a).
Neither statement gives G >= 0 everywhere. Under (T+) alone the preceding proof has not removed additional components
meeting an axis, so it cannot identify the component exclusion with (S). In particular its finite index formula remains
(53.9), with its possible k term. If no component lies wholly in Q1, Theorem 56(a) nevertheless applies directly to that
exclusion, without an axis-zero exclusion, and its temperature M is nonnegative by (59.20). This is an input from
Theorem 56(a), not a further conclusion special to Theorem 59.

5. The measurable balance and orbit signs.

Theorem 44(a) gives

  grad Ly = 3W + Omega W^perp + y grad Theta,
  W.grad Ly = 3|W|^2,    d Ly = y d Theta on zero arcs.    (59.21)

Theorem 36 yields grad Ly = 6X + O(r^(1/2)) and, by integration along radii,

  Ly(X) = 3r^2 + O(r^(3/2)).

Indeed Omega W = O(r^(1/2)) and y grad Theta = O(1). Thus exp(-lambda Ly) and |W|^2 exp(-lambda Ly) are integrable over
Q1.

For an invariant measurable B, change variables by the smooth flow, whose Jacobian is exp(4t):

  int_B exp(-lambda Ly(X)) dX
    = int_B exp(4t) exp(-lambda Ly(Phi_t Y)) dY.

For t in a fixed small interval, the linear growth bound on W and its backward version compare 1+|Phi_t Y| and 1+|Y| in
both directions. The time derivative of the integrand is therefore bounded by a polynomial times exp(-c|Y|^2), uniformly
in that interval, for some c > 0. Dominated differentiation at t = 0 gives (59.15). Division by the finite positive
weighted measure gives its mean formula. No boundary regularity of B is assumed. Taking B = Q1 or B = {Theta=c} cap Q1
recovers the corresponding cases of Theorem 56(g); those cases are not new.

For a regular escaping X in Q1, Theorem 39(a),(d) gives q in Z cap N, L(X) != 0, a(X) = lim_{t -> infinity}
e^(-2t)|Phi_t X| > 0, and

  J(X) = lim_{t -> infinity} e^t Omega(Phi_t X),
  G(phi_inf) = a(X)^(1/2)J(X),
  H'(phi_inf) = -2a(X)^2/L(X),
  J(X) = (3/L(X)) int_{-infinity}^{infinity}
                         e^(-3t)(y(Phi_t X)-q_y) dt.     (59.22)

For completeness, the displacement at negative times is O(e^(4t)) by Theorem 39(a), so its weighted integrand is O(e^t).
At positive times the natural tail gives |Phi_t X| = O(e^(2t)), making the integrand O(e^(-t)). This proves absolute
convergence at both ends. Equivalently, the last identity follows by integrating the cofactor formula Theta_x(Phi_t X) =
e^(-4t)W_2(Phi_t X)/L(X) over all times in the vorticity equation, and integrating the derivative of y-q_y by parts;
these same estimates make both boundary terms zero.

Under (V+), J >= 0 since the orbit remains in Q1. When J > 0, (59.22) gives sign I_* = sign L = -sign H'. When J = 0,
I_* = 0 and G(phi_inf) = 0. The nonzero value H'(phi_inf) = -2a(X)^2/L(X), together with (59.6), then gives
H'(phi_inf) > 0. Positivity of y along the orbit does not prescribe the sign of y-q_y. This proves (f).

6. Explicit angular data.

Set a = A/3 and b = 2A/3. Define

  eta(t) = exp(-1/t) for t > 0, and eta(t) = 0 for t <= 0,
  chi(t) = eta(t)/(eta(t)+eta(1-t)).

The denominator is positive for every real t. The function chi is smooth, equals 0 for t <= 0 and 1 for t >= 1, is
strictly between 0 and 1 for 0 < t < 1, and is flat at both transition endpoints. Put

  f0(phi) = chi(2(a-phi)/a)                    on [0,a],
  g0(phi) = (A-phi) chi(2(phi-b)/(A-b))         on [b,A],
  F0 = int_0^a f0(s) ds,    B0 = int_b^A g0(s) ds,
  f = f0/F0,    g = g0/B0.

Both normalization integrals are finite and strictly positive. Define

  H(phi) = int_0^phi f(s) ds                   for 0 <= phi <= a,
  H(phi) = 1                                 for a <= phi <= b,
  H(phi) = int_phi^A g(s) ds                   for b <= phi <= A,

  G(phi) = phi f(phi)^2                       for 0 <= phi < a,
  G(phi) = 0                                 for a <= phi <= b,
  G(phi) = g(phi)                             for b < phi <= A.

The functions f and g are positive on their open passages and flat with value zero at a and b, respectively. Their
integrals are both 1. Hence H is smooth, rises strictly to 1, has exactly the plateau [a,b], and falls strictly to 0.
Every value in (0,1) has exactly two preimages. Near 0, H(phi) = phi/F0; near A, H(phi) = (A-phi)^2/(2B0). It follows
that H'(0) = 1/F0 > 0, H''(A) = 1/B0 > 0, and reflection makes H smooth with its required odd/even A2 parities.

The function G is flat at a and b, is positive on (0,a) and (b,A), and vanishes exactly on {0,A} union [a,b]. Near 0 it
is phi/F0^2; near A it is (A-phi)/B0. Its odd reflections across both axes are smooth, with G'(0) = 1/F0^2 > 0 and G'(A)
= -1/B0 < 0. All interior critical angles of H belong to [a,b], where H'' = G = 0. Thus (59.6)-(59.7) hold.

Define p by the positive kernel integral in Step 2. It is positive and strictly concave with the asserted endpoint
derivatives and unique maximum, and on [a,b] its equation reduces to p''+(9/4)p = 0. Its smooth odd extension follows
directly from the ODE: p = G = 0 at each endpoint implies p'' = 0 there; repeated differentiation shows that every even
derivative of p vanishes there, since the even derivatives of G do. The resulting function is the unique 2pi-periodic
solution because 3/2 is not an integer.

These data also admit all the angular first-correction coefficients in Theorem 45(f). Define H1 and G1 by (59.17), and
let p1 be the odd-odd solution of -(p1''+p1) = G1. The right side is smooth and odd-odd. The Dirichlet problem on [0,A]
is invertible since sin(A) != 0, and odd reflection gives p1; no first-harmonic solvability condition remains in this
parity class. On the plateau H1 = G1 = 0 and p1''+p1 = 0. This verifies the correction equations, without claiming an
asymptotic realization.

The same construction with the first piece of G replaced by zero satisfies all the angular inequalities and implications
above, but G then vanishes on the increasing passage as well. In particular the listed angular conditions do not imply
strict positivity there. This second angular example is not a counterexample profile.

The conditional regular-level count is compatible with the first example at N = 1, since each intermediate value has two
angular preimages. Its nonconstant plateau makes H nonanalytic; G also vanishes on an interval without vanishing
identically, so neither is a trigonometric polynomial. No finite-angular-support profile prohibited by Theorem 49 is
being constructed.

Remark 56.1 also gives the angular marginal equation B_c' = -2(A_c+1_{H=c}), with B_c(0) = B_c(A) = 0. For every c the
formal assignments A_c = -1_{H=c}, B_c = 0 satisfy this equation, including the positive-length maximum plateau. They
need not be the radial marginals of any common spatial fields. The same remark's signed-density conclusion for b = H' is
a spatial restriction and does not become a sign obstruction from the angular example. Remark 39.1 discusses higher
formal coefficients: pure powers have resonance conditions starting at order 7, while allowing logarithms gives formal
solvability at every finite order. Neither pure-power continuation nor convergence is asserted here.

The flow-dependent conditions of Theorems 33, 36, 39, 40, 44, 46-48, 53 and 56 still require a common launch map,
backward-limit map, zero set and spatial fields. Neither this construction nor the preceding sign arguments supply them.
This proves precisely the consistency assertion in (g). QED.

### Theorem 60 (beta > 2: interior zeros under a finite simple x-axis chain)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2, with beta > 2. In particular the fields are smooth, U
is the canonical uniformly sublinear velocity, and Theta and Omega have polynomial growth. Theta is even in x and odd in
y, Omega is odd in each coordinate, U_1 is odd in x and even in y, and U_2 is even in x and odd in y. The temperature
satisfies Theta(0,y) = 0 and Theta = a0 x^2 y + O(|X|^5) near the origin, with a0 != 0. With X = (x,y), the equations
are

  W = beta X + U,                 div W = 2 beta,
  div U = 0,                     d_y U_1-d_x U_2 = Omega,
  kappa = beta - 2,               b = beta + 2,
  W.grad Theta = kappa Theta,     W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x.
                                                               (60.1)

Write Phi_t for the complete flow, Z = {W = 0}, O = (0,0), and Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}. Assume:

  (A) All positive zeros of w(x) = W_1(x,0) are finitely many
      and simple.
  (B) v(y) = W_2(0,y) has no positive zero.

Use the notation of Theorem 58(a). The positive x-axis zeros, in increasing order, are R_0 = P, Q_1, R_1, ..., Q_n, R_n,
where Q_j = (x_(2j),0) are axis saddles and R_j = (x_(2j+1),0) are sources. Their upper unstable branches at Q_j are
gamma_j, and

  m_j >= 1,    p_j = m_j + 1,    a_j = b/m_j,
  DW(R_j) = diag(b,kappa),       DW(Q_j) = diag(-a_j,2 beta+a_j).
                                                               (60.2)

Here m_j are integers. A subscript distinguishes the saddle Q_j from the open quadrant Q1. Let r_n be the x-coordinate
of R_n, put S = [-r_n,r_n] x {0}, and let K be the set of points with bounded forward orbit. A zero is nondegenerate
when its derivative DW is invertible. Total order means the degree of the first nonzero Taylor polynomial; flatness
means vanishing of every derivative, including the value.

(a) Every bounded forward orbit converges to a single zero. Moreover,

  K intersect ({x = 0} union {y = 0}) = S,
  Z intersect Q1 != empty
    if and only if some gamma_j is bounded forward
    if and only if K != S.                                    (60.3)

Every bounded gamma_j has its forward limit in Q1. The limit is either a hyperbolic saddle or a zero with spectrum {0,2
beta}.

(b) Suppose gamma_j is bounded and its forward limit Q* is hyperbolic. Put m = m_j and p = m+1. If its spectrum is
{-a,c}, where a > 0 and c = 2 beta+a, then

  i = (p c-kappa)/a,    ell = (m c+1)/a,    k = (beta+1)/a
  are positive integers,
  i > p,    ell > m,    i-ell = k+1 >= 2.                       (60.4)

In linear orthonormal eigen-coordinates (s,u) at Q*, with s stable and u unstable, the first nonzero homogeneous
polynomials are

  Theta_lead = C s^i u^p,
  Omega_lead = D s^ell u^m,    C D != 0.                        (60.5)

In particular,

  N = (2m-1)/a and beta N are positive integers,                (60.6)

so beta is rational.

(c) If beta is irrational and every zero in Q1 is nondegenerate, then Z intersect Q1 is empty. Thus the conclusions of
Theorem 58(c),(d) hold under these hypotheses and (A),(B).

More generally, the same conclusion holds if there are no degenerate interior zeros and, for each interior saddle with
spectrum {-a,2 beta+a} and each m in {m_1,...,m_n}, the two numbers i and ell in (60.4) are not both integers. For
irrational beta, (B) can be replaced by simplicity of every positive zero of v.

(d) Fix a bounded gamma_j, put p = p_j and m = m_j, and parametrize it by flow time. Choose a smooth transverse section
Sigma through gamma_j(0), with parameter z and

  J = det(W(gamma_j(0)),Sigma'(0)) > 0,
  Theta(Sigma(z)) = theta_p z^p + O(z^(p+1)),
  theta_p != 0.                                               (60.7)

Write gamma_j(t) = (x(t),y(t)), W_perp = (-W_2,W_1), and set

  I(t) = exp(-(beta+1)t)y(t)
         + (beta+1) integral_(-infinity)^t
                       exp(-(beta+1)s)y(s) ds,
  I_infinity = (beta+1) integral_(-infinity)^infinity
                       exp(-(beta+1)s)y(s) ds,
  I(t) > 0,    I(t) -> I_infinity,    0 < I_infinity < infinity.
                                                               (60.8)

Identify covectors with vectors by the Euclidean inner product. At every finite time the Cartesian derivative tensors
satisfy

  D^p Theta(gamma_j(t))
    = p! theta_p J^(-p) exp(-(2 beta p-kappa)t)
                    tensor_power(W_perp(gamma_j(t)),p),         (60.9)

  D^m Omega(gamma_j(t))
    = -m! p theta_p J^(-m-1) I(t) exp(-(1+2 beta m)t)
                    tensor_power(W_perp(gamma_j(t)),m).         (60.10)

If the forward limit Q* is degenerate, both tensor norms are o(|gamma_j(t)-Q*|^L) for every L > 0. This is consistent
with the flatness of both fields at Q* given by Theorem 43(b3),(c). A hyperbolic forward limit of this particular branch
cannot have flat temperature, by (b).

(e) Suppose every zero in Q1 is nondegenerate. Then K is a finite tree whose vertices are zeros and whose edges are
heteroclinic orbits. The closure of each connected component of K intersect Q1 meets the x-axis at exactly one Q_j, and
contains gamma_j as its unique connection from the axis.

If Q1 contains exactly one source S* and one saddle Q*, then, for one j, its bounded connections are precisely

  Q_j --> Q* <-- S*.                                         (60.11)

The two unstable branches of Q* escape. The total temperature order at S* is p_j, and

  spec DW(S*) = {kappa/p_j, 2 beta-kappa/p_j}.                 (60.12)

Near S*, the temperature zero set is its strong unstable curve. One branch goes to Q*, and its other branch escapes. In
particular, grad Theta(S*) = 0; a regular source cannot occur in this configuration.

(f) In the configuration of (e), let delta be the connection from S* to Q*, parametrized by flow time, and let y_S be
the height of S*. With k from (60.4), the signed moment

  M_S = integral_(-infinity)^infinity
             exp(-(beta+1)t)(delta_2(t)-y_S) dt
  satisfies    0 < |M_S| < infinity,    sgn M_S = (-1)^k.      (60.13)

Its sign is independent of the time origin. If beta = P/R in lowest terms with P,R odd, then k is even and M_S > 0.
Consequently delta contains a point above the height y_S.

Scope. These are necessary conditions and conditional exclusions for a hypothetical A2-broad profile with beta > 2. The
finite simple x-axis chain and (B) are additional hypotheses. Parts (c),(e),(f) have the further hypotheses specified
there. Neither (A),(B) alone nor nondegeneracy alone for arbitrary rational beta is shown to exclude interior zeros.
Degenerate forward limits and simultaneous rational resonances remain open. No realization of a connection, a local
profile or a global profile is asserted. If {X in Q1 : sgn(a0) Omega(X) < 0} is bounded, every zero of W in the closed
first quadrant is nondegenerate and W_2(0, y) has no positive zero, then Theorems 77(a) and 52(b) give (H1) for every
beta > 2, rational beta included; without these added hypotheses the rational and degenerate possibilities stated above
remain open.

Proof.

We first prove forward convergence and the attachment criterion. We then transport the two nonzero coefficients to a
forward saddle, before treating the finite tree and the source connection.

Theorem 52(a) supplies compactness, connectedness and full invariance of K, as well as Z contained in K and Theta = 0 on
K. Uniform sublinearity supplies R_* such that X.W(X) >= (beta/2)|X|^2 for |X| >= R_*. An orbit entering that exterior
stays there and its radius grows at least exponentially. Thus every unbounded forward orbit escapes. Every backward
orbit is bounded, as in Theorem 44(b).

The scalar x-axis flow and the signs in Theorem 58(a) show that every point of S has bounded forward orbit. Outside S
the flow moves outward and has no further zero; a bounded scalar orbit there would converge to a further zero, which is
impossible. The origin jet gives v'(0) = 3 beta+2, so (B) gives v > 0 on y > 0. The same scalar argument excludes
bounded nonzero y-axis orbits. Reflection proves the first assertion of (60.3).

Let Ly be the smooth function of Theorem 44, normalized by Ly(O) = 0. For a bounded forward orbit X(t), equation (44.1)
gives

  d_t Ly(X(t)) = (2 beta-1)|W(X(t))|^2,
  integral_0^infinity |W(X(t))|^2 dt < infinity.              (60.14)

Indeed Ly is bounded on the compact orbit closure. The derivative of |W(X(t))|^2 is 2 W.DW W, which is bounded there.
Uniform continuity and integrability imply W(X(t)) -> 0: otherwise disjoint intervals of a fixed positive length would
give a positive lower bound on the integral. The omega-limit set A is consequently a nonempty compact connected subset
of Z.

Here connectedness alone does not prove that A is a singleton. We use the nonzero trace, without assuming Z finite. If A
has two distinct points, choose a curve chart about one that omits the other. Such a chart exists because tr DW = 2 beta
implies that some component W_i has nonzero gradient at the chosen zero. The implicit function theorem puts {W_i = 0},
and hence the local zero set, on the horizontal axis of a rectangle.

If there are points outside A on both sides of the center on this horizontal axis, take them as the vertical sides of a
smaller closed rectangle. Its boundary misses A. Its intersection with A is nonempty, proper, and both open and closed
relative to A, a contradiction. Thus a one-sided interval of the horizontal axis belongs to A. In particular A contains
an open smooth arc of zeros. This is the local connectedness argument in the proof of Theorem 44(b).

At an interior point of that arc, use smooth coordinates (u,v) in which it is v = 0. Smooth division gives

  u' = v A_0(u,v),    v' = v B_0(u,v),
  B_0(u,0) = 2 beta.                                        (60.15)

The last equality follows because, at an equilibrium, coordinate change conjugates the derivative of the field. On a
small rectangle |u| <= d, |v| <= eta, arrange B_0 >= beta, |A_0| <= M, and M eta/beta < d/4. A nonstationary orbit
entering |u| < d/2, |v| < eta/2 has v != 0. Until its exit, |v| increases at least exponentially, and its total
horizontal displacement is at most M eta/beta, by integrating |u'| <= (M/beta) d_t|v|. It exits in finite time through
|v| = eta with |u| < 3d/4. On that compact exit set W is bounded away from zero. Arbitrarily late entries near the arc
point, which membership in A requires, therefore give arbitrarily late such exits. This contradicts W(X(t)) -> 0. The
stationary case is immediate. Thus A is a singleton, and compactness gives convergence.

A source has no nonconstant forward stable orbit. At O and at every Q_j the invariant x-axis supplies the local stable
manifold. Uniqueness of that manifold, and invariance of the axis under inverse flow, put the entire stable set on the
x-axis. A bounded gamma_j therefore cannot end on an axis or at a source. Theorem 43(a) leaves exactly the two
alternatives in (a).

We next determine how K can approach S from off the axis. Write T(x) = Theta_y(x,0). At O the prescribed jet gives Theta
= x^2 y A_0(x,y), with A_0(0,0) != 0. At every other point of S except the axis saddles, Theta = y A_1 with A_1(x,0) =
Theta_y(x,0) != 0, by Theorem 58(a) and reflection.

At Q_j, suppress j and straighten the unstable manifold as in Theorem 58(a), with u = x-x_(2j)-chi(y), where chi is
smooth and even. The field is u' = u A(u,y), y' = y C(u,y), with A(0,0) = -a_j, C(0,0) = c_j = 2 beta+a_j. Put H_l(y) =
partial_u^l Theta(0,y)/l!. Inductively, if the lower coefficients vanish, then

  y C(0,y) H_l'(y) = (kappa-l A(0,y))H_l(y).                (60.16)

For 0 <= l < p_j, the exponent (kappa+l a_j)/c_j lies strictly between zero and one. Subtracting this exponent divided
by y from the logarithmic derivative leaves a smooth function. A nonzero solution on either side would therefore be a
nonzero multiple of |y| to that exponent times a smooth nonvanishing factor. Smoothness at zero excludes it. This proves
the vanishing of every coefficient below p_j on both sides. At l = p_j the exponent is one, and Theorem 58(a) gives
H_(p_j)'(0) = T^(p_j)(x_(2j))/p_j! != 0.

Repeated smooth division first by u, and then by y using Theta(u,0) = 0, now gives the full neighborhood identity

  Theta = u^(p_j) y A_j(u,y),    A_j(0,0) != 0.             (60.17)

Thus the local zero set consists exactly of the axis and the two unstable branches. This conclusion uses all
coefficients below p_j, not just the first Taylor polynomial.

If every upper gamma_j escapes, so does its reflection below the axis; none of these branches meets K. The local
descriptions just proved give an open neighborhood V of S with K intersect V = S. Compactness makes S closed in K, and
this equality makes it relatively open. Connectedness of K gives K = S. Conversely a bounded gamma_j lies in K off S and
has an interior zero as its forward limit. Since Z is contained in K, an interior zero also forces K != S. This proves
(60.3). For n = 0 the conclusion agrees with Theorem 52(b).

Fix now a bounded gamma = gamma_j and the section (60.7). Set X(t,z) = Phi_t Sigma(z). Theorem 58(a) gives exact
transverse orders p and m = p-1 at every finite point of gamma, including the vanishing of all lower Cartesian
derivatives. Write omega_m(t) for the coefficient of z^m in Omega(X(t,z)). The coefficient calculation in Theorem 58(a),
equations (58.19)-(58.21), gives

  Theta(X(t,z)) = exp(kappa t)(theta_p z^p+O(z^(p+1))),
  exp(t)omega_m(t) = -(p theta_p/J) I(t).                    (60.18)

Its negative-time boundary condition is valid for each axis saddle: the exponent in (58.20) is positive because
1+c_j-m_j a_j = beta-1+a_j > 0. Also y(t) = O(exp((c_j-epsilon)t)) as t -> -infinity, where c_j > beta+1. This proves
negative-time convergence in (60.8). Positive-time convergence follows from boundedness of y; positivity follows from
y(t) > 0. No sign of y'(t) is needed.

At z = 0, Liouville's formula gives

  det(X_t,X_z) = exp(2 beta t)J,
  grad z = exp(-2 beta t)W_perp(gamma(t))/J.                  (60.19)

The leading chain rule has no lower-derivative terms. Applying it to (60.18) with (60.19) proves (60.9),(60.10).

Suppose the forward limit is a hyperbolic saddle Q*. By Theorem 46(a), DW(Q*) is symmetric. Straighten its smooth stable
and unstable manifolds simultaneously, using a chart whose derivative at Q* is an orthonormal eigen-coordinate change.
This straightens the manifolds; it does not assert a linearization of the field. In these smooth coordinates,

  s' = s A(s,u),    u' = u C(s,u),
  A(0,0) = -a,     C(0,0) = c = 2 beta+a.                   (60.20)

Choose s > 0 on gamma near Q*. The stable convergence is exponential. Integrating s'/s = -a+O(s) gives s(t) = C_s exp(-a
t)(1+o(1)), with C_s > 0. The transverse variation v(t) = partial_z u(X(t,0)) is nonzero and solves v' = C(s(t),0)v. The
error C(s(t),0)-c is integrable, so

  s(t) = C_s exp(-a t)(1+o(1)),
  v(t) = C_u exp(c t)(1+o(1)),    C_u != 0.                 (60.21)

Let h_p(s) and g_m(s) be the coefficients of u^p and u^m in Theta and Omega in this chart. All lower transverse
coefficients vanish for s > 0, by the exact orders on gamma. The leading chain rule is therefore exact and gives

  h_p(s(t)) = theta_p exp(kappa t)/v(t)^p,
  g_m(s(t)) = omega_m(t)/v(t)^m,
  h_p(s) = C_1 s^i(1+o(1)),
  g_m(s) = D_1 s^ell(1+o(1)),    C_1 D_1 != 0              (60.22)

as s decreases to zero, with i,ell as in (60.4). The nonzero limit I_infinity is essential for D_1 != 0.

A smooth one-variable function asymptotic to a nonzero multiple of s^r, with r >= 0, has integral r. If r were
nonintegral, its Taylor coefficients through floor(r) would vanish, and Taylor's theorem would make it O(s^ceil(r)),
contradicting that asymptotic. For integral r the derivative of order r is nonzero. Applying this to (60.22) proves
integrality of i,ell. In particular neither coefficient is flat.

We must also exclude lower total-degree terms involving higher transverse powers. All Taylor coefficients with u-degree
below p in Theta vanish, since the corresponding smooth functions vanish for s > 0. The coefficient h_p supplies a
nonzero term of degree i+p. If the first temperature polynomial had smaller degree, Theorem 43(b2) would make it a
single monomial s^r u^l with l >= p and -a r+c l = kappa. This forces r >= i, a contradiction. At degree i+p the
eigenvalue equation has a unique monomial. Thus Theta_lead is as in (60.5).

Next,

  i-ell = 1+(beta+1)/a > 1,
  ell+m < i+p-1,
  ((-a s,c u).grad+1) Omega_lead = 0
       below degree i+p-1.                                (60.23)

The forcing Theta_x has no term below degree i+p-1; a smooth coordinate change does not lower this bound. Any first
vorticity polynomial below degree ell+m would therefore be unforced. Its monomials have u-degree l >= m and r = (c
l+1)/a >= ell, which is impossible at that smaller degree. The nonzero coefficient in (60.22) proves the vorticity
assertion in (60.5). For fixed total degree the eigenvalue equation permits only one monomial. Since the chart
derivative is the chosen eigen-coordinate change, these first homogeneous polynomials are also the polynomials in the
linear eigen-coordinates of the statement.

This argument permits nonlinear resonances in the vector field. The scalar asymptotics have nonzero limits, so
logarithmic or flat terms cannot replace the leading powers in (60.22). No smooth conjugacy to a linear field has been
used.

For the arithmetic, put

  r_0 = i-p = (2 beta p-kappa)/a,
  s_0 = ell-m = (2 beta m+1)/a,
  r_0-s_0 = k = (beta+1)/a,
  2m k-s_0 = N = (2m-1)/a,
  s_0-k = beta N.                                          (60.24)

All are integers, and k,N,beta N are positive. This proves (b). Part (a) and the alternative in (b) prove (c). For the
stated replacement of (B), Theorem 30(c) applies with the explicit hypothesis that every positive y-axis zero is simple.
Once the interior zero set is empty, all hypotheses of Theorem 58(c),(d) are satisfied.

At a degenerate forward limit, Theorem 43(b3),(c) gives flatness of both fields. Its derivative is symmetric with
spectrum {0,2 beta}. If z(t) = gamma(t)-Q*, then for every epsilon > 0, sufficiently near the endpoint,

  z.W(Q*+z) >= -epsilon |z|^2,
  |z(t)| >= |z(T)|exp(-epsilon(t-T))    for t >= T.           (60.25)

The second inequality follows by differentiation of |z|; the orbit cannot reach its limit at a finite time. Both
exponents 2 beta p-kappa and 1+2 beta m in (60.9),(60.10) are positive. For any L > 0 choose epsilon with L epsilon
smaller than both exponents. Boundedness of W and I and (60.25) then prove the little-o assertions in (d). They make no
existence assertion at a degenerate endpoint.

Assume next that all interior zeros are nondegenerate. By reflection, (A),(B), and the origin spectrum, every full-plane
zero is nondegenerate. Compactness of Z and isolation give finiteness, as in Remark 43.1. Theorem 52(c) gives
nonflatness at every zero.

By (a), every nonstationary orbit in K tends forward to a saddle and is one of its two stable branches. Each such branch
is one complete orbit, bounded forward and backward. Theorem 44(b) supplies its backward endpoint. The endpoints are
distinct, since Theorem 58(e) strictly orders nonconstant connections by L_tilde. The closure of an orbit is an embedded
compact arc: use its two endpoint limits to extend a time parametrization to a compact interval, then use flow
uniqueness and the distinct endpoints for injectivity. Different arcs meet only at endpoints. There are at most two such
arcs for each saddle. They and the finitely many zeros form K, so K is a finite connected graph.

Any graph cycle contains a simple closed curve made of complete orbit arcs and zeros. This curve is compact and
invariant, regardless of the orientations of its edges. Its bounded complementary region contradicts Theorem 4. Thus K
is a tree. The segment S is a subtree. Each component of K intersect Q1 consequently has exactly one attachment to S:
two attachments, together with the intervening path in S, would give a graph cycle; no attachment would contradict
connectedness. The local descriptions leading to (60.17), together with (60.3), identify that attachment as exactly one
Q_j with its bounded gamma_j.

For later use, the index computation in Remark 43.1 is

  index sum on the x-axis = -1+2(n+1)-2n = 1,
  1+4(number of sources in Q1-number of saddles in Q1) = 1.
                                                               (60.26)

Thus the two interior numbers are equal. This is the existing index balance, not an additional obstruction.

Suppose there is just one interior source S* and one interior saddle Q*. Part (a) forces a connection Q_j --> Q*. Its
other stable branch cannot come from another axis saddle, by the unique attachment just proved. It cannot come from Q*
itself. An axis source has no upper zero-temperature orbit in its basin, by Theorem 58(b), and O has its entire unstable
set on the y-axis. Theorem 44(b) therefore identifies the backward endpoint of the other branch as S*. No unstable
branch of Q* can end at an axis zero, a source, or itself. Hence both escape.

We justify the temperature order on the second stable branch, which is not a consequence of knowing the incoming order
at just one regular point. In (60.20), write h_l(s) for the coefficient of u^l. Both stable branches have bounded
forward orbits, so h_0 = 0. When the lower coefficients vanish, their equation is

  s A(s,0) h_l'(s) = (kappa-l C(s,0))h_l(s).                (60.27)

Every nonzero solution on either side is a nonzero constant times |s|^((l c-kappa)/a) times a smooth nonvanishing
factor. This follows by subtracting the simple pole from its logarithmic derivative. For l < p, h_l vanishes on s > 0,
hence is flat at zero. No nonzero solution on s < 0 of this scalar equation is flat. Induction gives h_l = 0 on both
sides for l < p. For l = p, the nonzero derivative of order i at zero persists on both sides. Thus both stable branches
have exact transverse temperature order p. Finite-time flow preserves that order along delta.

A nonflat source of total temperature order d_0 has, by Theorem 43(b1), eigenvalues lambda = kappa/d_0 and c_S = 2
beta-lambda, with leading polynomial C u^(d_0) in the weak coordinate u. Its smooth strong unstable curve exists by the
strong unstable manifold theorem. Straighten it to u = 0 and use s on the curve, so u' = u A_S(u,s), s' = s C_S(s) on u
= 0, with A_S(0,0) = lambda and C_S(0) = c_S.

For the coefficient H_l(s) of u^l, once lower ones vanish, a nonzero solution has the form

  H_l(s) = constant times |s|^((kappa-l lambda)/c_S)
                      times a smooth nonvanishing factor.   (60.28)

For 0 <= l < d_0 the exponent lies strictly between zero and one, since c_S > kappa. Smoothness on both sides forces all
these coefficients to vanish. At l = d_0, H_l(0) != 0. Smooth division proves Theta = u^(d_0) B(u,s), with B(0,0) != 0.
Its local zero set is exactly the strong unstable curve and its transverse order there is d_0.

Apply this to S*. The connection delta lies in that zero curve and has order p, so d_0 = p. This proves (60.12) and
excludes a regular source. The other branch of the strong curve cannot also end at Q*, since the two arcs would make a
graph cycle. No other forward zero is available, so it escapes. This proves (e).

For the moment calculation we also need vorticity coefficients on the second stable branch. Let g_l(s) be its
coefficients in (60.20). For l < m the forcing vanishes, since Theta is divisible by u^p and a first derivative has
order at least p-1. Inductively,

  s A(s,0)g_l'(s) = -(1+l C(s,0))g_l(s),
  nonzero-solution exponent = (1+l c)/a.                    (60.29)

These coefficients vanish on s > 0 and hence are flat at zero. The scalar equation excludes a nonzero flat solution on s
< 0. Thus they vanish there as well. The coefficient g_m has leading Taylor term D s^ell on both sides, by
(60.5),(60.22). In particular it is nonzero near Q* on delta. Propagating the vanishing lower coefficients by their
homogeneous transport equations makes them zero along the whole delta.

Choose an oriented transverse section on delta with determinant J_delta > 0, and write theta_delta != 0 for its
temperature coefficient of order p and omega_delta(t) for its vorticity coefficient of order m. Both are defined using
its flow coordinates. At the source, backward flow contracts every tangent vector exponentially in a suitable equivalent
norm. Since derivatives of Omega are bounded and all lower ones vanish along delta, the leading chain rule gives
exp(t)omega_delta(t) -> 0 as t -> -infinity.

The coefficient calculation (58.19) now gives

  exp(t)omega_delta(t) = -(p theta_delta/J_delta) I_S(t),
  I_S(t) = exp(-(beta+1)t)(delta_2(t)-y_S)
       + (beta+1) integral_(-infinity)^t
                    exp(-(beta+1)s)(delta_2(s)-y_S) ds,
  I_S(infinity) = (beta+1) M_S.                             (60.30)

Indeed along the strong curve delta(t)-S* = O(exp((c_S-epsilon)t)) as t -> -infinity, and c_S = 2 beta-kappa/p > beta+1.
Thus the negative-time integral and boundary term converge after subtracting y_S. The positive-time convergence follows
from boundedness. This proves absolute convergence of M_S.

Orient the chart (s,u) at Q* positively, retaining s > 0 on gamma. For a positively oriented flow section, the
transverse variation has the sign of s': in coordinates det(W,X_z) = s' u_z on u = 0, and the physical determinant has
the same sign. Thus u_z < 0 on gamma and u_z > 0 on delta.

On gamma, (60.18),(60.22) imply
