  sgn(g_m/h_p) = sgn(-I(t)u_z/J) = +1.
  On delta near Q*:
  sgn(g_m/h_p) = (-1)^(ell-i) = (-1)^(k+1).                (60.31)

The latter sign follows from the nonzero Taylor coefficients on the two sides, so in particular D/C > 0 in this
orientation. On delta, (60.30) instead gives sgn(g_m/h_p) = -sgn I_S(t), whenever I_S(t) != 0. The limiting I_S cannot
be zero: as in (60.21), on delta s(t) = -C_s exp(-a t)(1+o(1)) and u_z(t) = C_u exp(c t)(1+o(1)), with C_s,C_u > 0.
Consequently the nonzero term D s^ell gives exp(t)omega_delta(t) a nonzero limit, since 1-a ell+c m = 0. Equation
(60.30) proves I_S(infinity) != 0. Comparing signs in (60.31) proves (60.13). A time shift multiplies M_S by a positive
exponential, so its sign is unchanged.

Finally suppose beta = P/R is reduced and P,R are odd. By (60.6), N = R t_0 for a positive integer t_0. It follows that

  k = (P+R)t_0/(2m-1).                                    (60.32)

The numerator is even and the denominator odd. Integrality of k therefore makes k even. A positive M_S requires
delta_2(t)-y_S > 0 somewhere. QED.

Remark 60.1 (arithmetic consistency, not realization).

The values beta = 3, m = 1 and a = 1 give

  kappa = 1,    p = 2,    c = 7,
  i = 13,    ell = 8,    k = 4,    N = 1,
  spec DW(S*) = {1/2,11/2}.                                 (60.33)

The candidate monomials C s^13 u^2 and D s^8 u have transport eigenvalues 1 and -1. Their total degrees are 15 and 9,
and Theta_x begins no earlier than degree 14. The required source moment is positive. These identities check the
arithmetic conditions only; they supply no local or global solution.

### Theorem 61 (beta = 2: orbit deficits and nonnegative zero jets)

Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2, and assume (V+): Omega >= 0 on Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}. Put
W = 2X + U, Z = {W = 0}, and N = {grad Theta != 0}. Thus div W = 4, Omega = d_y W_1 - d_x W_2, W.grad Theta = 0, and
W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x. Use the smooth angular functions H and G of Theorem 36, and grad^perp f = (-f_y,f_x).

On N put L = W.grad^perp Theta/|grad Theta|^2. Write X(theta,l) = (x(theta,l),y(theta,l)) for an inverse coordinate map
of Theorem 39(b), and q(theta) = X(theta,0). A regular zero means a point of Z cap N. For a fixed theta with q(theta) in
Q1, both half-fibres lie in Q1. For eps in {-1,+1} and s >= 0 put Y_eps(s) = y(theta,eps s),
omega_eps(s) = Omega(X(theta,eps s)), and q_y = y(theta,0). The negative branch means L < 0; on either branch s
increases in forward flow time.

(a) For every s > 0,

  s^(-3/4)(Y_eps(s)-q_y)
    + (3/4) int_0^s t^(-7/4)(Y_eps(t)-q_y) dt
      = eps s^(1/4) omega_eps(s).                         (61.1)

The left side is nonpositive on the negative branch and nonnegative on the positive branch. These signs for every s are
equivalent to nonnegative vorticity on the respective branches. If Y_-(s) > q_y, then Y_-(t) < q_y for some 0 < t < s.
In particular, every escaping negative branch with an interior exit angle dips below its source height. If
Omega(q(theta)) > 0, then Y_-'(0) = -Omega(q(theta))/4 < 0, so the dip occurs for all sufficiently small positive s.

(b) Suppose a branch in (a) escapes. Let phi_eps be its exit angle and, for any point X on that branch, let
a(X) = lim_(t -> infinity) exp(-2t)|Phi_t X|. Then phi_eps is in (0,pi/2), and the constants

  k_eps = a(X)/sqrt(|L(X)|) = sqrt(|H'(phi_eps)|/2),
  b_eps = k_eps sin(phi_eps) > 0,
  D_eps = G(phi_eps)/sqrt(k_eps) >= 0,
  eps = -sgn H'(phi_eps)                                  (61.2)

are independent of X. For each fixed escaping branch,

  |X(theta,eps s)| = k_eps sqrt(s) + O(s^(1/4)),
  Y_eps(s) = b_eps sqrt(s) + O(s^(1/4)),
  Y_eps'(s) = (b_eps/2)s^(-1/2) + O(s^(-3/4)),
  s^(1/4) omega_eps(s) -> D_eps.                          (61.3)

Suppose now that the negative branch escapes, and write Y = Y_-. With z_+ = max(z,0), define

  A_- = int_0^infinity s^(-7/4)(q_y-Y(s))_+ ds,
  A_+ = int_0^infinity s^(-7/4)(Y(s)-q_y)_+ ds.
  Then 0 < A_+ < infinity and
  A_- = A_+ + (4/3)D_- < infinity.                        (61.4)

Put delta = q_y - min_(s >= 0) Y(s) and K = sup_(s >= 0) |Y'(s)|. Then 0 < delta < q_y, 0 < K < infinity, and

  A_+ + (4/3)D_- <= (16/3)K^(3/4)delta^(1/4).            (61.5)

Choose S > 0 so large that Y(s) >= (b_-/2)sqrt(s) for every s >= S and q_y <= (b_-/4)sqrt(S). Then

  delta >= [(3b_- S^(-1/4) + 4D_-)/(16K^(3/4))]^4.        (61.6)

The dip set E = {s > 0: Y(s) < q_y} satisfies

  int_E s^(-7/4) ds >= [A_+ + (4/3)D_-]/delta.            (61.7)

An infinite left side is allowed. These bounds use the indicated orbit data; no universal positive depth or duration
bound is asserted.

(c) On every regular zero arc in Q1, parametrized by theta = Theta, put o = Omega(q(theta)) and tau = Theta_y(q(theta)).
Then

  q_x'(theta) = o(4-tau)/[4(o^2+tau^2)],
  q_y'(theta) = (o^2+4tau)/[4(o^2+tau^2)].                (61.8)

For the remaining assertions of this part, let C and Q+ be as in Theorem 16, put M = Theta(Q+), and assume (I), that no
component of Z lies wholly in Q1, and (R), that C excluding its two endpoints consists of regular zeros. For
0 < theta < M let q(theta) be the unique zero of temperature theta in Q1, and use its two regular half-fibres.

Fix a sufficiently small closed disc of radius rho about Q+ contained in Q1. For every integer n > 1 choose C_n > 0 such
that |grad Theta(X)| <= C_n |X-Q+|^n throughout this disc. Put d_theta = |q(theta)-Q+|, and let sigma_eps(theta) be the
first s > 0 at which X(theta,eps s) reaches the boundary of the disc. For theta sufficiently close to M, both exit
parameters are finite and

  sigma_eps(theta) >=
    4[d_theta^(1-n)-rho^(1-n)]/[C_n(n-1)].                (61.9)

For every p > 0, min(sigma_-(theta),sigma_+(theta)) d_theta^p tends to infinity as theta increases to M. Also
X(theta,l) -> Q+ uniformly on bounded l intervals, and k_eps(theta), b_eps(theta) -> 0.

(d) Let Q in Z cap Q1 satisfy Omega(Q) = 0 and grad Theta(Q) != 0. Put tau = Theta_y(Q), which is nonzero. In the
original Cartesian directions,

  DW(Q) = diag(4,0),    D^2 W(Q) = 0,
  Omega_xy(Q) = 0,
  (tau-108)Omega_xx(Q) = 4 Omega_yy(Q),
  D^2 Omega(Q) is positive semidefinite.                  (61.10)

Thus D^2 Omega(Q) = 0 if tau < 108. If tau = 108, only Omega_xx(Q) can be nonzero, and it is nonnegative. If tau > 108
and the Hessian is nonzero, both its diagonal entries are positive.

If Omega is not flat at Q, translate Q to (u,v) = (0,0) without rotating the axes. Let m be its first nonzero Taylor
degree and write the homogeneous term, with no factorials in the coefficients, as R_m(u,v) = sum_(j=0)^m c_j u^j
v^(m-j). Then m is even, m >= 2, R_m is nonnegative on R^2, and

  Lambda_j = 4(j+1)(4j+1),
  j(tau-Lambda_j)c_j
    = 4(m-j+2)(m-j+1)(4j-7)c_(j-2),    1 <= j <= m,
  c_(-1) = c_(-2) = 0.                                  (61.11)

If tau < 108, m cannot be congruent to 2 modulo 4. If m = 4, then

  tau <= -8 or tau >= 340.                               (61.12)

Consequently, if -8 < tau < 108, every derivative of Omega of order at most 7 vanishes at Q, whether or not Omega is
flat.

(e) Suppose J is a connected open regular zero arc in Q1 and Omega vanishes identically on J. Then J is vertical. If
Omega is not flat at Q in J, tau(Q) = Theta_y(Q) belongs to {Lambda_2,Lambda_4,Lambda_6,...}, and tau is constant with
that value on a neighbourhood of Q in J. In particular, Omega is flat at every point of J where tau < 108, and at every
point where tau is not locally constant with a value in that set.

At every Q in N cap Q1 where Omega is flat, D^k W(Q) = 0 for every k >= 2; this conclusion does not require W(Q) = 0.

The resonance values have the following local consistency statements. For any even k >= 2 and a > 0, the fields

  W = (4u,-a u^(k+1)/(k+1)),
  Omega = a u^k,
  Theta = Lambda_k v + a(4k+1)u^(k+1)/(k+1)              (61.13)

satisfy the two transport equations, div W = 4 and d_v W_1-d_u W_2 = Omega exactly. They have nonnegative vorticity and
the regular vertical zero arc {u = 0}. They are local consistency statements, not A2-broad profiles.

Scope. These are necessary conditions and restricted exclusions inside (V+). Existence or nonexistence under (V+),
including under (I) and (R), is not settled. Case (II), in which some component of Z lies wholly in Q1, remains
unexcluded. Neither finiteness of the zero components nor a regular zero of Omega on C cap Q1 is asserted. The
additional vanishing-on-an-arc hypothesis in (e) is not a consequence of (V+). Propagation of flatness from a stationary
point or a zero arc to a neighbourhood or to nonstationary orbits remains open. Theorem 12 forces a critical zero; the
flat critical endpoints and the potential regions in Theorems 16, 44, 47, 53, 56 and 59 do not force the regular zero
configurations required for the jet and arc restrictions.

Proof.

Step 1. Coordinate orientation and finite displacements.

Theorem 39(b),(c) gives

  det(X_theta,X_l) = 1/4,
  X_l = grad^perp Theta(X)/4,
  W(X) = 4l X_l,
  4l Omega_l + Omega = 4y_l.                             (61.14)

The determinant has this order of columns because the Jacobian of (Theta,L) is +4. Since l(t) = exp(4t)l(0), s = |l|
increases in forward time on both branches. Small segments of the two branches lie in Q1 near q(theta), and their
complete orbits stay in Q1 by invariance of the axes and uniqueness of the flow.

The chain rule gives y_l(theta,eps s) = eps Y_eps'(s). Therefore

  s omega_eps'(s) + omega_eps(s)/4 = eps Y_eps'(s),
  int_0^s t^(-3/4)Y_eps'(t) dt
    = eps s^(1/4)omega_eps(s).                           (61.15)

The coordinate map is smooth at l = 0. Thus omega_eps is bounded there, so s^(1/4)omega_eps(s) -> 0 as s decreases to
zero. This is the boundary condition used in integrating the first equation. Also Y_eps(s)-q_y = O(s), so
s^(-3/4)(Y_eps(s)-q_y) -> 0 at zero. Integration by parts in the second equation proves (61.1), with an integrable
O(t^(-3/4)) integrand near zero.

If Y_-(t) >= q_y on [0,s] and Y_-(s) > q_y, the left side of (61.1) is strictly positive, a contradiction. At s = 0 the
first equation of (61.15) gives Y_eps'(0) = eps Omega(q(theta))/4. This proves the finite-parameter assertions in (a).

Step 2. Escape and the quantitative deficit.

Fix X0 on an escaping branch and put s0 = |L(X0)|. Theorem 39(d) gives a = a(X0) > 0 and H'(phi_eps) = -2a^2/L(X0).
Along this orbit s = s0 exp(4t), so k_eps = a/sqrt(s0) is exactly the constant in (61.2), including its sign rule.
Theorem 36(d) identifies the exit angle with the image of the launch angle under an increasing circle diffeomorphism
fixing the axes. An orbit in Q1 meets the launch circle at an interior angle, so phi_eps is interior. The uniform
angular limit of Omega in Theorem 36(b) gives G >= 0 on this interval, also recorded in Theorem 59(b), equation (59.5).

Theorem 36(b) gives |U| = O(r^(1/2)). Since r exp(-2t) -> a > 0, d_t(log r-2t) = U_r/r = O(exp(-t)) and d_t
phi = U_phi/r = O(exp(-t)). Integrating to infinity gives r = a exp(2t) + O(exp(t)) and phi = phi_eps + O(exp(-t)).
These prove the first two estimates in (61.3). Since d_s Y_eps = W_2/(4s) and W_2 = 2Y_eps + O(r^(1/2)), the derivative
estimate follows from the equation itself, without differentiating an uncontrolled remainder. Finally Theorem 36(b)
gives Omega = r^(-1/2)G(phi) + O(r^(-1)) uniformly in angle. Substituting the preceding radial and angular estimates
gives the last limit in (61.3). In particular Y_- tends to infinity when it escapes, which completes (a).

For an escaping negative branch, the absolute displacement moment integrand is O(s^(-3/4)) at zero and O(s^(-5/4)) at
infinity. Both moments in (61.4) are finite, and A_+ > 0 because Y tends to infinity. The boundary term
s^(-3/4)(Y(s)-q_y) tends to zero at infinity. Passing to that limit in (61.1) gives (3/4)(A_+-A_-) = -D_-, proving
(61.4).

Continuity, strict positivity of Y and its limit at infinity give an attained strictly positive minimum. Part (a) makes
this minimum less than q_y. Smoothness for finite s and the derivative estimate in (61.3) give 0 < K < infinity. Since
Y(0) = q_y,

  (q_y-Y(s))_+ <= min(Ks,delta),
  int_0^infinity s^(-7/4)min(Ks,delta) ds
    = (16/3)K^(3/4)delta^(1/4).                          (61.16)

The integral is evaluated by splitting at s = delta/K. Its two terms are 4K^(3/4)delta^(1/4) and
(4/3)K^(3/4)delta^(1/4). This proves (61.5). For S as in the statement, Y(s)-q_y >= (b_-/4)sqrt(s) when s >= S. Hence
A_+ >= b_- S^(-1/4), and (61.5) gives (61.6). The bound (q_y-Y(s))_+ <= delta 1_E(s) proves (61.7).

Step 3. The source curve and the endpoint parameter.

At a regular zero Theorem 59(d), equation (59.10), gives Theta_x = Omega = o. Put h = grad Theta = (o,tau) and
R(a,b) = (-b,a). At L = 0, Theorem 39(b),(c) gives grad L.Rh = 4 and grad L.h = -o. Consequently

  grad L = [4Rh-o h]/|h|^2,
  q'(theta) = (L_y,-L_x)/4 = -R grad L/4.                (61.17)

The second equality is the inverse Jacobian formula at l = 0. Substitution proves (61.8).

Under (V+), Theorem 59(a), equation (59.4), identifies (I) with (S) of Theorem 48. Theorem 59(c), including (59.9), and
Theorem 48(e) give M > 0, the increasing passage (0,phi_2), the plateau [phi_2,phi_3], and the decreasing passage
(phi_3,pi/2). Theorem 39(b) makes Theta strictly increasing along the regular half-arc from P to Q+. Hence each theta in
(0,M) is attained at exactly one zero in Q1. There are no critical points of this temperature in Q1: otherwise their
backward limits, by Theorem 44(b),(d), would be critical zeros of the same temperature in the closed quadrant. Under (I)
and (R) the only such critical zeros are O and Q+, with temperatures 0 and M. Thus Theorem 39(b) describes the full
intermediate level by its one source and two orbits. Both escape by Theorem 53(d). Theorem 53(h) also gives precisely
two angular preimages of this level. The sign rule in (61.2) identifies the negative branch with the increasing passage.

As theta increases to M, q(theta) tends to Q+. By Theorem 16, Theta-M is flat there, which supplies the constants C_n
for every n. The auxiliary equation for each half-fibre is

  d_s X(theta,eps s) = (eps/4)grad^perp Theta(X(theta,eps s)),
  |d'(s)| <= C_n d(s)^n/4,
  d_s[d(s)^(1-n)] >= -(n-1)C_n/4,                        (61.18)

where d(s) = |X(theta,eps s)-Q+| before exit. Uniqueness for the smooth auxiliary equation ensures d(s) > 0: a solution
starting away from its equilibrium Q+ cannot reach it in finite s. Integration from d(0) = d_theta to d(sigma_eps) = rho
proves (61.9). Escape makes each exit finite. For any fixed p > 0, choose n > p+1 in that estimate to obtain the
asserted growth of both exit parameters.

Continuous dependence on the initial point in the auxiliary equation gives X(theta,l) -> Q+ uniformly on bounded signed
l intervals. Equivalently, a local Lipschitz bound K0 for grad Theta gives distance at most d_theta exp(K0 |l|/4) while
in the disc. The two exit angles tend to phi_2 and phi_3. Smoothness of H and its constancy on the plateau give H' = 0
at both endpoints. Equation (61.2) therefore gives k_eps,b_eps -> 0. No estimate for the ratio defining D_eps is
required.

Remark. The small-temperature limit adds no axis exclusion. Put g = Omega_y(x,0), T = Theta_y(x,0), and w = W_1(x,0).
Theorem 59, equation (59.16), gives T > 0; on the axis l = -w/T and dl/dx = -4/T. Smoothness and parity give
y(theta,l) = theta/T(x_l) + O(theta^3) and Omega(theta,l) = theta g(x_l)/T(x_l) + O(theta^3) on bounded l intervals,
where x_l is the inverse axis coordinate. Dividing (61.15) by theta and taking the limit gives g >= 0 and w
g' + (5-w')g = T', precisely the trace condition and equation used in Theorem 21(b).

Step 4. The quadratic jet.

At Q in (d), nonnegativity on an open neighbourhood of Q makes grad Omega(Q) = 0 and D^2 Omega(Q) positive semidefinite.
Theorem 59(d), equations (59.10)-(59.12), gives Theta_x = Theta_xx = Theta_xy = 0 there. Regularity then gives tau != 0.
The curl is zero at Q, so DW(Q) is symmetric; differentiated temperature transport gives its vertical kernel, and its
trace is 4. Thus DW(Q) = diag(4,0).

Twice differentiating W.grad Theta = 0 now leaves only tau D^2 W_2. Indeed W(Q) = 0, and the only possibly nonzero entry
of D^2 Theta is its yy entry, whereas DW(Q) has only its xx entry nonzero. Thus D^2 W_2(Q) = 0. In terms of the stream
function, W_2 = 2y + Psi_x, so Psi_xxx = Psi_xxy = Psi_xyy = 0. The identity Omega_y = -Psi_xxy-Psi_yyy = 0 also gives
Psi_yyy = 0. Hence D^3 Psi(Q) = 0 and D^2 W(Q) = 0.

Twice differentiating vorticity transport gives

  Theta_xxx = 9 Omega_xx,
  Theta_xxy = 5 Omega_xy,
  Theta_xyy = Omega_yy.                                 (61.19)

All derivatives in this step are evaluated at Q. Each x derivative hitting the linear part of W contributes 4, each y
derivative contributes zero, and the Omega term contributes 1. Three derivatives of temperature transport consequently
give

  tau Psi_xyyy = 0,
  tau Psi_xxxy = -40 Omega_xy,
  tau Psi_xxxx = -108 Omega_xx,
  tau Psi_xxyy = -4 Omega_yy.                            (61.20)

Since tau != 0, Psi_xyyy = 0. Using -Lap Psi = Omega now gives

  (tau-40)Omega_xy = 0,
  (tau-108)Omega_xx = 4 Omega_yy.                         (61.21)

If tau < 108, nonnegativity of the two diagonal Hessian entries forces both to vanish, and positive semidefiniteness
forces the off-diagonal entry to vanish too. If tau >= 108, tau != 40, so the first equation kills that entry directly.
The second equation then gives the two remaining cases in (61.10).

Step 5. The first nonzero jet.

If R_m is the first nonzero homogeneous term of Omega, expansion along each ray at Q gives R_m >= 0. A nonzero odd
homogeneous polynomial cannot be nonnegative on R^2, so m is even and m >= 2. Write the finite Taylor terms of W as
(4u,0) + sum_(j >= 2) W_j, and those of Theta as Theta(Q) + tau v + sum_(j >= 2) Theta_j. Only finite jets are used;
convergence is not assumed.

The vorticity equation and the absence of Omega terms of degree less than m show that Theta_j depends only on v for
j <= m. Inductively W_j = 0 for 2 <= j <= m. Indeed, after the earlier W_i have vanished, degree j of temperature
transport reads 4u partial_u Theta_j + tau (W_j)_2 = 0, so (W_j)_2 = 0. Degree j-1 of the divergence equation gives
partial_u (W_j)_1 = 0, and degree j-1 of the curl equation gives partial_v (W_j)_1 = 0. A homogeneous term of positive
degree with both derivatives zero is zero. This proves the induction.

Put W_(m+1) = (A,B). The first remaining equations are

  partial_u Theta_(m+1) = (4u partial_u+1)R_m,
  B = -(4/tau)u(4u partial_u+1)R_m,
  A_u+B_v = 0,    A_v-B_u = R_m.                         (61.22)

Differentiate the last equations to eliminate A. They give Lap B = -partial_u R_m, hence

  tau partial_u R_m
    = 4 Lap[u(4u partial_u+1)R_m].                       (61.23)

In degree u^(j-1)v^(m-j), the u second derivative on the right contributes 4j(j+1)(4j+1)c_j. The v second derivative
contributes 4(m-j+2)(m-j+1)(4j-7)c_(j-2). Comparing with the left side proves (61.11) for every j.

Average R_m(u,v) and R_m(-u,v). The resulting even polynomial is nonnegative and nonzero: if the average were
identically zero, both nonnegative summands would vanish everywhere. Its even coefficients still satisfy (61.11). If
tau < 108, none of the even denominators tau-Lambda_j vanishes. Its coefficient c_0 must be positive, since c_0 = 0
would recursively kill every even coefficient. Successive even coefficients have alternating signs, because 4j-7 > 0 for
even j >= 2. If m is 2 modulo 4, this gives c_m < 0, contradicting nonnegativity at v = 0.

For m = 4 and tau distinct from 108 and 340, the even polynomial is

  c_0[v^4 + 24u^2 v^2/(tau-108)
          + 432u^4/((tau-108)(tau-340))],    c_0 > 0.    (61.24)

At tau = 108 the j = 2 equation first gives c_0 = 0, and the j = 4 equation gives c_4 = 18c_2/(108-340). Nonnegativity
of c_2 u^2 v^2 + c_4 u^4 requires c_2,c_4 >= 0, so both vanish, a contradiction. At tau = 340 the equations give
c_0 = c_2 = 0 and permit c_4 > 0.

If 108 < tau < 340, (61.24) has c_4 < 0, which is impossible. If tau < 108, put A = 24/(tau-108) < 0 and
B = 432/((tau-108)(tau-340)) > 0. Nonnegativity of 1 + A z + B z^2 for z >= 0 requires 4B-A^2 >= 0, since its minimum
occurs at the positive point -A/(2B). Here

  4B-A^2 = 1152(tau+8)/[(tau-108)^2(tau-340)].            (61.25)

Thus tau <= -8. This proves (61.12), including the resonant cases. If -8 < tau < 108, a first degree 2 is excluded by
(61.10), degree 4 by (61.12), and degree 6 by the congruence argument. Odd first degrees are impossible. All derivatives
through order 7 therefore vanish, proving (d).

Step 6. A zero-vorticity regular arc and local consistency.

On J, equation (61.8) gives q_x' = 0 and q_y' = 1/tau != 0. Thus each local segment is vertical, and connectedness
places J on one vertical line. All pure vertical derivatives of Omega vanish along J. At a nonflat point, the polynomial
R_m therefore has c_0 = 0. Let k be its least u degree with nonzero coefficient. The polynomial R_m(u,1) is nonnegative
for both signs of u near zero, so k is even and c_k > 0. In particular k >= 2. The j = k equation of (61.11), with
c_(k-2) = 0, forces tau = Lambda_k.

A derivative of order m that is nonzero at Q stays nonzero on a sufficiently small connected segment of J containing Q.
At every point of that segment the first nonzero degree is at most m, so tau belongs to the finite set of Lambda_k with
2 <= k <= m and k even. Continuity makes tau constant there. This proves the local constancy and both flatness
conclusions.

For the velocity assertion, stationarity is unnecessary. If Omega is flat at Q in N, the equation Theta_x = W.grad
Omega + Omega makes Theta_x flat at Q. Thus Theta_y(Q) != 0. In a neighbourhood where Theta_y is nonzero, temperature
transport gives W_2 = -W_1 Theta_x/Theta_y, so W_2 is flat at Q. The divergence and curl equations now give
W_1,x-4 = -W_2,y and W_1,y = Omega+W_2,x, both flat at Q. Every derivative of W of order at least 2 therefore vanishes.

Finally (61.13) has divergence 4 and curl a u^k. Both sides of vorticity transport equal a(4k+1)u^k. Temperature
transport equals a[4(4k+1)-Lambda_k/(k+1)]u^(k+1), which is zero. Its zero set is {u = 0}, its temperature gradient
there is (0,Lambda_k), and a u^k is nonnegative. This checks all four local equations and the claimed regularity. The
polynomial velocity does not satisfy the sublinear A2-broad condition. No global realization is asserted. QED.

### Theorem 62 (the negative branch a0 < 0: a restricted exclusion at beta > 2 and necessary conditions)

Let (beta,Theta,Omega,U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2, with beta >= 2 and a0 < 0. Thus the fields are smooth on
R^2, Theta and Omega have at most polynomial growth, and

  W = beta X + U,                 div W = 2 beta,
  W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x, W.grad Theta = (beta-2)Theta,
  U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x),             -Lap Psi = Omega.

The velocity is canonical and U(X)=o(|X|) uniformly at infinity. Theta is even in x and odd in y, Omega and Psi are odd
in both coordinates, Theta(0,y)=0, and Theta=x^2 y(a0+O(|X|^2)) near O=(0,0).

Put Q1={x>0,y>0}, alpha=pi/2, b=beta+2, D=2 beta+1, d=2 beta-1, kappa=beta-2, h=1/beta and b0=2a0/D. Let P=(L,0) be the
first positive x-axis zero of W from Theorem 2. Write Phi_t for the flow of W and Z={W=0}. Hypothesis (H1) means Z cap
closure(Q1)={O,P}. Use the traces

  w(x)=W_1(x,0), T(x)=Theta_y(x,0), g(x)=Omega_y(x,0),
  v(y)=W_2(0,y), E(y)=Theta_xx(0,y)/2, K(y)=Omega_x(0,y).

Write Omega_+=max(Omega,0), Omega_-=max(-Omega,0), G(phi)=lim_(r->infinity)r^h Omega(r,phi), and, at beta=2,
H(phi)=lim_(r->infinity)Theta(r,phi). These limits are smooth, with the uniform differentiated expansions of Theorems 36
and 42. Let

  S_+={phi in (0,alpha): Omega(r,phi)>0 for some r>0}.

For an angular interval I, condition Ray(I) means that no phi in I and no three radii 0<r1<r2<r3 satisfy
Omega(r1,phi)<0, Omega(r2,phi)>0 and Omega(r3,phi)<0.

(a) Suppose beta>2. There is no profile satisfying all three conditions:

  (i)   {Theta=0} has empty interior relative to Q1;
  (ii)  {Omega>0} cap Q1 is bounded;
  (iii) Ray((0,alpha)).

Condition (i) holds under (H1), under all the hypotheses of the finite basin decomposition in Theorem 58(c), and under
nondegeneracy of every zero of W in the closed first quadrant (Theorem 80(b)).

For every beta>=2, S_+ is nonempty and open. Under Ray((0,alpha)),

  S_+ subset {phi in (0,alpha): G(phi)>=0}.                (62.1)

Thus Ray((0,alpha)) is impossible if {G>=0} has empty interior. If the positive set is bounded and Ray((0,alpha)) holds,
then for some R,

  Omega(r,phi)=0 for r>=R and phi in S_+,
  G=0 on S_+.                                            (62.2)

In particular these two conditions are impossible if {G=0} has empty interior. Without condition (i), at beta>2 they
force a nonempty exterior open sector on which Theta=Omega=0. At beta=2 they force a nonempty exterior open sector on
which Theta is constant, Omega=0 and U is harmonic.

The same sector conclusions, and the exclusion at beta>2 under (i), hold with (ii) and (iii) replaced by the following
weaker hypotheses: G<=0 on (0,alpha), and there are a nonempty open interval I with I cap S_+ nonempty and R>0 such that
Omega(r,phi)<=0 for r>=R, phi in I, and Ray(I) holds. For the constant-temperature sector conclusion at beta=2, the
local hypotheses on I suffice without G<=0.

(b) There exists delta in (0,L/2) such that Omega_- >= |b0|xy/2 in Q1 cap {r<delta}. Define the kernels of Theorems 9
and 55 by

  K0=xy/r^4, Q_L=(L^2+r^2)^2-4L^2x^2,
  N_L=4Lxy/(pi Q_L),
  M_L=N_L[1+2h-4L^2(L^2-x^2+y^2)/Q_L].                  (62.3)

With C0=pi(beta+1)/2, the following integrals converge absolutely:

  int_Q1 K0 Omega_+
    = C0+int_Q1 K0 Omega_-
    >= C0+pi|b0|delta^2/64,
  int_Q1 N_L Omega_+
    = beta L+int_Q1 N_L Omega_-
    >= beta L+L|b0|delta^6/[48(L^2+delta^2)^2].            (62.4)

Let R_+ be the infimum radius of the positive set and C_*=sup_Q1 r^h Omega_+. Then delta<=R_+<infinity, 0<C_*<infinity,
and

  C0+pi|b0|delta^2/64
    <= C_* R_+^(-h) h^(-1) int_(S_+) cos(phi)sin(phi)dphi
    <= C_*/(2h R_+^h).                                   (62.5)

Put gamma=1+2h and define

  t_c(phi)=[-(1-2h)cos(2phi)
    +sqrt((1-2h)^2 cos(2phi)^2+gamma(3-2h))]/gamma,
  rho(phi)=L sqrt(t_c(phi)),
  L<=rho(phi)<=L sqrt((3-2h)/(1+2h)).                     (62.6)

The kernel M_L is negative on D_in={0<r<rho(phi),0<phi<alpha} and positive on D_out={r>rho(phi),0<phi<alpha}. Its
balance is

  int_D_in |M_L|Omega_+ + int_D_out M_L Omega_-
    = int_D_in |M_L|Omega_- + int_D_out M_L Omega_+ >0.    (62.7)

Negative vorticity always occurs in D_out. Consequently this identity does not by itself force positive vorticity in
D_in. Estimate (62.5) depends on C_* and the negative core; it is not a universal bound on R_+/L.

(c) With A=T(L)<0, the traces satisfy

  wT'=(w'-b)T,                 wg'+(D-w')g=T',
  T'(L)=A w''(L)/b,
  g(L)=A w''(L)/[b(beta-1)].                              (62.8)

If w=-bx+c3 x^3+O(x^5), then

  T=a0 x^2-a0 c3 x^4/(2b)+O(x^6),
  g=b0 x-b0 c3 x^3/b+O(x^5),
  g'''(0)=-b0 w'''(0)/b.                                 (62.9)

If Omega<=0 on a neighbourhood of the closed segment OP on its Q1 side, or throughout {0<x<L,y>0}, then g<=0 on (0,L]
and w''(L)>=0. For every beta>=2,

  g<=0 on (0,infinity)
    implies w>0 on (L,infinity) and T<0 on (0,infinity).  (62.10)

For beta>2, adding v>0 on (0,infinity) to the hypothesis in (62.10) gives (H1).

(d) Assume beta>2 and (H1). Then E(y)<0 and K(y)<0 for y>0. Every positive y-axis point has a neighbourhood on its Q1
side where Omega<0. There is also an epsilon>0 such that Omega(r,phi)<0 for all sufficiently large r and
alpha-epsilon<phi<alpha.

Let chi_t be the scalar flow of w on the positive axis. For every x>0,

  g(x)=int_0^infinity e^(-s) T'(chi_(-s)x)
       exp(-int_0^s [2 beta-w'(chi_(-t)x)]dt)ds.           (62.11)

This integral converges absolutely. Thus T'<=0 along the backward axis orbit from x implies g(x)<=0. If w''(L)!=0, both
Theta_x and Omega have sign sgn(A w''(L)) in a sufficiently small upper neighbourhood of P, and at all sufficiently
negative times on each Q1 orbit. No sign of w''(L) is asserted.

(e) Assume beta>2. Put e_2=(0,1) and W^perp=(-W_2,W_1). Let Bern be the potential of dW+Omega W^perp-Theta e_2
normalized by Bern(O)=0, and set Ly=Bern+yTheta, as in Theorem 44. At every x-axis source R=(r,0) of Theorem 58(b), with
A_R=T(r)!=0 and DW(R)=diag(b,kappa), the functions

  Hc(X)=kappa Theta(X) int_0^infinity
                        e^(-kappa s)[Phi_(-s)X]_2 ds,
  L_tilde=Ly-Hc                                           (62.12)

from Theorem 58(e) are smooth throughout B_R={X:Phi_(-s)X->R as s->infinity}. The function L_tilde has exactly one
critical point in B_R, namely R, which is its strict minimum on B_R and is nondegenerate. With (u tensor v)_ij=u_i v_j,

  D^2 Hc(R)=A_R e_2 tensor e_2,
  D^2 L_tilde(R)=d diag(b,kappa).                         (62.13)

In particular this minimum imposes no inequality A_R>=-d kappa.

(f) Suppose beta=2. Let X(theta,l) be a regular level chart from Theorem 39 with q(theta)=X(theta,0) in Q1. Fix an
escaping half-fibre, write l=eps s with eps in {-1,+1}, s>0, and put Y(s)=y(theta,eps s), omega(s)=Omega(X(theta,eps s))
and q_y=y(theta,0). Without a sign hypothesis on Omega,

  s^(-3/4)(Y(s)-q_y)
    +(3/4)int_0^s t^(-7/4)(Y(t)-q_y)dt
      =eps s^(1/4)omega(s).                              (62.14)

Its exit angle phi lies in (0,alpha). Define

  k=sqrt(|H'(phi)|/2)>0, B=k sin(phi)>0,
  D_e=G(phi)/sqrt(k), eps=-sgn H'(phi).
  Then Y(s)=B sqrt(s)+O(s^(1/4)),
  s^(1/4)omega(s)->D_e.                                  (62.15)

The displacement moments satisfy

  A_+=int_0^infinity s^(-7/4)(Y(s)-q_y)_+ ds,
  A_-=int_0^infinity s^(-7/4)(q_y-Y(s))_+ ds,
  0<A_+<infinity, 0<=A_-<infinity,
  A_+-A_-=(4/3)eps D_e.                                  (62.16)

Hence eps G(phi)<=0 forces Y(s)<q_y for some s>0. The identity alone does not force a dip when eps G(phi)>0.

(g) Suppose beta=2. Let C be the zero component through P and Q+ its upper endpoint from Theorems 16 and 53. Put
M=Theta(Q+). Under (R), meaning grad Theta!=0 on C except at its two endpoints, M<0. This conclusion does not require
(S).

If also (S), meaning Z cap Q1=C cap Q1, holds, let [phi2,phi3] be the constant interval at height M in Theorem 48(e). If
in addition w>0 on (L,infinity), v>0 on (0,infinity), the positive vorticity set is bounded and Ray((0,alpha)) holds,
then

  0<phi2<phi3<alpha, S_+ subset (phi2,phi3).              (62.17)

Scope. These are necessary conditions and the restricted exclusion in (a). The negative branch remains unresolved in
general if boundedness of the positive set or the ray condition is omitted. At beta=2 the constant-temperature
potential-sector alternative remains unresolved. The smoothness in (e) is confined to regular source basins; no
transverse smoothness across their boundaries is asserted. The moments in (b) and the trace equations in (c) are only
necessary conditions. Smooth data satisfying those equations alone are not profiles.

Proof.

First prove (a). Smooth division by the two axes gives Omega=xy[b0+O(r^2)] with b0<0. Thus a fixed sufficiently small
quarter-disc has strictly negative vorticity. Theorem 21(a), or the positive strain identity of Theorem 9, supplies a
positive point. Positivity is open; fixing the radius of any positive point and varying its angle proves that S_+ is
open.

If phi is in S_+ and G(phi)<0, choose a positive point on that ray, an earlier point in the negative quarter-disc, and a
sufficiently late negative point. The last point exists by r^h Omega(r,phi)->G(phi). These three points violate
Ray((0,alpha)), proving (62.1). Since S_+ is nonempty and open, its inclusion in {G>=0} proves the first empty-interior
exclusion.

Choose R with the positive set contained in {r<R}. For every phi in S_+, choose r_p<R with Omega(r_p,phi)>0. The ray
condition and an earlier negative point prohibit every negative value at a radius greater than r_p. Boundedness
prohibits every positive value at r>=R. The tail is therefore exactly zero, proving (62.2). This argument uses the
prohibition of a later negative value after a positive value on a ray with an earlier negative value. It does not assume
that a nonpositive tail contains a strictly negative point. The same reasoning applies to I under the localized
hypotheses.

Boundedness of the full positive set implies G<=0 on (0,alpha): any angle with G>0 would have positive vorticity at all
sufficiently large radii. At beta>2 Theorem 41(b) gives an open interval where G has the sign of a0. At beta=2 the
corresponding statement is Theorem 34(b). Thus in either case G is negative somewhere.

Set a=2-h and denote by p the angular stream coefficient called P in Theorems 36 and 41. Their conclusions give

  -p''-a^2 p=G, p(0)=p(alpha)=0,
  r^(h-1)U_phi(r,phi)->a p(phi) uniformly in phi.          (62.18)

For beta>2 this is exactly Theorem 41(b); for beta=2 it is Theorem 36(a),(b). The 2 pi-periodic solution is unique
because a is not an integer. The reflection symmetries of G and uniqueness give the odd-odd symmetries of p, hence both
Dirichlet values. The velocity convention is U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), so a stream term r^a p(phi) contributes
U_phi=partial_r(r^a p)=a r^(1-h)p, with the positive sign in (62.18).

Here 3/2<=a<2, and consequently 0<a alpha<pi. The Dirichlet Green kernel is

  K_a(phi,t)=sin(a min(phi,t))
             sin(a(alpha-max(phi,t)))/[a sin(a alpha)],
  p(phi)=int_0^alpha K_a(phi,t)G(t)dt.                    (62.19)

The kernel vanishes at the endpoints, solves the homogeneous equation off phi=t, and its first phi derivative has jump
-1 there. These facts verify the inverse of -partial_phi^2-a^2. Every sine in (62.19) is positive at interior phi,t. It
follows that G<=0 and G negative somewhere imply p<0 throughout (0,alpha).

Choose an open interval J whose closure lies in S_+, or in I cap S_+ in the localized case. The zero tail contains,
after increasing the height Y0, a cone

  E_*={y>Y0, c1 y<x<c2 y}, 0<c1<c2<infinity,
  Theta(x,y)=F(y), W_2(x,y)>0 on E_*,
  F'(y)=kappa F(y)/W_2(c0 y,y), c1<c0<c2.               (62.20)

Indeed choose c1,c2 so that the closed angular interval between arctan(1/c2) and arctan(1/c1) lies in J, and choose Y0
so that E_* is beyond the zero-tail radius. On E_*, Omega and its derivatives vanish. Equation (V) gives Theta_x=0. Each
horizontal section of E_* is an interval, so Theta=F(y) with F smooth. Since r<=sqrt(1+c2^2)y there, uniform
sublinearity gives W_2>=beta y/2 after another increase of Y0. Equation (T) on x=c0 y gives the regular scalar equation
in (62.20).

Uniqueness for this homogeneous linear equation makes F either identically zero or nowhere zero on y>Y0. If beta>2 and F
is nowhere zero, then F' is nowhere zero. Equation (T) on the whole cone implies W_2=V(y)=kappa F/F'. Divergence and
vorticity then give

  W_1=(2 beta-V'(y))x+C(y),
  Omega=partial_y W_1-partial_x W_2=-V''(y)x+C'(y)=0,
  V(y)=c y+e2, C(y)=e1.                                  (62.21)

For each fixed y the identity holds on a nonempty interval in x, so V''=C'=0. The usual curl partial_x W_2-partial_y W_1
equals -Omega, consistently with (62.21). Along x=c0 y, the condition U_2/y->0 forces c=beta. Hence U=(e1,e2) throughout
E_*.

For each fixed ray in this cone a constant U has r^(h-1)U_phi->0, because h<1. This contradicts (62.18) and p<0.
Therefore F=0. The cone contains a sector {r>R2,phi in J2} for a sufficiently large R2 and a smaller open angular
interval J2. This proves the common zero sector at beta>2 and the exclusion under (i). Under (H1), condition (i) follows
from Theta<0 in Theorem 8(ii). Under Theorem 58(c), Theta is nonzero on every upper source basin by Theorem 58(b), and
the complement is the finite union of the separatrices in (58.6). Each separatrix is the smooth image of a real time
interval and is covered by countably many compact smooth curve segments. Each segment has planar measure zero. The
finite union therefore has measure zero and cannot contain an open subset of Q1.

At beta=2, (62.20) instead gives F'=0 directly. Thus Theta is constant and Omega=0 on E_*. Zero divergence and zero curl
make each component of U harmonic on E_*. There is no conclusion that W_2 depends only on y, so the affine argument does
not apply. This proves the stated alternative, consistently with Theorems 44, 47 and 56, and completes (a).

For (b), choose delta<L/2 so that the smooth quotient Omega/(xy) is at most b0/2 on the disc. The strain identity in
Theorem 9 and the origin value Psi_xy(0)=2 beta+2 give int_Q1 K0 Omega=C0. Theorem 55 gives int_Q1 N_L Omega=beta L and
int_Q1 M_L Omega=0. Absolute convergence follows from Theorems 36 and 42, together with the local kernel estimates in
Theorem 55.

The angular integrals of cos(phi)sin(phi) and cos(phi)^2 sin(phi)^2 over (0,alpha) are 1/2 and pi/16. Thus the
quarter-disc integral of K0 |b0|xy/2 is pi|b0|delta^2/64. On this disc Q_L<=(L^2+delta^2)^2, while Q_L>0 in Q1. The
quarter-disc integral of N_L |b0|xy/2 is at least

  [2L|b0|/(pi(L^2+delta^2)^2)] (delta^6/6)(pi/16)
    =L|b0|delta^6/[48(L^2+delta^2)^2].

Splitting the first two balances by signs proves (62.4). The estimate Omega=O(r^(-h)) and smoothness on compact sets
show C_*<infinity. Positivity somewhere shows C_*>0. In polar coordinates K0 dX=cos(phi)sin(phi)dr dphi/r. Bound Omega_+
by C_*r^(-h), restrict angles to S_+ and radii to r>=R_+, and integrate to obtain (62.5).

The sign numerator of M_L, divided by L^4 and with t=(r/L)^2, is gamma t^2+2(1-2h)cos(2phi)t+(2h-3). Its constant term
is negative, so it has exactly one positive root. The quadratic formula gives (62.6). Since 1-2h>=0, that root decreases
as cos(2phi) increases; at cos(2phi)=1 it is 1, and at cos(2phi)=-1 it is (3-2h)/(1+2h). At beta=2 both values are 1.

Splitting int_Q1 M_L Omega=0 by the signs of both factors gives (62.7). The right side is positive because M_L<0 and
Omega<0 on a sufficiently small quarter-disc. Finally choose a compact angular interval on which G is strictly negative,
using Theorem 34(b) or 41(b). Uniform convergence makes Omega strictly negative there at every sufficiently large
radius. The bound for rho in (62.6) puts these points in D_out. This proves (b).

For (c), parity gives W_2=partial_y W_1=0 on the x-axis, and divergence gives partial_y W_2=2 beta-w'. Differentiating
(T) and (V) once in y gives the two trace equations in (62.8). Differentiate the T equation in x at L, where w=0, w'=b
and T=A<0 by Theorem 2. This gives bT'(L)=A w''(L). The g equation at L gives (beta-1)g(L)=T'(L). Comparing coefficients
of x^2,x^4 in the T equation and of x,x^3 in the g equation gives (62.9).

Under either local nonpositive-vorticity hypothesis, divide Omega(x,y)<=0 by y and take y->0+ for 0<x<L. Continuity
gives g(L)<=0. Since A<0, the source relation yields w''(L)>=0.

To prove (62.10), suppose R1>L is the first later zero of w. Theorem 2 gives w>0 just after L, so w>0 on (L,R1) and
w'(R1)<=0. The homogeneous T equation preserves T<0 on this interval. Put H0=g/T>=0. Direct substitution gives

  wH0'+(beta-1)H0=(w'-b)/w,
  H0'<=-b/(2w^2) sufficiently near R1.                   (62.22)

The inequality uses w'-b<=-b/2, w>0 and H0>=0. Smoothness and w(R1)=0 give 0<w(x)<=C(R1-x) there. Therefore the integral
of w^(-2) diverges at R1. Integrating (62.22) from any fixed nearby point forces H0 to be negative before R1, a
contradiction. This includes a degenerate later zero. There is no later zero, and the homogeneous T equation gives T<0
everywhere. The last assertion of (c) is Theorem 52(b).

For (d), (H1) gives v>0 on the positive y-axis. Its trace equations, from Theorems 27 and 30, are

  vE'=(2v'-(3 beta+2))E,
  vK'+(D-v')K=2E.                                        (62.23)

The jet E=a0 y+O(y^3) is negative initially, so the first equation preserves E<0. Since v=(3 beta+2)y+O(y^3), a positive
integrating factor mu for the second equation satisfies mu(y)=C y^(-(beta+1)/(3 beta+2))(1+O(y^2)). The product mu K
tends to zero at zero, using K=b0 y+O(y^3). Also mu(2E/v) is negative and integrable there, because (beta+1)/(3
beta+2)<1. Integrating (mu K)'=mu(2E/v) from zero proves K<0.

Smooth oddness gives Omega(x,y)=x K(y)+O(x^3) near each fixed positive y-axis point. This proves the local sign.
Theorem 50(c) explicitly uses sigma=sgn(a0); with sigma=-1 it gives G'(alpha)>0. Theorem 42 gives convergence of r^h
Omega(r,.) to G in C^1. Both functions vanish at alpha. Their angular derivatives are positive on a fixed interval
[alpha-epsilon,alpha] for every sufficiently large r. Integrating from alpha gives the asserted exterior negative wedge.

The transverse derivative of the backward flow on the axis is

  J(s,x)=partial_y[Phi_(-s)(x,0)]_2
    =exp(-int_0^s [2 beta-w'(chi_(-t)x)]dt).               (62.24)

The first component has zero transverse derivative there. The Remark after Theorem 8 gives the backward representation
of Omega. Its transverse derivative is (62.11). To justify this derivative, each fixed x>0 has backward limit P by
Theorem 50(a). Choose a small backward invariant ball about P on which the symmetric part of D(-W) is at most -a1 I for
some a1>0. A common finite backward time sends a neighbourhood of (x,0) into this ball. All first derivatives of the
subsequent backward flow are bounded by C exp(-a1 s), uniformly on a smaller neighbourhood. The second derivatives of
Theta are bounded in the ball. Thus the differentiated integrand is dominated by C exp(-(1+a1)s) on the tail, with a
bounded finite initial part. This proves differentiation under the integral and absolute convergence.

The sign implication follows from the positive kernel in (62.11). Near P, smooth parity factors give
Theta_x=y[T'(L)+O(|x-L|+y^2)] and Omega=y[g(L)+O(|x-L|+y^2)]. Equation (62.8) gives the common sign when w''(L)!=0.
Theorem 8(i) puts every Q1 backward orbit in this upper neighbourhood eventually. This proves (d).

For (e), write I(X)=int_0^infinity e^(-kappa s)[Phi_(-s)X]_2 ds. In a small backward invariant ball about R the
symmetric part of D(-W) is bounded above by -a1 I. Consequently the backward flow and its first spatial derivative
converge exponentially to R and zero, respectively. Differentiating the flow equation m times gives the same stable
linear homogeneous equation for its m-th derivative; for m>=2 its forcing is a sum of products of at least two lower
derivatives. Induction bounds that forcing by C_m exp(-2a1 s). Variation of constants gives an O(exp(-a1 s)) bound for
the m-th derivative as well, uniformly on a smaller ball.

The defining integral is therefore differentiable in every spatial order near R. At R the linearized y component of the
backward flow is exp(-kappa s)y. Since R has y coordinate zero,

  I(R)=0, DI(R)=e_2/(2kappa),
  Theta(R)=0, DTheta(R)=A_R e_2.                         (62.25)

The product Hc=kappa Theta I gives D^2 Hc(R)=A_R e_2 tensor e_2. From Theorem 44(a), grad Ly=dW+Omega W^perp+y grad
Theta. At R, W=Omega=y=0, so D^2 Ly(R)=d DW(R)+A_R e_2 tensor e_2, also the formula (58.10). Subtraction proves (62.13).

For any X in B_R, a finite backward time sends a neighbourhood of X into the preceding ball. Splitting I at that time
expresses it as a smooth finite-time integral plus exp(-kappa times that time) multiplied by I composed with a smooth
finite-time flow. Thus Hc and L_tilde are smooth on B_R. Equation (58.14) gives grad L_tilde.W=d|W|^2. A critical point
must therefore be a zero of W; the only such point in B_R is R. Formula (62.25) gives grad L_tilde(R)=0. Its positive
definite Hessian makes it a nondegenerate minimum. Along every other basin orbit L_tilde strictly increases from its
backward limit L_tilde(R), so the minimum is strict throughout B_R.

The cancellation of A_R in (62.13) prevents the stated lower bound from following from this minimum. It is also
compatible locally with arbitrary A_R: in source coordinates u=x-r, the fields W=(bu,kappa y), Omega=0, Theta=A_R y
solve both transport equations, have divergence 2 beta and zero curl. The associated U=W-beta X is divergence-free and
has a harmonic stream function. These local fields are not A2-broad profiles. This proves (e).

For (f), Theorem 39(b),(c) gives W=4l X_l and Theta_x=4y_l. On l=eps s, (V) becomes

  s omega'(s)+omega(s)/4=eps Y'(s),
  (s^(1/4)omega(s))'=eps s^(-3/4)Y'(s).                 (62.26)

Smoothness at the source gives Y(s)-q_y=O(s) and bounded omega(s). Integrating (62.26) from zero and integrating Y' by
parts after subtracting q_y proves (62.14); both lower boundary terms vanish.

Choose a point on the escaping fibre with coordinate l0!=0. Its launch angle lies strictly inside the quadrant, and the
limiting angular diffeomorphism of Theorem 36(d) fixes both axes, so its exit angle phi is interior. Theorem 39(d) gives
a positive radial amplitude a_r=lim_(t->infinity)exp(-2t)|Phi_t X| and H'(phi)=-2a_r^2/l0. Since s=|l0|exp(4t), this
proves k=a_r/sqrt(|l0|), H'(phi)!=0 and eps=-sgn H'(phi).

Theorem 36 gives U=O(r^(1/2)). Along this orbit r is comparable to exp(2t), so the derivative of exp(-2t)Phi_t X is
O(exp(-t)). Integrating to its limiting vector a_r(cos(phi),sin(phi)) gives Phi_t
X=exp(2t)a_r(cos(phi),sin(phi))+O(exp(t)). This proves the height asymptotic in (62.15). Uniform vorticity convergence
and r/sqrt(s)->k give s^(1/4)omega(s)->G(phi)/sqrt(k).

The displacement moment integrands are O(s^(-3/4)) at zero and O(s^(-5/4)) at infinity. Both moments converge. The term
s^(-3/4)(Y-q_y) tends to zero at infinity, so (62.14) gives (62.16). Since B>0, Y-q_y is positive for all sufficiently
large s, and A_+>0. If eps G(phi)<=0, then A_->=A_+>0, proving the dip.

For the limitation of that implication, take q_y>0, B>0 and Y(s)=q_y+B(sqrt(1+s)-1). Define omega(s)=eps s^(-1/4)int_0^s
t^(-3/4)Y'(t)dt. This solves (62.26), is smooth at zero after substituting t=su, and has outgoing amplitude of sign eps
because the integral over (0,infinity) is finite and positive. The height increases everywhere. These are data for the
scalar fibre equation only, proving that the opposite sign in (62.16) does not force a dip. This completes (f).

Finally, the tangent of C at P is vertical by Theorem 3, and Theta_y(P)=A<0. Thus Theta initially decreases along the
upper arc. Under (R), Theorem 39(b) makes its derivative along the connected regular arc nonzero everywhere. That
derivative cannot change sign, so Theta strictly decreases up to Q+. A fixed upper interior point already has negative
temperature; continuity then gives M<0. No use of (S) is needed here.

Under (S) and (R), Theorem 48(e) applies with sigma=-1. With the two additional axis hypotheses its possible zero end
intervals disappear. The only open interval where H is constant is the central interval (phi2,phi3), and H is strictly
monotone on the two passages. By (62.2) and the beta=2 cone argument, H is locally constant at every angle in S_+. Hence
S_+ cannot meet either passage. It cannot contain either plateau endpoint, because it is open and each endpoint adjoins
a strictly monotone passage. This proves (62.17) and completes the proof.

### Theorem 63 (bounded forward orbits and open potential regions)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta >= 2. Thus the fields are smooth on R^2, U is the canonical
uniformly sublinear velocity, and Theta and Omega have at most polynomial growth. The temperature is even in x and odd
in y, Omega is odd in both variables, U_1 is odd in x and even in y, and U_2 is even in x and odd in y. Write O = (0,0).
The temperature satisfies Theta(0,y) = 0 and Theta = x^2 y a(x^2,y^2) near O, with a smooth and a0 = a(0,0) != 0. Put
X = (x,y), r = |X|, Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, and

  W = beta X + U,    Z = {W = 0},    kappa = beta-2,
  div W = 2 beta,    d_y U_1-d_x U_2 = Omega,
  W.grad Theta = kappa Theta,
  W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x.                           (63.1)

Let Phi_t be the complete flow of W and Ly the smooth function of Theorem 44(a). Let P = (x1,0) be the first positive
x-axis zero of Theorem 2. At beta = 2 let C be the zero component through P, Q+ its upper endpoint from Theorem 16, and
M = Theta(Q+); let H and G be the smooth angular limits of Theta(r,phi) and r^(1/2) Omega(r,phi) from Theorem 36. A zero
component is isolated if some open neighbourhood meets Z in precisely that component; its index is the planar
vector-field index on an isolating boundary.

(a) Every bounded forward orbit converges to a single point S+ of Z. For beta > 2, Theta vanishes on the complete orbit.
If the orbit is nonstationary, it also has a backward limit S- in Z, the limits are distinct, and

  Ly(S+) - Ly(S-)
    = (2 beta-1) integral_(-infinity)^infinity
                         |W(Phi_t X)|^2 dt > 0.             (63.2)

The integral is finite. At beta = 2 the common temperature of the orbit and its two limits need not be zero. In
particular there is no nonstationary homoclinic orbit.

(b) Suppose beta = 2 and some component of Z is isolated and has index +1. There exist a real number c, a nonempty open
connected set S contained in Q1, and a nonempty open interval J contained in (0,pi/2), such that S is invariant for
every real time, has infinite area, and

  Theta = c and Omega = 0 on S,
  H = c and G = 0 on J.                                    (63.3)

The velocity U is harmonic and real analytic on S. The number c is the temperature of a zero in the closed first
quadrant.

(c) If beta = 2 and Z has finitely many connected components, the hypothesis and conclusions of (b) hold.

Scope. These are necessary conditions on a hypothetical A2-broad profile, not an existence or nonexistence theorem for
the full class. Part (a) uses no zero-component, axis-chain, regularity-of-zeros or vorticity-sign hypothesis. Its
beta = 2 conclusions are already in Theorems 48(a) and 56(a); the absence of homoclinic loops is already in Theorem 4.
Parts (b) and (c) use no sign assumption, and require neither (S) nor (R) of Theorem 48. They exclude profiles
satisfying their respective component hypothesis for which {Omega = 0} has no interior point in Q1, or for which {phi in
(0,pi/2): G(phi) = 0} has empty interior. They do not identify c with M = Theta(Q+) or with zero. They leave unresolved
the general case of infinitely many zero components at beta = 2, including the case in which no isolated component has
index +1, and whether every orbit in Q1 escapes at beta > 2.

Proof.

Uniform sublinearity and smoothness give a complete flow and a radius R_* such that

  X.W(X) >= (beta/2)|X|^2 for |X| >= R_*,
  det D Phi_t(X) = exp(2 beta t),
  Theta(Phi_t X) = exp(kappa t) Theta(X).                   (63.4)

The last identity follows by solving the scalar equation (T) along the orbit. Every backward orbit stays in a compact
disc, as in Theorem 44(b). An orbit reaching the exterior of that disc in forward time stays outside and its radius
grows at least exponentially.

First prove (a). At beta = 2, forward convergence is Theorem 48(a). For beta > 2, let X(t) = Phi_t X0 have bounded
forward orbit. Smoothness bounds Theta on its compact closure. Since kappa > 0, (63.4) forces Theta(X0) = 0 and then
Theta(X(t)) = 0 for every real t. Theorem 44(a), restricted to this orbit, gives

  d_t Ly(X(t)) = (2 beta-1)|W(X(t))|^2,
  integral_0^infinity |W(X(t))|^2 dt < infinity.             (63.5)

Indeed Ly is bounded on the compact forward orbit closure. On that closure the derivative of |W(X(t))|^2 is 2 W.DW W and
is bounded. Thus |W(X(t))|^2 is uniformly continuous. A nonnegative integrable uniformly continuous function tends to
zero: otherwise a sequence of positive peaks supplies disjoint intervals of a fixed positive length on which the
function has a fixed positive lower bound. Consequently W(X(t)) tends to zero.

The omega-limit set A is the intersection of the closures of the forward tails. These are nested nonempty compact
connected sets, so A is nonempty, compact and connected, and A is contained in Z. We give the two local arguments needed
to show that A is a point. They use tr DW = 2 beta and do not use the beta = 2 component classification.

An interior point R of a smooth open zero arc cannot belong to the omega-limit set of a nonstationary orbit. Straighten
a short segment of the arc by smooth coordinates (u,v), with R at (0,0) and the arc at v = 0. Since the field vanishes
on that segment, division by v gives

  u' = v a(u,v),    v' = v b(u,v),
  b(u,0) = 2 beta.                                        (63.6)

To check the last identity, the derivative of the transformed field at (u,0) is the matrix with rows (0,a(u,0)) and
(0,b(u,0)). At a zero it is conjugate to DW in the original coordinates. Its trace is therefore 2 beta. Equivalently,
the tangent to the zero arc is a zero eigenvector and the other eigenvalue is 2 beta. This reasoning also applies to
arcs contained in or crossing an axis.

Choose a closed coordinate rectangle B = {|u| <= d, |v| <= e}, with X0 outside B, on which b >= beta and |a| <= A0. In
backward time tau, as long as an orbit stays in B,

  |v(tau)| <= |v(0)| exp(-beta tau),
  |u(tau)-u(0)| <= A0 |v(0)|/beta.                         (63.7)

Choose e0 < e so that A0 e0/beta < d/4. Initial points with |u(0)| < d/2 and |v(0)| < e0 cannot have a first backward
exit from B: (63.7) keeps both coordinates strictly inside its boundary. If R belonged to A, some positive-time point
X(T) would lie in this smaller rectangle. Following it backwards for time T would put X0 in B, a contradiction.

A compact connected subset A of Z with more than one point contains a smooth open zero arc. Choose distinct R,R' in A.
Since tr DW(R) != 0, at least one scalar component W_i has nonzero gradient at R. The implicit function theorem gives a
coordinate rectangle about R, not containing R', in which {W_i = 0} is v = 0 and Z is contained in that curve. Suppose
there are points of this curve outside A arbitrarily close to R on both sides. Choose two such points (u1,0) and (u2,0),
with u1 < 0 < u2, and a thin closed rectangle [u1,u2] x [-e1,e1] inside the chart. Its horizontal sides miss the
containing curve, and its vertical sides meet that curve only at the two chosen points outside A. Its boundary therefore
misses A. Its intersection with A equals its interior intersection with A, so is relatively open and closed in A. It
contains R and misses R', contradicting connectedness. Thus one side of R contains a full interval of the curve lying in
A. The interior of that interval is the required smooth open zero arc.

If A were not a singleton, the preceding paragraph would produce an open zero arc in A, while (63.6)-(63.7) exclude its
interior points from A. Thus A = {S+}. Compactness of the forward orbit closure now implies X(t) -> S+. A stationary
orbit causes no exception.

Theorem 44(b) supplies a single backward limit S- for every orbit. At beta > 2, Theta = 0 on the complete orbit under
consideration; at beta = 2, kappa = 0. In either case Theorem 44(a) gives the first identity of (63.5) for every real t.
Integrating on [-T,T] and passing to the two point limits proves (63.2), with finiteness from continuity of Ly. For a
nonstationary orbit the integral over some finite time interval is positive, so S- != S+. Temperature invariance at
beta = 2 also gives the asserted common temperature. This completes (a).

We next find a positive-index component under the hypothesis of (c). Theorem 53(a) applies at beta = 2 without
finiteness or (S): every nontrivial component of Z is a compact smooth embedded arc, and every singleton component is
critical. With finitely many components each is isolated, because the components are compact and disjoint. Theorem 53(f)
gives the index of an isolated arc as half the sum of its two endpoint signs, with outgoing sign +1 and incoming sign
-1. At an isolated point its derivative is symmetric with trace 4 by Theorem 44(d). If nonsingular it is a source or a
saddle, with index +1 or -1. If singular it has spectrum {0,4}, and Theorem 53(f) gives the same half-branch formula.
Thus every component index is in {-1,0,+1}.

On a sufficiently large circle the homotopy 2X+tU(X), 0 <= t <= 1, has positive radial component and no zero. Its index
is that of 2X, namely 1. Index additivity therefore gives

  sum_(D a component of Z) ind(D) = 1.                    (63.8)

Here the origin contributes -1. The points P and -P belong to the two arc components C and its reflection across the
y-axis; they are not counted as isolated point zeros. Their contributions and those of all the other components are
exactly the finite balance (53.8) of Theorem 53(f). Since no component index exceeds +1, (63.8) forces a component of
index +1. It remains to prove (b), using only isolation of the selected component.

Suppose first that this component is a point R. Theorem 56(c), in its assertion independent of finiteness and of the
direction of Q+, gives two possibilities: R is a hyperbolic source, or its spectrum is {0,4} and both centre
half-branches are outgoing. In either case that theorem already gives a full neighbourhood with backward limit R,
constant temperature and zero vorticity. We choose a bounded backward invariant open set inside such a neighbourhood.

For a hyperbolic source put A_R = DW(R). Its two eigenvalues are positive real numbers by Theorem 56(c). With xi = X-R
define

  P_R = integral_0^infinity
                     exp(-A_R^T t) exp(-A_R t) dt,
  A_R^T P_R + P_R A_R = I,
  d_tau (xi^T P_R xi) = -|xi|^2 + O(|xi|^3)               (63.9)

along reversed flow. The integral converges and is positive definite; its matrix identity follows by integrating the
derivative of exp(-A_R^T t) exp(-A_R t). A sufficiently small sublevel ellipsoid is backward invariant, and the last
inequality, together with equivalence of the two quadratic norms, gives backward convergence to R. The ellipsoid has
positive finite area.

For a degenerate point either outgoing centre half-branch admits the construction below. This uses only a C^2 centre
curve and does not require that curve to be analytic. The stronger full-neighbourhood conclusion of Theorem 56(c) is
consistent with this smaller choice.

Suppose instead that the selected component is an arc. Theorem 53(f) and index +1 imply that both endpoints are
outgoing. Choose one, R. By Theorem 53(a) its spectrum is {0,4}. As in the local construction in Theorems 35 and 53(f),
take a C^2 invariant centre curve through R. In a chart straightening that curve, its normal equation has the form
z' = a(s,z)z with a(0,0) = 4. Consequently all nearby zeros lie on the curve. It therefore contains the terminal zero
arc. Isolation and the endpoint property ensure that its opposite branch is zero-free sufficiently near R. Orient s so
that this branch is s > 0.

Both the degenerate point case and the outgoing arc endpoint case have the local form

  z' = a(s,z)z,    s' = b(s)+z c0(s,z),
  a(0,0) = 4,    b(0) = b'(0) = 0,
  b(s) > 0 for 0 < s <= delta.                            (63.10)

The functions a,c0 are continuous and b is C^1. Shrink the chart and choose eta > 0 so that

  a >= 2,    |b'| <= 1/4,    |c0| <= C0,
  eta C0 <= 1/2.                                         (63.11)

After decreasing delta if necessary, the closure of the cusp fits inside the chart:

  D = {0 < s < delta, |z| < eta b(s)}.                     (63.12)

This set is open, connected, bounded and has positive area, since b > 0 on (0,delta). In backward time tau, within D,

  -(3/2)b(s) <= d_tau s <= -(1/2)b(s),
  d_tau log(|z|/b(s))
    = -a + b'(s)(1+z c0/b(s))
    <= -2+3/8 < 0,    z != 0.                            (63.13)

The upper face s = delta and the side faces |z|/b(s) = eta cannot be crossed outwards in backward time. The set z = 0 is
invariant. Also b(s) <= C s near zero, so the first inequality gives d_tau s >= -(3C/2)s and prevents reaching s = 0 in
finite time. These estimates prove backward invariance. The decreasing coordinate s has a limit; a positive limit would
contradict d_tau s <= -b(s)/2 and positivity of b there. Thus s tends to zero, and |z| <= eta b(s) tends to zero. Every
backward orbit from D therefore converges to R. The same conclusion holds for the ellipsoid in the hyperbolic case.

Temperature is constant along orbits at beta = 2. Continuity at R gives Theta = Theta(R) on D. Since D is open,
Theta_x = 0 there. Backward invariance and (V) give

  Omega(Phi_(-tau) X) = exp(tau) Omega(X),    X in D.       (63.14)

The left side stays bounded as its argument tends to R, so Omega = 0 on D.

The field W is equivariant under both axis reflections. Reflect D if necessary so that its intersection with Q1 is
nonempty. A reflection across the y-axis leaves the constant temperature unchanged, while a reflection across the x-axis
changes its sign; zero vorticity remains zero. Call the resulting constant c and the reflected limiting zero R again.
Choose a connected component D1 of D cap Q1. It is open, bounded and of positive area. For each point of D1 the backward
path stays in D cap Q1, because D and Q1 are backward invariant; continuity keeps that path in its original connected
component. Thus D1 is backward invariant and R is in the closed first quadrant.

Set

  S = union_(t >= 0) Phi_t(D1),
  |Phi_t(D1)| = exp(4t)|D1|.                              (63.15)

Backward invariance of D1 makes the sets in this union nested. They are open and connected, so S is open and connected,
and the same nesting shows Phi_t(S) = S for every real t. Axis invariance gives S contained in Q1. Temperature
invariance gives Theta = c on S. Openness then gives Theta_x = 0 on S, and (V) propagates Omega = 0 from D1. The area
identity in (63.15) follows from (63.4), and implies |S| = infinity. Zero divergence and zero curl of U on S imply that
each component of U is harmonic and hence real analytic.

Choose a launch radius R0 for Theorem 36 so large that D1 lies inside its circle. Infinite area makes S unbounded. Since
S is connected and meets the inside of that circle, it meets the circle; its openness gives an open arc of launch labels
I with closure in (0,pi/2). All their complete orbits stay in S. In the notation of Theorem 36(d),

  Theta(r,F_r(alpha)) = c,
  Omega(r,F_r(alpha)) = 0,
  alpha in I,    r >= R0.                                 (63.16)

That theorem gives uniform convergence F_r -> F, with F a smooth diffeomorphism fixing the axis directions, and uniform
angular limits for Theta and r^(1/2) Omega. Passing to the limit in (63.16) gives H(F(alpha)) = c and G(F(alpha)) = 0.
Hence J = F(I) is a nonempty open interval in (0,pi/2) satisfying (63.3). This proves (b) and (c), including the
restricted exclusions in the Scope. QED.

### Theorem 64 (zero-vorticity sets for beta > 2 and bounded opposite-sign vorticity)

Let (beta,Theta,Omega,U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2, with beta >= 2. Thus the fields are smooth, U is
canonical and uniformly sublinear, and Theta and Omega have at most polynomial growth. The temperature is even in x and
odd in y, with Theta(0,y)=0 and Theta=a0 x^2 y+O(|X|^5) near the origin, where a0!=0. The vorticity is odd in each
coordinate; U_1 is odd in x and even in y, while U_2 is even in x and odd in y. Put

  Q1={x>0,y>0}, L=pi/2, sigma=sgn(a0),
  kappa=beta-2, h=1/beta, q=kappa/beta, a=2-h,
  W=beta X+U, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), -Lap Psi=Omega,
  div W=2 beta, d_y W_1-d_x W_2=Omega,
  W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x, W.grad Theta=kappa Theta.
                                                               (64.1)

Write Phi_t for the complete flow, Z={W=0} and Crit={grad Theta=0}. The hypothesis (H1) means Z cap
closure(Q1)={O,P_ax}, where O=(0,0) and P_ax is the first positive x-axis zero of Theorem 2. All connected open sets
below are nonempty.

Use the smooth angular functions f,G,P of Theorems 41 and 42 for beta>2, and H,G,P of Theorems 33 and 36 for beta=2.
Here P is the angular stream coefficient, with normalization

  r^(-q)Theta(r,phi)->f(phi)                 if beta>2,
  Theta(r,phi)->H(phi)                      if beta=2,
  r^h Omega(r,phi)->G(phi),
  r^(h-1)(U_r,U_phi)(r,phi)->(-P',aP)(phi),
  -P''-a^2 P=G, P(0)=P(L)=0.                          (64.2)

These limits are uniform in angle. For an unbounded set V, Lambda(V) is the set of limits of arg X_j on the angle circle
along sequences X_j in V with |X_j|->infinity. For V contained in Q1, regard Lambda(V) as a subset of [0,L]. Define

  B={X in Q1: sigma Omega(X)<0},
  S_B={phi in (0,L): sigma Omega(r,phi)<0 for some r>0}.
                                                               (64.3)

(a) Suppose B is bounded. Then sigma G>=0 on [0,L], G is not identically zero, and

  sigma P>0, sigma P''<0 on (0,L),
  sigma P'(0)>0, sigma P'(L)<0.                         (64.4)

In particular P and P' have no common zero in [0,L]. If beta>2, every unbounded connected open subset of {Omega=0} cap
Q1 has Theta identically zero. Consequently no such subset exists when {Theta=0} has empty interior in Q1.

(b) Suppose B is bounded and no ray in Q1 contains radii 0<r1<r2<r3 with strict vorticity signs (sigma,-sigma,sigma).
Choose R_B>0 with B contained in {r<R_B}. Then S_B is open and

  Omega(r,phi)=0 for r>=R_B and phi in S_B.              (64.5)

If beta>2 and B is nonempty, there is a nonempty exterior open sector in Q1 on which Theta=Omega=0. Thus, at beta>2,

  {Theta=0} has empty interior in Q1,
  B bounded, and no ray has (sigma,-sigma,sigma)
  imply B is empty.                                    (64.6)

For a0<0 these hypotheses are impossible; for a0>0 they imply Omega>=0 on Q1 and all the beta>2 conclusions of Theorem
57(a). For a0<0 this is the exclusion of Theorem 62(a) by a different route. The empty-interior hypothesis holds under
(H1), under all the hypotheses of Theorem 58(c), and under nondegeneracy of every zero of W in the closed first quadrant
(Theorem 80(b)).

(c) Suppose beta>2, B is bounded, and {Theta=0} has empty interior in Q1. For every positive integer n the set

  A_n={phi in (0,L):
          sigma Omega(r,phi)>0 for some r>n}             (64.7)

is open and dense. The intersection A_infinity of these sets is dense and residual in (0,L). If B is nonempty, a dense
residual subset of S_B has a triple (sigma,-sigma,sigma) whose last radius can be chosen arbitrarily large. For every
fixed M>=0 the set of angles in S_B admitting such a triple with r3>M is open and dense in S_B.

Consequently, these hypotheses are inconsistent with either of the following additional conditions: triples are
forbidden on a dense subset of an open interval J with J cap S_B nonempty; or, for one fixed M, triples with r3>M are
forbidden on every ray in such a J. The set of angles in (0,L) on which Omega is eventually identically zero is meagre.

(d) Suppose beta>2 and V is connected and open, with Omega=0 and Theta nowhere zero on V. There are real constants
c,e1,e2,C, with C!=0, such that

  W=((2 beta-c)x+e1,cy+e2),
  U=((beta-c)x+e1,(c-beta)y+e2),                         (64.8)

and

  Theta=C|cy+e2|^(kappa/c)                  if c!=0,
  Theta=C exp(kappa y/e2), e2!=0           if c=0.      (64.9)

In the first case cy+e2 is nowhere zero and has one sign on V. No restriction c>0 is required. All constants are global
on V, without any assumption on its horizontal slices. The set V cannot meet either axis.

(e) Suppose beta>2 and V is connected and open, with Omega=0 and Theta nonzero somewhere on V. The affine velocity in
(64.8) holds throughout V. If V is unbounded, then c=beta, Theta is nowhere zero on V, and

  U=(e1,e2), Theta=C|beta y+e2|^q, C!=0, 0<q<1.         (64.10)

At every phi_* in Lambda(V),

  P(phi_*)=P'(phi_*)=G(phi_*)=0,
  f(phi_*)=C beta^q |sin(phi_*)|^q.                     (64.11)

Every angular derivative of P and G vanishes at phi_*. If V is contained in Q1, Lambda(V) is a nonempty compact subset
of (0,L), and the absolute value on sin(phi_*) can be omitted. If {Theta=0} has empty interior in Q1, these conclusions
apply to every unbounded connected open subset of {Omega=0} cap Q1, without assuming B bounded. Such a set cannot
contain an exterior sector over an interval on which P or G is not identically zero.

(f) Suppose beta>2 and V is connected and open, with Theta=Omega=0. Its full flow saturation

  S=union_(t in R) Phi_t(V)                             (64.12)

is connected, open and invariant, has infinite area, and satisfies Theta=Omega=0. If V is contained in Q1, so is S, and
S supplies a nonempty open angular interval on which f=G=0. If V is also unbounded, every angular derivative of f and G
vanishes at every point of Lambda(V).

(g) Suppose beta=2, B is bounded and nonempty, and the ray prohibition of (b) holds. There are a nonempty open interval
I with closure in (0,L), R>0 and a real constant c such that the exterior sector E={r>R,phi in I} satisfies

  Omega=0, Theta=c, grad Theta=0 on E,
  H=c, G=0 on I,
  P(phi)=A sin(3phi/2)+B1 cos(3phi/2) on I.             (64.13)

The last expression has strict sign sigma on I. The saturation S of E is connected, open and invariant, lies in Q1, has
infinite area, and satisfies Theta=c and Omega=0. Every orbit in S escapes. Every backward limit is a point of Z cap
Crit cap closure(Q1) with temperature c, and lies in Q1 if c!=0. In particular c belongs to Theta(Z cap Crit cap
closure(Q1)); the full temperature range is the compact interval of Theorem 53(h).

The set J of exit angles of S is an open interval containing I, and H=c, G=0 on J.

(h) Suppose beta=2 and B is bounded, without a ray hypothesis. At interior angles, in addition to H'=0 implying G=0 from
Theorem 47(a), one has

  H'=0 implies H''=0,
  G=0 implies sigma H'>=0,
  sigma H'<0 implies sigma G>0.                         (64.14)

Scope. Parts (d)-(f) are local and asymptotic necessary conditions. Parts (a)-(c) give the restricted exclusion and the
positive-branch reduction. Bounded opposite-sign vorticity without a ray hypothesis remains open in general, including
under (H1): no negative-branch exclusion or positive-branch reduction is asserted in that generality. Parts (g)-(h)
leave the beta=2 constant-temperature potential alternative unexcluded. The value c is not identified with zero or with
an extremal temperature. Local formulas do not construct A2-broad profiles.

Proof.

First prove (d) and (e), which supply the rigidity needed in (a).

On a zero-vorticity open set the vorticity equation gives Theta_x=0. Under the nonvanishing hypothesis of (d),
temperature transport becomes W_2 Theta_y=kappa Theta!=0. Both factors on the left are therefore nowhere zero.
Differentiating in x gives (d_x W_2)Theta_y=0, since Theta_xy=0. The curl and divergence identities in (64.1) now give

  d_x W_2=0, d_y W_1=0,
  d_x W_1+d_y W_2=2 beta,
  d_xx W_1=0, d_yy W_2=0.                              (64.15)

The last line follows by differentiating the divergence identity and commuting mixed derivatives. Thus every entry of DW
has zero gradient. Connectedness makes DW constant; integrating the resulting zero gradients of the affine differences
gives (64.8) with single constants on V.

If c!=0, the continuous nonzero function cy+e2 has one sign. Both components of the gradient of
log|Theta|-(kappa/c)log|cy+e2| vanish. Connectedness, and the constant sign of Theta, give the first formula of (64.9).
If c=0, nonvanishing of W_2 gives e2!=0, and log|Theta|-kappa y/e2 has zero gradient. This proves the second formula.
Both A2 axis traces of Theta are zero, so V cannot meet either axis. This proves (d).

For (e), divergence and the curl convention give

  Lap U_1=d_y Omega, Lap U_2=-d_x Omega.                (64.16)

For example d_y Omega=U_1,yy-U_2,xy=U_1,yy+U_1,xx; the second identity follows by interchanging the roles of x and y
with the indicated sign. Hence U has harmonic components on V. A small ball about a point with nonzero temperature
satisfies (d). Each component of U minus the affine field obtained there is harmonic on V and vanishes on that ball.

For completeness, a harmonic function vanishing on a nonempty open subset of a connected open set vanishes everywhere on
that set. Harmonic functions have convergent local power series. The set of points having a zero neighbourhood is open;
at any of its limit points inside the domain all derivatives vanish by continuity, so the local power series gives a
zero neighbourhood there as well. The set is therefore also relatively closed. This proves continuation of the affine
field to V.

Its linear part is (beta-c)diag(1,-1), so

  |U(X)| >= |beta-c||X|-|(e1,e2)|.                      (64.17)

Uniform sublinearity along any unbounded sequence in V forces c=beta. Let D be a connected component of {Theta!=0} cap V
containing a nonzero point. On D, (d) gives (64.10). At a relative boundary point Y of D in V, if beta Y_y+e2!=0,
continuity gives Theta(Y)!=0. A small connected ball about Y in {Theta!=0} cap V then meets D and belongs to the same
component, a contradiction. Thus beta Y_y+e2=0. But on D,

  |Theta_y|=kappa |C||beta y+e2|^(q-1), q-1=-2h<0,     (64.18)

which diverges along a sequence in D tending to Y. This contradicts smoothness at Y. Hence D is relatively closed as
well as open in V, so D=V.

Let X_j=r_j e(phi_j) define a limit direction phi_*. Theorem 41(b) gives exactly the uniform polar velocity limit in
(64.2); in Cartesian components it is V0(phi)=-P'(phi)e_r(phi)+aP(phi)e_phi(phi). Since U is constant on V and h<1, its
normalized value tends to zero along the sequence. Thus V0(phi_*)=0, which gives P(phi_*)=P'(phi_*)=0. Zero vorticity
gives G(phi_*)=0. The temperature normalization in Theorem 41(b) is r^(-q)Theta, so (64.10) gives the stated value of f,
with no launch-radius factor.

Theorem 42(b) also gives, for each fixed integer m>=0, uniformly in phi,

  d_phi^m[r^(h-1)U(r e(phi))-V0(phi)]=O(r^(-h)).        (64.19)

Indeed d_phi=-y d_x+x d_y, and each term in its m-th power is a polynomial of degree k times a Cartesian derivative of
order k<=m. Applying the O_infty(r^(1-2h)) remainder of that theorem gives (64.19). For m>=1 the angular derivative of
the Cartesian field U is zero at each X_j, since U is constant on an open neighbourhood there. For m=0 its normalized
value tends to zero. Hence every derivative of V0 vanishes at phi_*. Since aP=V0.e_phi, all derivatives of P vanish
there; the angular equation then gives the same conclusion for G. The constants in (64.19) may depend on m, which is
sufficient.

If V is contained in Q1, combine (64.18) with the gradient bound in Theorem 41(a). For all sufficiently large X in V
this gives

  |beta y+e2|/|X| >= (kappa |C|/C_1)^(1/(2h))>0.       (64.20)

This excludes the direction 0. The direction L is excluded by f(L)=0, inherited from Theta(0,y)=0, since (64.11) would
give f(L)=C beta^q!=0. The set Lambda(V) is nonempty and compact: it is the intersection, over positive integers n, of
the nonempty compact closures in [0,L] of the directions of points of V outside {r<=n}. Conversely, a point in this
intersection is realized by choosing a point outside each disc whose direction is within 1/n of it. Thus Lambda(V) lies
in a compact subinterval of (0,L).

If the temperature zero set has empty interior, every nonempty open V in Q1 contains a nonzero-temperature point. Under
(H1), this hypothesis follows from Theorem 8(ii). Under the hypotheses of Theorem 58(c), the source basins in its
decomposition have nonzero temperature by Theorem 58(b). The remaining finitely many separatrices are smooth orbit
images and have zero planar area: each is a countable union of images of bounded time intervals, on which its
parametrization is Lipschitz. They cannot contain an open set. Finally, an exterior sector supplies each of its angles
as a limit direction, so (64.11) proves the last assertion of (e).

Now prove (a). Boundedness of B gives sigma Omega>=0 on Q1 outside a disc. The uniform angular limits give sigma G>=0 on
[0,L]. Theorem 41(b) for beta>2, and Theorem 34(b) for beta=2, give an open interval where sigma G>0. In particular the
angular source is not zero.

For 3/2<=a<2 one has 0<aL<pi. The Dirichlet inverse of -d_phi^2-a^2 is

  K_a(phi,t)=sin(a min(phi,t))sin(a(L-max(phi,t)))
               /[a sin(aL)],
  P(phi)=int_0^L K_a(phi,t)G(t) dt.                     (64.21)

The kernel vanishes at both endpoints, solves the homogeneous equation away from phi=t, and its first phi derivative has
jump -1 at phi=t. Thus applying -d_phi^2-a^2 gives the unit point mass. The homogeneous Dirichlet solution is zero
because sin(aL)!=0, which proves the inverse formula. The kernel is strictly positive in the open square. Since sigma G
is nonnegative and positive on an interval, sigma P>0. The equation gives sigma P''=-a^2 sigma P-sigma G<0. At the
endpoints,

  P'(0)=int_0^L sin(a(L-t))G(t)/sin(aL) dt,
  P'(L)=-int_0^L sin(at)G(t)/sin(aL) dt.                (64.22)

The signs are strict. Thus P and P' have no common zero, including at the endpoints. If beta>2 and an unbounded
connected zero-vorticity open set in Q1 contained a nonzero-temperature point, (e) and nonemptiness of Lambda(V) would
give such a common zero. This proves (a).

For (b), smooth division by the axes and oddness of Omega give Omega=xy b(x,y), with b smooth and even in both
variables. Its origin value is b0=2a0/(2 beta+1), as in Theorem 57. Therefore b=b0+O(r^2) uniformly near O. There is one
delta>0 such that sigma Omega>0 on every interior ray for 0<r<delta; no angular lower bound on xy is needed.

If phi belongs to S_B, choose r2<R_B with sigma Omega(r2,phi)<0 and then r1<min(delta,r2) with sigma Omega(r1,phi)>0. A
point with sigma Omega>0 at any r3>=R_B would complete the forbidden triple. A point with sigma Omega<0 there is ruled
out by boundedness of B. This proves (64.5). A negative value at one fixed radius persists for nearby angles, so S_B is
open. If nonempty, it contains an open interval I with closure in S_B. Its exterior sector r>R_B is connected, open and
unbounded. At beta>2, (a) forces Theta=0 throughout this sector.

The empty-interior hypothesis now gives B empty. When a0<0, this would mean Omega<=0 on Q1, contrary to Theorem 21(a).
When a0>0, it means Omega>=0, so Theorem 57(a), including its axis conclusions and Theorem 50(a)-(f), applies. This
proof uses only Theorems 1-60 and the preceding calculations. The assertions about (H1) and Theorem 58(c) were justified
in the proof of (e).

For (c), openness of A_n follows from a strict inequality at one radius. If it were not dense, some nonempty open
interval I would miss it. On I there would be no strictly sigma-signed value for r>n. For r>max(n,R_B), exterior weak
sign would then give Omega=0 on the whole sector. This contradicts (a) and the empty-interior hypothesis. This also
shows that n>=R_B is unnecessary.

Here is a direct Baire argument. Inside any nonempty open interval choose a closed interval K_1 of positive length
contained in A_1 and in that interval. Inductively choose a closed interval K_(n+1) of positive length contained in the
interior of K_n and in A_(n+1), with lengths tending to zero. Density and openness permit each choice. Compactness gives
a point in their intersection; it lies in every A_n and in the original interval. Thus A_infinity is dense. Its
complement is a countable union of relatively closed sets with empty interior, so it is residual.

For phi in A_infinity cap S_B, use an initial sigma-signed point and an opposite-sign point as in (b), then choose a
