strictly sigma-signed point beyond both that point and any prescribed bound. This gives arbitrarily late triples. The
intersection is dense and residual relative to S_B. For fixed M, a triple with r3>M persists at its three fixed radii
for nearby angles. Its angle set is therefore open as well as dense in S_B. An open triple set cannot avoid a dense
subset of J if J cap S_B is nonempty, which proves both weakened prohibitions.

For each positive integer m put

  Z_m={phi in (0,L): Omega(r,phi)=0 for every r>=m}.     (64.23)

This is relatively closed, being an intersection of zero sets of continuous angular functions. It has empty interior by
(a). The eventual-zero angles are exactly the union of these sets and are therefore meagre.

For (f), the open set V lies in Crit. Theorem 44(d) makes Crit invariant and gives Omega=0 on it; temperature transport
keeps Theta=0 along every orbit through V. The saturation is open, invariant and connected, the last assertion following
because it is the continuous image of R times V. Choose a ball D contained in V. Liouville's formula gives
|Phi_t(D)|=exp(2 beta t)|D|, and these sets all lie in S, so S has infinite area. The velocity parities make both axes
invariant. Uniqueness in both time directions prevents an orbit in Q1 from reaching an axis in finite time, so V
contained in Q1 implies S contained in Q1.

Choose a point X0 in S and a launch radius R0>|X0| admissible in Theorem 38. Infinite area makes S unbounded. Since S is
connected, its radial image is an interval containing radii on both sides of R0. Thus S meets the launch circle;
openness supplies an arc of launch labels. On these orbits theta_0=0 and J0=0. The exact angular formulas of
Theorem 38(b),(d), with J0 continuous at every label by Theorem 41(c), are

  f o F=R0^(-q)exp(kappa d_inf)theta_0,
  G o F=R0^h exp(-d_inf)J0.                            (64.24)

They give f=G=0 on the image arc under the exit diffeomorphism F. If V is unbounded, all spatial and hence all angular
derivatives of Theta and Omega vanish at points of V. The O_infty bounds of Theorem 42(b), converted as in (64.19), give
uniform convergence in every angular derivative of r^(-q)Theta to f and of r^h Omega to G. Passing along each defining
sequence for Lambda(V) proves the flatness in (f).

There is no conclusion P=P'=0 in (f) from these local equations and angular limits alone. On an exterior sector the
fields Theta=Omega=0 and a stream function

  Psi=r^(2-h)[A sin((2-h)phi)+B1 cos((2-h)phi)]          (64.25)

solve those local equations and have sublinear velocity; the stream coefficient need not vanish. This example concerns
only the sector equations and does not provide a full-plane A2 extension or satisfy the origin jet.

For (g), (64.5) holds also at beta=2. Choose an open I with closure contained in S_B and in (0,L). On its exterior
sector y>=c_I r for some c_I>0. Uniform sublinearity gives W_2=2y+o(r)>0 after increasing the radius. The vorticity
equation gives Theta_x=0; temperature transport then gives W_2 Theta_y=0. Thus Theta is one constant c on this connected
sector. Theorem 36 gives H=c, G=0 on I. The angular equation gives the sine and cosine formula in (64.13), whose strict
sign follows from (a).

The same saturation argument as in (f), using Theorem 44(d) and temperature invariance at beta=2, gives all its stated
set and field properties. Choose E beyond a radius where W_r>=r. Every orbit through E escapes, and hence every orbit in
its saturation does. By Theorem 44(b) each has a single backward limit in Z cap closure(Q1). Closedness of Crit and
continuity of temperature place this limit in Crit with value c. If c!=0, the zero axis traces exclude an axis limit.
The precise range identity in Theorem 53(h) is H([0,L])=closure(Theta(Q1))=Theta(Z cap closure(Q1)); the claimed
membership is consistent with, and more specific than, membership in this full range.

The escaping set in Q1 has the flow coordinates R times (0,L) of Theorems 33(b) and 36(d), with a smooth exit
diffeomorphism F fixing the axes. The inverse image of S is open and connected; its projection to launch labels is an
open interval. Its image J under F is therefore an open interval. The exact launch formulas in Theorem 36(d) give H=c
and G=0 there. If phi is in I, the orbit with launch label F^(-1)(phi) has hitting angle tending to phi as the radius
tends to infinity. Eventually that angle lies in I and the point lies in E. Thus the orbit belongs to S and phi belongs
to J. This proves I contained in J.

Finally prove (h). At an interior zero of G, the inequality sigma G>=0 from (a) and smoothness imply G'=0. Theorem 45(f)
gives the full first correction, uniformly in angle,

  Omega=r^(-1/2)G+r^(-1)G1+O_infty(r^(-3/2)),
  G1=(1/2)P'G+(3/2)PG'+sin(phi)H'.                    (64.26)

At the fixed angle where G=G'=0 this yields lim_(r->infinity) r Omega(r,phi)=sin(phi)H'(phi). Exterior weak sign and
sin(phi)>0 prove the second implication of (64.14). The third follows by contraposition and sigma G>=0.

Let H'(phi_c)=0 and take alpha_c=F^(-1)(phi_c). The launch identity theta_0=H o F of Theorem 36(d), together with W_r>0
and temperature transport, makes the launch point critical, as in the proof of Theorem 47(a). Its whole orbit lies in
Crit and has Omega=0 by Theorem 44(d).

Choose the launch radius R0 larger than R_B and large enough for W_r>0 throughout the exterior. With X(t,alpha)=Phi_t(R0
e(alpha)), the nearby interior labels stay outside the disc containing B for every t>=0. Thus
g(t,alpha)=Omega(X(t,alpha)) has sigma g>=0 near alpha_c and g(t,alpha_c)=0. For every t>=0, g_alpha(t,alpha_c)=0.
Differentiating the identity g_t+g=Theta_x(X(t,alpha)) in alpha and differentiating this zero function in t gives
d_alpha[Theta_x(X(t,alpha_c))]=0 for t>0.

Put lambda(alpha)=grad Theta(X(0,alpha)).(W_2,-W_1)/|W|^2 at launch. Theorem 33(c), with its clockwise rotation
(v1,v2)->(v2,-v1), gives

  Theta_x(X(t,alpha))
    =lambda(alpha)exp(-4t)W_2(X(t,alpha)),
  theta_0'(alpha)=-R0 W_r(X(0,alpha))lambda(alpha).      (64.27)

Here lambda(alpha_c)=0. The critical orbit escapes with interior angle phi_c, so W_2/|X|->2sin(phi_c)>0. Differentiating
the first identity in alpha at any sufficiently large t therefore gives lambda'(alpha_c)=0. Differentiating the second
gives theta_0''(alpha_c)=0. Since F is smooth and F'>0, differentiation of theta_0=H o F now gives
0=H''(phi_c)F'(alpha_c)^2. Hence H''(phi_c)=0. For an A2-broad profile these arguments use the vorticity sign only
outside a disc, together with the global critical-orbit conclusion of Theorems 44(d) and 47(a); a constant interval of H
satisfies the resulting angular conditions. QED.

### Theorem 65 (nonnegative vorticity for beta > 2: zeros, orbit moments and source constraints)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2, with beta > 2 and Omega >= 0 on Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}.
The fields are smooth, U is the canonical uniformly sublinear velocity, Theta and Omega have at most polynomial growth,
Theta is even in x and odd in y, and Omega is odd in both variables. The velocity component U_1 is odd in x and even in
y, while U_2 is even in x and odd in y. The temperature vanishes on both axes and has the nonzero jet Theta = a0 x^2
y + O(|X|^5) at the origin. Write X = (x,y) = r(cos(phi),sin(phi)), e_r = (cos(phi),sin(phi)) and
e_phi = (-sin(phi),cos(phi)). Put

  W = beta X + U,  U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x),  -Lap Psi = Omega,
  div W = 2 beta,  d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = Omega,
  W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x,
  W.grad Theta = kappa Theta,
  kappa = beta - 2,  lambda = beta + 2,  h = 1/beta,
  q = 1 - 2h,  a = 2 - h,  d = 2 beta - 1.                 (65.1)

Let Phi_t be the complete flow of W, P_ax = (L,0) the first positive x-axis zero of W, A = Theta_y(P_ax), and
alpha = pi/2. Theorem 57(a) gives a0 > 0, A > 0, (H1), Theta > 0 on Q1, and all conclusions of Theorem 50. Here (H1)
means that the zeros of W in the closed first quadrant are exactly (0,0) and P_ax. Write f, G and P for the smooth
angular temperature, vorticity and stream-function coefficients of Theorems 41 and 42, normalized by r^(-q)Theta -> f,
r^h Omega -> G and r^(h-2)Psi -> P, with Psi(0) = 0. The far-field angular expansions used below have uniform remainder
estimates on the closed quadrant. Define

  B(phi) = q cos(phi) f(phi) - sin(phi) f'(phi),
  C(phi) = (a-1)[a P(phi) cos(2phi) - P'(phi) sin(2phi)]
             - G(phi) sin(phi)^2.                         (65.2)

(a) At any X in Q1 with Omega(X) = 0, put tau = Theta_y(X), b = d_x W_2(X), and H = D^2 Omega(X). Then

  grad Omega = 0,  Theta_x = 0,  H >= 0,
  W_2 tau = kappa Theta > 0,
  H W = grad Theta_x,
  W.H W = -tau b >= 0,  W_2 b <= 0.                       (65.3)

Here H >= 0 means positive semidefinite, and all quantities in this display are evaluated at X. If W_2 b = 0, then H
W = 0 and grad Theta_x = 0.

(b) Suppose an open interval of a nonstationary orbit lies in {Omega = 0} cap Q1. On that interval D^2 W = 0 and DW is
one constant diagonal matrix. More precisely, for constants a1, a2, e1, e2 depending on the interval,

  a1 + a2 = 2 beta,
  DW = diag(a1,a2),
  W(X(t)) = (a1 x(t) + e1, a2 y(t) + e2).                (65.4)

At a spatially flat zero of Omega in Q1, meaning that every Cartesian derivative of Omega vanishes there, D^j W = 0 for
every j >= 2.

There exist R > 0 and c_* > 0, depending on the profile, such that

  |D^2 W(X)[e_r,e_r]| >= c_* |X|^(-1-h)
       for X in Q1, |X| >= R, e_r = X/|X|.              (65.5)

Every zero orbit segment and every point of Q1 where Omega is flat lies in {|X| < R}. If X(t0) is outside this disc and
Omega(X(t0)) = 0, then, with omega(t) = Omega(X(t)),

  either omega''(t0) > 0,
  or omega''(t0) = 0 and omega''''(t0) > 0.              (65.6)

In particular the zero is isolated in flow time. Every Q1 orbit has strictly positive vorticity at arbitrarily large
positive times. The interior of {Omega = 0} cap Q1 is contained in {|X| < R}.

(c) The angular functions satisfy

  G >= 0,  G not identically zero,
  P > 0,  P'' < 0 on (0,alpha),
  P'(0) > 0,  P'(alpha) < 0,
  G(phi) = 0 implies B(phi) <= 0
       for 0 < phi < alpha.                             (65.7)

There are epsilon > 0 and R1 > 0 such that Omega(r,phi) > 0 for r >= R1 and

  0 < phi < epsilon
       or alpha-epsilon < phi < alpha.                 (65.8)

If Omega(X_n) = 0, X_n in Q1, and |X_n| tends to infinity, then every limit angle phi_* is interior and satisfies

  G(phi_*) = B(phi_*) = 0,  C(phi_*) <= 0.               (65.9)

If the second flow derivative of Omega vanishes at every X_n, then C(phi_*) = 0 as well.

Consequently, if no interior angle satisfies (65.9), Omega is strictly positive outside a disc in Q1. This is a
conditional conclusion; absence of such an angle is not asserted.

(d) Use any unit-Jacobian chart Hc = (xi,eta) of Theorem 50, with eta = Theta/A. This chart is C^1 across the x-axis and
smooth in Q1. Set

  p = lambda/kappa,  n = (beta+1)/kappa,
  c = xi/eta^p,  Z(c,s) = Hc^(-1)(c s^p,s),
  Y(c,s) = [Z(c,s)]_2,  s > 0.                          (65.10)

Write phi(c) = lim_(s -> infinity) arg Z(c,s) for the limiting angle of this orbit, given by Theorem 50(b). For every c
in R and s > 0,

  Omega(Z(c,s))
    = -(A/kappa) s^(-1/kappa)
          integral_0^s v^(-n-1) Y_c(c,v) dv.             (65.11)

The integral is absolutely convergent. Thus nonnegative vorticity is equivalent to the nonpositivity of every cumulative
integral on the right before its negative prefactor. For a fixed c0, define

  M(c) = integral_0^infinity
             v^(-n-1)[Y(c,v)-Y(c0,v)] dv.
  Then
  M'(c) = -(kappa/A)
             [f(phi(c))/A]^(1/kappa) G(phi(c)) <= 0.     (65.12)

The defining integral is absolutely convergent, M is C^1, and differentiation under the integral is valid. The function
M is not constant on all of R. In particular, for c1 < c2,

  integral_0^infinity
       v^(-n-1)[Y(c2,v)-Y(c1,v)] dv <= 0.               (65.13)

For every C^1 compactly supported function chi on R there is also the absolutely convergent balance

  integral_R integral_0^infinity
      chi(c) exp(-s)(kappa s-d) Omega(Z(c,s)) s^p ds dc
    = A integral_R integral_0^infinity
      chi'(c) exp(-s) Y(c,s) ds dc.                     (65.14)

(e) Write w(x) = W_1(x,0), T(x) = Theta_y(x,0), and g(x) = Omega_y(x,0). Then g >= 0, T > 0, and

  T'(L) = A w''(L)/lambda,
  g(L) = A w''(L)/[lambda(beta-1)],
  w''(L) >= 0.                                         (65.15)

On x > L use the increasing coordinate xi = A w/(lambda T). Let x(xi) denote its inverse and put

  H0(xi) = A/T(x(xi)),  mu = (beta-1)/lambda,
  t0 = f'(0) > 0,
  c0_axis = A beta/(lambda t0).
  Then
  integral_0^infinity xi^(mu-2)[H0(xi)-1] dxi
    = -(lambda^2/3) c0_axis^mu G'(0)/t0 <= 0.            (65.16)

This integral is absolutely convergent. There is some x > L with T(x) > A. Moreover g(x) > 0 for all sufficiently large
x.

(f) If g(L) = 0, then w''(L) = w'''(L) = 0. In coordinates u = x-L, v = y, there are numbers c2, c0 >= 0 such that

  Omega(L+u,v) = c2 u^2 v + c0 v^3 + O((|u|+|v|)^4),

  [A - 9(beta+2)(beta+1)] c2
       = 3(3beta-2)(3beta-5)c0.                         (65.17)

If A < 9(beta+2)(beta+1), every derivative of Omega at P_ax of total order at most four vanishes. If A equals this
threshold, c0 = 0. These are conditional source restrictions and do not assert g(L) = 0.

(g) The following exact local solutions specify limits of purely local exclusions.

For any l > 0 and b1 > 0, set u = x-l and

  v0(u) = (lambda/b1)[exp(b1 u)-1],
  W = (v0(u), [2 beta-v0'(u)]y),
  Psi = [beta x-v0(u)]y,
  Omega = lambda b1 exp(b1 u)y,
  Theta = lambda(beta-1) exp(b1 u)y.                    (65.18)

They satisfy all equations in (65.1), with a source at (l,0) of derivative diag(lambda,kappa), and Theta, Omega > 0 on
y > 0. They have the required y-reflection parities near that source.

For b2 > 0, in Cartesian coordinates (u,v), set

  tau0 = (3lambda-kappa)(2lambda+1),
  W = (lambda u, kappa v-b2 u^3/3),
  U = W-beta(u,v),  Psi = -2u v-b2 u^4/12,
  Omega = b2 u^2,
  Theta = tau0 v + b2(2lambda+1)u^3/3.                  (65.19)

These fields satisfy the two transport equations, div W = 2 beta and d_v W_1-d_u W_2 = Omega. They have nonnegative
vorticity, positive temperature near each (0,v0) with v0 > 0, and a zero orbit segment through that point.

Finally, choose D > 0, c1 > 0, 0 < m < M1 and B1 > c1 M1. For y > 0 define

  V0(y) = D y^(1-h)/(1-h) + c1 y^q/q,
  U = (V0(y),0),  W = (beta x+V0(y), beta y),
  Psi = -D y^(2-h)/[(1-h)(2-h)]
          -c1 y^(2-2h)/[q(2-2h)],
  Omega = D y^(-h) + c1 y^(-2h),
  Theta = B1 y^q - c1 x y^(-2h)
          -c1 D y^(1-3h)/(1-h)
          -c1^2 y^(1-4h)/(2q).                         (65.20)

All profile equations hold on y > 0. On the exterior sector m < x/y < M1, y sufficiently large, the velocity is
sublinear, Theta and Omega are strictly positive, and Theta_x < 0. None of (65.18)-(65.20) is an A2-broad profile.

(h) The following restricted exterior extension holds. Replace Omega >= 0 on Q1 by a0 > 0 and boundedness of {Omega < 0}
cap Q1; retain all other A2-broad hypotheses and beta > 2. The angular inequalities in (65.7), including G = 0 implies
B <= 0, and the radial lower bound (65.5) still hold.

There is a common exterior radius beyond which W_2 > 0. At every vorticity zero there with Theta != 0, the identities of
(a) hold with the sign assertions replaced by

  W_2 tau = kappa Theta != 0,
  W.H W = -tau b >= 0,  Theta b <= 0.                  (65.21)

The equality conclusion of (a), the alternatives (65.6), and isolation in flow time hold at these zeros. No exterior
zero orbit segment with nonzero temperature and no exterior spatially flat vorticity zero with nonzero temperature
exists. Every Q1 orbit with nonzero temperature has positive vorticity at arbitrarily large positive times. Outside this
radius, every interior point of {Omega = 0} cap Q1 has Theta = 0.

For an unbounded sequence of such zeros and any limit angle phi_* in [0,alpha], G(phi_*) = B(phi_*) = 0. If the
temperature has the fixed sign eps in {-1,1} on a convergent subsequence, then eps C(phi_*) <= 0. If its second flow
derivative of Omega vanishes on that subsequence, then C(phi_*) = 0. This extension does not assert the positive axis
sectors in (65.8), exclusion of endpoint limit angles, or a globally positive temperature.

Scope. These are necessary conditions and exact local compatibility statements. Neither existence nor nonexistence of
the nonnegative class is established. Strict positivity throughout Q1, exclusion of bounded open zero regions, and
exclusion of isolated vorticity zeros remain open. Isolation in flow time does not mean isolation in the plane. The
orbit comparisons are convergent signed comparisons. The local solutions are not A2-broad profiles and provide no global
extension with the required parities, origin jet and canonical velocity. Part (h) is only the explicitly stated exterior
extension.

Proof.

Theorem 57(a) supplies the reduction stated after (65.1). In particular every point of Q1 has backward limit P_ax and
every Q1 orbit escapes with an interior exit angle, by Theorems 8 and 50. These facts will be used only with those
hypotheses already satisfied.

First establish the angular positivity needed below. The uniform vorticity limit in Theorem 41 gives G >= 0, and the
same theorem gives its nonvanishing. Theorem 42 gives

  -P''-a^2 P = G,  P(0) = P(alpha) = 0.

  K_a(phi,t)
    = sin(a min(phi,t)) sin(a(alpha-max(phi,t)))
         /[a sin(a alpha)],
  P(phi) = integral_0^alpha K_a(phi,t) G(t) dt.           (65.22)

The kernel is zero at the endpoints, solves the homogeneous equation away from phi = t, and its first phi derivative has
jump -1 there. Thus the operator in (65.22) applied to it is a unit point mass. The homogeneous Dirichlet problem has
only the zero solution because 0 < a alpha < pi. This verifies the inverse formula. Every interior sine factor is
positive; a nonzero continuous nonnegative G is positive on an interval. Therefore P > 0 inside. Its differential
equation gives P'' < 0. Differentiating the kernel at either endpoint gives

  P'(0) = integral_0^alpha
                sin(a(alpha-t)) G(t)/sin(a alpha) dt > 0,
  P'(alpha) = -integral_0^alpha
                sin(at) G(t)/sin(a alpha) dt < 0.        (65.23)

This argument proves the stream-function assertions directly from Theorems 41 and 42. Theorem 59(b) gives the
corresponding statement at beta = 2, with a = 3/2. For comparison, Theorem 64(a) includes the present angular
inequalities; none of its assertions is used here.

For (a), a zero of the nonnegative smooth function Omega at an interior point is a local minimum. Hence grad Omega = 0
and H >= 0. The vorticity equation gives Theta_x = 0, and the temperature equation gives W_2 tau = kappa Theta > 0. In
particular both W_2 and tau are nonzero. Differentiating the vorticity equation gives grad Theta_x = D^2 Omega
W + (DW^T+I)grad Omega, hence H W = grad Theta_x at this point. The x derivative of temperature transport is W.grad
Theta_x + (d_x W_1-kappa)Theta_x + b tau = 0. Taking the scalar product of H W = grad Theta_x with W therefore gives W.H
W = -b tau >= 0. Since W_2 tau > 0, the signs of tau and W_2 agree, proving W_2 b <= 0. If equality holds, W.H W = 0;
diagonalizing the real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix H shows H W = 0, and therefore grad Theta_x = 0.

We give a useful finite-order version of the zero-segment argument for (b). Along any orbit write F(t) = grad
Omega(X(t)) and J(t) = DW(X(t)). Differentiated vorticity transport reads

  grad Theta_x(X(t)) = F'(t) + [J(t)^T+I]F(t).           (65.24)

Suppose at a zero time t0 that omega''(t0) = omega''''(t0) = 0. Since omega is nonnegative, its first derivative
vanishes there. Taylor's theorem and nonnegativity successively force its third and fifth derivatives to vanish as well.
Therefore omega(t) = O(|t-t0|^6).

For completeness, local nonnegativity also gives |grad Omega|^2 <= C Omega near X(t0). Choose a ball compactly contained
in Q1 and a positive upper bound K for the norm of D^2 Omega on that ball. On a smaller ball, continuity of grad Omega
and grad Omega(X(t0)) = 0 ensure that the displacement -grad Omega/K remains in the larger ball. Taylor's upper bound
along that displacement and nonnegativity give 0 <= Omega-|grad Omega|^2/(2K). This proves the stated inequality, after
increasing K if necessary.

Here and in (65.24), gradients are column vectors and J_ij = d_j W_i. In components, d_i(W_j d_j Omega) = (d_i W_j)d_j
Omega + W_j d_j d_i Omega; differentiation of the term Omega contributes F itself. This verifies both the transpose and
the identity matrix in (65.24).

It follows that F(t) = O(|t-t0|^3). Thus F, F' and F'' vanish at t0. If Q(t) = grad Theta_x(X(t)), then (65.24) gives
Q' = F'' + (J^T)'F + (J^T+I)F'. Hence Q and Q' vanish there. Also Theta_x = 0. Differentiated temperature transport is
the identity

  W.grad Theta_x + (d_x W_1-kappa)Theta_x
       + (d_x W_2)Theta_y = 0.                          (65.25)

As tau != 0 by (a), it first gives b = d_x W_2 = 0. For a constant Cartesian vector e, the spatial derivative of (65.25)
has exactly the following six terms:

  (d_e W).grad Theta_x + W.grad(d_e Theta_x)
    + (d_e d_x W_1)Theta_x
    + (d_x W_1-kappa)d_e Theta_x
    + (d_e b)Theta_y + b d_e Theta_y = 0.              (65.26)

The first and fourth terms vanish because Q = 0, the third because Theta_x = 0, and the sixth because b = 0. Since e is
constant and the scalar Hessian is symmetric, the second term is e.D^2 Theta_x W = e.Q' = 0. Thus tau d_e b = 0 for both
Cartesian directions, proving grad b = 0.

In particular W_2,xx = W_2,xy = 0. The two derivatives of curl give W_1,xy = Omega_x + W_2,xx = 0 and
W_1,yy = Omega_y + W_2,xy = 0. The two derivatives of divergence give W_1,xx = -W_2,yx = 0 and W_2,yy = -W_1,xy = 0. We
have proved

  omega(t0) = omega''(t0) = omega''''(t0) = 0
       implies D^2 W(X(t0)) = 0.                        (65.27)

On a zero orbit segment these hypotheses hold at every time. At such times (65.24) gives grad Theta_x = 0, and (65.25)
gives b = 0. Zero curl makes DW diagonal. Its derivative along the orbit is D^2 W applied to W, so it is constant. The
derivative of W(X(t))-diag(a1,a2)X(t) is zero. This proves (65.4).

At a spatially flat zero, every derivative of W.grad Omega + Omega vanishes by the product rule, so Theta_x is flat too.
In a neighbourhood of that point Theta_y != 0 by (a), and temperature transport gives

  W_2 = kappa Theta/Theta_y - W_1 Theta_x/Theta_y,
  d_x W_2 = kappa Theta_x/Theta_y
    - kappa Theta Theta_xy/Theta_y^2
    - (d_x W_1)Theta_x/Theta_y
    - W_1 Theta_xx/Theta_y
    + W_1 Theta_x Theta_xy/Theta_y^2.                  (65.28)

Each of the five terms in d_x W_2 contains Theta_x or a derivative of it. The other factors are smooth, including the
reciprocals of Theta_y. Every further derivative is therefore zero at the point. Curl gives d_y W_1 = Omega + d_x W_2,
which is flat. These facts already make W_2,xx, W_2,xy, W_1,xy and W_1,yy flat. Divergence gives W_1,xx = -W_2,yx and
W_2,yy = -W_1,xy, so these last two entries are flat as well. All second derivatives of W are flat, which proves D^j
W = 0 for every j >= 2.

To prove (65.5), put

  U0(r,phi) = r^(1-h) V(phi),
  V(phi) = -P'(phi)e_r + a P(phi)e_phi.
  V_1 = -P' cos(phi)-a P sin(phi),
  V_2 = -P' sin(phi)+a P cos(phi).

  D^2 U0[e_r,e_r]
       = -h(1-h) r^(-1-h) V(phi).                      (65.29)

The leading velocity is exactly that of Theorem 42, from psi_0 = r^a P and U0 = (-d_y psi_0,d_x psi_0). Its second
radial derivative is taken along a straight ray with phi fixed, so the displayed Cartesian components of V are fixed
during differentiation. This proves the last line of (65.29). In the interior, P > 0; at either endpoint P = 0 but
P' != 0 by (65.23). Consequently P and P' have no common zero, and |V|^2 = (P')^2 + a^2 P^2 has a positive minimum m_*^2
on [0,alpha]. Theorem 42(b) states U-U0 = O_infty(r^(1-2h)); its definition in Theorem 36, at Cartesian derivative order
two, gives |D^2(U-U0)| <= C r^(-1-2h) uniformly in angle. Choose R with C R^(-h) <= h(1-h)m_*/2. Since D^2 W = D^2 U,
(65.5) follows with c_* = h(1-h)m_*/2.

Equation (65.27) now proves (65.6): if the second derivative of a nonnegative function vanishes at a zero, its third
derivative is zero and its fourth derivative is nonnegative; it cannot also be zero here. Taylor's theorem gives a
positive quadratic or quartic leading term and makes the zero isolated in flow time. It also excludes every point of a
zero segment and every spatially flat zero outside the disc. An interior point of an open zero region lies on a short
zero orbit segment, since W has no zero in Q1 by Theorem 57(a). Finally, by Theorems 8 and 50 every Q1 orbit has
positive temperature and escapes. If it had no positive vorticity after some time, nonnegativity would make its
remaining tail a zero segment, contradicting the exterior bound.

We complete (c). By Theorem 42(c), the first vorticity correction is

  Omega(r,phi)
    = r^(-h)G(phi) + r^(-2h)G1(phi) + O(r^(-3h)),
  G1 = h P'G + a P G' - B.                             (65.30)

An interior zero of G is a minimum, so G' = 0 there. Multiplying (65.30) at that angle by r^(2h) and taking the limit
proves -B >= 0. This gives the last implication in (65.7).

Here the coefficient is precisely G1 = h P'G + (2-h)PG' - q cos(phi)f + sin(phi)f' in Theorem 42(c), and the remainder
is O_infty(r^(-3h)). The temperature coefficient has the normalization f = lim r^(-q)Theta, without a change of sign.

At the x-axis, parity gives f(0) = G(0) = P(0) = 0. Theorem 50(c), with sgn(a0) = 1, gives t0 = f'(0) > 0, and G >= 0
gives G'(0) >= 0. Since B'(0) = (q-1)f'(0) = -2h f'(0) and h+a = 2, differentiating (65.30) at zero gives

  G1'(0) = 2 P'(0)G'(0) + 2h f'(0) > 0.               (65.31)

Choose epsilon so that G1(phi) >= c phi on [0,epsilon], for some c > 0. Let E3 be the remainder in (65.30). Oddness
gives E3(r,0) = 0. Since partial_phi = r e_phi.grad, the first Cartesian derivative bound from Theorem 42(c) gives
|partial_phi E3| <= C r^(-3h). Hence |E3(r,phi)| <= C r^(-3h)phi. Thus Omega >= r^(-2h)phi(c-C r^(-h)) > 0 near the
x-axis for large r. At the y-axis, Theorem 50(c) gives G'(alpha) < 0, so G(phi) >= c(alpha-phi) near alpha. For
E2 = Omega-r^(-h)G, parity gives E2(r,alpha) = 0 and Theorem 42(b) gives |partial_phi E2| <= C r^(-2h). Hence |E2| <= C
r^(-2h)(alpha-phi), proving positivity in the other sector of (65.8).

Consider now an unbounded sequence of zeros. The two sectors just proved keep its angles in a compact interior interval.
Uniform limits give G(phi_*) = 0 along any convergent angular subsequence. At every actual zero Theta_x = 0 by (a),
while Theorem 42 gives r^(2h)Theta_x = B(phi)+O(r^(-h)). Consequently B(phi_*) = 0. Direct Cartesian differentiation of
r^(2-h)P gives

  r^h d_x W_2(r,phi) = C(phi) + O(r^(-h)).              (65.32)

Indeed, in the orthonormal basis (e_r,e_phi), the Hessian of psi_0 = r^a P has entries r^(-h) times a(a-1)P, (a-1)P',
and aP+P'' = -a(a-1)P-G. Since e_x = cos(phi)e_r-sin(phi)e_phi, its xx entry is

  r^h (psi_0)_xx
    = a(a-1)P cos(phi)^2
      - 2(a-1)P' cos(phi)sin(phi)
      + (aP+P'')sin(phi)^2 = C(phi).                  (65.33)

There is no dilation contribution to d_x W_2: d_x(beta y) = 0. The first Cartesian derivative of U-U0 in Theorem 42(b)
is O(r^(-2h)), proving (65.32). On a compact interior angular interval, sin(phi) >= c > 0 and W_2 = beta r
sin(phi)+O(r^(1-h)) > 0 for large r. Part (a) then gives d_x W_2 <= 0 at the zeros. Passing to the limit proves
C(phi_*) <= 0. At an actual zero, omega'' = W.H W because grad Omega = 0. If omega'' = 0, then -tau b = 0 and tau != 0
gives b = 0, so C(phi_*) = 0 for a sequence of such points. If the indicated angular set were empty, an unbounded zero
sequence would contradict compactness. This proves only the conditional assertion.

For (d), Theorem 50(a),(b) gives det D Hc = 1, Phi_t Z(c,s) = Z(c,exp(kappa t)s), and dX = s^p dc ds. If
(x,y) = Hc^(-1)(xi,eta), the inverse of the matrix with rows (xi_x,xi_y) and (eta_x,eta_y) has lower left entry -eta_x.
Thus y_xi = -eta_x. At fixed s, d_c(c s^p,s) = (s^p,0), giving

  Y_c(c,s) = -s^p eta_x(Z(c,s)),
  Theta_x(Z(c,s)) = -A s^(-p)Y_c(c,s).

  kappa s partial_s Omega(Z(c,s)) + Omega(Z(c,s))
       = -A s^(-p)Y_c(c,s).                             (65.34)

For c in a compact interval and s decreasing to zero, (c s^p,s) tends to (0,0) uniformly. The C^1 inverse chart with
derivative I gives Z(c,s) -> P_ax and y = s+o(s), uniformly. Smooth oddness of Theta in y gives eta_x = O(y) near P_ax.
Therefore Y_c = O(s^(p+1)), uniformly on that interval. Also Omega(Z(c,s)) = O(s), by oddness of Omega in y. No higher
regularity of Hc at the axis is needed, including when p is an even integer. Multiply the last equation of (65.34) by
s^(1/kappa-1)/kappa and integrate from zero. Its left side is partial_s[s^(1/kappa)Omega]. The endpoint value vanishes.
Since 1/kappa-p = -n and p-n = 1/kappa, the right integrand is O(s^(1/kappa)) at zero. This proves the absolute
convergence and formula (65.11); its negative prefactor proves the equivalence of signs.

We record the estimates at infinity required for (65.12). Compact intervals of c on the section s = 1 have a common
finite escape time, by continuity, a finite subcover, and forward invariance of the exterior of a sufficiently large
circle. There r' >= beta r/2. Thus the error in d_t log r = beta+O(r^(-h)) is integrable, uniformly for this family of
orbits. Integrating proves that r exp(-beta t) stays between two positive constants. Since s grows as exp(kappa t), this
gives the first estimate below:

  |Z(c,s)| comparable to s^(beta/kappa),
  |partial_c Z(c,s)| <= C s^(beta/kappa)
       for s >= 1, c in a fixed compact interval.        (65.35)

For the derivative bound, the variational equation along an orbit is D Phi_t' = (beta I+DU)D Phi_t. After the common
escape time, the bound DU = O(r^(-h)) and the radial comparison make its normalized coefficient integrable in time,
bounded by C exp(-t). Gronwall bounds exp(-beta t)D Phi_t. Before that time smoothness on a compact set supplies the
bound. Apply it to the bounded derivative of Z(c,1) to obtain (65.35).

Integrate the bound for Y_c over the segment between c0 and c. The difference Y(c,s)-Y(c0,s), and its c derivative, are
O(s^(p+1)) at zero and O(s^(beta/kappa)) at infinity, uniformly when c ranges in a compact interval containing c0. After
multiplication by s^(-n-1) the exponents are p-n = 1/kappa and beta/kappa-n-1 = -1-1/kappa. Both are integrable at the
indicated endpoints. Dominated differentiation proves absolute convergence and the C^1 assertion in (65.12).

The temperature identity Theta(Z(c,s)) = As and the leading temperature expansion give, for each c,

  s^(1/kappa) Omega(Z(c,s))
       -> [f(phi(c))/A]^(1/kappa) G(phi(c)).             (65.36)

Indeed, for the actual angle phi_s of Z(c,s), Theorem 42(b) gives As/r^q = f(phi_s)+O(r^(-h)) -> f(phi(c)) > 0 by
Theorem 50(b). Thus s^(1/kappa)r^(-h) -> [f(phi(c))/A]^(1/kappa), since q/kappa = h. Multiply by r^h Omega -> G(phi(c))
to obtain (65.36), including its exponent and normalization. Taking s to infinity in (65.11) gives the derivative
formula (65.12). The continuous nonnegative G is positive on some interior interval, and the exit map in Theorem 50(b)
is onto (0,alpha). Hence M' is strictly negative on an interval and M is not constant. Integrating M' between c1 and c2
proves (65.13).

For (65.14), integrate div(Omega W) = d Omega+Theta_x against chi(c)exp(-s), first with s restricted to [epsilon,S]. In
these coordinates W = kappa s partial_s and the area element is s^p dc ds. The flux through an s boundary is kappa
chi(c)exp(-s)s^(p+1)Omega, which is O(s^(p+2)) at zero and tends to zero at infinity. For the latter limit, (65.35) and
Theorem 41 give polynomial bounds and exp(-s) dominates them. Since W.grad[chi(c)exp(-s)] = -kappa s chi(c)exp(-s),
integration by parts puts (kappa s-d) on the left side of (65.14). By (65.34), the remaining right side is -A integral
chi(c)exp(-s)Y_c dc ds. Integration by parts in c gives (65.14), with zero boundary term because chi has compact
support. At zero, Omega = O(s), Y = O(s) and Y_c = O(s^(p+1)); at infinity (65.35) bounds Y and Y_c polynomially. These
bounds prove absolute convergence separately before taking either limit or performing the integration by parts.

We next prove (e). Nonnegativity on the upper side of the axis gives g >= 0, and Theorem 57(a) gives T > 0. The trace
equations of Theorems 2 and 14 are

  w T' = (w'-lambda)T,
  w g' + (2 beta+1-w')g = T'.                            (65.37)

Although Theorem 14 states its bounded-solution assertion on (0,L), its trace equation comes from differentiating the
smooth profile equation in y and is valid on the entire positive axis. Differentiate the first equation in (65.37) to
obtain w T'' + lambda T' = w''T. Evaluation at L gives lambda T'(L) = A w''(L). The second equation at L gives
(beta-1)g(L) = T'(L). This proves (65.15), including w''(L) >= 0 since A > 0 and g(L) >= 0. For comparison,
Theorem 62(c) records these trace identities with A < 0; this derivation is independent of that theorem.

Theorem 50(a) identifies xi = A w/(lambda T) on the axis. Directly, (w/T)' = lambda/T by (65.37), so xi_x = A/T > 0 and
xi(L) = 0. The asymptotics below give xi -> infinity; hence the range on x > L is (0,infinity). The coordinate is smooth
along this axis because w,T are smooth and T > 0, regardless of the transverse regularity of Hc. Put
R0(xi) = g(x(xi))/T(x(xi)). The equation for the quotient is w d_x(g/T)+(beta-1)g/T = T'/T. Since w xi_x = lambda xi and
H0'(xi) = -T'/T, this becomes

  lambda xi R0'(xi) + (beta-1)R0(xi) = -H0'(xi),

  xi^mu R0(xi)
    = -(1/lambda) integral_0^xi t^(mu-1)H0'(t) dt.        (65.38)

Multiplication of the first equation by xi^(mu-1)/lambda gives the second after integration, because R0 is bounded at
zero and mu > 0. A prime on H0 or R0 here means a derivative in xi; a prime on w,T or g means a derivative in x.

By Theorem 42 and the endpoint temperature sign in Theorem 50,

  T(x) = t0 x^(-2h) + O(x^(-3h)),
  g(x) = G'(0)x^(-1-h) + O(x^(-1-2h)),
  xi(x) = c0_axis x^(1+2h)[1+O(x^(-h))].               (65.39)

For the first line, evaluate d_y of the temperature expansion of Theorem 42(b) on (x,0), using d_y = x^(-1)partial_phi
there. This gives T = t0 x^(-2h)+O(x^(-3h)), with t0 > 0 from Theorem 50(c). The same axis derivative of the vorticity
expansion gives the second line. Theorem 42(b) also gives w = beta x-P'(0)x^(1-h)+O(x^(1-2h)), and substitution into
xi = A w/(lambda T) gives the third line with the stated positive constant c0_axis.

All these remainders can be differentiated in x: after j derivatives, their orders are respectively x^(-3h-j),
x^(-1-2h-j), and x^(1+h-j), for every fixed j >= 0, where the third expression refers to xi-c0_axis x^(1+2h). In
particular T' = -2h t0 x^(-2h-1)+O(x^(-3h-1)), and xi' = (A/t0)x^(2h)[1+O(x^(-h))], consistently with xi_x = A/T. The
derivative of g has leading term -(1+h)G'(0)x^(-2-h) and remainder O(x^(-2-2h)).

Since 1+2h = lambda/beta, these formulas give H0(xi) comparable to xi^(2/lambda) and
H0'(xi) = -T'/T = O(xi^(2/lambda-1)) at infinity. At zero H0(0) = 1 and H0-1 = O(xi). The absolute integrability in
(65.16) follows: the exponent is mu-1 > -1 at zero and mu-2+2/lambda = -1-1/lambda at infinity. The integral of
t^(mu-1)H0' has the same bounds and also converges absolutely.

Integration by parts with H0-1 gives

  integral_0^infinity t^(mu-1)H0'(t) dt
    = (1-mu) integral_0^infinity
                    t^(mu-2)[H0(t)-1] dt.              (65.40)

The boundary product t^(mu-1)(H0-1) is O(t^mu) at zero and O(t^(-1/lambda)) at infinity, and so vanishes at both
endpoints. Moreover (1+2h)mu = 1-h, and (65.39) gives xi^mu R0 -> c0_axis^mu G'(0)/t0. Taking xi to infinity in (65.38),
then using (65.40) and 1-mu = 3/lambda, gives exactly the factor -lambda^2/3 on the right side of (65.16).

Since T(x) tends to zero, H0(xi) tends to infinity. If T never exceeded A on x > L, H0-1 would be nonnegative everywhere
and strictly positive eventually, contradicting (65.16). This proves the strict overshoot. If G'(0) > 0, (65.39) gives
eventual positivity of g. If G'(0) = 0, differentiate (65.30) at the x-axis and use (65.31) to obtain g(x) = 2h t0
x^(-1-2h)+O(x^(-1-3h)), again strictly positive for large x.

For (f), g(L) = 0 and g >= 0 imply g'(L) = 0. Equation (65.15) gives w''(L) = T'(L) = 0. The derivative of the second
equation of (65.37) is w g''+(2 beta+1)g'-w''g = T''. Hence T''(L) = 0. Differentiating w T''+lambda T' = w''T gives w
T'''+(w'+lambda)T'' = w'''T+w''T'; at L this is 2 lambda T''(L) = A w'''(L), so w'''(L) = 0.

At P_ax, the only possible linear and quadratic vorticity terms are g(L)v and g'(L)uv, by oddness in v. Both vanish.
Write the cubic homogeneous part as Omega_3 = c2 u^2 v+c0 v^3. For each fixed u and v > 0, division of Omega(L+epsilon
u,epsilon v) >= 0 by epsilon^3 v and passage to epsilon -> 0+ gives c2 u^2+c0 v^2 >= 0. Taking u = 0 and then letting
|u|/v grow proves c0,c2 >= 0.

Since W = (lambda u,kappa v)+O((|u|+|v|)^2) and Omega has order at least three, vorticity transport implies
Theta_u = O((|u|+|v|)^3). Oddness in v permits only uv at degree two and u^2v,v^3 at degree three in Theta. The u
derivatives exclude uv and u^2v, leaving a possible temperature term t3 v^3.

Write the degree-two velocity terms as W1,2 = a20 u^2+a02 v^2 and W2,2 = b11 uv. Since Theta_2 = 0, degree-two
temperature transport gives A b11 uv = 0, hence b11 = 0. Degree-one divergence and curl give 2a20+b11 = 0 and
2a02-b11 = 0, so a20 = a02 = 0.

Write the degree-three velocity terms as W1,3 = a30 u^3+a12 uv^2 and W2,3 = b21 u^2v+b03 v^3. Degree-three temperature
transport gives A b21 = 0 and A b03+2kappa t3 = 0. The sign convention for curl and constant divergence implies

  Lap W_2 = -d_x Omega.                              (65.41)

Indeed, d_x Omega = W_1,xy-W_2,xx and W_1,xy = -W_2,yy. Since d_x Omega starts at degree two, the degree-one part of
(65.41) gives 2b21+6b03 = 0. Thus b21 = b03 = t3 = 0. Degree-two divergence now gives 3a30+b21 = 0 and a12+3b03 = 0, so
a30 = a12 = 0. The remaining degree-two curl coefficient 2a12-2b21 is zero as required. We have proved W = (lambda
u,kappa v)+O((|u|+|v|)^4) and Theta = A v+O((|u|+|v|)^4).

Let Theta4 and W2,4 denote their degree-four homogeneous terms. Degree-three vorticity transport gives partial_u
Theta4 = (2lambda+kappa+1)c2 u^2v+(3kappa+1)c0 v^3. Integrating in u gives the first line below. Degree-four temperature
transport is (lambda u partial_u+kappa v partial_v-kappa)Theta4+A W2,4 = 0, giving the second line:

  Theta4 = (3kappa+1)c0 u v^3
              + (2lambda+kappa+1)c2 u^3 v/3,

  W2,4 = -[(lambda+2kappa)(3kappa+1)c0 u v^3
              + lambda(2lambda+kappa+1)c2 u^3 v]/A.     (65.42)

There is no integration term depending only on v in Theta4, because v^4 has the wrong parity. Apply (65.41) at degree
two. The Laplacians of uv^3 and u^3v both equal 6uv, whereas -partial_u Omega_3 = -2c2 uv. Equating the uv coefficients
and multiplying by -A/2 gives

  A c2 = 3(lambda+2kappa)(3kappa+1)c0
               + 3lambda(2lambda+kappa+1)c2.            (65.43)

Since lambda+2kappa = 3beta-2, 3kappa+1 = 3beta-5 and 2lambda+kappa+1 = 3beta+3, this is (65.17). All its factors on the
right are positive for beta > 2. Below the stated threshold it forces c2 = c0 = 0. A possible next, degree-four
homogeneous vorticity term is odd in v and hence odd in u, because its total degree is even. Nonnegativity on v > 0
forces that term to be zero. This proves vanishing through degree four. At equality the same coefficient identity gives
c0 = 0.

It remains to verify (g). For (65.18), v0' = lambda exp(b1 u), v0'' = lambda b1 exp(b1 u), and b1 v0 = v0'-lambda.
Divergence is 2 beta, and -Lap Psi = v0'' y = Omega. Temperature transport reduces to

  b1 v0 + 2 beta-v0' = kappa.

Vorticity transport reduces to the same expression plus one, namely kappa+1 = beta-1. Thus W.grad
Omega+Omega = (beta-1)Omega = Theta_x. The source derivative and positivity follow directly from the displayed formulas.

For (65.19), divergence is lambda+kappa = 2 beta and the stated curl is b2 u^2. Vorticity transport gives W.grad
Omega+Omega = b2(2lambda+1)u^2 = Theta_u. In temperature transport the coefficient of v is kappa tau0, and the
coefficient of u^3 agrees precisely because tau0 = (3lambda-kappa)(2lambda+1). On u = 0 the field is (0,kappa v), so a
small orbit segment through (0,v0), v0 > 0, is a zero segment with positive temperature. A stream function for
U = W-beta(u,v) is Psi = -2u v-b2 u^4/12; thus this example also has -Lap Psi = Omega.

For (65.20), -Psi_y = V0 and -Lap Psi = V0' = Omega, so divergence and curl hold. Since Omega depends only on y,

  W.grad Omega+Omega = -c1 y^(-2h) = Theta_x.            (65.44)

The dilation operator beta(x partial_x+y partial_y)-kappa annihilates B1 y^q-c1 x y^(-2h), multiplies y^(1-3h) by -1,
and multiplies y^(1-4h) by -2. Its action on the two remaining temperature terms therefore cancels V0 Theta_x exactly.
This proves temperature transport. On the sector, the leading temperature is at least (B1-c1 M1)y^q > 0. The two
corrections are smaller by respectively y^(-h) and y^(-2h), uniformly there, so temperature is positive sufficiently far
out. The other signs are immediate, and U = O(|X|^(1-h)) on that sector.

The first example has exponential growth and lacks the required x parity and origin jet. The second has a cubic velocity
which is not uniformly sublinear and lacks the A2 vorticity parity in v. The third is defined only on y > 0 and has no
smooth A2 extension across the axes with its stated formulas. In particular its vorticity is positive and unbounded as y
decreases to zero. These failures verify the qualification in (g).

For (h), choose R_B with {Omega < 0} cap Q1 contained in {r < R_B}. Theorem 41 gives G >= 0 by taking the limit on each
ray outside this disc, and also gives G not identically zero without any sign hypothesis. Thus the Green formula
(65.22), its endpoint derivatives, and the proof of (65.5) apply unchanged. At an interior zero of G, G' = 0, and the
first correction in Theorem 42(c), evaluated on that fixed ray for r > R_B, gives -B = G1 >= 0. This proves all the
stated angular inequalities without Theorem 57 or Theorem 64.

Theorem 42(a) also gives W_2 > 0 throughout the exterior of Q1. To check uniformity near the x-axis, split into two
regions. If y >= r/2, then W_2 = beta y+O(r^(1-h)) > 0 for large r. If y < r/2, then x > sqrt(3)r/2, and oddness of U_2
in y gives

  W_2(x,y)
    = y[beta+integral_0^1 d_y U_2(x,t y) dt]
    = y[beta+O(x^(-h))] > 0.                          (65.45)

The derivative estimate is uniform along this vertical segment because |(x,t y)| >= x. Increase a single radius R beyond
R_B and the radii for (65.5) and (65.45).

At a vorticity zero with r >= R and Theta != 0, there is a neighbourhood where Omega >= 0. The proof of (a) uses that
local nonnegativity and gives grad Omega = 0, H >= 0, Theta_x = 0, H W = grad Theta_x, W_2 tau = kappa Theta != 0 and
W.H W = -tau b >= 0. Since W_2 > 0, tau has the sign of Theta, proving (65.21). Equality again implies H W = 0. The
proof of (65.27) needs only local nonnegativity and tau != 0, so (65.5) gives the quadratic or quartic alternative and
isolation in flow time. The zero-segment and spatial-flatness arguments also need only these two local facts and are
therefore excluded at such exterior points. In particular an exterior interior point of the zero set cannot have nonzero
temperature.

If a Q1 orbit has nonzero temperature, its temperature is nonzero for every time and grows in magnitude as exp(kappa t).
Theorem 7 therefore makes the forward orbit unbounded, and uniform sublinearity makes it escape once it crosses a
sufficiently large circle. Eventually Omega >= 0 on it. If Omega had no positive value after some time, its tail would
be an exterior zero segment with nonzero temperature, just excluded.

For an unbounded sequence of the indicated zeros, pass to any convergent angular subsequence in [0,alpha]. The uniform
vorticity limit gives G(phi_*) = 0. At every such zero Theta_x = 0, and the differentiated temperature expansion of
Theorem 42(b) gives r^(2h)Theta_x = B(phi)+O(r^(-h)), so B(phi_*) = 0. If eps Theta > 0 on the subsequence, (65.21)
gives eps b <= 0, and (65.32) gives eps C(phi_*) <= 0. If omega'' = 0 there, then tau != 0 gives b = 0 and the same
limit gives C(phi_*) = 0. None of this supplies the endpoint temperature derivatives of Theorem 50(c) without its
hypotheses, which is why the extension has the stated scope. QED.

### Theorem 66 (bounded opposite-sign vorticity for beta > 2: transport balances, crossings and angular contact)

Let (beta,Theta,Omega,U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2. Assume beta>2, {Theta=0} has empty interior in Q1, and B
is bounded and nonempty, where

  Q1={x>0,y>0}, alpha=pi/2, e(phi)=(cos(phi),sin(phi)),
  sigma=sgn(a0), kappa=beta-2,
  h=1/beta, q=1-2h, a=2-h, d=2 beta-1,
  theta=sigma Theta, z=sigma Omega, B={X in Q1:z(X)<0},
  W=beta X+U, div W=2 beta,
  W.grad theta=kappa theta, W.grad z+z=theta_x.             (66.1)

Thus the fields are smooth on the plane, U is canonical and uniformly sublinear, and Theta and Omega have at most
polynomial growth. The temperature is even in x and odd in y, Theta(0,y)=0, and Theta=a0 x^2 y+O(|X|^5) with a0!=0.
Vorticity is odd in each coordinate. The velocity U_1 is odd in x and even in y, and U_2 is even in x and odd in y. The
coupling is U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x) and -Lap Psi=Omega. In particular d_y W_1-d_x W_2=Omega. The unsigned equations W.grad
Theta=kappa Theta and W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x are denoted by (T) and (V), respectively.

Write Phi_t for the complete flow. Use f,G,P from Theorems 41 and 42 with the normalization of Theorem 64:

  r^(-q)Theta->f, r^h Omega->G,
  r^(h-1)(U_r,U_phi)->(-P',aP),
  -P''-a^2 P=G, P(0)=P(alpha)=0.                             (66.2)

The limits are uniform in angle as r tends to infinity. Let O=(0,0) and P_ax=(L,0) be the first positive x-axis zero of
W from Theorem 2. Put F=sigma f and g=sigma G. A prime on an angular function denotes an angular derivative, and a prime
on an axis trace denotes an x derivative. Hypothesis (H1) means {W=0} cap closure(Q1)={O,P_ax}. A component means a
connected component. Integrals over planar sets use area measure unless another measure is displayed.

(a) Let D be any component of B and put b=-z on D. For every real r>=1 and every C^1 function A on a neighbourhood of
the compact range of theta on closure(D),

  r int_D A(theta)b^(r-1)theta_x
    =int_D [(2 beta-r)A(theta)+kappa theta A'(theta)]b^r.
                                                               (66.3)

All these integrals converge absolutely. No regularity of boundary(D) is required. In particular,

  int_D theta_x=d int_D b>0,
  r int_D b^(r-1)theta_x=(2 beta-r)int_D b^r.              (66.4)

The function theta_x takes both strict signs in D. If M_D=max_D b, this maximum is positive and attained in D, and
theta_x=-M_D at every point attaining it. The weighted source integral int_D b^(r-1)theta_x is positive for 1<=r<2 beta,
zero for r=2 beta and negative for r>2 beta.

(b) Assume in addition (H1), and put s=d/kappa=2+3/kappa. Then theta>0 on Q1. For every component D of B and every
epsilon>0,

  int_D (theta+epsilon)^(-s)theta_x
    =d epsilon int_D (theta+epsilon)^(-s-1)b>0.           (66.5)

Both integrals converge absolutely. If closure(D) is contained in Q1, then the left side tends to int_D
theta^(-s)theta_x=0 as epsilon decreases to zero, with absolute convergence. Formula (66.5) makes no assertion that this
last integral exists when closure(D) meets an axis.

(c) Suppose D is a component of B, closure(D) is contained in Q1, and grad z is nowhere zero on boundary(D). Let n be
its outward unit normal. Then

  W.n=theta_x/|grad z| on boundary(D),
  int_boundary(D) theta_x/|grad z| dl=2 beta |D|>0.       (66.6)

If theta is positive on closure(D), in particular under (H1), W crosses this boundary in both directions. At every
boundary point minimizing theta on closure(D), W.n<0 and theta_x<0. At every boundary point maximizing theta, W.n>0 and
theta_x>0. Under (H1), both directions occur on each connected component of boundary(D), including every inner boundary
curve.

(d) Every backward orbit from Q1 converges to a single point of {W=0} cap closure(Q1). Under (H1) this point is P_ax for
every X in Q1. Let X in B have an escaping forward orbit. The limit J(X) below exists, is nonnegative, and the two
integrals converge absolutely:

  z(X)=int_(-infinity)^0 e^t theta_x(Phi_t X) dt,
  J(X)=lim_(t->infinity)e^t z(Phi_t X)
      =z(X)+int_0^infinity e^t theta_x(Phi_t X) dt>=0.
                                                               (66.7)

More precisely, e^t z(Phi_t X)=J(X)+O_X(e^(-t)) as t tends to infinity. There is rho(X)>0 such that |Phi_t
X|=rho(X)e^(beta t)[1+O_X(e^(-t))], and J(X)=rho(X)^(-h)g(phi_*), where phi_* is the limiting angle.

Let (u,v) be the component of {t:z(Phi_t X)<0} containing zero. Then v is finite, u is finite or -infinity, and, for
every u<t<v,

  int_u^t e^s theta_x(Phi_s X) ds=e^t z(Phi_t X)<0,
  int_t^v e^s theta_x(Phi_s X) ds=-e^t z(Phi_t X)>0.
                                                               (66.8)

Thus theta_x is strictly negative at some earlier point and strictly positive at some later point of this same negative
excursion. The positive and negative parts of e^t theta_x have equal integrals over the full excursion.

Choose the launch radius R0 of Theorem 38 larger than a disc containing B. Write X(t,ell)=Phi_t(R0 e(ell)), 0<ell<alpha,
and put

  S={ell:z(X(t,ell))<0 for some real t},
  C_n={ell:z(X(t,ell))>0 for some t>n}, n=1,2,... .
                                                               (66.9)

The set S is nonempty and open. Each C_n is open and dense in (0,alpha). Thus a dense residual subset of S consists of
orbits that meet B and later have z>0 at arbitrarily large times. Escaping points are dense in B.

For the following additional conclusion assume a0<0 and (H1), and write w(x)=W_1(x,0). If w''(L)>0, a dense residual
subset of S has three increasing times with vorticity signs (sigma,-sigma,sigma), the last time arbitrarily large. Hence
an orbit prohibition of this triple, even on a dense subset of a nonempty open subinterval of S, is inconsistent with
w''(L)>0. This remains true if only triples whose last time exceeds one fixed bound are prohibited. If w''(L)<0, every
orbit in Q1 meets B at all sufficiently negative times and S=(0,alpha). No conclusion about the initial vorticity sign
is asserted when w''(L)=0.

(e) Define the smooth angular functions

  D0=q cos(phi)F-sin(phi)F',
  F1=-qP'F+aPF',
  g1=hP'g+aPg'-D0.                                      (66.10)

At every interior angle,

  g=0 implies D0<=0,
  D0>0 implies g>0.                                    (66.11)

If X_j are zeros of Omega in Q1 with |X_j| tending to infinity and arg X_j tending to phi_* in (0,alpha), then

  g(phi_*)=D0(phi_*)=0.                                (66.12)

At every sufficiently distant zero of Omega in Q1 one also has

  grad z=0, theta_x=0,
  W.grad theta_x=W^T(D^2 z)W=-(d_x W_2)theta_y>=0.
                                                               (66.13)

Under (H1), this implies W_2 d_x W_2<=0 at each such zero.

Under (H1), F>0 on (0,alpha), so g>0 at every interior critical point of F. At any interior zero of g the derivative of
F/sin(phi)^q is nonnegative. Every interior limit angle in (66.12) is a critical point of this quotient.

Under (H1), put gamma=g'(0)>=0 and c=F'(0)>0. Then

  sigma Omega_y(x,0)
    =gamma x^(-1-h)
      +[2P'(0)gamma+2hc]x^(-1-2h)+O(x^(-1-3h)).        (66.14)

In particular this trace is strictly positive for all sufficiently large x, including when gamma=0. There are epsilon>0
and R>0 such that z>0 for r>R and either 0<phi<epsilon or alpha-epsilon<phi<alpha. Consequently every unbounded sequence
of vorticity zeros in Q1 has a subsequence whose angles converge to an interior angle satisfying (66.12) and the
inequalities (66.17).

For an outgoing orbit with limiting angle phi_* in (0,alpha), its angle at radius r satisfies

  phi(r)=phi_*-aP(phi_*)r^(-h)+O(r^(-2h)).              (66.15)

In particular it approaches its limiting angle from below when sigma=1 and from above when sigma=-1. These statements
apply for all sufficiently large r on the fixed orbit.

(f) At an interior angle where g=D0=0, define

  C0=q(1-h)F[
          2P'cos(phi)-aP cos(2phi)/sin(phi)].             (66.16)

Then, with all quantities evaluated at that angle,

  C0>=0,    (D0')^2<=g'' C0.                            (66.17)

In particular g''=0 implies D0'=0. Under (H1), the bracket in (66.16) is nonnegative at every such angle. For a0<0 under
(H1), it is strictly negative on some interval immediately to the right of zero; consequently that interval has no
simultaneous zero of g and D0. Without (H1), the conclusion f=f'=0 implies f''=0 still holds at every interior angle.

(g) Assume a0<0 and (H1). In addition to being bounded, B has positive distance from the positive y-axis. Define the
positive temperature trace T0 and the signed vorticity trace k0 by

  T0(x)=-Theta_y(x,0)>0, k0(x)=-Omega_y(x,0),
  E={x>0:k0(x)<0}, b_axis=-k0 on E.                     (66.18)

The set E is open and bounded and is separated from zero; it may be empty. There is the exact identity, valid for all
x>0 including L,

  (w k0/T0^2)'=T0'/T0^2+3k0/T0^2.                     (66.19)

For every component (l,r) of E,

  1/T0(l)-1/T0(r)
      =3 int_l^r b_axis/T0^2 dx>0,
  T0(r)>T0(l).                                         (66.20)

If L belongs to (l,r), then T0(L)>T0(l) and T0(r)>T0(L). All these integrals converge absolutely. Thus every
opposite-sign trace interval has a strict net increase in the positive temperature trace across its endpoints, despite
the eventual decrease of T0 at infinity. If w''(L)<0, T0 has a local maximum to the left of L, a local minimum to its
right, and a second local maximum farther to the right. The minimum is smaller than T0(L), and both maxima are larger
than T0(L). These extrema need not be strict or nondegenerate.

(h) The local equations do not prescribe a common direction of crossing at a regular vorticity zero. More precisely, fix
beta>2, sigma in {-1,1}, x_*>0, y_*>0, v_*>0, T_*>0 and c!=beta+2. There are smooth fields on a rectangle about
(x_*,y_*) satisfying div W=2 beta, d_y W_1-d_x W_2=Omega, (V) and (T), with sigma Theta>0, Omega=0 at (x_*,y_*), and

  sigma Theta_x(x_*,y_*)
      =y_* T_*[c-(beta+2)]/v_*.                         (66.21)

The vorticity zero is regular and is crossed transversely. Values of c on opposite sides of beta+2 give opposite
crossing directions. These local fields are not asserted to have the origin jet, the global A2 parities, the canonical
velocity or the far field of a profile.

Scope. Parts (a)-(g) are necessary conditions for bounded nonempty B, with the additional hypotheses explicitly stated
in the individual parts. They do not exclude this configuration, including a0<0 under (H1). Part (d) gives a conditional
exclusion using an orbit sign prohibition and a positive value of w''(L); it does not establish that sign. Its
prohibition concerns three increasing flow times on a trajectory, whereas Theorem 64(b) concerns three increasing radii
on a fixed ray. These conditions are not identified. Part (h) concerns exact local solutions only and supplies no global
A2 extension. No A2-broad profile, and no global realization of the bounded opposite-sign configuration, is constructed.

Proof.

First record the accepted inputs. Theorem 64(a), applied with the stated hypotheses, gives g>=0, g not identically zero,
sigma P>0 on (0,alpha), and the strict endpoint slopes. It also excludes an unbounded connected open zero-vorticity set
in Q1, because the temperature zero set has empty interior. Theorems 41 and 42 give the uniform differentiated far-field
bounds and the first corrections used below. Under (H1), Theorem 8(ii) gives theta>0 in Q1, and Theorem 50(b) gives F>0
on (0,alpha). Parts (a)-(e) of Theorem 50, including its endpoint inequalities in (c), allow either sign of a0; only its
Lyapunov classification in (f) assumes a0>0. The canonical velocity, smoothness and sublinearity hypotheses required by
these theorems are part of A2-broad.

To prove (a), extend b=-z on D by zero outside D to a function b_D on the whole plane. This is a compactly supported
Lipschitz function. Here D is bounded and z=0 on boundary(D): a boundary point in Q1 with z<0 would have a connected
negative neighbourhood meeting D and hence contained in D, while oddness of Omega makes z=0 on both axes. To check the
Lipschitz assertion, take a disc containing closure(D), on which z is Lipschitz. For a point in D and a point outside D,
the segment between them has a first boundary point; the Lipschitz estimate for z between the first point and that
boundary point bounds the difference of b_D by a constant times the original distance. The cases with both points in D
or both outside are immediate. A larger disc handles the zero extension.

Almost everywhere, grad b_D=-grad z on D and is zero outside D. A Lipschitz function that is constant on a measurable
set has zero gradient almost everywhere on that set: at a density point where it is differentiable, a nonzero derivative
would exclude a fixed cone of positive relative measure from the level set in every sufficiently small ball. This proves
the assertion also on the zero set.

Extend A, without changing it near the compact range of theta on closure(D), to a C^1 function on R. Such an extension
is obtained with a smooth cutoff supported in its original domain. The chain and product rules for locally Lipschitz
functions, first on D and then almost everywhere on the plane, give the distributional identity

  div(A(theta)b_D^r W)
    =[(2 beta-r)A(theta)+kappa theta A'(theta)]b_D^r
       -r 1_D A(theta)b^(r-1)theta_x.                    (66.22)

For r=1 the last factor is interpreted only on D. The vector field on the left is Lipschitz and compactly supported; for
real r>=1 the map t -> t^r has bounded derivative on the nonnegative range of b_D. Integrate against a smooth function
equal to one on its support. Its divergence has integral zero, which proves (66.3). All factors on the right are bounded
on that compact support, so absolute convergence follows. Taking A=1 gives (66.4).

The maximum of b_D is positive and attained. It cannot be attained outside D, where b_D=0. At an attaining point grad
z=0, so (66.1) gives theta_x=z=-M_D<0. Continuity gives a nonempty open subset of D with theta_x<0. The first identity
in (66.4) forces theta_x>0 somewhere in D. The remaining assertions in (a) follow directly from the second identity.

For (b), apply (66.3) with r=1 and A(t)=(t+epsilon)^(-s). Under (H1), theta is nonnegative on closure(D), and this A is
C^1 on a neighbourhood of its range. Since kappa s=d, the coefficient in (66.3) is

  d A(t)+kappa t A'(t)
    =d epsilon (t+epsilon)^(-s-1).                       (66.23)

This proves (66.5) and its strict sign. If closure(D) lies in Q1, its compactness and theta>0 give theta>=m>0 there. The
left integrand is dominated by m^(-s)|theta_x|, which is integrable on D, and the absolute value of the right side is at
most d epsilon m^(-s-1) int_D b, which tends to zero. Dominated convergence proves the asserted limit. Equivalently, use
(66.3) directly with A(t)=t^(-s). When closure(D) meets an axis, theta vanishes there, so this positive lower bound is
absent and neither domination nor vanishing of the regularized right side follows.

For (c), the implicit function theorem makes boundary(D) smooth. Compactness gives a finite cover by regular level
charts, so the ordinary divergence theorem applies. Since z<0 on its inside, grad z=|grad z|n on boundary(D). Equation
(66.1) at z=0 gives the first identity in (66.6); integrating div W gives the second.

When theta>0 on closure(D), (66.1) implies grad theta!=0 throughout that closure. Thus neither its minimum nor its
maximum is attained in D. At a boundary minimum, the tangential derivatives vanish and the inward normal derivative is
positive: it is nonnegative by the minimum property and cannot be zero because grad theta!=0. Consequently grad theta=-c
n with c>0. The identity W.grad theta=kappa theta>0 gives W.n<0. At a boundary maximum, grad theta=c n with c>0, giving
W.n>0. Formula (66.6) transfers these strict signs to theta_x.

Under (H1), each connected component of the compact regular boundary is a smooth embedded circle. Its bounded Jordan
region has compact closure in Q1: every coordinate there lies between the corresponding extrema on the circle, since a
linear coordinate has no local extremum in an open planar region. This region is the bounded side of the particular
circle, also when that side is a hole of D. On its closure theta>0 and grad theta!=0. The same minimum and maximum
argument therefore gives both signs of W relative to its outward normal. The outward normal of D along the outer circle
is this normal; along an inner circle it is its negative. Equivalently, on any one circle the two continuous unit
normals agree everywhere or are opposite everywhere. Both crossing signs persist in either case. This proves the
additional assertion for each boundary circle.

For (d), set j(t)=e^t z(Phi_t X). Equation (66.1) gives

  j'(t)=e^t theta_x(Phi_t X).                            (66.24)

Theorem 44(b) says that every backward orbit is contained in a compact disc and converges to a single stagnation point.
Invariance of Q1 places this point in {W=0} cap closure(Q1); Theorem 6(a) makes its temperature zero. Under (H1),
Theorem 8(i) identifies this point as P_ax for every point of Q1. The positive y-axis instead has backward limit O.
Therefore theta_x and z are bounded on the backward orbit, j(t) tends to zero as t tends to -infinity, and the
negative-time integral of |j'| is finite. This proves the first identity in (66.7); it is also the signed version of the
representation in the Remark following Theorem 8.

An escaping orbit reaches the launch circle of Theorem 38 in finite time. Theorem 38(b) gives a limiting angle and
|Phi_t X|=rho(X)e^(beta t)[1+O_X(e^(-t))] with rho(X)>0. Theorem 41(c), with a time translation, gives both absolute
convergence and e^t z(Phi_t X)=J(X)+O_X(e^(-t)) for every such orbit, rather than only for almost every launch label.
Equivalently, the radial estimate and Theorem 41(a) give |theta_x(Phi_t X)|=O_X(e^(-2t)). The uniform vorticity
expansion in Theorem 42 and convergence of the angle then identify J(X)=rho(X)^(-h)g(phi_*). Since B is bounded and the
orbit escapes, z(Phi_t X)>=0 eventually, so J(X)>=0.

The upper endpoint v of a negative excursion is finite because the orbit eventually leaves the disc containing B. At a
finite endpoint continuity gives z=0. At an endpoint u=-infinity the already proved limit j(u)=0 applies. Integrating
(66.24) proves both identities (66.8). Their strict signs give the two source signs inside the excursion, in the stated
temporal order. Adding them gives integral zero on the whole excursion. The absolute convergence already established
justifies splitting into positive and negative parts.

Theorem 38(c) makes the escaping set open and identifies it smoothly with the cylinder of times and labels.
Nonzero-temperature points escape by Theorem 7 and the outward radial velocity at large radius. They are dense in every
open subset of Q1 by the empty-interior hypothesis. This proves density in B and nonemptiness of S. A strict negative
value at one fixed time persists on nearby labels, so S is open; the same argument proves openness of every C_n.

If C_n missed a nonempty open interval I, then z(X(t,ell)) could not be positive for t>n and ell in I. Since t>0 puts
these points outside the launch circle, boundedness of B makes z nonnegative there. Thus z=0 on the image of
(n,infinity) x I. This image is a connected, unbounded, open subset of Q1 by the launch diffeomorphism and outward
growth. It contradicts Theorem 64(a). Hence each C_n is dense. The Baire theorem for the open interval gives the dense
residual intersection and the assertions about S. This argument proves the claim for launch angles. It does not replace
trajectories by the rays occurring in Theorem 64(b),(c).

Under a0<0 and (H1), set T0=-Theta_y(x,0) and k0=-Omega_y(x,0). The axis argument in Theorem 50(a) gives T0>0 for all
x>0. Theorem 62(c) gives w(L)=0, w'(L)=beta+2 and the trace equations displayed in (66.36) below. Differentiating their
first equation and evaluating at L gives T0'(L)=w''(L)T0(L)/(beta+2). Their second equation at L then gives
k0(L)=w''(L)T0(L)/[(beta+2)(beta-1)]. These identities agree with Theorem 62(c). Oddness in y gives
z(x,y)=y[k0(L)+O(|x-L|+y^2)] and theta_x(x,y)=y[T0'(L)+O(|x-L|+y^2)]. Thus, when w''(L)!=0, both signed fields have the
sign of w''(L) throughout a sufficiently small upper half disc about P_ax, as also stated in Theorem 62(d). Theorem 8(i)
puts every Q1 orbit in that half disc at all sufficiently negative times. Consequently z initially has the sign of
w''(L). If this derivative is positive, any label in S has an initial positive value and a later negative value; the
residual returns just proved give the third value at arbitrarily large times. For each fixed time bound the set of
labels with such a triple is open, and its intersection with every open subinterval of S is nonempty by the same
residual argument. A dense set of labels prohibiting triples in such an interval is therefore impossible. If w''(L)<0,
every Q1 orbit initially lies in B. Theorem 50(b) says every such orbit escapes, proving S=(0,alpha).

For (e), multiply the temperature and vorticity expansions of Theorem 42(c) by sigma. The stream coefficients P and P1
remain the original signed coefficients of that theorem; in particular F1=sigma f1 and g1=sigma G1. With the notation
(66.10), the resulting expansions hold uniformly in angle, with differentiated remainders:

  z(r,phi)=r^(-h)[g(phi)+r^(-h)g1(phi)]+O(r^(-3h)),
  theta_x(r,phi)=r^(-2h)[D0(phi)+O(r^(-h))].            (66.25)

At an interior zero of the nonnegative smooth function g, one has g'=0. The first equation at that fixed angle then
reads z=-D0 r^(-2h)+O(r^(-3h)). Since z>=0 for all sufficiently large r, this forces D0<=0 and proves (66.11).

At any sufficiently distant zero X_j, z is nonnegative on a neighbourhood in Q1, hence grad z(X_j)=0. Equation (66.1)
yields theta_x(X_j)=0. The uniform limits in (66.25) give (66.12). Under (H1), F>0 by Theorem 50(b). At such a zero D^2
z is positive semidefinite. Differentiating the vorticity equation in space gives grad theta_x=(D^2 z)W there, because
grad z=0. Differentiating the temperature equation in x gives W.grad theta_x=-(d_x W_2)theta_y, because theta_x=0. These
identities prove (66.13). Under (H1), the temperature equation at the zero is W_2 theta_y=kappa theta>0, so multiplying
the last inequality by the positive ratio W_2/theta_y proves W_2 d_x W_2<=0. For comparison, these are the signed
versions of the zero identities in Theorem 65(a),(h), using nonnegativity of z in the exterior and, for the last sign,
positivity of theta under (H1).

At F'=0, D0=q cos(phi)F>0, giving g>0. Direct differentiation gives

  (F/sin(phi)^q)'=-D0/sin(phi)^(q+1).                   (66.26)

This proves the quotient assertions. For comparison, the angular B(phi) in Theorem 65 equals sigma D0, so
(66.11)-(66.12) agree with Theorem 65(c),(h) on their common hypotheses a0>0; the positive axis sectors proved below use
(H1), which is available in Theorem 65(c) but is not assumed in Theorem 65(h).

Under (H1), Theorem 50(c) gives c=F'(0)>0 and g'(alpha)<0 for both signs of a0. Nonnegativity of g gives gamma=g'(0)>=0.
Differentiate (66.10) at zero, using P(0)=g(0)=F(0)=0, h+a=2 and q-1=-2h. This gives
g1'(0)=(h+a)P'(0)gamma-(q-1)c=2P'(0)gamma+2hc. The differentiated expansion (66.25), and d_y=x^(-1)d_phi on the positive
x-axis, prove (66.14).

If gamma>0, g(phi)>=gamma phi/2 on a sufficiently small interval 0<phi<epsilon. The remainder after the leading term of
z vanishes at phi=0 and has angular derivative O(r^(-2h)), so it is bounded by C phi r^(-2h) on that interval. This
proves strict positivity there for large r. If gamma=0, then g1'(0)=2hc>0, so g1(phi)>=hc phi after shrinking epsilon.
Now use g>=0 and the remainder after the first correction: it vanishes at phi=0 and is bounded by C phi r^(-3h). Again
z>0 uniformly for large r. The same leading-term argument at alpha, using g'(alpha)<0 and the vanishing of the remainder
on that axis, gives the other wedge. An unbounded sequence of zeros is therefore eventually confined to a compact
interior angular interval. A convergent subsequence and (66.12), followed by (f), give the stated conditions.

Theorem 42(b) gives U_phi=aP(phi)r^(1-h)+O(r^(1-2h)) and U_r=-P'(phi)r^(1-h)+O(r^(1-2h)). Along an outgoing orbit this
implies

  d phi/dr=(a/beta)P(phi)r^(-1-h)+O(r^(-1-2h)).         (66.27)

Theorem 38(b) first gives phi(r)-phi_*=O(r^(-h)). Substituting this estimate into P in (66.27), and integrating from r
to infinity, gives phi_*-phi(r)=aP(phi_*)r^(-h)+O(r^(-2h)), because beta h=1. This is (66.15). Its strict side follows
from sigma P>0 in Theorem 64(a).

For (f), it is necessary to determine one further vorticity coefficient. Let P1 be the stream correction in
Theorem 42(c), and put

  D1=(q-h)cos(phi)F1-sin(phi)F1',
  g2=[2hP'g1+aPg1'+hP1'g+(2-2h)P1g'-D1]/2.            (66.28)

We claim the uniform expansion

  z=r^(-h)g+r^(-2h)g1+r^(-3h)g2+O(r^(-4h)).           (66.29)

Here only the stated uniform remainder is needed. To prove it, write L_r=beta r d_r+1. Theorem 42(c) gives the first two
terms of z and U with differentiated remainders, and the first two terms of theta with a differentiated remainder.
Substitute these into L_r z=theta_x-U.grad z. The terms of order r^(-3h) on the right are
D1-2hP'g1-aPg1'-hP1'g-(2-2h)P1g', which is -2g2. Every unused term is O(r^(-4h)): for example U's leading term times the
gradient of z's O_infty(r^(-3h)) remainder has that order, as does the x derivative of theta's O_infty(r^(q-2h))
remainder.

Since L_r(r^(-jh))=(1-j)r^(-jh), the remainder E2 after subtracting the three displayed terms satisfies E2=O(r^(-3h))
and L_r E2=O(r^(-4h)). At fixed angle,

  (r^h E2)'=h r^(h-1)L_r E2,
  E2(r)=-h r^(-h)int_r^infinity t^(h-1)L_t E2(t) dt.
                                                               (66.30)

The boundary term at infinity vanishes because E2=O(r^(-3h)). The uniform bound on the integral is O(r^(-4h)), proving
(66.29). This is a finite additional expansion, not an assertion about an infinite series.

Fix an interior angle phi0 with g=D0=0. Nonnegativity gives g'=0 and g''>=0 there, and g1=0. For any fixed real u,
substitute phi=phi0+u r^(-h) into (66.29). Taylor expansion and z>=0 give

  (g''/2)u^2+g1'u+g2>=0 for every real u.                (66.31)

All coefficients in the remainder of the proof of (f) are at phi0. From (66.10) and (66.28),

  g1'=aP g''-D0',
  2g2=a^2 P^2 g''-aP D0'-D1.                          (66.32)

The terms containing P1 have disappeared because g=g'=0. Thus the quadratic in (66.31), on writing v=u+aP, becomes

  (g''/2)v^2-D0'v+(aP D0'-D1)/2.                      (66.33)

We compute its constant coefficient without leaving a sign implicit. At g=0 the angular stream equation gives P''=-a^2
P. At D0=0 one has F'=q cot(phi)F, including when F=0. Differentiate D0 and F1 in (66.10):

  D0'=-q sin(phi)F+(q-1)cos(phi)F'-sin(phi)F'',
  F1'=-qP''F+(a-q)P'F'+aPF''.                         (66.34)

In aP D0'-D1 the F'' terms cancel. Substituting P'' and F' just obtained, and using a=2-h, gives

  aP D0'-D1
    =q(1-h)F[2P'cos(phi)-aP cos(2phi)/sin(phi)]
    =C0.                                               (66.35)

Evaluating (66.33) at v=0 gives C0>=0. If g''>0, evaluating it at v=D0'/g'' gives (D0')^2<=g''C0. If g''=0, a nonzero
linear coefficient would make (66.33) negative in one direction, so D0'=0 and the same inequality holds. This proves
(66.17).

For comparison, let C(phi)=(a-1)[aP cos(2phi)-P' sin(2phi)]-G sin(phi)^2, the expression in (65.2); then at g=D0=0 one
has C0=-q F C(phi)/sin(phi)=-q sigma f C(phi)/sin(phi), so under (H1) the assertion C0>=0 is precisely C(phi)<=0 for
either sign of a0, agreeing with (65.9) on their common hypotheses, while (D0')^2<=g''C0 is an additional restriction;
without (H1), when f!=0 it gives sigma sgn(f) C(phi)<=0, agreeing for a0>0 with the sign-conditioned conclusion of
Theorem 65(h), since a nonzero f fixes the temperature sign along a sequence with that limit angle.

Under (H1), q(1-h)F>0, so the bracket has the asserted sign. Since P(0)=0, the limit of this bracket at zero is
(2-a)P'(0)=hP'(0). For a0<0 the endpoint sign in Theorem 64(a) gives P'(0)<0. Continuity then excludes simultaneous
zeros on an interval adjacent to zero. Finally, if F=F'=0 at an interior angle, Theorem 47(a) gives g=0. Also D0=C0=0,
so (66.17) gives D0'=0. Formula (66.34) then reads D0'=-sin(phi)F'', and F''=0 follows.

For (g), Theorem 62(d) supplies a neighbourhood on the Q1 side of each positive y-axis point on which Omega<0. The
origin jet, as used in Theorem 64(b), supplies a single small quarter disc on which z>0. If B had distance zero from the
positive y-axis, boundedness would give a sequence in B converging to a point of the closed positive y-axis. The origin
case is excluded by that quarter disc, and every other case by the just cited neighbourhoods. This proves the
separation.

The axis argument in the proof of Theorem 50(a) gives T0>0 on x>0. Continuity of Omega_y and boundedness of B imply
k0>=0 for sufficiently large x: otherwise Omega(x,y)>0 for arbitrarily small positive y at that fixed x. Near zero the
vorticity jet gives k0>0. Thus E is open, bounded and separated from zero.

Here is a direct derivation of the signed trace equations, also recorded in Theorem 62(c). On y=0, parity gives W_2=d_y
W_1=0 and theta_x=z_x=0, while divergence gives d_y W_2=2 beta-w'. Differentiating the two transport equations in y on
this axis yields w T0'+(2 beta-w')T0=kappa T0 and w k0'+(2 beta-w')k0+k0=T0'. Thus

  w T0'=(w'-(beta+2))T0,
  w k0'+(2 beta+1-w')k0=T0'.                            (66.36)

For comparison with Theorem 65(e), the source identities T0'(L)=T0(L)w''(L)/(beta+2) and
k0(L)=T0(L)w''(L)/[(beta+2)(beta-1)] are the same trace identities after replacing its T,g,A by T0,k0,T0(L), but its
conclusion w''(L)>=0 uses a nonnegative vorticity trace, which boundedness of B does not supply at L.

Differentiate w k0/T0^2 and use these two equations without dividing by w. Its numerator becomes T0'+(2w'-(2
beta+1))k0-2(w'-(beta+2))k0=T0'+3k0. This proves (66.19), including at w=0.

For a component (l,r) of E, both endpoints are finite and positive, T0 is bounded away from zero on [l,r], and k0
vanishes at the endpoints. Integrate (66.19) on this interval. The boundary terms vanish and the integral of T0'/T0^2 is
1/T0(l)-1/T0(r). This proves (66.20) and absolute convergence. If L lies inside, the boundary term w k0/T0^2 also
vanishes at L because w(L)=0. Apply the same calculation to (l,L) and (L,r); the strict positivity of their integrands
gives both further inequalities. Finally (66.36) and w=beta x+O(x^(1-h)), w'=beta+O(x^(-h)), from Theorem 42(a), imply
T0'/T0=-2/(beta x)+O(x^(-1-h)), which is negative for sufficiently large x and, upon integration, gives T0(x)->0. More
precisely, Theorem 42(b) differentiated on the axis and Theorem 50(c) give T0(x)=c x^(-2h)+O(x^(-3h)) with c=F'(0)>0.

If w''(L)<0, Theorem 62(c) gives T0'(L)=T0(L)w''(L)/(beta+2)<0 and k0(L)=T0'(L)/(beta-1)<0. Let (l,r) be the component
of E containing L. The two endpoint inequalities just proved show T0(l)<T0(L)<T0(r). There is a point just to the left
of L where T0>T0(L), so the maximum of T0 on [l,L] is attained in its interior and exceeds T0(L). There is a point just
to the right of L where T0<T0(L), so the minimum on [L,r] is attained at an interior point m and is smaller than T0(L).
Choose R>r with T0(R)<T0(r). The maximum on [m,R] is attained in its interior, is at least T0(r), and occurs strictly to
the right of m. These three interior extrema have the properties asserted in (g).

For (h), the following local ordinary differential equations provide all the claimed fields:

  v'=p, p'=k,
  T'=[p-(beta+2)]T/v,
  k'={T'-(2 beta+1-p)k}/v,
  v(x_*)=v_*, p(x_*)=c, k(x_*)=0, T(x_*)=sigma T_*.
                                                               (66.37)

The right sides are smooth where v!=0. The local existence theorem for ordinary differential equations gives a smooth
solution on a sufficiently small interval, with v>0 and sigma T>0. Define there

  W=(v(x),(2 beta-v'(x))y),
  Omega=y v''(x), Theta=y T(x),
  Psi=(beta x-v(x))y, U=W-beta X.                        (66.38)

Direct differentiation gives div W=2 beta, d_y W_1-d_x W_2=yv''=Omega, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), and -Lap Psi=Omega. The
temperature equation reduces to the T equation in (66.37). The vorticity equation reduces to v v'''+(2 beta+1-v')v''=T',
which is its k equation. Thus all stated local equations hold exactly.

At x=x_*, v''=0 and v'''=[c-(beta+2)]sigma T_*/v_*^2!=0. Hence the vorticity zero is regular. Moreover theta_x=y_*
T_*[c-(beta+2)]/v_*, which proves (66.21). At this zero W.grad z=theta_x is nonzero, so the crossing is transverse and
has either sign as claimed. The construction only defines a local rectangle and supplies none of the omitted global
conditions. Its displayed separated formulas cannot themselves define a uniformly sublinear velocity on the whole strip:
for each fixed x, letting |y| tend to infinity in U_2=(beta-v'(x))y would force v'(x)=beta throughout the interval,
contradicting v'''(x_*)!=0. This does not rule out a different continuation of local data; no such continuation is
provided. QED.

### Theorem 67 (beta > 2: the formal natural far field and compatibility of the far-field necessary conditions)

Fix beta>2 and put alpha=pi/2. Write X=r(cos(phi),sin(phi)), Q1={x>0,y>0}, e_r=(cos(phi),sin(phi)),
e_phi=(-sin(phi),cos(phi)), and z=log r. Use the notation and conventions

  h=1/beta, q=1-2h, a=2-h, kappa=beta-2,
  W=beta X+U, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), -Lap Psi=Omega,
  W.grad Theta=kappa Theta, W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x,
  div W=2 beta, d_y W_1-d_x W_2=Omega.                    (67.1)

Thus 0<h<1/2. Primes on angular functions mean angular derivatives. The temperature is even in x and odd in y and
vanishes on both axes. The additional condition Theta(0,y)=0 is imposed separately from its even x parity. Vorticity and
stream function are odd in both variables. The corresponding velocity parities are those of Setting A2.

For comparison with an actual A2-broad profile, a0 is its nonzero coefficient of x^2 y at the origin, sigma=sgn(a0), and
P_ax=(L,0) is its first positive x-axis zero of W from Theorem 2. Hypothesis (H1) means {W=0} cap closure(Q1)={O,P_ax}.
The letter P below denotes an angular stream coefficient. As in Theorem 42, O_infty(r^t) means that every Cartesian
derivative of order k is O(r^(t-k)). All exterior estimates are uniform up to both axes.

(a) Let f,G be smooth real functions on [0,alpha] such that, for every integer k>=0,
