  f^(2k)(0)=0, f^(2k+1)(alpha)=0, f(alpha)=0,
  G^(2k)(0)=G^(2k)(alpha)=0.                              (67.2)

These are exactly the angular endpoint conditions imposed by the A2 parities and the axis value on the smooth limits of
Theorems 41 and 42. They are not all the necessary conditions for actual profile limits. In particular, Theorem 47(a)
supplies an additional implication at interior zeros of f and f'.

There is a unique smooth odd-odd angular function P satisfying

  -P''-a^2 P=G, P(0)=P(alpha)=0.                          (67.3)

For every pair satisfying (67.2) and every prescribed real sequence (c_m)_(m>=1), the system (67.1) has a formal
expansion to every finite order of the following form. No finite coefficient equation imposes another condition on f,G.

(b) Define an allowed set of grades and the expansion by

  K={0,4,6,8,...}, S={n h+K0:n>=0, K0 in K},
  b_m=2+2m,
  Theta ~ sum_(delta in S) r^(q-delta) F_delta(z,phi),
  Omega ~ sum_(delta in S) r^(-h-delta) G_delta(z,phi),
  Psi ~ sum_(delta in S) r^(a-delta) P_delta(z,phi)
          +sum_(m>=1) c_m r^(-2m) sin(2m phi).             (67.4)

The coefficients are polynomials in z with smooth angular coefficients. The leading coefficients are F_0=f, G_0=G,
P_0=P. Equal real grades are collected into one coefficient. The set S is locally finite even when h is irrational. Each
polynomial coefficient of F_delta satisfies the temperature conditions in (67.2); those of G_delta and P_delta satisfy
the odd-odd endpoint conditions.

The harmonic stream term with index m acts in transport with grade increment b_m. There is no independent harmonic
increment 2. This does not exclude the numerical grade 2: for example, it equals 6h when beta=3. No scalar grade outside
S is generated. The harmonic stream terms themselves are displayed separately in (67.4).

If all c_m vanish, the expansion is supported on delta=jh, including when logarithms occur. When all coefficients
involved are independent of z, write F_j,G_j,P_j for these coefficients and mu_j=2-(j+1)h. Then

  j F_j=sum_(k+l=j-1) [
             -(q-lh)P_k'F_l+mu_k P_k F_l'],
  j G_j=sum_(k+l=j-1) [
             (l+1)h P_k'G_l+mu_k P_k G_l']
             -(q-(j-1)h)cos(phi)F_(j-1)
             +sin(phi)F_(j-1)',
  -P_j''-mu_j^2 P_j=G_j, P_j(0)=P_j(alpha)=0.            (67.5)

Here j>=1. The transport steps are algebraic in angle. Their dilation multipliers and the general polynomial inverse are

  (beta r d_r-kappa)r^(q-jh)F=-j r^(q-jh)F,
  (beta r d_r+1)r^(-h-jh)H=-j r^(-h-jh)H,
  [beta(delta-d_z)]^(-1)H
    =sum_(k=0)^d d_z^k H/(beta delta^(k+1)),
       delta>0, degree_z H<=d.                           (67.6)

(c) At grade delta put mu=a-delta. The elliptic equation is

  -[d_phi^2+(mu+d_z)^2]P_delta=G_delta,
  P_delta(z,0)=P_delta(z,alpha)=0.                        (67.7)

Its only possible resonances are mu=-2m, m>=1. At a pure grade this means (j+1)h=2+2m; at a general grade the condition
is

  delta=nh+K0, (n+1)h+K0=2+2m, K0 in K.                 (67.8)

On a resonant sine mode let H(z) be the source coefficient. Its normalized particular solution is the polynomial p
determined by

  p(z)=integral_0^z [(4m-d_t)^(-1)H](t) dt, p(0)=0,
  (4m d_z-d_z^2)p=H.
  In particular H constant gives p(z)=H z/(4m).          (67.9)

The inverse inside the integral is its terminating polynomial inverse. The remaining constant on that mode is c_m. This
convention prevents double counting. Nonresonant modes have unique polynomial solutions. Consequently f,G and the c_m
determine the entire normalized expansion.

There is no Fredholm obstruction when logarithms are allowed. For these expansions a generated logarithm requires
rational beta; rationality alone does not force its coefficient to be nonzero. A logarithm can subsequently propagate to
a nonresonant grade. The resonant terms are compatible with a sublinear canonical velocity and with the orders of the
actual-profile expansion in Theorem 42(c). The constants c_m record possible interior information in the canonical
inverse. They are not freely addable harmonic fields for a fixed whole-plane vorticity.

(d) For every N>0 a finite truncation gives smooth fields on r>1, with smooth reflection across both axes, satisfying
the elliptic, divergence and curl identities in (67.1) exactly, U=o(r), and

  W.grad Theta-kappa Theta=O_infty(r^(-N)),
  W.grad Omega+Omega-Theta_x=O_infty(r^(-N)).              (67.10)

The truncations can all be taken from one formal expansion.

(e) For either sigma=1 or sigma=-1 the following data and forced first corrections will be used:

  p0=1/[h(4-h)], s=sin(phi), c=cos(phi),
  f=sigma s c^2, G=sigma sin(2phi), P=sigma p0 sin(2phi),
  f1=2p0 s c^2[(1+h)-(4+h)s^2],
  A2=sigma(h-1)/2, A4=2p0+sigma(1+h)/4,
  G1=A2 sin(2phi)+A4 sin(4phi),
  P1=A2 sin(2phi)/[4-(2-2h)^2]
       +A4 sin(4phi)/[16-(2-2h)^2].                     (67.11)

These are precisely the first corrections of Theorem 42(c). In particular,

  F=sigma f=s c^2>0, g=sigma G=sin(2phi)>0
       for 0<phi<alpha,
  F'(0)=1, F''(alpha)=2, g'(0)=2, g'(alpha)=-2,
  sigma P>0, sigma P''<0,
  sigma P'(0)=2p0, sigma P'(alpha)=-2p0,
  D0=q c F-s F'=2s c[(1+h)s^2-h].                       (67.12)

Every finite truncation with these data, including arbitrary fixed values of its finitely many harmonic constants, has a
radius R beyond which

  sigma Theta>0, sigma Omega>0 in Q1,
  Theta=Omega=0 on the axes, |W|>=beta r/2.              (67.13)

The signs are uniform in angle in the sense of the quotients proved below. The radius may depend on the truncation and
its constants.

(f) Compatibility has the following restricted meaning. The same data in (67.11), with their forced corrections, satisfy
the angular conditions in Theorems 41, 42, 47(a), 50(b),(c), and 64(a), the natural exterior bounds and nonvanishing
requirements in Theorems 31, 32, 37, 38, 40, 41 and 45, and the exterior consequences of the sign-change assertions in
Theorems 50, 55 and 57. They have the temperature-weight divergence in Remark 55.1 on the positive branch. They satisfy
the exterior requirements of Theorems 58, 60, 62 and 63 that apply without additional interior configurations.

For comparison with Theorems 65 and 66, they satisfy (65.7)-(65.9) on the positive branch, (66.11)-(66.17) whenever the
bounded opposite-sign hypotheses are imposed, and the far-field axis expansions used in those theorems. The implications
at interior common zeros of g and D0 have empty hypotheses here.

Global integral balances, source conditions, and conditions involving complete orbits or an additional chain of zeros
are not claimed to be realized. On the negative branch a nonempty bounded positive-vorticity region would still be
necessary. No prohibition on ray or orbit sign triples is included. Thus the assertion is simultaneous compatibility of
the stated far-field tests, together with formal solvability, not simultaneous realization of all hypotheses and
conclusions for an actual profile.

Scope. The extension beyond Theorem 42(c) is formal only. There is no claim of convergence, summability, an exact
exterior solution, or a whole-plane A2-broad profile. The origin jet, (H1), global balances and the required interior
structure are not constructed. In particular, formal solvability for every pair satisfying (67.2) does not mean that
every such pair is admissible for an actual profile. Nor does the result show that far-field arguments cannot decide
existence or nonexistence.

Proof.

First consider the coefficient equations, without any sign hypotheses and without using Theorems 65 or 66.

Theorems 41 and 42 supply the angular limits and their smoothness for actual profiles. Smooth odd reflection at an
endpoint is equivalent to vanishing of all even derivatives there; smooth even reflection is equivalent to vanishing of
all odd derivatives. Applying these facts at 0 and alpha, and imposing the extra temperature value at alpha, gives
exactly (67.2). Repeated reflections give smooth 2pi-periodic functions. The odd-odd angular basis is sin(2m phi), m>=1.

On this basis the eigenvalues of -d_phi^2-a^2 are 4m^2-a^2>0. Division of the rapidly decreasing Fourier coefficients by
these numbers gives a smooth P and proves uniqueness in (67.3), in agreement with Theorem 41(b).

For the full recursion it is convenient to index a stream term by its transport decrement lambda. Write it as
r^(2-lambda)A_lambda(z,phi). Its radial and angular velocity components and its transport action on r^t H are

  U_r=-r^(1-lambda)A_lambda,phi,
  U_phi=r^(1-lambda)[(2-lambda)A_lambda+A_lambda,z],
  U.grad(r^t H)=r^(t-lambda)T_(lambda,t)(A_lambda,H),
  T_(lambda,t)(A,H)
    =-A_phi(t+d_z)H+[(2-lambda)A+A_z]H_phi,
  d_x(r^t H)=r^(t-1)X_t(H),
  X_t(H)=cos(phi)(t+d_z)H-sin(phi)H_phi.                 (67.14)

The particular stream term at delta has lambda=h+delta. A decaying harmonic has lambda=b_m=2+2m. Temperature
differentiation contributes vorticity grade epsilon+h from temperature grade epsilon. Therefore all scalar grades are
generated by the positive increment h, the increments b_m, and their sums. The additive semigroup generated by the b_m
is K: every even integer at least 4 is already one of them, their sums remain in that set, and the empty sum is 0. This
proves the allowed grading S.

More explicitly, if delta,epsilon belong to S, the transport interaction of a particular stream coefficient and a scalar
coefficient has grade h+delta+epsilon in S. A harmonic acting on a scalar coefficient gives b_m+epsilon in S. Repeated
such operations include interactions mediated by the fields already generated by other harmonics. There is no separate
harmonic-harmonic vorticity term, since each harmonic has zero Laplacian. The angular mode m=0, including a log r stream
term, is excluded by odd-odd parity. This explains the absence of an independent increment 2, without excluding 2 when
it belongs to S.

Below any D there are only finitely many possible K0 and n, since K0<=D and n<=D/h. This proves local finiteness,
irrespective of rationality. If all c_m=0, induction uses only increments h and sums of preceding pure grades. Resonance
changes logarithmic degree, not the radial grade. This proves the assertion about pure grades.

Let Lambda=(h+S) union {b_m:m>=1}. At a given lambda, A_lambda is P_(lambda-h) if that grade belongs to S, together with
the harmonic coefficient c_m sin(2m phi) if lambda=b_m. Missing terms are zero. With the normalized convention of (c),
this includes a resonant particular coefficient and its independent constant just once. Collecting (67.14) in the two
transport equations gives, for delta>0,

  beta(delta-d_z)F_delta
    =sum_(lambda+epsilon=delta)
          T_(lambda,q-epsilon)(A_lambda,F_epsilon),
  beta(delta-d_z)G_delta
    =sum_(lambda+epsilon=delta)
          T_(lambda,-h-epsilon)(A_lambda,G_epsilon)
       -X_(q-delta+h)(F_(delta-h)).                       (67.15)

The sums have lambda in Lambda and epsilon in S. The last term is zero if delta-h is not in S. Every coefficient on the
right has already been found: epsilon<delta and lambda-h<=delta-h<delta. The signs follow directly by moving the
nonlinear terms to the right of the dilation equations and then multiplying by -1. Formula (67.6) is the terminating
geometric inverse, since d_z is nilpotent on each finite-degree polynomial space. It proves the unique transport steps.
Removing d_z and setting delta=jh in (67.15) gives (67.5), including its temperature derivative term.

For completeness, all products in these equations preserve the required endpoint classes. At 0, A and F are odd, A_phi
and F_phi are even, and G is odd. Thus both A_phi F and A F_phi are odd, and the same assertion holds with F replaced by
G. At alpha, A and G are odd, A_phi is even, F is even, and F_phi is odd. The temperature products are even and the
vorticity products odd. Moreover A=A_z=0 there and F=F_z=0 there, so every temperature source has value zero at alpha.
At 0, cos(phi)F and sin(phi)F_phi are odd; at alpha they are odd because cos(phi) is odd and sin(phi) is even about that
endpoint. The z derivatives do not change any of these statements. Reflection parity implies all the corresponding
derivative conditions, not just the endpoint values.

It remains to solve the elliptic step. On sin(2m phi), (67.7) is the polynomial operator

  gap-2mu d_z-d_z^2, gap=4m^2-mu^2.
  If gap!=0, its inverse on a polynomial H is
  (1/gap) sum_(j>=0) [(2mu d_z+d_z^2)/gap]^j H,           (67.16)

where the sum terminates. For large m the denominators grow quadratically. The inverse therefore preserves rapid
decrease of the angular Fourier coefficients, for every angular derivative. There are only finitely many small modes to
consider separately. This proves smoothness and the odd-odd endpoint conditions for P_delta.

Since mu=a-delta<=a<2, mu=+2m cannot occur. At mu=-2m the operator is d_z(4m-d_z), so (67.9) solves it with exactly one
free constant. There is no mode m=0. The elementary identity

  -Lap[r^(-2m)log r sin(2m phi)]
       =4m r^(-2m-2)sin(2m phi)                         (67.17)

also verifies the sign and normalization of the first logarithm. These inverses complete the induction.

Any first logarithm must arise at a resonance, since the other operators take constant polynomials to constant
polynomials. Equation (67.8) makes h rational at such a resonance, hence beta rational. If the resonant source
projection vanishes, no logarithm is forced there. In particular rationality is not sufficient, as is already clear from
the zero formal solution with every c_m=0. Subsequent logarithmic sources can pass through nonresonant inverses.

There is no conflict with the canonical inverse of Setting A2 and Theorem 9. For angular mode n=2m its radial Green
formula is (1/(2n)) times the sum of r^(-n) integral_0^r rho^(n+1)omega_n(rho) d rho and r^n integral_r^infinity
rho^(1-n)omega_n(rho) d rho. For a source rho^(mu-2) times a polynomial in log rho, the outer integral converges because
mu<=a<2<=n. At mu=-n the inner integral generates precisely the logarithmic polynomial in (67.9); the remaining multiple
of r^(-n) is absorbed in c_m. Its velocity is O(r^(-n-1) times a polynomial in log r), and is sublinear. The growing
homogeneous term r^n would violate sublinearity and is excluded. The first possible resonant stream exponent is -2,
strictly below 2-3h>1/2, the stream remainder exponent in Theorem 42(c). Thus that theorem imposes no vanishing
logarithmic projection. A separately imposed absence of logarithms would impose such a condition, but is not an A2
hypothesis.

For a fixed whole-plane source the inner Green integral fixes its constants. For a finite list of modes, smooth sources
supported on an interior annulus can alter their r^(-n) coefficients independently in this elliptic formula. This
statement concerns only the linear inverse, not a coupled solution or a sign-preserving completion. An arbitrary
infinite sequence in (67.4) is only a formal sequence; no convergence or growth assertion about that sequence is
required.

To prove (d), retain all scalar and particular stream grades delta<=D and all harmonics with b_m<=h+D. The latter cutoff
includes every harmonic whose stream degree is at least a-D. Each retained particular stream term has exactly its
retained vorticity as negative Laplacian, including all its logarithmic derivatives. The harmonics have zero Laplacian.
Thus the three linear identities hold exactly. Reflection gives smooth fields for r>1 up to and across both axes. Their
leading velocity is O(r^(1-h)); every other term has a strictly smaller power, possibly multiplied by a polynomial in
log r. Hence U=o(r).

No omitted stream coefficient can contribute to a residual grade <=D. The transport induction therefore cancels all such
grades. Let delta_+ be the least member of S strictly larger than D. For some finite M depending on the truncation, the
residuals satisfy

  R_T=O_infty(r^(q-delta_+)(1+log r)^M),
  R_V=O_infty(r^(-h-delta_+)(1+log r)^M).                 (67.18)

The notation here permits the same polynomial factor after each Cartesian derivative. A finite sum permits a common M;
differentiation does not increase its logarithmic degree. Taking D>N+q+1 absorbs the logarithmic factor and proves
(67.10) for all derivatives.

Next prove (e) and the comparisons in (f). The leading elliptic equation follows from 4-a^2=h(4-h). Theorem 42(c), or
the j=1 case of (67.5), gives f1=-qP'f+aPf' and G1=hP'G+aPG'-qcf+sf'. Substitution gives (67.11). In particular
hP'G+aPG'=2p0 sin(4phi); decomposing the remaining term -qcf+sf' gives A2 and the remaining part of A4. Dividing the two
sine coefficients by their nonzero elliptic eigenvalues gives P1. This verifies all first corrections with the
conventions in (67.1), rather than prescribing them independently.

The uniform signs require more than absolute angular remainders. For any smooth temperature coefficient H in (67.2) and
any smooth odd-odd coefficient J there are smooth functions Hhat,Jhat on the closed interval such that

  H=sin(phi)cos(phi)^2 Hhat,
  J=sin(2phi)Jhat.                                       (67.19)

Indeed H has a zero of order at least one at 0, and its value and first derivative vanish at alpha. Taylor's formula
with integral remainder permits division by phi at 0 and by (alpha-phi)^2 at alpha. The corresponding trigonometric
factors differ from these by smooth nonzero factors. The same argument uses first-order zeros at both endpoints for J.
Apply it separately to every logarithmic coefficient; it also applies to every sine harmonic. The quotients are bounded
with all angular derivatives on the compact interval.

For a fixed finite truncation all nonleading scalar grades are positive. Thus (67.19) yields uniform limits, with the
endpoint quotients interpreted by continuity,

  sigma Theta/[r^q sin(phi)cos(phi)^2]=1+o(1),
  sigma Omega/[r^(-h)sin(2phi)]=1+o(1).                  (67.20)

Each error is a finite sum of r^(-delta) times logarithmic polynomials with bounded angular coefficients. This proves
(67.13) for temperature and vorticity, including angles approaching either axis at arbitrary rates. Since U=o(r),
|W|>=beta r-|U| gives its last assertion. In fact W_r>0 in this exterior. Velocity parity and the differentiated bound
DU=O(r^(-h)) also give W_1/x=beta+O(r^(-h)) and W_2/y=beta+O(r^(-h)) there, with the quotients extended to the axes.

The elementary signed angular calculations needed for the comparisons are (67.12) and

  F'=c(1-3s^2),
  q s F+c F'=c^2[1-2(1+h)s^2],
  (F/s^q)'=-D0/s^(q+1).                                 (67.21)

Thus F has a single interior critical point, at s^2=1/3, where g>0. The only interior zero of D0 is s^2=h/(1+h), where
g=2sqrt(h)/(1+h)>0. There is no interior common zero of f,f', and there is no interior zero of g. Theorem 47(a) is
therefore satisfied. The endpoint inequalities of Theorem 50(c) are exactly those in (67.12).

To check the additional angular expressions of Theorems 65 and 66, their functions C and C0 specialize to

  C=-sigma sin(2phi)[(1-h)+(2+h)s^2]/(4-h),
  C0=2sigma h q(1-h)p0 s c^3 cos(2phi).                  (67.22)

The first formula follows by substituting P,G in (65.2). The second follows from (66.16), with its signed F. The
condition C<=0 in (65.9) is required only at a limiting zero angle satisfying G=B=0. No such angle exists here.
Similarly (66.17) is required only where g=D0=0; it does not require C0>=0 everywhere. Near 0 the bracket in (66.16) has
sign sigma, agreeing with the negative-branch statement of Theorem 66(f). The implication f=f'=0 implies f''=0 there
concerns interior angles only and is also satisfied. It must not be imposed at alpha, where F''=2.

For comparison at the next order, set F1=sigma f1, g1=sigma G1 and D1=(q-h)cF1-sF1'. The signed j=2 vorticity
coefficient is

  g2=(1/2)[2hP'g1+aPg1'+hP1'g+(2-2h)P1g'-D1].          (67.23)

This follows from (67.5), independently of Theorem 66. It agrees with the second coefficient used in deriving its
contact inequality. There is no resonance at this order.

Here are the differentiated axis expansions, for truncations retaining the first correction:

  sigma Theta_y(x,0)
    =x^(-2h)+2sigma p0(1+h)x^(-3h)+O(x^(-4h)),
  sigma Omega_y(x,0)
    =2x^(-1-h)+(8sigma p0+2h)x^(-1-2h)+O(x^(-1-3h)),
  sigma Theta_xx(0,y)/2
    =y^(-1-2h)-6sigma p0 y^(-1-3h)+O(y^(-1-4h)),
  sigma Omega_x(0,y)
    =2y^(-1-h)-(8sigma p0+2)y^(-1-2h)+O(y^(-1-3h)).
                                                               (67.24)

They follow by evaluating f1'(0)=2p0(1+h), f1''(alpha)=-12p0, sigma G1'(0)=8sigma p0+2h, and sigma G1'(alpha)=8sigma
p0+2, and using d_y=r^(-1)d_phi on the x-axis and d_x=-r^(-1)d_phi on the y-axis. The second x derivative of the
temperature on that axis uses f(alpha)=f'(alpha)=0. The bounds hold after all further axis derivatives.

In the notation w=W_1(.,0), v=W_2(0,.), E=Theta_xx(0,.)/2 and K_axis=Omega_x(0,.), one also obtains

  w(x)=beta x-2sigma p0 x^(1-h)+O(x^(1-2h)),
  v(y)=beta y+2sigma p0 y^(1-h)+O(y^(1-2h)),
  K_axis(y)/E(y)=2y^h[1+O(y^(-h))],
  1/v(y)-h/y=O(y^(-1-h)).                               (67.25)

These are the trace signs and clock convergence in Theorems 31, 45(e), 50(c) and 62(d). The leading positive branch also
has v>beta y eventually, as required by Theorem 57(a). Formula (66.14) has gamma=2, c=1 and P'(0)=2sigma p0, so its
second coefficient is exactly the one in (67.24). Both endpoint sectors in (65.8) and Theorem 66(e) follow already from
(67.20).

The escape law in Theorem 50(b) is a real angular restriction and can be checked without constructing a chart. For any
nonzero A of sign sigma define, with a fixed interior phi0,

  ell(phi)=-(1/q) integral_phi0^phi (|A|/F(t))^(2/q) dt.
  Then dphi/dell=-q(f(phi)/A)^(2/q).                    (67.26)

Since F is comparable to phi near 0 and to (alpha-phi)^2 near alpha, the integral diverges at both endpoints, with
opposite signs. It gives a decreasing smooth diffeomorphism from (0,alpha) onto R. Its inverse therefore has exactly the
law and range in Theorem 50(b). This is an angular parametrization; no unit-Jacobian chart for a coupled global solution
has been constructed.

Along an exterior orbit with interior limit angle phi_*, (67.14) gives dphi/dr=(a/beta)P(phi)r^(-1-h)+O(r^(-1-2h)).
Integration first gives phi-phi_*=O(r^(-h)); substitution back then gives phi=phi_*-aP(phi_*)r^(-h)+O(r^(-2h)), as in
(66.15). The sign of P proves the stated side of approach. For any orbit starting in the exterior open quadrant its
limit remains interior: division of the angular equation by phi(alpha-phi), using the endpoint zeros of its angular
numerator, gives an integrable logarithmic derivative for phi/(alpha-phi).

The radial Hessian test of Theorem 65(b), and its extension in 65(h), also causes no problem. If V=-P'e_r+aP e_phi, then

  |V|^2=p0^2[4cos(2phi)^2+a^2 sin(2phi)^2]>=a^2p0^2,
  D^2 W[e_r,e_r]
    =-h(1-h)r^(-1-h)V+O(r^(-1-2h)).                    (67.27)

Thus its norm is at least h(1-h)a p0 r^(-1-h)/2 eventually, uniformly in angle. There are no exterior vorticity zero
segments or flat vorticity zeros here in any case.

The growth tests require no new construction. Equations (67.11) and (67.20) give the natural nonzero outgoing vorticity,
nonzero temperature, and differentiated bounds of Theorems 31, 32, 37, 38, 41 and 45. Polar integration gives exterior
L^p integrability of Omega precisely for p>2/h=2beta, and a nonzero weak L^(2beta) tail. Its leading homogeneous field
has the corresponding nonzero homogeneous distribution law of Theorem 40. Nonzero angular leading terms also give the
positive annular limits for temperature gradient, vorticity, velocity and velocity gradient in Theorem 38. In particular
the annular velocity energy grows as a positive constant times R^(4-2h). The bounded-velocity and smaller-energy
hypotheses in Theorems 19, 23, 24 and 28 are not met when they would imply exclusion. No whole-plane integrability or
orbit-distribution assertion is inferred for the truncations.

The signs of the leading coefficients of sigma Theta_x, sigma Theta_y and sigma Theta_phi are respectively D0 and the
two expressions in (67.21). Each takes both signs in the open quadrant. Fixed interior angles preserve these signs for
large r. They give both signs on every sufficiently high horizontal line, every sufficiently distant vertical line, and
every sufficiently large quadrant arc. The demands on every smaller line or arc in Theorems 50(e) and 57(b) involve the
unconstructed interior. Also sigma Theta_r/(r^(q-1)F) tends uniformly to q>0. The zero-limit and opposite-sign
hypotheses in Theorem 57(c) are absent for each interior ray of these data.

Theorem 55 requires a radial sign change somewhere, not negativity of the corresponding expression at infinity. Here
(67.19) gives

  sigma [r d_r Omega+(1+2h)Omega]
    =(1+h)r^(-h)sin(2phi)[1+o(1)]>0                    (67.28)

throughout the exterior open quadrant. Any global realization must therefore have the negative open set required by
Theorem 55 inside a bounded region. Its positive-kernel balance is not an identity on this exterior alone.

There is also a positive-weight test that is entirely visible at infinity. On the positive branch and for zeta in a
compact subinterval of (0,infinity), put x=zeta y^(1/2+h). Taylor expansion at the y-axis using (67.24), with the
uniform differentiated bounds, gives

  Theta(x,y)=zeta^2+o(1),
  Omega(x,y)=y^(-1/2)[2zeta+o(1)],
  dx=y^(1/2+h) d zeta.                                  (67.29)

The temperature Taylor error has order y^(-1+2h); the vorticity error has that relative order. Both tend to zero. For
any continuous nonnegative H on (0,infinity), H not identically zero, choose a compact zeta interval where H(zeta^2) is
bounded below by a positive constant. Its row contribution to H(Theta)Omega is at least C y^h for large y. The exterior
integral therefore diverges to positive infinity, as required by Remark 55.1.

The other weighted assertions in that remark have a different status. Its estimate phi_K,x=O(r^(-3)) and Theta=O(r^q),
q<1, make the exterior integral of |Theta phi_K,x| finite. The two infinite signed parts in (55.16) arise in the source
region in its proof. They cannot be required to diverge in the far field. Likewise the ordered identity (55.15) retains
the interior contributions. The leading formula for phi_K,x in (55.17) has angular factor
sin(phi)[sin(phi)^2-3cos(phi)^2], with both signs, and presents no exterior sign conflict.

To compare the axis requirement behind Theorem 65(e), take sigma=1, write lambda=beta+2, and let A>0 denote the
unspecified source value Theta_y(P_ax). Equations (67.24)-(67.25) give

  xi=A w/(lambda T)
    =c_axis x^(1+2h)
       [1-2p0(1+2h)x^(-h)+O(x^(-2h))],
  c_axis=A beta/lambda, T=Theta_y(.,0),
  H0(xi)=A/T(x(xi)) comparable to xi^(2/(beta+2)),
  mu=(beta-1)/(beta+2).                                  (67.30)

Differentiation gives H0'=O(xi^(2/(beta+2)-1)). Consequently xi^(mu-2)(H0-1) has a positive integrable tail: its leading
exponent is -1-1/(beta+2). The right side of (65.16) for these data is -(2lambda^2/3)c_axis^mu<0, since t0=1 and
G'(0)=2. That identity would require a negative contribution before the tail, and hence an overshoot T>A, exactly as
Theorem 65(e) asserts. It is a condition on an interior axis completion, not an identity already realized by the formal
expansion. The source restrictions on w''(L) and higher derivatives remain unassigned. The orbit moments in 65(d)
likewise require the complete height function; their prescribed derivative has the correct negative sign because f/A>0
and G>0.

On the negative branch, the traces of Theorem 66(g) are T0=-Theta_y and k0=-Omega_y. From (67.24)-(67.25),

  w k0/T0^2=2beta x^(3h)[1+O(x^(-h))],
  (w k0/T0^2)'=6x^(3h-1)+O(x^(2h-1)),
  3k0/T0^2=6x^(3h-1)+O(x^(2h-1)),
  T0'/T0^2=-2h x^(2h-1)[1+O(x^(-h))].                  (67.31)

Thus the leading terms agree in (66.19); the formal trace equations give its coefficientwise agreement to arbitrary
order. Its boundary term at infinity diverges. It cannot be discarded to obtain a zero-boundary global moment. The
bounded opposite-sign trace intervals and their required net temperature increases in (66.20) are interior data;
eventual positivity of k0 and decrease of T0 are precisely the required tail behavior.

We finally specify the remaining limits of the comparisons. The strain and axis kernel integrals in Theorems 9, 45, 50,
54 and 55 have absolutely convergent tails for (67.11): each relevant kernel at a fixed axis abscissa is O(r^(-2)), and
Omega=O(r^(-h)). Their vorticity tails are O(R^(-h)). Their fixed total values, however, require the interior and, where
present, L. The positive mass requirements of Theorem 62(b) have the same limitation. Negative exterior vorticity on the
negative branch already supplies its required negative region in D_out. The local jets and source trace conditions of
Theorems 26, 27, 29 and 62(c) are not fixed by the far-field coefficients.

The finite-chain angular restrictions in Theorem 58(c), and the outgoing zero orders in Theorems 46, 54 and 60, are
conditional on additional saddles and their escaping branches. These data have no interior angular zero, so a
realization with the stated exhaustive chain decomposition could only have n=0. This agrees with the intended (H1)
comparison; it does not construct it. The proper growth in Theorem 58(e) is consistent with Ly=(2beta-1)beta
r^2/2+O(r^(2-h)) and Hc=O(r^(2-2h)). Its global potentials and complete backward orbits are not defined by the formal
series. Theorem 62(e) does not impose a sign bound on the source temperature through the Hessian of its corrected
Lyapunov function.

Theorem 63(a) concerns bounded complete connections with zero temperature. There is no such exterior orbit because W_r>0
and sigma Theta>0 there. Its remaining parts concern beta=2. The ray prohibitions in Theorems 62(a) and 64(b) are
additional hypotheses and are not imposed here. On the negative branch the positive interior region required by
Theorem 21(a), if realized, would give negative-positive-negative ray triples using the origin jet and (67.13).
Theorems 64(c) and 66(d) require late positive signed vorticity on appropriate rays and escaping orbits; (67.13)
supplies the exterior sign, but not those orbits' earlier history. The open potential and dead-region alternatives in
Theorem 64(d)-(f) are absent in the exterior, and its forced dead angular intervals cannot occur for these data.
Component balances and crossing conditions in Theorem 66(a)-(d) concern a bounded opposite-sign region that remains to
be constructed.

None of this turns (67.2) into a characterization of actual leading pairs. For example the endpoint-smooth pair

  f_alt=sin(phi)cos(phi)^2 cos(2phi)^2,
  G_alt=sin(2phi)                                        (67.32)

has f_alt=f_alt'=0 and G_alt=1 at phi=pi/4. It is formally solvable by (a)-(d) but is excluded as actual leading data by
Theorem 47(a). The explicit pair (67.11) avoids that obstruction. This distinction proves the stated, restricted
compatibility assertion and explains why it gives neither a global realization nor a limit on possible far-field
arguments. QED.

### Theorem 68 (beta = 2: the formal natural far field and compatibility of the far-field necessary conditions)

Work at beta = 2. References to an actual profile mean an A2-broad profile. Put alpha = pi/2, Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0},
X = r(cos(phi),sin(phi)), z = log r, and S_j(phi) = sin(j phi). Primes denote angular derivatives. Use
U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x), W = 2X+U, and the curl convention d_y U_1-d_x U_2 = Omega. For an actual profile, a0 != 0 is the
coefficient of x^2 y in the origin jet of Theta, sigma = sgn(a0), Z = {W = 0}, and S_+ is the set of angles in (0,alpha)
whose ray contains a point with Omega > 0. A polynomial coefficient means a polynomial in z with smooth angular
coefficients. The notation O_infty is that of Theorem 36. The interior symbols C, Q+, M and conditional hypotheses (S),
(R), (X), (Y), (V+), (I) retain their meanings in Theorems 48 and 59.

(a) The reflection and axis conditions on smooth leading data H,G are exactly

  H^(2j)(0) = 0, H^(2j+1)(alpha) = 0, H(alpha) = 0,
  G^(2j)(0) = G^(2j)(alpha) = 0, j = 0,1,2,... .         (68.1)

These are the endpoint conditions supplied by the A2 parities, Theta(0,y) = 0, and Theorems 33, 34, 36 and 45. They are
not a list of all necessary conditions on an actual profile. In particular, those theorems also require H and G to be
nonzero, and Theorem 34 requires sgn(a0)G > 0 on an interval.

For every smooth pair satisfying (68.1), including pairs without those nontriviality properties, there is a formal
expansion to every finite order

  Theta ~ sum_(n>=0) r^(-n/2) H_n(z,phi),
  Omega ~ sum_(n>=0) r^(-(n+1)/2) G_n(z,phi),
  Psi   ~ sum_(n>=0) r^((3-n)/2) P_n(z,phi).              (68.2)

Here H_0 = H, G_0 = G, and P_0 = P is the unique odd-odd solution of -P''-(9/4)P = G. All coefficients are polynomial
coefficients. Each H_n satisfies the endpoint conditions of H, including H_n(z,alpha) = 0. Each G_n and P_n has smooth
odd reflection at both endpoints. The equations W.grad Theta = 0, W.grad Omega+Omega = Theta_x and -Lap Psi = Omega hold
formally.

Once the preceding coefficients are fixed, the only freedom occurs at n = 4m+3, m >= 1. It is one real constant c_m in

  P_(4m+3): c_m S_(2m),
  Psi:     c_m r^(-2m) S_(2m).                           (68.3)

The constants are fixed by the interior if an actual globally smooth canonical solution exists. They are free parameters
of the formal exterior construction.

(b) At each resonant order, every polynomial resonant forcing has a polynomial inverse. A nonzero resonant forcing
requires a nonconstant polynomial in z in that angular mode of P_n. Thus the recursion imposes no further condition on
H,G when logarithms are allowed.

At the first resonance nonzero forcing is an open dense condition in the real space of smooth pairs satisfying (68.1),
with its usual smooth topology. At every later resonance it is an open dense condition jointly in that pair and the
finitely many preceding constants c_j. This does not assert nonvanishing for each fixed choice of preceding constants,
or relative density in any additional sign or plateau class.

Theorems 36 and 45 do not exclude these logarithms. Nor do the smooth angular coordinates of Theorem 36(d), the regular
backward coordinates of Theorem 39, the outgoing-amplitude estimate of Theorem 40(e), or the axis estimate of
Theorem 45(e) impose a log-free expansion at the resonant orders.

(c) Truncate all three sums in (68.2) at the same index N >= 0, and define U_N and W_N from Psi_N. Poisson, divergence
and curl are exact: -Lap Psi_N = Omega_N, div U_N = 0, and d_y U_(N,1)-d_x U_(N,2) = Omega_N. If R_T = W_N.grad Theta_N
and R_V = W_N.grad Omega_N+Omega_N-(Theta_N)_x, there is an integer d_N >= 0 such that, for every Cartesian multi-index
nu,

  partial_X^nu R_T =
    O(r^(-(N+1)/2-|nu|)(1+log r)^d_N),
  partial_X^nu R_V =
    O(r^(-(N+2)/2-|nu|)(1+log r)^d_N), r >= 2.           (68.4)

The constants in these estimates can depend on N, nu and the chosen data.

(d) There are explicit smooth pairs for either sign sigma in {-1,+1} that satisfy all the angular necessary conditions
in Theorems 1-65 applicable to the following classes: finitely many components of Z = {W=0}; Omega >= 0 on Q1, with
sigma = +1; and a0 < 0 with bounded {Omega > 0} cap Q1, with sigma = -1. Here compatibility means the angular conditions
and asymptotic axis signs, with the hypotheses of each cited theorem retained. It does not mean satisfaction of
identities involving an unknown interior, source curve or flow.

The pairs also have the stronger one-excursion angular pattern of Theorem 48(e). More precisely, a = alpha/3,
b = 2alpha/3 and J = (a,b) can be used, with

  sigma H > 0 on (0,alpha), H = sigma on [a,b],
  sigma H' > 0 on (0,a), sigma H' < 0 on (b,alpha),
  {G = 0} = {0,alpha} union [a,b],
  sigma G > 0 on (0,a) union (b,alpha).                  (68.5)

Every intermediate signed temperature has exactly two angular preimages. The plateau meets the angular conclusion of
Theorem 63(c). For the negative pair, any nonempty open interval with closure in J meets the necessary angular
inclusions for S_+ in Theorem 62 when its additional ray hypotheses hold; no planar positive-vorticity set is being
constructed.

For every choice of the constants in (68.3), all positive-order H_n and all G_n vanish on J. Every finite truncation
therefore solves the full equations exactly on the sector phi in J, with Theta_N = sigma, Omega_N = 0 and harmonic
Psi_N.

Scope. The construction is formal. No convergence, global profile, prescribed interior jet, or exact solution on the
whole exterior of a disc is asserted. The exact solution on the plateau sector is the only exterior existence assertion
here. The global identities and interior structures in the cited theorems are not realized. No uniform eventual
vorticity sign through a shrinking angular transition is asserted. The result does not show that every far-field
argument must fail. No result for beta > 2 is used.

Proof.

First consider the endpoint conditions. Smooth odd reflection at an endpoint is equivalent to vanishing of all even
derivatives there, and smooth even reflection is equivalent to vanishing of all odd derivatives. Thus the parities and
the additional y-axis temperature condition give precisely (68.1). Conversely, those conditions give the required smooth
reflections on the angle circle. The endpoint and regularity assertions of Theorems 33, 36 and 45 impose no additional
endpoint equations. In particular they do not prescribe vanishing or nonvanishing of H'(0), H''(alpha), G'(0) or
G'(alpha). The sign and nontriviality conclusions of Theorem 34 are separate, as are the later conditional endpoint
inequalities in Theorems 57 and 59.

Put D = partial_z and a_n = (3-n)/2. Direct polar differentiation gives

  U[r^a P] = r^(a-1)(-P' e_r+((a+D)P)e_phi),
  -Lap(r^a P) = -r^(a-2)[partial_phi^2+(a+D)^2]P.        (68.6)

A velocity term of index k acting on a temperature term of index l has radial exponent -(k+l+1)/2. Acting on a vorticity
term it has exponent -(k+l+2)/2. Also d_x = cos(phi)partial_r-r^(-1)sin(phi)partial_phi. Equating coefficients in the
two transport equations therefore gives, for n >= 1,

  (n-2D)H_n =
    sum_(k+l=n-1) [-P_k'(D-l/2)H_l
                         + ((a_k+D)P_k)H_l'],
  (n-2D)G_n =
    sum_(k+l=n-1) [-P_k'(D-(l+1)/2)G_l
                         + ((a_k+D)P_k)G_l']
    + cos(phi)((n-1)/2-D)H_(n-1)+sin(phi)H_(n-1)',
  -[partial_phi^2+(a_n+D)^2]P_n = G_n.                  (68.7)

Each D on a right side acts only on its immediately following coefficient. The linear radial terms in the transport
equations are (2D-n)H_n and (2D-n)G_n, respectively, which fixes the signs in (68.7). With D = 0 this is the recursion
in Remark 39.1.

The first two right sides involve only preceding indices. On polynomials of degree at most d their inverse is

  (n-2D)^(-1) = (1/n) sum_(i=0)^d (2D/n)^i.             (68.8)

Multiplication telescopes, since D^(d+1) = 0. The top coefficient of a nonzero polynomial is multiplied by n, so the
kernel on all polynomials is zero.

On smooth odd-odd angular functions, let A_n = -partial_phi^2-a_n^2. The sine basis is S_(2m), m >= 1, with eigenvalues
4m^2-a_n^2. At a nonresonant order, division of the rapidly decreasing sine coefficients by these eigenvalues preserves
smoothness and all reflection conditions. The inverse on polynomial coefficients is the finite sum

  [A_n-2a_nD-D^2]^(-1)
    = sum_(i=0)^d [A_n^(-1)(2a_nD+D^2)]^i A_n^(-1).     (68.9)

The factors commute and 2a_nD+D^2 lowers degree, so telescoping proves the formula. The top-degree argument proves
uniqueness.

An eigenvalue vanishes exactly when |3-n| = 4m. For n >= 0 and m >= 1, this means n = 4m+3. In particular n = 3 is not
resonant; a constant angular mode is not odd-odd. At a resonance, (68.9) applies on the orthogonal complement of S_(2m).
If g(z) is the coefficient of S_(2m) in G_n, its remaining equation and all its polynomial solutions are

  D(4m-D)p = g,
  p(z) = c_m+int_0^z [(4m-D)^(-1)g](t) dt,
  (4m-D)^(-1)g = (1/(4m))sum_(i=0)^d (D/(4m))^i g.      (68.10)

The same telescoping calculation verifies the inverse. The homogeneous equation gives p' = 0. If g has top term g_d z^d,
with g_d != 0, the top term of p is g_d z^(d+1)/(4m(d+1)). This proves both existence and the asserted logarithmic
forcing.

Reflection invariance of the equations, or direct inspection of (68.7), preserves all parities. The extra temperature
boundary value follows separately by induction. At phi = alpha, each summand in the first equation contains either H_l
or D H_l, which vanish there, or P_k or D P_k, which also vanish there. The inverse (68.8) preserves this zero boundary
value. The initial Dirichlet inverse is nonresonant. Induction now proves (a).

There are no polynomial homogeneous temperature or vorticity solutions at positive index by (68.8). Nonpolynomial
solutions of the homogeneous transport operator are outside (68.2). Growing odd-odd harmonic stream functions
r^(2m)S_(2m) have velocities of order r^(2m-1), contrary to U = o(r), including m = 1. A constant or radial logarithmic
stream function has the wrong parity. Within (68.2) only the decaying terms (68.3) remain. They cannot be freely added
to a globally smooth solution, since they are singular at the origin. Equivalently, an entire harmonic velocity
difference of sublinear growth is constant by the interior derivative estimate for harmonic functions; its A2 parities
make that constant zero.

At n = 1, (68.7) gives precisely Theorem 45(f):

  H_1 = (3/2)PH',
  G_1 = (1/2)P'G+(3/2)PG'+sin(phi)H',
  -P_1''-P_1 = G_1, P_1(0) = P_1(alpha) = 0.            (68.11)

Here and below the sine coefficient of a function means (2/alpha) times its integral against that sine on [0,alpha].

For completeness, finite algebraic certificates show that every resonant forcing map in (b) is nonzero. At the first
resonance take h = (S_1+S_3)/4 and G_0 = 0. Through index 6 the odd H indices and even G indices vanish. Direct
substitution in the nonresonant recursion gives

  G_1 = -S_2/4+3S_4/8,
  H_2 = 29S_1/1920-7S_3/1920-9S_5/640+3S_7/640,
  G_3 = 3S_2/160+S_4/48-9S_6/160+3S_8/160,
  H_4 = 161S_1/921600-337S_3/307200+247S_5/368640
          +581S_7/614400-171S_9/204800+33S_11/204800,
  G_5 = 133S_2/307200-1303S_4/409600-7S_6/368640
          +147S_8/20480-1089S_10/204800+429S_12/409600,
  H_6 = 841S_1/73728000-107S_3/24576000
          +19069S_5/221184000-24349S_7/221184000
          -493S_9/11059200+91S_11/819200
          -203S_13/4096000+7S_15/1024000,
  [S_2]G_7 = 203/7372800,
  [z S_2]P_7 = 203/29491200.                            (68.12)

One way to verify each line is to divide the S_j coefficient of G_n by j^2-(3-n)^2/4 to obtain P_n, and use S_i cos(j
phi) = (S_(i+j)+S_(i-j))/2 in (68.7) with D = 0. These rules, starting with P_0 = 0, determine every entry in (68.12),
including the last forcing. The use of G_0 = 0 here is a test of a polynomial map, not a candidate A2 profile. For a
nonzero leading G, the pair of Remark 39.1, namely H_0 = h and G_0 = -sin(phi)h', has the additional certificate

  [S_2]G_7 =
    -248652665830143836372937708761809789
      /5600812026228230278370435051520000000000.          (68.13)

For the later resonances take m >= 2, K = 2m-2, J0 = 2K+3, H_0 = t h and G_0 = 0. Set the preceding free constants to
zero except for c S_K in P_(J0). Extract the coefficient of c t^2 in G_(J0+4). The following finite formulas specify
that coefficient completely. Define the fixed angular functions

  g = -S_2/4+3S_4/8, p = -S_2/12+S_4/40,
  u = p h'/2,
  v = (p'g+pg'+cos(phi)u+sin(phi)u')/3.                 (68.14)

Thus u and v are the coefficients of t^2 in H_2 and G_3. Write s_K = S_K, and set

  A = -K s_K h'/(J0+1),
  B = [s_K'g-K s_K g'
           +((J0+1)/2)cos(phi)A+sin(phi)A']/(J0+2),
  -C''-(K+1)^2 C = B, C(0) = C(alpha) = 0,
  E = [s_K'u-K s_K u'+((J0+1)/2)p'A+pA'
                                      -(K+1)C h']/(J0+3),
  F = [2s_K'v-K s_K v'+((J0+3)/2)p'B+pB'
           +C'g-(K+1)Cg'
           +((J0+3)/2)cos(phi)E+sin(phi)E']/(J0+4).
                                                               (68.15)

The inverse defining C is nonresonant since K+1 is odd. The functions A,B,C,E,F are, in order, the relevant coefficients
of H_(J0+1), G_(J0+2), P_(J0+2), H_(J0+3), G_(J0+4). This follows by extracting powers of c,t in (68.7). Terms of degree
at least 3 in t or at least 2 in c cannot contribute. The first background logarithm has degree 4 in t, so no omitted
logarithm contributes either. In this quotient of the parameter polynomial ring all derivatives D are zero.

Expansion by the same sine product rule gives

  [S_(K+2)]F =
    K(K+1)^2(224K^4+1624K^3+3788K^2+3194K+695)
      /[256(K+3)(2K-1)(2K+1)(2K+3)(2K+5)^2(2K+7)]
                                      for even K >= 4,
  [S_4]F = -30203/554400                for K = 2.       (68.16)

To account for the exceptional value, the signed frequencies in (68.15) are K+d with d in {0,+2,-2,+4,-4,+6,-6,+8,-8}.
For even K >= 4 no additional frequency is the negative of K+2. At K = 2, K-6 = -(K+2); its extra contribution is
-193/3200. The uncollided rational expression at K = 2 is 12937/2217600, giving exactly the second line of (68.16). All
factors in the first expression are positive for K >= 4. Thus the forcing map is nonzero at every later resonance.

At each fixed index the recursion is a continuous polynomial map of the smooth leading pair and the preceding real
constants. Indeed multiplication, angular differentiation, the smooth angular inverses, the finite sums in
(68.8)-(68.10), and integration in z have this property. Induction bounds the polynomial degree in z at each fixed
index. Hence each fixed angular and z coefficient of a resonant forcing is a continuous real polynomial. The
certificates (68.12) and (68.16) show that at least one such polynomial is nonzero at each resonance.

A nonzero continuous real polynomial on this vector space cannot vanish on a nonempty open set: restrict to the line
from a point of that set to an arbitrary point, and apply the one-variable polynomial identity theorem. The zero set of
the entire forcing is closed and is contained in the zero set of this nonzero scalar polynomial. It therefore has empty
interior. This proves the open dense assertions, also on restriction to any nonempty open nontriviality and
sign-at-some-angle conditions. It proves no relative density assertion on the nonlinear plateau classes.

For the remainder issue, every smooth angular function A, integer d >= 0 and epsilon > 0 satisfy

  r^q(log r)^d A(phi) = O_infty(r^(q+epsilon)).           (68.17)

Each Cartesian derivative is r^(-1) times a smooth angular combination of r partial_r and partial_phi. It does not
increase the logarithmic degree. The inequality (log r)^d <= C_epsilon r^epsilon proves (68.17) at every derivative
order. The first possible logarithm is in P_7, contributing r^(-2)log r to Psi and r^(-3)log r to U. Its first possible
transport contribution has index 8, contributing r^(-4)log r to Theta and r^(-9/2)log r to Omega. All these orders lie
strictly below the remainders asserted in Theorems 36 and 45.

Theorem 36(d) asserts smoothness in the launch angle and convergence in angular smooth norms with error O(r^(-1/2)). It
asserts no smooth extension in r^(-1/2) at zero. The smooth variable exp(4t) in Theorem 39 concerns approach to a finite
regular backward zero, not approach to spatial infinity. Theorem 40(e) follows from the leading natural estimates and
allows an O(exp(-t)) outgoing-amplitude error. The logarithmic terms above are smaller. Finally, Theorem 45(e) uses
integrability of 1/v(y)-1/(2y), which already follows from v(y)=2y+O(y^(1/2)); these logarithms do not affect it. These
results give no resonant vanishing equation. This proves (b).

To prove (c), apply (68.6) separately to each term. The third equation of (68.7), including index zero, gives exact
Poisson, and the stream representation gives exact divergence and curl. In R_T all coefficients through radial exponent
-N/2 cancel. The remaining nonlinear products have k+l >= N, with smallest exponent -(N+1)/2. In R_V the products not
cancelled have smallest exponent -(N+2)/2; the last temperature derivative has that exponent as well. There are only
finitely many remaining terms, each a radial power times a polynomial in log r. Their maximum polynomial degree supplies
d_N, and Cartesian differentiation proves (68.4).

We next specify the data in (d). Use the positive angular construction already established in Theorem 59(g). In the
present notation it is

  eta(t) = exp(-1/t) for t > 0, eta(t) = 0 for t <= 0,
  chi(t) = eta(t)/(eta(t)+eta(1-t)),
  f_0(phi) = chi(2(a-phi)/a), 0 <= phi <= a,
  g_0(phi) = (alpha-phi)chi(2(phi-b)/(alpha-b)),
                                             b <= phi <= alpha,
  F_0 = int_0^a f_0(phi)dphi, B_0 = int_b^alpha g_0(phi)dphi,
  f = f_0/F_0, g = g_0/B_0.                             (68.18)

Both normalizing constants are positive. Define

  h(phi) = int_0^phi f(t)dt,             0 <= phi <= a,
           1,                          a <= phi <= b,
           int_phi^alpha g(t)dt,        b <= phi <= alpha;
  j(phi) = phi f(phi)^2,                0 <= phi <= a,
           0,                          a <= phi <= b,
           g(phi),                     b <= phi <= alpha.
                                                               (68.19)

Theorem 59(g) proves smoothness, flat transitions, strict signs on both passages, and the single plateau for these
functions. In particular the formulas near the axes are exact:

  h(phi) = phi/F_0, j(phi) = phi/F_0^2 near 0,
  h(phi) = (alpha-phi)^2/(2B_0),
  j(phi) = (alpha-phi)/B_0 near alpha.                   (68.20)

They verify every condition in (68.1). The same theorem gives the Dirichlet Green formula and its positivity. For
explicitness, with k_0 = 3/2 it is

  p(phi) = int_0^alpha K(phi,t)j(t)dt,
  K(phi,t) =
    sin(k_0 min(phi,t))sin(k_0(alpha-max(phi,t)))
      /[k_0 sin(k_0 alpha)].                            (68.21)

Its angular derivative has jump -1. Since k_0 alpha = 3pi/4, the kernel is positive in the open square and the
homogeneous Dirichlet problem has zero kernel. Thus -p''-(9/4)p = j. The positivity and strict concavity conclusions of
Theorem 59(g) give

  p > 0, p'' < 0 on (0,alpha),
  p'(0) = int_0^alpha sin(k_0(alpha-t))j(t)dt
                                      /sin(k_0 alpha) > 0,
  p'(alpha) = -int_0^alpha sin(k_0 t)j(t)dt
                                      /sin(k_0 alpha) < 0.
                                                               (68.22)

In particular p' has exactly one zero. The differential equation and the even endpoint derivative conditions for j give
the same odd-odd smooth reflection for p.

Take H = sigma h, G = sigma j and P = sigma p. Formula (68.11) now specifies the first corrections without a further
choice:

  H_1 = (3/2)p h',
  G_1 = (1/2)p'j+(3/2)pj'+sigma sin(phi)h',
  -P_1''-P_1 = G_1, P_1(0) = P_1(alpha) = 0.            (68.23)

The common quadratic terms do not change sign under simultaneous negation of H,G,P. This is why the two formal
continuations are not obtained by negating every coefficient.

We check the angular consequences of Theorems 1-65, retaining each conditional hypothesis. Theorems 33, 34, 36 and 45
require the nonzero natural tail, its reflections, the Dirichlet equation and the first corrections. These have all been
verified. The energy coefficient in Theorem 33(e) is positive because P is nonzero. The tail has vorticity exponent 1/2,
integrable p-th power exactly for p > 4 at infinity, and a nonzero weak L^4 tail, as in Theorem 45. Thus the
faster-decay, bounded-velocity and critical-energy hypotheses of Theorems 15, 19, 24, 25 and 28 are not inadvertently
imposed. The exclusions of finite energy and finite velocity or temperature integrals in Theorems 17, 18, 20 and 23 are
consistent with this tail. The finite angular-bandwidth exclusions of Theorems 10 and 49 do not apply to a smooth
function with a nontrivial flat plateau and nonconstant passages.

The critical angles of H in the open quadrant are exactly [a,b], where H'' = G = 0. Elsewhere H' != 0 and sigma G > 0.
This proves H'=0 implies G=0, as required by Theorem 47(a), the nonzero critical value of Theorem 48(c), and all the
implications in Theorem 64(h). In particular G=0 implies sigma H'>=0 with equality on the plateau; it does not require a
positive derivative there. The strict sign on the decreasing passage required by Theorem 59(b),(c) holds. Equations
(68.20) and (68.22) give H'(0)=sigma/F_0, H''(alpha)=sigma/B_0, G'(0)=sigma/F_0^2 and G'(alpha)=-sigma/B_0. For sigma=+1
these include all the endpoint inequalities of Theorems 57 and 59.

The range is [0,1] for sigma=+1 and [-1,0] for sigma=-1. Every intermediate signed level has one preimage on each
passage. This supplies the range and two-crossing pattern required by Theorem 53(h) and the N=1 case of
Theorem 56(d),(e), when their additional hypotheses hold. It does not choose the unknown temperature range or zero count
of a global flow. The conditional pattern of Theorem 48(e) has phi_1=0, phi_2=a, phi_3=b, phi_4=alpha and m=1. These
also give the stronger endpoint pattern in Theorem 59(c),(d). Different conditional interior configurations leading to
that same pattern are not being asserted simultaneously.

The constant interval required under the respective hypotheses of Theorems 35, 44, 47(d), 48(d), 51, 53(d), 56(a)-(c)
and 63(b),(c) is present. Its nonzero value is permitted: Theorem 63 does not identify its value with zero or require an
extremal value. Under the additional regular-component hypotheses the value can be the distinguished endpoint
temperature M=sigma. A connected zero arc can contain uncountably many regular zeros, so the regular-label conclusion of
Theorem 47(c) is not inconsistent with finite component count. Neither the actual arc nor its derivative matrix is
constructed here.

For sigma=+1, (68.22) gives all the stream signs in (59.5). The leading angular velocity is (3/2)p, and the leading
radial velocity is -p'. The sign assertions around the unique zero of p' follow on compact subintervals of strict sign.
Also U.grad Theta has leading term (3/2)p h' r^(-1/2), with both signs on the passages, as required in Theorem 59(b).
The leading Cartesian temperature derivatives are -sin(phi)H'/r and cos(phi)H'/r; their angular signs change on the two
passages.

The half-line tests of Theorem 57(b) also fit. For each fixed y_0>0, the endpoint expansion and reflected derivative
bounds give Theta(x,y_0)~sigma y_0/(F_0 x) as x tends to infinity. For each fixed x_0>0, they give Theta(x_0,y)~sigma
x_0^2/(2B_0 y^2) as y tends to infinity. Both are strictly signed and tend to zero. Together with the zero value at the
other, finite-axis end of either half-line, they force both derivative signs by the mean value theorem for any smooth
extension having the A2 axis values. The angular derivative test holds on every sufficiently large quadrant arc by the
two passages. The assertion about all finite radii retains its interior content.

For sigma=-1, bounded positive vorticity requires G<=0 and the signed stream inequalities of Theorem 64(a), all of which
hold. Theorem 62(a) requires S_+ to be nonempty and open. Under its additional ray prohibition, (62.1)-(62.2) require
S_+ subset {G>=0} and G=0 on S_+. Any open interval with closure in J obeys these inclusions. Under the further
hypotheses of Theorem 62(g), M=-1 has the required sign and that interval lies strictly inside the plateau. Bounded
positive vorticity alone does not imply the ray prohibition. On J the Green solution satisfies the local formula P=A
sin(3phi/2)+B1 cos(3phi/2), with strict sign sigma, as required by Theorem 64(g). No Dirichlet conditions are imposed at
a,b.

The asymptotic axis traces implied by the data are

  Theta_y(x,0) ~ sigma/(F_0 x),
  Omega_y(x,0) ~ sigma/(F_0^2 x^(3/2)),
  Theta_xx(0,y)/2 ~ sigma/(2B_0 y^2),
  Omega_x(0,y) ~ sigma/(B_0 y^(3/2)),
  Omega_x(0,y)/(Theta_xx(0,y)/2) ~ 2 sqrt(y),
  W_1(x,0) = 2x-P'(0)sqrt(x)+O(1),
  W_2(0,y) = 2y-P'(alpha)sqrt(y)+O(1).                 (68.24)

The minus sign in Omega_x(0,y) = -G'(alpha)y^(-3/2)+lower orders is included here. These formulas meet the outgoing-axis
consequences of Theorems 30, 31, 45(e), 57 and 62(c). They do not specify the finite-axis zeros, trace jets or integral
identities of Theorems 2, 14, 26, 27, 29 and 62(c).

The fibre requirements also need this distinction. At a regular angle Theorems 61(b) and 62(f) specify the constants

  k = sqrt(|H'(phi)|/2), B_e = k sin(phi)>0,
  D_e = G(phi)/sqrt(k), eps = -sgn H'(phi).
  On (0,a): D_e = sigma 2^(1/4) phi f^(7/4);
  on (b,alpha): D_e = sigma 2^(1/4) g^(3/4).             (68.25)

They are finite on each passage and have the required sign. As an angle tends to its adjoining plateau endpoint,
k,B_e,D_e tend to zero. In particular the k,B_e degeneration in Theorem 61(c) holds at the angular level. That theorem
does not require D_e to tend to zero; this additional limit is a property of the present data. Its superalgebraic
exit-parameter lower bounds, convergence on bounded fibre intervals, source-curve identity and the jet restrictions of
parts (d),(e) involve an unknown interior. The latter parts require a regular zero, so they cannot be inferred merely
from critical plateau angles. The displacement identities and dip bounds in Theorems 61(a),(b) and 62(f) likewise
involve the full half-fibre and its source height. Formula (68.25) does not assert those global identities.

The constancy on the plateau persists through the recursion. Assume preceding positive-index H_l and all preceding G_l
vanish on J. In the first equation of (68.7) the l=0 term vanishes because H_0 is constant there; all other terms vanish
by induction. The second equation vanishes for the same reason. The polynomial transport inverse is unique. Therefore

  H_n = 0 on J for n >= 1, G_n = 0 on J for n >= 0,
  [partial_phi^2+(a_n+D)^2]P_n = 0 on J for n >= 0.       (68.26)

This proves the exact sector assertion for finite truncations. The powers of z in the last equation can be coupled. For
example r^(-2)[log r sin(2phi)-phi cos(2phi)] is harmonic on an angular interval: the angular operator partial_phi^2+4
applied to -phi cos(2phi) gives 4sin(2phi), cancelling the radial logarithmic term. Thus a local potential sector does
not require the global expansion to be log-free. Smoothness gives flat vanishing of H_n,G_n at the transitions, but
gives no uniform eventual sign across them.

Finally, the global integral conditions are not angular normalizations. The strain identity of Theorems 9, 39(e) and
45(d) requires the full quadrant integral to be 3pi/2. Its exterior portion is only

  int_(Q1 cap {r>R}) xy r^(-4) Omega dX
    = 2R^(-1/2)int_0^alpha cos(phi)sin(phi)G(phi)dphi
      +O(R^(-1)).                                      (68.27)

It tends to zero and is negative for the negative pair at sufficiently large R. Thus positive interior vorticity is
necessary in that case, as already required by Theorem 62. The budgets in Theorem 62(b) also contain the core, its size,
and the unknown positive-vorticity bound. They are not verified by prescribing G.

At beta=2, Theorem 55 requires sigma(r partial_r+2)Omega<0 somewhere and gives the two x-axis Green-kernel balances. The
leading tail on a passage instead has sigma(r partial_r+2)Omega = (3/2)j r^(-1/2)+O(r^(-1))>0. The theorem does not
require its negative region to occur arbitrarily far out. Indeed, if an exact profile had the sector in (68.26), its
positive signed origin jet followed by zero vorticity on a plateau ray would require a decrease of r^2 sigma Omega
somewhere along that ray. This is compatible with Theorem 55. The kernel balances still depend on the interior and the
first axis zero.

For the isothermal restrictions of Theorems 48(f) and 53(i), with a smooth test function b_0 supported in the open
angular quadrant, the identity is

  int_({Theta=c} cap Q1)
    r^(-3)(-2b_0(phi)U_r+b_0'(phi)U_phi)dX
      = 2int_({H=c} cap (0,alpha)) b_0(phi)dphi.         (68.28)

The left integral uses planar measure over the full isothermal set. At c=sigma the plateau gives a nonzero right side
for suitable b_0. It is not permissible to replace the left side by the exterior sector. The full radial version in
Theorem 56(a) and the weighted identities in Theorems 56(g) and 59(f) have the same interior dependence. The outgoing
identities of Theorems 33, 39 and 40 either use the unknown flow coordinates or define an asymptotic constant, rather
than prescribe a numerical normalization of H,G.

The remaining component, local-jet and finite-orbit results in Theorems 1-65 make no additional standalone angular
demand beyond those checked above. Their interior hypotheses and conclusions have not been supplied by this
construction. Theorem 66 concerns beta>2 and has no specialization used here. This proves (d), with exactly the stated
scope.

### Theorem 69 (beta > 2: exact exterior solutions with the natural tail)

Put alpha = pi/2, h = 1/beta, q = 1-2h, a = 2-h and kappa = beta-2, where beta > 2. A prime denotes an angular
derivative. The A2 parities are even-odd for temperature, odd-odd for vorticity and stream function, odd-even for U_1,
and even-odd for U_2. Temperature is also required to vanish on the y-axis. Write Q1 = {x > 0,y > 0} and rcurl v = d_y
v_1-d_x v_2 for a plane vector field v, so that the curl convention reads rcurl U = Omega. The notation O_infty(r^b)
means that each Cartesian derivative of order j is O(r^(b-j)), uniformly in angle.

(a) Suppose f,G are smooth on [0,alpha] and, for every integer j >= 0, satisfy

  f^(2j)(0) = 0, f^(2j+1)(alpha) = 0, f(alpha) = 0,
  G^(2j)(0) = G^(2j)(alpha) = 0.                                (69.1)

Extend them by the indicated reflections. Let P be the unique odd-odd solution of -P''-a^2 P = G. Fix any smooth
compactly supported odd-odd function Omega_in, and fix a smooth radial cutoff shape 0 <= chi_0 <= 1, equal to zero on
[0,1] and to one on [2,infinity).

There is R such that smooth functions Theta,Omega exist on r > R, up to and across the axes, with these parities. Set
chi(X) = chi_0(|X|/R) and

  Omega_tot = Omega_in+chi Omega,
  U = BS(Omega_tot), W = beta X+U,
  U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x), -Lap Psi = Omega_tot.                     (69.2)

Here chi Omega is extended by zero, and BS is the canonical parity-grouped whole-plane Biot-Savart inverse. The
functions Omega_tot,U,Psi are smooth on the plane; Psi is odd-odd. The velocity is uniformly sublinear and has the A2
parities. On r > 2R the equations

  W.grad Theta = kappa Theta,
  W.grad Omega+Omega = Theta_x,
  div W = 2 beta, d_y W_1-d_x W_2 = Omega                       (69.3)

hold exactly. The radial velocity is positive there. Define

  f1 = -qP'f+aPf',
  G1 = hP'G+aPG'-q cos(phi)f+sin(phi)f',
  -P1''-(2-2h)^2 P1 = G1,
  psi_0 = r^a P, psi_1 = r^(2-2h)P1,
  u_i = (-d_y psi_i,d_x psi_i), i = 0,1.                        (69.4)

P1 is the unique odd-odd solution. The following estimates hold:

  Theta = r^q(f+r^(-h)f1)+O_infty(r^(q-2h)),
  Omega = r^(-h)(G+r^(-h)G1)+O_infty(r^(-3h)),
  U = u_0+u_1+O_infty(r^(1-3h)),
  Psi = psi_0+psi_1+O_infty(r^(2-3h)).                          (69.5)

In particular all derivative bounds and the first corrections in Theorem 42 hold on the exterior. No nonvanishing
condition on f or G is required for this existence assertion.

(b) There is a precise small class in which a cutoff construction is unique. Fix 0 < vartheta < 1. For a scalar, vector
or tensor v on r > s, define

  ||v||_(b,k,vartheta;s)
     = sup_(rho >= s) rho^(-b)
         ||v(rho .)||_(C^(k,vartheta)({1 <= |z| <= 2})).
                                                               (69.6)

One-sided limits at the inner circle are used. Equivalent norms using slightly overlapping annuli have the same meaning.
There are M,C_* > 0, depending only on beta,vartheta,chi_0 and finitely many norms of f,G, such that the construction
below, with uniform angular limits r^(-q)Theta -> f and r^h Omega -> G, is unique among smooth auxiliary solutions whose
odd-odd vorticity remainders lie in

  Omega = r^(-h)G+omega_rem,
  ||omega_rem||_(-2h,1,vartheta;R/2) <= M.                      (69.7)

For this assertion both transport equations in (69.3), with auxiliary Omega, are imposed on r > R/2, and Omega_tot is
defined by (69.2). The auxiliary equation rcurl U = Omega is not imposed in the cutoff region; there rcurl U = chi
Omega. Temperature has the stated A2 parities and vanishes on the y-axis. Its uniform leading limit is part of the
uniqueness prescription. Choose R >= 2 so that supp Omega_in is contained in r < R/4, the normalized C^(2,vartheta) norm
of BS(Omega_in) in weight 1-h on r > R/2 is at most one, and

  M(R/2)^(-h) <= 1, C_*(R/2)^(-h) <= 1/2.                       (69.8)

Increasing C_* includes the radial-velocity lower bound. The contraction metric is
||omega_rem,1-omega_rem,2||_(-2h,0,vartheta;R/2). Thus uniqueness in (b) includes a fixed auxiliary prescription in the
cutoff region.

Uniqueness from only f,G,Omega_in and the exterior equations in (a) is false, even with chi fixed, smooth remainders,
and the expansions (69.5). Vorticity in the transition annulus is additional data.

(c) The decaying harmonic velocity terms are determined by the whole vorticity, not an additional velocity gauge. More
explicitly, fix r_b > 2R and write Omega_tot = sum_(m >= 1) omega_m(r)sin(2m phi). On r > r_b,

  Psi = sum_(m >= 1) [
       (1/(4m))r^(-2m)int_(r_b)^r t^(2m+1)omega_m(t)dt
       +(1/(4m))r^(2m)int_r^infinity t^(1-2m)omega_m(t)dt
       +c_m(r_b)r^(-2m)]sin(2m phi),
  c_m(r_b) = (1/(4m))int_0^r_b t^(2m+1)omega_m(t)dt.            (69.9)

The harmonic sum converges smoothly on every closed exterior r >= r_b+epsilon. Its velocity terms are
c_m(r_b)r^(-2m-1)(-2m cos(2m phi),-2m sin(2m phi)) in polar components. These are exact Green-formula constants with the
particular inverse normalized at r_b. Their numerical values are not identified with the formal constants c_m of
Theorem 67 without matching its particular-solution normalization. For any fixed normalization, the coefficient is
determined by Omega_tot. A different normalization of the particular inverse, including normalization of formal
logarithmic terms, changes the displayed constants by the corresponding particular harmonic coefficients. None can be
independently added while Omega_tot is fixed.

The construction gives an explicit description of the failure of the whole-plane transport equations. Put
Theta_tot = chi Theta. Since chi vanishes on r <= R, this is a smooth completion. On R < r < 2R its residuals are

  W.grad Theta_tot-kappa Theta_tot = (W.grad chi)Theta,
  W.grad Omega_tot+Omega_tot-(Theta_tot)_x
       = (W.grad chi)Omega-chi_x Theta.                         (69.10)

On r < R they are respectively zero and W.grad Omega_in+Omega_in. These are formulas for the residuals, not assertions
that each is nonzero everywhere. The elliptic, divergence and curl equations for Omega_tot hold everywhere.

(d) For either sigma = 1 or sigma = -1, put s = sin(phi), c = cos(phi), p0 = 1/[h(4-h)], and choose

  f = sigma s c^2, G = sigma sin(2phi),
  P = sigma p0 sin(2phi),
  f1 = 2p0 s c^2[(1+h)-(4+h)s^2],
  G1 = sigma(h-1)sin(2phi)/2
           +[2p0+sigma(1+h)/4]sin(4phi).                        (69.11)

The solutions in (a) then satisfy sigma Theta > 0 and sigma Omega > 0 throughout Q1 cap {r > R'} for a sufficiently
large R'. They have no zero of W there. Their tails satisfy the exterior bounds and limits in Theorems 41, 42 and 45;
the angular implication in Theorem 47(a); the angular and eventual axis signs in Theorem 50(b),(c); the sign changes on
sufficiently high horizontal lines, sufficiently distant vertical lines and sufficiently large arcs in Theorems 50(e)
and 57(b), and the eventual radial sign in Theorem 57(c); the angular signs and absence of open exterior vorticity-zero
regions in Theorem 64(a); and the conclusions about angular data, eventual axis signs and exterior zero contacts in
Theorems 65(b),(c),(h) on the positive branch, and the signed conclusions in Theorem 66(e),(f) on either branch. The
positive branch also has the eventual signs in Theorem 57(a); the negative branch has the eventual axis signs in
Theorem 62(c),(d).

All statements here refer to exterior restrictions of those conclusions. In particular, Theorems 65 and 66 are not being
applied with their full whole-plane hypotheses. The forward integral and angle laws meaningful in the exterior, the
exterior potential, and the precise status of the source-normalized orbit label are given in the proof.

(e) Consequently, no condition implied solely by the exterior system, canonical whole-plane inversion, and these natural
tails can exclude all the examples (69.11). This does not remove angular restrictions on actual profiles whose proofs
use the interior. It does not assert that the exterior of a profile is parametrized by only its leading pair and
Omega_in.

Scope. Exterior solutions are not profiles. The interior equations, the nonzero origin jet, P_ax, and (H1) are not
realized. Complete backward-orbit identities, balances involving the origin or an axis source, and global sign or
source-basin hypotheses are not consequences of this construction. Neither a full asymptotic expansion nor convergence
of the formal series of Theorem 67 is asserted. No assertion at beta = 2 is made.

Proof.

We first give the analytic estimates used to construct the fields. This also records the derivative counts in the fixed
point.

The reflections in (69.1) give smooth functions on the circle: odd reflection matches precisely the even derivatives
that vanish, and even reflection matches precisely the odd derivatives that vanish. Odd-odd functions have the basis
sin(2m phi), m >= 1. Since 0 < a < 2, the multipliers 4m^2-a^2 are positive. Division by these multipliers gives a
smooth P, with the asserted uniqueness. The same argument applies to P1 because 1 < 2-2h < 2.

Let K(z) = (z_2,-z_1)/(2pi|z|^2). If 0 < gamma < 2, v is odd-odd, supported in r >= R, and has a finite norm in weight
-gamma, its grouped inverse satisfies

  ||BS(v)||_(1-gamma,k+1,vartheta;R/2)
        <= C ||v||_(-gamma,k,vartheta;R/2),                     (69.12)

where the norm of a cut-off function on the right can be bounded by the exterior norm before cutoff. Constants are
independent of R >= 2. The same estimate applies to differences.

Here is the needed justification. For r = |X|, split the integral into |Y| < r/2, r/2 <= |Y| <= 2r, and |Y| > 2r. The
first part is bounded by C r^(-1)int_0^r t^(1-gamma)dt, hence C r^(1-gamma). The middle part has the same bound by local
integrability of |X-Y|^(-1). In the last part subtract K(-Y). Its integral over every centered annulus is zero by
parity, while |K(X-Y)-K(-Y)| <= C r |Y|^(-2). The resulting bound is C r int_(2r)^infinity t^(-1-gamma)dt. These
estimates prove convergence, the size estimate, and uniform sublinearity. They also work with a smooth bounded core in
place of the vanishing core. The derivative gain on an annulus is the local div-curl estimate proved in Theorem 36,
(36.4), applied after scaling and combined with the size bound. Multiplication by chi has uniformly bounded scaled
derivatives; it vanishes on a neighborhood of the inner circle R/2. This proves (69.12). This estimate is independent of
beta and of the transport equations. The divergence version is already proved in Step 1 of Theorem 42: add the curl-free
potential with kernel z/(2pi|z|^2) for the localized divergence. At finite C^(k,vartheta) regularity the same localized
potentials have the asserted Schauder bounds, and the remaining field is distributionally harmonic, hence smooth.
Equivalently, mollify on a slightly larger annulus, use uniform estimates, pass to a smaller Holder exponent, and retain
the original seminorm by pointwise limits of difference quotients. Convergence of mollifiers in the original Holder norm
is not required.

A compact smooth odd-odd source has zero mass and zero first moments. Taylor expansion of K(X-Y) for |X| beyond twice
its support radius therefore gives BS(Omega_in) = O_infty(r^(-3)). In particular its norm in (b) tends to zero as R
increases. The grouped inverse has the stated parities and curl. Two entire uniformly sublinear velocities with the same
divergence, curl and parities differ by an entire harmonic vector field. The interior gradient estimate on a disc of
radius T bounds its derivative at any fixed point by o(T)/T. Letting T tend to infinity proves that the difference is
constant, and parity makes the constant zero. This proves the canonical assertion.

We also need a transport estimate. Suppose ||U||_(1-h,k,vartheta;R/2) <= B_vel, with k = 1 or 2, and B_vel(R/2)^(-h)
sufficiently small. Every forward orbit from r >= R/2 remains in that region. Along an orbit,

  d_t |Phi_t X|^h = |Phi_t X|^h+O(B_vel),
  C^(-1)e^(beta t)|X| <= |Phi_t X| <= C e^(beta t)|X|.
                                                               (69.13)

The first identity uses beta h = 1. Multiplication by e^(-t) and integration give the second, with constants uniform in
the starting point. On a starting annulus |X|~rho, the normalized flow e^(-beta t)Phi_t(rho z)/rho has uniformly bounded
C^(k,vartheta) norms. Indeed its equation has the form d_t Y = rho^(-h)e^(-t)u_(rho e^(beta t))(Y), where
u_l(z) = l^(h-1)U(lz). It stays in a fixed annulus by (69.13). Differentiating this equation once or twice, and taking
Holder differences, gives linear inequalities with integrable coefficient C B_vel rho^(-h)e^(-t). Gronwall bounds the
first derivative; the second derivative equation has the already bounded first derivatives as its inhomogeneous term.
The same inequalities for differences bound the Holder seminorms. They also show that this normalized flow converges in
C^(k,vartheta). These arguments work at any higher finite order once the corresponding norm of U is known.

For m and lambda with lambda+beta m < 0, define

  I_(lambda,U) S(X)
      = -int_0^infinity e^(lambda t)S(Phi_t X)dt.
  Then (W.grad+lambda)I_(lambda,U)S = S,
  ||I_(lambda,U)S||_(m,k,vartheta;R/2)
      <= C_(m,lambda,B_vel) ||S||_(m,k,vartheta;R/2).           (69.14)

To verify the estimate, scale a starting annulus by rho. The normalized C^(k,vartheta) norm of S at time t is bounded by
C rho^m e^(beta m t)||S||, by the flow bounds and the composition rule. Integrating e^((lambda+beta m)t) proves the
assertion, including its Holder seminorm. Shifting the lower integration endpoint along an orbit and differentiating
proves the equation. If (W.grad+lambda)v = 0 and e^(lambda t)v(Phi_t X) tends to zero, v = 0. Thus (69.14) is also the
unique solution with that terminal condition.

Put Theta_0 = r^q f and Omega_0 = r^(-h)G on r > R/2. For an omega_rem in (69.7), form
U_trial = BS(Omega_in+chi(Omega_0+omega_rem)). Define Theta_trial and the output Omega_trial by

  Theta_trial = Theta_0+
        I_(-kappa,U_trial)(-U_trial.grad Theta_0),
  Omega_trial = Omega_0+
        I_(1,U_trial)((Theta_trial)_x-U_trial.grad Omega_0).
                                                               (69.15)

The radial identities (beta X.grad-kappa)Theta_0 = 0 and (beta X.grad+1)Omega_0 = 0 show that both auxiliary transport
equations hold for these outputs with velocity U_trial. Their terminal leading data are f,G.

We specify the uniform bounds before taking differences. Let B_data bound 1 and the C^(3,vartheta) norm of f and
C^(2,vartheta) norm of G. If M(R/2)^(-h) <= 1, then ||Omega_0+omega_rem||_(-h,1,vartheta;R/2) <= C(B_data+1). Equation
(69.12) gives a C^(2,vartheta) bound for U_trial in weight 1-h depending only on beta,vartheta,chi_0,B_data and the core
bound one. The first source in (69.15) is in C^(2,vartheta), weight q-h. Its transport exponent is
-kappa+beta(q-h) = -1. Hence Theta_trial-Theta_0 has that weight and regularity, uniformly. In particular Theta_trial
has a uniform C^(2,vartheta) bound in weight q. The second source is in C^(1,vartheta), weight -2h, and
1+beta(-2h) = -1. Thus

  ||Theta_trial-Theta_0||_(q-h,2,vartheta;R/2) <= C_0,
  ||Omega_trial-Omega_0||_(-2h,1,vartheta;R/2) <= C_0.          (69.16)

Fix B_data first and then its resulting velocity bound B_vel. Subject to B_vel(R/2)^(-h) being below a fixed small
constant, the normalized flow constants are bounded in terms of these data alone. Consequently C_0 is independent of M
and R under these conditions and M(R/2)^(-h) <= 1. Choose M = 2C_0, then C_* to include the flow and difference
constants, and finally R. Thus (69.8) does not enter circularly into the choice of C_0. This proves invariance of the
ball.

For two inputs, let delta denote their difference and dist their distance in the metric in (b). From (69.12), ||delta
U||_(1-2h,1,vartheta;R/2) <= C dist. Taking the difference of the temperature equations and using the first velocity on
the left gives

  (W_1.grad-kappa)delta Theta
        = -delta U.grad Theta_2,
  (W_1.grad+1)delta Omega_output
        = (delta Theta)_x-delta U.grad Omega_output,2.
                                                               (69.17)

In the first equation the right side has weight q-2h and C^(1,vartheta) norm at most C dist: this is where the uniform
C^(2,vartheta) bound on Theta_2 is used. The terminal difference is zero. Equation (69.14), now with exponent -2, gives
the same bound for delta Theta. In the second equation the two sources have weights -4h and -3h in C^(0,vartheta); the
C^(1,vartheta) bound on Omega_output,2 suffices. Their transport exponents are -3 and -2, respectively. On r >= R/2 >= 1
the first is bounded in weight -3h as well. Applying (69.14) gives

  ||delta Omega_output||_(-3h,0,vartheta;R/2) <= C_1 dist,
  ||delta Omega_output||_(-2h,0,vartheta;R/2)
        <= C_1(R/2)^(-h)dist.                                   (69.18)

The difference formulas are legitimate applications of terminal uniqueness: both temperature remainders have weight q-h,
and both vorticity remainders have weight -2h. The corresponding weighted values tend to zero along forward orbits.

Increase C_* in (69.8) to include C_1 and the preceding flow constants. The map is a contraction. Its domain is complete
in the weaker metric: a Cauchy sequence converges in the weighted C^(0,vartheta) norm, and on each compact annulus its
derivatives have uniformly bounded C^(0,vartheta) norms. Compactness at every smaller Holder exponent and integration of
the limiting derivatives identify a C^(1,vartheta) limit. The derivative Holder bound passes to the limit pointwise in
pairs of points. Taking the supremum over annuli retains the bound M. Consequently Banach's contraction theorem gives
the fixed point and precisely the uniqueness stated in (b).

Reflections preserve the grouped inverse, the vector field, the flow, and both formulas (69.15). They preserve the
terminal data, so the fixed point has all A2 parities. The temperature on either axis is zero. One may check the y-axis
separately: Theta_0 = 0 there and its tangential derivative vanishes there, so U_trial.grad Theta_0 = 0 on that
invariant axis. The same argument applies to the x-axis. This also proves the extra temperature vanishing that does not
follow from evenness in x alone.
