We next prove smoothness; a contraction at one Holder order does not by itself prove it. The argument is the directional
div-curl gain of Theorem 42 with terminal, rather than initial, data.

First work outside 2R, where the physical curl is Omega. For a scaling radius rho put u_rho = rho^(h-1)U(rho .),
omega_rho = rho^h Omega(rho .), g_rho = rho^(2h)grad Theta(rho .), Z_rho = beta z+epsilon u_rho, epsilon = rho^(-h), and
F_rho = Du_rho Z_rho. Direct differentiation gives

  div F_rho = epsilon tr((Du_rho)^2),
  rcurl F_rho = (beta-1)omega_rho+epsilon(g_rho)_1,
  rcurl v = d_2 v_1-d_1 v_2.                                    (69.19)

For the second identity use rcurl((z.grad)u) = omega+z.grad omega and rcurl((u.grad)u) = u.grad omega for
divergence-free u; then use vorticity transport. Thus if omega_rho,g_rho are bounded in C^(k,vartheta) and u_rho in
C^(k+1,vartheta) on enlarged annuli, the div-curl estimate bounds F_rho in C^(k+1,vartheta) on smaller annuli. No
derivative of omega_rho or g_rho occurs on the right.

Launch from any fixed sufficiently distant circle, using angle ell and time t >= 0. The map Y(t,ell) = e^(-beta
t)X(t,ell) converges to Xi(ell) = rho_inf(ell)e(phi_inf(ell)). If u_rho has bounded C^(k+1,vartheta) norms, the
differentiated normalized flow equation used in (69.13) gives this convergence in C^(k+1,vartheta). Its derivatives
converge because their time derivatives have the integrable factor e^(-t). The rescaled finite-width flow charts and
their inverses have the same regularity and uniform bounds. For each target annulus first choose a slightly larger
annulus and then a strip wide enough to cover it, as in Lemma 42.1. The strip width and the constants may depend on that
annulus. To check the inverse bound, use det(W,X_ell) = r0 W_r(r0e(ell))e^(2beta t); after scaling this determinant
stays bounded away from zero on each fixed-width time strip. The inverse function formula and differentiation give the
asserted bounds. This is also the argument of Lemma 42.1.

Write e = W/|W|, n = (-e_2,e_1), k1 = e.DUe, k3 = n.DUe, and E = e^(2t)grad Theta.e, B = e^(2t)grad Theta.n, j = e^t
Omega along the launched orbits. Since (T) holds, E = kappa Theta(r0e(ell))e^(beta t)/|W|. Eliminating the remaining
component of DU by rcurl U = Omega gives

  B' = e^(-t)[k1_hat B-(j+2k3_hat)E],
  j' = e^(-t)(E e_1+B n_1),
  k1_hat = e^t k1, k3_hat = e^t k3.                             (69.20)

For example, in the orthonormal frame (e,n), write DU = [[k1,k2],[k3,-k1]]. Then k2-k3 = Omega and e' = k3 n.
Differentiating B gives k1 B-(k2+k3)E before multiplication by the normalized factors, which is (69.20).

The starting bounds (69.16) imply the differentiated leading temperature limit and hence the terminal values

  j_infinity = rho_inf^(-h)G(phi_inf),
  B_infinity = rho_inf^(-2h)f'(phi_inf).                        (69.21)

Indeed the differentiated error in Theta is O(r^(q-h-1)); after multiplication by e^(2t) it tends to zero. Also n tends
to e_phi(phi_inf). The leading error for Omega proves the other limit. The temperature identity similarly gives
Theta(r0e(ell)) = rho_inf^q f(phi_inf).

Suppose omega_rho,g_rho have uniform C^(k,vartheta) bounds and u_rho has uniform C^(k+1,vartheta) bounds. This holds
initially for k = 1 by the construction. The coefficients E,e,n in (69.20) have C^(k+1,vartheta) bounds in the flow
charts. The same is true of k1_hat,k3_hat by (69.19): DU enters them only through Du_rho e = F_rho/|Z_rho|, or
physically DUe = rho^(-h)F_rho/|Z_rho|. On the strip t = T+s with rho = e^(beta T), this gives e^t DUe = e^s
F_rho/|Z_rho|. The identity Theta(r0e(ell)) = rho_inf^q f(phi_inf) gives the required regularity of the launch
temperature from the old limiting flow, without assuming the new regularity of grad Theta. The terminal data (69.21)
have C^(k+1,vartheta) regularity because Xi does and f,G are smooth.

Treat (69.20) as an affine linear system with these already specified coefficients; adjoining a constant component 1
makes it homogeneous. Its terminal integral equation has a unique bounded solution in C^(k+1,vartheta) of the label. To
see this without a smallness assumption at order k, expand its Volterra series. If C bounds the coefficient norm, the
n-fold ordered integral of C e^(-t) is at most C^n/n!. In the Banach algebra C^(k+1,vartheta) the ordered products obey
this bound after increasing C for its multiplication constant. The series therefore converges in that space, including
its Holder seminorm. The continuous terminal solution is unique by the corresponding backward Gronwall inequality. It is
consequently the existing pair B,j. Time derivatives in the charts follow directly from (69.20); differentiating at most
k times on its right gives the mixed derivatives of total order k+1. The highest pure label derivative is Lipschitz in
time, because its time derivative is bounded by the same equation. Thus the bounds are joint C^(k+1,vartheta) bounds on
each fixed-width strip. Reconstructing grad Theta and Omega from E,B,j, and using the old inverse chart, gives uniform
C^(k+1,vartheta) bounds for g_rho,omega_rho. The elliptic inverse then gives C^(k+2,vartheta) for u_rho. Lemma 42.1 then
upgrades the charts last. This completes the induction at the already chosen radius; no smallness depending on k is
needed.

The same induction supplies smoothness throughout r > R/2, locally away from its inner boundary. There Omega_in = 0 but
rcurl U = chi Omega. In (69.19) replace its second line by

  rcurl F_rho = (beta-1)chi_rho omega_rho
       +epsilon chi_rho(g_rho)_1
       +(Z_rho.grad chi_rho)omega_rho,
  chi_rho(z) = chi(rho z).                                      (69.22)

In (69.20) replace j in the first line by chi(X(t,ell))j. These identities follow by the product rule and have the
identical derivative gain. All extra cutoff coefficients are smooth, are bounded on scaled annuli, and vanish or become
constant at large radii. For any closed exterior r >= s > R/2, use slightly larger annuli contained in r > R/2 and
launch at a radius between R/2 and s. The old induction hypothesis holds on every such larger exterior. The induction
assertion is made simultaneously for every s > R/2, so shrinking an annulus uses only the preceding-order assertion on
another such exterior. Thus there is no loss from the inner boundary. No regularity on the artificial circle r = R/2
itself is needed or asserted. This proves smoothness near r = R as well as all natural differentiated bounds at
infinity. Multiplication by chi now proves the global smoothness in (69.2).

The exterior bounds now verify the inputs of the local radial argument in Steps 6-8 of Theorem 42. We record its
equations and coefficients, which use only the exterior equations, to specify the remainders here. Put Th = r^(-q)Theta,
Om = r^h Omega and (v_r,v_phi) = r^(h-1)(U_r,U_phi). On r > 2R the exact radial equations are

  (beta+r^(-h)v_r)r Th_r
       = -r^(-h)(qv_r Th+v_phi Th_phi),
  (beta+r^(-h)v_r)r Om_r
       = r^(-h)[hv_r Om-v_phi Om_phi
          +q cos(phi)Th-sin(phi)Th_phi
          +cos(phi)r Th_r].                                     (69.23)

All normalized derivatives are bounded by the induction. The denominator is at least beta/2. Therefore every normalized
derivative of r Th_r and r Om_r is O(r^(-h)). Integrating in dr/r from infinity, and using the known limits f,G, shows
Th-f = O_infty(r^(-h)) and Om-G = O_infty(r^(-h)), in the normalized sense. The rule converting normalized derivatives
to Cartesian derivatives is obtained by writing r d_x and r d_y as smooth angular combinations of r d_r and d_phi, and
iterating.

Cut off psi_0 smoothly inside a fixed disc. Its curl agrees with r^(-h)G outside that disc. The remaining whole-plane
source is O_infty(r^(-2h)); (69.12), with a smooth core, gives U-u_0 = O_infty(r^(1-2h)). Inserting these three leading
approximations in (69.23) gives

  r Th_r = -h r^(-h)f1+O_infty(r^(-2h)),
  r Om_r = -h r^(-h)G1+O_infty(r^(-2h)).                        (69.24)

Every derivative of these errors has the same normalized bound. Integration from infinity proves the first two
expansions in (69.5). Cutting off psi_1 and applying (69.12) to the remaining source with gamma = 3h < 3/2 < 2 proves
the velocity expansion. Its constant core is harmless in the three-region estimate. Integrating its rotated gradient
along rays proves the stream-function expansion: 2-3h > 0 absorbs the constant of integration. Odd-odd parity fixes the
additive constant globally; bounded ray-dependent initial values are absorbed in the positive remainder power. These are
the coefficients and remainder orders of Theorem 42(c). In particular q-2h = 1-4h can be nonnegative, and the
temperature remainder is not claimed to tend to zero in that range.

Formula (69.9) follows by solving the radial equation for each sine coefficient of -Lap Psi = Omega_tot. Its two
homogeneous solutions are r^(2m) and r^(-2m), with Wronskian -4m/r. Regularity at zero removes the negative-power
solution there, and uniform sublinearity of velocity removes an independently added positive-power solution at infinity.
Variation of parameters gives (4m)^(-1)[r^(-2m)int_0^r t^(2m+1)omega_m(t)dt+r^(2m)int_r^infinity t^(1-2m)omega_m(t)dt].
The second integral converges because omega_m = O(t^(-h)). Splitting the first integral at r_b proves (69.9). For its
harmonic sum, smoothness on r <= r_b bounds the moments by C_N r_b^(2m+2)(1+m)^(-N); the factor (r_b/r)^(2m) gives
convergence with every derivative on r >= r_b+epsilon. The full modal solution agrees with the grouped inverse by
canonical uniqueness. In particular a harmonic coefficient is not extra freedom once the whole source and the particular
normalization are fixed. No convergence of a formal asymptotic series is used in this argument.

For (69.10), differentiate chi Theta and chi Omega and use the two auxiliary transport equations. The term chi Theta_x
cancels the same term in (chi Theta)_x, leaving -chi_x Theta in vorticity transport. The support choice for Omega_in
separates the core and annular formulas. This proves (a), the construction assertion in (b), and (c).

We prove the failure of the unrestricted uniqueness assertion for nonzero as well as zero leading data. Choose a smooth
nonnegative radial bump b_patch supported in an interval compactly contained in (1,2) on which chi_0 is strictly
positive, with b_patch not identically zero. Put zeta_R(X) = tau R^(-h)b_patch(r/R)sin(2phi), where tau is a small fixed
real parameter. Perform exactly the preceding fixed point with velocity BS(Omega_in+zeta_R+chi Omega). The bounds remain
uniform for |tau| <= 1: the added velocity has size O(|tau|) in weight 1-h, and R can be chosen uniformly. For the
smoothness argument put xi_rho(z) = rho^h zeta_R(rho z). Add beta xi_rho+Z_rho.grad xi_rho to (69.22), and add e^t
zeta_R(X) to the physical normalized curl chi(X)j in (69.20). These are specified smooth coefficients and have the same
derivative count.

Denote the auxiliary fixed point by Omega^(tau), with temperature Theta^(tau). On r > R set

  Omega_tilde^(tau) = Omega^(tau)+zeta_R/chi,                   (69.25)

where the quotient is extended by zero outside the support of the bump. This is smooth. Its total vorticity has exactly
the prescribed form Omega_in+chi Omega_tilde^(tau), with the original Omega_in and the original chi. Outside 2R it
equals Omega^(tau), so all the required equations and tails hold there.

These exterior velocities need not agree. The difference estimates used in (69.17), with the additional prescribed
velocity BS(zeta_R), give ||Omega^(tau)-Omega^(0)||_(-2h,0,vartheta;R/2) <= C|tau|. For this estimate the temperature
difference has weight q-h and the direct vorticity source has weight -2h; the part depending on the unknown difference
is absorbed by (69.18). Hence the induced velocity of chi(Omega^(tau)-Omega^(0)) at r = 3R is O(|tau|R^(1-2h)).

On the other hand let C_patch = (1/4)int_1^2 t^3 b_patch(t)dt > 0. The direct added source has exterior stream function
tau C_patch R^(4-h)r^(-2)sin(2phi). Its velocity at (3R,0) is (-2tau C_patch R^(1-h)/27,0). For R sufficiently large
this cannot be canceled by the preceding O(|tau|R^(1-2h)) error when tau != 0. By continuity the velocities differ also
at nearby open-quadrant points. Thus there are distinct exterior fields with the same f,G,Omega_in,chi and with (69.5).
The modified annular vorticity is extra data. It need not solve the auxiliary transport prescription in (b), so the
distinct exterior fields do not contradict that uniqueness assertion. This proves the nonuniqueness assertion.

We now check the explicit sign examples and the cited exterior statements. Substitution into (69.4) gives (69.11); the
first identity is quadratic in sigma and the forcing part of the second is linear in sigma. Write F = sigma f = s c^2
and g = sigma G = sin(2phi). Direct differentiation gives

  F > 0, g > 0 on (0,alpha),
  F'(0) = 1, F''(alpha) = 2, g'(0) = 2, g'(alpha) = -2,
  sigma P > 0, sigma P'' < 0 on (0,alpha),
  sigma P'(0) = 2p0, sigma P'(alpha) = -2p0.                    (69.26)

Every smooth temperature angular remainder here is divisible by s c^2, and every smooth odd-odd vorticity remainder by
sin(2phi). For the first assertion use oddness at zero and vanishing of the value and first derivative at alpha.
Integral Taylor formulas bound the quotient by a constant times the C^2 norm; the smooth nonzero ratios sin(phi)/phi and
cos(phi)/(alpha-phi) transfer these divisions to s and c. For vorticity a first-order division suffices at either
endpoint. Apply these bounds to the normalized remainders in (69.5), uniformly in r. They prove

  sigma Theta/(r^q s c^2) = 1+O(r^(-h)),
  sigma Omega/(r^(-h)sin(2phi)) = 1+O(r^(-h))                   (69.27)

on the closed interval, with continuously extended quotients. This proves strict signs throughout the exterior open
quadrant, not only in sectors away from the axes. The radial derivative satisfies the same division estimate and has
leading quotient q > 0. Also W_r = beta r+O(r^(1-h)) > 0.

The exterior bounds, smoothness and limits of Theorems 41 and 42 have already been proved. In particular (DT) holds
because Theta_x = O(r^(-2h)), and (S) holds because DU = O(r^(-h)) tends to zero. The nonzero angular data and their
sign intervals in Theorem 41(b) are explicit. For any exterior launch point the flow estimates and vorticity transport
give, with rho_inf(X) > 0 and limiting angle phi_*,

  J(X) = rho_inf(X)^(-h)G(phi_*),
  e^t Omega(Phi_t X) = J(X)+O_X(e^(-t)),
  J(X) = Omega(X)+int_0^infinity e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X)dt.
                                                               (69.28)

The integral is absolutely convergent since Theta_x(Phi_t X) = O_X(e^(-2t)). This is the exterior content of
Theorem 41(c) and the forward half of Theorem 66(d). The error is uniform for launch points on a fixed exterior circle.
The scattering angle map is a smooth orientation-preserving circle diffeomorphism fixing the axes: passage to the limit
in the determinant formula gives beta rho_inf(ell)^2 phi_inf'(ell) = r0 W_r(r0e(ell)) > 0. Its degree is one, as it is
uniformly close to the identity when the circle is sufficiently large. Thus interior exterior orbits have interior limit
angles.

Theorem 45(a)-(c) has its full tail meaning. On a closed interior angular interval (69.27) gives a lower bound c r^(-h)
for |Omega|, and globally there is the upper bound C r^(-h). Consequently the exterior integral of |Omega|^p converges
exactly when hp > 2. For small levels lambda the measure of the exterior set {|Omega| > lambda} is bounded above and
below by positive multiples of lambda^(-2/h). This follows by integrating r dr between a fixed radius and a constant
multiple of lambda^(-1/h). A smooth compact completion does not change these assertions; boundedness of that completion
supplies the weak upper bound also at larger levels. Decay faster than r^(-h) is impossible. More precisely, the
little-o hypothesis of Theorem 24 holds for 0 < eta < h by the bound C R^(eta-h), fails for eta = h by the sector lower
bound, and fails for eta > h because r^eta |Omega| is unbounded along a ray in that sector. Thus the fast-decay
hypothesis in Theorem 15 also fails. Each of the four integrands in Theorem 45(d) is absolutely integrable at infinity:
K0 Omega has size O(r^(-2-h)), and the other three have size O(r^(-2-2h)), where K0 = xy/r^4. Their whole-plane values
are not prescribed. Along the positive y-axis, 1/W_2(0,y)-1/(beta y) = O(y^(-1-h)); hence the time-minus-logarithm limit
in Theorem 45(e) exists. The additional axis amplitude in that theorem requires its specified axis history.

The exact weak distribution law of Theorem 40 uses complete orbits. Its exterior counterpart can be stated precisely. On
a launch circle r_b, write Delta(ell) = r_b W_r(r_b e(ell)) and J_b(ell) = J(r_b e(ell)). The transport law J(Phi_t
X) = e^(-t)J(X) and the area density Delta(ell)e^(2beta t) give measure{r > r_b:|J| > lambda} = (1/(2beta))int_0^(2pi)
Delta(ell)[(|J_b(ell)|/lambda)^(2beta)-1]_+ d_ell. The small-level coefficient is (1/2)int_0^(2pi)|G(phi)|^(2beta)d_phi,
since Delta = beta rho_inf^2 phi_inf'. The subtraction is the contribution of the omitted backward part. The full
identity for every lambda and the local singularity in Theorem 40(d) are not exterior requirements.

The explicit pairs also satisfy the growth requirements behind the restricted exclusions in Theorems 17(b), 19 and 23.
Their temperature grows like r^q on a sector, so it is in no finite L^p space. The critical-energy hypothesis of
Theorem 28 fails as well. Their velocity has magnitude of order r^(1-h), and direct integration of its squared leading
term gives lim_(T -> infinity) T^(-4+2h)int_(T < r < 2T)|U|^2 = pi p0^2(4+a^2)(2^(4-2h)-1)/(4-2h) > 0. Indeed the
angular integrals of sin(2phi)^2 and cos(2phi)^2 over the full circle are both pi, and the radial integral is
int_T^(2T)r^(3-2h)dr. The velocity error contributes only O(T^(4-3h)). In particular the energy is not below the
critical order T^(4-4h).

The angular implication of Theorem 47(a) holds for these data: F never vanishes in (0,alpha), and G vanishes on the
axes. In the exterior itself grad Theta is nowhere zero in Q1 because W.grad Theta = kappa Theta and Theta has a strict
sign. This does not prove Theorem 47(a) for arbitrary data in (69.1). Its proof uses Theorem 44(d), which makes Omega
vanish on the critical set by following a complete backward orbit. Exterior critical orbits can instead carry a nonzero
solution of homogeneous vorticity transport. Thus that angular implication is an additional restriction on profiles
whose derivation is not exterior.

The sign statements in Theorem 50(c), and the angular positivity in Theorem 50(b), are exactly (69.26). One can also
check the escape-label law, without asserting a source chart. For any A_ext of sign sigma, fix phi0 in (0,alpha) and
define

  c_label(phi) = -(1/q)int_phi0^phi (|A_ext|/F(t))^(2/q)dt.
                                                               (69.29)

Its derivative is negative. Since F~phi at zero and F~(alpha-phi)^2 at alpha, both endpoint integrals diverge, with
opposite signs. Thus it is a smooth decreasing diffeomorphism onto the real line and its inverse obeys
phi'(c_label) = -q(f(phi)/A_ext)^(2/q), as in Theorem 50(b). For actual exterior flow lines, assign c_label to their
limiting angle. It is a smooth first integral there.

In fact the area normalization in Theorem 50(b) can also be realized in the exterior. Put eta = Theta/A_ext,
p = (beta+2)/kappa and xi = c_label eta^p. Then W.grad(xi,eta) = (lambda xi,kappa eta), where lambda = beta+2.
Differentiating these equations shows that Jac = det D(xi,eta) satisfies W.grad Jac = (lambda+kappa-div W)Jac = 0; this
determinant identity follows by expansion even before Jac is known to be nonzero. The normalized flow estimate gives
phi_*(X) = phi+O_infty(r^(-h)) locally in interior angles. Together with (69.5), it gives Jac -> -q
c_label'(phi)(f(phi)/A_ext)^(p+1) = 1, because q(p+1) = 2. Every exterior orbit has an interior limit angle, so Jac = 1
everywhere in exterior Q1. The map (xi,eta) is injective: c_label distinguishes the orbits and eta increases strictly on
each orbit. Its image is the part eta > eta_b(c_label), where eta_b is its positive value on a fixed sufficiently
distant launch circle. In (c_label,eta) coordinates the area element is eta^p dc_label d_eta. This proves the exterior
coordinate and escape laws, with the inner circle as boundary. A_ext is an arbitrary exterior normalization. The
normalization A = Theta_y(P_ax) of Theorem 50, and extension of this chart through P_ax, have not been constructed.

The infinite endpoints of the orbit moments in Theorem 65(d) are meaningful as well. Write Z(c,v) for the inverse
exterior chart in coordinates (c_label,eta), Y for its second Cartesian component, and n = (beta+1)/kappa as in (65.10)
(an exponent, not the frame vector above). On compact c intervals, (69.5) and the smooth angle law give
Y,Y_c = O(v^(1/q)). Thus v^(-n-1)Y_c and v^(-n-1)[Y(c,v)-Y(c0,v)] are O(v^(-1-h/q)) and integrable at infinity. The same
estimate after a c derivative justifies differentiation of the second integral on compact c intervals. The area formula
gives Theta_x(Z) = -A_ext v^(-p)Y_c. Vorticity transport therefore gives the precise future identity
v^(1/kappa)Omega(Z(c,v)) = (f(phi(c))/A_ext)^(1/kappa)G(phi(c))
  +(A_ext/kappa)int_v^infinity u^(-n-1)Y_c(c,u)du.
Its terminal constant follows directly from (69.5), using h/q = 1/kappa. This is obtained by integrating the derivative
of v^(1/kappa)Omega, so every sign is fixed. Its terminal constant cannot be replaced by an integral starting at zero
without the source identity in Theorem 65(d). The factors exp(-v) in its further balance cause no difficulty at infinity
on compact c intervals. Integrals down to v = 0, and their asserted source normalizations, are not supplied.

The eventual axis expansions, with differentiated errors, are

  sigma Theta_y(x,0)
      = x^(-2h)+2sigma p0(1+h)x^(-3h)+O(x^(-4h)),
  sigma Theta_xx(0,y)/2
      = y^(-1-2h)-6sigma p0 y^(-1-3h)+O(y^(-1-4h)),
  sigma Omega_y(x,0)
      = 2x^(-1-h)+(8sigma p0+2h)x^(-1-2h)
                      +O(x^(-1-3h)),
  sigma Omega_x(0,y)
      = 2y^(-1-h)-(8sigma p0+2)y^(-1-2h)
                      +O(y^(-1-3h)),
  W_1(x,0) = beta x-2sigma p0 x^(1-h)+O(x^(1-2h)),
  W_2(0,y) = beta y+2sigma p0 y^(1-h)+O(y^(1-2h)).
                                                               (69.30)

For example at the positive x-axis d_y = x^(-1)d_phi, while at the positive y-axis d_x = -y^(-1)d_phi. The temperature
and its first angular derivative vanish on the y-axis, so its second x derivative is y^(-2)Theta_phiphi there. From
(69.11), f1'(0) = 2p0(1+h), f1''(alpha) = -12p0, sigma G1'(0) = 8sigma p0+2h, and sigma G1'(alpha) = 8sigma p0+2. These
identities prove every coefficient in (69.30). They check the eventual portions of Theorems 57(a), 62(c),(d), 65(e), and
the exact coefficient in Theorem 66(e), (66.14). In particular W_2(0,y) > beta y eventually on the positive branch; E,K
are negative eventually on the negative branch. The trace equations themselves follow by differentiating (69.3) on the
exterior axes.

For the positive branch, the axis coordinate xi = A_ext w/(lambda T) of Theorems 50(a) and 65(e), with any A_ext > 0, is
increasing in the exterior: its derivative is A_ext/T by wT' = (w'-lambda)T. Here xi is of order x^(1+2h), and
H0 = A_ext/T is of order xi^(2h/(1+2h)). With nu_ax = (1-h)/(1+2h), the integrand xi^(nu_ax-2)[H0-1] in Theorem 65(e) is
O(xi^(-1-h/(1+2h))) at infinity. Its infinite endpoint is therefore absolutely integrable. Its full value, its lower
endpoint at the source, and the conclusion T > A_ext somewhere are not exterior assertions.

The leading Cartesian velocity coefficients are r^(h-1)U_1 = -2sigma p0 c[1-hs^2]+O(r^(-h)) and r^(h-1)U_2 = 2sigma p0
s[1-hc^2]+O(r^(-h)). The errors have the respective factors c and s, with bounded quotients, by parity and the
differentiated bounds. Consequently W_1,W_2 > 0 throughout sufficiently distant Q1, as required in the exterior part of
Theorem 65(h). On the positive branch U_2 > 0 there as well.

The local axis identity of Theorem 66(g) also holds. On the negative branch set T0 = -Theta_y(x,0), k0 = -Omega_y(x,0).
Exterior axis differentiation gives wT0' = (w'-beta-2)T0 and wk0'+(2beta+1-w')k0 = T0'. Differentiating wk0/T0^2 and
substituting these equations gives (wk0/T0^2)' = T0'/T0^2+3k0/T0^2. Here T0 > 0, T0' < 0 and k0 > 0 for sufficiently
large x by (69.30). Thus there are no exterior opposite-sign trace intervals. The integral over such an interval through
finite source positions is a different, global assertion.

For the sign changes in Theorems 50(e) and 57(b),(c), compute

  r^(2h)sigma Theta_x -> D0 = 2sc[(1+h)s^2-h],
  r^(2h)sigma Theta_y -> c^2[1-2(1+h)s^2],
  r^(-q)sigma Theta_phi -> c(1-3s^2).                           (69.31)

The thresholds h/(1+h), 1/[2(1+h)] and 1/3 all lie in (0,1). Choose fixed interior angles on opposite sides of each
relevant threshold. Their intersections with every sufficiently high horizontal line, or sufficiently distant vertical
line, lie in the exterior and preserve the corresponding strict signs. The last limit gives both signs on every
sufficiently large quadrant arc. Positivity of sigma Theta on those portions also follows from (69.27). The radial
derivative has strict sign sigma everywhere in the exterior quadrant by the division argument. Assertions requiring both
radial signs on a whole ray from the origin do not apply to these positive F. Likewise, a horizontal half-line at a
small fixed height is not wholly exterior, so the every-height assertion of Theorem 57(b) is not claimed.

Theorem 64(a)'s angular inequalities are (69.26), and there is no open vorticity-zero region in the exterior. The lower
bound in Theorem 65(b), (65.5), follows by twice differentiating U on a ray:

  |D^2 W[e_r,e_r]|
      = h(1-h)r^(-1-h)sqrt(P'^2+a^2 P^2)
                        +O(r^(-1-2h)),
  P'^2+a^2P^2 = p0^2[4cos(2phi)^2+a^2sin(2phi)^2]
                         >= a^2p0^2.                            (69.32)

It holds uniformly in angle, for either sign. All exterior zero-segment, flat-zero and zero-contact implications in
Theorem 65 have empty hypotheses for these examples. Its positive axis sectors hold by (69.27). Every future orbit
starting in the exterior Q1 has strict signed vorticity at all future times, which is stronger there than eventual
positive returns.

For the angular assertions in Theorems 65(c) and 66(e),(f), g > 0 has no interior zero. Thus g = 0 implies D0 <= 0, and
all common-zero contact inequalities, hold with empty antecedents. The only critical point of F in the interior has
s^2 = 1/3 and g > 0. The identity (F/sin(phi)^q)' = -D0/sin(phi)^(q+1) checks the quotient normalization. The unique
interior zero of D0 has s^2 = h/(1+h), where g = 2sqrt(h)/(1+h) > 0. For either branch, substitution in the expression C
of Theorem 65, (65.2), gives C = -sigma sin(2phi)[(1-h)c^2+3s^2]/(4-h). It is strictly negative on the positive branch.
This introduces no zero-angle condition because G has no interior zero. There are no unbounded exterior sequences of
vorticity zeros. The implication f = f' = 0 implies f'' = 0 in Theorem 66(f) has no interior hypothesis for these data.
On the negative branch the bracket in (66.16) is indeed negative near zero: it equals 2sigma p0[2c cos(2phi)-a c
cos(2phi)] = 2sigma h p0 c cos(2phi). The full expression in (66.16) is consequently C_contact = 2sigma q(1-h)h p0 s c^3
cos(2phi). Its sign is negative for small positive phi when sigma = -1. The inequality in Theorem 66(f) is required only
at common zeros of g and D0; it is not a pointwise nonnegativity condition on this expression. Here g is strictly
positive.

Finally the angular velocity equation gives

  d_phi/dr = (a/beta)P(phi)r^(-1-h)+O(r^(-1-2h)),
  phi(r) = phi_*-aP(phi_*)r^(-h)+O(r^(-2h)).                    (69.33)

The first right side is integrable, giving phi-phi_* = O(r^(-h)). Replacing P(phi) by P(phi_*) in its integral costs
O(r^(-2h)), and beta h = 1 gives the coefficient in the second line. This is Theorem 66(e)'s outgoing-angle law, with
approach from below for sigma = 1 and from above for sigma = -1.

There are two further meaningful exterior parts of Theorem 50. The future weight v_K(X) = int_0^infinity
e^((2beta-1)t)K0(Phi_t X)dt exists on exterior Q1, is positive, is O(r^(-2)), and satisfies -(2beta-1)v_K-W.grad
v_K = K0. Convergence and differentiation follow from (69.13) and the differentiated flow bounds; the integrand is
O(r^(-2)e^(-t)). For r_b sufficiently large, integration of div(v_K Omega W) over Q1 cap {r_b < r < T}, followed by T
tending to infinity, gives the actual exterior balance

  int_(Q1,r > r_b) v_K Theta_x
      = int_(Q1,r > r_b) K0 Omega
       -r_b int_0^alpha v_K(r_b,phi)Omega(r_b,phi)W_r(r_b,phi)dphi.
                                                               (69.34)

There is no axis flux. The outer flux tends to zero by its O(T^(-h)) bound. This proves why the constant whole-quadrant
balance in Theorem 50(d) cannot be imposed without the interior boundary contribution.

Remark 55.1 has a further conclusion which does hold entirely at infinity on the positive branch. For any continuous
H:(0,infinity) -> [0,infinity), H not identically zero, the exterior integral of H(Theta)Omega is infinite. Indeed put
x = z y^(1/2+h), with z in a compact positive interval. The axis expansions and Taylor's formula with the differentiated
remainder give Theta(x,y) = z^2+o(1), Omega(x,y) = y^(-1/2)(2z+o(1)) uniformly on that interval: the relative Taylor
errors are O(y^(-1+2h)) and tend to zero. Choose the interval with H(z^2) bounded below by a positive constant. Its
x-integral is at least C y^h, since dx = y^(1/2+h)dz, proving divergence. In contrast, Theta d_x v_K = O(r^(-2-2h)) is
absolutely integrable on the exterior. The two infinite signed parts in Remark 55.1, (55.16), are not generated there.
The weighted velocity estimate also gives v_K = K0+O_infty(r^(-2-h)), so d_x v_K has leading term y(y^2-3x^2)/r^6 and
has both signs on every sufficiently high horizontal line.

Put delta_B = 2beta-1 and W^perp = (-W_2,W_1). The vector field delta_B W+Omega W^perp-Theta e_2 has zero usual curl on
the exterior. In fact its curl is -delta_B Omega+div(Omega W)-Theta_x = 0 by (V), div W = 2beta and usual curl
W = -Omega. Its circulation around a circle is zero: the A2 velocity reflection parity preserves its one-form and
reverses the circle's orientation. It therefore has a single-valued potential Bern on the full exterior. For
Ly = Bern+yTheta,

  grad Ly = delta_B W+Omega W^perp+y grad Theta,
  Ly = delta_B beta r^2/2+O(r^(2-h)),
  W.grad Ly = delta_B|W|^2+kappa yTheta > 0
                         for sufficiently large r.              (69.35)

The gradient formula follows by differentiation. The leading gradient is delta_B beta X+O(r^(1-h)); integration on rays
and the bounded initial circle give its stated growth. The last inequality holds for both branches, since its first term
is of order r^2 and the possible negative term is O(r^(2-2h)). Thus Ly tends to infinity at infinity and is proper on
each sufficiently distant closed exterior. These are the growth and monotonicity assertions meaningful here from
Theorem 50(f), with no assertion about critical points or values in the interior.

We finish by specifying the limits of the conclusion. The canonical Green and strain representations of Theorem 9 hold
for the completed stream function. Their origin coefficient is the one determined by Omega_tot; the profile value
Psi_xy(0) = 2beta+2 is not prescribed. The corresponding transport balances in Theorem 45(d) require the interior
equations. The same qualification applies to the first axis zero and its jet in Theorem 2; the axis-jet, axis-chain and
source-basin conclusions of Theorems 8, 13, 14, 26, 27, 29, 30, 43, 46, 52, 54, 58 and 60; the complete backward-orbit
assertions of Theorems 44 and 47; or the global balances and radial sign requirement of Theorems 50(d), 54(e) and 55.
For the present examples, sigma[r Omega_r+(1+2h)Omega] = (1+h)r^(-h)g+O_infty(r^(-2h)), with an error divisible by
sin(2phi) uniformly. This expression is strictly positive throughout the sufficiently distant quadrant. The negative
region required by Theorem 55, if an actual profile existed, would have to occur in the missing interior. For instance
the exterior contribution to int K0 Omega is O(r_b^(-h)) beyond radius r_b, and does not prescribe the nonzero origin
strain.

The positive-vorticity-to-(H1) implication in Theorems 21 and 57 assumes the whole quadrant and the origin jet. The
negative-branch exclusion and quantitative balances in Theorem 62(a),(b) use a nonempty positive set, the negative
origin jet, and, where stated, radial sign triples. The source-corrected potential in Theorem 62(e) uses an integral
along the complete backward orbit to its source. The ray prohibitions and reductions in Theorem 64(b),(c) also use the
interior sign configuration. The source and complete-orbit moments of Theorem 65(d)-(f), and the component balances,
negative excursions and axis-source restrictions of Theorem 66(a)-(d),(g), are not supplied by an eventually signed
exterior. The local zero identities in Theorems 64-66 are meaningful where the local equations hold; for the examples
above there are no such exterior zeros. The local existence examples in Theorems 65(g) and 66(h) are not further
necessary conditions. The exact global angular-support restrictions in Theorems 10 and 49 are restrictions on all
coefficients of a profile, not on these leading trigonometric polynomials.

Some necessary conditions have angular conclusions but interior proofs. Theorem 47(a) is an explicit example. Taking
f = 0 and a nonzero G in (69.1) yields an exterior solution by (a). Formula (69.15) makes Theta identically zero, so it
violates that implication on every interior angle where G != 0. This does not contradict Theorem 47, whose profile
hypotheses are absent. It also illustrates why the homogeneous-vorticity conclusion of Theorem 1 uses the full backward
orbit. This example has f'' = 0, so a different example is needed for the last implication in Theorem 66(f). Take
f = sin(phi)cos(phi)^2[sin(phi)^2-1/2]^2, G = sin(2phi). These satisfy (69.1), and at phi = pi/4 one has f = f' = 0,
f'' = sqrt(2)/2 and G = 1. Part (a) again constructs an exterior solution. Thus f = f' = 0 implies f'' = 0 is also not
an exterior-only condition. Its proof in Theorem 66(f) invokes Theorem 47(a). For the nonzero examples (69.11) these
implications and all the other angular checks above hold.

Accordingly the theorem excludes a contradiction based only on the stated exterior problem for these examples. A further
obstruction to their completion must use information absent from that problem, possibly transmitted to infinity through
a global identity. It need not be formulated as a pointwise condition near the origin. This is the precise sense of (e).
QED.

### Theorem 70 (beta = 2: exact exterior solutions with the natural tail)

Put alpha = pi/2, Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, X = r e_r(phi), e_r(phi) = (cos(phi),sin(phi)),
e_phi(phi) = (-sin(phi),cos(phi)), e_2 = (0,1), O = (0,0), h = 1/2 and q = kappa = 0. A prime denotes an angular
derivative. The A2 parities are even in x and odd in y for Theta, odd in both variables for Omega and Psi, odd-even for
U_1, and even-odd for U_2. Use U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x), W = 2X+U, rcurl U = d_y U_1-d_x U_2, v^perp = (-v_2,v_1),
grad^perp f = (-f_y,f_x), and {f,g} = f_x g_y-f_y g_x. The stream function is normalized to be odd-odd. The notation
O_infty(r^mu_w) has the meaning of Theorem 36: every Cartesian derivative of order j is O(r^(mu_w-j)), uniformly in
angle. With an additional factor (1+log r)^N_log, the same factor is allowed in each derivative estimate. Put
a = alpha/3, b = 2alpha/3 and I_pl = (a,b); Theorem 68 denotes this interval by J. The leading stream degree is 3/2; it
is not denoted by a here. The profile symbols a0, b0, L, P_ax, A and c retain their origin and axis meanings, J(X)
denotes only the forward amplitude, and B and d retain their meanings in Theorem 66. None of these profile data is
prescribed here. We use delta for the Holder exponent, k_reg for a derivative order, mu_w for a weight, omega_rem for a
vorticity remainder, and N_log for a logarithmic power. Primes on traces or orbit functions denote differentiation in
their displayed variable.

(a) Let H,G be arbitrary smooth real functions on [0,alpha] satisfying

  H^(2j)(0) = 0, H^(2j+1)(alpha) = 0, H(alpha) = 0,
  G^(2j)(0) = G^(2j)(alpha) = 0, j = 0,1,2,... .
                                                               (70.1)

These are (68.1); nonzero H or G is not needed for existence. Reflect the functions with the A2 parities, and let P be
the unique odd-odd solution of -P''-(9/4)P = G. Fix a smooth compactly supported odd-odd Omega_in and a smooth radial
cutoff shape chi_0 with 0 <= chi_0 <= 1, chi_0 = 0 on [0,1] and chi_0 = 1 on [2,infinity).

There is R > 0, with supp Omega_in contained in {r < R/4}, and smooth Theta,Omega on {r > R}, including across the axes,
such that Theta has the additional value zero on the y-axis. With chi(X) = chi_0(r/R), set

  Omega_tot = Omega_in+chi Omega,
  U = BS(Omega_tot), W = 2X+U,
  -Lap Psi = Omega_tot, U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x).                     (70.2)

The product chi Omega is extended by zero. The fields Omega_tot,U,Psi are smooth on the plane. Here BS is the canonical
parity-grouped whole-plane inverse; no harmonic velocity is added. On r > 2R,

  W.grad Theta = 0, W.grad Omega+Omega = Theta_x,
  div W = 4, rcurl W = Omega, W_r > 0.                          (70.3)

The convergence Theta -> H and r^(1/2)Omega -> G is uniform in angle. More precisely, put

  H1 = (3/2)PH',
  G1 = (1/2)P'G+(3/2)PG'+sin(phi)H',
  -P1''-P1 = G1, P1 odd-odd,
  psi_0 = r^(3/2)P, psi_1 = r P1,
  u_i = (-d_y psi_i,d_x psi_i), i = 0,1.
  Then
  Theta = H+r^(-1/2)H1+O_infty(r^(-1)),
  Omega = r^(-1/2)G+r^(-1)G1+O_infty(r^(-3/2)),
  U = u_0+u_1+O_infty(r^(-1/2)),
  Psi = psi_0+psi_1+O_infty(r^(1/2)).                           (70.4)

Thus the derivative bounds and first corrections of Theorems 36 and 45(f) hold.

(b) The solution has the expansion of Theorem 68 to every finite order. In the normalization z = log r and
mu_n = (3-n)/2, let H_n,G_n,P_n be its polynomial coefficients, with H_0 = H, G_0 = G, P_0 = P. For each N >= 0 there is
an integer N_log_N >= 0 such that

  Theta - sum_(n=0)^N r^(-n/2)H_n(z,phi)
     = O_infty(r^(-(N+1)/2)(1+log r)^N_log_N),
  Omega - sum_(n=0)^N r^(-(n+1)/2)G_n(z,phi)
     = O_infty(r^(-(N+2)/2)(1+log r)^N_log_N),
  Psi - sum_(n=0)^N r^mu_n P_n(z,phi)
     = O_infty(r^((2-N)/2)(1+log r)^N_log_N).                   (70.5)

The velocity expansion follows by differentiating Psi. The constants c_m in (68.3) are fixed by Omega_tot, with the
polynomial resonant particular solution normalized to have zero constant coefficient as in (68.10). In particular, if
g_7 is the sine coefficient (2/alpha)int_0^alpha G_7(phi)sin(2phi)dphi, the first logarithmic term is

  (g_7/4) r^(-2) log r sin(2phi) in Psi.                        (70.6)

The set g_7 != 0 is open and dense in the real C^infinity Frechet space defined by (70.1), with its usual seminorm
topology. This statement holds for every prescribed core and every cutoff construction in (a). It is not a density
assertion within a sign or plateau subclass. When g_7 = 0 the displayed logarithmic term is absent; later resonances can
still produce logarithms.

(c) There is a specific small class in which the construction is unique. Fix 0 < delta < 1 and define, with one-sided
values at r = r_base,

  ||v||_(mu_w,k_reg,delta;r_base)
     = sup_(r_scale>=r_base) r_scale^(-mu_w)
        ||v(r_scale .)||_(C^(k_reg,delta)({1 <= |zeta| <= 2})).
  Omega = r^(-1/2)G+omega_rem, omega_rem odd-odd,
  ||omega_rem||_(-1,1,delta;R/2) <= M_* .                       (70.7)

Here M_* depends only on chi_0, delta and finitely many norms of H,G. The two auxiliary transport equations are imposed
on all r > R/2, and (70.2) specifies the physical curl there. Uniqueness is in this class with the stated leading
terminal data, for sufficiently large R. The contraction metric is ||omega_rem_1-omega_rem_2||_(-1,0,delta;R/2). There
is no uniqueness assertion from H,G,Omega_in and (70.3) alone. Even with chi fixed, the vorticity in R < r < 2R is
additional data.

The whole-plane inversion makes the harmonic data explicit. Write Omega_tot = sum_(m>=1) omega_m(r)sin(2m phi). For any
fixed r_b > 2R and r > r_b,

  Psi = sum_(m>=1) sin(2m phi)/(4m) [
    r^(-2m) int_(r_b)^r t^(2m+1)omega_m(t)dt
    +r^(2m) int_r^infinity t^(1-2m)omega_m(t)dt
    +r^(-2m) int_0^(r_b) t^(2m+1)omega_m(t)dt ].
                                                               (70.8)

The last terms form a smoothly convergent harmonic sum on r >= r_b+epsilon_gap, for every epsilon_gap > 0. They are the
harmonic constants for this integral normalization. They are not in general the constants c_m for the polynomial
normalization in (b); the latter are given precisely in the proof.

For the smooth completion Theta_tot = chi Theta, the transport residuals are, on R < r < 2R,

  W.grad Theta_tot = (W.grad chi)Theta,
  W.grad Omega_tot+Omega_tot-(Theta_tot)_x
     = (W.grad chi)Omega-chi_x Theta.                           (70.9)

On r < R they are zero and W.grad Omega_in+Omega_in, respectively. These formulas locate possible failures, without
claiming a residual is nonzero at every point of its support. Poisson, divergence and curl hold on the whole plane.

(d) Take the explicit pairs (68.5), with either sigma = 1 or sigma = -1. There is R' > 2R such that every forward orbit
starting in r > R' remains there, has an interior limit angle ell(X) when X is in Q1, and

  sigma Theta > 0 on Q1 cap {r > R'},
  S = {X in Q1: r > R', ell(X) in (a,b)}
    is open, connected, forward invariant and of infinite area,
  Theta = sigma, Omega = 0, Lap Psi = 0 on S,
  {Omega = 0} cap Q1 cap {r > R'}
     = {X in Q1: r > R', ell(X) in [a,b]},
  sigma Omega > 0 where ell(X) is in (0,a) or (b,alpha).
                                                               (70.10)

The two boundary orbits ell = a,b also have Theta = sigma and Omega = 0. All derivatives of Theta-sigma and Omega vanish
on them. They need not bound straight angular sectors. Every closed interval contained in I_pl does give an exact
straight potential sector at sufficiently large radii. There is no zero of W in the exterior.

The bounds, local identities, forward laws and angular conclusions used in the three comparisons of Theorem 68(d) hold
on these exteriors, with inner boundary fluxes in all integrated identities. Those comparisons concern profiles with
finitely many zero components, nonnegative vorticity with positive temperature, or negative temperature and bounded
positive vorticity. Their interior hypotheses are retained, not asserted. For the positive pair a core nonnegative on Q1
gives a canonical vorticity completion nonnegative on Q1 when R is sufficiently large. For the negative pair the
physical positive-vorticity set {X in Q1: Omega_tot(X) > 0} is bounded. With zero core, either pair admits a canonical
completion whose only zero of W is O.

(e) The angular conclusion of Theorem 47(a) at beta = 2 is not an exterior consequence. For example the admissible data

  H(phi) = sin(phi)cos(phi)^2, G(phi) = sin(2phi),
  phi_c = arcsin(1/sqrt(3))
  satisfy H'(phi_c) = 0 and G(phi_c) > 0.                       (70.11)

Their solutions in (a) have Theta > 0 and Omega > 0 throughout the sufficiently distant open first quadrant, and have a
critical escaping orbit with positive vorticity. This does not contradict Theorem 47, whose proof uses bounded complete
backward orbits.

(f) No necessary condition implied solely by the exact exterior equations, canonical whole-plane inversion and the
natural tail can exclude the plateau examples in (d). Conditions about extension through the interior, including angular
conclusions proved using that extension, are outside this assertion.

Scope. Exterior solutions are not profiles. The construction supplies no realization of the interior equations, the
nonzero origin jet, P_ax, the strain identity with value 3 pi/2 or (H1) as profile data. Complete backward-orbit
statements, source curves and global balances are not supplied by the construction. No convergence of the formal series
is asserted. No assertion for beta > 2 is made.

Proof.

We first construct the fields at one fixed regularity, then prove smoothness at the chosen radius. The higher order
asymptotics will follow from the equations and a separate estimate for the angular modes of Poisson's equation.

Reflection and inversion. The smooth reflections, the angular inverses for P and P1, and preservation of the extra value
at alpha are as in Theorem 68(a). The odd-odd angular modes are sin(2m phi), m >= 1; the two eigenvalues are 4m^2-9/4
and 4m^2-1.

We use the common inverse estimate proved in Theorem 69, (69.12):

  ||BS(v)||_(1-gamma,k_reg+1,delta;R/2)
     <= C ||v||_(-gamma,k_reg,delta;R/2), 0 < gamma < 2.        (70.12)

Here v is odd-odd and smoothly cut off on r <= R, k_reg >= 0, and C is independent of R >= 2. The same result includes
differences, uniformly scaled cutoff derivatives, and a fixed smooth core. The proof of (69.12) explicitly does not
depend on beta or transport. Its local div-curl estimate, including a prescribed divergence, is therefore available at
beta = 2. The compact odd-odd core has zero mass and first moments, so its velocity is O_infty(r^(-3)). Its weighted
exterior norm tends to zero. The canonical uniqueness and velocity parities are those established with that estimate in
Theorem 69.

Terminal transport. Suppose ||U||_(1/2,k_reg,delta;r_base) <= C_*, with k_reg = 1 or 2, and C_* r_base^(-1/2)
sufficiently small. Every forward orbit starting at r >= r_base stays there. Writing Phi_t for this forward flow gives

  d_t |Phi_t X|^(1/2) = |Phi_t X|^(1/2)+O(C_*),
  C_lo e^(2t)|X| <= |Phi_t X| <= C e^(2t)|X|.                   (70.13)

These are the flow bounds proved in Theorem 69, (69.13). That argument requires h > 0 and beta h = 1, both satisfied
here. In particular, on a starting annulus of radius r_scale the normalized flow e^(-2t)Phi_t(r_scale zeta)/r_scale has
uniformly bounded C^(k_reg,delta) norms and converges in that space. Its equation has the integrable coefficient
r_scale^(-1/2)e^(-t). This holds at every finite order for which the corresponding velocity norm is available.

If lambda_tr+2mu_w < 0, define

  I_(lambda_tr,U)F_src(X) = -int_0^infinity e^(lambda_tr t)F_src(Phi_t X)dt.
  Then (W.grad+lambda_tr)I_(lambda_tr,U)F_src = F_src,
  ||I_(lambda_tr,U)F_src||_(mu_w,k_reg,delta;r_base)
     <= C ||F_src||_(mu_w,k_reg,delta;r_base).                  (70.14)

This is the terminal inverse proved in Theorem 69, (69.14), with beta = 2. Its proof uses only the strict inequality
lambda_tr+beta mu_w < 0 and the preceding flow estimates. It also proves uniqueness among solutions with e^(lambda_tr
t)-weighted value tending to zero on every forward orbit. The applications below have strictly negative exponents;
kappa = 0 causes no loss of integrability.

The fixed point. Put r_base = R/2, Theta_0 = H(phi) and Omega_0 = r^(-1/2)G(phi). For an input omega_rem in (70.7), set

  U_trial = BS(Omega_in+chi(Omega_0+omega_rem)),
  Theta_trial = Theta_0+I_(0,U_trial)(-U_trial.grad Theta_0),
  Omega_trial = Omega_0+
    I_(1,U_trial)((Theta_trial)_x-U_trial.grad Omega_0).
                                                               (70.15)

We use omega_rem -> Omega_trial-Omega_0 as the map. The identities 2X.grad Theta_0 = 0 and (2X.grad+1)Omega_0 = 0 show
that its outputs solve both auxiliary transport equations with velocity U_trial.

Let a bound C_data control 1, the C^(3,delta) norm of H and the C^(2,delta) norm of G. Provided M_* r_base^(-1/2) <= 1
and the core norm is at most 1, the input source is bounded in C^(1,delta), weight -1/2, by a constant depending only on
C_data and chi_0. Equation (70.12) with gamma = 1/2 gives a uniform C^(2,delta) velocity bound in weight 1/2. The
temperature source U_trial.grad H has weight -1/2 and regularity C^(2,delta). Its transport exponent is 0+2(-1/2) = -1,
not zero. Consequently the temperature correction has weight -1/2 and that regularity. The vorticity source has weight
-1 and regularity C^(1,delta); its exponent is 1+2(-1) = -1. It follows that

  ||Theta_trial-H||_(-1/2,2,delta;r_base) <= C_0,
  ||Omega_trial-Omega_0||_(-1,1,delta;r_base) <= C_0.           (70.16)

Here C_0 is independent of M_* and R under these smallness conditions. Choose M_* = 2C_0 and then enlarge R.

For two inputs let dist_aux be their distance in the metric of (c). Use parenthesized superscripts to distinguish their
full fields and put Delta U = U^(1)-U^(2), with analogous differences for the outputs. Equation (70.12), now with
gamma = 1, gives ||Delta U||_(0,1,delta;r_base) <= C dist_aux. Subtracting the output equations, with W^(1) on the left,
gives

  W^(1).grad Delta Theta = -Delta U.grad Theta^(2),
  (W^(1).grad+1)Delta Omega
     = (Delta Theta)_x-Delta U.grad Omega^(2).                  (70.17)

The first source is C^(1,delta), weight -1, because Theta^(2) is uniformly C^(2,delta), weight 0. The exponent in
(70.14) is -2. Thus Delta Theta is bounded by C dist_aux in C^(1,delta), weight -1. The two sources in the second
equation have weights -2 and -3/2 in C^(0,delta), respectively. Its output satisfies

  ||Delta Omega||_(-3/2,0,delta;r_base) <= C_1 dist_aux,
  ||Delta Omega||_(-1,0,delta;r_base) <= C_1 r_base^(-1/2)dist_aux.
                                                               (70.18)

For the two source weights the transport exponents are -3 and -2. The terminal differences vanish: the original
temperature remainders tend to zero, and e^t times the original vorticity remainders tends to zero by their weight -1.
Hence terminal uniqueness justifies using (70.14) in the difference equations; no assumption about a common limiting
angle for the two flows is being made.

Choose R so that all flow smallness conditions hold and C_1 r_base^(-1/2) <= 1/2. The ball is complete in the weaker
metric. Indeed a Cauchy sequence converges in weighted C^(0,delta). On each compact annulus its first derivatives are
uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. Subsequence convergence, integration along segments in local charts and uniqueness
of the function limit identify its first derivatives. Their delta seminorm bound passes to the limit for each pair of
points. Taking the supremum over the annuli preserves the bound M_*. The limit is therefore in the ball. Banach's
theorem proves existence and precisely the uniqueness in (c).

The symmetries preserve the inverse, the vector field and its flow, and both formulas in (70.15). They therefore hold
for the fixed point. Both axes are invariant. On the y-axis H is zero and its tangential derivative is zero, so U.grad H
is zero there; (70.15) gives Theta = 0. Oddness gives its zero value on the x-axis as well. This verifies the additional
axis condition separately from evenness in x.

Smoothness at the fixed radius. The fixed point initially gives Omega in C^(1,delta), Theta in C^(2,delta), U in
C^(2,delta), with the weights already stated. A separate derivative gain is necessary; repeating the contraction at
successively higher orders with increasing radii would not prove the assertion.

On an exterior annulus of radius r_scale define u(zeta) = r_scale^(-1/2)U(r_scale zeta),
vort_scaled(zeta) = r_scale^(1/2)Omega(r_scale zeta), grad_scaled(zeta) = r_scale grad Theta(r_scale zeta),
epsilon = r_scale^(-1/2), Z_scaled = 2zeta+epsilon u and F_acc = Du Z_scaled. Where chi = 1, direct differentiation
gives

  div F_acc = epsilon tr((Du)^2),
  rcurl F_acc = vort_scaled+epsilon grad_scaled_1.
  In the transition region the second identity is
  rcurl F_acc = chi_scale vort_scaled+epsilon chi_scale grad_scaled_1
                   +(Z_scaled.grad chi_scale)vort_scaled,
  chi_scale(zeta) = chi(r_scale zeta).                          (70.19)

The core is absent on r > r_base. To verify the curl formula, if curl_scaled = rcurl u, then rcurl(Du
Z_scaled) = 2curl_scaled+Z_scaled.grad curl_scaled. For curl_scaled = vort_scaled use Z_scaled.grad
vort_scaled+vort_scaled = epsilon grad_scaled_1; for curl_scaled = chi_scale vort_scaled use the product rule. The
divergence formula uses div u = 0. In particular no derivative of vort_scaled or grad_scaled appears in these sources.

Assume vort_scaled,grad_scaled are bounded in C^(k_reg,delta) on normalized annuli, and u in C^(k_reg+1,delta). This
holds initially for k_reg = 1. The cited div-curl estimate gives F_acc in C^(k_reg+1,delta) on smaller annuli. Launch
from a circle r = r_launch > r_base. Write X(t,l) for the flow, rho_launch(l)e_r(ell_launch(l)) = lim e^(-2t)X(t,l),
t_hat = W/|W| and n_hat = (-t_hat_2,t_hat_1). Put K_11 = t_hat.DU t_hat and

  E_fr = e^(2t)grad Theta.t_hat = 0,
  B_fr = e^(2t)grad Theta.n_hat, j_fr = e^t Omega.
  Then B_fr' = K_11 B_fr, j_fr' = e^(-t)B_fr n_hat_1.           (70.20)

The vanishing E_fr follows from W.grad Theta = 0. To check the other equations, in the moving orthonormal frame write
DU = [[K_11,K_12],[K_21,-K_11]]. The direction satisfies t_hat' = K_21 n_hat, and grad Theta satisfies its
differentiated transport equation. Hence B_fr' = K_11 B_fr-(K_12+K_21)E_fr = K_11 B_fr. The second equation is exactly
vorticity transport. Thus no division by kappa and no nonzero longitudinal gradient component is used at beta = 2.

The normalized flow and its limiting vector have C^(k_reg+1,delta) regularity by (70.13). Flow charts have uniformly
regular inverses on fixed-width normalized time strips. Indeed det(W,X_l) = r_launch W_r(r_launch e_r(l))e^(4t); after
scaling this determinant is bounded away from zero, and differentiating the inverse matrix formula gives the inverse
estimates. Moreover DU t_hat is obtained from F_acc by division by |Z_scaled| and multiplication by r_scale^(-1/2). Thus
e^t K_11 has C^(k_reg+1,delta) bounds in the label and normalized charts, with the additional size r_launch^(-1/2).

The already differentiated leading limits in (70.16) give the terminal values and solutions

  B_fr_infinity = rho_launch^(-1)H'(ell_launch),
  j_fr_infinity = rho_launch^(-1/2)G(ell_launch),
  B_fr(t) = B_fr_infinity exp(-int_t^infinity K_11(v)dv),
  j_fr(t) = j_fr_infinity-int_t^infinity e^(-v)B_fr(v)n_hat_1(v)dv.
                                                               (70.21)

All terminal data on the right have C^(k_reg+1,delta) regularity. The coefficient bounds are integrable with the factor
e^(-t), so differentiation and Holder differences pass under the integrals. If the launch radius is r_launch, use
r_launch B_fr and sqrt(r_launch)j_fr; their norms and terminal norms are uniformly bounded. This proves one additional
label derivative for grad_scaled and vort_scaled. Time derivatives of total order k_reg+1 follow by differentiating
(70.20) at most k_reg times, so the full normalized chart regularity improves by one. The inverse charts transfer the
gain to Cartesian annuli, and Poisson inversion gives u in C^(k_reg+2,delta). This closes the induction.

The same argument works throughout r > r_base using the cutoff version of (70.19); (70.20) is unchanged. Formally the
induction assertion is made for every closed exterior r >= r_outer > r_base. To prove the next order on one such
exterior, launch at r_inner with r_base < r_inner < r_outer and use slightly larger annuli still inside r > r_base. The
old assertion is available at that r_inner. For uniform weighted estimates on distant annuli, launch instead at a fixed
fraction of the annulus radius; the normalized estimates just proved are uniform in that launch radius. Thus R is fixed
once and for all, while constants can depend on derivative order and on r_outer-r_base. The result is smoothness on
r > r_base, including a neighbourhood of r = R, and all the natural differentiated bounds at infinity. Flatness of the
cutoff at r = R now proves the claimed global smoothness of (70.2).

First corrections. Put Temp_scaled = Theta, Vort_scaled = r^(1/2)Omega and (v_r,v_phi) = r^(-1/2)(U_r,U_phi). On r > 2R
the exact polar equations are

  (2+r^(-1/2)v_r) r Temp_scaled_r = -r^(-1/2)v_phi Temp_scaled_phi,
  (2+r^(-1/2)v_r) r Vort_scaled_r
     = r^(-1/2)[(1/2)v_r Vort_scaled-v_phi Vort_scaled_phi
                       -sin(phi)Temp_scaled_phi+cos(phi)r Temp_scaled_r].
                                                               (70.22)

All normalized derivatives are bounded, and the denominator is at least 1 after increasing the radius. Uniform angular
convergence and the bounded higher angular derivatives imply convergence in every finite angular C^j norm: compactness
gives subsequential convergence of those derivatives, and integration identifies each limit with the corresponding
derivative of H or G. The right sides show that all normalized derivatives of r Temp_scaled_r and r Vort_scaled_r are
O(r^(-1/2)). Integrating in dr/r from infinity, using these differentiated leading limits, gives Temp_scaled-H and
Vort_scaled-G of order O_infty(r^(-1/2)). To convert normalized derivatives to Cartesian ones, write r d_x and r d_y as
smooth angular combinations of r d_r and d_phi and iterate.

Cut off psi_0 in a fixed disc. Its smooth global curl equals Omega_0 outside that disc and its sublinear velocity is
canonical by uniqueness. The difference source is O_infty(r^(-1)); (70.12) with gamma = 1, allowing its smooth core,
gives U-u_0 = O_infty(1). Substitution in (70.22) now yields

  r Temp_scaled_r = -(1/2)r^(-1/2)H1+O_infty(r^(-1)),
  r Vort_scaled_r = -(1/2)r^(-1/2)G1+O_infty(r^(-1)).           (70.23)

The exterior integration argument of Theorem 45(f) now applies verbatim: its only inputs are these differentiated
equations, terminal leading limits, canonical inversion and the local angular Poisson equations. Its three inverse
weights are gamma = 1/2, 1 and 3/2, all in the range of (70.12). It yields every expansion in (70.4), including
-P1''-P1 = G1. The positive stream remainder degree 1/2 absorbs the finite integration constant. No interior profile
assertion is used in this step.

Poisson remainders and resonances. We give the additional estimate needed beyond those three weights. Suppose psi_rem is
smooth and odd-odd on r >= r_b, psi_rem = O_infty(r^mu_old(1+log r)^N_log), mu_old < 2, and -Lap
psi_rem = F_src = O_infty(r^(mu_new-2)(1+log r)^N_log), where mu_new = mu_old-1/2. Assume mu_old is an integer multiple
of 1/2. Then, after subtracting a single term c_harm r^mu_old sin(-mu_old phi) if mu_old is a negative even integer, one
has psi_rem = O_infty(r^mu_new(1+log r)^(N_log+1)). If mu_old is not a negative even integer there is no term to
subtract.

Here is a proof including uniform angular control. Write nu_mode = 2m and let psi_rem_m,F_src_m be the sine
coefficients. Since mu_new < 2 <= nu_mode, the integral at infinity in the following formula converges:

  psi_rem_m(r) = C_m r^(-nu_mode)+(1/(2nu_mode))[
    r^(-nu_mode) int_(r_b)^r t^(nu_mode+1)F_src_m(t)dt
    +r^nu_mode int_r^infinity t^(1-nu_mode)F_src_m(t)dt ].
                                                               (70.24)

This is variation of parameters for -psi_rem_m''-r^(-1)psi_rem_m'+nu_mode^2r^(-2)psi_rem_m = F_src_m. Its Wronskian is
-2nu_mode/r. A possible r^nu_mode term is excluded by the assumed growth of psi_rem. If nu_mode+mu_new > 0 the first
integral is O(r^(nu_mode+mu_new)(1+log r)^N_log). If nu_mode+mu_new = 0 it is O((1+log r)^(N_log+1)). If
nu_mode+mu_new < 0, split it into its finite integral to infinity and the negative of its tail; the finite integral
changes C_m, and the tail has size O(r^(nu_mode+mu_new)(1+log r)^N_log). The second integral always contributes
O(r^mu_new(1+log r)^N_log) after its prefactor.

Only finitely many modes have nu_mode+mu_new <= 0. In those with -nu_mode > mu_old, the total r^(-nu_mode) coefficient
must vanish, by the assumed bound on psi_rem. In the interval [mu_new,mu_old] the only possible value -nu_mode > mu_new
is -nu_mode = mu_old: negative even integers are separated by 2 and the interval has length 1/2. This leaves exactly the
term stated. At -nu_mode = mu_new the allowed logarithmic bound already includes the harmonic term.

For every integer j and every N_four, the coefficients of (r partial_r)^j F_src are bounded by
C_(j,N_four)(1+m)^(-N_four)r^(mu_new-2)(1+log r)^N_log, by integration by parts on the smoothly reflected angle circle.
The same rapid decrease holds for the boundary data psi_rem_m(r_b). For all sufficiently large m the denominators
nu_mode, nu_mode+mu_new and nu_mode-mu_new in the integral estimates have size comparable to m. Boundary terms decay
like (r_b/r)^nu_mode. These bounds sum after any number of angular and radial differentiations on r >= 2r_b; the finite
remaining annulus is harmless by smoothness. This proves the asserted O_infty estimate, rather than only a modewise
assertion. It also proves uniqueness of the extracted coefficient.

We can now prove (70.5) by induction without a weighted Biot-Savart assertion outside its proved range. At the beginning
of step n >= 1, suppose the coefficients through n-1 have been subtracted and the errors are

  Theta error = O_infty(r^(-n/2)(1+log r)^N_log),
  Omega error = O_infty(r^(-(n+1)/2)(1+log r)^N_log),
  Psi error = O_infty(r^mu_n(1+log r)^N_log).                   (70.25)

The case n = 1 was proved above. The corresponding velocity error has exponent mu_n-1 = (1-n)/2. Replacing the true
fields by the known sums in U.grad Theta creates an error of exponent at most -(n+1)/2: the largest term is the velocity
error acting on H. In U.grad Omega the analogous largest exponent is -(n+2)/2, from the velocity error acting on
r^(-1/2)G. The missing temperature derivative in vorticity transport also has exponent -(n+2)/2. Products of two errors
have at least these decay rates.

Consequently the coefficient equations are precisely (68.7), with mu_n = (3-n)/2 and D_z = partial_z in our notation.
Use its polynomial transport inverses and angular reflection statements. No new coefficient equation is needed. After
subtracting H_n and G_n, the radial equations with 2r partial_r on the left have errors of exponents -(n+1)/2 and
-(n+2)/2, respectively. For 2r f_r+lambda_tr f = F_src the terminal inverse is -(1/2)r^(-lambda_tr/2) int_r^infinity
t^(lambda_tr/2-1)F_src(t)dt. With lambda_tr = 0 and 1 these improved exponents give strict convergence and a gain of
half a radial power. Radial derivatives follow from the equation and angular derivatives pass under the integral. The
old remainder bounds exclude a homogeneous constant temperature or r^(-1/2) vorticity.

Choose the polynomial Poisson solution in (68.7) as in Theorem 68. Subtract it from the true stream function. Its old
bound has exponent mu_n and its new source bound exponent mu_n-5/2. Apply (70.24) with mu_new = mu_n-1/2. At n = 4m+3,
mu_n = -2m, extract its one remaining harmonic coefficient and include it in P_n. At every other n nothing is extracted.
The new stream error has exponent mu_n-1/2, with at most another finite power of log r. This is (70.25) for the next
step and proves (70.5) for every N.

Theorem 68(b) supplies the polynomial Poisson inverses and their normalization. The first permitted resonance is n = 7,
since parity excludes the constant angular mode. There are no earlier logarithms or harmonic constants. Thus its
resonant coefficient is c_1+(g_7/4)z. The nonzero polynomial forcing map and its open dense nonzero set are those of
Theorem 68(b): for H = (sin(phi)+sin(3phi))/4 and G = 0, (68.12) gives g_7 = 203/7372800 and g_7/4 = 203/29491200. The
actual expansion has exactly those coefficients before the first free harmonic constant, so the assertion is independent
of the prescribed core and annular data. The topology is the usual real C^infinity topology, not a relative topology on
a sign or plateau subclass.

Harmonic normalization and annular data. The modal formula (70.8) follows from (70.24), now with the actual source, by
regularity at the origin and sublinear velocity at infinity. The origin eliminates the singular homogeneous mode there;
sublinearity eliminates the growing mode. Smooth angular coefficients of a compact source have rapidly decreasing
moments, and the factor (r_b/r)^(2m) gives smooth convergence of the displayed harmonic sum. The full modal inverse
equals the grouped inverse by canonical uniqueness.

The precise constants in (b) can be defined without a possibly divergent unrenormalized moment. At n = 4m+3 let P_n^0 be
the polynomial solution whose resonant constant is zero, with all earlier constants already fixed. For a function f
write [f]_(2m) for its sin(2m phi) coefficient. Then

  c_m = lim_(r->infinity) [
    r^(2m) [Psi(r,.)]_(2m)
    -sum_(j=0)^(n-1) r^(2m+mu_j)[P_j(log r,.)]_(2m)
    -[P_n^0(log r,.)]_(2m) ].
                                                               (70.26)

The remainder estimate at step n is O(r^(-1/2)(1+log r)^N_log), so this limit exists. Equations (70.8) and (70.26) fix
c_m from Omega_tot and exactly the normalization (68.10), with z = log r. Changing the logarithmic length scale or the
particular inverse would change its displayed constant. No such change is made here.

We substantiate the limitation on uniqueness. Choose a smooth nonnegative nonzero function bump(t) supported in a
compact interval of (1,2) where chi_0 > 0, and prescribe

  omega_bump(X) = tau R^(-1/2)bump(r/R)sin(2phi).               (70.27)

Run the same fixed point with velocity BS(Omega_in+omega_bump+chi Omega). For |tau| <= 1 all bounds are uniform. The
known additional smooth curl contributes only known smooth terms to (70.19), so the smoothness proof is unchanged.
Replace the resulting auxiliary Omega by Omega+omega_bump/chi on r > R, extending the quotient by zero outside the
support of bump. The physical source again has the form (70.2), with the original Omega_in and chi, and all equations
outside 2R and all asymptotic assertions persist.

Denote the auxiliary solutions before the quotient is added by Omega_aux^(tau). The same difference estimates, including
the direct forcing from omega_bump, give ||Omega_aux^(tau)-Omega_aux^(0)||_(-1,0,delta;r_base) <= C|tau|. Here the
prescribed velocity is bounded by C|tau| in weight 1/2, the direct temperature difference has weight -1/2, and the
direct vorticity difference weight -1; the remaining unknown difference is absorbed by (70.18). The velocity induced by
this auxiliary difference at r = 3R is therefore O(|tau|). The absorbed annular quotient itself has weighted norm of
size |tau|sqrt(R); it is not included in this comparison. In contrast, put c_bump = (1/4)int_1^2 t^3 bump(t)dt > 0. The
prescribed source has exterior stream tau c_bump R^(7/2)r^(-2)sin(2phi) and velocity (-2tau c_bump sqrt(R)/27,0) at
(3R,0). For large R this cannot be canceled by O(|tau|). Thus even the exterior velocities differ. The annular freedom
is real. Finally, the product rule gives (70.9) and the stated core residuals.

The plateau formula. We spell out the data of Theorem 68(d), retaining its normalization. Put

  flat(t) = exp(-1/t) for t > 0, flat(t) = 0 for t <= 0,
  step(t) = flat(t)/(flat(t)+flat(1-t)),
  f_raw(phi) = step(2(a-phi)/a), 0 <= phi <= a,
  g_raw(phi) = (alpha-phi)step(2(phi-b)/(alpha-b)),
                                      b <= phi <= alpha,
  N_left = int_0^a f_raw, N_right = int_b^alpha g_raw,
  f_left = f_raw/N_left, g_right = g_raw/N_right,
  H_pos(phi) = int_0^phi f_left on [0,a], 1 on [a,b],
             int_phi^alpha g_right on [b,alpha],
  G_pos(phi) = phi f_left(phi)^2 on [0,a], 0 on [a,b],
             g_right(phi) on [b,alpha],
  H = sigma H_pos, G = sigma G_pos, P = sigma P_pos.            (70.28)

Both normalization constants are positive. The cutoff step is flat at 0 and 1, so all pieces fit smoothly. Both passages
have strict signs, and near the axes

  H_pos = phi/N_left, G_pos = phi/N_left^2 near 0,
  H_pos = (alpha-phi)^2/(2N_right),
  G_pos = (alpha-phi)/N_right near alpha.                       (70.29)

These formulas verify every condition in (70.1). The Dirichlet Green formula, also used in Theorem 59(g), is

  P_pos(phi) = int_0^alpha
    sin((3/2)min(phi,t))sin((3/2)(alpha-max(phi,t)))
       G_pos(t)dt / [(3/2)sin(3alpha/2)].
                                                               (70.30)

Its derivative jump is -1. Since 3alpha/2 = 3pi/4, its kernel is positive in the open square. Thus P_pos > 0, and
P_pos'' = -G_pos-(9/4)P_pos < 0 throughout (0,alpha), including on the plateau. Differentiating at the endpoints gives
P_pos'(0) > 0 and P_pos'(alpha) < 0. Hence P_pos' has exactly one zero. These are precisely the signed angular stream
inequalities in Theorems 59(b) and 64(a).

For an arbitrary exterior point define the smooth scattering data

  rho(X)e_r(ell(X)) = lim_(t->infinity)e^(-2t)Phi_t X.
  Then rho(X)/r = 1+O_infty(r^(-1/2)),
  ell(X)-phi = O_infty(r^(-1/2)),
  rho(Phi_t X) = e^(2t)rho(X),
  ell(Phi_t X) = ell(X).                                        (70.31)

For the first two estimates, O_infty is applied to the scalar ratio and the locally lifted angle difference. They follow
by integrating the normalized flow equation and its differentiated equations. On each sufficiently distant circle the
angular map ell is close to the identity in C^k_reg and fixes both axes. Its angular derivative is positive.
Equivalently, the determinant identity for a launch circle gives 2rho_launch(l)^2 ell_launch'(l) = r_launch W_r(r_launch
e_r(l)) > 0. Consequently ell takes (0,alpha) diffeomorphically onto (0,alpha) on each large quadrant arc.

Temperature invariance and terminal vorticity transport give the exact pointwise formula

  Theta(X) = H(ell(X)),
  Omega(X) = rho(X)^(-1/2)G(ell(X))+b_T(X)H'(ell(X)),
  b_T(X) = -int_0^infinity e^t ell_x(Phi_t X)dt.
                                                               (70.32)

The integral defining b_T converges with all derivatives by the preceding flow estimates. To verify its sign uniformly
near the axes, (70.31) in C^2 gives |r ell_x+sin(phi)| <= C r^(-1/2). The left error vanishes on the x-axis and has
angular derivative O(r^(-1/2)), by reflection. On [0,alpha/2], the mean value theorem therefore improves the estimate to
C r^(-1/2)sin(phi); on [alpha/2,alpha] the original estimate has that form after changing C. Thus

  -ell_x(X) = (sin(phi)/r)(1+O(r^(-1/2))) > 0 in Q1,
  ell_y(X) = (cos(phi)/r)(1+O(r^(-1/2))) > 0 in Q1,
  0 < b_T(X) <= C r^(-1)sin(ell(X)),
  b_T(X)/rho(X)^(-1/2) <= C r^(-1/2).                           (70.33)

For the ell_y formula, ell is constant with value alpha on the positive y-axis, so ell_y vanishes there. Its Cartesian
derivative error therefore vanishes there as well, and the same C^2 estimate and mean value argument apply with
alpha-phi. Along the integral in (70.32), sin(arg Phi_t X) is comparable to sin(ell(X)), because the angular maps and
their endpoint derivatives are uniformly close to the identity. Combine this with |Phi_t X| comparable to e^(2t)r to
prove the last two estimates.

On the increasing passage, (70.28) and (70.32) give sigma Omega = rho^(-1/2)ell f_left(ell)^2+b_T f_left(ell) > 0. On
the decreasing passage they give sigma Omega = g_right(ell)(rho^(-1/2)-b_T) > 0 for sufficiently large r, uniformly all
the way to its flat endpoint. On ell in [a,b] both G and H' vanish, so Omega = 0 exactly. Temperature has the asserted
strict sign because ell is an interior angle. This proves the sign claims without dividing an asymptotic remainder by a
flat function.

The inverse angular map on every circle identifies S with (R',infinity) x (a,b). It is therefore open and connected; it
is forward invariant by (70.31). Its angular width tends to b-a > 0, so its area is infinite. The transport formula
gives Theta = sigma there and Poisson gives harmonic Psi. The boundary levels ell = a,b are smooth curves, because
ell_phi > 0, and W is tangent to them and has positive radial component. Flatness of H_pos-1 and G_pos at a,b, and
(70.32), prove flatness on these curves. Compact subintervals of I_pl belong to S for all large radii by (70.31). This
proves all of (d)'s geometric assertions.

We now check the exterior content of the earlier results. The following calculations apply to both plateau signs, with a
sign hypothesis imposed only where stated.

On the two passages, (70.32)-(70.33) give the exact derivative signs

  sgn Theta_x = -sgn H'(ell), sgn Theta_y = sgn H'(ell),
  Theta_phi = H'(ell)ell_phi.
  On compact passage intervals,
  U.grad Theta = (3/2)PH' r^(-1/2)+O(r^(-1)).
                                                               (70.34)

The first three assertions also hold arbitrarily near a flat transition, with zero on its boundary. The last has both
signs for either sigma, because PH' = P_pos H_pos'. Every sufficiently distant horizontal half-line y = y_0 and vertical
half-line x = x_0 traverses both passages: its radius stays exterior, its limit angle approaches the two endpoint angles
at its two ends, and ell_x < 0 or ell_y > 0 supplies strict monotonicity. Thus both strict derivative signs in
Theorem 57(b) occur on each of these half-lines. They also occur on every sufficiently large quadrant arc. A low
horizontal or vertical line truncated by the inner disc need not contain both signs. The assertion in Theorem 57 about
every complete half-line and every radius uses the interior. The radial premise H(phi) = 0 in Theorem 57(c) never holds
at an interior angle for these data.

The velocity signs in Theorem 59(b) also follow: for sigma = 1, U_phi > 0 eventually on every compact angular
subinterval; U_r < 0 on compact intervals to the left of the unique zero of P_pos', and U_r > 0 on compact intervals to
its right. Multiplying each assertion by sigma gives the signed version. Moreover sigma Psi > 0 on the whole
sufficiently distant quadrant, uniformly up to its axes. Indeed P_pos is bounded below by a positive constant times
min(phi,alpha-phi), while the O(r) stream error and its angular derivative are bounded by C r and vanish at each axis.
The mean value theorem gives the same endpoint factor for that error.

For every exterior launch point the forward equations imply

  J(X) = lim_(t->infinity)e^t Omega(Phi_t X)
        = rho(X)^(-1/2)G(ell(X)),
  J(X) = Omega(X)+int_0^infinity e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X)dt,
  e^t Omega(Phi_t X)-J(X) = O_X(e^(-t)).
                                                               (70.35)

The integral is absolutely convergent because Theta_x(Phi_t X) = O_X(e^(-2t)); the error is uniform on a fixed launch
circle. This verifies the forward amplitude assertions of Theorems 31-34, 36(d), 37(a), 40(e) and 46(c) wherever they
concern that exterior.

For precision concerning the regular coordinates of Theorem 39, put lambda = W.grad^perp Theta/|grad Theta|^2 on grad
Theta != 0. On an exterior regular component one has

  W = lambda grad^perp Theta, {Theta,lambda} = 4,
  W.grad lambda = 4lambda,
  grad Theta(Phi_t X) = -e^(-4t)W(Phi_t X)^perp/lambda(X),
  H'(ell(X)) = -2rho(X)^2/lambda(X),
  Omega = -div(lambda grad Theta),
  4lambda Omega_lambda+Omega = 4y_lambda.                       (70.36)

The first two identities follow by taking divergence, the cofactor identity by differentiating Theta o Phi_t = Theta,
and the last equation follows either from (V) or from the Jacobian {Theta,lambda} = 4. Its area element is
dX = (1/4)dTheta dlambda with positive orientation. These are local equations and forward coordinate laws. A passage
gives a regular half-fibre only beyond its intersection with the inner boundary, not down to lambda = 0. The source
q_src(theta), the parametrization at lambda = 0 and the integrals starting there in Theorem 39(a)-(d) are not
constructed.

There is also a genuine exterior version of the distribution calculation in Theorem 40. For a launch circle
r_launch > R', write Jac_launch(l) = r_launch W_r(r_launch e_r(l)) and J_launch(l) = J(r_launch e_r(l)). The forward
cylinder has area Jac_launch(l)e^(4t)dt dl. Consequently

  |{r > r_launch: |J(X)| > z_level}|
     = (1/4)int_0^(2pi) Jac_launch(l)
                         ((|J_launch(l)|/z_level)^4-1)_+ dl.
                                                               (70.37)

This is not the exact whole-plane power law (40.3); its subtraction and positive part record the inner boundary. In
particular J is bounded on this exterior. The interior singularity and the failure of local critical Sobolev regularity
in Theorem 40(c),(d) cannot be deduced on the exterior. The forward potential of Theorem 37(a),
V_future(X) = int_0^infinity e^(-3t)[Phi_t X]_2 dt, is smooth there; its derivatives converge because the normalized
flow derivatives are bounded. The cofactor identity gives {Theta,y o Phi_t} = e^(4t)Theta_x o Phi_t; integrating with
weight e^(-3t) therefore gives J = Omega+{Theta,V_future}, exactly as in that theorem, with no assertion about V_future
inside the circle.

The nonzero natural tail gives all integrability and growth comparisons directly, for real p_int > 0 and z_level > 0:

  int_(r>T) |Omega|^p_int dX < infinity exactly when p_int > 4,
  |{r > R': |Omega| > z_level}| is comparable to z_level^(-4)
                                      as z_level decreases to 0,
  lim_(T->infinity) T^(-3)int_(T<r<2T)|U|^2 dX
     = (7/3)int_0^(2pi)(P'^2+(9/4)P^2)dphi > 0.
                                                               (70.38)

The upper vorticity bound is uniform and a lower bound C_lo r^(-1/2) holds on a closed subinterval of either passage.
Integrating r^(1-p_int/2) and the corresponding level-set annuli proves the first two claims; a bounded smooth core does
not change them. The velocity limit and int_T^(2T)r^2dr = (7/3)T^3 prove the last. Also Theta and U belong to no finite
L^p_int space at infinity, since their nonzero leading terms have respective degrees 0 and 1/2 on a sector. These facts
check Theorems 15, 17(b), 18-20, 23-25, 28, 33(e), 34(b),(c), and 45(a)-(c). The restrictive faster-decay,
bounded-velocity and critical-energy hypotheses fail. The little-o assumption of Theorem 24 holds precisely for
0 < eta_decay < 1/2 among its permitted decay exponents for these examples. Neither H nor G has finite angular
bandwidth: a nonconstant trigonometric polynomial cannot have a flat interval. The angular Poisson equation then implies
that P has infinitely many modes as well. Uniform angular limits would preserve any fixed finite bandwidth for Theta or
Psi. The finite-mode hypotheses of Theorems 10 and 49 are therefore absent.

The asymptotic axis data, including their signs, are

  Theta_y(x,0) = sigma/(N_left x)+O(x^(-3/2)),
  Omega_y(x,0) = sigma/(N_left^2 x^(3/2))+O(x^(-2)),
  Theta_xx(0,y)/2 = sigma/(2N_right y^2)+O(y^(-5/2)),
  Omega_x(0,y) = sigma/(N_right y^(3/2))+O(y^(-2)),
  Omega_x(0,y)/(Theta_xx(0,y)/2) ~ 2sqrt(y),
  W_1(x,0) = 2x-P'(0)sqrt(x)+O(1),
  W_2(0,y) = 2y-P'(alpha)sqrt(y)+O(1).                          (70.39)

Taylor division at the endpoints and the differentiated bounds in (70.4) prove these formulas uniformly. In particular
the y-axis curl derivative is -G'(alpha)y^(-3/2), giving the displayed plus sign. Writing w_ax = W_1(x,0),
