v_ax = W_2(0,y), T_ax = Theta_y(x,0), g_ax = Omega_y(x,0), E_ax = Theta_xx(0,y)/2 and K_ax = Omega_x(0,y), direct
differentiation of the exterior equations gives

  w_ax T_ax' = (w_ax'-4)T_ax,
  w_ax g_ax'+(5-w_ax')g_ax = T_ax',
  v_ax E_ax' = (2v_ax'-8)E_ax,
  v_ax K_ax'+(5-v_ax')K_ax = 2E_ax.                             (70.40)

Thus their quotient q_ax = K_ax/E_ax satisfies v_ax q_ax'+(v_ax'-3)q_ax = 2. The coordinate t_ax'(y) = 1/v_ax(y) obeys
t_ax(y)-(1/2)log y -> a finite limit, because 1/v_ax-1/(2y) = O(y^(-3/2)). For these examples q_ax ~ 2sqrt(y), realizing
the exterior growth in Theorems 31 and 45(e). Its source-normalized axis integral still depends on the omitted axis
segment. The eventual signs in Theorems 57(a), 59(a),(b),(e) for sigma = 1 and in Theorem 62(c) for sigma = -1 follow
from (70.29),(70.30),(70.39). In particular v_ax > 2y eventually for the positive sign, and w_ax < 2x eventually;
neither is asserted near an unspecified interior point. The jets, finite-part conditions and first-zero identities in
Theorems 2, 14, 26, 27, 29, 30 and 62(c) cannot be checked from the exterior.

The forward axis derivative in Theorem 31(c),(e) also holds. At (0,y), differentiating (70.35) gives
J_x = rho^(-1/2)G'(alpha)ell_x, which has sign sigma and equals sigma/(N_right y^(3/2))+O(y^(-2)). If x_lin(t) is the
transverse linearization of an exterior y-axis orbit, then x_lin' = (4-v_ax')x_lin and x_lin(0) = 1. Differentiating the
forward vorticity identity gives J_x(0,y) = K_ax(y)+2int_0^infinity e^t E_ax(y(t))x_lin(t)dt. The integrand is
O(e^(-t)); the representation using an integral from negative infinity in Theorem 31 requires additional interior data.

The potential identity in Theorem 44(a) is meaningful on the exterior. There the vector field 3W+Omega W^perp-Theta e_2
is curl-free by (V) and div W = 4. Its period around a centered circle is zero: W.e_phi has odd-odd angular parity,
Omega W_r is odd-odd, and Theta cos(phi) has zero angular integral by reflection. A closed field with this zero period
on an annulus has a single-valued potential Bern. Therefore, up to an additive constant,

  grad Ly = 3W+Omega W^perp+y grad Theta,
  Ly = Bern+yTheta, W.grad Ly = 3|W|^2,
  Ly = 3r^2+O(r^(3/2)).                                         (70.41)

The last bound follows by integrating its gradient, whose difference from 6X is O(r^(1/2)). This proves the exterior
Lyapunov assertion and all local monotonicity statements that use it. It does not identify Ly with the normalization at
O. All exterior orbits already escape because W_r > 0; there are no exterior bounded forward orbits, zeros, cycles, or
connections between zeros. Thus Theorem 4's exterior prohibitions hold, while its whole-plane invariant-set conclusions
and the zero and backward-limit assertions of Theorems 1, 3, 5, 6(a), 11, 12, 16, 21, 22, 39, 44(b)-(f), 46, 47(c),(d),
48(a),(b),(d), 51, 53(a)-(g), 55, 56(a)-(f), 59(a),(c),(d), 61(c)-(e), 62 and 63 retain their stated interior
hypotheses.

We make the distinction for balances explicit. Let F_test be a smooth function on the temperature range, put
K_strain = xy/r^4, fix a constant nu > 0, and integrate over Q1 cap {r > r_launch}, with r_launch > R'. Define the inner
radial fluxes using the positive radial vector. The local divergence identities are

  div(F_test(Theta)Omega^4 W) = 4F_test(Theta)Omega^3 Theta_x,
  div(F_test(Theta)|Omega|^p_int W)
     = (4-p_int)F_test(Theta)|Omega|^p_int
                  +p_int F_test(Theta)|Omega|^(p_int-2)Omega Theta_x,
  div(F_test(Theta)|grad Theta|^2 W)
     = -2F_test(Theta)grad Theta.(DU grad Theta),
  div(K_strain Omega W) = K_strain Theta_x+Omega U.grad K_strain-Omega K_strain,
  div(F_test(Theta)e^(-nu Ly)W)
     = F_test(Theta)e^(-nu Ly)(4-3nu|W|^2).
                                                               (70.42)

Here the p_int identity is used for p_int > 4; its differentiability at Omega = 0 is then sufficient. For the first
identity the flux at infinity is 2int_0^alpha F_test(H)G^4; for the gradient identity it is 2int_0^alpha
F_test(H)(H')^2. In each case the integral of the divergence equals that outer flux minus r_launch int_0^alpha of the
displayed density times W_r at the inner circle. The p_int > 4, strain and exponential outer fluxes tend to zero. All
terms are absolutely integrable at infinity by (70.4) and (70.41). This verifies the local equations behind
Theorems 39(e), 45(d), 56(g) and 59(f) and explains exactly why their full-domain constants or zero right sides are not
exterior identities.

The measurable invariant sets in Theorem 59(f) require no smooth-indicator argument. Their exterior portions consist of
forward orbits from a measurable set of launch labels. Along each orbit the derivative of e^(4t-nu Ly(Phi_t X)) is
e^(4t-nu Ly)(4-3nu|W|^2). Its value at infinity is zero. Integrating in time and then in the launch labels gives exactly
the negative inner flux, also for such sets.

The isothermal identities of Theorems 48(f), 53(i) and 56(a) have the same issue, even for a plateau. Take an angular
test function test_ang in C^1([0,alpha]), and first use a smooth function F_test of Theta. Since W.grad
F_test(Theta) = 0 and div(2X r^(-2)test_ang) = 0,

  div(F_test(Theta)r^(-2)test_ang(phi)W)
     = F_test(Theta)r^(-3)(-2test_ang U_r+test_ang' U_phi).
                                                               (70.43)

Its exterior integral is 2int_0^alpha test_ang F_test(H)dphi minus r_launch^(-1)int_0^alpha test_ang
F_test(Theta(r_launch,phi))W_r(r_launch,phi)dphi. There is no flux through either axis because W is tangent there; no
endpoint condition on test_ang is needed. Approximate the indicator of a temperature level by bounded smooth functions
converging pointwise to it. Dominated convergence applies to the integrable right side and both boundary integrals. This
gives the exterior level-set identity, with the same inner flux, also for test_ang = 1. At temperature level sigma the
inner flux tends to 2int_a^b test_ang as r_launch tends to infinity and cannot be discarded; the open plateau region is
not the full-domain isothermal set of those theorems.

The actual canonical strain is Psi_xy(O) = (4/pi)int_Q1 K_strain Omega_tot dX, as in Theorem 9, but its value need not
be 6. This integral is absolutely convergent: odd-odd smoothness gives Omega_tot = O(r^2) near O, and the tail gives
K_strain Omega_tot = O(r^(-5/2)) at infinity. The exterior part of its quadrant integral is

  int_(Q1 cap {r > T}) xy r^(-4)Omega dX
     = 2T^(-1/2)int_0^alpha cos(phi)sin(phi)G(phi)dphi
                          +O(T^(-1)).                           (70.44)

It tends to zero, with sign sigma for large T. The additional integration by parts in Theorem 45(d) also retains an
inner term: the exterior integral of K_strain Theta_x equals that of Theta y(3x^2-y^2)r^(-6), minus
r_launch^(-1)int_0^alpha Theta(r_launch,phi)cos(phi)^2 sin(phi)dphi. The outer boundary term vanishes. The value 3 pi/2
in Theorems 9, 39(e) and 45(d) requires the origin temperature jet and the interior equations. For sigma = -1 any
completion meeting that identity would need positive interior vorticity, consistently with Theorems 21(a) and 62(a),(b).
The two axis Green balances and the existence of a negative signed radial derivative in Theorem 55 use P_ax and that
jet. On each compact passage interval the exterior instead has sigma(r partial_r+2)Omega = (3/2)G_pos
r^(-1/2)+O(r^(-1)) > 0; no sign is inferred uniformly through a moving flat transition. Theorem 55 does not place its
required negative region at arbitrarily large radii.

For the angular conditions, the critical set of H in (0,alpha) is [a,b], and there H'' = G = 0. Outside it sigma G > 0.
Thus the angular implications of Theorems 47(a), 48(c), 59(b) and 64(h) hold for the plateau pairs, including G = 0
implying sigma H' >= 0. The nonzero critical value is sigma. Their range on the closed angular quadrant, and the closure
of the exterior quadrant temperature range, are [0,1] or [-1,0]; each intermediate signed level has exactly two angular
preimages. This verifies the angular side of Theorem 53(h) and the single-excursion pattern of Theorem 56(d),(e), with
their additional regular-source hypotheses retained rather than asserted. Theorem 56(d),(e) as stated has M > 0; for the
negative pair only its signed angular pattern is being compared. The endpoint formulas of Theorem 48(e) follow by
differentiating Theta = H(ell) on a launch circle: H'(0) = r_launch T_ax(r_launch)/ell_launch'(0) and
H''(alpha) = 2r_launch^2 E_ax(r_launch)/ell_launch'(alpha)^2. Formula (70.10) supplies the potential-region conclusions
at infinity of Theorems 35, 44(f), 47(d), 48(d), 51(a), 53(d), 56(a)-(c), 59(c) and 63(b),(c). It supplies neither their
generating zero nor the local geometry or analytic noncontinuation at that zero.

For the two regular passages the exterior lambda coordinate in (70.36) gives the exact constants of Theorems 61(b) and
62(f):

  k_exit = rho/sqrt(|lambda|) = sqrt(|H'(ell)|/2),
  b_exit = k_exit sin(ell) > 0, D_exit = G(ell)/sqrt(k_exit),
  eps_branch = sgn lambda = -sgn H'(ell),
  r = k_exit sqrt(s_fiber)+O(s_fiber^(1/4)),
  y = b_exit sqrt(s_fiber)+O(s_fiber^(1/4)),
  partial_(s_fiber) y = (b_exit/2)s_fiber^(-1/2)+O(s_fiber^(-3/4)),
  s_fiber^(1/4)Omega -> D_exit, s_fiber = |lambda| -> infinity.
                                                               (70.45)

On the orbit launched at X0, the errors follow from |Phi_t X0| = rho(X0)e^(2t)(1+O(e^(-t))) and the flow equation, with
s_fiber growing like e^(4t). For the positive pair D_exit >= 0. On the left passage D_exit = sigma 2^(1/4)ell
f_left(ell)^(7/4), and on the right D_exit = sigma 2^(1/4)g_right(ell)^(3/4). In particular k_exit,b_exit and also
D_exit tend to zero at the adjoining plateau endpoints. This checks the angular degeneration in Theorem 61(c). Its
superalgebraic exit bounds, the displacement and dip integrals of Theorems 61(a),(b) and 62(f), and their source height
require the full half-fibre down to s_fiber = 0 and are not exterior assertions. The regular-zero and vertical-arc jet
restrictions of Theorem 61(c)-(e) do not apply to these exterior critical boundary orbits: on them grad Theta = 0 and
W != 0. The local minimum implication grad Omega = 0, Theta_x = 0 at a vorticity zero in Theorem 59(d) is verified
directly by the flatness in (70.10).

For sigma = -1 the set {X in Q1 : Omega_tot(X) > 0} is bounded, because Omega_tot <= 0 at every sufficiently distant
point of Q1. Nonemptiness of that set, the negative origin jet, the budgets and the ray history required in Theorem
62(a),(b),(g) are separate. In particular boundedness does not supply the ray prohibition. If one prescribes positive
vorticity at interior radii and demands that prohibition, Theorems 62 and 64 require its angles to belong to an eventual
zero sector. Any closed subinterval of I_pl is available for precisely that angular requirement by (70.10). The theorem
does not claim that an arbitrary prescribed core meets that ray condition. On I_pl the angular stream is c_s
sin(3phi/2)+c_c cos(3phi/2), of sign sigma, by its homogeneous equation; no boundary condition is imposed at a,b. This
checks the exterior part of Theorem 64(g), whose full saturation and backward limits are not supplied.

For sigma = 1, (70.10) gives nonnegative exterior vorticity on Q1, with a nonempty zero region there. If a smooth
whole-plane completion whose vorticity is nonnegative on Q1 is desired, choose Omega_in >= 0 on Q1 and increase the
original R so that the sign proof applies on r >= R. Its low-order constants are uniform in that choice of R by (70.16)
and (70.31)-(70.33); hence chi Omega >= 0 there and Omega_tot >= 0 on Q1. This still does not make the interior
transport equations true. The positive stream and eventual axis conclusions were checked above. Strict positivity of
vorticity throughout Q1, excluded at beta = 2 by Theorems 12 and 21(c), is not being imposed.

For the finite-component comparison in Theorems 53, 56 and 63, there is no exterior zero at all. Their index counts,
existence of a positive-index interior component and its source properties require a completion satisfying the interior
equations and origin jet. Their resulting exterior demand, an open constant-temperature potential region and angular
plateau, is realized by (70.10). One can even choose Omega_in = 0 and make the canonical completion have only the zero
O: inside r < R/2 the derivative kernel estimate gives |DU| <= C R^(-1/2), and outside it (70.12) gives the same bound.
Since U(O) = 0, |U(X)| <= C R^(-1/2)|X| on the whole plane. For large R, X.W > 0 for X != O. This observation realizes
finiteness for a smooth canonical completion, but its origin jet and transport equations are still absent.

The beta > 2-only Theorems 7, 8, 13, 38, 41-43, 50, 52, 54, 58, 60, 65 and 66 impose no beta = 2 conclusion. In the
remaining mixed-beta results, all beta = 2 exterior bounds, local identities, forward laws, angular and eventual axis
conclusions have been checked above. Theorems 1 and 5 cannot be used to kill a homogeneous exterior vorticity on a
critical orbit: their bounded backward arguments require the equations through the inner boundary. The near-origin
nonzero-amplitude assertion of Theorem 34(a) is likewise not an exterior assertion; part (a) here even allows G = 0 with
H != 0. Exterior components of strict temperature superlevels or sublevels are unbounded, as in the exterior part of
Theorem 6(b), since any of their points carries a forward orbit of that same temperature to infinity. No assertion about
their interior attachment follows. The plateau temperature is not real analytic across either of its boundary orbits:
all derivatives of Theta-sigma vanish there, but the function is nonconstant on the adjacent passage. The actual
velocity is not real analytic across either boundary either, since its curl vanishes on the open potential side and is
nonzero arbitrarily close on the other side. Thus the analytic hypotheses in Theorems 11 and 17(a) are absent. This does
not assert noncontinuation of a holomorphic function defined only on the potential side, which is a different claim in
Theorems 51 and 53.

Finally consider (70.11). Its endpoint reflections and value on the y-axis satisfy (70.1), and
H' = cos(phi)(1-3sin(phi)^2). At phi_c, sin(2phi_c) = 2sqrt(2)/3 > 0. By (70.32), along the orbit with ell = phi_c the
temperature gradient is zero and Omega = rho^(-1/2)G(phi_c) > 0. It solves homogeneous vorticity transport there.
Following that homogeneous solution backwards only to the inner boundary causes no contradiction. The proof of
Theorem 47(a), in contrast, invokes Theorem 44(d), where a bounded complete backward orbit forces this homogeneous
amplitude to vanish. In fact H is positive in the open angular quadrant. Where H' >= 0, the exact formula makes
Omega > 0. Where H' < 0, write u_ang = sin(ell). Then |H'(ell)|/G(ell) = (3u_ang^2-1)/(2u_ang) <= 1, for
1/sqrt(3) < u_ang < 1. Hence Omega >= G(ell)(rho^(-1/2)-b_T) > 0 there also, uniformly up to the y-axis. This proves the
strict signs throughout the distant open quadrant. The strict-sign exclusions in Theorems 12 and 21(c), and the angular
implication in Theorem 47(a), are conclusions about whole-plane profiles. This verifies both the example and the precise
limitation in (e). Every plateau pair has already been realized by (70.2)-(70.10); any condition following solely from
those exterior properties is therefore satisfied by those examples, which proves (f).

### Theorem 71 (beta > 2: further x-axis saddles force unbounded opposite-sign vorticity; source basins for either sign)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2, with beta > 2. Thus the fields are smooth on R^2, U is
canonical and uniformly sublinear, Theta and Omega have polynomial growth, and

  W = beta X + U, div W = 2 beta,
  W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x, W.grad Theta = kappa Theta,
  U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x), -Lap Psi = Omega.

The temperature is even in x and odd in y, Omega is odd in each coordinate, U_1 is odd in x and even in y, and U_2 is
even in x and odd in y. Moreover Theta(0,y) = 0 and Theta = a0 x^2 y + O(|X|^5) near O = (0,0), with a0 != 0. Put

  kappa = beta - 2, b = beta + 2, d = 2 beta - 1,
  h = 1/beta, sigma = sgn(a0), Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0},
  X = r(cos(phi), sin(phi)), Z = {W = 0},
  w(x) = W_1(x,0), T(x) = Theta_y(x,0), v(y) = W_2(0,y).

Write Phi_t for the complete flow of W and P = (x_1,0) for its first positive x-axis zero, supplied by Theorem 2. Define

  B_R = {X : Phi_(-s)X -> R as s -> infinity},
  B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0}.

Hypothesis (H1) means Z cap closure(Q1) = {O,P}, as in Theorem 8. Let G be the continuous angular limit of Theorem 41,
normalized by r^h Omega(r,phi) -> G(phi) uniformly in phi. For a source R as in Theorem 58(b), let J_R be the interval
of limiting angles of the forward orbits in B_R cap Q1.

Put e_2 = (0,1) and W^perp = (-W_2,W_1). Let Bern be the potential of d W + Omega W^perp - Theta e_2 normalized by
Bern(O) = 0, and set Ly = Bern + y Theta, as in Theorem 44(a). Use the functions of Theorem 58(e):

  I(X) = int_0^infinity e^(-kappa s)[Phi_(-s)X]_2 ds,
  Hc(X) = kappa Theta(X) I(X), L_tilde = Ly - Hc.

(a) Assume that all positive zeros of w are finitely many and simple, v has no positive zero, and W has no zero in Q1.
By Theorem 58(a), the positive x-axis zeros form the alternating chain

  R_0 = P, Q_1, R_1, ..., Q_n, R_n,

where n >= 0, the R_j are sources and the Q_j are saddles. If n >= 1, there are R_* > 0 and nonempty open intervals I_+,
I_-, whose closures are contained in J_(R_0), such that

  Omega > 0 on {r > R_*, phi in I_+},
  Omega < 0 on {r > R_*, phi in I_-}.                           (71.1)

Consequently Omega takes both strict signs in Q1 cap {R < |X| < 2R} for every R > R_*. The set B contains an exterior
open sector and is unbounded. Thus, under the hypotheses of this part, boundedness of B forces n = 0, P to be the only
positive x-axis zero, and (H1).

(b) The conclusions of (a) also hold under the following alternative hypotheses: beta is irrational, all positive zeros
of w are finitely many and simple, every positive zero of v is simple, and every zero of W in Q1 is nondegenerate. Here
nondegeneracy means that DW is invertible at the zero.

(c) For either sign of a0, let R = (r_0,0), r_0 > 0, be any zero with A_R = T(r_0) != 0 and DW(R) = diag(b,kappa). The
basin B_R is open, and I, Hc and L_tilde are smooth on B_R. The function L_tilde has exactly one critical point there,
namely R, which is its nondegenerate strict minimum throughout B_R. With (u tensor v)_ij = u_i v_j,

  D^2 Hc(R) = A_R e_2 tensor e_2,
  D^2 L_tilde(R) = d diag(b,kappa).                             (71.2)

Scope. Part (a) is a restricted exclusion under the hypotheses of Theorem 58(c), and (b) supplies alternative sufficient
hypotheses through Theorems 30(c) and 60(c). Neither part excludes longer chains without boundedness of B. No ray
condition or separate hypothesis on the interior of {Theta = 0} is imposed. Boundedness of B is not shown to imply
B = empty under (H1); the additional ray prohibition of Theorem 64(b) is sufficient for that conclusion. Part (c)
requires none of the additional zero-set hypotheses in (a) or (b) and extends Theorem 62(e) to either sign of a0. It
concerns individual open source basins; no smoothness across their boundaries or global Morse classification of L_tilde
is asserted. The positive Hessian in (71.2) imposes no inequality A_R >= -d kappa.

Proof. (a) The hypotheses are precisely those of Theorem 58(c). That theorem states that G takes both signs in J_(R_j)
for every 0 <= j < n. If n >= 1, it applies to j = 0. Its ordered-angle description gives

  J_(R_0) = (phi_1,pi/2), 0 < phi_1 < pi/2.

In particular this is a nonempty open interval contained in (0,pi/2). The signs can also be read directly from that
theorem: G has sign -sigma just above phi_1 and sign sigma just below pi/2.

Choose phi_+, phi_- in J_(R_0) with G(phi_+) > 0 > G(phi_-). Continuity gives compact intervals K_+, K_- contained in
J_(R_0), each with nonempty interior, and a number c > 0 such that G >= 2c on K_+ and G <= -2c on K_-. The uniform
Eulerian limit in Theorem 41(b) gives R_* > 0 such that

  sup_(0 <= phi <= pi/2)
    |r^h Omega(r,phi) - G(phi)| < c
                    for every r > R_*.                          (71.3)

This estimate holds for every sufficiently large radius. On the interiors I_+, I_- of K_+, K_-, respectively, it yields
Omega > c r^(-h) and Omega < -c r^(-h). This proves (71.1). Both sectors lie in Q1, since their angles are strictly
between 0 and pi/2, and both meet every annulus in the statement.

If sigma = 1, the sector with angles in I_- lies in B. If sigma = -1, the sector with angles in I_+ lies in B. In either
case B contains a nonempty open sector extending to every radius greater than R_*, so it is unbounded.

If B is bounded, n >= 1 is therefore impossible. Theorem 58(a) gives exactly 2n+1 positive x-axis zeros, so n = 0 leaves
only P. Parity gives W(x,0) = (w(x),0) and W(0,y) = (0,v(y)). There is no positive y-axis zero by hypothesis, and there
is no zero in Q1 by hypothesis. Since W(O) = 0, this accounts for every point of the closed quadrant and gives Z cap
closure(Q1) = {O,P}, exactly (H1). Theorem 52(b) gives the same conclusion from the two axis conditions.

(b) Theorem 30(c) applies because beta is irrational and every positive zero of v is simple. It gives that v has no
positive zero. Thus (A) of Theorem 60 holds by the hypothesis on w, and (B) of that theorem now holds by Theorem 30(c).
Irrationality and nondegeneracy of every interior zero are the further hypotheses of Theorem 60(c), which therefore
gives Z cap Q1 = empty. Equivalently, one may use its explicit provision replacing (B) by simplicity of every positive
zero of v when beta is irrational. All hypotheses of (a) have now been obtained, so its conclusions apply.

(c) Theorem 58(e) defines I, Hc and L_tilde for every A2-broad profile with beta > 2, without a sign assumption. The
backward radial bound used there makes I converge locally uniformly. We prove its smoothness on B_R and compute its
derivatives at R.

Let Id denote the identity matrix. Since D(-W)(R) = -diag(b,kappa) and b,kappa > 0, there are a_1 > 0 and a small closed
ball D centred at R on which the symmetric part of D(-W) is at most -a_1 Id. For X in D, integrating DW along the
segment from R to X gives

  (X-R).W(X) >= a_1 |X-R|^2.

Consequently D is invariant under the backward flow. With Y_s(X) = Phi_(-s)X, differentiation of |Y_s(X)-R|^2 gives

  |Y_s(X)-R| <= e^(-a_1 s)|X-R|,
  |D_X Y_s(X)| <= e^(-a_1 s), s >= 0.                           (71.4)

For the second estimate, the first variational equation has coefficient -DW(Y_s(X)), whose symmetric part has the stated
negative bound. Its evolution operator E(s,t;X), for s >= t >= 0, satisfies |E(s,t;X)| <= e^(-a_1(s-t)).

For m >= 2, differentiating the flow equation m times gives

  partial_s D_X^m Y_s
     = -DW(Y_s) D_X^m Y_s + F_m(s,X).

Every term in F_m is a bounded derivative of W evaluated at Y_s, applied to at least two derivatives of Y_s of orders
between 1 and m-1. If these lower derivatives are bounded by constants times e^(-a_1 s), then |F_m(s,X)| <= C_m e^(-2a_1
s). Since D_X^m Y_0 = 0, variation of constants gives

  |D_X^m Y_s|
     <= C_m int_0^s e^(-a_1(s-t)) e^(-2a_1 t) dt
     <= (C_m/a_1)e^(-a_1 s).                                    (71.5)

Induction starting with (71.4) proves this estimate in every fixed order, uniformly for initial points in a smaller
ball. Since R_2 = 0, (71.4) also bounds |[Y_s(X)]_2| by a constant times e^(-a_1 s). Thus the integrand defining I and
each of its spatial derivatives have an integrable bound C_m e^(-(kappa+a_1)s). Differentiation under the integral
proves that I is smooth near R.

Let V be the interior of a sufficiently small such ball. Every point in V tends backward to R, and every point in B_R
enters V after a finite backward time. Hence B_R is the union of the open sets Phi_t(V), t >= 0, and is open. Given X in
B_R, choose T > 0 such that a whole neighbourhood of X is mapped into V by Phi_(-T). The flow property gives on that
neighbourhood

  I(X) = int_0^T e^(-kappa s)[Phi_(-s)X]_2 ds
                  + e^(-kappa T) I(Phi_(-T)X).                  (71.6)

The finite integral and the composition on the right are smooth. This proves smoothness of I, Hc and L_tilde throughout
B_R.

At R the orbit is constant and its linearized backward flow is diag(e^(-bs),e^(-kappa s)). Identifying covectors with
vectors by the Euclidean inner product, it follows that

  I(R) = 0, DI(R) = e_2 int_0^infinity e^(-2kappa s) ds
                   = e_2/(2kappa),
  Theta(R) = 0, DTheta(R) = A_R e_2.                            (71.7)

The last two identities follow from the temperature parity and the definition of A_R. Therefore DHc(R) = 0, and the
product rule gives

  D^2 Hc(R)
     = kappa (DTheta tensor DI + DI tensor DTheta)(R)
     = A_R e_2 tensor e_2.                                      (71.8)

The terms containing Theta(R) or I(R) vanish.

Theorem 44(a) and Ly = Bern + y Theta give

  grad Ly = d W + Omega W^perp + y grad Theta.                  (71.9)

At R, W = 0, Omega = 0 and y = 0. The vorticity vanishes by oddness in y. Thus grad Ly(R) = 0. Both terms in the
derivative of Omega W^perp vanish at R, while the derivative of y grad Theta is A_R e_2 tensor e_2 there. Consequently

  D^2 Ly(R) = d DW(R) + A_R e_2 tensor e_2
            = diag(db,d kappa + A_R).                           (71.10)

This derives the identity used in Theorem 58(d), without its sign hypothesis for the Lyapunov classification of Ly.
Subtracting (71.8) proves (71.2), and also grad L_tilde(R) = 0. Since d,b,kappa > 0, its Hessian is positive definite.

By Theorem 58(e), the derivative of L_tilde along every orbit is d|W|^2. On B_R smoothness therefore gives grad
L_tilde.W = d|W|^2. Every critical point in B_R is a zero of W, and a zero is its own backward limit. Hence R is the
only critical point in B_R.

For X in B_R with X != R, integrate this orbit identity from time -T to time 0 and let T tend to infinity. Continuity at
R and the exponential estimate (71.4), together with |W(Y)| <= C|Y-R| near R, justify the limit and give

  L_tilde(X) - L_tilde(R)
     = d int_(-infinity)^0 |W(Phi_t X)|^2 dt > 0.               (71.11)

The integral is finite. It is strictly positive because a nonconstant orbit never reaches a zero at a finite time. This
proves the strict minimum on the entire basin. Every step uses kappa > 0 and the specified source linearization, with no
condition on the sign of a0 or A_R. QED.

### Theorem 72 (beta = 2: zero arcs, endpoint transport reduction, and vorticity along strong unstable orbits)

Local system. Let D be an open disc, W a smooth real vector field on D, and Theta and Omega smooth real scalar
functions. The equations are

  div W = 4, d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = Omega,
  W.grad Theta = 0, W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x.             (72.1)

Put U = W - 2X, identify X = (x,y) with z = x + i y, and set f = U_1 - i U_2. Then d_zbar f = (i/2) Omega. Every
A2-broad profile at beta = 2 satisfies these equations. Write Phi_t for the flow wherever it is defined, and
Z = {W = 0}. Flatness includes the value and all derivatives. The derivative d_x always means the Cartesian
x-derivative; changes of coordinates below do not change this convention. A first integral is a continuous function
constant on the portions of flow orbits under consideration.

(a) (Interior points of zero arcs.) Suppose W vanishes on a smooth embedded arc C, and Y0 is an interior point of C.
There is a neighbourhood N of Y0, the image of a coordinate rectangle under a smooth diffeomorphism R, such that R(s,0)
parametrizes C, Z cap N = C cap N, and

  W.grad = 4 t d_t.                                             (72.2)

The rectangle, and hence N, can be chosen backward invariant. The fibres {s = const} are the strong unstable fibres.
Their backward-limit projection is alpha(R(s,t)) = R(s,0). Every continuous first integral is its trace on C composed
with alpha. For fixed smooth W and Theta, after choosing a sufficiently small rectangle, the unique bounded classical
solution of the vorticity transport equation is smooth and is

  Omega(R(s,t)) = (1/4) int_0^1 q^(-3/4) Theta_x(R(s,q t)) dq.    (72.3)

In particular Omega = Theta_x on C. If s is oriented arclength on C, tau = (tau_x,tau_y) its unit tangent, theta its
temperature trace, and k = d theta/ds, every solution of (72.1) satisfies

  (4 - k tau_y) Omega = 4 k tau_x on C.                         (72.4)

For example, the analytic data gamma(s) = (s/sqrt(2),s/sqrt(2)) and theta(s) = 4 sqrt(2) s admit no such solution:
(72.4) would read 0 = 16.

(b) (Nonanalytic regular arcs.) For every smooth function T of one variable,

  Theta = T(x), W = (0,4y - T(x)), Omega = T'(x)                (72.5)

solve all four equations (72.1), and Z = {y = T(x)/4}. Let eps != 0 and T(x) = x + eps eta(x), where
eta(x) = exp(-1/x^2) for x > 0 and eta(x) = 0 for x <= 0. On a sufficiently small disc about O, grad Theta != 0. The
zero arc and its temperature trace in arclength are both nonanalytic at O. This is an example at an interior point of a
zero arc.

(c) (Endpoint reduction on an invariant neighbourhood.) Call W a geometric field at Q if W is smooth on a disc D about
Q, div W = 4, its entire zero set in D is a smooth embedded arc C ending at Q, DW(Q) has eigenvalues 0 and 4, and a
local C^2 invariant centre curve through Q has a zero-free branch opposite to C whose forward flow points away from Q. A
centre curve is tangent to ker DW(Q).

Such a field has a smooth local strong unstable curve Gamma through Q. The construction of Gamma and the
backward-convergence argument in Steps 1-3 of Theorem 51 use only W. The subsequent temperature, vorticity and
holomorphy conclusions of Step 3 require (72.1).

There are an open backward invariant neighbourhood N of Q with closure contained in D and, inside N, a smaller Euclidean
disc B about Q with the following properties. Both N minus Gamma and B minus Gamma have two connected components,
denoted N+, N- and B+, B-. The minus sides contain C minus Q locally; the plus sides contain the opposite centre branch.
Every point of N+ has backward limit Q. Every point of N- has a backward limit in C cap N, and Gamma cap N is backward
invariant with backward limit Q.

On a neighbourhood of closure(N-) there is a smooth function sigma with d sigma != 0, sigma = 0 exactly on Gamma there,
and sigma < 0 on N-. It is constant on orbits in N-, and its restriction to C cap N is a regular parameter, with
sigma(Q) = 0. Its value labels the backward limit.

Let M be real and theta be a smooth one-sided trace near 0, on s <= 0, with theta - M flat at 0. Choose N small enough
that this trace is defined smoothly beyond the closed range needed on C cap N. On N put

  Theta_W = theta(sigma) on N-, Theta_W = M on N+ cup Gamma,
  Omega_W(X) = int_(-infinity)^0 e^tau (Theta_W)_x(Phi_tau X) d tau on N-,
  Omega_W = 0 on N+ cup Gamma.                                  (72.6)

All backward orbits in this formula remain in N. The functions are smooth and bounded after the indicated choice of N;
Theta_W - M and Omega_W are flat along Gamma cap N. They solve both transport equations in (72.1). On N, Theta_W is the
unique continuous first integral with the prescribed trace on C cap N and value M on N+, and Omega_W is the unique
bounded classical solution of the vorticity transport equation with that temperature. These are uniqueness statements
for fixed W and theta, and consequently for local germs. They are not uniqueness assertions for transport posed only on
an arbitrary smaller Euclidean disc.

The constructed triple solves (72.1) precisely when

  d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = Omega_W on N.                             (72.7)

The construction and equivalence can be restricted to smaller invariant neighbourhoods and then to a disc.

Call a smooth solution of (72.1) an (E') configuration at Q if it has the geometric hypotheses above and Theta - M and
Omega are flat at Q, where M = Theta(Q). Every (E') configuration, restricted to a sufficiently small N, is given by
(72.6), with theta its trace in the parameter sigma, and satisfies (72.7). Conversely, a geometric field and a trace
theta with theta - M flat at 0, satisfying (72.7), give an (E') configuration on a smaller disc.

Call it an (E) configuration if also grad Theta != 0 on the terminal punctured zero arc and the trace is strictly
monotone there. For (E), the reduction requires in addition theta'(s) != 0 on a terminal interval (-delta,0). Conversely
this derivative condition gives both additional properties of (E). Thus (72.7) is the remaining coupled equation for
(E'), and for (E) with this additional condition on the trace.

(d) (Vorticity along the separator and its orbits.) In an (E') configuration, use the disc B and the objects constructed
in (c). After shrinking B:

  (i) theta is not constant on any terminal interval (-delta,0);
  (ii) every point of Gamma cap B, including Q, belongs to the closure of
       {X in B- : Omega(X) != 0}.

Thus Omega is flat along Gamma but vanishes on no open neighbourhood of any point of Gamma cap B.

Now let (2,Theta,Omega,U) be an A2-broad profile satisfying (S) of Theorem 48, and take Q = Q+ from Theorem 16 and
M = Theta(Q+). For every value of M, including zero, this is an (E') configuration near Q+. Conclusions (i) and (ii)
hold, and

  (iii) for every Y in Gamma minus {Q+} sufficiently near Q+ and every real t,
        Phi_t(Y) belongs to the closure of {Omega != 0}.

The Gamma segment used here is chosen backward invariant. The complete orbits in (iii) refer to the full-plane profile,
not just to a local field.

(e) (A geometric field with a potential side that cannot be completed.) Put zeta = y - i x, and let
L(zeta) = exp(-zeta^(-1/2)) on the principal branch in |arg zeta| < 3 pi/4. Choose a smooth even angular cutoff chi that
is 1 for |arg zeta| <= 2 pi/3 and vanishes near the boundary of |arg zeta| < 3 pi/4. For eps > 0 put

  q = -eps chi(arg zeta) Im L(zeta), q = 0 outside the sector and at O,
  W = (4x - q_y,q_x).                                           (72.8)

The field is smooth near O, W - (4x,0) is flat there, and div W = 4. It is a geometric field with C = {x = 0,y <= 0} and
outgoing centre branch {x = 0,y > 0}. The whole y-axis is a smooth invariant centre curve near O.

Its smooth strong unstable curve is a graph y = g(x), where g is flat and nonanalytic at 0. In fact no local
real-analytic invariant curve through O tangent to the x-axis exists. On the full side B+ = {y > g(x)} in a sufficiently
small disc, the curl -Lap q vanishes and

  f = 2z - i eps L'(-i z)

is holomorphic. It has no holomorphic continuation from that side to a disc about O. The side consists of points with
backward limit O, and -Lap q is flat along Gamma. Nevertheless no smooth temperature and vorticity complete this W to an
(E') configuration: -Lap q vanishes on a neighbourhood of every point of Gamma minus {O}, violating (d)(ii).

Scope. Existence or nonexistence of (E) and (E') in general remains unresolved by this theorem. Part (c) solves the
transport and flat-gluing problem on suitable backward invariant neighbourhoods; the curl equation remains unsolved in
general. For (E) the trace must also have nonvanishing derivative on the terminal punctured arc. Parts (a) and (b)
concern interior points and construct no endpoint. Part (d) is a necessary condition. For profiles under (S), it rules
out an open zero-vorticity neighbourhood at every point on the indicated complete orbits. It does not assert that
vorticity is nonzero on those orbits, or describe all possible enlargements of a potential region. Part (e) realizes the
velocity geometry, potential side, noncontinuation and nonanalyticity conclusions relevant to Theorem 51, but is not a
solution of (72.1). Its exclusion follows from the coupled necessary condition (d)(ii); no claim is made that this is
the only way to exclude it. Part (d)(i) is the local terminal-constant exclusion corresponding to Theorem 53(e). All
proofs here are informal; no formal verification is claimed.

Proof.

(a) Write the physical coordinate map as X = R0(s,r), with C = {r = 0}. If F and G are the coordinate components of W,
then F(s,0) = G(s,0) = 0. The integral form of Hadamard's lemma gives F = r a(s,r), G = r b(s,r), with smooth
coefficients.

Under a coordinate map H, the transformed vector field is DH W. At a zero X, its derivative is DH(X) DW(X) DH(X)^(-1),
because the term containing D^2 H is multiplied by W(X) = 0. Thus the trace at a zero remains the physical divergence,
namely 4. This does not assert invariance of coordinate divergence away from zeros. The tangential column of the
coordinate derivative is zero; its matrix at r = 0 is [[0,a(s,0)],[0,b(s,0)]]. Therefore b(s,0) = 4. Shrink so that
b > 0; there are no other zeros.

The nonsingular ODE ds/dr = a(s,r)/b(s,r), with initial value s0 at r = 0, gives a smooth local diffeomorphism
(s0,r) -> (s,r). Its inverse labels each curve by s0. In these coordinates W = r b~(s0,r) d_r and b~(s0,0) = 4. Set

  t = r exp(int_0^r (4/b~(s0,v) - 1)/v dv).

Since 4/b~(s0,0) - 1 = 0, the quotient in the integrand is smooth jointly in s0 and v, including v = 0. Hence t is
smooth, t_r(s0,0) = 1, and differentiation gives r b~ t_r = 4t. This proves (72.2). Choose a rectangle in (s0,t), rename
s0 as s, and shrink its closure inside the coordinate domain. Its backward flow is R(s,t) -> R(s,e^(4 tau)t) for
tau <= 0. This proves backward invariance, the limit projection, and the assertion about continuous first integrals.

Write omega(s,t) = Omega(R(s,t)) and h(s,t) = Theta_x(R(s,t)). The vorticity equation is 4t omega_t + omega = h. For
q > 0,

  d/dq [q^(1/4) omega(s,qt)] = (1/4) q^(-3/4) h(s,qt).

Boundedness makes the lower endpoint term vanish on integration to q = 0. This gives (72.3) on both sides of t = 0. A
derivative with respect to t introduces a nonnegative power of q; derivatives with respect to s do not worsen q^(-3/4).
On a rectangle with compact closure the derivatives of h are bounded, so every differentiated integral converges
uniformly. The formula is smooth and satisfies the equation, also at t = 0, where omega = h. The homogeneous solutions
on t > 0 and t < 0 are c_+(s)t^(-1/4) and c_-(s)|t|^(-1/4). Boundedness forces both coefficients to vanish. The equation
at t = 0 fixes the value there.

For (72.4), let n = (-tau_y,tau_x), so (tau,n) is an oriented orthonormal basis. As DW tau = 0, there is a vector w with
DW = w tensor n. Its trace is w.n = 4. Write w = 4n + c tau. With the stated curl convention,

  d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = w_1 n_2 - w_2 n_1
                     = c(tau_1 n_2 - tau_2 n_1) = c.

Thus c = Omega. Differentiating W.grad Theta = 0 at a zero gives (DW)^T grad Theta = 0. Write grad Theta = k tau + mu n.
The last identity gives 4mu + Omega k = 0. Since Omega = Theta_x at a zero,

  Omega = k tau_x + mu n_x
         = k tau_x + (Omega k/4) tau_y,

which is (72.4). For the displayed gamma and theta, tau_x = tau_y = 1/sqrt(2) and k = 4 sqrt(2), so the left coefficient
is zero and the right side is 16.

(b) Direct differentiation gives

  div W = 4,
  d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = T'(x),
  W.grad Theta = 0,
  W.grad Omega + Omega = T'(x) = Theta_x.

The first component is identically zero and the second vanishes exactly when y = T(x)/4. Every right derivative of eta
is a polynomial in 1/x times exp(-1/x^2), and tends to zero at 0. Thus eta is smooth and flat but is nonzero arbitrarily
near 0 on the right. It is not analytic. Since T'(0) = 1, T' > 0 after shrinking.

If the zero arc were an analytic submanifold near O, its nonvertical tangent would make it an analytic graph over x.
This would make T analytic, a contradiction. Parametrize the arc by arclength with x_s > 0. Its temperature trace is
T(x(s)) = 4y(s). If this trace were analytic, y(s) would be analytic, and

  x_s = sqrt(1 - y_s^2) > 0

would be analytic as well. Integrating and using the analytic inverse function theorem would make x(s), its inverse, and
T(x) = 4y(s(x)) analytic. This is the second contradiction.

(c) We first establish the geometry and the precise domains.

The eigenvalues 4 and 0 are distinct. In real linear eigencoordinates (u,v), with u in the direction for 4, write

  u' = 4u + P(u,v), v' = R(u,v),

where P,R and their first derivatives vanish at 0. For a general geometric field this eigenbasis need not be
orthonormal. No orthogonality is used in the following construction.

Here is the construction in Theorem 51, Step 1. Multiply P,R by a cutoff in a sufficiently small ball to obtain smooth
functions with bounded derivatives and Lipschitz constant L < 1 in the maximum norm. On continuous paths for t <= 0 use
the norm sup e^(-2t) max(|u(t)|,|v(t)|). For each a the map

  u(t) -> e^(4t)a - int_t^0 e^(4(t-r)) P(u(r),v(r)) dr,
  v(t) -> int_(-infinity)^t R(u(r),v(r)) dr

is a contraction with constant at most L/2. Its fixed point has norm at most |a|/(1-L/2). All derivatives of the map in
the path variable exist and are bounded multilinear operators: for a j-fold increment the integrands gain e^(2jr), which
is at most e^(2r) for r <= 0. Smooth dependence and the implicit function theorem therefore give a smooth fixed path
depending on a. Evaluation at t = 0 gives a smooth graph through 0 with tangent the u-axis. For small a its entire past
stays where the cutoff equals 1. Shifting a fixed path backwards gives the fixed path with the corresponding new
u-coordinate. Thus the graph is backward invariant and, by ODE uniqueness, locally invariant. This is Gamma. Restricting
its parameter interval makes its backward motion stay on the local segment.

A local C^2 centre curve K contains every nearby zero. Indeed, in a C^2 chart straightening K, the normal component of W
has the form z A0(s,z), with A0 continuous and A0(0,0) = 4. It has no zero with z != 0 sufficiently near Q. In
particular K contains C near Q.

We need a smooth chart for the minus-side projection, not just this C^2 chart. Extend a smooth regular parametrization
c(s) of the half-arc C, s <= 0, smoothly across 0, and parametrize Gamma smoothly by gamma(r), with c(0) = gamma(0) = Q.
Their tangent vectors are independent. The map

  (s,r) -> c(s) + gamma(r) - Q

is a smooth local diffeomorphism. It simultaneously gives C = {r = 0,s <= 0} and Gamma = {s = 0}. A smooth embedded arc
with boundary supplies the stated smooth extension of c in its definition. In this chart K is a C^2 graph r = h(s), and
h(s) = 0 for s <= 0. Put z = r - h(s). This last chart is C^2, preserves Gamma = {s = 0}, and makes K = {z = 0}.

Invariance of Gamma in the smooth (s,r) chart gives s' = s m~(s,r), with m~ smooth. In the (s,z) chart invariance of K
gives

  s' = s m(s,z), z' = z A(s,z).

Here A is continuous, A(0,0) = 4, m is continuous and uniformly Lipschitz in z on a small closed box, and

  A >= 2, |m(s,z)-m(s,0)| <= K0 |z|,
  m(s,0) = 0 for s <= 0, m(s,0) > 0 for s > 0.

The positive inequality is exactly the outgoing condition.

Choose delta and eps small enough that a larger closed box remains in D and in both charts. Define N by

  |z| < eps, |s| exp(K0 |z|/2) < delta.

This is an open connected neighbourhood of Q, with compact closure in the larger box. It has two connected sides s > 0
and s < 0, and contains a smaller Euclidean disc B whose two sides are likewise connected. For the last assertion choose
the disc sufficiently small that the smooth regular curve Gamma crosses its boundary exactly twice; Gamma is a graph
with nonzero tangent, and its two local sides are then the two components of the disc complement.

Let nu denote backward time. Away from s = 0 and z = 0,

  d|z|/d nu = -A |z| <= -2|z|,
  d log|s|/d nu = -m(s,z),
  d/d nu [log|s| + K0 |z|/2] <= -m(s,0) <= 0.

The sign of s is preserved by uniqueness, as is z = 0. The same bounds hold on z = 0 directly. Thus an orbit starting in
N cannot reach its boundary in backward time; its two defining quantities remain bounded strictly below their boundary
values. The orbit exists for all negative time because it remains in a compact subset of the larger coordinate box. This
proves backward invariance of N. On Gamma the z-bound gives convergence to Q.

For s < 0, m(s,0) = 0. Hence |d log(-s)/d nu| <= K0 |z(0)| e^(-2nu), which is integrable. Therefore s tends to a
strictly negative limit ell, z tends to zero, and |ell| < delta by the invariant bound. The limit (ell,0) belongs to C
cap N.

For s > 0, put I(nu) = K0 int_0^nu |z(rho)| d rho and p(nu) = s(nu) exp(-I(nu)). Then

  p' <= -p m(s,0) <= 0.

The function I has a finite limit, so s has a limit ell >= 0. If ell > 0, continuity and positivity give m(s,0) >= c > 0
eventually; since z tends to zero, d log s/d nu <= -c/2 eventually, a contradiction. Thus ell = 0. Every point of N+,
and therefore every point of the full disc side B+, has backward limit Q. This is the velocity-only portion of
Theorem 51, Steps 2-3, with an additional invariant choice of domain.

Return to the smooth (s,r) chart. Write its smooth vector field components as F(s,r),G(s,r). They vanish at r = 0 for
s <= 0. Define on a full slightly larger chart

  a(s,r) = int_0^1 F_r(s,lambda r) d lambda,
  b(s,r) = int_0^1 G_r(s,lambda r) d lambda.

Then F = r a and G = r b on s <= 0. At r = 0 on that half, trace invariance at zeros gives b(s,0) = 4. Invariance of
Gamma gives F(0,r) = 0 for all r, so a(0,r) = 0. Consequently

  c0(s,r) = int_0^1 a_s(lambda s,r) d lambda

is smooth on the full chart and a = s c0 there. These explicit formulas provide the needed extensions; they do not
assert that F = r a and G = r b on the positive half. Shrink the full chart so that b > 0.

Solve ds/dr = s c0(s,r)/b(s,r). Smooth ODE dependence gives a smooth initial-value label sigma(s,r), equal to s at
r = 0. Its s-derivative never vanishes after shrinking. The equation preserves s = 0 and the sign of s, so sigma = 0
precisely on Gamma and sigma has the sign of s. On the negative half its solution curves are exactly the nonstationary
W-orbits, supplemented by their points on C. Backward convergence established above identifies sigma as their limit
label. The construction is on a full chart containing closure(N-), after choosing N smaller if needed; in particular
sigma is smooth up to and beyond Gamma.

In coordinates (sigma,r), write b~(sigma,r) = b(s(sigma,r),r). This is smooth on a full chart and b~(sigma,0) = 4 for
sigma <= 0. Set

  b_hat(sigma,r) = b~(sigma,r) - b~(sigma,0) + 4.

It equals b~ on the closed negative half, is positive after shrinking, and equals 4 at r = 0 for every sigma in the full
chart. Apply the formula in (a), with b_hat in place of b~, to define t smoothly on the full chart. It gives a smooth
coordinate map R(sigma,t), with W = 4t d_t on the closed negative half. Nothing on the positive half is required to be
linearized.

On N-, the temperature in (72.6) is a first integral and

  (Theta_W)_x = theta'(sigma) sigma_x.

Every entire past orbit in the formula stays in N and has sigma constant. The substitution q = e^(4 tau) gives

  Omega_W(R(sigma,t)) = theta'(sigma) K_W(sigma,t),
  K_W(sigma,t) = (1/4) int_0^1 q^(-3/4) sigma_x(R(sigma,q t)) dq.

The past segments (sigma,q t), 0 <= q <= 1, lie in the constructed coordinate domain, with q = 0 on C or on Q. The
integrable estimates from (a), including all derivatives, show that K_W is smooth up to sigma = 0. Thus every derivative
of Theta_W - M and of Omega_W tends to zero from N- at Gamma, since theta - M and theta' are flat at 0. Extending by M
and 0 across the hypersurface sigma = 0 is smooth: in these coordinates each one-sided partial derivative has the same
zero boundary trace, and induction on the differentiation order proves smoothness of the glued function. This also
proves flatness along the whole local Gamma, not just at Q.

The temperature transport equation is immediate on either side. Formula (72.3) proves the vorticity transport equation
on N-. Both equations hold on N+ because the functions are constant there, and on Gamma by smoothness and continuity.
Compactly contained choices of coordinates and trace interval make the constructed functions bounded.

For uniqueness, every backward orbit stays in N and converges to a point of C cap N or to Q. Continuity and the
prescribed trace therefore fix every first integral, including on Gamma. If v is the difference of two bounded classical
solutions of the vorticity equation, then

  v(Phi_tau X) = e^(-tau) v(X), tau <= 0.

Its boundedness on N forces v(X) = 0. At a zero the equation itself gives v = 0. Since the divergence was imposed in the
definition of geometric field, (72.7) is exactly the remaining equation.

For an (E') solution initially defined on D, choose closure(N) contained in D. Its temperature and vorticity are bounded
on N. First-integral continuity gives Theta = M on N+. On that open set Theta_x = 0; backward invariance and boundedness
in the vorticity equation give Omega = 0 there. The trace on C is flat relative to M at Q. The preceding uniqueness
proves (72.6). Conversely (72.6) gives the required flatness and both transport equations, and (72.7) supplies the curl.
This proves the equivalence.

On the punctured zero arc, grad Theta = theta'(sigma) grad sigma. Since grad sigma != 0, regularity is equivalent to
theta' != 0. A continuous nonvanishing derivative on a connected terminal interval has constant sign and gives strict
monotonicity. This proves the assertion for (E).

(d) We check explicitly the local noncontinuation result used here. The purely local Scope of Theorem 51 assumes the
smooth equations, spectrum {0,4}, the one-sided zero arc and an outgoing zero-free opposite centre branch; M is
arbitrary. These assumptions hold for (E'). Its initial flatness hypotheses are not needed for the geometric basin
argument. Indeed, on N+ backward convergence and the transport equations give Theta = M and Omega = 0 as above, and
smoothness then gives their flatness along Gamma. In particular Omega(Q) = 0, so the physical matrix DW(Q) is symmetric,
as in Theorem 51. This explains why the orthonormal eigencoordinates used in that theorem are legitimate for the coupled
problem.

For completeness, the relevant argument from Theorem 51, Step 4, is as follows. Suppose a holomorphic function H on a
disc about Q agrees with f on the potential side. Define

  W_a = 2X + (Re H,-Im H).

It is real analytic and agrees with W on the open plus side. Therefore every derivative of W_a-W vanishes at Q.
Translate Q to 0 and use orthonormal eigenvectors, with coordinates (u,v) corresponding to 4 and 0, and orient v so that
the terminal zero arc has v <= 0. The analytic implicit function theorem gives

  (W_a)_u(u,v) = a(u,v)(u-k(v)), a(0,0) = 4,

where a,k are analytic and k(0) = k'(0) = 0. The actual smooth arc is (c(v),v), v <= 0, with c(0) = c'(0) = 0. Flatness
of W_a-W and W = 0 on that arc give, for every integer n,

  |W_a(c(v),v)| <= C_n |v|^n, |c(v)-k(v)| <= C'_n |v|^n

as v tends to zero from below. Boundedness of d_u (W_a)_v then gives

  |(W_a)_v(k(v),v)| <= C''_n |v|^n.

The expression on the left without absolute values is analytic in v. It cannot have a first nonzero Taylor term and is
therefore identically zero near 0. Hence W_a vanishes on (k(v),v) for both signs of v. The curve Gamma is v = gamma0(u),
with gamma0(u) = O(u^2), while k(v) = O(v^2). For small v > 0,

  v - gamma0(k(v)) = v + O(v^4) > 0.

These points lie on the plus side, where W = W_a. They would be zeros outside C, contrary to the geometric zero-set
hypothesis. This proves Theorem 51(b) in exactly the local form required here, for every M, without an independent use
of endpoint flatness.

If theta is constant on a terminal interval, continuity at zero makes the constant M. Choose a smaller invariant N
within the range of that interval. Formula (72.6), including its entire past orbits, gives Theta = M and Omega = 0 on N.
Then f is holomorphic on a disc about Q and provides the prohibited continuation. This proves (i). This is the local
content of Theorem 53(e); it requires no global backward-limit theorem.

For (ii), take Y in Gamma cap B and suppose Omega vanishes on a disc V about Y contained in B. Then d_zbar f = 0 there,
so f is holomorphic and W is real analytic. The vorticity equation gives Theta_x = 0, and the temperature equation
becomes W_2 Theta_y = 0.

If W_2 is not identically zero on the connected disc V, its nonzero set is dense there by the identity theorem for
real-analytic functions. Thus Theta_y = 0 by continuity. The temperature is constant on V, with value M since V meets
B+. As sigma is a submersion, local coordinates (sigma,t) at Y show that sigma(V cap B-) contains (-delta,0) for some
delta > 0. In more detail, an open coordinate rectangle about (0,t(Y)) lies in V, and its negative sigma values give
that interval. Therefore theta is constant on a terminal interval, contradicting (i).

If W_2 is identically zero on V, the divergence and curl equations give d_x W_1 = 4 and d_y W_1 = 0. Hence W_1 = 4x + c
and f = 2z + c on V, with c real. Since B+ is connected, f is holomorphic there, and V cap B+ is a nonempty open set,
the identity theorem gives f = 2z + c on B+. This again provides a continuation to Q, a contradiction.

The argument also applies to Y = Q. Thus no such V exists. Since Omega = 0 on B+ cup Gamma, its nonzero values in
arbitrarily small neighbourhoods of Y must lie in B-. This proves (ii).

For the profile assertion, Theorem 16 supplies Q+ in the open first quadrant, its smooth terminal zero arc, spectrum
{0,4}, and flatness of Theta-M and Omega. Hypothesis (S), as defined in Theorem 48, isolates this arc locally. Step 0 of
Theorem 51 gives an outgoing centre branch for M != 0. For all M, including zero, Theorem 53(d) supplies outgoingness
under (S) and explicitly validates the same local conclusions of Theorem 51. Thus the local hypotheses just checked
apply for the actual value M, without an assumption (R).

An A2-broad profile has U(X) = o(|X|), so W = 2X+U has at most linear growth. Smoothness and this bound imply existence
of its flow for every finite positive or negative time. Choose the local Gamma segment backward invariant as in (c).
Then, for t <= 0, Phi_t(Y) remains on that segment and (ii) proves (iii).

For t > 0 set

  S_t = union_{0 <= s <= t} Phi_s(B+).

Each Phi_s is a diffeomorphism of the plane, so S_t is open. It is connected as the continuous image of the connected
set [0,t] times B+. Temperature invariance gives Theta = M on every Phi_s(B+), hence on their open union; in particular
Theta_x = 0 throughout S_t. For X in B+, its orbit segment from time 0 to s stays in S_t. The equation
dOmega/ds = -Omega and Omega(X) = 0 therefore give Omega = 0 throughout S_t.

Suppose Omega = 0 on a disc V' about Y' = Phi_t(Y). Since Y is in closure(B+), continuity of Phi_t gives Y' in
closure(Phi_t(B+)), so V' meets S_t in a nonempty open set. On V', W is analytic and Theta_x = 0. If W_2 is not
identically zero there, the same argument as above gives Theta constant, and the intersection with S_t fixes the value
as M. Flow invariance gives Theta = M on Phi_(-t)(V'), an open neighbourhood of Y. Its intersection with the local B-
has sigma-image containing a terminal interval, by the same coordinate-rectangle argument. This contradicts (i).

If W_2 is identically zero on V', then f = 2z + c there. The function f is holomorphic on connected S_t and agrees with
this polynomial on V' cap S_t. The identity theorem makes f = 2z + c on S_t, in particular on B+, contradicting the
local noncontinuation proved above. Hence no such V' exists. This proves (iii).

(e) On the sector in question,

  Re zeta^(-1/2) >= cos(3 pi/8) |zeta|^(-1/2).

Every Cartesian derivative of L is bounded by a fixed negative power of |zeta| times exp(-c |zeta|^(-1/2)), with c > 0.
Derivatives of the angular cutoff add only further negative powers. For every derivative order and every N, the
resulting derivative of q is O(|zeta|^N). Near the sector edges q is zero on an angular neighbourhood because the cutoff
is. Thus the zero extension is smooth away from O, and the displayed estimates prove its smoothness and flatness at O.
The same holds for W-(4x,0). Differentiation gives

  div W = 4 - q_yx + q_xy = 4,
  d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = -q_yy - q_xx = -Lap q.

Complex conjugation sends x to -x and preserves y. Since L(conj zeta) = conj L(zeta) on the chosen branch and chi is
even, q(-x,y) = -q(x,y). Therefore W_1(0,y) = -q_y(0,y) = 0. Flatness gives d_x W_1 = 4-q_xy > 2 on a sufficiently small
disc. Each horizontal segment in that disc contains x = 0, so W_1 vanishes there only at x = 0.

For y < 0 the field q is identically zero near (0,y), hence W(0,y) = 0. For y > 0 the cutoff is 1 near (0,y), and
differentiation gives

  W_2(0,y) = q_x(0,y) = eps L'(y)
            = (eps/2) y^(-3/2) exp(-y^(-1/2)) > 0.

Thus the asserted half-axis is exactly the zero set. The whole y-axis is invariant, since W_1 = 0 on it; it is smooth
through O, tangent to the kernel of DW(O) = diag(4,0), and its positive branch is zero-free and outgoing. This verifies
the centre-curve hypothesis in its C^2, two-sided sense.

The strong unstable curve from (c) is a smooth graph y = g(x), with g(0) = g'(0) = 0, and invariance gives

  W_2(x,g(x)) = g'(x) W_1(x,g(x)).

If a_m x^m, m >= 2, were its first nonzero Taylor term, the left side would have zero Taylor series because W_2 is flat.
On the right, W_1(x,g(x)) = 4x plus a flat term, so the coefficient of x^m would be 4m a_m. This is impossible. Hence g
is flat. The same reasoning applies to any smooth invariant graph tangent to the x-axis.

For x > 0, zeta = -ix has argument -pi/2, where chi = 1. Since L'(zeta) = (1/2) zeta^(-3/2) exp(-zeta^(-1/2)),

  W_2(x,0) = eps Re L'(-ix)
            = (eps/2) x^(-3/2) exp(-x^(-1/2)/sqrt(2))
             cos(3 pi/4 - x^(-1/2)/sqrt(2)).

For instance x_n = 1/[2(2 pi n + 3 pi/4)^2] tends to zero and makes the cosine equal to 1. Thus the x-axis is not
invariant in any neighbourhood of O. An analytic invariant graph tangent to that axis would be flat by the preceding
argument and therefore identically zero, contradicting this computation. This proves both the nonanalyticity of g and
the stronger exclusion of any analytic transverse invariant curve.

For zeta = y-ix, the sector |arg zeta| < 2 pi/3 is equivalently

  y > -|x|/sqrt(3).

Since g(x) = o(|x|), for sufficiently small nonzero x one has g(x) > -|x|/sqrt(3). If x = 0 and y > g(0), then y > 0.
Therefore the whole local side y > g(x) lies in this open sector. Each point (x,g(x)) with x != 0 sufficiently small
lies strictly in it as well. It has a neighbourhood inside the sector, away from O, on which chi = 1.

On this sector F(z) = L(-iz) is holomorphic and q = -eps Im F. The Cauchy-Riemann equations give

  q_y + i q_x = -eps F'(z).

Consequently q is harmonic, its curl contribution is zero, and

  f = 2z - q_y - i q_x = 2z + eps F'(z)
     = 2z - i eps L'(-iz).

All derivatives of the correction are flat at O from this side. If it had a holomorphic continuation to a disc, its
Taylor series at O would have all coefficients zero: equivalently compare the continuation with the ambient smooth f on
the open plus side and take derivative limits at O. The correction would therefore vanish near O. But on z = iy with
y > 0 it is -i eps L'(y) != 0. This proves noncontinuation.

The geometry from (c) makes this full side a backward basin of O. The curl is zero on it, zero on a neighbourhood of
each punctured Gamma point, and flat at O; hence it is flat along Gamma. If a smooth Theta and Omega completed W to
(E'), its vorticity would necessarily equal -Lap q and would vanish near every punctured Gamma point. This contradicts
(d)(ii). All assertions follow. QED.

### Theorem 73 (beta > 2: finite exceptional rays and orbits, shear reversal, and a local vorticity pocket)

All conclusions concerning global profiles are conditional on the stated profile hypotheses. Part (e) is an independent
local existence statement.

For parts (a)-(d), let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2 satisfying (H1), and
assume that B is bounded and nonempty. Thus the fields are smooth on the plane, U is canonical and uniformly sublinear,
Theta and Omega have at most polynomial growth, and the profile equations hold. The temperature is even in x and odd in
y, Theta(0,y) = 0, and Theta = a0 x^2 y + O(|X|^5) near the origin, with a0 != 0. Vorticity is odd in each coordinate.
The velocity U_1 is odd in x and even in y, while U_2 is even in x and odd in y. Set

  Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, alpha = pi/2, sigma = sgn(a0), kappa = beta - 2,
  h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h, a = 2 - h, d = 2 beta - 1, s = d/kappa,
  theta = sigma Theta, z = sigma Omega, B = {X in Q1 : z(X) < 0}, W = beta X + U.

The signed equations and the curl convention are

  W.grad theta = kappa theta, W.grad z + z = theta_x,
  div W = 2 beta, d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = sigma z.

Write Phi_t for the complete flow. Let O = (0,0) and P_ax = (L,0) be the first positive x-axis zero from Theorem 2.
Hypothesis (H1) is {W = 0} cap closure(Q1) = {O,P_ax}. Let f, G, P be the angular functions of Theorems 41, 42 and 64,
normalized by

  r^(-q) Theta -> f, r^h Omega -> G,
  r^(h-1)(U_r,U_phi) -> (-P',aP),
  -P'' - a^2 P = G, P(0) = P(alpha) = 0.

All these limits are uniform in angle. Put F = sigma f and g = sigma G. In particular P retains its original sign:
-P'' - a^2 P = sigma g. A prime on an angular function denotes an angular derivative. Define, as in (66.10),

  D0 = q cos(phi) F - sin(phi) F',
  F1 = -q P' F + a P F',
  g1 = h P' g + a P g' - D0.

Let P1 be the original signed stream correction of Theorem 42(c), so

  -P1'' - (2 - 2h)^2 P1 = sigma g1, P1(0) = P1(alpha) = 0,
  D1 = (q - h) cos(phi) F1 - sin(phi) F1',
  g2 = [2h P' g1 + a P g1' + h P1' g + (2 - 2h) P1 g' - D1]/2.

These are (66.28). Put

  K = 2 P' cos(phi) - a P cos(2 phi)/sin(phi),
  C0 = q(1 - h) F K.                                            (73.1)

The expression C0 extends the formula (66.16) to all interior angles. Under (H1), every orbit in Q1 tends backward to
P_ax and escapes forward; its limiting angle belongs to (0,alpha). By Theorem 50(b), limiting angle is a bijection from
the set of complete orbits in Q1 onto (0,alpha). On a fixed orbit, X(r) denotes the unique point of radius r on its
sufficiently late forward end.

(a) (Common zeros of g and K.) The set {phi in (0,alpha) : g(phi) = K(phi) = 0} is finite. At every point of this set,

  K' = 2 a (2 - a) cos(phi) P / sin(2 phi)^2 != 0.              (73.2)

(b) (Exceptional rays.) The set

  E = {phi in (0,alpha) : liminf_(r -> infinity) r^(3h) z(r,phi) = 0}    (73.3)

equals {g = g1 = g2 = 0} and is finite. If phi is not in E, there are c_phi > 0 and R_phi > 0 such that
z(r,phi) >= c_phi r^(-3h) for r >= R_phi. If phi is in E, z(r,phi) = O(r^(-4h)). The constants and thresholds in these
statements may depend on the ray. Consequently the profile hypotheses are incompatible with infinitely many distinct
angles satisfying the condition in (73.3). The ray prohibition of Theorem 64(b) implies that condition for every angle
of the nonempty open set S_B = {phi in (0,alpha) : z(r,phi) < 0 for some r > 0}.

(c) (Exceptional trajectories.) Put E_orb = {phi in (0,alpha) : g = D0 = C0 = 0}. This set is contained in the finite
set in (a). For the orbit with limiting angle phi_*,

  if phi_* is not in E_orb: liminf_(r -> infinity) r^(3h) z(X(r)) > 0;
  if phi_* is in E_orb: z(X(r)) = O(r^(-4h)).                   (73.4)

Here a lower limit of +infinity is allowed. Thus all but finitely many complete orbits in Q1 satisfy z(X) >= c_orb
|X|^(-3h) at every sufficiently late point, with c_orb > 0 and a threshold depending on the orbit. E_orb is exactly the
set of limiting angles for which r^(3h) z(X(r)) tends to zero. No equality between E and E_orb is asserted.

If moreover a0 < 0 and w''(L) > 0, where w(x) = W_1(x,0), all but finitely many orbits in Q1 that meet B have three
increasing times with strict vorticity signs (sigma,-sigma,sigma). The last time can be chosen arbitrarily large.
Accordingly, when a0 < 0, forbidding this triple on infinitely many distinct complete orbits meeting B is inconsistent
with w''(L) > 0.

(d) (Shear reversal.) For X in Q1, let (u,v) be any component of {t : z(Phi_t X) < 0}. Then v is finite, and there is t
in (u,v) such that

  W_2 d_x W_2 < 0 at Phi_t X.                                   (73.5)

In particular W_2 d_x W_2 >= 0 cannot hold throughout any component of B.

(e) (A local pocket.) Independently of the global profile hypotheses, fix beta > 2, sigma in {-1,1}, an interior point
(x_*,y_*) in Q1, and constants v_*, c_*, T_*, M > 0. Put kappa = beta - 2, d = 2 beta - 1 and s = d/kappa. In the
coordinates xi = x - x_* and eta = y - y_*, prescribe analytic data on eta = 0:

  W_1 = 0, W_2 = v_* - c_* xi, theta = T_*, z = M xi^2 - epsilon.    (73.6)

Consider the system

  d_eta W_1 = d_xi W_2 + sigma z, d_eta W_2 = 2 beta - d_xi W_1,
  d_eta theta = (kappa theta - W_1 d_xi theta)/W_2,
  d_eta z = (d_xi theta - z - W_1 d_xi z)/W_2.                  (73.7)

There is a fixed open disc N centered at (x_*,y_*), with closure(N) contained in Q1, such that for every sufficiently
small epsilon > 0 the analytic solution exists on a neighbourhood of closure(N). On that neighbourhood it satisfies the
four signed equations displayed above, with theta > T_*/2 and W_2 > v_*/2 on closure(N). The set D = {X in N : z(X) < 0}
is nonempty and strictly convex, closure(D) is a compact subset of N, and its boundary is a smooth closed curve with
nonvanishing grad z and strictly positive curvature.

By a maximal trajectory segment in N, mean a solution X:I -> N on a maximal connected time interval during which the
trajectory remains in N. Each such segment meets D in either no times or a single interval (u,v) whose closure lies
inside I and whose endpoints are finite. In the latter case it enters D transversely with theta_x(X(u)) < 0 and leaves
transversely with theta_x(X(v)) > 0.

For D, the identities (66.3), (66.4), (66.5), including its absolutely convergent limit int_D theta^(-s) theta_x = 0,
and (66.6) hold. The regularization parameter in (66.5) is any delta > 0, independently of the small construction
parameter epsilon. Identity (66.8) holds on each negative interval (u,v) just described. With U = W - beta X, there is
an analytic stream function Psi on N such that U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x) and -Lap Psi = sigma z.

Scope. Parts (a)-(d) are necessary conditions for a bounded nonempty set B under (H1). They do not exclude such a
profile for either sign of a0. Part (b) excludes an additional condition weaker than the ray prohibition of
Theorem 64(b): infinitely many distinct rays carry z = o(r^(-3h)) along a sequence of radii tending to infinity on each
ray. The sequences need not agree between rays. Boundedness of B makes z eventually nonnegative, so this sequence
condition is exactly (73.3) on each selected ray. The ray prohibition forces z = 0 beyond one common radius on every ray
of S_B; the sequence condition permits ray sign triples.

For comparison, z = C x y exp(-|X|^2)(|X|^2 - 1)(|X|^2 - 4), with C > 0, is smooth, odd in each coordinate, and has
origin jet 4Cxy + O(|X|^4). Its negative set in Q1 is {1 < |X| < 2}; every interior ray has a positive-negative-positive
triple, while z = o(r^(-3h)) on every ray. This field is not claimed to solve the profile equations. Thus the strict
weakening concerns extra conditions on fields; it is not an existence assertion about the excluded profile classes.

Part (c) strengthens the late-positivity conclusion of Theorem 66(d) from a dense residual family to all but finitely
many orbits. Its triple conclusion retains a0 < 0 and w''(L) > 0; no sign of w''(L) is proved. Part (d) is a pointwise
restriction on velocity. No implication between that restriction and the ray or orbit prohibitions is proved. It is
consistent with (66.13), which gives W_2 d_x W_2 <= 0 at sufficiently distant vorticity zeros. Part (e) supplies exact
local solutions with curl coupling, the listed component and excursion identities, and one negative interval per maximal
trajectory segment in N. It supplies no origin jet, smooth A2 extension across the axes, canonical velocity, natural far
field, or global basin of P_ax. It is not a counterexample to a global nonexistence statement.

No extension of parts (b)-(e) to beta = 2 is asserted. Theorem 3 shows that (H1) itself fails there: a stagnation curve
passes through P_ax and enters Q1. There are nevertheless analogous differentiated first corrections at beta = 2 in
Theorem 45(f), and the radial argument below also produces a third vorticity term with O(r^(-2)) remainder at h = 1/2.
Thus the absence of expansions is not the obstruction. At q = 0, C0 vanishes identically and its flatness gives no
information about K; positivity of kappa theta in (d) and the positive second Hessian entry in (73.9) are also lost.
Theorem 64(g) leaves a constant-temperature zero-vorticity sector unexcluded. This is not an existence result. The
angular conclusion (a), by itself, remains valid for beta = 2 under boundedness of B, as justified at the end of the
proof. The finite-domain balances (66.3), (66.4), the regular-boundary identity (66.6), and the finite-endpoint
integrating-factor identity (66.8) also remain valid at beta = 2 under their respective local hypotheses. The weight
s = d/kappa in (66.5) is not defined there. Failure of (73.9) at beta = 2 is a failure of this pocket construction, not
a proof against every possible local construction.

Proof. By Theorems 8(ii), 50(b) and 66(b), theta > 0 on Q1 and F > 0 on (0,alpha). Thus {Theta = 0} has empty interior
in Q1, and all the hypotheses of Theorem 66 are satisfied. Theorem 64(a) gives g >= 0, sigma P > 0 in (0,alpha), sigma
P'(0) > 0 and sigma P'(alpha) < 0. Theorem 50(c) gives F'(0) > 0 and g'(alpha) < 0, for either sign of a0. Since
g(0) = 0 and g >= 0, gamma = g'(0) >= 0. The endpoint vanishing of F, g and P at zero follows from the parities;
g(alpha) = P(alpha) = 0 as well. The angular functions are smooth on the closed angular interval. The quotient
P/sin(phi) has a smooth extension at zero, because both numerator and denominator vanish there and sin'(0) != 0. Hence K
also extends smoothly there. Its formula is regular at alpha.

(a) On the interior interval, write

  K = 2 cos(phi)[P' - a cot(2 phi) P].

At a common zero of g and K, G = sigma g = 0, so the angular stream equation gives P'' = -a^2 P. Also P' = a cot(2 phi)
P. Differentiating before making these substitutions gives

  K' = -2 sin(phi)[P' - a cot(2 phi) P]
       + 2 cos(phi)[P'' - a cot(2 phi) P' + 2 a P/sin(2 phi)^2].

The first bracket vanishes. The second becomes

  a P[-a - a cot(2 phi)^2 + 2/sin(2 phi)^2]
     = a(2 - a) P/sin(2 phi)^2.

This proves (73.2). Its factors are nonzero: 0 < a < 2, cos(phi) > 0, sin(2 phi) > 0 and P != 0. Every such point is
therefore an isolated zero of K. As phi decreases to zero,

  P/sin(phi) -> P'(0), K -> (2 - a) P'(0) = h P'(0) != 0.

There are no zeros of K near zero. Since g(alpha) = 0 and g'(alpha) < 0, g is strictly positive just below alpha. The
simultaneous-zero set is consequently contained in a compact interior angular interval. It is closed there, and an
infinite subset would have an accumulation point that is itself a simultaneous zero, contradicting its isolation. This
proves finiteness.

(b) We first verify the additional expansion, rather than assume a formal series. Theorem 42(c) gives, uniformly in
angle and with differentiated remainders,

  z = r^(-h) g + r^(-2h) g1 + O_infty(r^(-3h)),
  theta = r^q F + r^(q-h) F1 + O_infty(r^(q-2h)),
  (U_r,U_phi) = r^(1-h)(-P',aP)
               + r^(1-2h)(-P1',(2 - 2h)P1) + O_infty(r^(1-3h)).

Here O_infty(r^m) means that each Cartesian derivative of order k is O(r^(m-k)), uniformly in angle. With L_r = beta r
d_r + 1, the vorticity equation is L_r z = theta_x - U.grad z. Its right side has coefficient -g1 at r^(-2h) and
coefficient

  D1 - 2h P' g1 - a P g1' - h P1' g - (2 - 2h) P1 g' = -2g2

at r^(-3h). Every unused term is O(r^(-4h)) uniformly in angle. For example, the leading velocity times the gradient of
z's O_infty(r^(-3h)) remainder has order r^(1-h) r^(-3h-1) = r^(-4h), and the x derivative of the temperature remainder
has order r^(q-2h-1) = r^(-4h). The velocity remainder times the leading vorticity gradient has the same order. Since
L_r(r^(-jh)) = (1-j)r^(-jh), the error R2 after subtracting the three terms satisfies R2 = O(r^(-3h)) and L_r
R2 = O(r^(-4h)). At each fixed angle,

  (r^h R2)' = h r^(h-1) L_r R2,
  R2(r,phi) = -h r^(-h) int_r^infinity t^(h-1) L_t R2(t,phi) dt.

The boundary term at infinity vanishes since r^h R2 = O(r^(-2h)). The integral is bounded uniformly by a constant times
r^(-3h); multiplication by r^(-h) therefore proves

  z = r^(-h) g + r^(-2h) g1 + r^(-3h) g2 + O(r^(-4h)),          (73.8)

uniformly in angle. This is exactly the argument in (66.28)-(66.30), in the proof of Theorem 66(f). Only this
undifferentiated uniform remainder is needed after the upgrade; no infinite expansion is assumed.

Boundedness of B gives z(r,phi) >= 0 for every interior angle and all r >= R_B, where R_B contains B. Fix an angle. If
g > 0, (73.8) gives r^(3h) z -> +infinity. If g = 0, it first gives g1 >= 0; if g1 > 0, again r^(3h) z -> +infinity. If
g = g1 = 0, it gives r^(3h) z -> g2 >= 0. Therefore E = {g = g1 = g2 = 0}, the lower bound off E follows, and
z = O(r^(-4h)) on E. An interior zero of the nonnegative function g has g' = 0, and hence g1 = -D0 there. In particular
E is contained in {g = D0 = 0}.

At an angle with g = D0 = 0, (66.32) gives

  g1' = a P g'' - D0',
  2g2 = a^2 P^2 g'' - a P D0' - D1.

For clarity, differentiating the definitions at this angle gives

  D0' = -q sin(phi) F + (q - 1) cos(phi) F' - sin(phi) F'',
  F1' = -q P'' F + (a - q) P' F' + a P F''.

Here P'' = -a^2 P because G = 0, and F' = q cot(phi) F because D0 = 0. In a P D0' - D1 the terms involving F'' cancel.
After substituting these two relations and q = 1 - 2h, a = 2 - h, the remaining terms equal q(1-h) F[2 P' cos(phi) - a P
cos(2 phi)/sin(phi)] = C0. Thus (66.35) gives

  2g2 = a^2 P^2 g'' - 2 a P D0' + C0.

There is no accumulation of E at zero. Indeed D0(0) = 0 and g1(0) = 0, and differentiation at zero yields

  D0'(0) = (q - 1) F'(0) = -2h F'(0),
  g1'(0) = (h + a) P'(0) gamma - D0'(0)
           = 2 P'(0) gamma + 2h F'(0).

These are the coefficients in (66.14). If gamma > 0, then g > 0 just to the right of zero. If gamma = 0, then
g1'(0) = 2h F'(0) > 0, so g1 > 0 there. Either case excludes E from an interval adjacent to zero. At alpha the strict
inequality g'(alpha) < 0 excludes E in the same way using g alone.

If E were infinite, choose distinct phi_j in E converging to an interior point phi_*. A smooth function of one real
variable with distinct zeros accumulating at an interior point is flat there: otherwise its first nonzero Taylor
coefficient gives an isolated zero. Apply this to g and D0, both of which vanish at every phi_j. In particular Taylor's
formula for their derivatives gives

  g''(phi_j) = O(|phi_j - phi_*|^2),
  D0'(phi_j) = O(|phi_j - phi_*|^2).

Since g2(phi_j) = 0, the displayed contact identity gives C0(phi_j) = O(|phi_j - phi_*|^2). Continuity first gives
C0(phi_*) = 0, and the difference quotient along phi_j then gives C0'(phi_*) = 0. The positive smooth factor q(1-h) F
converts these equalities to K(phi_*) = K'(phi_*) = 0. Also g(phi_*) = 0 by continuity. This contradicts (73.2), so E is
finite.

For the comparison with Theorem 64(b), its origin-jet argument gives z > 0 on every interior ray at all sufficiently
small positive radii. If a ray meets B and a positive value occurred on it at r >= R_B, these three values would form a
prohibited triple. A negative value there is excluded by boundedness of B. Thus the ray prohibition gives z = 0 for
r >= R_B on every angle in S_B, exactly (64.5). The set S_B is nonempty and open, since B is nonempty and a strict
negative value persists under a small angular perturbation at a fixed radius. All its angles would belong to E, which
contradicts finiteness.

(c) Theorem 66(e), equation (66.15), gives along an outgoing orbit

  phi(r) = phi_* - a P(phi_*) r^(-h) + O(r^(-2h)).

It follows by integrating d phi/dr = (a/beta) P(phi) r^(-1-h) + O(r^(-1-2h)); the leading integral has coefficient a
because beta h = 1. Since (73.8) is uniform in angle, it is valid at phi = phi(r).

If g(phi_*) > 0, smoothness gives z(X(r)) = r^(-h) g(phi_*) + O(r^(-2h)). If g(phi_*) = 0, nonnegativity gives
g'(phi_*) = 0, so g(phi(r)) = O(r^(-2h)). It follows that z(X(r)) = r^(-2h) g1(phi_*) + O(r^(-3h)), where
g1(phi_*) = -D0(phi_*) >= 0 by (66.11).

It remains to treat g(phi_*) = D0(phi_*) = 0. Put u(r) = (phi(r) - phi_*) r^h = -a P(phi_*) + O(r^(-h)). Taylor
expansion of g through order two, g1 through order one, and g2 through order zero gives, with all coefficients below at
phi_*,

  z(X(r)) = r^(-3h)[(g''/2) u(r)^2 + g1' u(r) + g2] + O(r^(-4h))
           = r^(-3h)[(a^2 P^2/2) g'' - a P g1' + g2] + O(r^(-4h)).

The remainders have this order since phi(r) - phi_* = O(r^(-h)); the O(r^(-h)) correction to u(r) also contributes only
O(r^(-4h)). Using g1' = a P g'' - D0' and the formula for 2g2 from (b), the bracket equals C0(phi_*)/2. Equation (66.17)
gives C0(phi_*) >= 0; this sign also follows directly from eventual nonnegativity of z on the orbit. Thus r^(3h) z(X(r))
tends to +infinity if g > 0 or if g = 0 and D0 < 0, and tends to C0/2 if g = D0 = 0. These three cases give (73.4) and
the stated exact description of the exceptional orbit angles.

Because F > 0 and q(1-h) > 0, C0 = 0 is equivalent to K = 0 on (0,alpha). Therefore E_orb is contained in {g = K = 0},
finite by (a). The bijection of Theorem 50(b) converts a finite set of angles into a finite set of complete orbits,
rather than merely a finite set of possible directions for many orbits.

Suppose now a0 < 0 and w''(L) > 0. Theorem 2(c) gives A_ax = Theta_y(P_ax) < 0. Theorem 62(d) states that Omega has the
sign of A_ax w''(L) in a sufficiently small upper neighbourhood of P_ax, and at every sufficiently negative time on each
Q1 orbit. Hence Omega < 0 there and z = -Omega > 0. A visit to B supplies a later negative z value. For every orbit
outside the finite exceptional family, (73.4) supplies positive z at every sufficiently late time. Multiplying these
three z signs by sigma gives the claimed vorticity triple. Distinct points on one orbit do not count as distinct orbits
in the final prohibition statement.

(d) Every orbit in Q1 escapes by Theorem 50(b). It therefore eventually leaves a disc containing B forever, so every
negative excursion has finite upper endpoint v. At a finite excursion endpoint continuity gives z = 0. If the lower
endpoint is -infinity, the backward limit P_ax makes z and theta_x bounded there, so e^t z(Phi_t X) -> 0 and the
backward integral of e^t |theta_x(Phi_t X)| converges. Differentiating along the orbit gives

  d(e^t z(Phi_t X))/dt = e^t theta_x(Phi_t X).

Integration from the lower endpoint to an interior time and from that time to v gives exactly (66.8), for this
excursion. This also explains its applicability to an excursion not containing the original time zero: one can choose an
