interior point and translate time. The first integral is strictly negative and the second strictly positive, so there
are t_- < t_+ in (u,v) such that theta_x(Phi_(t_-) X) < 0 < theta_x(Phi_(t_+) X).

Put f_orb(t) = theta_x(Phi_t X). Differentiating the temperature transport equation in x gives

  f_orb' = (kappa - d_x W_1) f_orb - (d_x W_2) theta_y,

with the spatial quantities evaluated on the orbit. Suppose W_2 d_x W_2 >= 0 throughout (u,v). Define

  t_0 = sup{t in [t_-,t_+] : f_orb(t) <= 0}.

The set is nonempty and closed, f_orb(t_-) < 0, and f_orb(t_+) > 0. Continuity consequently gives t_- < t_0 < t_+,
f_orb(t_0) = 0, and f_orb > 0 on (t_0,t_+]. At t_0, temperature transport gives

  W_2 theta_y = kappa theta > 0.

Thus W_2 != 0 there and on a small closed interval [t_0,t_0+delta] contained in [t_0,t_+]. Eliminating theta_y on this
interval gives

  f_orb' = A_orb(t) f_orb - kappa theta (W_2 d_x W_2)/W_2^2,
  A_orb(t) = kappa - d_x W_1 + W_1 d_x W_2/W_2.

The coefficient A_orb is continuous and the final term is nonpositive. For the positive integrating factor
mu(t) = exp(-int_(t_0)^t A_orb(tau) d tau), one has (mu f_orb)' <= 0 and mu(t_0) f_orb(t_0) = 0. Hence f_orb <= 0 on the
small interval, contrary to its strict positivity. This proves (73.5). A connected negative time interval maps into one
connected component of B. Choosing its initial point in any prescribed component proves the final component assertion.

(e) The right sides of (73.7) are analytic functions of xi, the unknown fields, and their xi derivatives wherever
W_2 != 0. The analytic initial data have W_2 = v_* at xi = 0. Apply the first-order Cauchy-Kowalevski theorem with eta
as the normal variable and (xi,epsilon) as tangential variables; the right sides contain no epsilon derivatives. It
provides a solution analytic jointly in (xi,eta,epsilon) near (0,0,0). This application is noncharacteristic because the
system is solved for every eta derivative and its denominators are nonzero at the data. In particular there is a common
product neighbourhood for all sufficiently small |epsilon|. Shrink it so that W_2 > v_*/2 and theta > T_*/2. The first
two equations are exactly divergence and signed curl, and the remaining two are the transport equations.

At epsilon = 0, evaluate at the origin of the translated coordinates. The initial line gives

  z = M xi^2, z_eta = -M xi^2/(v_* - c_* xi),
  theta_eta = kappa T_*/(v_* - c_* xi).

It follows that z = z_xi = z_eta = z_xi,eta = 0 and z_xi,xi = 2M at the centre, and theta_xi,eta = c_* kappa T_*/v_*^2.
Differentiate W_2 z_eta = theta_xi - z - W_1 z_xi in eta at the centre. All terms except W_2 z_eta,eta and theta_xi,eta
vanish, because W_1 = z_xi = z_eta = 0 there. Therefore

  z = 0, grad z = 0,
  D^2 z = diag(2M, c_* kappa T_*/v_*^3).                        (73.9)

This Hessian is positive definite. At the same point W = (0,v_*), and the term involving grad z in a second transport
derivative vanishes. Hence

  (W.grad)^2 z = W^T(D^2 z)W = c_* kappa T_*/v_* > 0.

Choose a closed disc K0 of radius rho > 0 centered at this point, compactly contained in the common spatial domain and
in Q1, on which at epsilon = 0 both D^2 z and (W.grad)^2 z are strictly positive in their respective senses. Compactness
gives uniform positive lower bounds. Since z and grad z vanish at the centre, integrating the Hessian along a radial
segment shows that z_0(X) > 0 at every other point of K0. In particular its minimum on the boundary circle is positive.

Joint analyticity gives uniform convergence of the fields and their derivatives through order two on K0 as epsilon tends
to zero. Thus, for all sufficiently small epsilon > 0, the positive Hessian lower bound, positivity of (W.grad)^2 z,
positivity of z on the boundary circle, and the bounds on W_2 and theta persist on this same disc. The data give
z_epsilon(0,0) = -epsilon < 0. Let N be the interior of K0.

The negative set D is nonempty and has compact closure in N because z is positive on the boundary circle. The positive
Hessian makes z strictly convex on the convex set K0. Its minimum is negative, attained in the interior, and is its
unique critical point. Thus grad z != 0 on {z = 0} in K0. For two distinct points of closure(D), strict convexity gives
z < 0 on the open segment between them. This proves strict convexity of D and connectedness. From the unique minimum,
each ray reaches the boundary circle with positive z and has exactly one zero, with positive radial derivative. The
implicit function theorem gives a smooth closed boundary curve. On it, the curvature magnitude is D^2 z[tau,tau]/|grad
z| > 0, where tau is a unit tangent. This proves the stated geometry without changing the disc to a flow box.

Let X:I -> N be a maximal trajectory segment. Since dy/dt = W_2 > v_*/2 and the vertical diameter of N is 2rho, any
t1 < t2 in I satisfy (v_*/2)(t2-t1) < 2rho. Hence I has finite length, at most 4rho/v_*, and both its endpoints are
finite. The fields extend smoothly to a neighbourhood of closure(N); their bounded speed gives a limit at each endpoint,
and ODE continuation puts both limits on the boundary circle. The positivity of z on that circle consequently gives
positive z near both endpoints of I.

Along the whole segment, d^2 z(X(t))/dt^2 = (W.grad)^2 z(X(t)) > 0. Strict convexity in time shows that the negative
time set is an interval or empty. If nonempty, write it as (u,v); the endpoint positivity just proved places [u,v]
inside I, with finite u,v and z(X(u)) = z(X(v)) = 0. For any t in (u,v), convexity gives

  d z(X(u))/dt <= z(X(t))/(t-u) < 0,
  d z(X(v))/dt >= -z(X(t))/(v-t) > 0.

At z = 0, the vorticity equation identifies d z/dt with theta_x. Thus the crossings are transverse with the asserted
entry and exit signs. These assertions concern maximal segments in N; an arbitrarily truncated subsegment need not
contain its entry or exit.

Set U = W - beta X. Since div U = 0, the one-form U_2 dx - U_1 dy is closed. The disc is simply connected, so it has an
analytic potential Psi with Psi_x = U_2 and Psi_y = -U_1. The curl convention then gives

  -Lap Psi = d_y U_1 - d_x U_2 = d_y W_1 - d_x W_2 = sigma z.

It remains to check the identities listed in the statement. Write b = -z > 0 on D. For every real p >= 1 and every C^1
function A defined near the compact temperature range on closure(D), differentiation gives

  div(A(theta) b^p W)
     = [(2 beta - p) A(theta) + kappa theta A'(theta)] b^p
      - p A(theta) b^(p-1) theta_x.

The notation p here is the exponent called r in (66.3). The factor b^p vanishes on the smooth boundary, so its flux has
zero integral. For nonintegral p >= 1 one may extend b^p as (max(-z,0))^p to apply the Lipschitz divergence theorem, or
approximate inside D. All factors are bounded on a compact set. Thus

  p int_D A(theta) b^(p-1) theta_x
     = int_D [(2 beta - p) A(theta) + kappa theta A'(theta)] b^p,

with absolute convergence. This is (66.3). Taking A = 1 gives

  int_D theta_x = d int_D b > 0,
  p int_D b^(p-1) theta_x = (2 beta - p) int_D b^p,

which is (66.4). In particular theta_x takes both signs: its integral is positive, while at the interior maximum M_D > 0
of b, grad z = 0 and the vorticity equation gives theta_x = z = -M_D < 0.

For an independent regularization parameter delta > 0, take p = 1 and A(t) = (t+delta)^(-s). Since kappa s = d,

  int_D (theta+delta)^(-s) theta_x
     = d delta int_D (theta+delta)^(-s-1) b > 0.

This is exactly (66.5). Put m = min_closure(D) theta > 0. The right side is at most d delta m^(-s-1) int_D b and tends
to zero. The left integrands converge with the integrable majorant m^(-s)|theta_x|. Therefore int_D theta^(-s)
theta_x = 0, with absolute convergence. Equivalently, choose p = 1 and A(t) = t^(-s) directly in (66.3).

On the boundary, grad z = |grad z| n, where n is the outward normal. The vorticity equation and divergence theorem give

  W.n = theta_x/|grad z|,
  int_boundary(D) theta_x/|grad z| dl = 2 beta |D| > 0,

which is (66.6). Both crossing directions occur by taking a maximal segment through any point of D. The usual extremum
conclusions also hold: W.grad theta = kappa theta > 0 ensures grad theta != 0; at a minimum of theta on closure(D), grad
theta is a strictly negative multiple of n, and at a maximum a strictly positive multiple. Transport therefore gives
W.n < 0 at every boundary minimum and W.n > 0 at every boundary maximum.

Finally, for each negative interval (u,v) and each u < t < v,

  int_u^t e^tau theta_x(X(tau)) d tau = e^t z(X(t)) < 0,
  int_t^v e^tau theta_x(X(tau)) d tau = -e^t z(X(t)) > 0.

These follow by integrating d(e^t z)/dt = e^t theta_x from the two zero endpoints and are precisely (66.8). All
intervals here are finite and all integrands extend continuously to their closures, so convergence is absolute. This
completes the local construction.

To justify the scope statements at beta = 2, (73.2) still holds with h = 1/2 and a = 3/2. Theorem 64(a) still gives the
strict endpoint slopes of P. The zero-endpoint limit remains h P'(0) != 0. At the other endpoint, putting
delta = alpha - phi and using P(phi) = -P'(alpha) delta + O(delta^2), one obtains

  K(phi) = h P'(alpha) delta + O(delta^2).

Thus K itself is nonzero just below alpha, without using the beta > 2 assertion g'(alpha) < 0. This confines its common
zeros with g to a compact interior interval; (73.2) then proves finiteness exactly as in (a). For the expansion,
Theorem 45(f) supplies the three differentiated input remainders used in the derivation of (73.8) at h = 1/2, with
F = sigma H and q = 0. The same L_r integration gives a uniform O(r^(-4h)) = O(r^(-2)) remainder. Its availability does
not restore the step C0 = C0' = 0 implies K = K' = 0, because C0 = q(1-h) F K is now identically zero. In (d), W_2
theta_y = kappa theta at a zero of theta_x has zero right side and gives no nonvanishing of W_2. In (e), the second
entry of (73.9) vanishes. The unweighted and general finite-domain identities and the finite-endpoint excursion
integrations above have no division by kappa, so they retain precisely the local validity stated in Scope. QED.

### Theorem 74 (beta = 2: the endpoint equation (72.7) in area coordinates; compatibility, linear Cauchy instability, potential matching and tests)

Setting. Use the local system (72.1), the notation f = U_1 - i U_2, d_zbar f = (i/2) Omega of Theorem 72, and the
reverse-curl convention rc W = d_y W_1 - d_x W_2. Let W be a geometric field at Q with the objects N, N+, N-, Gamma, C
and sigma of Theorem 72(c), let M be real and let theta be a smooth trace on s <= 0 with theta - M flat at 0. Write
h = theta'. For a smooth map R(s,t) write u = R_s, v = R_t, A = |v|^2, n = (v_2,-v_1), B = v_t.n, and

  rho = (u.v)/A,
  K(s,t) = (1/4) int_0^1 q^(-3/4) v_2(s,q t) dq,
  F = h K/(4A) - 2t B/A^2.                                      (74.1)

(a) (Area chart.) After shrinking N there are delta, eps > 0 and a smooth embedding R of a neighbourhood of the closed
half-rectangle H- = {-delta < s <= 0, |t| < eps} such that R(H-) is a relative neighbourhood of Q in closure(N-), and

  det DR = 1, W(R(s,t)) = 4t R_t(s,t) on H-,
  R({s = 0}) is contained in Gamma, R({t = 0, s <= 0}) is contained in C, R(0,0) = Q.

The label is a function of s alone, sigma(R(s,t)) = S1(s) with S1 smooth, S1' > 0 and S1(0) = 0; write theta again for
the trace theta o S1 in the parameter s (theta - M is still flat at 0, and theta' != 0 exactly where the old trace
derivative is nonzero). Then grad s = n o R^(-1), u = rho v + n/A, (Theta_W)_x o R = h v_2, Omega_W o R = h K, and

  (rc W) o R = 4A(rho - t rho_t) + 8t B/A.                      (74.2)

Consequently (72.7) holds on R(H-) if and only if

  rho - t rho_t = F on H-.                                      (74.3)

On N+, Omega_W = 0, so (72.7) holds there if and only if W is irrotational on N+.

(b) (Solvability in t, the first compatibility condition, gauge, and the first jets.) For a smooth function F on H-, the
equation (74.3) for an unknown smooth rho has a smooth solution if and only if F_t(s,0) = 0; its smooth solutions are
then exactly

  rho(s,t) = F(s,0) + c(s) t - t int_0^t [F(s,r) - F(s,0)]/r^2 dr,  (74.4)

with c an arbitrary smooth function. On t = 0 write v_t = a v + b n. Then

  F_t(s,0) = -[9 h v_2 a + (40 + h v_1) b]/(20 A),

so every (E') configuration satisfies, in every chart of (a),

  (40 + h v_1) b = -9 h v_2 a on t = 0.                         (74.5)

On their common closed minus side, the charts of (a) are related exactly by S = S(s), T = t/p(s), with p = S' > 0 and
S(0) = 0. Under such a change c = rho_t(s,0) becomes c/p + p'/p^2, and the difference of the two sides of (74.5) is
multiplied by p. Thus c can be removed by a reparametrization of C, and (74.5) is invariant. No transition law is
asserted for the arbitrary extensions of these charts to the plus side.

Let gamma(s) = R(s,0) and d1 = |gamma'|^2 - h gamma_2'/4. Where d1 != 0, the area equation and (74.3) at t = 0 determine

  v(s,0) = (h/4 - gamma_2', gamma_1')/d1, rho(s,0) = h v_2/(4A).  (74.6)

Put ell = v_s.v/A, m = v_s.n/A and d2 = 40 + h v_1 + (9/4) h^2 v_2^2. Where d2 != 0, (74.5) and the identity R_st = R_ts
at t = 0 determine

  b = 9 h v_2 A m/d2, a = A(rho(s,0) b - m), c = ell - rho(s,0) a + b/A.  (74.7)

If gamma is regular and theta - M is flat at 0, then d1 -> |gamma'(0)|^2 > 0 and d2 -> 40, and for every such pair
(gamma, theta), on a sufficiently short interval -delta < s <= 0, the jets (74.6)-(74.7) are the first two t-derivatives
at t = 0 of an area chart R in which, with W(R) = 4t R_t, Theta = theta(s) and Omega = h K, the curl residual rc
W - Omega vanishes to second order on t = 0. This is a statement about finite jets; it is not a local existence
statement. Condition (74.5) does not follow from the area equation and the value of (74.3) at t = 0: the chart
R(s,t) = (s + d t^2/2, t), d != 0, with constant theta, satisfies both and has a = 0, b = d.

In every (E') configuration the separator Gamma has zero curvature at Q.

(c) (Linear Cauchy instability in s.) At a point with t != 0 the principal part of the system formed by det DR = 1 and
(74.2) = h K, for perturbations R + r exp(lambda s + i eta t) with eta real and nonzero, has nontrivial solutions
exactly for

  lambda = i rho eta + |eta|/A and lambda = i rho eta - |eta|/A.  (74.8)

At the exact solution R0(s,t) = (s,t), theta = M (so W = (0,4y) and Omega = 0), the linearized system for R = R0 + (xi1,
xi2), with theta unperturbed, is

  xi1_s + xi2_t = 0, xi1_t + xi2_s + t(xi1_tt - xi2_st) = 0.        (74.9)

With Si(z) = int_0^z sin(r)/r dr, k > 0 and e in {1,-1}, the functions

  xi1 = (e/4) exp(e k s) Si(k t), xi2 = -(1/4) exp(e k s) [cos(k t) + k t Si(k t)]   (74.10)

are real analytic, also at t = 0, and solve (74.9). Fix L > 0. After multiplication by exp(-k L), every C^j norm of
(xi1, xi2) on {s = 0, |t| <= 1} tends to zero as k -> infinity, while xi2(e L, 0) exp(-k L) = -1/4 for every k. The full
perturbation is not uniquely determined by its trace: the system has gauge solutions (xi1,xi2) = (a(s),-a'(s)t).
Nevertheless xi2(s,0) is uniquely determined by the trace of (xi1,xi2) on s = 0, among smooth solutions on a connected
rectangle meeting t = 0. On traces admitting such solutions to distance L, evaluation at (e L,0) is therefore a
well-defined map, and the displayed sequence proves that it is not continuous at zero in any C^j norm, or in the
C^infinity topology. Consequently no choice of full solutions can be continuous from these data to that value, in either
direction of s (e = -1 is the direction from Gamma into N-).

(d) (Matching with a potential side.) Let Gamma' be a smooth embedded curve dividing a disc into two sides. Let W- be
smooth up to Gamma' on the minus side with div W- = 4 and rc W- flat along Gamma', and put
f- = (W-_1 - 2x) - i(W-_2 - 2y). Let f+ be holomorphic on the plus side and smooth up to Gamma'. If f+ = f- on Gamma',
all derivatives of f+ and f- agree on Gamma', and the field equal to W- on the minus side and to 2X + (Re f+, -Im f+) on
the plus side is smooth, with divergence 4. There is at most one such f+ on a connected plus side. In a chart of (a),
with z(t) = R_1(0,t) + i R_2(0,t), the required boundary values are

  f+(z(t)) = 4t conj(z'(t)) - 2 conj(z(t)).                      (74.11)

(e) (Tests.) (i) For the field (72.8) of Theorem 72(e) and every trace theta with theta - M flat at 0, for instance the
strictly increasing trace theta(s) = M - exp(-1/s^2) (s < 0), theta(0) = M, the triple (W, Theta_W, Omega_W) of (72.6)
solves (72.1) on a neighbourhood of every point of C minus {Q} and on N+, and rc W - Omega_W is flat along Gamma. Hence
every identity obtained by differentiating (72.1) any number of times and restricting to C, including (74.5), holds, and
so does flatness of the residual along Gamma; but by Theorem 72(e) no temperature completes W to an (E') configuration.
(ii) Suppose a chart of (a) satisfies (74.3) on a connected rectangle H- and every fibre is affine,
R(s,t) = gamma(s) + t v(s). Then after a change as in (b) there are a constant unit vector e, n_e = (e_2,-e_1) and a
constant vector X0 with

  R(S,T) = X0 + S n_e + (T + e_2 theta(S)/4) e,                   (74.12)

and conversely (74.12) gives exact solutions of (72.1), with Theta = theta(S), W(R) = 4T e and Omega = e_2 theta'(S).
These are the solutions (72.5) rotated, with the buoyancy factor e_2. No (E') configuration has such a chart.

(f) (The remaining assertion.) Consider the assertion L: there are delta, eps > 0, a smooth embedding R of a
neighbourhood of H- and a smooth trace theta on s <= 0 with theta - M flat at 0, such that (1) det DR = 1 and (74.3)
hold on H-; (2) on the side of Gamma0 = R({s = 0}) opposite to R(H-), locally near Q = R(0,0), the function in (74.11)
is the boundary value of a holomorphic function f+ smooth up to Gamma0; (3) the field 2X + (Re f+, -Im f+) has no zero
on that side, and the glued field of (d) has a C^2 invariant centre curve through Q containing R({t = 0, s <= 0}) whose
other branch is zero-free and outgoing. Then L holds if and only if an (E') configuration exists locally; L together
with theta' != 0 on (-delta,0) holds if and only if an (E) configuration exists locally.

Scope. This theorem neither constructs nor excludes an (E') or (E) configuration, and it constructs or excludes no
A2-broad profile. Part (b) states finite-jet facts and one necessary condition; the realization of the jets is not a
solution. Part (c) is a statement about the principal part and about the linearization at one exact solution; it is not
a nonlinear nonexistence theorem, and it does not exclude solutions for specially chosen data. Part (d) shows that, once
the minus side is a solution with curl flat on Gamma, smooth matching to a potential side reduces to equality of
boundary values; it does not show that the boundary values (74.11) of any minus-side solution extend holomorphically.
Part (e)(i) shows that the identities on C at every order, flatness along Gamma, the potential side and the
noncontinuation of Theorem 51(b) do not suffice to ensure that a given geometric field admits an (E') completion, even
with a strictly monotone trace; the obstruction used for (72.8) is Theorem 72(d)(ii). Its example and exclusion are
those of Theorem 72(e); the all-orders tests on C and the strictly monotone trace are the additions here. Part (f)
restates the reduction of Theorem 72(c) in area coordinates with explicit potential matching; the existence part of L is
unproved. The transport and flatness assertions in (a) are also from Theorem 72(c), after relabelling. All proofs are
informal; no formal verification is claimed.

Proof.

(a) The proof of Theorem 72(c) constructs, on a full chart containing closure(N-), smooth coordinates (sigma,t) with
physical map R(sigma,t), sigma < 0 on N-, sigma = 0 on Gamma, t = 0 on C, and W = 4t d_t on the closed negative half,
that is W(R) = 4t R_t. Replacing t by -t if necessary, J = det DR > 0. For a field W = 4t d_t in coordinates with area
density J, the physical divergence is J^(-1) d_t(4t J) = 4 + 4t J_t/J. Since div W = 4, J_t = 0 for t != 0, and by
continuity also at t = 0 on the closed negative half: J = J(sigma,0) there. Extend the label change by
s = S1^(-1)(sigma) = int_0^sigma J(r,0) dr on the full chart. In the coordinates (s,t) the determinant is one on the
closed negative half, and W = 4t d_t is unchanged there. Restricting to a small closed half-rectangle and shrinking N
gives the stated chart. The trace statements follow because S1 is a diffeomorphism fixing 0.

Since det(u,v) = 1, the inverse of DR has rows grad s = (v_2,-v_1) = n and grad t = (-u_2,u_1). As det(n,v) = A and
v.n = 0, u = rho v + n/A. The temperature of (72.6) is Theta_W o R = theta(s), so (Theta_W)_x o R = h s_x = h v_2. In
the proof of Theorem 72(c), Omega_W(R(sigma,t)) = theta'(sigma) (1/4) int_0^1 q^(-3/4) sigma_x(R(sigma,q t)) dq; in the
new label this is h K, since theta_old'(sigma) sigma_x = h s_x.

For (74.2), let lambda = W_1 dx + W_2 dy. With the reverse-curl convention, d lambda = -(rc W) dx ^ dy, and
dx ^ dy = ds ^ dt. The pull-back is R^*lambda = 4t (v.u) ds + 4t A dt. Its exterior derivative is [d_s(4t A) - d_t(4t
v.u)] ds ^ dt. Using u_t = v_s and A_s = 2 v.v_s,

  rc W o R = d_t(4t v.u) - d_s(4t A) = 4 v.u + 4t(v_t.u - v.u_t).

Differentiate u = rho v + n/A in t. Since v.n = 0 and n_t = (v_2t,-v_1t), v.n_t = -v_t.n = -B. Then v.u_t = rho_t
A + rho v.v_t - B/A and v_t.u = rho v.v_t + B/A, so v_t.u - v.u_t = 2B/A - A rho_t. With v.u = rho A this gives (74.2).
Equation (72.7) on R(H-) is (74.2) = h K, which is (74.3) after division by 4A. On N+ the statement is immediate from
(72.6).

(b) Differentiating (74.3) gives -t rho_tt = F_t, so F_t(s,0) = 0 is necessary. If it holds, Taylor's formula with
integral remainder gives F(s,t) - F(s,0) = t^2 H(s,t) with H smooth, so (74.4) is smooth; with G(t) = int_0^t
[F(s,r) - F(s,0)]/r^2 dr, rho_t = c - G - [F(s,t) - F(s,0)]/t, and rho - t rho_t = F. The difference of two smooth
solutions solves rho - t rho_t = 0, so it equals c_+(s) t on t > 0 and c_-(s) t on t < 0; smoothness at t = 0 forces
c_+ = c_-.

At t = 0: K = v_2 and K_t = (1/4) int_0^1 q^(1/4) dq v_2t = v_2t/5; A_t = 2 v.v_t = 2aA; B = bA; and v_2t = a v_2 - b
v_1. Hence

  F_t(s,0) = h[(a v_2 - b v_1)/(20A) - a v_2/(2A)] - 2b/A = -[9 h v_2 a + (40 + h v_1) b]/(20A).

An (E') configuration solves (74.3) by (a) and Theorem 72(c), so (74.5) holds.

For the gauge: on the common closed minus side a change of charts preserving the form 4t d_t satisfies t S_t = 0 and t
T_t = T; smoothness across t = 0 gives S = S(s) and T = d(s) t, and equality of the determinants gives S' d = 1.
Preserving the minus side and Q gives p = S' > 0 and S(0) = 0. With R_new(S,T) = R(s, pT): (R_new)_T = p v and
(R_new)_S = u/p + (p'T/p) v. Hence rho_new = rho/p^2 + (p'/p^2) T, so c_new = c/p + p'/p^2. Also A_new = p^2 A,
h_new = h/p, K_new = p K and B_new = p^3 B, so F_new = F/p^2 and (F_new)_T = F_t/p at T = 0; the bracket in F_t is
therefore multiplied by p. Solving p' = -c p removes c.

At t = 0, u = gamma'; the area equation is gamma_1' v_2 - gamma_2' v_1 = 1, and (74.3) at t = 0 reads rho(s,0) = h
v_2/(4A), that is gamma_1' v_1 + (gamma_2' - h/4) v_2 = 0. Solving gives (74.6). Differentiate u = rho v + n/A in t at
t = 0, using v_t = a v + b n, n_t = a n - b v and A_t = 2aA:

  u_t = (c + rho a - b/A) v + (rho b - a/A) n.

Since u_t = v_s, comparing components with v_s = ell v + m n gives a = A(rho b - m) and c = ell - rho a + b/A at t = 0.
Substituting a into (74.5) and using A rho(s,0) = h v_2/4 gives d2 b = 9 h v_2 A m. This proves (74.7). If theta - M is
flat, h(s) -> 0, so d1 -> |gamma'(0)|^2 and d2 -> 40.

Realization of the jets: put w = a v + b n with v, a, b from (74.6)-(74.7) and P(s,r) = gamma(s) + r v(s) + (r^2/2)
w(s). At r = 0 its Jacobian is det(gamma',v) = 1, and its r-derivative is det(v_s,v) + det(gamma',w) = m A + a - rho b
A = 0. So J_P = 1 + O(r^2), smoothly in s. The substitution t = int_0^r J_P(s,q) dq, so that r = t + O(t^3), gives an
area chart R(s,t) = P(s,r(s,t)) with R(s,0) = gamma, R_t(s,0) = v and R_tt(s,0) = w. For any area chart the residual rc
W - h K equals 4A(rho - t rho_t - F) by (74.2). Its value at t = 0 vanishes by (74.6), and its t-derivative at t = 0
equals 4A(-t rho_tt - F_t) = -4A F_t(s,0), which vanishes because a, b satisfy (74.5). Hence the residual is O(t^2).

For the counterexample R = (s + d t^2/2, t): det DR = 1, gamma(s) = (s,0), v(s,0) = (0,1), u = (1,0) at t = 0, so
rho(s,0) = 0 = F(s,0) for constant theta; v_t = (d,0) = d n at t = 0, so a = 0 and b = d, and (74.5) would require 40
d = 0. (Directly, W = (4d y^2, 4y), rc W = 8d y, while the transported vorticity is 0.)

Zero curvature of Gamma at Q. In an (E') configuration Omega and its first derivatives vanish at Q, so DW(Q) is
symmetric with eigenvalues 0 and 4. Take positively oriented orthonormal coordinates centred at Q, with the tangent of C
along the x-axis, the eigenvalue-4 direction along the y-axis, and C contained in a curve y = kappa x^2/2 + O(|x|^3),
x <= 0. For this argument use the transformed vector components of W and redefine f = (W_1 - 2x) - i(W_2 - 2y) in these
coordinates. The divergence and reverse-curl identity is unchanged; no transformation of the buoyancy equation is used.
Since d_zbar f = (i/2) Omega = O(|z|^2) and f(0) = 0, f = -2z + f2 z^2 + O(|z|^3). Thus W_1 = Re(f2 z^2) + O(|z|^3) and
W_2 = 4y - Im(f2 z^2) + O(|z|^3). Vanishing on C at order x^2 gives Re f2 = 0 and Im f2 = 2 kappa. If Gamma is
x = lambda y^2/2 + O(|y|^3), then on Gamma W_1 = Re(2i kappa (-y^2)) + O(|y|^3) = O(|y|^3), while invariance gives
W_1 = x'(y) W_2 = 4 lambda y^2 + O(|y|^3). Hence lambda = 0.

(c) Freeze u and v at a point with t != 0. The terms of highest order in the area equation linearize to det(r_s,
v) + det(u, r_t), and those of (74.2) to 4t(r_tt.u - v.r_st); the source h K involves at most one t-derivative of R
inside an integral and contributes no principal term. For r exp(lambda s + i eta t) with a constant complex vector r and
w = lambda v - i eta u, these become det(r, w) = 0 and -4 i t eta (w.r) = 0, with the bilinear dot product. As u, v are
independent, w != 0; det(r,w) = 0 makes r a multiple of w, so a nontrivial solution exists exactly when w.w = 0:

  A lambda^2 - 2 i eta (u.v) lambda - eta^2 |u|^2 = 0.

Since u.v = rho A and A|u|^2 - (u.v)^2 = det(u,v)^2 = 1, the roots are (74.8).

At R0 = (s,t), theta = M: u = (1,0), v = (0,1), the area equation det DR = 1 and the curl equation 4
v.u + 4t(v_t.u - v.u_t) = 0 hold. Their linearizations are xi1_s + xi2_t = 0 and
4(xi1_t + xi2_s) + 4t(xi1_tt - xi2_st) = 0, which is (74.9). For (74.10), with E = exp(e k s): xi1_s = (k/4) E Si(kt)
and xi2_t = -(1/4) E [-k sin(kt) + k Si(kt) + k sin(kt)] = -(k/4) E Si(kt), so the first equation holds. Next
xi1_t = (e/4) E sin(kt)/t, xi1_tt = (e/4) E [k cos(kt)/t - sin(kt)/t^2], xi2_s = -(e k/4) E [cos(kt) + kt Si(kt)] and
xi2_st = -(e k^2/4) E Si(kt). Then

  xi1_t + xi2_s + t xi1_tt - t xi2_st
    = (e/4) E [sin(kt)/t - k cos(kt) - k^2 t Si(kt) + k cos(kt) - sin(kt)/t + k^2 t Si(kt)] = 0

for t != 0, and at t = 0 by continuity. Si is entire, so the functions are real analytic. (Equivalently, the
perturbation of W at fixed physical points, 4(t xi1_t, t xi2_t - xi2) = (e E sin(kt), E cos(kt)), is the gradient of E
sin(kt)/k, a harmonic function.) Since Si(kt) = int_0^1 sin(k t q)/q dq, the j-th t-derivative of Si(kt) is bounded on
|t| <= 1 by k^j for j >= 1 and Si is bounded; so every C^j norm of the data on s = 0 is at most a polynomial in k, and
multiplication by exp(-kL) sends it to zero. At s = e L, t = 0, exp(-kL) xi2 = -(1/4) exp(-kL) exp(kL) = -1/4.

To justify the evaluation-map assertion, for any solution of (74.9) put

  P = 4t xi1_t, Q1 = 4(t xi2_t - xi2).

The two equations give P_s + (Q1)_t = 0 and P_t - (Q1)_s = 0, so P - i Q1 is holomorphic in s + i t. The trace of
(xi1,xi2) on s = 0 determines the trace of P - i Q1 by tangential differentiation. Two solutions with the same trace
therefore have identical P - i Q1: for an interior fibre this is the holomorphic identity theorem; for a boundary fibre,
their holomorphic difference with zero boundary values extends by zero across the straight boundary, by the matching
argument of (d), and the same identity theorem applies. Connectedness propagates equality. Their difference then
satisfies t xi1_t = 0 and t xi2_t - xi2 = 0. Smoothness across t = 0 and the area equation give precisely
(xi1,xi2) = (a(s),-a'(s)t); zero trace imposes a(0) = a'(0) = 0. In particular every such difference has xi2(s,0) = 0.
This proves uniqueness of the evaluated value and the claimed discontinuity. The analytic coefficients alone do not
supply uniqueness of the full perturbation. If one also fixes the linearized gauge rho_t(s,0) = 0, a'' = 0 removes the
zero-trace ambiguity; the modes (74.10) already satisfy this gauge.

(d) For a field with divergence 4, d_zbar f = (1/2)[(d_x U_1 + d_y U_2) + i(d_y U_1 - d_x U_2)] = (i/2) rc W, where
U = W - 2X. Choose smooth coordinates (s,t) near Gamma' with Gamma' = {s = 0}; then d_zbar = a(s,t) d_s + b(s,t) d_t
with a = (s_x + i s_y)/2 != 0. The boundary values of f+ and f-, hence all their t-derivatives, agree on s = 0. On the
minus side d_zbar f- is flat on s = 0, and on the plus side d_zbar f+ = 0. Solving the equation for d_s f gives d_s
f = a^(-1)(d_zbar f - b d_t f), so the first normal derivatives agree on s = 0; differentiating this relation and
inducting on the number of normal derivatives shows that all mixed derivatives agree. Functions smooth up to s = 0 from
both sides with equal one-sided derivatives of every order glue to a smooth function. The glued field has divergence 4
on both sides and therefore everywhere. For uniqueness, the difference of two such f+ extended by 0 to the minus side is
smooth by the same argument and satisfies d_zbar = 0 on the disc, so it is holomorphic and vanishes on an open set,
hence on the connected plus side. On Gamma in a chart of (a), W(R(0,t)) = 4t R_t(0,t), that is W_1 + i W_2 = 4t z'(t),
and f = (W_1 - i W_2) - 2 conj(z); this is (74.11).

(e)(i) The cutoff in (72.8) vanishes near every point (0,y0) with y0 < 0, so there W = (4x,0), the orbits are the
horizontal lines with backward limit (0,y), and the label sigma is a function of y alone. Hence
Theta_W = theta(sigma(y)) there, (Theta_W)_x = 0, and the bounded transported vorticity is Omega_W = 0, while rc W = 0.
So (72.1) holds on a neighbourhood of every point of C minus {Q}. On N+, W is irrotational by Theorem 72(e), and
Theta_W = M and Omega_W = 0 by (72.6), so (72.1) holds there. By Theorem 72(c) Omega_W is flat along Gamma, and by
Theorem 72(e) rc W = -Lap q is flat along Gamma; so their difference is flat along Gamma, in particular at Q. Every
derivative of every equation of (72.1) therefore vanishes at every point of C minus {Q}, and at Q by flatness. The trace
M - exp(-1/s^2) has derivative -2 s^(-3) exp(-1/s^2) > 0 for s < 0 and is flat relative to M at 0. Theorem 72(e) proves
that no smooth temperature and vorticity complete W.

(e)(ii) If R = gamma + t v, the area equation reads det(gamma',v) + t det(v',v) = 1, so det(gamma',v) = 1 and v' is
parallel to v; on a connected interval v = r1(s) e with e a constant unit vector and r1 > 0. Since R_tt = 0, B = 0,
K = v_2 and rho - t rho_t = gamma'.v/A, so (74.3) reads 4 gamma'.v = h v_2, that is gamma'.e = h e_2/4; and det(gamma',
e) = gamma'.n_e = 1/r1. The change S' = 1/r1, T = r1 t of (b) gives R = gamma(s) + T e with gamma_S = n_e + (theta_S
e_2/4) e, which integrates to (74.12). Conversely R_S = n_e + (theta_S e_2/4) e and R_T = e have det = det(n_e, e) = 1;
grad S = n_e, so Theta_x = e_2 theta'(S); rho = e_2 theta'(S)/4 does not depend on T and B = 0, so by (74.2) rc W = e_2
theta'(S) = Omega, and W.grad Omega = 4T d_T Omega = 0, so the vorticity equation W.grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x holds;
the temperature equation holds since Theta depends on S alone. With e = (0,1), (74.12) is x = S + X0_1,
y = T + theta(S)/4 + X0_2, the form (72.5). In such a chart Gamma0 is the straight segment T -> X0 + T e + (e_2
theta(0)/4) e and W(R(0,T)) = 4T e. On a straight line z = z0 + e T (e also read as a complex number of modulus one),
T = (z - z0)/e and conj(z) = conj(z0) + conj(e) (z - z0)/e, so the boundary values (74.11) are those of a polynomial of
degree one in z. By the uniqueness in (d), the potential side of an (E') configuration would carry this polynomial,
which continues holomorphically to a disc about Q; this contradicts Theorem 51(b) in the local form proved in
Theorem 72(d).

(f) Suppose L holds. On R(H-) put W(R) = 4t R_t, Theta(R) = theta(s), Omega(R) = h K. By (a) (whose computation uses
only det DR = 1 and W(R) = 4t R_t), (74.3) gives div W = 4 and rc W = Omega there, the temperature equation holds since
W.grad s = 0, and the vorticity equation 4t omega_t + omega = h v_2 holds for omega = h K by differentiation under the
integral (as in the proof of Theorem 72(a)), with Theta_x o R = h v_2. Since theta - M and h are flat at 0 and K is
smooth up to s = 0, Theta - M and Omega are flat along Gamma0. On the plus side put Theta = M, Omega = 0 and
W = 2X + (Re f+, -Im f+); all four equations hold there. By (d) the glued W is smooth with divergence 4; Theta and Omega
glue smoothly by flatness, and the equations hold across Gamma0 by continuity. On R(H-), W = 0 exactly on t = 0 because
R_t != 0; by (3) the zero set near Q is R({t = 0, s <= 0}). Differentiating W(R) = 4t R_t at (0,0) gives DW(Q)
DR(0,0) = DR(0,0) diag(0,4). Thus DW(Q) is conjugate by DR(Q) to diag(0,4). With (3), W is a geometric field at Q and
the triple is an (E') configuration on a small disc. If moreover theta' != 0 on (-delta,0), then grad Theta = theta'
(n o R^(-1)) != 0 on the punctured zero arc and the trace is strictly monotone, which gives (E). Conversely, for an (E')
configuration, (a) gives a chart with (1) by Theorem 72(c); f is holomorphic on N+ (Omega = 0 there) and smooth up to
Gamma, and its boundary values are (74.11) by (d), which gives (2); (3) is part of the definition of a geometric field.
For (E), Theorem 72(c) gives theta' != 0 on a terminal interval. QED.

Remark 74.1 (the reach of L, integral matching, and unique continuation).
Use the notation of Theorems 16, 53, 56, 72 and 74.

(i) (Reach.) Let (2,Theta,Omega,U) be an A2-broad profile such that no component of Z = {W = 0}
is wholly contained in Q1, and put M = Theta(Q+). The fields are smooth, and div W = 4.
By Theorems 16 and 53(a), C is a compact smooth embedded arc ending at Q+, DW(Q+) has
eigenvalues 0 and 4, and Theta-M and Omega vanish to infinite order at Q+.
By Theorem 53(c), zeros outside C cannot accumulate at Q+: such accumulation would produce
entire components of Z wholly contained in Q1. By Theorem 53(d), also 56(a), Q+ is outgoing:
a local C^2 invariant centre curve has a zero-free opposite branch whose forward flow points
away from Q+. Thus, on a sufficiently small disc D about Q+, the entire zero set of W is a
terminal subarc of C and W is a geometric field in the sense of Theorem 72(c). Equation (53.1)
and the stated flatness make the restricted profile an (E') configuration, for its actual
value M, including M = 0.

By Theorem 74(f), L holds. Consequently, if L is false, every A2-broad profile at beta = 2
has a component of Z wholly contained in Q1. Theorems 53 and 56 do not exclude this alternative.
Hypothesis (S) of Theorem 48 implies the component exclusion: any component wholly in Q1
would meet C and hence equal C, whereas C contains the x-axis point P. Under (S), this gives
the reduction stated in Theorem 72(d).

If no (E) configuration exists, then in every A2-broad beta = 2 profile with no component
of Z wholly in Q1, the ambient critical points of Theta on C minus {Q+} accumulate at Q+.
Otherwise a terminal punctured subarc would be regular;
Theorem 53(a) makes its trace strictly monotone, giving an (E) configuration by Theorem 72(c).

(ii) (One integral identity.) All equivalences in this part are local: the half-rectangle
and the discs may be shrunk. Holomorphic functions on discs about q are compared as germs.
Identify X with z = x+i y and put

  r = R_1+i R_2, gamma(s) = r(s,0), q = r(0,0), h = theta'.

Let R be a smooth embedding of a neighbourhood of
H- = {-delta < s <= 0, |t| < eps}, with det DR = 1 on H-. Let theta be a smooth real trace
on s <= 0 with theta-M flat at 0. Define A, B, rho, K and F by (74.1), and put
Gamma0 = R({s = 0}) and C0 = R({t = 0, s <= 0}) locally.
Choose a disc D1 about q inside the extended chart, small enough that Gamma0 divides it into
two connected sides and its minus side lies in R(H-). Set

  Omega_* = (hK) o R^(-1) on the minus side, and Omega_* = 0 on the plus side.

Since h is flat at 0 and K is smooth, Omega_* is smooth on D1 and flat along Gamma0.
Choose a real smooth cutoff chi compactly supported in D1 and equal to one on a smaller
disc D2 about q. Extend chi Omega_* by zero outside D1 and, with dA = dx dy, put

  G(z) = (i/(2 pi)) int_{R^2} chi(w) Omega_*(w)/(z-w) dA(w).                     (74.13)

The plane is identified with the complex plane. The kernel is locally integrable,
and d_zbar(1/(pi z)) = delta_0 for d_zbar = (d_x+i d_y)/2. Hence G is smooth and
d_zbar G = (i/2) chi Omega_*.

Conditions (1) and (2) of L hold locally if and only if there is a function H holomorphic
on a full disc about q such that

  4t conj(r_t(s,t))-2 conj(r(s,t)) = G(r(s,t))+H(r(s,t))                         (74.14)

on a sufficiently small H-. For a given holomorphic H, (74.14) is equivalent to (74.3)
together with

  H(gamma(s)) = -2 conj(gamma(s))-G(gamma(s))

on a terminal interval -delta' < s < 0.

Indeed, define W_R(R(s,t)) = 4t R_t(s,t) and
f_R(R(s,t)) = 4t conj(r_t(s,t))-2 conj(r(s,t)). The determinant condition gives div W_R = 4.
For any field with divergence four and f = (W_1-2x)-i(W_2-2y),

  d_zbar f = (i/2) rc W.

Moreover, (74.1)-(74.2) give

  (rc W_R-Omega_*) o R = 4A(rho-t rho_t-F).

Shrink H- so that R(H-) is contained in D2, where chi = 1.
Thus f_R-G is holomorphic on the open minus side near q exactly when (74.3) holds.
The terminal punctured arc C0 minus {q} lies in that open side: s < 0 and t = 0 are
interior parameter values. Restrict to a smaller connected minus-side chart inside the
domains of G and H. The identity theorem applies to f_R-G-H on this connected domain;
the trace on C0 therefore implies (74.14), also on s = 0 by continuity.

If (74.14) holds, f+ = G+H is holomorphic on the plus side, smooth up to Gamma0, and has
the boundary values (74.11). Conversely, under (1) and (2), Theorem 74(d) glues the two
complex velocities smoothly, with d_zbar f = (i/2) Omega_* on a full smaller disc.
Then H = f-G is holomorphic there. The trace determines H uniquely as a germ. Changing
chi changes G by a holomorphic germ J and changes H by -J.

The possible H can be determined from the minus-side data. For s <= 0 define

  b(s) = -2 conj(gamma(s))-G(gamma(s)),
  D_gamma = (1/gamma'(s)) d/ds,
  a_j = (D_gamma^j b)(0)/j!,

where gamma'(s) = r_s(s,0) is a nonzero complex number and derivatives at 0 are one-sided.
A holomorphic germ H with H(gamma(s)) = b(s) on a terminal interval exists if and only if,
for some C_*, r0 > 0,

  |a_j| <= C_* r0^(-j) for all j >= 0,
  b(s) = sum_{j >= 0} a_j (gamma(s)-q)^j on a terminal interval.

The interval is chosen inside the convergence disc. In that case

  H(z) = sum_{j >= 0} a_j (z-q)^j.

Necessity follows from D_gamma^j(H o gamma) = H^(j) o gamma and Cauchy estimates;
the convergent series and its stated trace give sufficiency. A bound on coefficients
alone is insufficient for general smooth traces: for gamma(s) = s,
b(s) = exp(-1/s^2) for s < 0 and b(0) = 0, every a_j is zero but b is not zero.
This is a test of the interpolation criterion, not a proposed solution of (74.3).

Consequently L is equivalent to the following assertion. There are R and theta as above
such that sum_{j >= 0} a_j (z-q)^j has positive radius of convergence, (74.14) holds on a
smaller H- with H equal to that series, and the following geometric condition holds.
For f+ = G+H, the field 2X+(Re f+,-Im f+) has no zero on the open plus side near q.
The glued field has a C^2 invariant centre curve through q containing
R({t = 0, s <= 0}) locally, whose opposite branch is zero-free and outgoing.
This is condition (3) of L in full. Formula (74.14) already supplies the interpolation
equality. R and theta are the only independent field and trace unknowns; the discs and
cutoff are auxiliary choices.

(iii) (Unique continuation.) Flat agreement with a potential solution along a curve does
not force a smooth solution of (72.1) to be potential on the other side, even with the
source form hK in (74.3). Let

  a(x) = exp(-1/x^2) for x < 0, and a(x) = 0 for x >= 0.

Then W = (0,4y-a(x)), Theta = M+a(x), Omega = a'(x) solve (72.1), since

  div W = 4, rc W = a' = Omega,
  W.grad Theta = 0, W.grad Omega+Omega = a' = Theta_x.

They agree with the potential solution ((0,4y),M,0) on x >= 0 and to every order along
x = 0, but Omega != 0 for every x < 0. In (74.12), take e = (0,1),
X0 = (0,-M/4) and theta(s) = M+a(s). The resulting chart and coefficients are

  R(s,t) = (s,t+a(s)/4), det DR = 1, W(R) = 4t R_t,
  A = K = 1, B = 0, hK = a', rho = F = a'/4.

Their zero set is the full curve y = a(x)/4 through q = (0,0); on the plus side it
contains y = 0. Thus they fail condition (3) and are not (E') configurations,
in agreement with the affine-fibre exclusion of Theorem 74(e)(ii).

The example refutes unique continuation based only on (72.1), flat agreement with a
potential solution, and the source form hK. It does not refute a uniqueness theorem
using additional hypotheses, such as the endpoint geometry required for (E').

The full first-order system (72.1) is not elliptic. For perturbations
(w_1,w_2,vartheta,omega), with rows ordered as divergence, reverse curl, temperature
and vorticity, its principal symbol, omitting the common Fourier factor i, is

  [ xi_x   xi_y       0          0     ]
  [ xi_y  -xi_x       0          0     ]
  [  0      0       W.xi        0     ]
  [  0      0      -xi_x       W.xi   ].

Its determinant is -|xi|^2 (W.xi)^2. At nonstationary points it vanishes on the
conormals of the orbits; at zeros of W it vanishes for every covector.
The rates (74.8) concern the frozen principal part of the reduced chart equations
at t != 0, viewed in the s direction. They do not supply a unique-continuation
theorem for the full coupled system.

None of (i)-(iii) proves or disproves L. No (E') or (E) configuration or A2-broad
profile is constructed, and no general nonexistence statement for these classes
is proved. All arguments are informal.

### Theorem 75 (beta > 2: finite exceptional rays and orbits when B is bounded, possibly empty; nonnegative vorticity)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2 satisfying (H1). Use the notation of
Theorem 73: Q1, alpha = pi/2, sigma = sgn(a0), h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h, a = 2 - h, theta = sigma Theta, z = sigma Omega,
B = {X in Q1 : z(X) < 0}, the angular functions F, g, P, D0, F1, g1, P1, D1, g2, K and C0 of (73.1) and the lines before
it, and, on a complete orbit in Q1, the point X(r) of radius r on its sufficiently late forward end. Assume that B is
bounded. The case B = {} is allowed.

(a) The set {phi in (0,alpha) : g(phi) = K(phi) = 0} is finite, and (73.2) holds at each of its points.

(b) Uniformly for phi in [0,alpha],

  z(r,phi) = r^(-h) g(phi) + r^(-2h) g1(phi) + r^(-3h) g2(phi) + O(r^(-4h)).        (75.1)

The set E of (73.3) equals {g = g1 = g2 = 0} and is finite. If phi is in (0,alpha) and not in E, there are c_phi > 0 and
R_phi > 0 such that z(r,phi) >= c_phi r^(-3h) for r >= R_phi. If phi is in E, z(r,phi) = O(r^(-4h)).

(c) Put E_orb = {phi in (0,alpha) : g = D0 = C0 = 0}. This set is contained in the finite set in (a), and (73.4) holds
for the orbit with limiting angle phi_*. If g(phi_*) = D0(phi_*) = 0, then C0(phi_*) >= 0 and

  r^(3h) z(X(r)) -> C0(phi_*)/2   as r -> infinity.                                  (75.2)

Thus all but finitely many complete orbits in Q1 satisfy z(X) >= c_orb |X|^(-3h) at every sufficiently late point, with
c_orb > 0 and a threshold depending on the orbit.

(d) (Nonnegative vorticity.) Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2 and
Omega >= 0 on Q1. Then (H1) holds, a0 > 0 and B = {}, so (a)-(c) apply with sigma = 1 and z = Omega. In particular, for
all but finitely many phi in (0,alpha) there are c_phi > 0 and R_phi > 0 with Omega(r,phi) >= c_phi r^(-3/beta) for
r >= R_phi, and all but finitely many complete orbits in Q1 satisfy Omega(X) >= c_orb |X|^(-3/beta) at every
sufficiently late point.

Scope. For bounded nonempty B, (a)-(c) are contained in Theorem 73(a)-(c); the new content is the case B = {}, which
covers the class Omega >= 0 on Q1 in (d). The last sentence of Theorem 73(b) and the sign-triple assertion of
Theorem 73(c) concern points of B and are not part of this theorem. No equality between E and E_orb, no uniform constant
or threshold, no boundedness of {Omega = 0} cap Q1 and no nonexistence statement is asserted. Part (d) neither
constructs nor excludes a profile with Omega >= 0 on Q1. The finite-exception argument does not extend to beta = 2:
there q = 0, C0 vanishes identically, and its flatness gives no information about K.

Proof. Theorem 8(ii) gives theta > 0 on Q1. Theorem 50(b),(c) gives F > 0 on (0,alpha), F'(0) > 0 and g'(alpha) < 0.
Theorem 64(a) uses only boundedness of B; it gives g >= 0 on [0,alpha], sigma P > 0 on (0,alpha), sigma P'(0) > 0 and
sigma P'(alpha) < 0. By the parities, F(0) = g(0) = P(0) = 0 and g(alpha) = P(alpha) = 0, and the angular functions are
smooth on the closed interval. As in the proof of Theorem 73, K extends smoothly to the closed interval. Theorem 66 is
not used.

(a) On (0,alpha), K = 2 cos(phi)[P' - a cot(2 phi) P]. At a common zero of g and K, G = sigma g = 0 gives P'' = -a^2 P,
and P' = a cot(2 phi) P. Differentiation and these substitutions give

  K' = 2 cos(phi) a P [2 - a sin(2 phi)^2 - a cos(2 phi)^2]/sin(2 phi)^2
     = 2 a (2 - a) cos(phi) P/sin(2 phi)^2,

which is nonzero because a > 0, 2 - a = h > 0, cos(phi) != 0 and sigma P > 0. As phi -> 0, K -> (2 - a) P'(0) = h
P'(0) != 0, so common zeros do not accumulate at 0. Since g(alpha) = 0 and g'(alpha) < 0, g > 0 on an interval
(alpha - eps, alpha). The common-zero set is therefore a closed subset of a compact subinterval of (0,alpha), and each
of its points is isolated because K' != 0 there. It is finite.

(b) Theorem 42(b),(c), multiplied by sigma, give

  z = r^(-h) g + r^(-2h) g1 + O_infty(r^(-3h)),
  theta = r^q F + r^(q-h) F1 + O_infty(r^(q-2h)),
  U = u_0 + u_1 + O_infty(r^(1-3h)),

with u_0 = r^(1-h)(-P' e_r + a P e_phi) and u_1 = r^(1-2h)(-P1' e_r + (2 - 2h) P1 e_phi); here sigma G1 = g1, sigma
f1 = F1, and P1 is the signed solution of -P1'' - (2 - 2h)^2 P1 = sigma g1 of Theorem 73. For an angular function m,
d_x(r^c m) = r^(c-1)[c cos(phi) m - sin(phi) m'] and u_0 . grad(r^c m) = r^(c-h)[-c P' m + a P m']. With these rules and
q - 1 = -2h, the right side of

  (beta r d_r + 1) z = theta_x - U . grad z

equals -g1 r^(-2h) - 2 g2 r^(-3h) + O(r^(-4h)): at order r^(-2h) the terms are D0 - h P' g - a P g' = -g1, and at order
r^(-3h) they are D1 - 2h P' g1 - a P g1' - h P1' g - (2 - 2h) P1 g' = -2 g2. Every other term is O(r^(-4h)); for example
d_x O_infty(r^(q-2h)) = O(r^(-4h)), u_0 . grad O_infty(r^(-3h)) = O(r^(-4h)) and u_1 . grad(r^(-2h) g1) = O(r^(-4h)).
Since (beta r d_r + 1) r^(-h) = 0, (beta r d_r + 1) r^(-2h) = -r^(-2h) and (beta r d_r + 1) r^(-3h) = -2 r^(-3h), the
remainder R = z - r^(-h) g - r^(-2h) g1 - r^(-3h) g2 satisfies R = O(r^(-3h)) and (beta r d_r + 1) R = O(r^(-4h)),
uniformly in angle. As beta h = 1, d_r(r^h R) = h r^(h-1) (beta r d_r + 1) R, and r^h R -> 0, so

  R(r,phi) = -h r^(-h) integral_r^infinity t^(h-1) (beta t d_t + 1) R(t,phi) dt = O(r^(-4h)).

This proves (75.1).

Boundedness of B gives z >= 0 on Q1 outside a disc. Fix phi in (0,alpha). By (75.1), g(phi) >= 0; if g(phi) > 0, r^(3h)
z(r,phi) -> +infinity. If g(phi) = 0, then g1(phi) >= 0, and g1(phi) > 0 again gives +infinity. If g(phi) = g1(phi) = 0,
then r^(3h) z(r,phi) -> g2(phi) >= 0. Hence E = {g = g1 = g2 = 0}, the lower bound holds off E, and
z(r,phi) = O(r^(-4h)) on E.

An interior zero of g >= 0 has g' = 0, so g1 = -D0 there. At a point with g = D0 = 0 (hence g' = g1 = 0),
differentiation of the definitions gives g1' = a P g'' - D0' and 2 g2 = a^2 P^2 g'' - a P D0' - D1. There also
P'' = -a^2 P and F' = q cot(phi) F. Expanding D0', F1' and D1 with these substitutions, the F'' terms cancel and

  a P D0' - D1 = q(a - h) cos(phi) P' F - a q(1 - h) P F cos(2 phi)/sin(phi) = C0,

since a - h = 2(1 - h). Hence, at every point with g = D0 = 0,

  2 g2 = a^2 P^2 g'' - 2 a P D0' + C0.                                               (75.3)

Near 0: put gamma = g'(0) >= 0. Since F(0) = P(0) = g(0) = 0, D0(0) = 0, D0'(0) = (q - 1) F'(0) = -2h F'(0) and
g1'(0) = (h + a) P'(0) gamma + 2h F'(0) = 2 P'(0) gamma + 2h F'(0). If gamma > 0, g > 0 on some (0,eps). If gamma = 0,
then g1(0) = 0 and g1'(0) = 2h F'(0) > 0, so g1 > 0 on some (0,eps). Near alpha, g > 0 on some (alpha - eps, alpha).
Thus E lies in a compact subinterval of (0,alpha).

Suppose E is infinite, and let phi_j in E be distinct with phi_j -> phi_*, an interior angle. Since g and D0 vanish at
every phi_j and are smooth, every derivative of each vanishes at phi_*: a first nonzero Taylor coefficient would make
the zero at phi_* isolated. Taylor's formula then gives g''(phi_j) = O(|phi_j - phi_*|^2) and
D0'(phi_j) = O(|phi_j - phi_*|^2). As g2(phi_j) = 0, (75.3) gives C0(phi_j) = O(|phi_j - phi_*|^2), so C0(phi_*) = 0 and
C0'(phi_*) = 0. Since q(1 - h) F > 0 near phi_*, K(phi_*) = K'(phi_*) = 0, while g(phi_*) = 0. This contradicts (a).
Hence E is finite.

(c) By Theorem 50(b), limiting angle is a bijection from the complete orbits in Q1 onto (0,alpha). On the late part of
an orbit with limiting angle phi_*, d_t r = beta r + U_r > 0 and r d_t phi = U_phi, so by Theorem 42(b),

  d phi/d r = (a/beta) P(phi) r^(-1-h) + O(r^(-1-2h)),
  phi(r) = phi_* - a P(phi_*) r^(-h) + O(r^(-2h)),

using beta h = 1 in the integration from r to infinity. Substitute this into (75.1); the uniform remainder permits it.
If g(phi_*) > 0, r^(h) z(X(r)) -> g(phi_*) > 0. If g(phi_*) = 0, then g'(phi_*) = 0 and the coefficient of r^(-2h) is
g1(phi_*) = -D0(phi_*); eventual nonnegativity of z forces D0(phi_*) <= 0, and if D0(phi_*) < 0 then r^(2h)
z(X(r)) -> -D0(phi_*) > 0. If g(phi_*) = D0(phi_*) = 0, Taylor expansion gives the coefficient of r^(-3h) as

  (a^2 P^2/2) g'' - a P g1' + g2 = C0/2

at phi_*, by g1' = a P g'' - D0' and (75.3), with remainder O(r^(-4h)). This is (75.2), and eventual nonnegativity of z
gives C0(phi_*) >= 0. Hence r^(3h) z(X(r)) has a positive lower limit (possibly +infinity) exactly when phi_* is not in
E_orb, and z(X(r)) = O(r^(-4h)) when phi_* is in E_orb. Since F > 0, E_orb is contained in {g = K = 0}, which is finite
by (a). The bijection of Theorem 50(b) turns this finite set of angles into a finite set of complete orbits.

(d) Theorem 57(a) gives a0 > 0, (H1) and Theta > 0 on Q1. Hence sigma = 1, z = Omega >= 0 on Q1 and B = {}, which is
bounded. Parts (a)-(c) apply, and 3h = 3/beta. QED.

### Theorem 76 (beta = 2: every A2-broad profile has the expansion of Theorem 68 to every finite order)

Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2, and let Psi be its odd-odd stream function, so
U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x) and -Lap Psi = Omega. Let H, G and P be the angular functions of Theorem 36, put z = log r and
mu_n = (3-n)/2, and use the notation O_infty of Theorem 36, with an additional factor (1+log r)^N_log allowed in each
derivative estimate as in Theorem 70. Then there are unique real constants c_m, m >= 1, with the following property. Let
H_n, G_n, P_n be the polynomial coefficients of (68.2), computed by (68.7) from H_0 = H, G_0 = G and P_0 = P, with the
polynomial Poisson inverses normalized as in (68.10) and with these constants c_m in (68.3). For every N >= 0 there is
an integer N_log_N >= 0 such that

  Theta - sum_(n=0)^N r^(-n/2)H_n(z,phi)
     = O_infty(r^(-(N+1)/2)(1+log r)^N_log_N),
  Omega - sum_(n=0)^N r^(-(n+1)/2)G_n(z,phi)
     = O_infty(r^(-(N+2)/2)(1+log r)^N_log_N),
  Psi - sum_(n=0)^N r^mu_n P_n(z,phi)
     = O_infty(r^((2-N)/2)(1+log r)^N_log_N).                   (76.1)

The constant c_m is given by (70.26), with Psi the stream function of the profile. In particular the truncations of
(76.1) are the truncations of Theorem 68(c), and their transport residuals satisfy (68.4).

Scope. The theorem gives an asymptotic expansion with a remainder at each finite order. It asserts neither convergence
of the series nor existence of an A2-broad profile. It determines the constants c_m from the profile, but supplies no
additional restrictions on their values or on the leading pair (H,G) beyond the preceding results. For a fixed profile,
put g_7 = (2/alpha)int_0^alpha G_7(phi)sin(2phi)dphi, where alpha = pi/2. Its first possible stream logarithm is
(g_7/4)r^(-2)log r sin(2phi); it is present exactly when g_7 != 0. If g_7 = 0, later resonances may still force
logarithms. Whether all actual profiles are log-free, or any actual profile has a nonzero logarithmic coefficient, is
not decided: the open dense nonvanishing of the first resonant forcing in Theorem 68(b) concerns unrestricted smooth
pairs satisfying (68.1), and is not transferred to the leading pairs of actual profiles. No all-order expansion of
actual profiles at beta > 2 is asserted; Theorem 42(c) gives the first correction there.

Proof. Theorem 36(b) gives the temperature and vorticity estimates for N = 0. Its bound U-u_0 = O_infty(1), integrated
along rays from a fixed circle, gives Psi-psi_0 = O(r); positive-order derivatives follow directly from the velocity
bound. Thus Psi-psi_0 = O_infty(r), completing N = 0. The case N = 1 is Theorem 45(f): by (68.11), its coefficients H_1,
G_1, P_1 are those of (68.7), and Psi-psi_0-psi_1 = O_infty(r^(1/2)). Hence (70.25) holds at n = 2, with N_log = 0.

The induction step in the proof of Theorem 70(b), from (70.25) to (70.25) with n replaced by n+1, uses the following
inputs on an exterior region r >= r_b: smoothness of Theta, Omega and Psi there, including across the axes; oddness of
Psi in x and y; the exterior equations W.grad Theta = 0, W.grad Omega+Omega = Theta_x and -Lap Psi = Omega, with
W = 2X+U and U = (-Psi_y,Psi_x); the differentiated leading bounds and the current bounds (70.25); the preceding
coefficient equations and angular reflection conditions of Theorem 68; the polynomial inverses (68.8)-(68.10), radial
terminal integration, and the modal estimate based on (70.24). It uses no property of the core, cutoff, fixed point or
uniqueness class of Theorem 70(a),(c), and no further weighted inverse. The actual profile has the required smoothness,
parities and equations. Theorems 36 and 45(f) give the initial bounds; Theorem 68 supplies the coefficient identities
and reflections at each stage. Bounds valid at infinity extend to r >= 1 by smoothness on the remaining compact annulus.
We recall the step. Given (70.25) at index n, substitution of the known sums into U.grad Theta and U.grad Omega leaves
errors of exponents -(n+1)/2 and -(n+2)/2, and the missing temperature derivative in the vorticity equation has exponent
-(n+2)/2. The coefficient equations at the next order are therefore exactly (68.7). After H_n and G_n are subtracted,
the terminal inverses of 2r d_r and 2r d_r+1 improve the temperature and vorticity errors by half a radial power; the
old error bounds exclude a homogeneous constant temperature term and a homogeneous r^(-1/2) vorticity term. After the
polynomial Poisson solution of (68.7) is subtracted from the stream sum remainder, the remainder is smooth and odd-odd
with old exponent mu_n and source exponent mu_n-5/2. At a resonance choose P_n^0 with zero resonant constant as in
(68.10), with all earlier constants already fixed. The modal estimate with mu_new = mu_n-1/2 gives the new stream error,
after extraction of one possible harmonic term c r^(-2m)sin(2m phi) exactly when n = 4m+3, mu_n = -2m. Its uniform
differentiated estimates apply because the source has O_infty bounds and the remainder has smooth reflected angular data
at r_b, hence rapidly decreasing Fourier coefficients there. The summation argument following (70.24) applies without
change. The extracted c is c_m and is included in P_n through (68.3). After completing this step the stream remainder is
O_infty(r^(-2m-1/2)(1+log r)^N_log). Its sin(2m phi) coefficient multiplied by r^(2m) is O(r^(-1/2)(1+log r)^N_log), so
(70.26) exists and equals c_m. Induction proves (76.1) for every N.

Uniqueness: suppose two choices of constants satisfy (76.1) for every N, and let m be the least index at which they
differ. All coefficients with index below n = 4m+3 agree, and P_n differs by (c_m-c_m')sin(2m phi). Subtracting the two
stream expansions at order N = n gives (c_m-c_m')r^(-2m)sin(2m phi) = O(r^(-2m-1/2)(1+log r)^N_log), so c_m = c_m'. The
final assertion is Theorem 68(c) applied to the pair (H,G), which satisfies (68.1) by Theorem 68(a). For the conditional
logarithm formula: H_0, G_0 and P_0 are independent of z, the inverses (68.8) and (68.9) map z-independent data to
z-independent coefficients, and the first resonance is n = 7, so all coefficients through index 6, and also G_7, are
independent of z. Then (68.10) with m = 1 and g = g_7 shows that the coefficient of sin(2phi) in P_7 is c_1+(g_7/4)z.
QED.

### Theorem 77 (beta > 2: bounded B and nondegenerate zeros exclude further x-axis zeros and restrict y-axis zeros)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2. Use the notation of Theorem 54: W = beta
X + U, kappa = beta - 2, b = beta + 2, L = 3 beta + 2, D = 2 beta + 1, sigma = sgn(a0), O = (0,0), Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0},
P = (x1,0), w(x) = W_1(x,0), v(y) = W_2(0,y), Phi_t the flow, Z = {W = 0} and B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0}. Let Ly
be the function of Theorem 44(a). Assume

  (BB) B is bounded; B = {} is allowed;
  (ND) det DW(S) != 0 at every zero S of W in the closed first quadrant.

(a) W has no zero on {(x,0) : x > x1}, and w > 0 on (x1, infinity).

(b) If v has a positive zero and y1 is the first one, then d0 = 1/|v'(y1)| is an odd positive integer and beta d0 is an
    even positive integer. Hence beta is rational and, in lowest terms, has even numerator and odd denominator.

(c) If beta is irrational, or beta = N/M in lowest terms with N odd, then v has no positive zero and (H1) holds. In this
    case the conclusions of Theorem 75(a)-(c) hold.

Scope. No absence of positive y-axis zeros or interior zeros is assumed. Hypothesis (ND) implies finiteness and
simplicity of the positive zeros of w, which is (A) of Theorem 60; its condition (B), the absence of positive zeros of
v, is not assumed. The absence of y-axis and interior zeros required in Theorem 71(a) is also not assumed here. For
exclusion of positive y-axis zeros, the added parameters beyond Theorem 30(c), under (BB) and (ND), are beta = N/M in
lowest terms with N odd and M even. Part (c) also uses part (a) and Theorem 52(b) to obtain (H1). Under (BB) and (ND),
failure of (H1) therefore requires beta = N/M in lowest terms with N even and M odd, together with a positive zero of v.
Interior zeros are not excluded in that case, and no such configuration is asserted to exist. Configurations involving
degenerate zeros, zeros with flat temperature or nonisolated zero sets are outside this argument. Boundedness of B
remains a hypothesis. No existence or nonexistence result for the full A2-broad class is asserted, and no endpoint
follows.

Proof. Step 1 (zeros and bounded orbits). As in the proof of Theorem 52(a), X.W(X) >= (beta/2)|X|^2 for |X| >= R0, so Z
lies in the closed disc of radius R0. By (ND) the zeros in the closed first quadrant are isolated, so they are finitely
many. Let S be one of them. By Theorem 43(a) the eigenvalues of DW(S) are real, and their sum is div W = 2 beta; by (ND)
neither is zero. Hence S is a hyperbolic source or a hyperbolic saddle with eigenvalues -a and c = 2 beta + a, a > 0. At
a saddle grad Theta(S) = 0, since otherwise S is a source by Theorem 43(a); then Omega(S) = 0 and DW(S) is symmetric.
The quadrant Q1 is invariant, because both axes are invariant. No orbit other than S converges forward to a hyperbolic
source S. By Theorem 63(a), every bounded nonstationary forward orbit gamma converges forward to a zero S+ and backward
to a zero S-, Theta = 0 on gamma, and Ly(S+) > Ly(S-) by (63.2). In particular S+ is a saddle.

Step 2 (no return to the boundary of Q1). Let gamma_0, ..., gamma_k (k >= 0) be bounded nonstationary orbits in Q1.
Suppose the backward limit S_0 of gamma_0 lies on the boundary of Q1, and that for 1 <= j <= k the forward limit of
gamma_(j-1) is the backward limit S_j of gamma_j and lies in Q1. Then the forward limit S_(k+1) of gamma_k lies in Q1.

Indeed, Ly(S_0) < Ly(S_1) < ... < Ly(S_(k+1)) by Step 1, so the S_j are distinct. Each set gamma_j cup {S_j, S_(j+1)} is
an embedded closed arc, distinct orbits are disjoint and no orbit contains a zero; so the union Gam of the gamma_j and
the S_j is an embedded arc from S_0 to S_(k+1). Suppose S_(k+1) lies on the boundary of Q1. Let Gam' be the arc in the
boundary of Q1 from S_(k+1) to S_0: the closed segment between them if they lie on one closed positive half-axis, and
otherwise the union of the two closed segments from O to S_0 and from O to S_(k+1). The axes are invariant and the
endpoints of these segments are zeros, so Gam' is invariant. Gam and Gam' meet only at S_0 and S_(k+1), because Gam
minus these two points lies in Q1. Thus Gam cup Gam' is an invariant Jordan curve. Let V be its bounded complementary
component. For X in V, the continuous path t -> Phi_t(X) never meets Gam cup Gam', since that curve is invariant. The
path starts in V, so it remains in the same complementary component for every real t. Hence Phi_t(V) is contained in V
for every real t. Applying the same inclusion to Phi_(-t) gives Phi_t(V) = V. Since det DPhi_t = e^(2 beta t), the area
satisfies |V| = |Phi_t(V)| = e^(2 beta t)|V| with 0 < |V| < infinity, which is impossible for t != 0. This is the
argument of Theorem 4.

Step 3 (transfer through an interior saddle). Let S in Q1 be a saddle with eigenvalues -a, c = 2 beta + a, and let gamma
in Q1 be a nonstationary orbit whose forward limit is S. Let Sigma(z) be a smooth section through Sigma(0) in gamma,
transverse to W, and X(t,z) = Phi_t Sigma(z). Suppose there are integers p >= m + 1 and m >= 1 such that, at every fixed
t,

  Theta(Sigma(z)) = theta z^p + O(z^(p+1)),   theta != 0,
  Omega(X(t,z)) = omega_m(t) z^m + O(z^(m+1)),   e^t omega_m(t) -> L_* != 0 as t -> infinity.                   (77.1)

(Theta(X(t,z)) = e^(kappa t) Theta(Sigma(z)) by (T).) Put

  i = (p c - kappa)/a,   ell = (m c + 1)/a.                                                                     (77.2)

We show: i and ell are positive integers with i - ell >= 2; on each of the two unstable branches of S, which lie in Q1,
(77.1) holds with (p, m) replaced by (i, ell), with nonzero theta and with e^t omega_ell(t) constant and nonzero; and if
gamma is contained in the closure of B, then so is one of these unstable branches.

The stable and unstable manifolds of S are C^infinity curves tangent to orthogonal eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix
DW(S). Choose C^infinity coordinates (s,u) on a neighbourhood N of S in Q1, with S = (0,0) and derivative at S an
orthogonal matrix, in which the stable manifold is {u = 0} and the unstable manifold is {s = 0}. Since these curves are
invariant, in N

  ds/dt = s A(s,u),   du/dt = u C(s,u),   A(0,0) = -a,   C(0,0) = c,                                            (77.3)

with A and C smooth. Let Lam be the operator -a s d_s + c u d_u on homogeneous polynomials; it multiplies s^r u^j by
cj - ar. In N, (T) and (V) read s A Theta_s + u C Theta_u = kappa Theta and s A Omega_s + u C Omega_u + Omega = Theta_x,
where Theta_x = s_x Theta_s + u_x Theta_u. If F is smooth with first nonzero homogeneous Taylor polynomial F_n at S, the
degree-n part of s A F_s + u C F_u is Lam F_n.

Orient s so that gamma enters N along {u = 0, s > 0}, and shift t so that gamma(t) is in N for t >= 0. Then
s(t) = s(gamma(t)) solves s' = s A(s,0); since A(s,0) + a = O(s), s(t) = c_s e^(-at)(1 + o(1)) with c_s > 0, and s(t)
decreases to 0 for large t. Differentiating du/dt = u C in z at z = 0 shows that u_z(t) = d_z u(X(t,z)) at z = 0 solves
u_z' = C(s(t),0) u_z, so u_z(t) = c_u e^(ct)(1 + o(1)) with c_u != 0 (the section is transverse to {u = 0}). Put
h_j(s) = d_u^j Theta(s,0)/j! and g_j(s) = d_u^j Omega(s,0)/j!. Since u(X(t,z)) = u_z(t) z + O(z^2) and
s(X(t,z)) = s(t) + O(z), induction on j in (77.1) gives h_j = 0 for j < p and g_j = 0 for j < m on an interval (0, s_0),
and h_p(s(t)) u_z(t)^p = e^(kappa t) theta, g_m(s(t)) u_z(t)^m = omega_m(t). Therefore, as s -> 0+,

  h_p(s) = C_0 s^i (1 + o(1)),   g_m(s) = D_0 s^ell (1 + o(1)),   C_0 D_0 != 0.                                 (77.4)

A C^infinity function on [0, s_0) asymptotic to a nonzero multiple of s^r with r > 0 has r integral, by Taylor's
theorem, and its derivatives of order less than r vanish at 0 while that of order r does not. So i and ell are positive
integers, and the Taylor coefficients at S of s^i u^p in Theta and of s^ell u^m in Omega are C_0 and D_0. With
d = p - m >= 1,

  i - ell = (d c - kappa - 1)/a = d + (2 beta d - beta + 1)/a > d,   so   i - ell >= 2.                         (77.5)

Since h_j = 0 on (0, s_0) for j < p, every Taylor coefficient of Theta at S of a monomial s^r u^j with j < p vanishes;
likewise for Omega with j < m. Let Theta_n be the first nonzero homogeneous Taylor polynomial of Theta at S; n <= i + p.
Then Lam Theta_n = kappa Theta_n, so each of its monomials s^r u^j has c j - a r = kappa and j >= p, hence r >= i and
r + j >= i + p. So n = i + p; at fixed total degree c j - a r = kappa determines j, so Theta_(i+p) = C_0 s^i u^p. Hence
Theta_x has no Taylor term of degree below i + p - 1. Let Omega_n' be the first nonzero homogeneous Taylor polynomial of
Omega at S; n' <= ell + m < i + p - 1 by (77.5). Then (Lam + 1) Omega_n' = 0, so each monomial has c j - a r = -1 and
j >= m, hence r >= ell, and as before

  Theta_lead = C_0 s^i u^p,   Omega_lead = D_0 s^ell u^m.                                                       (77.6)

Outgoing orders. We use: if A_0, B_0 are smooth near 0, A_0(0) != 0, and H is smooth with u A_0(u) H' = B_0(u) H on
0 < +-u < u_0, then on each side H = b_+- |u|^e E_+-(u) with e = B_0(0)/A_0(0), constants b_+-, and E_+- smooth and
nonvanishing up to u = 0 (integrate H'/H = e/u + smooth). Let H_j(u) = d_s^j Theta(0,u)/j! and R_j(u) = d_s^j
Omega(0,u)/j!. Applying d_s^j at s = 0 to (T): if H_0 = ... = H_(j-1) = 0, then u C(0,u) H_j' = (kappa - j A(0,u)) H_j,
with exponent e_j = (kappa + j a)/c. For 0 <= j < i, 0 < e_j < p. If e_j is not an integer, smoothness at u = 0 forces
b_+- = 0. If e_j is an integer and b_+ or b_- is nonzero, the Taylor coefficient of s^j u^(e_j) at S is nonzero, with
j + e_j < i + p, contrary to (77.6). By induction H_j = 0 for j < i, and e_i = p with (77.6) gives H_i(u) = u^p
(C_0 + O(u)). Thus Theta is divisible by s^i near {s = 0}, so Theta_s, Theta_u and Theta_x are divisible by s^(i-1), and
i - 1 > ell. Applying d_s^j at s = 0 to (V) for j <= ell: if R_0 = ... = R_(j-1) = 0, then u C(0,u) R_j' = -(1 + j
A(0,u)) R_j, with exponent (j a - 1)/c, which is less than m for j < ell. A negative exponent contradicts boundedness, a
nonintegral one smoothness, and a nonnegative integral one with b_+ or b_- nonzero gives a nonzero Taylor coefficient of
total degree below ell + m, contrary to (77.6). So R_j = 0 for j < ell and R_ell(u) = u^m (D_0 + O(u)).

Hence, at points (0,u) with 0 < |u| small, Theta and Omega have exact transverse orders i and ell along the unstable
manifold. Both unstable branches gamma'_+ = {s = 0, u > 0} and gamma'_- = {s = 0, u < 0}, continued by the flow, lie in
Q1. Along a section X'(t,z) = Phi_t Sigma'(z) through a point of either branch, Theta(X'(t,z)) = e^(kappa t)
Theta(Sigma'(z)) has exact order i with a nonzero coefficient theta', Theta_x(X'(t,z)) = O(z^(i-1)), and the
coefficients of z^j in (V), d/dt(e^t omega'_j(t)) = e^t [Theta_x]_j(t), have no forcing for j <= i - 2. As omega'_j = 0
for j < ell and omega'_ell != 0 near S, omega'_j = 0 for j < ell at all t and e^t omega'_ell(t) is a nonzero constant.
This is (77.1) for gamma'_+ and gamma'_- with (i, ell).

Sign transfer. Suppose gamma is contained in the closure of B. Fix t so large that gamma(t) = (s(t),0) is in N and sgn
g_m(s(t)) = sgn D_0. Near gamma(t), Omega(s,u) = g_m(s) u^m (1 + O(u)), so points with sigma Omega < 0 near gamma(t)
have u != 0 and sigma D_0 eps^m < 0 for eps = sgn u. On gamma'_eps near S, sigma R_ell(u) has the sign of sigma D_0
eps^m, so sigma Omega(s,u) = s^ell sigma R_ell(u) + O(s^(ell+1)) < 0 for small s > 0. Thus every point of gamma'_eps
near S is a limit of points of B. Along a transported section the sign of sigma omega'_ell(t) z^ell on a fixed side z of
fixed sign does not change, since e^t omega'_ell is constant. So gamma'_eps is contained in the closure of B.

Step 4 (chains). There is no nonstationary orbit gamma_0 in Q1, contained in the closure of B, whose backward limit lies
on the boundary of Q1 and which satisfies (77.1) for some integers p >= m + 1, m >= 1 and some L_* != 0. Suppose there
is. Since B is bounded, gamma_0 is bounded. By Steps 1 and 2, its forward limit S_1 is a saddle in Q1. Step 3 gives an
unstable branch gamma_1 of S_1 contained in the closure of B and satisfying (77.1) with a gap of at least two between
its orders. It is bounded, and by Steps 1 and 2, applied to gamma_0 and gamma_1, its forward limit S_2 is a saddle in
Q1. Repeating gives saddles S_1, S_2, ... in Q1 with Ly(S_1) < Ly(S_2) < ..., by (63.2). They are distinct, contrary to
the finiteness in Step 1. If B = {}, no such gamma_0 exists trivially.

Step 5 (proof of (a)). Suppose w has a zero after x1, let x2 be the first and Q_x = (x2,0). By (54.3),
DW(Q_x) = diag(-a, 2 beta + a) with a = -w'(x2) >= 0, and a > 0 by (ND). By Theorem 54(a), including (54.5) and the
transverse-order statement that follows it, a = b/m for a positive integer m, and the unstable branch gamma_x in Q1 has
exact transverse orders p = m + 1 for Theta and m for Omega at every nonstationary point. Its backward limit Q_x lies on
the boundary of Q1. In the coordinates (u, eta) = (x - x2 - chi(y), y) of (54.29), Omega(u,eta) = R_m(eta)
u^m + O(u^(m+1)) near Q_x, where R_m is odd, R_m'(0) = p H_p'(0)/(beta - 1 + a) by (54.32), and H_p'(0) = T^(p)(x2)/p!
with T(x) = Theta_y(x,0). Theorem 54(a) gives T of sign sigma on (x1,x2), and Theorem 27 gives its exact order p at x2,
as used in the proof of Theorem 54. Thus H_p'(0) and R_m'(0) have the sign (-1)^p sigma.
Hence, for each small eta > 0, sigma Omega(u,eta) has the sign of (-1)^m (-1)^(m+1) = -1 for all sufficiently small
u < 0. So points of B accumulate at every point of gamma_x near Q_x. By (54.37), on a section with J_* > 0, e^t
omega_m(t) = -(p theta_p/J_*) I(t) with I(t) > 0, so the sign of omega_m does not change along gamma_x, and gamma_x is
contained in the closure of B. Hence gamma_x is bounded, so e^(-(beta+1)t) y(t) -> 0 and I(t) converges to (beta+1)
int_(-infinity)^infinity e^(-(beta+1)s) y(s) ds, which lies in (0, infinity). Thus (77.1) holds for gamma_x with
p = m + 1, m and L_* != 0, contrary to Step 4. So w has no zero on (x1, infinity). Since w(x) >= (beta/2) x for large x,
w > 0 on (x1, infinity).

Step 6 (proof of (b) and (c)). Suppose v has a positive zero and let y1 be the first, Q_y = (0,y1). By (54.7),
DW(Q_y) = diag(2 beta + a, -a) with a = -v'(y1) >= 0, and a > 0 by (ND). By (54.9) and (54.10), d0 = 1/a and beta d0 are
positive integers, and the unstable branch gamma_y in Q1 has exact transverse orders p = n + 2 = L d0 + 2 for Theta and
k = ell + 1 = D d0 + 1 for Omega at every nonstationary point, with p - k = (beta + 1) d0 + 1 >= 2. Its backward limit
Q_y lies on the boundary of Q1. Along a section through a point of gamma_y, Theta_x has order at least p - 1 > k, so, as
in Step 3, e^t omega_k(t) is a nonzero constant, and (77.1) holds with (p, k) and L_* != 0.

Suppose d0 is even. Then k = 2 beta d0 + d0 + 1 is odd. Since Omega has exact odd transverse order k at every point of
gamma_y, it takes both strict signs at points arbitrarily close to each point of gamma_y in Q1, so gamma_y is contained
in the closure of B. This contradicts Step 4. Hence d0 is odd.

The positive zeros of v are zeros of W, since W_1(0,y) = 0 by parity, so they are finitely many by Step 1. At (0,y), the
parities give DW = diag(d_x W_1(0,y), v'(y)), so (ND) makes every positive zero of v simple. Since v = L y + O(y^3) near
0 (proof of Theorem 30) and v(y) >= (beta/2) y for large y, v has an even number of positive zeros, at least two; in
particular the second positive zero y2 exists and is simple. Theorem 30(a),(b) gives v'(y1) = -1/d with d = d0 and
(beta + 1) d0 odd. As d0 is odd, beta d0 = (beta + 1) d0 - d0 is even. Write beta = N/M in lowest terms. Since beta d0
is an integer, M divides d0, so M is odd, and beta d0 = N (d0/M) with d0/M odd, so N is even. This proves (b).

Finally, if beta is irrational, or beta = N/M in lowest terms with N odd, (b) shows that v has no positive zero.
Together with (a), Theorem 52(b) gives (H1). Theorem 75 assumes only (H1) and bounded B, so its conclusions (a)-(c)
hold. This proves (c).

### Theorem 78 (beta > 2: real analytic vorticity excludes degenerate zeros; a weaker form of (ND) in Theorem 77)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2, and use the notation of Theorem 77. A
zero S of W is called degenerate if det DW(S) = 0.

(a) If Omega is real analytic on Q1, then W has no degenerate zero in Q1. If Omega is real analytic on R^2 (in
    particular, if W is), then W has no degenerate zero at all; hence (ND) holds, and the conclusions of Theorem
    77(a)-(c) hold under (BB) alone.

(b) The conclusions of Theorem 77(a)-(c) hold under (BB) and the following hypothesis in place of (ND):

  (ND') every positive zero of w and every positive zero of v is simple; every zero of W in Q1 is an isolated point of
        Z; and Omega vanishes identically on a neighbourhood of every degenerate zero of W in Q1.

    The last condition in (ND') holds at a degenerate zero S in Q1 whenever Omega is real analytic on a connected
    neighbourhood of S.

(c) Suppose v has a positive zero, its first positive zero y1 is simple, and d0 = 1/|v'(y1)| is odd. (Under (BB) and
    either (ND) or (ND'), d0 is odd by Theorem 77(b) or by part (b).) Let gamma_y be the unstable branch in Q1 of the
    saddle Q_y = (0,y1) (Theorem 54(b)). Then the exact transverse order k = D d0 + 1 of Omega along gamma_y is even,
    and every point of gamma_y has a neighbourhood on which sigma Omega >= 0. In particular gamma_y does not meet the
    closure of B.

Scope. Part (a) is a consequence of Theorem 43(b3),(c); real analyticity of A2-broad profiles is not proved, so (a) is a
conditional statement. Hypothesis (ND') admits degenerate zeros in Q1 only when Omega vanishes on a neighbourhood of
them; degenerate zeros in Q1 with nonzero vorticity at points arbitrarily close to them, nonsimple axis zeros and
nonisolated zero sets are not treated. Part (c) requires neither (BB) nor (ND) nor (ND'). Under (BB) and either
(ND) or (ND'), it applies to the remaining possibility in Theorem 77(b): a positive y-axis zero with beta = N/M
in lowest terms, N even and M odd. The order-transfer conclusions in Step 3 of Theorem 77 do not require the incoming
orbit to lie in the closure of B. Its sign-transfer conclusion uses that hypothesis, and Step 4 uses it to keep the
chain bounded. Part (c) shows that gamma_y cannot start that bounded-chain argument; boundedness of B therefore
supplies no bound on gamma_y by that argument. Part (c) does not prove that gamma_y is bounded or that it escapes,
and does not assert that such a configuration exists. No existence or nonexistence result for the full A2-broad
class is asserted, and no endpoint follows.

Proof. (a) Let S be a degenerate zero of W. By Theorem 43(a) the eigenvalues of DW(S) are real; their sum is
div W = 2 beta and their product is 0, so they are 0 and 2 beta. By Theorem 43(b3) Theta is flat at S, and then by
Theorem 43(c) Omega is flat at S. Suppose S is in Q1 and Omega is real analytic on Q1. Since Q1 is connected and every
derivative of Omega vanishes at S, Omega = 0 on Q1. Then (V) gives Theta_x = 0 on Q1, so for x, y > 0, Theta(x,y) is
the limit of Theta(x',y) as x' decreases to 0, which is Theta(0,y) = 0 by the axis condition of Section 1. This
contradicts Theta = x^2 y a(x^2,y^2) near O with a(0,0) = a0 != 0, at points of Q1 near O. If Omega is real analytic on
R^2 and S is any degenerate zero, the same argument on the connected set R^2 gives Omega = 0 on R^2, hence on Q1, and
the same contradiction. So W has no degenerate zero, (ND) holds, and Theorem 77 applies. If Omega is real analytic on a
connected neighbourhood G of a degenerate zero S, flatness at S gives Omega = 0 on G; this is the sufficient condition
stated after (ND').

(b) Assume (BB) and (ND'). We list the changes to the proof of Theorem 77; everything else is used unchanged.

In Step 1, finiteness and the types of the boundary zeros are obtained as follows. By the proof of Theorem 27,
w'(0) = -(beta + 2) and v'(0) = 3 beta + 2, so DW(O) = diag(-(beta + 2), 3 beta + 2) is nonsingular, and w < 0 < v on
some interval (0, eps). Since Z lies in the closed disc of radius R0, the positive zeros of w and of v lie in [eps, R0].
They are simple, hence isolated, hence finitely many. Theorem 27(x),(y) applies to all of them and shows that DW at each
of them is one of diag(beta + 2, beta - 2), diag(-(beta + 2)/m, 2 beta + (beta + 2)/m),
diag(2 beta + (3 beta + 2)/n, -(3 beta + 2)/n), diag((beta - 2)/2, (3 beta + 2)/2) and diag(-(beta + 2), 3 beta + 2),
with positive integers m and n; each is nonsingular since beta > 2. Thus every zero on the boundary of Q1 is
nondegenerate, every zero in Q1 is isolated by (ND'), and Z intersected with the closed first quadrant is compact and
discrete, hence finite. Nondegenerate zeros are hyperbolic sources or hyperbolic saddles exactly as in Step 1. By
Theorem 63(a), the forward limit S+ of a bounded nonstationary forward orbit is a zero, Ly(S+) > Ly(S-) by (63.2), and
S+ is not a source; so S+ is a hyperbolic saddle or a degenerate zero in Q1.

Steps 2 and 3 are unchanged; Step 3 concerns a hyperbolic saddle and Step 2 uses only (63.2), the invariance of the
axes and the area identity.

In Step 4, let gamma_0 be as there; it is bounded because B is, and by Step 2 its forward limit S_1 lies in Q1. It
is not a source. Suppose S_1 is degenerate. By (ND') there is an open neighbourhood N of S_1 on which Omega = 0. Then N
does not meet B, and since N is open it does not meet the closure of B. But gamma_0(t) is in N for all large t, and
gamma_0 is contained in the closure of B, a contradiction. Hence S_1 is a hyperbolic saddle in Q1. The same argument
