applies to every later S_j, and the rest of Step 4 is unchanged.

In Step 5, a = -w'(x2) > 0 because x2 is a simple zero of w. In Step 6, a = -v'(y1) > 0 because y1 is a simple zero of
v, the positive zeros of v are finitely many by the modified Step 1, and they are simple by (ND'). The remainder of
Steps 5 and 6, and the deduction of Theorem 77(c), are unchanged.

(c) By (54.9), d0, ell = D d0 and beta d0 are positive integers, and by (54.10) Omega has exact transverse order
k = ell + 1 = 2 beta d0 + d0 + 1 along gamma_y. Here 2 beta d0 is even and d0 + 1 is even, so k is even.

Use the coordinates (u,eta) = (y - y1 - chi(x), x) of (54.29) near Q_y, in which gamma_y near Q_y is {u = 0, eta > 0}.
By Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 54, R_j = d_u^j Omega(0, .)/j! vanishes for j < k, R_k is odd and
R_k'(0) = K_y^(k)(y1)/k! != 0, where K_y(y) = Omega_x(0,y). Hence Omega = u^k F(u,eta) with F smooth and
F(0,eta) = R_k(eta). Since chi is even, u is even in x, and Omega is odd in x; so F is odd in eta and F = eta G with G
smooth and G(0,0) = R_k'(0). By (54.8), sgn K_y = sigma on (0,y1), and K_y has exact order k at y1 (Step 2 of the proof
of Theorem 54); so K_y(y) = (K_y^(k)(y1)/k!)(y - y1)^k (1 + o(1)) as y increases to y1, and
sigma (-1)^k K_y^(k)(y1) > 0. As k is even, sigma G(0,0) > 0. Choose u0, eta0 > 0 with sigma G > 0 on
{|u| < u0, |eta| < eta0}. On the open set {|u| < u0, 0 < eta < eta0}, sigma Omega = u^k eta sigma G >= 0, and this set
contains every point of gamma_y close enough to Q_y.

Let X0 be any point of gamma_y. Choose a point X1 of gamma_y in the set above, with coordinates (u,eta) = (0,eta1),
and t0 with Phi_(t0) X1 = X0. Let Sigma(z) be the point with coordinates (z,eta1), for small |z|; this is a section
transverse to W at X1. Put X(t,z) = Phi_t Sigma(z). By Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 54 (and Step 6 of the proof of
Theorem 77), the z-derivatives of Omega(X(t,z)) of order less than k vanish at z = 0 for every t, and
Omega(X(t,z)) = omega_k(t) z^k + O(z^(k+1)) with e^t omega_k(t) a nonzero constant. So Omega(X(t,z)) = z^k F1(t,z)
with F1 smooth and F1(t,0) = omega_k(t). At t = 0, Omega(Sigma(z)) = z^k F(z,eta1), so omega_k(0) = F(0,eta1) =
eta1 G(0,eta1) and sigma omega_k(0) > 0; hence sigma omega_k(t) > 0 for every t. By continuity there is z1 > 0 with
sigma F1 > 0 on (t0 - 1, t0 + 1) x (-z1, z1). The map (t,z) -> X(t,z) is a diffeomorphism from a neighbourhood of
(t0,0) onto a neighbourhood of X0, because its partial derivatives at (t0,0) are W(X0) and D Phi_(t0) Sigma'(0), and
D Phi_(t0) is invertible and maps W(X1) to W(X0). On that neighbourhood, since k is even, sigma Omega = z^k sigma F1 is
nonnegative. So X0 has a neighbourhood that does not meet B, and X0 is not in the closure of B.

### Theorem 79 (beta > 2 without interior zeros: basins, the zero set of Theta and the ray condition)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2. Use the notation of Theorem 77, with
T(x) = Theta_y(x,0) and E(y) = Theta_xx(0,y)/2 as in Theorem 27. Assume (BB), (ND) and

  (NI) W has no zero in Q1.

For a zero S of W let A(S) = {X : Phi_(-s) X -> S as s -> infinity}.

(a) The positive zeros of v are finitely many and simple, and their number is even, say 2m with m >= 0; write them
    y1 < y2 < ... < y_(2m). For 1 <= j <= m, v'(y_(2j-1)) < 0 and (0,y_(2j-1)) is a hyperbolic saddle with DW =
    diag(2 beta + |v'(y_(2j-1))|, -|v'(y_(2j-1))|); and v'(y_(2j)) = L/2, so (0,y_(2j)) is a hyperbolic source with
    DW = diag(kappa/2, L/2) and E(y_(2j)) != 0. Let gamma_j be the branch in Q1 of the unstable manifold of
    (0,y_(2j-1)).

(b) For every X in Q1, |Phi_t X| -> infinity as t -> infinity. For each source S in {P, (0,y2), (0,y4), ...,
    (0,y_(2m))}, A(S) is open. The quadrant Q1 is the disjoint union of gamma_1, ..., gamma_m and the sets A(S) cap Q1
    for these sources S.

(c) Theta has no zero on A(S) cap Q1 for each of these sources S, and Theta = 0 on each gamma_j. Hence
    {Theta = 0} cap Q1 = gamma_1 cup ... cup gamma_m, a set of zero area; in particular {Theta = 0} has empty interior
    in Q1.

(d) If m = 1, then sigma Theta > 0 on Q1 \ gamma_1.

(e) If no ray in Q1 contains radii 0 < r1 < r2 < r3 at which Omega has the strict signs (sigma, -sigma, sigma), then
    a0 > 0, B is empty, Omega >= 0 on Q1, m = 0 and (H1) holds. Equivalently: if (BB), (ND) and (NI) hold and v has a
    positive zero, then some ray in Q1 contains three radii at which Omega has the strict signs (sigma, -sigma, sigma).

Scope. The hypotheses (BB), (ND), (NI) and, in (e), the ray condition are not proved for A2-broad profiles. When m = 0,
Theorem 77(a) and (NI) give (H1), and (e) is contained in Theorem 64(b). When m >= 1, Theorem 77(b) requires beta = N/M
in lowest terms with N even and M odd. Parts (b) and (c) for m = 0 follow from Theorems 8 and 52(b). For m = 1, the
escape and decomposition in (b) are Theorem 54(d); its proof gives the basin signs used here, and (d) also uses Theorem
77(b). Vanishing on the saddle branches is already in Theorem 46(b). Parts (a) to (d) use (V), (T), div W = 2 beta, d_y
W_1 - d_x W_2 = Omega, the A2 parities and jet, smoothness, uniform sublinearity, the index count and the cited
theorems. Part (e) also uses the origin strain identity, the positive y-axis kernel and the angular inverse underlying
Theorems 21, 57 and 64. Its additional application here is the exclusion with m >= 1. Profiles with an interior zero,
and exclusion of the residual y-axis configurations without the ray condition, are not resolved by this argument. No
configuration with m >= 1 is asserted to exist. No existence or nonexistence result for the full A2-broad class is
asserted, and no endpoint follows.

Proof. Step 1 (zeros and indices). By Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 77, X.W(X) >= (beta/2)|X|^2 for |X| >= R0, so Z
lies in the closed disc of radius R0, and Z cap closure(Q1) is finite. By Theorem 2 and Theorem 77(a), the zeros on the
positive x-axis reduce to P; by (NI) there is none in Q1. On the y-axis DW(0,y) = diag(2 beta - v'(y), v'(y)) at zeros
of v (the off-diagonal entries vanish by parity), so by (ND) every positive zero of v is simple. Since v'(0) = L > 0
and y v(y) >= (beta/2) y^2 for y >= R0, v > 0 near 0 and for y >= R0; hence the positive zeros of v are even in number,
2m, and the signs of v' at y1 < ... < y_(2m) alternate, starting with v'(y1) < 0. By Theorem 27(y), at odd j,
v'(y_j) = -L/n_j with n_j a positive integer, and DW(0,y_j) = diag(2 beta + L/n_j, -L/n_j) has determinant < 0; at
even j, v'(y_j) is L/2 or L, with DW(0,y_j) = diag(kappa/2, L/2) (determinant > 0) or diag(-b, L) (determinant < 0).
Also DW(O) = diag(-b, L) and DW(P) = diag(b, kappa) (Theorem 27(x) and its proof).

Reflection R in either axis maps Z to Z and DW(RS) = R DW(S) R, so every zero of W in R^2 is nondegenerate, Z
is finite, and its index sgn det DW(S) is invariant under R. On the circle |X| = R0 the fields t W + (1 - t) X,
0 <= t <= 1, do not vanish because X.(t W + (1 - t) X) > 0 there; so W has degree one on that circle, and the sum of
the indices of the zeros of W (all inside the circle) is 1. The zeros are O (index -1), P and -P (index +1 each) and
the points (0, +-y_i) (each of the pair with the index of (0,y_i)). Hence

  sum over i = 1, ..., 2m of ind(0,y_i) = 0.                                                                  (79.1)

The m zeros with odd i have index -1, so the m zeros with even i have index sum m, each index is +1 or -1, and all of
them have index +1. Thus v'(y_(2j)) = L/2 and DW(0,y_(2j)) = diag(kappa/2, L/2), a hyperbolic source since kappa > 0.
By Theorem 27(y), E vanishes at y_(2j) to order 0, that is, E(y_(2j)) != 0. This proves (a).

Step 2 (escape and basins). The axes are invariant, so Q1 is invariant. A nonstationary orbit does not converge forward
to a hyperbolic source. At the saddle O the stable eigenvector is (1,0) and at the saddle (0,y_(2j-1)) it is (0,1). The
corresponding axis is invariant, and the flow on it near the saddle converges to the saddle; by uniqueness of the local
stable manifold, that manifold is a segment of the axis, and every orbit converging forward to the saddle lies on the
axis. Likewise the local unstable manifold of O is a segment of the y-axis. Let X be in Q1. If its forward orbit were
bounded, it would converge to a zero S+ in closure(Q1) by Theorem 63(a); S+ is not in Q1 by (NI), is not a source,
and is not O or (0,y_(2j-1)) by the above. Hence the forward orbit is unbounded. Once the radius r(t) = |Phi_t X| is
at least R0, the derivative of r(t)^2 is 2 Phi_t X.W(Phi_t X) >= beta r(t)^2, so the orbit never returns into the
disc of radius R0 and r(t) -> infinity.

By Theorem 44(b), Phi_(-s) X converges as s -> infinity to a point of Z, which lies in closure(Q1). It is not O, because
the local unstable manifold of O lies on the y-axis. If it is (0,y_(2j-1)), then X lies on the unstable manifold of this
saddle, which is tangent to (1,0) and is mapped to itself by the reflection x -> -x; its branch in Q1 is gamma_j.
Otherwise it is one of the sources P, (0,y_(2j)). The basin A(S) of a hyperbolic source S is open: a small open
neighbourhood N of S is mapped into itself by Phi_(-s) for s > 0, with Phi_(-s) Y -> S uniformly on N, and A(S) is the
union of the open sets Phi_t(N), t >= 0. The limit is unique, so the union is disjoint. This proves (b).

Step 3 (temperature). By (T), Theta(Phi_t X) = e^(kappa t) Theta(X) for all t. Since Theta is odd in y, Theta = y h with
h smooth and h(x,0) = T(x); by Theorem 27(x), T(x1) != 0, and T = a0 x^2 + O(x^4) does not vanish on (0,x1], so
sigma T(x1) > 0. Hence sigma Theta > 0 on N cap Q1 for a small neighbourhood N of P. For X in A(P) cap Q1, Phi_(-s) X
lies in N cap Q1 for large s, and sigma Theta(X) = e^(kappa s) sigma Theta(Phi_(-s) X) > 0. Since Theta is even in x and
Theta(0,y) = 0, Theta = x^2 e with e(x,y) = int_0^1 (1 - s) Theta_xx(s x, y) ds smooth and e(0,y) = E(y). By (a),
E(y_(2j)) != 0, so Theta has the sign of E(y_(2j)) on N cap Q1 for a small neighbourhood N of (0,y_(2j)), and the same
argument gives this sign on A((0,y_(2j))) cap Q1.

Let S = (0,y_(2j-1)) and c = 2 beta + |v'(y_(2j-1))|, the unstable eigenvalue; c > kappa. Fix c' with kappa < c' < c.
For X in gamma_j, |Phi_(-s) X - S| <= C_X e^(-c' s) for s >= 0, by the standard estimate on the unstable manifold of a
hyperbolic saddle. Theta(S) = 0 and Theta is Lipschitz near S, so |Theta(X)| = e^(kappa s) |Theta(Phi_(-s) X)| <=
C'_X e^((kappa - c') s), which tends to 0. Thus Theta = 0 on gamma_j. Each gamma_j is an orbit, the image of R under a
smooth immersion, and has zero area. With (b) this proves (c).

Step 4 (m = 1). By Theorem 77(b), d0 = 1/|v'(y1)| is odd and beta d0 is even. With v'(y1) = -L/n_1 from Step 1,
n_1 = L d0 = 3 beta d0 + 2 d0 is even, and by Theorem 27(y) E vanishes at y1 to the exact order n_1 + 2, which is even.
By Theorem 27(y), sigma E > 0 on (0,y1), since E = a0 y + O(y^3); an exact zero of even order preserves the sign, and E
does not vanish on (y1,y2), so sigma E > 0 on (y1,y2) and, as E(y2) != 0, sigma E(y2) > 0. Step 3 gives sigma Theta > 0
on A(P) cap Q1 and on A((0,y2)) cap Q1, whose union is Q1 \ gamma_1 by (b). This proves (d).

Step 5 (the ray condition). By (c), {Theta = 0} has empty interior in Q1. With (BB) and the ray hypothesis, (64.6) of
Theorem 64(b) gives B empty, that is, sigma Omega >= 0 on Q1. If sigma = -1, then Omega <= 0 on Q1, which Theorem 21(a)
excludes. Hence sigma = 1 and Omega >= 0 on Q1, and Theorem 57(a) gives a0 > 0, v(y) > beta y for y > 0, so m = 0, and
(H1). The second sentence follows by contraposition from m = 0. Conversely, that sentence and the ray condition
exclude positive zeros of v. Theorem 77(a) and (NI) then give (H1), and Theorem 64(b) gives all the conclusions of
the first sentence. QED.

### Theorem 80 (beta > 2: under nondegeneracy Theta vanishes on no open set; the ray condition then gives (H1))

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2, and use the notation of Theorem 77.

(a) If Theta = 0 on a nonempty open set V, then Theta is flat at the backward limit of every point of V (a single
    zero of W, by Theorem 44(b)).

(b) If {Theta = 0} has nonempty interior in Q1, then Theta is flat at some zero of W in closure(Q1), and W has a
    zero in closure(Q1) at which det DW = 0. In particular, under (ND) the set {Theta = 0} has empty interior in Q1.

(c) Assume (BB) and (ND), and that no ray in Q1 contains radii 0 < r1 < r2 < r3 at which Omega has the strict signs
    (sigma, -sigma, sigma). Then a0 > 0, B is empty, Omega >= 0 and Theta > 0 on Q1, and (H1) holds. In particular,
    under (BB) and (ND), if (H1) fails, then some ray in Q1 contains three radii at which Omega has the strict signs
    (sigma, -sigma, sigma).

Scope. Part (b) supplies, under (ND) and without using (H1), the empty-interior condition in Theorem 62(a), in the last
consequence of Theorem 64(a), in Theorems 64(b), (c) and (e), and in Theorem 66. All other hypotheses of those
statements remain required, including (H1) wherever it is explicitly assumed. By Theorem 43(d), a flat source would
force Theta = Omega = 0 on its open basin; under (ND) this alternative is excluded, since every zero of W in the plane
is then nondegenerate and Theorem 52(c) makes Theta nonflat at every zero. Part (c) contains Theorem 79(e), whose
hypothesis (NI) excludes zeros of W in Q1. If Theta is real analytic on Q1, the identity principle on the connected set
Q1 and the expansion Theta = x^2 y a(x^2,y^2) near O with a(0,0) = a0 != 0 give the empty interior without (ND); with
(BB) and the ray condition, Theorems 64(b), 21(a) and 57(a) then give the conclusions of (c). The hypotheses (BB), (ND)
and the ray condition are not proved for A2-broad profiles, and real analyticity of profiles is not proved. Part (a)
uses only smoothness, the flow, (T) and Theorem 44(b); part (b) uses in addition the parities and Theorem 52(c); part
(c) uses in addition Theorems 64(b), 21(a) and 57(a). Theorem 77(a) is not needed. No existence or nonexistence result
for the full A2-broad class is asserted, and no endpoint follows.

Proof. (a) Choose X in V, and let S be the backward limit of X, that is, Phi_(-s) X -> S as s -> infinity (Theorem
44(b)). For every s >= 0, (T) gives Theta(Phi_(-s) Y) = e^(-kappa s) Theta(Y) = 0 for Y in V, so Theta = 0 on the open
set Phi_(-s)(V). Thus partial^alpha Theta(Phi_(-s) X) = 0 for every multi-index alpha and every s >= 0. Fix alpha; since
partial^alpha Theta is continuous and Phi_(-s) X -> S, partial^alpha Theta(S) = 0. As alpha was arbitrary, Theta is flat
at S. This proves (a).

(b) Let V be a nonempty open subset of Q1 with Theta = 0 on V, and choose X in V. Both axes are invariant under the flow
by the parities, so Q1 is invariant and the backward limit S of X lies in closure(Q1). By (a), Theta is flat at S. By
Theorem 52(c), Z contains a zero Q' with det DW(Q') = 0. For either axis reflection R, the parities give W(RY) = R W(Y),
hence DW(RQ) = R DW(Q) R and det DW(RQ) = det DW(Q) for every zero Q; applying at most two reflections to Q' gives a
zero in closure(Q1) at which det DW = 0. Under (ND) no such zero exists, so {Theta = 0} has empty interior in Q1. This
proves (b).

(c) By (b), {Theta = 0} has empty interior in Q1. With (BB) and the ray hypothesis, (64.6) of Theorem 64(b) gives B
empty, that is, sigma Omega >= 0 on Q1. If sigma = -1, then Omega <= 0 on Q1, which Theorem 21(a) excludes. Hence
sigma = 1, so a0 > 0 and Omega >= 0 on Q1, and Theorem 57(a) gives Theta > 0 on Q1 and (H1). The last sentence of (c) is
the contrapositive of the implication to (H1). QED.

### Theorem 81 (beta >= 2: the far-field vorticity sign and boundedness of B)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta >= 2. Put sigma = sgn(a0), h = 1/beta, Q1 =
{x > 0, y > 0}, X = r e(phi) and B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0}. Let G be the smooth angular vorticity function with
r^h Omega(r, .) -> G uniformly (Theorems 33(d) and 36(a) at beta = 2, Theorems 41(b) and 42(b) for beta > 2). G is odd
in x and in y, so G(0) = G(pi/2) = 0.

(a) If sigma G(phi0) < 0 for some phi0 in (0, pi/2), then there are R > 0 and delta > 0 such that every point r e(phi)
    with r > R and |phi - phi0| < delta lies in B; in particular B is unbounded. Equivalently, boundedness of B implies
    sigma G >= 0 on [0, pi/2] (Theorem 64(a)).

(b) If sigma G > 0 on (0, pi/2), sigma G'(0) > 0 and sigma G'(pi/2) < 0, then there is R > 0 such that sigma Omega > 0
    at every point of Q1 with |X| >= R. In particular B is contained in {|X| < R}, so B is bounded. At beta = 2 this
    hypothesis is never satisfied: by Theorem 47(a), G vanishes at some angle in (0, pi/2).

(c) In any statement whose hypotheses include boundedness of the set B defined above, that hypothesis may be replaced by
    the condition of (b), with the beta range and every other hypothesis retained. For beta > 2, this applies to the
    bounded-B clauses of Theorems 62(a), 64(a) to (c), 65(h), 66, 71(a), (b), 73(a) to (d), 75(a) to (c), 77, 78, 79,
    80(c) and 82(d); in Theorem 78 these are the bounded-B consequence in (a), part (b) and the sufficient hypotheses
    mentioned in (c), whose conclusion itself assumes no boundedness. At beta = 2 it applies to the bounded-B clauses of
    Theorems 62(a), (g) and 64(a), (b), (g), (h) and to the angular conclusion of Theorem 73(a) described in its Scope;
    these substitutions are vacuous, since the condition of (b) never holds at beta = 2. Retain the sign of a0 (a0 < 0
    in 62(a), (g) and a0 > 0 in 65(h)), nonemptiness of B, the axis and interior-zero assumptions, (H1), the ray
    condition and every other hypothesis wherever they occur. For beta > 2, W_2(0, y) > 0 for every y > 0 implies sigma
    G'(pi/2) < 0, where W = beta X + U; in particular this holds under (H1) (Theorem 50(c)).

Scope. Part (a) restates the uniform angular limit, and part (b) replaces the global hypothesis that B is bounded by a
strict sign condition on the leading far-field angular function G. Parts (a) and (b) do not characterize boundedness of
B. When sigma G >= 0 has an interior zero or a vanishing endpoint slope, these two implications do not decide
boundedness; higher far-field terms and other profile constraints may matter. For beta > 2, a0 > 0 and bounded B,
Theorem 65(h), through (65.7), gives the necessary condition q cos(phi) f(phi) - sin(phi) f'(phi) <= 0 at every interior
zero of G, with q = 1 - 2h. For beta > 2, the report does not prove the condition of (b) for every A2-broad profile.
Theorems 41(b), 47(a), 50(c) and 64(a) impose sign or zero constraints with their stated hypotheses. Theorem 67 gives a
formal natural far-field expansion for every smooth pair satisfying the parity and endpoint conditions (67.2).
Realization by a full profile remains unproved. Its explicit pair f = sigma sin(phi) cos(phi)^2, G = sigma sin(2 phi)
satisfies the condition of (b), since sigma G > 0 inside and its signed endpoint slopes are 2 and -2. For example, for
beta > 2, Theorem 80(c) and part (c) give: under (ND) and the condition of (b), if (H1) fails, some ray in Q1 contains
radii r1 < r2 < r3 at which Omega has the strict signs (sigma, -sigma, sigma), and r2 < R. At beta = 2, the condition of
(b) is impossible for an A2-broad profile: Theorem 47(a) forces G = 0 at an interior critical point of H = lim Theta.
Thus (b) and its bounded-B substitutions are vacuous there. Section 7 already records, using Theorems 44(d) and 47(a),
that a strict vorticity sign throughout the sufficiently distant open quadrant is impossible at beta = 2. The proof of
(a) and (b) uses the remainders of Theorems 36 and 42 and the parities; part (c) also uses the cited statements. No
existence or nonexistence result for the full A2-broad class is asserted, and no endpoint follows.

Proof. Choose R1 >= 1 such that the expansions of Theorem 36(b) (beta = 2, where h = 1/2) and Theorem 42(b) (beta > 2)
hold for |X| >= R1, and put E(X) = Omega(X) - r^(-h) G(phi) for |X| >= R1. By those expansions E = O_infty(r^(-2h)); in
particular there is a constant C1 such that, for |X| >= R1, |E(X)| <= C1 |X|^(-2h) and |grad E(X)| <= C1 |X|^(-2h-1).

(a) Put c0 = -sigma G(phi0) > 0. By continuity of G choose delta with 0 < delta < min(phi0, pi/2 - phi0) and sigma
G(phi) < -c0/2 for |phi - phi0| < delta. For such phi and r >= R1, sigma Omega(r e(phi)) <= r^(-h) (-c0/2 + C1 r^(-h)),
which is negative for r > R := max(R1, (2 C1/c0)^beta). These points lie in Q1. The equivalent form is the
contrapositive; it is also part of Theorem 64(a).

(b) Omega is odd in x and in y, and so is r^(-h) G(phi), because G is; hence E is odd in x and in y and vanishes on both
axes. Fix r >= R1 and phi in [0, pi/2]. The arc s -> r e(s), 0 <= s <= phi, lies on the circle |X| = r, and the
derivative of s -> E(r e(s)) is r e(s + pi/2) . grad E(r e(s)), of absolute value at most C1 r^(-2h). Since E(r e(0)) =
0, this gives |E(r e(phi))| <= C1 r^(-2h) phi. The arc from phi to pi/2 gives |E(r e(phi))| <= C1 r^(-2h) (pi/2 - phi)
in the same way. Thus, with m(phi) = min(phi, pi/2 - phi), the bound |E(r e(phi))| <= C1 r^(-2h) m(phi) holds. The
function g = sigma G/m is continuous and positive on (0, pi/2). Since G is C^1 and G(0) = G(pi/2) = 0, g(phi) tends to
sigma G'(0) > 0 as phi decreases to 0 and to -sigma G'(pi/2) > 0 as phi increases to pi/2. Hence c := inf of g over (0,
pi/2) is positive, and sigma G >= c m on [0, pi/2]. For 0 < phi < pi/2 and r >= R1, sigma Omega(r e(phi)) >= r^(-h)
sigma G(phi) - |E(r e(phi))| >= r^(-h) m(phi) (c - C1 r^(-h)), which is positive for r > (C1/c)^beta. So sigma Omega > 0
on Q1 cap {|X| >= R} for any R > max(R1, (C1/c)^beta), and B is contained in {|X| < R}.

(c) Part (b) supplies boundedness of B. Apply each cited clause with all its other hypotheses and beta range retained.
The final assertion follows from the explicit weakened hypothesis in Theorem 50(c): for beta > 2, v = W_2(0, .) > 0 on
(0, infinity) suffices. QED.

### Theorem 82 (beta > 2: flat points of the temperature and the zero set of Theta under nondegeneracy)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2. Put kappa = beta - 2, W = beta X + U,
let Phi_t be the complete flow of W, Z = {W = 0}, pi the backward-limit map of Theorem 44(b), Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0},
sigma = sgn(a0) and B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0}. Theta is flat at a point if all its derivatives of every order,
including order zero, vanish there. Write (ND) for the condition that det DW(Q) != 0 for every Q in Z cap closure(Q1).

(a) If Theta is flat at a point X of R^2, then Theta is flat at pi(X), and W has a zero Q' in the closed first quadrant
    with det DW(Q') = 0.

(b) Under (ND), Theta is flat at no point of R^2, and {Theta = 0} is contained in a countable union of smooth embedded
    curves; in particular {Theta = 0} has area zero.

(c) Under (ND), Z is finite and each of its points is a hyperbolic source or a hyperbolic saddle of W, and {Theta = 0}
    is the union of Z and of finitely many nonstationary orbits of W. The backward limit of each of these orbits lies in
    Z; forward, each of them either tends to infinity or converges to a saddle in Z.

(d) Suppose (ND) holds and B is bounded. Then the following are equivalent: (i) no ray in Q1 contains radii r1 < r2 < r3
    at which Omega has the strict signs (sigma, -sigma, sigma); (ii) B is empty; (iii) Omega >= 0 on Q1. Each of them
    implies a0 > 0, Theta > 0 on Q1 and (H1). If B is nonempty, let S_B be the set of angles phi in (0, pi/2) with sigma
    Omega(r, phi) < 0 for some r > 0; then for every M >= 0 the set of angles in S_B on whose ray such a triple exists
    with r3 > M is open and dense in S_B.

Scope. Parts (a) and (b) extend Theorem 80(a), (b), which concern open subsets of {Theta = 0}, to single flat points and
to sets of positive area. Nonflatness at zeros is already Theorem 52(c). Its proof also gives finiteness and the source
and saddle classification of Z, and the finite count of bounded nonstationary orbits. The additional conclusion in (c)
is finiteness of the escaping zero orbits, obtained from the restriction of Theta to a transverse circle. Part (c) uses
neither boundedness of B, nor (H1), nor the absence of zeros of W in Q1. It gives no profile-independent numerical bound
on the number of zeros or orbits, and decides neither whether there are saddles other than O nor whether every orbit in
Q1 escapes. Part (d) records consequences already available from Theorems 21(a), 57(a), 64(c) and 80(b), (c). In
particular, Theorem 80(b) already supplies the empty-interior condition, so the stronger conclusion of (b) is not needed
there. Part (d) does not exclude a nonempty B. Neither (ND) nor boundedness of B is proved for A2-broad profiles. No
existence or nonexistence result for the full A2-broad class is asserted, and no endpoint follows.

Proof. Equation (T) gives Theta(Phi_t Y) = e^{kappa t} Theta(Y) for all Y and all real t. The parities give W(RX) = R
W(X) for R = diag(-1, 1) and R = diag(1, -1), so Z is invariant under these reflections and DW(RQ) = R DW(Q) R; hence
(ND) implies det DW(Q) != 0 at every Q in Z, and every zero of W is the image of a zero in the closed first quadrant
under a composition of these reflections, with the same determinant.

(a) Fix s >= 0. Since Theta = e^{-kappa s} Theta o Phi_s and Phi_s is a smooth diffeomorphism with Phi_s(Phi_{-s}
X) = X, the chain rule, applied to each finite order separately, shows that Theta is flat at Phi_{-s} X. By Theorem
44(b), Phi_{-s} X tends to pi(X) in Z as s tends to infinity; since every derivative of Theta is continuous, every
derivative of Theta vanishes at pi(X). Thus Theta is flat at the zero pi(X), and Theorem 52(c) gives a zero Q' of W with
det DW(Q') = 0. A composition of the two reflections maps Q' into the closed first quadrant without changing the
determinant.

(b) Under (ND), (a) shows that Theta is flat nowhere. Let Theta(X) = 0 and let n >= 1 be the least order of a nonzero
derivative of Theta at X. Choose a multi-index alpha of order n with D^alpha Theta(X) != 0 and an index i with
alpha_i >= 1, and put g = D^(alpha - e_i) Theta. Then g(X) = 0 by the minimality of n (for n = 1, g = Theta), and d_i
g(X) = D^alpha Theta(X) != 0. So X lies in M(alpha, i) = {g = 0, d_i g != 0}, which by the implicit function theorem is
a smooth embedded curve, a countable union of graphs of smooth functions over open intervals. There are countably many
pairs (alpha, i), and each smooth curve has area zero.

(c) Uniform sublinearity of U gives R0 > 0 with X.W(X) >= (beta/2)|X|^2 for |X| >= R0. Hence Z lies in the open disc of
radius R0; it is closed, and by the inverse function theorem each of its points is isolated, since DW is invertible on
Z. So Z is finite. By Theorem 43(a) the eigenvalues of DW at a zero are real; their sum is div W = 2 beta > 0 and their
product is nonzero, so the zero is a hyperbolic source or a hyperbolic saddle. Put h(phi) = Theta(R0 e(phi)) on the
circle of radius R0. The map F(t, phi) = Phi_t(R0 e(phi)) has at (0, phi) the derivative with columns W(R0 e(phi)) and
R0 e(phi + pi/2), which are linearly independent because W(R0 e(phi)).e(phi) > 0; so F is a local diffeomorphism near
(0, phi), and Theta(F(t, phi)) = e^{kappa t} h(phi). If h were flat at phi0, then e^{kappa t} h(phi) would be flat at
(0, phi0), hence Theta would be flat at R0 e(phi0), contrary to (b). So every zero of h has finite order and is
isolated, and h has finitely many zeros on the compact circle. The set {Theta = 0} is invariant under the flow and
contains Z, because kappa Theta(Q) = W(Q).grad Theta(Q) = 0 at Q in Z. Let Y be a point of {Theta = 0} not in Z, and
gamma its orbit; its backward limit pi(Y) lies in Z (Theorem 44(b)). Along any orbit, d|X|^2/dt = 2 X.W >= beta |X|^2
while |X| >= R0. Hence an orbit meeting the circle at time t_* stays strictly outside it for t > t_*, and its radius
r(t) = |Phi_t Y| satisfies r(t)^2 >= R0^2 exp(beta (t - t_*)); it therefore tends to infinity and cannot meet the circle
again. If the forward orbit of Y is unbounded, the complete orbit gamma meets the circle at some real time t_*, since
its backward limit pi(Y) lies inside the disc; this time can be negative when Y is already outside. The crossing point
is a zero of h, so there are only finitely many such complete orbits. If the forward orbit of Y is bounded, it converges
to a point S+ of Z (Theorem 63(a)). A hyperbolic source is the forward limit of no nonstationary orbit, so S+ is a
saddle, and gamma is one of the two nonstationary orbits that form, with S+, the stable manifold of the hyperbolic
saddle S+. As Z is finite, these are finitely many orbits as well.

(d) By (b), {Theta = 0} has empty interior in Q1. If (i) holds, (64.6) of Theorem 64(b) gives (ii). If (ii) holds, then
sigma Omega >= 0 on Q1; sigma = -1 would give Omega <= 0 on Q1, which Theorem 21(a) excludes, so sigma = 1 and (iii)
holds. If (iii) holds, Theorem 21(a) excludes a0 < 0, so sigma = 1, no point of Q1 has sigma Omega < 0, and no ray
carries the middle sign -sigma, which is (i). Under (iii), Theorem 57(a) gives a0 > 0, (H1) and Theta > 0 on Q1 at
beta > 2. If B is nonempty, the last assertion is that of Theorem 64(c), whose empty-interior hypothesis is supplied by
(b). QED.

### Theorem 83 (beta = 2: every A2-broad profile has an invariant region of potential flow in the open quadrant)

Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile. Put W = 2X + U, Z = {W = 0}, Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, let Phi_t be the flow
of W, and let H and G be the smooth angular limits of Theta(r, phi) and r^(1/2) Omega(r, phi) from Theorem 36, as in
Theorem 63. A zero of W has spectrum {0, 4} if the eigenvalues of DW there are 0 and 4.

(a) There exist a real number c, a nonempty open connected set S contained in Q1 and a nonempty open interval J
    contained in (0, pi/2) such that S is invariant for every real time, has infinite area, Theta = c and Omega = 0 on
    S, and H = c and G = 0 on J. The velocity U is harmonic and real analytic on S. The number c is the temperature of a
    zero of W in the closed first quadrant.

(b) Suppose that Z has infinitely many connected components. Then Z contains a point S0 every neighbourhood of which
    meets infinitely many components of Z, and every such point has spectrum {0, 4}. Every neighbourhood N of such a
    point S0 contains a zero A of W and a nonempty open set D contained in N such that every backward orbit from D
    converges to A, and Theta = Theta(A) and Omega = 0 on D. The zero A is either a hyperbolic source of W or a zero
    with spectrum {0, 4} from which a zero-free half-branch of a local invariant C^2 curve through S0 is outgoing.

(c) Consequently there is no A2-broad profile at beta = 2 for which {Omega = 0} has no interior point in Q1, or for
    which {phi in (0, pi/2): G(phi) = 0} has no interior point. This contains the exclusion of real-analytic velocity in
    Theorem 17, by a different route.

Scope. Part (a) removes the assumption in Theorem 63(b), (c) of an isolated component of index +1 or of finitely many
components. No sign assumption is used, and neither (S) nor (R) of Theorem 48 is assumed. The gap orbits at an
accumulating Q+ are already in Theorem 53(c), and Theorem 56(f) gives their action limit; applying the constructions
(63.9) to (63.13) at their departing ends already gives open sets of constant temperature in that special configuration.
Part (b) extends the argument to every point whose neighbourhoods meet infinitely many zero components, and (a) combines
it with Theorem 63(c). The local cusp estimates and the global saturation argument are those of Theorem 63. The theorem
does not identify c with M = Theta(Q+) or with zero, does not decide whether Q+ is outgoing or incoming, and does not
exclude accumulation of zeros. It neither constructs nor excludes an A2-broad profile possessing such a region. It is a
necessary condition on a hypothetical A2-broad profile at beta = 2, not an existence or nonexistence result for the full
class.

Proof. Uniform sublinearity of U gives R_* with X.W(X) >= |X|^2 for |X| >= R_*, as in (63.4); hence Z is a compact
subset of the disc of radius R_*. If Z has finitely many connected components, (a) is Theorem 63(c). Assume from now on
that Z has infinitely many components.

Choose points X_n in pairwise distinct components of Z. By compactness a subsequence converges to a point S0 of Z, and
every neighbourhood of S0 contains X_n for infinitely many n, hence meets infinitely many components. Let S0 be any
point of Z with this property. If det DW(S0) were nonzero, the inverse function theorem would make S0 an isolated point
of Z, and a small disc about S0 would meet only the component {S0}. Hence det DW(S0) = 0. Since the trace of DW is div
W = 4, the spectrum of DW(S0) is {0, 4}.

Take a local invariant C^2 centre curve through S0 (centre manifold theorem, as in Theorems 35, 51 and 63) and a C^2
chart (s, z) on a neighbourhood N0 of S0 whose image is (-d0, d0) x (-e0, e0), with S0 at (0, 0) and the curve equal to
{z = 0}. As in (63.10), invariance of {z = 0} and division give

    z' = a(s, z) z, s' = b(s) + z c0(s, z),

with a and c0 continuous and b of class C^1. The linearization of the transformed field at a zero (s, 0) is the
upper triangular matrix with diagonal entries b'(s) and a(s, 0), and it is conjugate to DW at the corresponding zero
of W, so the two diagonal entries are the eigenvalues there and their sum is 4. At S0 the curve is tangent to the
kernel of DW(S0), so b'(0) = 0 and a(0, 0) = 4. Shrinking d0 and e0 we may assume a >= 2 and |b'| <= 1/4 on the
chart, and |c0| <= C0. Then z' = 0 forces z = 0, so the zeros of W in N0 are exactly the points (s, 0) with s in
K = {s in (-d0, d0): b(s) = 0}, a relatively closed set containing 0.

We claim that on one side of 0, say on s > 0 after the change of orientation s -> -s (which replaces b(s) by -b(-s) and
preserves the form above), K meets (0, e) and does not contain (0, e), for every e in (0, d0). Otherwise there is e in
(0, d0) such that each of K cap (0, e) and K cap (-e, 0) is empty or the whole interval. Then K cap (-e, e) is an
interval containing 0, and the zeros of W in the chart preimage N_e of (-e, e) x (-e0, e0) form a connected set
containing S0. Every component of Z meeting N_e then contains S0, so N_e meets only one component, contrary to the
choice of S0.

Given a neighbourhood N of S0, choose e in (0, d0) and h in (0, e0) such that the closure of the chart preimage V of the
rectangle (-e, e) x (-h, h) is contained in N and in N0. Choose s1 in (0, e) outside K, then k in K cap (0, s1), then s2
in (0, k) outside K. Let (g1, g2) be the connected component of (-d0, d0) minus K containing s2. Since K meets (0, s2)
and k > s2 lies in K, we have 0 < g1 < s2 < g2 <= k < e and g1, g2 lie in K. The function b has one strict sign on (g1,
g2). If it is negative there, replace s by -s once more; this replaces b(s) by -b(-s), keeps the form above, the bounds
on a, b' and c0 and the rectangle (-e, e) x (-h, h), and maps (g1, g2) onto (-g2, -g1), on which the new b is positive.
Writing (g1, g2) again for the image interval, we may therefore assume b > 0 on (g1, g2), with g1, g2 in K and both in
(-e, e). Let A be the zero of W with chart coordinates (g1, 0); the flow on the curve departs from A along (g1, g2).
Since b(g1) = 0 < b(s) for g1 < s < g2, b'(g1) >= 0.

If b'(g1) > 0, the eigenvalues of DW(A) are b'(g1) > 0 and a(g1, 0) >= 2, so A is a hyperbolic source. The construction
(63.9) in the proof of Theorem 63 gives a sublevel ellipsoid D, as small as we wish and hence contained in V, which is
open, bounded, of positive area and backward invariant, and whose backward orbits converge to A.

If b'(g1) = 0, then a(g1, 0) = 4, and in the chart translated by s -> s - g1 the field has the form (63.10) at A, with
b > 0 on (0, delta] for every delta < g2 - g1. The bounds (63.11) hold on the chart, with eta C0 <= 1/2, and, since the
translated b tends to 0 at A, for small delta the closure of the cusp (63.12) lies in the translated chart image of V.
The estimates (63.13) and the paragraph following them in the proof of Theorem 63 show that this cusp D is open,
bounded, of positive area and backward invariant, and that every backward orbit from D converges to A. The curve {z = 0}
is tangent at A to the kernel of the linearization, and its half-branch (g1, g2) is zero-free and outgoing from A.

In either case temperature transport at beta = 2 and continuity at A give Theta = Theta(A) on D. Since D is open,
Theta_x = 0 there. Backward invariance of D and (V) give (63.14), with A in place of R. Its left side stays bounded as
tau tends to infinity, since the argument tends to A, so Omega = 0 on D. This proves (b), with the existence of S0 shown
above.

For (a), we use the remaining part of the proof of Theorem 63(b), from the paragraph on reflection to the end. Besides
the standing A2 equations and parities, the completeness of the flow, the identities (63.4) (in particular det D
Phi_t = exp(4t)) and Theorem 36, that argument uses no further property of A or of its zero component. Reflect D so that
its intersection with Q1 is nonempty and choose a connected component D1 of that intersection; it is open, bounded, of
positive area and backward invariant. With S = union_(t >= 0) Phi_t(D1), the argument (63.15), (63.16) gives the set S,
the interval J and the constant c. The constant c is the temperature of the reflected zero in the closed first quadrant;
it equals Theta(A) or -Theta(A) according to the reflection used. This proves (a).

For (c), the first two assertions follow from (a), since S is a nonempty open subset of Q1 on which Omega = 0 and J is a
nonempty open interval on which G = 0. If U is real analytic on R^2, so is Omega = d_y U_1 - d_x U_2; it vanishes on the
nonempty open set S, hence on the connected plane, contrary to Omega = b0 x y + O(|X|^4) with 5 b0 = 2 a0 != 0. QED.

### Theorem 84 (beta > 2: under the strict far-field vorticity sign, nondegeneracy forces (H1))

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2, and use the notation of Theorem 77:
sigma = sgn(a0), Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0}, w(x) = W_1(x, 0), v(y) = W_2(0, y),
P = (x1,0), and (ND) is the condition that det DW(Q) != 0 for every zero Q of W in the closed first quadrant. Let G be
the angular vorticity function of Theorem 81, and write (FG) for the condition of Theorem 81(b): sigma G > 0 on (0,
pi/2), sigma G'(0) > 0 and sigma G'(pi/2) < 0.

(a) Under (FG), every orbit of W in Q1 on which Omega vanishes identically is bounded. In particular, every
    nonstationary orbit in Q1 whose backward limit is a hyperbolic saddle of W is bounded.

(b) Under (FG) and (ND), (H1) holds. Consequently, B is bounded, possibly empty, and the conclusions of Theorems 75(a),
    75(b) and 75(c) apply.

Scope. Part (b) holds for every beta > 2. In particular it removes, under (FG), the possibility left open by Theorem
77(b): a positive zero of v with beta = N/M in lowest terms, N even and M odd. By Theorem 78(c), in that case the
unstable branch in Q1 from the first positive y-axis zero does not meet the closure of B. Thus the containment argument
in Theorem 77 does not bound this branch. The additional input here is that Omega vanishes on that branch (Theorem
46(b)) while sigma Omega > 0 near infinity in Q1 (Theorem 81(b)); this bounds the branch whether or not it meets the
closure of B. No ray condition is assumed. Zeros of W in Q1 are allowed, but (ND) requires each of them to be
nondegenerate. Theorem 75(d) assumes in addition that Omega >= 0 throughout Q1, which is not derived here. The theorem
does not show that B is empty or that a0 > 0. Neither (FG) nor (ND) is proved for A2-broad profiles, and at beta = 2 the
condition (FG) is never satisfied (Theorem 81(b)). No existence or nonexistence result for the full A2-broad class is
asserted, and no endpoint follows.

Proof. (a) By Theorem 81(b) there is R > 0 such that sigma Omega > 0 at every point of Q1 with |X| >= R. An orbit in Q1
on which Omega = 0 therefore lies in the disc {|X| < R}. If gamma is a nonstationary orbit in Q1 whose backward limit is
a hyperbolic saddle, Theorem 46(b) gives Omega = 0 on gamma, so gamma is bounded.

(b) By Theorem 81(b), B is bounded, so (BB) of Theorem 77 holds, and Theorem 77(a) shows that w has no zero in (x1,
infinity). By Theorem 52(b) it remains to show that v has no positive zero. Steps 1 and 2 of the proof of Theorem 77 use
only (ND), not (BB): by Step 1, the zeros of W in the closed first quadrant are finitely many, each is a hyperbolic
source or a hyperbolic saddle, and every bounded nonstationary orbit in Q1 converges forward to a saddle S+ and backward
to a zero S-, with Theta = 0 on the orbit and Ly(S+) > Ly(S-); Step 2 is the no-return statement for chains of bounded
orbits.

Suppose v has a positive zero, and let y1 be the first one and Q_y = (0, y1). By the local identities of Section 1,
DW(O) = diag(-(beta + 2), 3 beta + 2), so v'(0) = 3 beta + 2 > 0 and v > 0 on (0, y1). Since W_1(0, y) = 0 for all y and
W_2 is even in x (Setting A2), d_y W_1 and d_x W_2 vanish on the y-axis, so DW(Q_y) = diag(d_x W_1(Q_y), v'(y1)). By
(ND), v'(y1) != 0, hence v'(y1) < 0, and since the trace of DW is 2 beta, DW(Q_y) = diag(2 beta + a, -a) with
a = -v'(y1) > 0. Thus Q_y is a hyperbolic saddle with stable direction along the invariant y-axis, and one of its two
unstable branches, gamma_0, starts into x > 0 near Q_y and hence lies in the invariant set Q1.

Put S_0 = Q_y. We construct inductively bounded nonstationary orbits gamma_0, gamma_1, ... in Q1 and hyperbolic saddles
S_1, S_2, ... in Q1 such that gamma_j has backward limit S_j and forward limit S_(j+1). By (a), gamma_0 is bounded.
Given gamma_0, ..., gamma_j bounded with these limits for indices below j, Step 1 shows that the forward limit S_(j+1)
of gamma_j is a hyperbolic saddle, and Step 2, applied to gamma_0, ..., gamma_j, shows that S_(j+1) lies in Q1. A
hyperbolic saddle in Q1 has two unstable branches; near the saddle they lie in the open set Q1, so by invariance of Q1
they lie in Q1; let gamma_(j+1) be one of them. By (a), gamma_(j+1) is bounded, and its backward limit is S_(j+1). By
Step 1, Ly(S_0) < Ly(S_1) < Ly(S_2) < ..., so the zeros S_j are pairwise distinct. This contradicts the finiteness of
the zeros of W in the closed first quadrant. Hence v has no positive zero, and Theorem 52(b) gives (H1).

Finally, (H1) holds and B is bounded, possibly empty. The hypotheses of Theorem 75(a) to (c) are therefore satisfied,
and those conclusions apply. QED.

### Theorem 85 (beta = 2: real analyticity on the open quadrant is excluded)

Let (2, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile, put W = 2X + U and Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, and let H and G be the angular
limits of Theta(r, phi) and r^(1/2) Omega(r, phi) from Theorem 33(d). Then none of the following holds:

(a) Theta is real analytic on Q1;

(b) Omega is real analytic on Q1; in particular, U is not real analytic on Q1, and neither is W;

(c) H is real analytic on (0, pi/2);

(d) G is real analytic on (0, pi/2).

Scope. Parts (a) to (d) are immediate corollaries of Theorem 83(a), the standing parities and jets, and Theorems 33(d)
and 34(b); parts (b) and (d) also follow from the empty-interior exclusions of Theorem 83(c). Part (b) strengthens the
exclusion of Theorem 17(a) by requiring analyticity only on Q1; the other parts record the corresponding exclusions for
Theta, H and G. Thus at beta = 2, Theta, Omega, U and W cannot be real analytic throughout Q1, and H and G cannot be
real analytic throughout (0, pi/2). This is compatible with local analyticity on the sets of Theorem 83(a): on S, Theta
and Omega are constant and U and W are real analytic, and on J, H and G are constant. These are restricted exclusions.
No existence or nonexistence result for the full A2-broad class at beta = 2 is asserted, and no endpoint follows.

Proof. By Theorem 83(a) there are a real number c, a nonempty open set S contained in Q1 and a nonempty open interval J
contained in (0, pi/2) such that Theta = c and Omega = 0 on S, and H = c and G = 0 on J. The sets Q1 and (0, pi/2) are
connected, so a real analytic function on one of them that is constant on a nonempty open subset is constant on all of
it.

(a) If Theta is real analytic on Q1, then Theta = c on Q1. Theta is continuous and Theta(0, y) = 0 for y > 0 (57.2), so
c is the limit of Theta(x, 1) as x decreases to 0, and c = 0. Then every derivative of Theta vanishes on Q1, and hence
at O, since Theta is smooth on R^2. But Theta = a0 x^2 y + O(|X|^5) gives d_x^2 d_y Theta(O) = 2 a0 != 0.

(b) If Omega is real analytic on Q1, then Omega = 0 on Q1, so every derivative of Omega vanishes on Q1 and at O. But
Omega = b0 x y + O(|X|^4) with b0 = 2 a0/5 != 0 by (57.2) at beta = 2, so d_x d_y Omega(O) = b0 != 0. If U is real
analytic on Q1, so is Omega = d_y U_1 - d_x U_2, and W = 2X + U is real analytic on Q1 exactly when U is.

(c) If H is real analytic on (0, pi/2), then H = c there. H is continuous with H(0) = 0 (Theorem 33(d)), so c = 0. The
symmetries H(-phi) = -H(phi) and H(pi - phi) = H(phi) and the value H(pi/2) = 0 from Theorem 33(d) then give H = 0 on
R/2piZ, contrary to Theorem 33(d), by which H is not identically zero.

(d) If G is real analytic on (0, pi/2), then G = 0 there. G is continuous, zero on both axes, and odd in x and in y
(Theorem 33(d)), that is G(pi - phi) = -G(phi) and G(-phi) = -G(phi); hence G = 0 on R/2piZ, contrary to Theorem 34(b).
QED.

### Theorem 86 (beta > 2: consequences of the strict far-field vorticity sign)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta > 2, and use the notation of Theorem 84:
sigma = sgn(a0), h = 1/beta, Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0}, w(x) = W_1(x, 0), v(y) = W_2(0,
y), P = (x1, 0), Z = {W = 0}, the condition (ND), and the condition (FG) of Theorem 81(b) on the angular vorticity
function G. Write X = r e(phi) with e(phi) = (cos phi, sin phi), put m(phi) = min(phi, pi/2 - phi), and let S_B be the
set of phi in (0, pi/2) such that sigma Omega(r e(phi)) < 0 for some r > 0, as in (64.3). Assume (FG).

(a) There are c > 0 and R > 0 such that sigma Omega(r e(phi)) >= c r^(-h) m(phi) for all r >= R and all phi in [0,
    pi/2]. In particular {Omega = 0} cap Q1 is contained in {|X| < R}, and r^h sigma Omega(r e(phi)) tends to sigma
    G(phi) > 0 as r tends to infinity, for every phi in (0, pi/2).

(b) For every phi in S_B and every M > 0 there are radii 0 < r1 < r2 < r3 with r3 > M at which Omega(r e(phi)) has the
    strict signs (sigma, -sigma, sigma). Consequently some ray in Q1 carries three radii with these strict signs if and
    only if B is nonempty. If B is empty, then a0 > 0, Omega >= 0 on Q1, Z = {O, P, -P}, (H1) holds and Theta > 0 on Q1.
    If a0 < 0, then B is nonempty.

(c) Suppose that every positive zero of w and every positive zero of v is simple, and that Omega vanishes identically on
    a neighbourhood of every zero S of W in Q1 with det DW(S) = 0. Then (ND) holds. In particular, under (FG) the
    hypothesis (ND') of Theorem 78(b) implies (ND), and (H1) then holds by Theorem 84(b).

(d) Suppose (ND) holds, or the hypothesis of (c). Then Z = {O, P, -P}, sigma Theta > 0 on Q1, and {Theta = 0} is the
    union of the two coordinate axes. Every point of Q1 has backward limit P. Every orbit in Q1 escapes, its polar angle
    converges to an angle phi_inf in (0, pi/2), and along it |X|^h sigma Omega(X) tends to sigma G(phi_inf) > 0.

(e) The set {Theta = 0} cap Q1 has empty interior.

Scope. Part (a) records the estimate obtained in the proof of Theorem 81(b), and its inclusion and limit are immediate
consequences; the factor m(phi) cannot be removed, since Omega vanishes on the axes, and no lower bound independent of
the angle is asserted. Part (b) is a corollary of Theorem 81(b) and the jet at the origin: under (FG), which gives
bounded B by Theorem 81(b), it yields on every angle of S_B the triples that Theorems 64(c) and 82(d) give on dense sets
of angles under bounded B together with the empty-interior hypothesis of Theorem 64(c) or with (ND), respectively; it is
a strengthening for profiles satisfying (FG), not of those bounded-B statements. Its statements for empty B restate
Theorems 21(a) and 57(a), and its last statement follows from Theorem 21(a) alone; it does not show that B is empty or
that a0 > 0. Part (c) is the substantive addition: under (FG) its hypotheses imply (ND), without the isolatedness clause
of (ND'). Part (d) is a consequence of Theorems 84(b), 8, 38 and 50 and reflection, with the vorticity limit of Theorem
81 evaluated along the orbits; its additional reach is the application under the hypothesis of (c). It gives no global
sign of Omega: B is bounded but may be nonempty, and zeros of Omega in Q1, as well as bounded open subsets of Q1 on
which Omega vanishes, are not excluded. The limits sigma G(phi_inf) tend to 0 as phi_inf approaches either axis, so they
have no positive lower bound uniform over the orbits. Part (e) gives under (FG) the exclusion of open zero sets of Theta
in Q1 that Theorem 80(b) gives under (ND). Neither (FG) nor (ND) is proved for A2-broad profiles, and at beta = 2 the
condition (FG) is never satisfied (Theorem 81(b)). No existence or nonexistence result for the full A2-broad class is
asserted, and no endpoint follows.

Proof. (a) The proof of Theorem 81(b) gives R1 >= 1, C1 >= 0 and c1 > 0 such that sigma Omega(r e(phi)) >= r^(-h) m(phi)
(c1 - C1 r^(-h)) for r >= R1 and 0 < phi < pi/2. Put R = max(R1, (2 C1/c1)^beta) and c = c1/2. For r >= R the bracket is
at least c1/2, which gives the bound for 0 < phi < pi/2; at phi = 0 and phi = pi/2 both sides vanish, since Omega is odd
in x and in y. Hence sigma Omega > 0 on Q1 cap {|X| >= R}, which gives the inclusion. The last assertion is the uniform
convergence of r^h Omega(r, .) to G (Theorem 81) together with sigma G > 0 on (0, pi/2).

(b) Fix phi in S_B and M > 0, and choose r2 > 0 with sigma Omega(r2 e(phi)) < 0. By (57.2), Omega = b0 x y + O(|X|^4)
with b0 = 2 a0/(2 beta + 1), so sigma b0 = |b0| > 0 and sigma Omega(r e(phi)) = r^2 (|b0| cos(phi) sin(phi) + O(r^2)),
which is positive for all sufficiently small r > 0 because cos(phi) sin(phi) > 0; choose such an r1 < r2. By (a),
r3 = max(R, r2, M) + 1 satisfies sigma Omega(r3 e(phi)) > 0. This gives the triple. If B is nonempty, the polar angle
of any of its points lies in S_B, so a triple exists; conversely, the middle radius of a triple gives a point of B. If
B is empty, then sigma Omega >= 0 on Q1. Theorem 21(a) excludes Omega <= 0 on Q1, so sigma = 1, that is a0 > 0, and
Omega >= 0 on Q1; Theorem 57(a) then gives Z = {O, P, -P}, (H1) and Theta > 0 on Q1 (57.4). If a0 < 0, Theorem 21(a)
shows that Omega takes both signs in Q1; in particular Omega > 0 somewhere in Q1, and such points lie in B = {X in Q1
: -Omega(X) < 0}.

(c) By (a), every subset of Q1 on which Omega vanishes lies in the disc {|X| < R} and has area at most pi R^2. Let S be
a zero of W in Q1 with det DW(S) = 0, and choose a connected open neighbourhood V of S, contained in Q1, on which
Omega = 0. If Theta = 0 on V, Theorem 64(f) shows that the flow saturation of V is contained in Q1, has infinite area
and carries Omega = 0, a contradiction. Otherwise Theta is nonzero somewhere on V, and Theorem 64(e) gives W = ((2
beta - c) x + e1, c y + e2) on V with real constants c, e1, e2. Then det DW(S) = c (2 beta - c) = 0, so c = 0 or c = 2
beta. If c = 0, then W(S) = 0 forces e2 = 0, and Z cap V is the intersection of V with the vertical line through S; if
c = 2 beta, then e1 = 0, and Z cap V is the intersection of V with the horizontal line through S. Let I be the connected
component of this intersection that contains S. It is an open segment, hence a connected one-dimensional embedded
C^infinity submanifold of R^2 without boundary, and it is contained in Z. By Theorem 44(e), (e1), the set B_I = {X :
pi(X) in I} is open, invariant, of infinite area, and Theta = Omega = 0 on B_I. The complement of Q1 is closed and
invariant under the flow, since W_1(0, y) = 0 and W_2(x, 0) = 0 by the parities, so the backward limit of a point
outside Q1 lies outside Q1. Hence B_I is contained in Q1, again a contradiction. Thus W has no zero S in Q1 with det
DW(S) = 0. On the positive x-axis, w(x) = beta x + U_1(x, 0) is positive for all large x since U = o(|X|), and w(0) = 0
with w'(0) = -(beta + 2) < 0, so the positive zeros of w lie in a compact subinterval of (0, infinity); being simple,
they are isolated, hence finitely many. The same holds for v, with v'(0) = 3 beta + 2 > 0. Theorem 27(x), (y), applied
to the complete lists of these zeros, shows that DW is diagonal at each of them, equal to diag(beta + 2, beta - 2) or
diag(-(beta + 2)/m, 2 beta + (beta + 2)/m) on the x-axis and to diag(2 beta + (3 beta + 2)/n, -(3 beta + 2)/n),
diag((beta - 2)/2, (3 beta + 2)/2) or diag(-(beta + 2), 3 beta + 2) on the y-axis, with positive integers m and n; each
of these matrices is nonsingular for beta > 2. Finally DW(O) = diag(-(beta + 2), 3 beta + 2). Hence det DW != 0 at every
zero of W in the closed first quadrant, which is (ND). The hypothesis (ND') of Theorem 78(b) contains the two
assumptions of (c), and Theorem 84(b) applies.

(d) Under the hypothesis of (c), (ND) holds by (c); in either case Theorem 84(b) gives (H1), that is Z cap
closure(Q1) = {O, P}. W_1 is odd in x and even in y, and W_2 is even in x and odd in y, so Z is invariant under both
reflections and Z = {O, P, -P}. Theorem 8(i), (ii) gives backward limit P for every point of Q1 and sigma Theta > 0 on
Q1. Theta is even in x and odd in y and vanishes on the y-axis, so it vanishes on both axes and is nonzero on each open
quadrant; this is the description of {Theta = 0}. By Theorem 50(b) every orbit in Q1 escapes, and its escape angle, the
limit of the polar angle along the orbit (Theorem 38), lies in (0, pi/2). Along such an orbit |X| tends to infinity and
the polar angle tends to phi_inf, so the uniform convergence of r^h Omega(r, .) to G and the continuity of G give |X|^h
Omega(X) -> G(phi_inf), and sigma G(phi_inf) > 0 by (FG).

(e) If {Theta = 0} cap Q1 had an interior point, it would contain an open disc V with Theta = 0 on V. Then grad
Theta = 0 on V, so V is contained in {grad Theta = 0} and Omega = 0 on V by Theorem 44(d). By Theorem 64(f), the flow
saturation of V is contained in Q1, has infinite area and carries Omega = 0; by (a) it lies in {|X| < R}, a
contradiction. QED.

### Theorem 87 (the negative branch: amplitude and area of the positive vorticity set)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile in Setting A2 with beta >= 2 and a0 < 0. Let Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0},
let P = (L, 0) be the first positive x-axis zero of W (Theorem 2), let N_L be the kernel (55.1), and put

  (87.1) B = {X in Q1 : Omega(X) > 0},    |B| = the area of B,    M_B = sup_B Omega.

Then B is nonempty and open, 0 < M_B < infinity and 0 < |B| <= infinity.

(a) For every measurable set E contained in Q1 with finite area A,

  (87.2) int_E N_L dY <= sqrt(A/pi).

(b) If |B| < infinity, then

  (87.3) beta L < int_B N_L Omega dY <= M_B sqrt(|B|/pi),

and in particular

  (87.4) M_B |B|^(1/2) > sqrt(pi) beta L.

(c) Let beta > 2 and assume the far-field sign condition of Theorem 81(b). Then B is bounded, and (87.4) holds. Thus no
A2-broad profile with beta > 2, a0 < 0 and this condition satisfies M_B |B|^(1/2) <= sqrt(pi) beta L.

Proof. B is open since Omega is continuous, and nonempty by Theorem 21(a). Omega is bounded on Q1: it is continuous, and
Omega = O(r^(-h)) at infinity with h = 1/beta (Theorem 36 at beta = 2, Theorem 41 at beta > 2). Hence 0 < M_B <
infinity, and |B| > 0 since B is open and nonempty.

(a) Put p_L(x, y) = y/(pi((x - L)^2 + y^2)) for y > 0. For (x, y) in Q1,

  N_L(x, y) = (y/pi) [1/((x - L)^2 + y^2) - 1/((x + L)^2 + y^2)],

so 0 < N_L < p_L on Q1. For t > 0, completing the square gives

  {p_L > t} = {(x - L)^2 + (y - 1/(2 pi t))^2 < 1/(4 pi^2 t^2)},

an open disc in the upper half-plane of area 1/(4 pi t^2). By Tonelli's theorem, applied to nonnegative functions,

  int_E p_L dY = int_0^infinity |E cap {p_L > t}| dt <= int_0^infinity min(A, 1/(4 pi t^2)) dt.

For A > 0 split the last integral at t0 = 1/(2 sqrt(pi A)); its value is A t0 + 1/(4 pi t0) = sqrt(A/pi). The case
A = 0 is immediate. Since N_L < p_L on E, (87.2) follows.

(b) Write Omega_+ = max(Omega, 0) and Omega_- = max(-Omega, 0); then Omega_+ = Omega on B and Omega_+ = 0 on Q1 \ B. By
(62.4) of Theorem 62(b), which holds for every beta >= 2 with a0 < 0, the integrals below converge absolutely and

  int_B N_L Omega dY = int_Q1 N_L Omega_+ dY = beta L + int_Q1 N_L Omega_- dY > beta L,

the last inequality because Omega_- >= |b0| x y/2 > 0 on Q1 cap {r < delta} (Theorem 62(b)) and N_L > 0 on Q1. Since
0 < Omega <= M_B on B, part (a) with E = B gives

  int_B N_L Omega dY <= M_B int_B N_L dY <= M_B sqrt(|B|/pi).

This is (87.3), and (87.4) follows by multiplying by sqrt(pi).

(c) For beta > 2, the condition of Theorem 81(b) implies that B = {X in Q1 : sigma Omega(X) < 0}, with sigma = sgn(a0)
= -1, is bounded (Theorem 81(b)); hence |B| < infinity and (b) applies. QED.

Scope. This is an immediate corollary of (62.4) and the elementary estimate (a): part (a) is a rearrangement estimate
for the kernel of the first identity of (55.3), (b) combines it with (62.4), and (c) adds only Theorem 81(b). (87.4) is
a necessary condition on the size of the positive vorticity set of the negative branch, not an exclusion of that branch.
It is invariant under the spatial scaling of Section 1: M_B is unchanged, while |B|^(1/2) and L are multiplied by the
same factor. It complements (62.5), which bounds sup_Q1 r^h Omega_+ from below in terms of the infimum radius of the
positive set. The constant in (87.2) is sharp: for the discs D_a = {(x - L)^2 + (y - a)^2 < a^2} with 0 < a < L,
int_{D_a} N_L dY = 4 L^2 a/(4 L^2 + a^2), so int_{D_a} N_L dY/|D_a|^(1/2) tends to 1/sqrt(pi) as a tends to 0; this
gives no optimality of (87.4) among profiles. The report proves no upper bound sufficient to contradict (87.4) under the
hypotheses of the first of the three sign cases in Section 7 (beta > 2, a0 < 0, the far-field sign condition of Theorem
81(b), and nondegenerate zeros of W in the closed first quadrant). This case remains open; the present result excludes
the additional condition M_B |B|^(1/2) <= sqrt(pi) beta L. As conditions on scalar vorticity fields, smallness of the
product of the positive amplitude and the square root of the positive area does not imply the ray prohibitions in
Theorems 62(a) and 64(b). The following example makes no assertion about profiles. With h = 1/beta and epsilon > 0, the
smooth function

  omega_eps = epsilon x y (r^2 - 1)(4 - r^2)/(1 + r^2)^(3 + h/2),

is odd in x and in y. On Q1 it is negative near O (omega_eps = -4 epsilon x y + O(|X|^4)) and in the far field (r^h
omega_eps(r e(phi)) tends to -epsilon cos(phi) sin(phi)), and positive exactly on {X in Q1 : 1 < r < 2}, of area 3 pi/4,
so that every ray in Q1 carries strict signs (-, +, -); its supremum there is at most 9 epsilon/16, hence the product of
its supremum on the positive set in Q1 and the square root of the area of that set is at most 9 sqrt(3 pi) epsilon/32,
which is smaller than any prescribed positive number for small epsilon. This function is not part of a profile.

### Theorem 88 (beta >= 2: an energy flux identity with pressure and a weighted condition on the flux)

Let (beta, Theta, Omega, U) be an A2-broad profile with beta >= 2, and put h = 1/beta, q = 1 - 2h, n = 4 - 2h and
c = 2 beta + 2 (Theorem 9). Let W = beta X + U, Q1 = {x > 0, y > 0}, D_R = Q1 cap {|X| < R}, Gamma_R = Q1 cap {|X| = R},
U_r = U.e_r, and

  (88.1) e = |U|^2/2 + y Theta.

(a) There is a unique C^infinity function Pi on R^2 with Pi(0) = 0 and

  (88.2) W.grad U + (1 - beta) U + grad Pi = -Theta e_2.

Pi is even in x and in y, Pi = -((c^2 - c) x^2 + (c^2 + c) y^2)/2 + O(|X|^4) at O, and

  (88.3) div(W e + Pi U) = (4 beta - 2) e   on R^2.

(b) For R > 0 put F(R) = int_{D_R} e dX and Q(R) = int_{Gamma_R} (e + Pi) U_r ds. Then, for every R > 0,

  (88.4) beta R F'(R) - beta n F(R) = -Q(R),    R^(-n) F(R) = -(1/beta) int_0^R s^(-n-1) Q(s) ds,

where the last integral converges absolutely at 0, and, as R tends to 0,

  (88.5) F(R) = pi c^2 R^4/16 + O(R^6),    Q(R) = -pi c^2 R^4/8 + O(R^6).

(c) In polar coordinates, let f be the uniform limit of r^(-q) Theta(r, .) and G the uniform limit of r^h Omega(r, .),
and let P be the unique 2 pi-periodic solution of -(P'' + (2 - h)^2 P) = G (unique since 2 - h is not an integer; f = H
and P of Theorem 36 at beta = 2, f and P of Theorem 42 at beta > 2). Then

  (88.6) R^(-n) F(R) -> C_inf := (1/n) int_0^{pi/2} [(P'(phi)^2 + (2 - h)^2 P(phi)^2)/2 + f(phi) sin(phi)] dphi

as R tends to infinity. Moreover Q(R) = O(R^(n-h)) as R tends to infinity, with a constant depending on the profile, so
int_0^infinity s^(-n-1) Q(s) ds converges absolutely, and it equals -beta C_inf. These conclusions require no sign
assumption on Theta.

(d) If Theta >= 0 on Q1 (for beta > 2 this holds when a0 > 0 and (H1) holds, by Theorem 8(ii)), then F(R) > 0 and
int_0^R s^(-n-1) Q(s) ds < 0 for every R > 0, and C_inf > 0, so int_0^infinity s^(-n-1) Q(s) ds = -beta C_inf < 0.

Proof. (a) Put A = W.grad U + (1 - beta) U and rcurl V = d_y V_1 - d_x V_2 for smooth vector fields V, so that rcurl
U = -Lap Psi = Omega. For smooth V, rcurl((X.grad) V) = rcurl V + X.grad(rcurl V), and, since div U = 0, rcurl((U.grad)
U) = U.grad Omega. Hence rcurl A = beta (Omega + X.grad Omega) + U.grad Omega + (1 - beta) Omega = W.grad
Omega + Omega = Theta_x by (V), while rcurl(Theta e_2) = -Theta_x. The smooth field A + Theta e_2 therefore has zero
rcurl on R^2, and Pi(X) = -int_0^1 (A + Theta e_2)(tX).X dt is the unique smooth solution of (88.2) with Pi(0) = 0. U_1
and W_1 are odd in x and even in y, U_2 and W_2 are even in x and odd in y, and Theta is even in x and odd in y; so the
first component of A + Theta e_2 is odd in x and even in y, the second is even in x and odd in y, and Pi is even in x
and in y. Near O, Psi = c x y + O(|X|^4) by Theorem 9 and parity, so U = (-c x, c y) + O(|X|^3), W = ((beta - c) x,
(beta + c) y) + O(|X|^3) and Theta = O(|X|^3); inserting these into (88.2) gives grad Pi = -((c^2 - c) x, (c^2 + c)
y) + O(|X|^3), whence the expansion of Pi. Taking the dot product of (88.2) with U, and using U.((W.grad)
U) = W.grad(|U|^2/2) and U.grad Pi = div(Pi U), gives W.grad(|U|^2/2) + div(Pi U) = (beta - 1)|U|^2 - Theta U_2. By (T)
and W_2 = beta y + U_2, W.grad(y Theta) = (beta - 2) y Theta + W_2 Theta = 2 (beta - 1) y Theta + Theta U_2. Adding,
W.grad e + div(Pi U) = 2 (beta - 1) e, and div(W e) = W.grad e + 2 beta e gives (88.3).

(b) Psi vanishes on both axes (it is odd in x and in y), so U_2 = Psi_x = 0 and W_2 = 0 on {y = 0}, and U_1 = -Psi_y = 0
and W_1 = 0 on {x = 0}: the normal components of W e + Pi U vanish on the two straight parts of the boundary of D_R. On
Gamma_R the outer normal is e_r and W.e_r = beta R + U_r. The divergence theorem on the sector D_R and (88.3) give beta
R int_{Gamma_R} e ds + Q(R) = (4 beta - 2) F(R). Since F'(R) = int_{Gamma_R} e ds and 4 beta - 2 = beta n, this is the
first identity of (88.4); it is equivalent to (R^(-n) F)' = -R^(-n-1) Q/beta. Near O, |U|^2 = c^2 |X|^2 + O(|X|^4) and y
Theta = O(|X|^4), so e = c^2 |X|^2/2 + O(|X|^4), and integration over the quarter disc gives the first part of (88.5).
With the expansion of Pi, e + Pi = (c/2)(x^2 - y^2) + O(|X|^4) = (c/2) r^2 cos(2 phi) + O(r^4), and U_r = -c r cos(2
phi) + O(r^3). Hence Q(R) = R int_0^{pi/2} (e + Pi) U_r dphi = -(c^2 R^4/2) int_0^{pi/2} cos(2 phi)^2
dphi + O(R^6) = -pi c^2 R^4/8 + O(R^6). Thus s^(-n-1) Q(s) = O(s^(2h-1)) is integrable at 0, rho^(-n)
F(rho) = O(rho^(2h)) tends to 0 as rho tends to 0, and integrating (R^(-n) F)' from rho to R and letting rho tend to 0
gives the second identity of (88.4).

(c) By Theorem 36(b) at beta = 2 and Theorem 42(b) at beta > 2, for |X| >= 1 (after enlarging the constants, since all
terms are bounded on compact annuli), U = u_0 + O(r^(1-2h)) with u_0 = r^(1-h) (-P' e_r + (2 - h) P e_phi), and
Theta = r^q f + O(r^(q-h)). Hence |U|^2 = r^(2-2h) (P'^2 + (2 - h)^2 P^2) + O(r^(2-3h)) and y Theta = r^(2-2h) f
sin(phi) + O(r^(2-3h)), so e = r^(2-2h) epsilon(phi) + O(r^(2-3h)), where epsilon is the integrand in (88.6).
Integrating over D_R \ D_1 gives F(R) = F(1) + ((R^n - 1)/n) int_0^{pi/2} epsilon dphi + O(1 + R^(n-h)), since
n - h = 4 - 3h > 0. Dividing by R^n gives (88.6), and (88.6) with the second identity of (88.4) gives the value of the
weighted integral over (0, infinity). Integrating the expansion of e over Gamma_R gives F'(R) = int_{Gamma_R} e
ds = R^(n-1) int_0^{pi/2} epsilon dphi + O(R^(n-h-1)) = n C_inf R^(n-1) + O(R^(n-h-1)) for R >= 1, and F(R) = C_inf
R^n + O(R^(n-h)); so the first identity of (88.4) gives Q(R) = beta (n F(R) - R F'(R)) = O(R^(n-h)). Hence
int_R^infinity s^(-n-1) |Q(s)| ds = O(R^(-h)), and the integral over (0, infinity) converges absolutely.

(d) If Theta >= 0 on Q1, then e >= |U|^2/2 >= 0 on Q1, and U is nonzero on Q1 near O, so F(R) > 0 for every R > 0; the
second identity of (88.4) gives the sign of the weighted integral. f >= 0 on [0, pi/2], as a limit of nonnegative
functions. Since Omega is odd in x and in y, G(-phi) = -G(phi) and G(pi - phi) = -G(phi), and by uniqueness
P(-phi) = -P(phi) and P(pi - phi) = -P(phi). Thus, if P vanished identically on [0, pi/2], it would vanish on the whole
circle, and G would vanish identically, contrary to Theorem 34(b) at beta = 2 or Theorem 41(b) at beta > 2. Therefore P
is not identically zero on [0, pi/2]. Hence the integrand of (88.6) is nonnegative and not identically zero on [0,
pi/2], and C_inf > 0. QED.

Scope. (88.3) is the energy law of the profile equations: the dot product of the velocity form (88.2) of (V) with U,
added to y times (T). The normalization Pi(0) = 0 does not affect Q, since int_{Gamma_R} U_r ds = 0 (Psi vanishes at
both ends of Gamma_R). Under the hypothesis Theta >= 0 on Q1 (supplied for beta > 2 by a0 > 0 and (H1), and an
assumption at beta = 2), part (d) is a necessary condition on the profile: every partial integral int_0^R s^(-n-1) Q(s)
ds is strictly negative. It is consistent with (88.5), which already makes Q negative at small radii. Part (c) bounds
Q(R) by a profile-dependent multiple of R^(n-h) at large radii, but gives no pointwise sign of Q at intermediate or
large radii. No general sign of C_inf when Theta takes negative values in Q1 is established, in particular for beta > 2
and a0 < 0 under (H1). The theorem neither constructs nor excludes a profile.

## 4. An exact family satisfying the local identities at O, at P and along [0, x1]

For every beta > 0, with b = beta + 2 and d = 2 beta + 1,
  Psi = (beta x + (b/2) sin 2x) y,  Omega = 2 b sin(2x) y,  Theta = 2 b d sin^2(x) y
solves (P) exactly on R^2 (symbolic check in the accompanying artifacts) and has the A2 parity and jet (a0 = 2bd > 0,
c = 2 beta + 2). On [0, pi/2] it satisfies the local identities and conclusions of Theorem 2: w = -(b/2) sin 2x, x1 = pi/2,
w'(x1) = beta + 2, f(x1) != 0. It is not admissible: w(x)/x -> 0 rather than beta, U_1(x,0)/x -> -beta, and (G) fails.
Consequently the local identities at O, at P and along [0, x1] cannot by themselves exclude the A2 class (with
a0 > 0; dilation preserves the sign of a0); an obstruction must use more, for instance the sublinear growth
U = o(|X|) globally. Particular jets or axis data can still fail compatibility conditions (Theorems 14, 26, 29).

Remark 4.1 (the separated class and the sign of a0). Write Psi = w(x) y, Theta = y F(x) and v = beta x - w, so that
W = (v(x), (2 beta - v'(x)) y) and Omega = v''(x) y. Then (P) holds if and only if
  v F' + (beta + 2 - v') F = 0,   F' = v v''' + (2 beta + 1 - v') v''.                                          (4.1)
The A2 parity and jet mean that v is odd with v'(0) = -(beta + 2) and F is even with F(0) = 0; then a0 = F''(0)/2.
Write v = -(beta + 2) x + sum_{m >= 1} v_{2m+1} x^{2m+1} and F = sum_{m >= 1} F_{2m} x^{2m} for the Taylor series. In
the first equation of (4.1) the coefficient of x^2 vanishes identically, and for m >= 2 the coefficient of x^{2m} is
-(2m - 2)(beta + 2) F_{2m} plus a polynomial in F_2, ..., F_{2m-2}, v_3, ..., v_{2m-1}. In the second equation, written
as F' - v v''' - (2 beta + 1 - v') v'' = 0, the coefficient of x is 2 F_2 - 6 (2 beta + 1) v_3, and for m >= 2 the
coefficient of x^{2m-1} is (2m + 1)(2m)((2m - 4) beta + 4m - 5) v_{2m+1} plus a polynomial in v_3, ..., v_{2m-1},
F_2, ..., F_{2m}. Both leading factors are nonzero for beta > 0, so all Taylor coefficients are determined by v_3, and
a0 = F_2 = 3 (2 beta + 1) v_3. The dilation (v, F)(x) -> (v(lam x)/lam, F(lam x)), lam > 0, preserves (4.1) and
multiplies v_3 by lam^2. The family above has v = -(b/2) sin 2x and v_3 = 2b/3. The fields
  Psi = (beta x + (b/2) sinh 2x) y,  Omega = -2 b sinh(2x) y,  Theta = -2 b d sinh^2(x) y
also solve (P) exactly on R^2 (symbolic check in the accompanying artifacts), with v = -(b/2) sinh 2x, v_3 = -2b/3,
the A2 parity, c = 2 beta + 2 and a0 = -2bd < 0. Hence every solution of (P) of the separated form with the A2 parity and jet coincides near 0 with a dilate of one
of these two families, the sign of v_3 being the sign of a0. If w is real analytic near 0 this follows from the Taylor
coefficients. If w is only smooth, (v, F) and the matching dilate (v*, F*) have the same Taylor series at 0, so their
difference is flat there. For x > 0 put s = log x, a = v/x, p = v', r = x v'' and H = F; with b = beta + 2 and
d = 2 beta + 1, (4.1) becomes the autonomous system
  da/ds = p - a,  dp/ds = r,  dr/ds = (1 - (d - p)/a) r + (p - b) H/a^2,  dH/ds = (p - b) H/a,
whose right side is smooth near the point (-b, -b, 0, 0) (b > 0), the limit of both solutions Y, Y* as s -> -infinity.
Let L0 be a Lipschitz constant on a neighbourhood of that point and choose s0 so that both solutions stay in it for
s <= s0. Flatness gives |Y(s) - Y*(s)| <= C_N e^{N s} for every N and s <= s0 (division by x and multiplication by x
preserve flatness), and Gronwall on [s, s0] gives |Y(s0) - Y*(s0)| <= C_N e^{L0 s0} e^{(N - L0) s}, which tends to 0
as s -> -infinity for N > L0. So the germs agree on (0, e^{s0}), and by parity near 0. For a0 < 0 the matching dilate
has v*(x) = -(b/(2 lam)) sinh(2 lam x) < 0 for x > 0. Where v != 0, (4.1) is the regular first-order system
v' = p, p' = r, F' = (p - b) F/v, r' = (p - b) F/v^2 - (d - p) r/v (here r = v''). If v had a first zero L > 0,
uniqueness for this system would give v = v* on (0, L), and v(L) = v*(L) < 0 by continuity, a contradiction. Hence
W_1(x, 0) = v(x) < 0 for every x > 0: no separated solution with a0 < 0 has a stagnation point P on the positive x-axis.
Whether the local identities at O, at P and along [0, x1] can be satisfied with a0 < 0 outside the separated class is
not decided here.
