Theta_y = (beta - 2) Theta_y at every zero of W on the x-axis ((T) differentiated in y, with Theta = Theta_x = d_y
W_1 = 0 on that axis by parity); here nu - (beta - 2) and Theta_y are certifiably nonzero, so (T) fails near a certified
point of each field to which the interval computation applies (for the second state, the field with rounded exponents),
and the pointwise ratio of the thermal residual to its normalization has supremum 1 in every punctured neighbourhood of
that zero. The same arithmetic, applied to three stored states of the branch a0 > 0 at beta = 2 (N = 112, 176 and 208,
with the far-field tail rows), certifies in each a nondegenerate saddle of W on the positive x-axis, at
x = 14.1826343893, 14.9730173576 and 15.5183937861, with nu = d_y W_2 = -0.4408146176, -0.2366441216 and -0.1635147426
(mu = 4 - nu) and Theta_y = 63.5023650059, 57.6823872546 and 57.1843947012 (values rounded to the digits shown;
enclosures of width 1e-22; independently checked). At beta = 2 an exact profile has nu = beta - 2 = 0 at such a zero;
here nu and Theta_y are certifiably nonzero, so the same conclusions hold, and the exact centre identities fail for all
three states. The certified |nu| decreases with N, which is compatible with convergence of these zeros and derivatives
to P, where DW(P) = diag(4, 0) at beta = 2 (Theorem 2); their location also moves with N, and no convergence statement
is made. No assertion is made that these zeros are the first positive zeros of W_1, or about the number of zeros. For
the state of the branch a0 < 0 at beta = 2 and N = 208, ball arithmetic at 2048 and 2816 bits, with the logarithmic
Taylor remainder of the canonical inverse bounded explicitly, certifies a unique nondegenerate zero of W in the closed
disc of radius 0.003 about (13.67859, 5.66655) in the open quadrant, and |grad Theta| >= 7.3 on that disc (independently
checked). An exact solution of (T) at beta = 2 has grad Theta = 0 at every nondegenerate zero of W (differentiate W.grad
Theta = 0 at the zero), and a contraction argument for the zero then gives a quantitative local exclusion: no pair (W,
Theta) with W of class C^1 and Theta of class C^2 satisfying W.grad Theta = 0 near that disc lies within 0.001 of the
trial in W, 0.01 in DW (operator norm) and 1 in grad Theta, uniformly on the disc; in particular no A2-broad profile at
beta = 2 is that close to this trial there (independently checked). The exclusion persists with a free exponent: writing
W = beta X + U and (T) as W.grad Theta = (beta - 2) Theta, no pair (U, Theta) with U of class C^1 and Theta of class C^2
satisfying (T) near that disc for some beta with |beta - 2| <= 1/50000 lies within 1/1000 of the trial in U, 1/100 in DU
(operator norm) and 1 in grad Theta, uniformly on the disc, and the same holds with |beta - 2| <= 1/20000 and 1/2000 in
U (independently checked); at a zero of W, differentiating (T) gives (DU + 2I)^T grad Theta = 0, in which beta cancels.
In the same two neighbourhoods, now with U and Theta only of class C^1 and no bound on Theta itself, every pair has
thermal residual R = W.grad Theta - (beta - 2) Theta with |R| > 0.06 at one of the two points (13.67859 +- 0.003,
5.66655), the point depending on the pair, and there |R| / (|W_1 Theta_x| + |W_2 Theta_y| + |beta - 2| |Theta|) > 0.08;
at beta = 2 with the bound 1/1000 in U this ratio exceeds 0.15 (independently checked). These concern one stored state
and one disc; they give no statement about other resolutions or about limits of the states. Apart from these local
statements, these tests give no quantitative finite-radius absolute residual bound, nearby-profile error estimate or
convergence statement.

Five further stored states of the branch a0 < 0 at beta = 2 (t-map basis, M = 28, N = 112; map scales L = 0.5, 1 and 2,
and two different weightings of the least-squares objective at L = 1; one state with L = 1 includes the far-field tail
rows and has relative misfit 5.889e-3; none is the beta = 2 state of the first item below) were evaluated by a second independent implementation: a full-quadrant physical inverse using the four
reflected images of the whole-plane kernel with Duffy triangles at quadrature orders 128, 192 and 256 and three
integration scales, a separately implemented adaptive modal inverse (frequencies 2 to 56), and centred differences of
formal order eight at two steps. At the point (15.375, 5.125) the thermal residuals R_Theta = W.grad Theta of the five
states (L = 0.5, 1, 2, then the two weightings) are 2.768, 52.55, -36.80, -23.61 and -24.10, with |R_Theta|/N_Theta = 1,
0.305, 0.0820, 0.161 and 0.284 (N_Theta as above with beta = 2, strictly positive there); over five sample points off
the axes the largest values of |R_Theta| are 36.78, 52.55, 41.72, 23.61 and 24.10, and those of |R_Omega| are 0.420,
0.972, 1.247, 0.279 and 1.895. The residual values above use the physical inverse at quadrature order 256 and
integration scale 1. At the four sample points other than (25.125, 0.03125), the two inverses agree to 4.4e-12. At the
four sample points other than (25.125, 0.03125), which lies close to the x-axis, the change from order 192 to order 256
is at most 3.3e-12, and at order 256 the values at the integration scales 0.5 and 2 differ from those at scale 1 by at
most 5.5e-12 (any two of the three scales by at most 7.9e-12); with that fifth point included, these three maxima are
2.4e-6, 3.5e-7 and 4.8e-7 (rounded upward). These are observed differences, not error bounds, and the
residuals are sampled values. Independently of these samples, none of the five stored tables is an exact profile,
whatever the velocity: write the stored fields as Theta = x^2 y a and Omega = x y b with a and b smooth and even in each
variable; for every smooth divergence-free U with the A2 parities, A = beta + U_1/x and B = beta + U_2/y are smooth with
A(0) + B(0) = 2 beta, and the vorticity residual is x y V with V = (A + B + 1) b + x A b_x + y B b_y - 2 a - x a_x, so
V(0) = 5 b0 - 2 a0 at beta = 2 (the centre relation (2 beta + 1) b0 = 2 a0 of Section 1). Exact integer arithmetic on
the stored binary64 coefficients gives 5 b0 - 2 a0 > 0 for each table (about 2.5e-9 to 9.2e-9), so the vorticity
residual is nonzero at points of the open quadrant near the origin (independently checked). This concerns the five
stored tables only; it gives no radius and no statement about nearby fields.

For the stored state of the branch a0 < 0 at beta = 2 and N = 208 of (iv) (reported relative least-squares
misfit 1.5e-3, the smallest of the four sequences tabulated by the numerical study at N = 208; 1.55e-3 for
the excluded control at beta = 1.9431 on the branch a0 > 0, against 1.883e-3 for the state at beta = 2 and
N = 208 of that branch), the same kind of independent evaluation (physical inverse at quadrature orders 192
to 320, adaptive modal cross-check, centred differences of formal order eight) at four fixed points,
approximately (13.68, 5.67), (24.32, 0.43), (24.5351, 0.02) and (60, 15) (coordinates and values rounded),
gives |R_Omega| <= 0.0979 and |R_Theta| <= 1.644, and |R_Omega|/N_Omega <= 0.0093; |R_Theta|/N_Theta is 1 at
(13.68, 5.67), next to the certified interior zero of W (there R_Theta = N_Theta = 0.146, the two transport
terms have the same sign), 0.995 at (24.5351, 0.02), next to the certified axis zero, and 0.0866 and 0.0099
at the other two points (independently checked). These are values at four points, not error bounds: at
quadrature order 192 the largest velocity-component differences between the physical and modal inverses are
6.0e-12, 5.3e-6, 3.6e-4 and 6.2e-12 at the four points; after refinement of the two points near the axis to
order 320 the spread over three integration scales is at most 1.2e-7.

For the stored state of the same branch at N = 240 (beta = 2, a0 < 0, 60 angular by 240 radial coefficients for
each field; reported relative least-squares misfit 1.096e-3), a separate independent evaluation (adaptive modal
integral, full physical-plane parity quartet with Duffy quadrature, Cartesian finite differences) at 72 equally
spaced points of the circle of radius 0.1 about the numerically located interior zero of W near (14.08234, 5.63423)
gives max |R_Theta| = 6.7257 and max |R_Omega| = 0.18728, with pointwise normalized maxima 1 and 0.0145
(independently checked). These are sampled values, not continuous-circle or error bounds; at quadrature order 256 the
physical and modal velocities differ by at most 7.2e-11 on 24 targets, an observed agreement and not an enclosure.
Exact rational arithmetic on the stored binary64 coefficients gives c - 6 < 0 (about -1.38e-8) and nonzero
coefficients of x y in R_Omega (exactly 962362477/2^60, about 8.3e-10) and of x^2 y in R_Theta ((6 - c) a0 < 0,
about -1.38e-8), so the stored state is not an exact solution (independently checked); this excludes no
neighbourhood of it. Rejected.

Further numerical studies. Fitting trajectories and diagnostics are solver-reported unless an independent evaluation or
exact certificate is identified below.
 - The branch a0 < 0 (gauge a0 = -1), by the same least-squares protocol: relative misfits 5.99e-3 at beta = 2 and
   7.23e-3 at beta = 3 (radial resolution N = 112), decreasing with N over the tested range as on the branch a0 > 0
   (6.30e-3 and 7.29e-3 there, with the same far-field weighting). At beta = 3 a numerically located interior zero of W
   has computed Theta = -62.37, whereas Theorem 6(a) gives Theta = 0 at an exact stagnation point (the root and its
   evaluation error are not certified). At beta = 2 the search found one interior stagnation point in the open first
   quadrant, with computed Omega = 4.39, and did not locate the zero-vorticity stagnation point required by Theorem 12
   (sampling does not show that none exists); the N = 80 and N = 112 fields have reported interior coordinates (10.4962, 4.8552) and
   (11.8559, 5.4974), respectively. These are different fitted fields, with no tracked root or matched-protocol
   assertion for this comparison. The estimated first positive x-axis zero has slope 4.42, against the exact value beta + 2 = 4 of Theorem 2. In both states r^{1/beta} Omega has both signs on the sampled set; at several fixed sampled angles its values
   change with radius, including sign changes, over r = 30 to 1e4 (beta = 2) and r = 100 to 1e4 (beta = 3).
   The finite representation has an exact angular limit as r -> infinity, but these finite samples do not establish
   an asymptotic regime or a uniform distance to that limit. Rejected.
 - The branch a0 > 0 at beta = 2 at radial resolution N = 240 (60 angular coefficients, far-field tail rows, 200
   iterations from the state at N = 208): reported relative misfit 1.379e-3, against 1.883e-3 at N = 208. The
   zero search reports an approximate zero of W on the positive x-axis near (16.003, 0) with computed DW =
   diag(4.116, -0.116) and Theta_y = 59.0, no positive y-axis zero found by the non-exhaustive search over 0.05
   <= y <= 300, and one approximate zero found in the open quadrant by the same finite search near (9.895, 3.730)
   with computed Jacobian eigenvalues 2 +- 0.757i, determinant 4.57 and |grad Theta| = 7.59. An exact profile at
   beta = 2 has d_y W_2 = beta - 2 = 0 at every zero of W on the x-axis with Theta_y != 0 (by the identity d_y
   W_2 Theta_y = (beta - 2) Theta_y stated above), and grad Theta = 0 at every nondegenerate zero of W; these
   computed values are not certified. On a circle of radius 0.1 about the reported interior point the sampled
   maximum of |R_Theta| is 5.17 (3.98 and 5.32 for the states of this branch at N = 176 and 208); on a diagnostic
   grid of 300 radii in [0.02, 2000] and 239 interior angles, including 120 collocation angles and 119
   intervening angles, the sampled maxima of |R_Theta| are 2.28, 14.5 and 10.6 in 1 <= r < 10, 10 <= r < 100 and
   r >= 100. Rejected.
 - Ray sign patterns on seven stored beta = 3 states: the three states of the table (N = 112, 144, 176), a refit at
   N = 208 with far-field tail rows, and three states of the branch a0 < 0 at N = 80, 112 and 144. With sigma the sign
   of the fitted a(0), which equals that of a0 in all seven, the signs of sigma Omega and sigma Theta were sampled on 90
   interior rays at 400 logarithmically spaced radii in [0.5, 1e6]. In each state, 57 to 71 of the 90 rays carry the
   strict signs (+, -, +) of sigma Omega at three increasing sampled radii, with smallest third radius about 101 to 105
   (a0 > 0) and 19.0 to 20.4 (a0 < 0); sigma Theta has the pattern (+, -, +) on 77 to 80 rays (a0 > 0) and 20 to 28 rays
   (a0 < 0). These signs are floating-point samples. For each of the seven states the pattern of sigma Omega has also
   been established exactly on one ray. The represented vorticity is x y times a positive factor depending on |X| only
   times a finite polynomial P in t = (1 + |X|^2)^(-1/6) and the real and imaginary parts of w = (x + iy)^2/(1 + |X|^2),
   with the stored coefficients, which as binary floating-point numbers are dyadic rationals. On the ray y = v x, with
   v = 1 (six states) or v = 1/2 (one state), at three rational values of t, P is a rational number; its exact rational
   evaluation, carried out in three independently organized ways and enclosed in rational intervals of one strict sign,
   gives the strict signs (+, -, +) of sigma P, with sigma the exact sign of the represented a0, at the radii
   (t^(-6) - 1)^(1/2), which are about 0.154, 44.9 to 70.4 and 1214 to 23014 (a0 > 0) and about 0.154, 4.87 to 5.41 and
   70.4 to 95.5 (a0 < 0). Hence each of the seven represented vorticities has the signs (sigma, -sigma, sigma) at three
   increasing radii on a ray in Q1, so none of them satisfies the ray hypothesis of Theorems 64(b), 79(e) and 80(c). The
   represented fields are not solutions; apart from these 21 points, three on each of the seven rays, the signs are
   uncertified, nondetection between or beyond the samples excludes nothing, and nothing follows about profiles.
 - Sampled elliptic defect of eleven fitted states (beta = 2 with a0 < 0 at N = 112, 144, 176, 208 and 240, beta = 2
   with a0 > 0 at N = 240, beta = 3 with a0 > 0 at N = 176 and with a0 < 0 at N = 144, and, at beta = 2 with a0 < 0, the
   dense-annulus refit at N = 144 and two map-scale variants at N = 112). The velocity was evaluated from the Green
   inverse used in the fit on a common grid of 10000 points (200 radii from 0.02 to about 2000 and 50 interior angles,
   disjoint from the collocation sets), and E, the difference between the vorticity computed from that velocity and the
   represented vorticity, was formed by fourth-order central differences in polar coordinates with radial steps of 1e-3,
   3e-4 and 1e-4 times the radius and angular steps of the same sizes in radians. Over the 132 combinations of state,
   step and region (r < 1, 1 <= r < 10, 10 <= r < 100, r >= 100) the sampled regional maxima of |E| lie between 3.5e-10
   and 4.2e-6; in the two outer regions the largest values occur at the largest step and fall by factors of 13 to 135 at
   the step 3e-4, and the ratios of the regional maxima of |E| to the sampled regional maxima of |R_Theta| (10.4 to 691
   there) lie between 2.8e-12 and 3.4e-7. These are floating-point samples on one grid, computed with the inverse of the
   fit; they do not separate differentiation error, field-evaluation error and the elliptic defect of the represented
   fields, and they bound neither E nor its effect on the residuals.
 - Initial singular-value studies of four N = 112 states (both signs of a0, beta = 2 and 3, beta free) reported
   smallest-to-largest singular-value ratios of about 1e-6, with 359 to 846 singular values below 1e-4 of the largest.
   For the positive beta = 2 state the initial study's objective had residual norm 8.53e-3, compared with 6.30e-3 in the later diagnostic. In a later
   four-state diagnostic, the smallest-singular-value directions had most of their coefficient energy in vorticity.
   Unit steps in that coefficient normalization changed beta by signed amounts from -0.1051 to +0.1152, changed the
   velocity by 3.6 to 5.3 times its sampled maximum, and increased the residual norm by factors of about 2.9 to 17.4.
   A weak linearized response therefore does not imply a small finite-step residual. The later beta-column norms
   were large, but their distances from the coefficient-column spans were small relative to those norms; these
   diagnostics do not show that beta is well determined. The initial studies reported fractions 0.629 to 0.999 of
   the residual norm outside the full Jacobian range. These projection and singular-value data indicate poor
   conditioning; they do not certify a local minimum or convergence of the optimizer.
 - Joint refits with beta free at N = 208, 176 and 144. Three stored states at N = 208 (beta = 2 with a0 < 0,
   beta = 2 with a0 > 0, beta = 3 with a0 > 0) were refitted for 200 iterations with beta as an additional unknown.
   The radial map, whose parameter b = 2, 2, 3 (the initial beta) fixes the far-field exponents of the
   representation, and the weights, targets and tail rows were otherwise unchanged. According to the full-precision
   saved fitting histories, beta and the residual norm decreased at each of the 200 saved iterations, beta to about
   1.96005, 1.99045 and 2.86061 and still decreasing at the last iteration, the residual norm by about 1.1, 0.68 and
   12.0 percent. An independent evaluation (its own full-plane modal inverse; exact rational arithmetic on the stored
   coefficients for the statements on defects) shows that none of the three stored coefficient tables represents a
   profile, for two separate reasons. First, the fitted beta differs from b. For these represented fields, whose
   expansions hold also after differentiation, if Theta = r^(1 - 2/b) f(phi) + O(r^(1 - 3/b)) and Omega = r^(-1/b)
   g(phi) + O(r^(-2/b)) on a fixed ray, then R_Theta = r^(1 - 2/b) [2 (1 - beta/b) f(phi) + O(r^(-1/b))] and
   R_Omega = r^(-1/b) [(1 - beta/b) g(phi) + O(r^(-1/b))] there. On the ray phi = pi/4 the leading coefficients are
   nonzero, about -0.622, 0.0791 and -0.508 for R_Theta/r^(1 - 2/b) and -2.09, -0.209 and -1.02 for r^(1/b) R_Omega,
   and the values computed at r = 1e30 agree with them to relative differences below 2e-5. So on that ray the thermal
   residual tends to a nonzero constant for b = 2 and grows like r^(1/3) for b = 3. This asymptotic obstruction also
   holds, with leading coefficients at least one quarter of the corresponding exact coefficients in absolute value,
   for every exponent within (b - beta)/2 of the fitted beta and every coefficient table of the same representation
   whose temperature and vorticity coefficients differ from the stored ones by at most |P_A|/2 and |P_G|/2 in the l1
   norm, where P_A and P_G are the angular sums of the far-field temperature and vorticity coefficients at phi = pi/4
   (about 44.0, 23.4 and 15.5, and 209, 87.3 and 43.9, in absolute value). For b = 2 this exponent interval lies
   below 2, where Theorem 1 already excludes profiles; for b = 3 it is about [2.791, 2.930]. Second, the exact centre
   defects (2 beta + 1) b0 - 2 a0 and c - (2 beta + 2) of the tables are nonzero, between 6e-11 and 3.5e-7 in
   absolute value. On three independent point sets per table, the sampled maxima of |R_Theta| have approximate minima
   and maxima of 33.7 and 36.6, 12.8 and 18.4, and 337 and 527, respectively. Two further refits of this kind, of the
   beta = 2, a0 < 0 states at N = 144 (with the far-field tail rows added to its objective) and at N = 176, for 200
   iterations each with b = 2, ended at beta about 1.93366 and 1.94180; for N = 144 beta did not decrease at every
   saved iteration. The independent evaluation gives the same two conclusions for these two tables: on the ray
   phi = pi/4 the leading coefficients are about -1.56 and -1.12 for R_Theta/r^(1 - 2/b) and 2.41 and -1.21 for
   r^(1/b) R_Omega, with leading coefficients at least one quarter of the corresponding exact coefficients in
   absolute value throughout the neighbourhoods defined as above (whose exponent intervals lie below 2), and the
   exact centre defects are between 5e-9 and 1.4e-7 in absolute value; on three independent point sets per table, the
   sampled maxima of |R_Theta| have approximate minima and maxima of 53.5 and 60.9, and 36.3 and 50.9, respectively. Two
   more refits of this kind, of the beta = 2, a0 > 0 states at N = 144 (with the far-field tail rows added to its
   objective and the radius scale of its radial residual weights changed from 20 to 30) and at N = 176, for 200
   iterations each with b = 2, ended at beta about 1.97901 and 1.98684; according to the saved fitting histories, beta
   decreased strictly from each saved iteration to the next, and the residual norm decreased by about 9.8 and 0.96
   percent from the first saved iteration to the last. The independent evaluation gives the same two conclusions for
   these two tables: on the ray phi = pi/4 the leading coefficients are about 0.0878 and 0.179 for R_Theta/r^(1 - 2/b)
   and -0.174 and -0.150 for r^(1/b) R_Omega, with leading coefficients at least one quarter of the corresponding exact
   coefficients in absolute value throughout the neighbourhoods defined as above (whose exponent intervals lie below 2),
   and the exact centre defects are between 1e-10 and 1.4e-8 in absolute value; on three independent point sets per
   table, the sampled maxima of |R_Theta| have approximate minima and maxima of 23.9 and 24.9, and 19.6 and 20.8,
   respectively. The seven refits differ in starting state and objective, so their final values of beta establish no
   resolution trend. The finite trajectories vary beta and the coefficients jointly; they do not measure the dependence
   of the objective on beta at fixed coefficients and identify neither a minimizing beta nor a limiting value. Controls
   with beta held at 2 and the same 200-iteration limit as the four joint refits with beta free at N = 144 and N = 176
   were also run. Within each pair, the recorded initialization paths and fixed row parameters agree. The residual norm
   decreased by about 11.9 and 0.34 percent for the a0 < 0 controls at N = 144 and N = 176 and by about 9.2 and 0.33
   percent for the a0 > 0 controls, against 13.6, 2.2, 9.8 and 0.96 percent for the corresponding joint refits with beta
   free. These percentages use each N = 144 run's own post-update label-0 norm and the stored starting norm for N = 176.
   The final norms of the joint refits are approximately 0.6 to 1.9 percent lower than those of the corresponding
   controls, relative to each control's final norm. At the final states of the joint refits beta differs from the
   exponent of the radial map, so these represented fields do not satisfy the far-field balance of their own
   representation (the nonzero leading coefficients above). These lower norms do not compare two representations both
   consistent with their far-field balance and do not by themselves show that a representation consistent at some beta
   below 2 attains a lower norm than at beta = 2. Theorem 1 excludes exact profiles with beta < 2; it does not by itself
   exclude approximate states with beta below 2 tending to 2 from approaching a profile at beta = 2. The exact
   obstruction concerns these represented fields and the stated neighbourhoods in this representation; it excludes no
   profile at beta = b and no profile represented otherwise, for instance with a radial map whose exponent equals beta.
   Runs on the branch a0 < 0 with a radial map re-adapted to or consistent with beta were also made. Two joint refits
   with beta free from the same starting states as those at N = 144 and N = 176 ran four rounds of 50 iterations; after
   each of the first three rounds the radial map, its prefactors and the residual normalizations were rebuilt with b
   equal to the current beta and the state was refitted onto the new basis. Beta was lower at the end of each round than
   at its start, ending at about 1.95038 and 1.95377 with b about 1.96215 and 1.96437 from the last rebuild. The limit
   of R_Theta/Theta, wherever the leading temperature amplitude is nonzero, is 2 beta + 2 - beta e_a/b. Here e_a is the
   cached binary64 exponent in the prefactor t^e_a of a, with t = (1 + r^2)^(-1/(2b)) in these L = 1 runs. For the ideal
   e_a = 2b + 2 this is 2 (1 - beta/b); for these stored tables it agrees with that expression to the quoted precision.
   The two limits are about 0.0120 and 0.0108, agreeing to the printed precision with the values at the eight sampled
   angles and requested r = 1e20, against about 0.066 and 0.058 for the joint refits with b = 2. Their final residual
   norms, about 3.526e-3 and 2.173e-3, are about 0.94 and 1.28 percent below those of the corresponding controls with
   beta held at 2 and about 0.97 and 0.56 percent above those of the corresponding joint refits with b = 2, each
   percentage relative to the final norm of the run compared. A run of the same kind on the branch a0 > 0, initialized
   from the beta = 2, a0 > 0 state at N = 144 and using far-field tail rows in all four rounds, ended at beta about
   1.97409 with b about 1.98077 from the last rebuild. The leading coefficient of R_Theta/Theta is about 0.0067,
   agreeing to this printed precision with the values at the eight sampled angles and requested r = 1e20. Its recorded
   residual norm is about 3.981e-3, about 1.83 and 1.22 percent below the control with beta held at 2 and the joint
   refit with b = 2 from the same initialization, relative to their final norms 4.0546e-3 and 4.0299e-3. A second such
   run, initialized from the beta = 2, a0 > 0 state at N = 176, ended at beta about 1.98094 with b about 1.98545 from
   the last rebuild; the leading coefficient of R_Theta/Theta is about 0.0045, and its recorded residual norm, about
   2.655e-3, is about 1.73 and 1.11 percent below the control with beta held at 2 and the joint refit with b = 2 from
   the same initialization, relative to their final norms 2.7019e-3 and 2.6848e-3. These are attained norms under
   different objectives and do not isolate a basis effect. A refit of the final state of the joint refit of the
   beta = 2, a0 < 0 state at N = 208, with beta held at the rounded value 1.960048 and b = 1.960048, whose cached
   exponents satisfy the leading far-field balance (the printed maximum of |R_Theta/Theta| at the eight sampled angles
   and requested r = 1e20 is about 2.626e-8), reached the residual norm 1.4878e-3 after 200 iterations: about 0.82
   percent below the stored state at beta = 2 and N = 208 (1.5001e-3), 0.27 percent above the joint refit with b = 2
   (1.4838e-3) and 3.8 percent below the excluded control with a0 target +1 at beta about 1.9431 and N = 208 (1.5471e-3;
   also with b = beta, obtained along a different sequence of fits), relative to these three norms. Rebuilding the
   radial map changes the radial nodes, the normalizations and the row weights, so these norms are values of different
   sampled objectives; equal iteration counts do not establish equal computational work. The path from the stored state
   at beta = 2 and N = 208 to the final state at beta = 1.960048 contains 400 further iterations: 200 in the joint refit
   and 200 in the fixed-beta refit, plus the transfers between representations. These finite comparisons under differing
   protocols locate no minimizing beta. Theorem 1 excludes exact profiles with beta < 2. A lower attained sampled norm
   under these differing protocols does not by itself certify an admissible exponent or proximity to a profile.
 - Dynamic rescaling: the time-dependent equations in self-similar variables were integrated in pseudo-time from the
   fitted states and from a generic start, in three normalizations. In the normalization fixing the speed of the time
   variable and a0, the origin strain collapses. That normalization leaves the time-translation mode free: for any
   profile (Omega*, Theta*, U*), the fields (m Omega*(X/m), m^3 Theta*(X/m), m^2 U*(X/m)) with m' = m(m - 1) solve the
   normalized equations, and for m(0) < 1 they show the same collapse, with the product of c and the origin vorticity
   coefficient conserved (in the computation it is conserved to 2e-6). Normalizations that remove
   this mode (fixing a0 and b0, or beta and a0) did not converge either, and after a pseudo-time of about 2 their far
   field is not represented by the velocity reconstruction. A trajectory that fails to converge is not evidence that
   no profile, attracting or not, lies near its starting point: an exact scalar example has an arbitrarily small
   residual at the starting point, a growing linearization there, a trajectory leaving the basin, and an attracting
   equilibrium at distance epsilon. These computations therefore bear neither on existence nor on nonexistence.

Annulus-penalized refit (independently evaluated). Starting from the beta = 2, a0 < 0 Gaussian-start state
B2_m_gauss_N144, the numerical study performed 300 additional iterations at radial resolution N = 144 and 36 angular
rows. It added least-squares rows w R_Theta/(100 sqrt(576)) at 24 x 24 nodes of the annular sector 9 < r < 20, 0 < phi <
pi/2, using w = 0.3 and, in a separate run from the same state, w = 1.0. Their squared Euclidean contribution is
(w/100)^2 times the equal-node mean of R_Theta^2. The recorded standard misfit, omitting these added rows, rose from
0.00359295 to 0.00511607 (42.39 percent) and 0.00583286 (62.34 percent), respectively. These objective values come from
the fitting logs, whose decomposition was arithmetically checked against the logged totals; for w = 0.3, the logged
initial and final penalty RMS values also agree with the independent evaluation to within 6e-9 in absolute value.

For the w = 0.3 state, an independent evaluator uses the canonical full-plane modal inverse and separately
implemented eighth-order centred Cartesian differences, with no fitting-code routines. It gives the following
sampled maxima of |R_Theta|.

The equal-node RMS on the 65 x 97 grid rose from 9.244 to 12.86. These two independently constructed grids are not

changes the sampled thermal residuals by at most 1.7e-7. Separate physical-space quadrature of the full-plane
Biot-Savart integral agrees with the modal velocity within 7.6e-13 at two selected points for the baseline and two for
the refit, each with quadrature orders 192 and 256; these observed differences are not error bounds. Improvement on the
penalty grid did not persist in either independent-grid maximum or RMS. This does not establish where all improvements
occur or compare continuous suprema.

A separate evaluation interprets the stored w = 0.3 coefficients as exact dyadic rationals and evaluates their
full-plane inverse in a finite closed form including its logarithmic terms, using exact algebra and outward-rounded
real-ball arithmetic. At the fixed exact dyadic point selected after the floating-point diagnostic, corresponding to
the largest sampled thermal residual on the 65 x 97 grid, it certifies 160 < R_Theta < 165 and positivity of both
Cartesian transport terms. Subject to the certificate's stated software, arithmetic and hardware assumptions, the
supremum of |R_Theta| over this annulus, and over the plane, therefore exceeds 160. This gives no upper bound for
either supremum, no rigorous comparison with the baseline's continuous supremum, for which no upper bound was
established, and no statement about distance to a solution or nearby functions. The exact centre defects are nonzero:
c - 6 is about -2.9e-8 and 5 b0 - 2 a0 is about 2.6e-9. Thus the literal stored function also fails the exact centre
relations.

Three approximate zeros of W in the sector were located and polished independently. Their computed Jacobians are
classified as a repelling node, a saddle and a repelling focus, and their computed |grad Theta| values are 3.97, 52.7
and 52.3. The roots, classifications and completeness of this list are not certified. At any exact zero of W in an exact
beta = 2 profile, differentiating the thermal equation gives (DW)^T grad Theta = 0; hence grad Theta = 0 when DW is
nonsingular. The fitted data fail this local diagnostic. Finite point penalties alone do not certify continuous residual
control or confine the zeros of W. This refit does not show that these residuals cannot be reduced in the
representation. The stored trial is rejected as a successful endpoint candidate; the broad A2 problem remains open.

## 7. Limitations and open obstacles

Neither accepted endpoint has been reached: there is no complete theorem excluding every A2-broad profile, and no
candidate has the independently reproduced, resolution-stable small residuals required of numerical existence
evidence (Section 6).

 - No result proves the absence of A2-broad profiles for any beta >= 2; every such profile, if it exists, has the
   natural tail. Theorem 8 uses the unproved hypothesis (H1). For beta > 2, by Theorem 52(b), a failure of (H1)
   requires a zero of W on {(x, 0): x > x1} or on {(0, y): y > 0}, so additional zeros confined to the open quadrant
   cannot by themselves cause it; a further zero is a hyperbolic source, a saddle with a resonant or flat temperature
   jet, or a degenerate zero (Remark 43.1, Theorem 43), and Theorems 27, 30 and 54 restrict the axis configurations,
   but none of these is excluded in general. If B = {X in Q1 : sgn(a0) Omega(X) < 0} is bounded and every zero of W in
   the closed first quadrant is nondegenerate, there is no zero of W on {(x, 0): x > x1}, and a zero on {(0, y): y > 0}
   requires beta = N/M in lowest terms with N even and M odd (Theorem 77), and is excluded for every beta > 2 if the
   far-field sign condition on G of Theorem 81(b) replaces boundedness of B (Theorem 84); boundedness of B is not
   proved, nor is the far-field sign condition on G that implies it (Theorem 81). For the conclusions of Theorem 77
   under bounded B, degenerate zeros in the open quadrant are admitted only when the positive zeros of W on the axes are
   simple, the zeros of W in the open quadrant are isolated and Omega vanishes on a neighbourhood of each degenerate
   one; the last condition holds when Omega is real analytic near it (Theorem 78(b)). Under the far-field sign condition
   of Theorem 81(b) the isolatedness requirement can be dropped: simple positive zeros of W on the axes and vanishing of
   Omega near each degenerate zero in the open quadrant then imply nondegeneracy, hence (H1) (Theorem 86(c)). For
   beta > 2, under the far-field sign condition of Theorem 81(b) and nondegeneracy of the zeros of W in the closed first
   quadrant, which together give (H1) (Theorem 84), no result of this report excludes any of the three cases a0 < 0;
   a0 > 0 with {Omega < 0} cap Q1 nonempty
   (it is then bounded, Theorem 81(b)); a0 > 0 with Omega >= 0 on Q1. The necessary conditions of Theorems 50, 55, 64,
   66, 73, 75 and 86 (among them ray sign conditions, fixed moments, pocket balances and shear requirements) apply in
   these cases as far as their hypotheses hold, and whether they can be met by a full-plane profile is not
   decided. In the first case B = {Omega > 0} cap Q1 is bounded, and Theorem 87 adds the necessary condition
   M_B |B|^(1/2) > sqrt(pi) beta L, with M_B the supremum of Omega on B; no upper bound sufficient to contradict it is
   proved. In the other two cases a0 > 0, so Theta > 0 on Q1 by (H1) and Theorem 8(ii), and Theorem 88(d) requires, in
   its notation, int_0^R s^(-n-1) Q(s) ds < 0 for every R > 0, where Q(s) is the flux of (e + Pi) U through the quarter
   arc of radius s; Q is negative near O by (88.5), and no sign of Q at larger radii is proved. Vorticity that changes
   sign in Q1, and, for beta > 2, vorticity that is strictly
   positive throughout Q1, are not excluded (Theorem 21). A nonnegative vorticity on Q1 is not excluded for any
   beta >= 2; it forces a0 > 0 and the axis signs (57.3), and for beta > 2 it reduces to (H1) with Theta > 0,
   where Theorem 50 applies (Theorem 57(a)) and the obstructions of Remark 55.1 hold by its weak-sign
   paragraph. For beta > 2 Theorem 65 adds that the zeros of the
   vorticity in Q1 outside a disc have order two or four along their orbits, that the vorticity is positive outside a
   disc in sectors at both axes, conditions at the limit angles of unbounded sequences of zeros in Q1, convergent orbit
   and axis moments, and a cubic relation at P when Omega_y(P) = 0; strict positivity of Omega on Q1, the exclusion of
   bounded open subsets of Q1 on which Omega vanishes, boundedness of {Omega = 0} cap Q1 and isolation of its zeros
   within Q1 remain open, and none of these conditions excludes a profile. Under the same sign and for beta > 2, Theorem
   75 adds that Omega >= c r^{-3/beta} beyond a radius on all but finitely many rays in Q1, and Omega >= c |X|^{-3/beta}
   at all sufficiently late points of all but finitely many complete orbits in Q1, with c > 0 and the thresholds
   depending on the ray or the orbit; these are necessary conditions as well. At beta = 2, under Omega >= 0 on Q1,
   Theorem 59 gives Psi > 0 on Q1, G >= 0, G = H'' = 0 at the interior critical angles of H and G'(pi/2) < 0, and, if no
   zero component lies wholly in Q1 and (R) holds, Theta > 0 on Q1; none of these conditions excludes a profile. In this
   case (88.4) makes the strict negativity of every partial integral in Theorem 88(d) equivalent to F(R) > 0 for every
   R > 0. The necessary angular conditions alone do not force a common sign for the far-field flux. At beta = 2,
   Q(R) = A R^(5/2) + O(R^2) as R tends to infinity, where A = int_0^(pi/2) (P' P1' + (3/2) P P' G) and P1 is the
   Dirichlet solution on (0, pi/2) of -P1'' - P1 = P'G/2 + 3PG'/2 + sin(phi) H'. Smooth angular data satisfying (68.1),
   (59.5)-(59.7) and (59.9), with G = 0 in (0, pi/2) exactly on the plateau of H, give either sign of A; no realization
   of these data by a full-plane profile is established. For specified H and G, A is determined and, when nonzero, fixes
   the eventual sign of Q. The invariant potential-flow region of Theorem 83 contains a far sector: forward invariance,
   openness and infinite area give a launch interval at a large radius, and convergence of the hitting maps in
   Theorem 36(d) gives a smaller fixed sector inside its forward image. On that simply connected sector, U = grad chi
   and e + Pi = k - 2r partial_r chi + 3chi with a constant k. The homogeneous term of degree 3/2 in chi cancels in this
   identity. These observations give no exclusion of a profile. Under the same sign, Theorem 61 adds an exact
   height-deficit identity along the half-fibres of regular zeros and vanishing of the vorticity jet through order 7 at
   regular zeros with Omega = 0 and -8 < Theta_y < 108; these are necessary conditions as well, and the case of a zero
   component wholly in Q1 remains open. Theorem 28 forces both signs in every large quadrant annulus under the critical
   energy bound, which fails throughout A2-broad (Theorems 34 and 38). In the natural regime the uniform limit
   r^{1/beta} Omega -> G, with G of the sign of a0 on an open interval of angles in (0, pi/2) (Theorems 33 and 34(b) at
   beta = 2, Theorem 41 for beta > 2), rules out sgn(a0) Omega <= 0 on the first quadrant outside a disc; an eventual
   weak sign sgn(a0) Omega >= 0 is not excluded. Under it, sgn(a0) P > 0 on (0, pi/2) with strict endpoint slopes
   (Theorem 64(a)); for beta > 2, if moreover {Theta = 0} has no interior point in Q1 and no ray carries vorticity of
   signs (sigma,-sigma,sigma) at three increasing radii, sigma = sgn(a0), the sign holds on all of Q1, which is
   impossible for a0 < 0 and for a0 > 0 is the nonnegative case above (Theorem 64(b)); without the ray condition this
   remains open, also under (H1). For beta > 2 and bounded nonempty {X in Q1 : sgn(a0) Omega(X) < 0} with {Theta = 0}
   without interior points in Q1, Theorem 66 adds exact transport balances on its components, the conditional
   boundary-crossing conclusions of its part (c), late returns of the sign of a0 along a dense residual set of orbits,
   far-field contact inequalities and, for a0 < 0 under (H1), a dichotomy by the sign of w''(L) and an axis trace
   identity; none of these excludes the configuration. For beta > 2, nondegeneracy of every zero of W in the closed

   selected proofs in this report, beyond the exterior equations, canonical whole-plane inversion and tail estimates.
   It describes these proofs only: it does not assert that another proof needs the same inputs, and it does not
   classify arguments that could exclude the natural branch. (i) The estimate and limit steps in Theorems 33(a),(d),
   excluding nonvanishing of H, 36, 38(a),(b), excluding nonvanishing of f, 41(a),(c), 42 and 45(f) use exterior
   estimates and forward orbits launched from an exterior circle, with the standing regularity and growth assumptions.
   This description concerns those steps, not the other conclusions or complete-orbit identifications established in
   the same proofs. (ii) Nonvanishing of H in Theorem 33(d), through Theorem 32(d), uses an open set where Theta != 0
   and its forward area expansion, as in Theorem 18. Nonvanishing of f in Theorem 38(b) uses a nonzero-temperature
   point and its forward escape, through Theorem 37(c). Nonvanishing of G and its sign agreement with a0 on an open
   interval in Theorems 34(b) and 41(b) use the origin jet, invariance of Q1, positivity of the weighted position V(X)
   = int_0^infinity exp(-(beta+1)t)y(Phi_t X) dt, and escaping near-origin points. The proof of 34(b) uses Theorem
   33(b),(c); the proof of 41(b) uses Theorem 37(a)-(d). The nonvanishing of J0 in Theorem 38(c) uses its
   escaping-chart identification and Theorem 37(a)-(c). Theorem 34(b) supplies the nonvanishing input in Theorem
   59(b), and Theorem 41(b) supplies it in Theorem 65(c). Theorem 64(a) uses Theorem 34(b) at beta = 2 and Theorem
   41(b) at beta > 2. The exterior constructions of Theorem 69(a) allow f = 0 or G = 0 under (69.1), and those of
   Theorem 70(a) allow H = 0 or G = 0 under (70.1); these constructions impose transport only in the exterior. (iii)
   The implication in Theorem 47(a) that G vanishes where f = f' = 0 for beta > 2, or where H' = 0 for beta = 2, uses
   bounded complete backward orbits through Theorem 44(d). Theorem 59(b) explicitly repeats that argument. (iv) The

   profile has a0 > 0, Omega >= 0 on Q1 and (H1) (Theorem 80(c)). Under the far-field sign condition of Theorem 81(b)
   alone, every ray in Q1 on which sgn(a0) Omega is somewhere negative is such a ray, with the last radius arbitrarily
   large, and {Theta = 0} has no interior point in Q1 (Theorem 86(b), (e)). Taken at face value, none of the four stored
   beta = 3 states tested has bounded B: for the real fields reconstructed exactly from their stored coefficients
   (a0 > 0 at N = 176 and 208, a0 < 0 at N = 112 and 144), exact rational evaluation gives rays in Q1 on which sgn(a0)
   Omega < 0 beyond explicit radii. These fields are not solutions of the profile equations, and nondegeneracy of their
   zeros was not established. Under bounded B and this nondegeneracy, without assuming the absence of such a ray, assume
   also that W has no zero in Q1. The positive zeros of W_2(0, y) are then finite and even in number, possibly none; in
   increasing order the odd-numbered zeros are saddles, where d_y W_2(0, y) < 0, and the even-numbered zeros are
   sources, where d_y W_2(0, y) = (3 beta + 2)/2. Every orbit in Q1 escapes, and {Theta = 0} cap Q1 is the union of the
   branches in Q1 of the unstable manifolds of these saddles (Theorem 79). If the positive zeros of W_1(x, 0) are
   finitely many and simple and W_2(0, y) has no positive zero, a zero of W in the open quadrant exists only if the
   upper unstable branch of an axis saddle is bounded; it is excluded for irrational beta with nondegenerate interior
   zeros, while for rational beta, and for branches ending at a degenerate zero, Theorem 60 gives only necessary
   conditions. Without these hypotheses every bounded forward orbit still converges to a single zero and carries
   Theta = 0 (Theorem 63(a)). The set K of points whose forward orbits are bounded is compact with Phi_t(K) = K for all
   t (Theorem 52(a)), and Phi_t multiplies area by e^{2 beta t} since div W = 2 beta; hence K has area zero. An
   unbounded forward orbit tends to infinity, since X.W(X) >= (beta/2)|X|^2 for all large |X| (Step 1 of the proof of
   Theorem 77). So almost every orbit in the open quadrant escapes; whether every orbit there escapes is open without
   additional hypotheses. Any degenerate zero of W has eigenvalues 0 and 2 beta, and Theta and Omega are flat there
   (Theorem 43(a) to (c)); so for beta > 2, if Omega is real analytic on R^2, W has no degenerate zero (Theorem 78(a)).
   For beta > 2, an open subset of Q1 on which Theta vanishes forces a zero of W in the closed first quadrant with det
   DW = 0 (Theorem 80(b)). Theorem 44 supplies single backward limits. By Theorem 54(c) an axis zero whose eigenvalue
   tangent to the axis is zero cannot be the backward limit of an outgoing label with nonzero G; Theorem 46(d) still
   permits the other flat degenerate zeros, in the open quadrant or on an axis with zero transverse eigenvalue, as
   backward limits of labels with nonzero amplitude. Theorem 45(e) proves convergence of t(y) - beta^{-1} log y; the
   nonzero outer-trace hypothesis (N) of Theorem 31 remains unproved in general.
 - The earlier runs of the numerical search with smooth bases reach relative least-squares misfits of 0.4 to 1 percent
   at fixed beta in [2, 6], decreasing with the radial resolution N over the tested range (the reported power fits are
   descriptive fits over finitely many resolutions; no asymptotic law or floor is established); the later states of the
   branch a0 < 0 at beta = 2 have reported misfits 1.5e-3 (N = 208) and 1.096e-3 (N = 240), against 1.55e-3 for the
   excluded control at beta = 1.9431 and N = 208 on the branch a0 > 0 (Section 6). The excluded beta < 2 control attains
   a comparable relative least-squares objective. On the branch a0 > 0 its reported misfit at N = 208 is about 17.8
   percent below the reported misfit 1.883e-3 of the state at beta = 2 and N = 208 of that branch (Section 6); the two
   fits use the same family of radial maps, the same number of iterations and the same far-field tail-row construction,
   while their physical nodes, evaluated rows and row weights depend on beta. On the branch a0 < 0, a refit at
   beta = 1.960048 and N = 208 with a radial map consistent with beta attains a residual norm about 0.82 percent below
   that of the stored state at beta = 2 and N = 208, under a differing protocol (Section 6). The reported objective
   sizes alone establish neither an exact profile nor global nonexistence, and provide no validated bound on distance to
   an exact solution. Comparisons across resolutions or normalizations do not by themselves establish a decrease of the
   continuous PDE residual. The separately measured residuals remain information about the particular stored states. The
   sampled residuals and geometric diagnostics of Section 6 do not validate any tested state as an exact profile and do
   not exclude unobserved stagnation points. The certified local tests of Section 6 exclude only the stated quantitative
   neighbourhoods of one stored state on one disc, including the stated ranges of beta; they give no exclusion outside
   those neighbourhoods. Section 6 reports states with both signs of a0. On both branches the reported least-squares
   misfit decreases over the tested resolution sequences, but no state of either sign meets the stated acceptance
   criterion. The sign of a0 is not a gauge. Within the separated class Psi = w(x) y no solution with a0 < 0 has a
   stagnation point on the positive x-axis (Remark 4.1); outside that class the sign a0 < 0 is not excluded. For
   beta > 2 Theorem 62(a) excludes it under three additional hypotheses: {Theta = 0} has no interior point in Q1,
   {Omega > 0} is bounded in Q1, and no ray carries vorticity of signs (-,+,-) at increasing radii; at beta = 2 these
   hypotheses leave a constant-temperature potential sector. For beta > 2 the first hypothesis may be replaced by
   nondegeneracy of every zero of W in the closed first quadrant (Theorem 80(b)). Dynamic rescaling did not converge in
   any normalization tried. A residual floor or a nonconvergent trajectory is not a proof. By Theorem 49(b) no finite
   trial whose stream function has finite angular support is an exact profile, whatever its temperature; this concerns
   exact finite support only and says nothing about whether such approximations converge to a profile of infinite
   angular support.
 - Strategies ruled out, and limits of the tests and arguments considered here. The following are restricted exclusions,
   compatibility results and reported numerical observations; each rules out a strategy only in the stated restricted
   sense. None settles existence or nonexistence in the full A2-broad class for any beta >= 2.
   (1) Integrability and energy. No A2-broad profile has Theta in L^p(R^2) (Theorem 17(b)) or U in L^p(R^2)
   (Theorem 23(a)) for any finite p > 0, and every A2-broad profile has the natural tail (Theorems 33, 34 and 36 at
   beta = 2, Theorem 38 at beta > 2), so that the annular energy E(R) is not O(R^{4-4/beta}). Hence nonexistence
   arguments that assume an integrable temperature, finite energy, an L^p velocity, or the critical energy bound (A) of
   Theorem 28 apply to no A2-broad profile. The literature paragraph cites Chae, math/0601060, for profile integrability
   assumptions.
   (2) Real analyticity at beta = 2. No A2-broad profile at beta = 2 has W real analytic on R^2 (Theorem 17(a)),
   velocity, vorticity or temperature real analytic throughout the open quadrant, or an angular limit H or G real
   analytic throughout (0, pi/2) (Theorem 85, a corollary of Theorem 83(a)). Representations or continuation arguments
   that presuppose analyticity of the profile at beta = 2 therefore cannot produce one. Locally, the equations at
   beta = 2 admit regular interior points of zero arcs at which the arc and its temperature trace in arclength are not
   real analytic (Theorem 72(b), an interior point, not an endpoint or an A2-broad profile), so analyticity of a zero
   arc does not follow from the local equations.
   (3) Local identities. The exact family of Section 4 satisfies (P), the A2 parities and jet with a0 > 0, and the local
   identities and conclusions of Theorem 2 at O, at P and along [0, x1], but is not admissible. These identities alone
   give no contradiction for a0 > 0. For beta > 2, the exact local solutions of Theorem 73(e), defined on a
   neighbourhood of a fixed closed disc in the open quadrant, have a strictly convex component of {sigma Omega < 0} with
   compact closure in that disc and satisfy (66.3)-(66.6) on it and (66.8) on the negative interval of each maximal
   trajectory segment in the disc. They are local solutions without an established A2 extension (no origin jet,
   extension across the axes, canonical velocity or far field is supplied), so these identities alone give no
   contradiction for such a local component; the pocket is not a counterexample to a global nonexistence statement.
   (4) Restricted ansatz classes. No A2-broad profile has Psi = x y h(x^2 + y^2) (Theorem 10) or a stream function with
   finite angular Fourier support, whatever the angular support of its temperature (Theorem 49). For a whole-plane
   solution in the separated class Psi = w(x) y of Remark 4.1, U = (-w(x), w'(x) y) and the A2 jet gives
   w'(0) = 2 beta + 2, so U_2(0, y) = (2 beta + 2) y and U = o(|X|) fails: no such solution is admissible.
   (5) Far field. For beta > 2 and beta = 2, Theorems 67 and 68 give formal natural expansions to every finite order,
   allowing logarithms, and leading data compatible with the specified far-field tests under their stated hypotheses.
   Theorems 69 (beta > 2) and 70 (beta = 2) give exact solutions on r > 2R with the A2 parities, the natural tail and
   the velocity given by the canonical whole-plane inverse of a smooth completed vorticity. No condition implied solely
   by these exterior requirements excludes all the examples of Theorem 69(d), nor, at beta = 2, all the plateau examples
   of Theorem 70(d); no whole-plane profile is constructed.
   (6) Integral identities with positive weights. For an A2-broad profile with beta > 2 and Omega >= 0 on Q1 (which
   forces a0 > 0, (H1) and Theta > 0 on Q1, Theorem 57(a)), by the weak-sign paragraph of Remark 55.1 the weight phi of
   (55.14) gives the valid ordered identity (55.15), but Theta phi_x has infinite positive and negative two-dimensional
   integrals and hence no two-dimensional Lebesgue integral (55.16). Every continuous F:(0,infinity) -> [0,infinity)
   that is not identically zero gives an infinite integral of F(Theta) against Omega (55.23). These obstructions concern
   those weights only; they do not show that every positive-weight argument fails.
   For beta > 2 the three moments of Omega fixed by Theorems 9 and 55 are attained by a positive measure with two atoms
   in Q1, and every real linear combination of the three kernels that is pointwise nonnegative on Q1 and not identically
   zero has a positive fixed moment value (Remark 55.2); hence no linear positivity certificate built from these three
   kernels, with coefficients constant on Q1, together with Omega >= 0 or Omega > 0 on Q1, can exclude the class. This
   does not concern arguments that use the transport equations, flow-dependent weights, the origin jet beyond these
   moments, or the source basin of the first positive x-axis zero P_ax of W.
   (7) Taylor identities at the beta = 2 endpoint. The example of Remark 51.1 satisfies every Taylor identity of the two
   transport equations at a flat endpoint of a one-sided zero arc, with either orientation of the centre branch, and
   fails (V) on every neighbourhood of the endpoint. So the endpoint jets alone do not decide the configuration. The
   field of Theorem 72(e) realizes the local velocity geometry and potential-side conclusions of Theorem 51 but has no
   smooth completion to the coupled endpoint system, so these conclusions alone do not ensure that a candidate field
   extends to a solution. With any trace whose difference from its endpoint value M is flat at the endpoint, even a
   strictly monotone one, that field also satisfies every identity on the arc obtained by differentiating the local
   equations, and its curl residual is flat along the strong unstable curve (Theorem 74(e)(i)); so the identities on the
   arc at every order give no contradiction by themselves and do not ensure that a given geometric field admits an (E')
   completion. For the linearization at the exact solution W = (0, 4y) with the temperature trace unperturbed, the value
   of the second component of the perturbation on the arc at distance L is determined by its data on a fibre, among data
   admitting a smooth linearized solution on a connected rectangle meeting the arc to that distance, but does not depend
   continuously on them in any C^j norm or in the C^infinity topology (Theorem 74(c), a linear statement, not a
   nonexistence or nonlinear ill-posedness result), so at the linear level marching the chart along the arc from data on
   a fibre is not continuous in these norms. Flat agreement with a potential solution along a curve, with a source of
   the form hK of (74.3), does not force a solution of the local equations to be potential on the other side (the shear
   of Remark 74.1(iii), which is not an (E') configuration), so unique continuation based only on these facts fails;
   this does not refute a uniqueness statement using the endpoint geometry of (E').
   (8) Size of the least-squares misfit (reported numerical observation, Sections 6 and 7). In the reported smooth-basis
   search, a control with 0 < beta < 2, excluded by Theorem 1, reaches relative misfits comparable to those at beta
   in [2, 6]. Their size alone establishes neither existence nor nonexistence. Dynamic rescaling did not converge in
   any normalization tried; this is a reported observation, not a proof.
 - An unproved counting heuristic (local index contributions at O and P, with the scaling symmetry and the free beta)
   suggests that for beta > 2 under (H1) the problem is overdetermined by one condition in C^{2,alpha}. An independent
   review found it not established (no Fredholm setting is available); it was used only to choose numerical diagnostics
   and is not a restriction on A2-broad. Persistence of a residual direction under refinement would not by itself
   identify an extra condition: a stationary least-squares residual satisfies J^T r = 0 whatever the continuum index,
   and representation error, local minima, weighting or missed geometry give the same symptom.

Context in the literature (as far as checked; no claim of completeness). The whole-plane blow-up of Elgindi and
Pasqualotto (arXiv 2310.19780) uses, after exchanging the coordinates, the same parities, but its temperature has a
nonzero linear term, the origin is a source of the self-similar flow and the profile is smooth only in r^alpha; it
is not an A2 profile. The boundary-setting works arXiv 2509.14185 and 2511.22819 are cited only as context for the
selection of exponents by smoothness at stagnation points; no result from them is used here. Nonexistence results
for self-similar Euler or Boussinesq blow-up (for example Chae, math/0601060) assume integrability conditions on
the profile. Theorems 17 and 23 exclude every finite integral of |Theta|^p and of |U|^p, 0 < p < infinity. The
bound |Omega| <= C r^{-1/beta} with a uniform, not identically zero angular limit (Theorems 33, 34, 41) determines
which integrals of |Omega|^p are finite (Theorem 45(b)). No external nonexistence theorem is applied here to decide
A2. The local step of Theorem 11 is close to a known result on smooth first integrals near curves of equilibria (X.
Zhang, arXiv 1712.09510, Theorem 2). A second check on 2026-10-21 found the following, none of which is used here.
Collot, Prange and Tan (arXiv 2507.17381) prove stable self-similar blow-up for the porous medium equation on a
periodic or bounded strip in the infinite-energy class of Castro, Cordoba, Gancedo and Orive, whose stream function
has the separated form y f(t, x) of Remark 4.1; Dembski (arXiv 2511.01827) treats Lipschitz porous-medium solutions
in wedges; Zheng (arXiv 2610.06544) proves unforced porous-medium gradient blow-up on the torus by a multiscale
layered construction; the companion paper arXiv 2310.19781 (revised 2025) of Elgindi and Pasqualotto shows by a
computer-assisted symbolic method that a linearized Boussinesq flow in self-similar coordinates gives an invertible
operator. A paper on discretely self-similar Euler solutions in R^3 (Chae and Wolf, J. Nonlinear Sci. 33 (2023),
article 115) concerns Euler without temperature; its statement was not checked. Chen and Hou prove finite-time
blow-up for the 2D Boussinesq equations in domains with boundary, first with C^{1,alpha} velocity (arXiv
1910.00173) and then for smooth initial data of finite energy, a nearly self-similar blow-up obtained from
nonlinear stability of an approximate self-similar profile (arXiv 2210.07191, with the computer-assisted estimates
of arXiv 2305.05660); these boundary results do not provide an A2 whole-plane profile. Abe, Ginsberg and Jeong
(arXiv 2410.21765) study stationary Boussinesq flows that are exactly homogeneous in space, posed in a half-plane
and identified with whole-plane flows by reflection; for rotational (-alpha)-homogeneous solutions with regular
profiles (classical away from the origin) they prove nonexistence in C^1 away from the origin for 0 <= alpha <= 1
and in C^2 away from the origin for -1/2 <= alpha < 0, and existence in C^2 away from the origin for alpha > 1 and
in C^1 for alpha < -2 (their Theorem 1.2, arXiv v1), and for -1 < alpha < 1 they construct rotational solutions
smooth away from the axes under a further reflection symmetry (their Theorem 1.3). These stationary homogeneous
flows do not decide the profiles studied here. Chae's Boussinesq Theorem 2.4 (math/0601060) assumes a velocity
profile in H^m, m > 2, and a temperature profile in L^{p1} and L^{p2} for some 0 < p1 < p2 <= infinity; Theorem
17(b) excludes the temperature hypothesis. The continuation criteria of Chae and Wolf (arXiv 1709.02030, Theorems
1.2 and 1.4) and of Chae and Constantin (arXiv 2103.10672, Theorem 2.1) assume velocity data in W^{2,q}(R^2) for
some q > 2 (and, in the first paper, temperature data in W^{2,p}(R^2)); for the self-similar solution of an A2
profile this would make U integrable to a finite power, which Theorem 23(a) excludes. The displayed pressure
conditions of Chae and Constantin (arXiv 2103.10672v1, Theorem 2.1(i), (ii), and the formulas in Theorem 2.2(i),
(ii)) fail for the self-similar solution of an A2 profile, with the local conditions failing on every ball whose
interior contains the centre. After translating the temperature sign to their convention, with tau = T - t and
c = 2 beta + 2, the velocity gradient at the centre is diag(-c, c)/tau and the pressure Hessian there is
diag(c - c^2, -c - c^2)/tau^2. At each fixed t < T, along z = tau^beta (eps^2, eps) as eps decreases to zero, their
two direction vectors are defined and tend to the same vertical unit vector, and the nonnegative pressure
quantities appearing in (2.1) and (2.2) tend respectively to c(c + 1)/tau^2 and c/tau^2. Continuity near these
points gives the corresponding essential-supremum lower bounds. Since c > 2, conditions (2.3), (2.4), (2.7) and
(2.8) fail, and the weighted time integrals (2.1), (2.2), (2.5) and (2.6) diverge. This checks only the displayed
sufficient conditions: Theorem 2.1's global W^{2,q} hypothesis is already excluded, and Theorem 2.2 is cited only
for its formulas, without resolving its printed system label (E). The calculation neither excludes nor produces a
profile, and the remaining hypotheses and theorem proofs were not checked. Ju, "On the profiles of locally
self-similar solutions for the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations" (J. Math. Anal. Appl. 484 (2020), article 123671;
DOI 10.1016/j.jmaa.2019.123671), concerns profiles of locally self-similar solutions of the 2D inviscid Boussinesq
equations. The available publisher records provided bibliographic metadata, but the abstract and full text were not
obtained in this audit. Its full theorem hypotheses were not compared with A2-broad, and no conclusion from it is
used. No published result found decides the A2 question.

## 9. Reproduction

Reproduction is incomplete: no tested claim-by-claim reproduction protocol is supplied, and no command was re-run
after the accompanying artifacts were assembled. The accompanying artifacts include documentation of the layout,
the software versions and exact commands for each part, and a list of SHA-256 digests of all files. They
contain the following.
 - Symbolic checks of the analysis: exact sympy and exact-fraction checks of the exact family and the
   separated class of Section 4, the single-mode algebra of Theorem 10, the x-axis and y-axis trace identities, the
   beta = 2 origin resonance coefficient, the beta = 2 formal recursion of Remark 39.1 with the check of (68.16) in
   Theorem 68, and the energy flux identity of Theorem 88, together with a numerical model study of a finite-part
   integral (not an exact check).
 - The numerical search: the fitting code (parity-compatible smooth bases with the coordinate maps
   named in Section 6, both signs of a0, beta free or fixed, and the excluded controls with beta < 2), its validation
   tests (among them a symbolic check of (A2-red) and the Taylor identities), the forward/Picard and dynamic-rescaling codes, the diagnostics, and 72 stored coefficient files of the
   states examined in Section 6, including the three earliest states of the table (the beta < 2 control, B1 and T4).
   Each file records beta, the resolutions, the coordinate map, the target a0, all solver options and, where recorded,
   the solver history (misfit against iteration). The accompanying artifacts give the commands that regenerate the states by the
   Levenberg-Marquardt fit and evaluate their residuals and diagnostics. All of these states are rejected.
 - The independent evaluation: the inverse and residual code written by the independent verifier
   separately from the fitting code (exact fourfold kernel cancellation with Duffy-type quadrature, a target-centred
   polar quadrature and an adaptive radial modal inverse), its manufactured tests, the exact rational evaluations of
   origin and tail coefficients of stored states, the integer-interval certificates of axis zeros and the
   python-flint certificate of one interior zero, with the stored inputs and outputs of these certificates. The
   certificate scripts check the compiled exact coefficients against their stored digests; the published state files
   are lossless re-archives with arrays identical to the evaluated copies, so a differing digest of a raw state file
   is reported rather than treated as an error. The accompanying artifacts also include a symbolic check of the reduced system (A2-red)
   and of the centre relations of Section 1.

Not included: the run logs and solver output logs, the run launch scripts, the dated work logs, the written
verification records and proofs of the independent verifier, the reports of the external referee (a second model),
and the provenance manifest compiled during the run with its dated errata file. The manifest indexes the verification
records, run files and report versions by their locations and digests on the machine on which the investigation ran;
since those records are not published, the claims of this report cannot be traced file by file to their verification
records from the accompanying artifacts alone. The verification events are dated in Section 8.

Environment. Linux (kernel 6.12, Amazon Linux 2023) on Intel Xeon Platinum 8275CL processors; every CPU process
single-threaded (OMP_NUM_THREADS = 1) and below 16 GB of memory; one NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU (driver 580.167.08),
shared with unrelated jobs, used for the least-squares fits. Software: Python 3.9.25, numpy 2.0.2, scipy 1.13.1, sympy
1.14.0, mpmath 1.3.0, torch 2.8.0+cu128 (float64 on the GPU) for the fitting code, and python-flint 0.9.0 (FLINT/Arb
interval arithmetic) for the interval certificates. The certified statements of Section 6 rely on the audited programs,
on the interval semantics of FLINT/Arb, on CPython and on the hardware; none is formally verified. Compute accounting of
the least-squares search through 2026-10-22 09:01 UTC (from the run logs, which are not among the accompanying artifacts; for each log the time from its first start
stamp to its last modification; the run notes record that the GPU was shared): 169 Levenberg-Marquardt log files with at
least 10 iteration records, 40.1 h of summed log span (about 1.0 h for N <= 80, 6.2 h for N = 112, 8.9 h for N = 144,
12.7 h for N = 176, 8.4 h for N = 208 and 2.8 h for N = 240); the four longest spans were about 86 to 207 min each, the
two longest each combining two starts and including the intervals between their starts. Log spans are neither GPU-active
time nor elapsed research time, and the logs are not deduplicated (a partial file is counted alongside the combined log
of which it is an exact prefix). These figures exclude log files below that iteration threshold. Dynamic rescaling
durations of 1 to 3 min per run and roughly nine hours of diagnostics are estimates recorded in the run notes, not
measurements. The retained histories include failed and aborted runs; incidents whose artifacts were removed or
overwritten are known only from the run notes unless supported by retained logs.
